las yang dag par 'das pa de la phyag 'tshal lo/ / zhes smras te/ shar phyogs su phyag btsal nas mngon par dga' zhing rang gi gnas su song ngo zhes gsungs te/ don de nyid thugs la gzhag nas slob dpon sna tshogs blo gros kyis rtsod pa mi mnga' bar bsten pa las/ 'dod pa mi snang 'brel med cing*/ / lta ba'i drwa ba bcom gyur pas/ / des na rtsod pa mi 'byung ste/ / rtsa ba med par ga la 'byung*/ / zhes gsungs so}

A sūtra also states: Venerable Mahākātyāyana was staying in Vārāṇasī along the banks of the muddy, murky river, when the brahman Daṇḍapāṇi approached and engaged in some pleasant discourse. Then, taking a seat to one side, he asked, “Kātyāyana, what causes a king to dispute with another king, or a farmer with a farmer, or a brahman [53] with a brahman, or a householder with a householder?” Kātyāyana replied, “Brahman, it is attachment, longing, relation, actual desire, and complete desire for sense {objects} that causes a king to dispute with a king or a householder to dispute with a householder.” “Kātyāyana,” the brahman said, “if it is attachment to sense objects that causes a king to dispute with a king and so on, then what causes the ordained to dispute with the ordained?” “Brahman, it is attachment, longing, relation, actual desire, and complete desire for views that causes the ordained to dispute with the ordained.” “Kātyāyana, if that is so, is there one who is now beyond attachment to sense objects and views . . . up to complete desire for sense objects and views?” “Brahman, that person exists, for my teacher, the Bhagavan Buddha, is beyond those because he is beyond attachment to sense objects and views . . . up to complete desire for sense objects and views.” “Kātyāyana,” the brahman said, “where does your teacher reside?” “Brahman, he is presently residing in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada at Prince Jeta’s Grove in the city of Śrāvastī to the east.” Then, with faith, the brahman Daṇḍapāṇi rose from his seat and with palms together said, “I pay homage to the Buddha, who is completely beyond attachment to any sense objects or views,” and having said that he prostrated to the east and returned joyfully to his abode.[322] Many masters, by keeping this point in mind, do not engage in intellectual dispute. Praise Beyond All Praise says: Since you neither acknowledge nor engage with sense objects and you destroy the net of views, dispute does not arise in you, for how could it arise when its root does not exist?[323]}

'du shes ni rab tu byung ba rnams kyi rtsod pa'i rtsa bar gyur pa yin te/ lta ba la lhag par zhen pas 'du shes phyin ci log tu gyur te/ rang gzhan gyi grub mtha' la bzang ngan gyi mtshan mar 'dzin pas dge sbyong dang dge sbyong la sogs pa rnams rtsod pa'i phyir ro/ / des na gnyis po rtsod pa'i rtsa bar gyur pa yin no zhes shes par bya ba'i phyir dang*/ bde ba la sogs pa'i tshor ba la chags pa la sogs pa dang ldan pa rnams las gsog cing*/ de yang 'du shes phyin ci log gis yin pas de dag 'khor ba'i rgyu'i gtso bo yin pa'i phyir ro zhes shes par bya ba'i phyir dang*/ rags pa la sogs pa 'og nas 'chad pa'i rim par ston pa'i rgyu mtshan bzhi yod pa'i phyir yang sems las byung ba gzhan rnams las tshor ba dang 'du shes ni logs shig tu phung por bcom ldan 'das kyis rnam par bzhag go zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Discernment is the root of dispute for the ordained because discernment becomes distorted through excessive attachment to views. Therefore śramaṇas dispute with other śramaṇas through holding their own views as valid and those of others as invalid. Thus both feeling and discernment should be understood as the root of dispute. (2) They are posited as separate aggregates because they are the main causes of saṃsāra. Those who possess attachment and so on to feelings of pleasure and so forth accumulate karma, and those with distorted discernment also accumulate karma. (3) They are posited as separate aggregates by the four reasons taught below regarding their order, such as from coarse to subtle and so on. Therefore it should be understood that from among the mental factors (caitta), feeling (vedanā) and discernment (saṃjñā) are posited by the Bhagavan as separate aggregates.
phung po dag tu 'dus ma byas/ / don du mi rung phyir ma bshad/ / rim ni rags dang kun nyon mongs/ / snod sogs don khams ji bzhin no/ / 22
Unconditioned phenomena are not explained among the aggregates because they have an incongruent nature. Their order accords with coarseness, affliction, vessel and so on, and realm. (1:22)
yang ci'i phyir skye mched dang khams dag tu 'dus ma byas kyang bshad la phung por ma bshad ce na/
Question: Again, why are unconditioned phenomena explained within the bases and elements but not in the aggregates?

phung po dag tu 'dus ma byas ma bshad de/ 'dus ma byas ni phung po lnga'i mtshan nyid dang mi ldan pas de dag de'i don du mi rung la/ phung po drug par yang mi rung ste/ chos 'das pa la sogs pa du ma spungs pa zhes bya ba'i don du mi rung ba'i phyir ro/ / gzhan yang kun nas nyon mongs kyi gzhi shes par bya ba'i phyir nyer len gyi phung po dang*/ kun nas nyon mongs dang rnam byang gnyis ka'i gzhi shes par bya ba'i phyir phung po bstan pa yin pa la/ 'dus ma byas ni de gnyis ka'i gzhi'i don du mi rung ba'i phyir ro/ / kha cig na re dper na bum pa chag pa bum pa ma yin pa bzhin du 'dus ma byas ni phung po zhig pa yin pas phung por mi 'os so zhes zer mod kyi/ de ni khams dang skye mched la'ang ha cang thal bar 'gyur pas mi 'thad do/ / skye mched dang khams kyi don du ni dmigs pa'i tshul gyis skye ba'i sgo dang rigs kyi don yod pa'i phyir bshad do/{ phung po lnga'i grangs nges ni bshad zin to/ /}

skye mched bcu gnyis su nges pa ni gzugs can ni bcur dngos po la nges la/ gzugs can ma yin pa dag yid dang chos gnyis su nges pa'i phyir ro/ / khams bco brgyad du nges pa ni gzugs can la bcu dang*/ gzugs can ma yin pa la chos dang sems gnyis su nges shing sems la rnam pa bdun du nges pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag ni dbang don de dag kho na la zhes bya ba la sogs par sngar bshad zin pa'i phyir 'dir ni skye mched dang khams kyi grangs nges ma bstan to zhes shes par bya'o/ / kun las btus las ni bdag tu 'dzin pa'i gzhi rnam pa lnga brjod pa'i phyir phung po lnga bstan te/ bdag gi gzhi las yongs su gzung ba dang bcas pa bstan pa'i phyir gzugs kyi phung po bstan te/ dbang po lnga ni lus dang yul lnga na gzung ba yin pa'i phyir ro/ / bdag gi gzhi longs spyod brjod pa'i dbang du byas nas tshor ba'i phung po bstan te/ bde ba la sogs pa ni lus dang gzung ba de la brten nas myong bar bya ba yin pa'i phyir ro/ / bdag gi gzhi tha snyad brjod pa'i dbang du byas na 'du shes kyi phung po bstan te/ de ni tha snyad sna tshogs 'dogs pa po yin pa'i phyir ro/ / bdag gi gzhi chos dang chos ma yin pa mngon par brjod pa'i dbang du byas nas 'du byed kyi phung po bstan te/ dad sogs ni blang bya dang*/ chags sogs blang bya ma yin pa'i 'du byed yin pa'i phyir ro/ / bdag gi gzhi de dag gi gnas brjod pa'i dbang du byas nas rnam shes kyi phung po bstan te/ rnam shes la bdag tu gzung ba las ni de dag la bdag gir 'dzin pa kun du 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ /

The bases are definitely twelve in number because form is definitely ten things, and that which is not form is definitely two: the mental base and the phenomena base. The elements are definitely eighteen in number because ten are form, and that which is not form is definitely two: phenomena and mind, and mind is definitely seven. However, the set number of bases and elements is not taught [extensively] here because they were explained above in the statement “Just those sense faculties and objects” (1:14a) and so on. The Compendium of Abhidharma indicates that the aggregates number five because they express the five types of basis held as the self. (1) The aggregate of form is taught as the basis of the self because it represents the body and the objects held, where the five sense faculties are the body and the five sense objects are the objects held. (2) The aggregate of feeling is taught from the perspective of enjoyment being the basis of the self because pleasure and so on are experienced in dependence on the body and the objects held. (3) The aggregate of discernment is taught from the perspective of the process of attributing names being the basis of the self because it is the agent that assigns diverse designations. (4) The aggregate of formation is taught from the perspective of Dharma and non-Dharma being the basis of the self because it is the formative factor that engages faith and so on that should be practiced and attachment and so forth that should not be practiced. (5) The aggregate of consciousness is taught from the perspective of being the domain of those bases of the self because through holding consciousness to be the self, the other four are continuously held as mine.[324]

skye mched bcu gnyis su nges pa ni lus dang yongs su gzung ba gnyis ma 'ongs pa'i nye bar spyod pa drug skye ba'i sgo'i dbang du byas nas gsungs te/ lus ni mig la sogs pa'i dbang po drug dang*/ yongs su gzung ba ni yul drug go /ma 'ongs pa'i nye bar spyod pa drug ni rnam shes drug skye ba'i sgo yin pa'i phyir ro/ / khams bco brgyad du nges pa ni lus dang yongs su gzung ba gnyis kyis 'das pa dang da ltar gyi nye bar spyod pa rnam pa drug 'dzin pa'i phyir te/ lus ni mig la sogs pa drug dang*/ yongs su gzung ba gzugs la sogs pa drug gis 'das pa dang da ltar gyi nye bar spyod pa mig la sogs pa'i rnam par shes pa drug gnas dang dmigs pa'i sgo nas 'dzin pa'i phyir ro zhes bya ba'i don du 'chad do/ / des ni 'di skad bstan pa yin te/ bdag tu 'dzin pa'i 'khrul pa'i gzhi lnga yin no zhes bya ba'i don du phung po lnga dang*/ rnam shes drug mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa skye ba'i rgyu'i dbang du byas nas skye mched bcu gnyis dang*/ rgyu 'bras bu dang bcas pa'i dbang du byas nas khams bco brgyad du bstan to zhes bya ba'o/ /

The bases are stated to be definitely twelve from the perspective of both the body and the objects held being gateways for generating the six future utilizing agents.[325] That is, the body is the six sense faculties of the eyes and so on, the objects held are the six objects, and together they are gateways for generating the six future utilizing agents, which are the six consciousnesses. The elements are definitely eighteen because the six types of past and present utilizing agents hold their objects due to both the body and the objects held. Therefore the six eye consciousnesses and so on, which are past and present utilizing agents, hold their objects both due to the body — the six organs such as the eyes, which is their domain — [55] and due to the objects held — the six objects such as form, which are their focal objects.[326] Therefore it is said that the five aggregates were taught because “there are five fields mistakenly held as a self,” the twelve bases were taught from the perspective of the causes that give rise to the six consciousnesses and their concomitant mental factors, and the eighteen elements were taught from the perspective of those causes plus their results.
lnga pa go rim nges pa la
Fixed sequence

re zhig phung po lnga'i rim pa ni thog mar gzugs ni gzugs can thogs bcas yin pas thams cad pas rags pa dang*/ de nas gzugs can ma yin pa las tshor ba rgyu ba rags pa la sogs pa'i phyir te/{ gzugs ni kun las rags te thogs pa dang bcas shing bstan du yod pas so/ / bzhi las tshor ba rags rkang pas tshor ro zhes sogs rtogs sla bas so/ / gsum las 'du shes rags te sngo sogs su mtshan mar 'dzin pas gnyis pas rtogs sla bas so/ / gnyis las 'du byed rags te bdag bde bar bya'o sdug bsngal bar mi bya'o zhes 'dod pas rtogs sla bas so/ / rnam shes ni kun las phra ste don gyi ngo bo tsam rig par 'byung bas rtogs dka' bas so/} rags pa dang phra ba ni 'dir rtogs par sla ba dang dka' ba la brjod do/ /

The order (krama) of the five aggregates here reveals their relative coarseness (udarika) in terms of the ease or difficulty of comprehending them. First, form is the coarsest of all, since it is impeded physically. Next, from among the nonphysical aggregates, feeling has the coarsest degree of movement and so on. {Form is the coarsest of all because it is impeded and demonstrable. Feeling is the coarsest of the remaining four since, for instance, the foot sensing its experiential objects and so on is easier to comprehend [than the other nonphysical aggregates]. Discernment is coarsest of the remaining three because apprehending the [defining] mark of blue and so on is easier to comprehend [than the later aggregates]. Formation is coarsest of the remaining two because the desire “May I have pleasure and not have pain” is easier to comprehend [than consciousness itself]. Consciousness is the subtlest of all since cognizing the mere essential nature of an object is the most difficult to comprehend.}

kun nas nyon mongs pa skye ba'i rim pa yod pa'i phyir yang ste/ thog ma med pa nas skye bo dag gzugs la mngon par dga' 'o/ / de las ni bde ba la sogs pa'i tshor ba la ro myang ba'i chags pa 'byung ngo*/ / de las ni{ gtsang bde sogs su} 'du shes phyin ci log 'byung ngo*/ / de las 'dod chags la sogs pa'i nyon mongs pa'i tshogs 'byung ngo*/ / des kyang sems kun nas nyon mongs par byed pa'i phyir ro/ / yang na snod dang sogs pa'i sgras gzung ba/ zas dang tshod ma dang byan po dang za ba po dang chos mthun pa'i don gyi phyir ro/ /

There is also the order in which affliction arises. Those born from beginningless time are attracted to form, then the desire to experience the feeling of pleasure and so on arises, then the wrong discernment {of the object being clean and blissful} arises, then the mass of afflictions such as attachment arises, and then the mind itself becomes completely afflicted. The meaning of the term “vessel (bhājana) and so on” indicates states compatible with food, cooking, the cook, and the eater.

{gzugs ni tshor ba'i rten yin pas snod lta bu yin no/ / tshor ba ni ro myang bar bya ba yin pa'i phyir zas lta bu yin no/ / 'du shes ni tshor ba la de'i mtshan mar 'dzin pas gsal bar byed pa'i phyir tshod ma lta bu yin no/ / sems pa ni rnam par smin pa'i tshor ba mngon par 'dus byas nas nye bar gtod pa'i phyir byan po lta bu yin no/ / rnam shes de la tshor bas phan 'dogs pa'i phyir rnam shes ni zab po lta bu yin pas snod sogs kyi go rim bzhin no/}

{Form is like a food vessel since it is the support of the feelings. Feelings are like food because they constitute the taste of the object experienced. Discernment is like cooking because in terms of feeling [represented by the food] it is the agent that brings out [the taste of each ingredient] since discernment apprehends the defining mark [of each object]. Intention is like the cook, since it is directed to manifesting feelings that mature.[327] Consciousness is like the eater because it is benefited [or stimulated] by feeling.}

yang na 'dod pa la sogs pa'i khams kyi go rim ji lta ba bzhin du bstan no zhes bya ste/ khams de dag ni gzugs la sogs pas rab tu phye ba'i phyir te/ 'di ltar 'dod khams ni gzugs kyis phye ste/ 'dod pa'i yon tan dag gzugs yin pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs kyi khams dag tshor bas phye ste/ bsam gtan dang po na bde ba dang yid bde dang*/ gnyis pa na yid bde dang*/ gsum pa na sems bde dang*/ bzhi pa na btang snyoms yod pas gzhag pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs med dang po gsum ni 'du shes kyis phye la srid rtse ni 'du byed tsam gyis phye{ ste des tshe bskal pa brgyad khrir 'phen} zhing rnam par shes pa ni de dag gi gzhi yin pa'i phyir de ltar go rim du bstan to/ / 'di dag gis ni grangs nges pa'ang 'grub bo zhes 'chad do/ /

Likewise, their order accords with (yathā) the order of the desire realm (dhātu) and so on because those realms are classified according to form and so forth. Thus the desire realm is classified as the form aggregate because sense objects are form. The form realm is classified in terms of feeling because the first absorption has pleasure and mental satisfaction, the second has mental satisfaction, the third has mental bliss (sukhacitta), and the fourth has equanimity. The first three levels of the formless realm are classified in terms of discernment. The summit of existence is classified in terms of formation alone {because it projects [or produces] a lifespan of eighty thousand eons}. Consciousness is their basis. This is said also to establish that they are definite in number.
skye mched drug gi go rim ni
THE ORDER OF THE SIX BASES
da lta'i don phyir dang po lnga/ / 'byung ba las gyur don phyir bzhi/ / gzhan ni ches ring myur 'jug phyir/ / yang na ji ltar gnas bzhin rim/ / 23

Five are first because they have present objects. Four are first because their objects are derived from the primary elements. Alternately they engage them at a greater distance or speed, or their order accords with their location. (1:23)

skye mched drug las da ltar ba'i don 'dzin pa'i phyir dang po mig la sogs pa gzugs can lnga sngon la bstan la/ yid ni dus gsum dang dus ma yin pa 'dus ma byas kyi yul can yang yin pa'i phyir phyis bshad do/ / lnga po de dag las kyang 'byung ba las gyur pa'i don 'bras bu'i gzugs kho na'i yul can yin pa'i phyir mig la sogs pa{ dang po} bzhi sngon la bstan la/ lus ni gnyis ka'i yul can yin pa'i phyir phyis bshad do/ / bzhi po de dag las kyang gzhan mig dang rna ba gnyis ni rgyang ring po la 'jug pa'i phyir sngar smos la/ sna dang lce ni phrad nas 'dzin pas yul nye ba kho na la 'jug pa'i phyir phyis bshad do/{ dang po gnyis kyis/ /} mig ni rna ba bas kyang ches rgyang ring ba la 'jug pa'i phyir sngar bshad do/ / {sna lce gnyis kyi'ang */}sna ni lce bas ches myur du 'jug pa'i phyir sngar bshad la lce ni de'i phyi la bshad do/ /

Among the six bases, the five physical sense bases [56] are taught first because they apprehend objects in the present (vartamāna). The mental base is taught later because it engages objects of all the three times as well as unconditioned phenomena, which exist outside of time. Among those five, the {first} four bases — the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue — are taught first because they take as their objects only resultant form derived from the primary elements (bhautika). The body base, since it takes both types of object, is explained later. Alternately, from among those four, both the eye and ear bases are mentioned first because they engage their objects at a distance. The nose and tongue bases are explained later because they only engage proximate objects by apprehending them through contact. {From among the first two,} eyes are explained first since they engage objects at a far greater distance (dūra) than the ears. {Of the nose and tongue,} the nose is explained first since it engages its object with greater speed (āśutara) than the tongue, and thus the tongue is explained later.

yang na ji ltar gnas pa'i rim pa bzhin bshad de/ mig ni dang po na gnas pa nas lus phal che ba 'og na gnas pa'i bar gyi phyir ro/ / de ltar na 'dis ni nang gi skye mched drug gi go rim bshad pa na phyi'i skye mched kyi go rim yang shes te/ yul can gyi rim pa ltar bstan pa'i phyir ro/ / des ni khams kyi go rim yang 'grub ste/ 'bras bu rnam shes kyi khams drug ni rgyu'i go rim ltar bstan pa'i phyir ro/ /

Or their order (krama) is said to accord with their location (sthāna), from the eyes, which are located highest, to the body, which is located lowest. The order of the external bases should be understood in accordance with the order of the six internal bases because they are presented in accordance with the order in which internal bases engage external objects. That also establishes the order of the elements because the six resultant elements of consciousness are taught in accordance with the order of their causes.
bye brag don dang gtso bo'i phyir/ / chos mang ba dang mchog bsdus phyir/ / gcig ni gzugs kyi skye mched dang/ / gcig ni chos zhes bya bar brjod/ / 24
One is called the “form base” because it is the specific object and the principal form. One is called the “phenomena base” because it includes many phenomena and the supreme phenomenon. (1:24)

yang ci'i phyir mig gi yul kho na la gzugs kyi skye mched dang khams dang*/ yid kyi yul kho na la chos kyi skye mched dang khams zhes brjod de/ mig la sogs pa bcu ga'ang gzugs yin pa'i phyir dang*/ skye mched dang khams thams cad kyang chos yin pa'i phyir ro zhe na/

Question: Because the ten bases and elements — the eyes and so on — are form, and all bases and elements are phenomena, why are just the objects of the eyes called “form base” and “form element” and why are just the objects of the mental faculty called “phenomena base” and “phenomena element”?

bcu po thams cad gzugs yin yang de dag so sor skye mched yin gyi spyir ni ma yin no zhes rtogs par bya ba'i phyir mig la sogs pa dgu ni rang rang gi ming gis bstan la/ ming gzhan med pa'i mig gi yul de gzugs zhes bya ba'i spyi'i sgras bye brag tu rtogs pa'i don gyi phyir mig gi yul gcig pu ni gzugs kyi skye mched dang khams zhes bya bar brjod de rtags med pa nyid kyis dmag la sogs pa bye brag tu rtogs pa bzhin no/ / yang na mig gi yul ni bstan du'ang yod la thogs pa dang bcas pas gzugs kyi gtso bo yin pa'i phyir yang de'i sgras brjod de mi'i mchog gis rgyal po go ba bzhin no/ / yang 'jig rten na yang de gzugs so zhes grags kyi gzhan dag la ni ma yin no/ / zhes 'grel pa las 'chad do/ /

Reply: Although all ten are form, the nine such as the eyes are represented by their individual name because they are comprehended as individual bases and not as form in general. Just one, the object of the eyes alone, is called the “form base” (rūpāyatana) and the form element because objects of the eyes lack other names, and it is the specific object (viśeṣanārtha) understood by the general term “form,” just as soldiers and so on are specifically understood in the absence of individual marks.[328] Moreover, the object of the eyes is designated by that term because it is the principal form (prādhānya) due to being demonstrable and impeded, just as the principal human is understood to be the king. The Autocommentary explains: In the world that is commonly held as form and not as something else.[329]

gzhan dag na re rnam pa nyi shus rags pa'i phyir dang*/{ rnam bshad rigs pa'i 'grel pa las/ sha'i spyan ni bdag cag lta bu'i yod pa gang yin pa'o/ / lha'i spyan ni mngon par shes pa'i spyan te/ bsam gtan dang po la sogs pa'i sa pa'o/ / 'phags pa'i shes rab kyi spyan ni zag pa med pa'i ye shes so/ / chos kyi spyan ni 'jig rten las 'das pa'i rjes las thob pa'i ye shes te/ gang gi chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa'o/ / sangs rgyas kyi spyan ni shes bya thams cad la rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa'o/ / zhes 'byung ba'i/} sha dang lha dang 'phags pa'i shes rab kyi mig gsum gyi spyod yul yin pa'i phyir mig gi yul kho na la gzugs kyi skye mched du bstan to zhes zer ro/ { thams cad la chos su brjod na skye mched gcig tu 'gyur ba'i phyir dang*/} yang skye mched dang khams thams cad chos yin pa bden yang yid kyi yul kho na la chos kyi skye mched dang khams kyi sgras brjod pa ni gzhan dag ni rang rang gi ming gis smos la/ ming gzhan med pa'i yid kyi yul la chos zhes spyi'i sgras yid kyi yul bye brag tu rtogs pa'i don gyi phyir te ming med nyid ming du gyur pa bzhin no/ / yang na tshor ba la sogs pa bsdu bya'i chos mang ba'i phyir dang*/ chos kyi mchog mya ngan las 'das pa so sor brtags 'gog kyang der bsdus pa'i phyir yid kyi yul gcig pu ni chos kyi skye mched dang khams zhes bya bar brjod do/ / de dag gis ni phung po dang skye mched dang khams kyi rang bzhin bshad zin to/ /

Others say: Only the object of the [ordinary] eye is taught to be the form base because the twenty types of form are coarse and because [subtle form] is the object field of the three eyes: [57] (1) the flesh eye, (2) the divine eye, and (3) the ārya wisdom eye[330] {for it is stated in the Commentary on the Rational System of Exposition: The flesh eye is like our eye. The divine eye is the eye of higher perception that exists on the level of the first absorption and so on. The wisdom eye of an ārya is uncontaminated transcendent wisdom. The eye of phenomena is post-equipoise transcendent wisdom that fully differentiates phenomena. The buddha eye comprehends all aspects of all objects of knowledge.[331]}
Though it is true that {if all are called “phenomena” they would constitute a single base and} all bases and elements are phenomena, just objects of the mental faculty are designated by the terms “phenomena base” and “phenomena element” and the others are designated by their individual names because objects of the mental faculty lack other names and they are objects specifically comprehended through the general term “phenomena,” like “nameless” being a name. Again, just one, the object of the mental faculty, is called the “phenomena base” (dharmāyatana) and phenomena element because it includes many phenomena, such as feelings, and because it includes the supreme (agra) phenomenon, which is analytical cessation or nirvāṇa. This concludes the explanation of the nature of aggregates, bases, and elements.
gnyis pa de dag gzhan yang 'dir bsdu ba
How other taxonomies are subsumed in these three
['di] la gnyis las
This has two headings: those designated aggregates are subsumed in the aggregates, and applying that to the other two.
phung po'i ming can phung por bsdu ba ni
THOSE DESIGNATED AGGREGATES ARE SUBSUMED IN THE AGGREGATES
chos kyi phung po brgyad khri dag / gang rnams thub pas gsungs de dag / tshig gam ming yin de dag ni/ / gzugs dang 'du byed dag tu 'dus/ / 25
The 80,000 aggregates of Dharma declared by the Sage are words or names included in form or formation. (1:25)

gal te 'dus byas thams cad phung po lnga dang*/ 'dus byas dang 'dus ma byas thams cad skye mched dang khams kyis bsdus na chos kyi phung po brgyad khri bzhi stong zhes bya ba la sogs pa dang*/ zad par dang zil gyis gnon pa'i skye mched la sogs pa dang*/ khams mang po pa'i mdo las khams drug cu rtsa gnyis bshad pa{ de dag dang*/ mdo gzhan dag las phung po la sogs pa'i ming can gzhan dag kyang 'byung na} de dag 'dir smos pa rnams kyis ma bsdus na de dag las tha dad pa'i chos yod{ pas de dag tu grangs ma nges} par 'gyur la bsdus na ji ltar bsdus she na/

Question: If all conditioned phenomena are aggregates and all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are included in the bases and elements, and if the 84,000 aggregates of Dharma, the bases of subjugation and elimination and so on, the sixty-two elements explained in the Multiple Elements Sūtra, {and the aggregates and so on that occur in other sūtras with other names} are not included in those mentioned here but are included in phenomena {beyond enumeration} distinct from them, then how would they be included?
de'i lan la{ gnyis las dang po chos kyi phung po phung por bsdu ba ni}
Reply: {There are two} answers to that: {The first[332] is that [the aggregate of] Dharma is included in the aggregates.}

The 80,000 aggregates [or bundles] of Dharma (dharmaskandha) have been declared by the Sage. Sautrāntikas assert that they [i.e., the aggregates of Dharma] are [either] objects of the ear, which are words (vāc), or {indicative speech} that is in essence words. Vaibhāṣikas assert that they are objects of the mental faculty, which are the essence of names (nāma). Therefore they are included respectively in the aggregate of form (rūpa) or the aggregate of formation (saṃskāra). Ābhidharmikas assert what is stated in the Attainment of Knowledge: What are the statements of the Buddha? They are any speech, statements, expressions, intonations, definitive statements, the course of statements, euphonic statements, the enlightened activity of speech, and revealing statements. And: What are these Dharmas called the statements of the Buddha? They are the serial formulation, the serial arrangement, and the serial correct application of the collection of nouns, the collection of predicated phrases, and the collection of letters.[333] Therefore they are included in both because they possess the nature of both. [58] Other schools assert 84,000 aggregates of Dharma. Because the Ānanda Sūtra states: I, Ānanda, actually received 81,000 aggregates of Dharma from the Bhagavan. Two were received from monks.[334] And the Rational System of Exposition declares that in terms of the Śrāvaka Vehicle [the teachings] were not included in 80,000 [aggregates] for the Ānanda Sūtra mentions that eighty-one thousand were received from the Bhagavan and two were received from monks.[335] Thus it can be inferred that Ānanda heard instructions while acting as the Buddha’s attendant for twenty-one years though he did not receive the Buddha’s instructions given prior to becoming his attendant, and since it is untenable that so little Dharma was uttered prior to him becoming the Buddha’s attendant, it is unreasonable that instruction given by the Buddha in this prior period was just those two received from monks alone. Elucidation of the Compendium of Abhidharma also articulates: In the context of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, any of the 84,000 aggregates of Dharma received by Ānanda constitutes the three piṭakas.[336] The scriptures of other schools assert 84,000 aggregates of Dharma. Therefore the assertion of 80,000 is the system of the Kāśmīri Vaibhāṣikas alone.

Some say: The measure (pramāṇa) of an aggregate of Dharma[337] is equal to Śāriputra’s inclusive treatise {in 6,000 verses}. Therefore it is said that 6,000 verses is one aggregate of Dharma because other views have mostly subsided. Thus there would be {1,680,000 sections and} 480,000,000 verses in 80,000 aggregates of Dharma. {In accordance with the Cittamātrins,} Elucidation of the Compendium of Abhidharma says: What is the measure of one aggregate of Dharma? Ten times one hundred is an aggregate of Dharma, making the final number one thousand.[338] This passage explains that for each aggregate of Dharma there are one thousand verses, and it further states: In this method of enumeration, the 84,000 aggregates of Dharma are 84,000,000 verses.[339]

Others assert: Each aggregate of Dharma is an entire discourse (kathā) that {completely} reveals a category of meaning such as the aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination, and so on. [59] There is no definite number of verses. Question: Why were these aggregates taught?

Reply: The {80,000} aggregates of Dharma {such as repulsiveness, love, dependent origination, the classification of elements, and so on} were stated as antidotes (pratipakṣa) to the 80,000 distinct actions (carita) {of afflicted sentient beings} such as attachment, delusion, aversion, pride, view, doubt, and so on. Jinaputra explains that [the Sanskrit particle] tu is stated for the purpose of either refuting or establishing the previous position.[341] Some say: The latter system is the system of the Master. One Tibetan master says: There are 84,000 aggregates of Dharma as antidotes since there are 21,000 actions motivated by each of the three poisons such as attachment, and a fourth with those three in equal measure. The Jewel Torch Dhāraṇī states: A conqueror establishes the welfare of reincarnating beings through teaching any of the 84,000 Dharmas and tames worldly beings who possess various dispositions through the gateway of specific Dharmas.[342] That is also stated in the Sūtra Requested by Vidyutprāpta.[343] These instances are from the shared perspective of both vehicles.[344] According to the Mahāyāna, it is clear that [the aggregates of Dharma] are not included even in the 84,000 because Master Dharmamitra writes: From the perspective of the highest vehicle, one aggregate of Dharma can be inscribed by the ink carried by Airāvata, the elephant of Indra.[345] Moreover, a sūtra says: Devadatta recited from memory the volumes carried by five thousand elephants.[346] {The Avataṃsaka Sūtra declares: In a southern mountain range in a region called the Gateway to the Ocean, the monk Sāgaramegha, who was the guru of the youthful Maṇibhadra, heard and retained in mind an amount of Dharma that, if written down, would require ink equal in measure to the water of the great ocean and pens equal in measure to Mount Meru. But even that would be insufficient to record such Dharma because each chapter, each heading, each principle of Dharma, or each category of Dharma would require that much or would not even be completed by that much.}[347] Repaying the Buddha’s Kindness Sūtra also mentions: Devadatta acquired and could recite from memory the sūtras carried by sixty thousand incense elephants.[348]

Question: It is said that you should acquire an aggregate of Dharma, but since they now don’t exist on this continent, where do they exist? Reply: Master Dharmamitra stated that some say they are practiced in other world systems and others say they are mostly practiced in the abode of nāgas.[349] The Letter to a Student explains: The teachings, like a supreme jewel, are pure and not to be forsaken. These means of purification should be respected like the great [60] crown ornament in the hood of the nāga, and they will abide in the depths of the earth and eliminate confusion.[350] Master Vasubandhu writes in his Rational System of Exposition: Because the basis containing the perfect teachings became corrupt, nothing was comprehended.[351] Commentary on Scriptural Inquiry states: After the passing of the Master, the brahman king called Jayamitra destroyed stūpas, killed monks, incinerated volumes of texts, and burned temples.[352] Due to that king and the beggar Sūryasiddhi and so on, the basis containing the perfect teachings degenerated and the aggregate of Dharma declined. For those who remained no Dharma appeared due to the presence of impurity. Master Jinaputra writes in his Subcommentary: Those aggregates of Dharma declined, and this alone is left.[353] And: The sūtra teaching the six pure causes was lost, and where formerly up to one hundred Dharmas were taught by elaborating a single scripture, now just ten or less are taught.[354]

In the sūtras} there are five, called the aggregates of (1) ethics, (2) concentration, (3) wisdom, (4) liberation, and (5) the liberated transcendent wisdom of seeing. Vaibhāṣikas assert that these [five] are included in the [standard] aggregates of form and formation.[355] They assert [the aggregate of] ethics to be form since it consists of the seven abandonments of body and speech. The other [four aggregates] are mental factors different from feeling and discernment[356] {since the last two aggregates are respectively subcategories of resolution and wisdom.} Specifically, that is because the aggregate of liberation is {nonlearner} resolution and the liberated transcendent wisdom of seeing is a subcategory of wisdom. {If the latter four possess a retinue, then that retinue will include either four or five [standard] aggregates because equipoise on the six levels of absorption also has nonindicative form [and that is included in the form aggregate].} Others such as the Sautrāntikas assert that all are included in the aggregate of formation because they assert the [61] aggregate of ethics to be a specific type of intention. So too, the aggregates of the confession of immorality, rejoicing, and prayer are included in the aggregate of formation because they are by nature [respectively] regret, faith, and aspiration. If they also have a retinue, it is included in four aggregates. Further, those called aggregates set on a correct path, aggregates set on a wrong path, and indeterminate aggregates are included in five aggregates because it is said: Āryas and those who commit heinous acts are [respectively] determined to be those set on a correct path or a wrong path.[357] This is stated from the perspective of persons who are āryas, those who commit heinous acts, and those who are neither.

Furthermore, the first eight of the ten bases of totality[358] (kṛtsnāyatana) are included in the phenomena base because they possess the nature of nonattachment since the Abhidharmakośa observes, “There are ten totalities. Eight are nonattachment” (8:36a). If they possess a complement, they are included in the mental and phenomena bases since they possess the nature of the five aggregates. Both space and consciousness possess the nature of the first two formless-realm states, since the Abhidharmakośa states, “Two are pure formless states” (8:36c). So too, the eight bases of subjugation are included in the phenomena base since they possess the nature of nonattachment. If they have a retinue they are included in the mental base and the phenomena base. Also, a sūtra states: Monks, when the Teacher or learned guru pure in conduct teaches Dharma, then in just the way the Teacher or learned guru pure in conduct teaches Dharma, analytical knowledge of meaning and analytical knowledge of phenomena arises with respect to those Dharmas. Then with respect to the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of phenomena, joy arises; reliant on that joy, mental joy arises; reliant on mental joy, physical pliancy arises; reliant on physical pliancy, pleasure is experienced; reliant on pleasure, equipoise arises; reliant on mental equipoise, you come to know and see the perfect state just as it is. Reliant on the view that knows and sees the perfect state just as it is, disappointment arises. When disappointment arises, freedom from attachment arises and when free from attachment, liberation arises. This is the first base of liberation.[359]

(1) Recognizing Dharma, (2) melodiously reciting it, (3) extensively teaching it to others, (4) extensively contemplating it, and (5) meditating on it [62] are called “the five bases of liberation.” Since they are wisdom they are included in the phenomena base, because recognizing Dharma and its meaning that is taught and recited by others is wisdom derived from hearing; recognizing Dharma and its meaning that is taught to others and contemplated is wisdom derived from contemplation; and recognizing Dharma and its meaning that is meditated on is wisdom derived from meditation. “Mental joy” is mental satisfaction, “physical pliancy” is flexibility of the body, “pleasure is experienced” refers to flexibility of the mind, “equipoise” is concentration that is the culmination of mental placement, “seeing {and knowing} the perfect state just as it is” is wisdom that is the culmination of insight, “disappointment arises” from the truths of suffering and origin, being “free from attachment” arises due to the path, and “liberation” should be understood as the manifestation of cessation. If they possess a complement, they are included in the base of sound, the mental base, and the phenomena base, since sound is heard in recitation and in teaching others, they have concomitant associates, and they have characteristics and so on. Again, the four [formless] states such as the base of infinite space and so on are included in the mental and phenomena bases because they are by nature the four aggregates that are other than form. A sūtra declares: There are embodied sentient beings devoid of discernment, and there are also those devoid of specific discernment. Such sentient beings devoid of discernment are the first base. There are formless sentient beings who pass beyond the base of “nothingness” and establish and abide in the base of “neither discernment nor nondiscernment.” Such beings who proceed to the base of “neither discernment nor nondiscernment” are the second base.[360] The state of nondiscernment is included in ten sense bases because it is included in (1–8) the eight physical bases, omitting smell and taste, and it is by nature (9–10) the mental and phenomena bases; and the mental faculty of such beings exists at birth and death. The base of neither discernment nor nondiscernment is included in the mental and phenomena bases because it is by nature the four aggregates.

{THOSE DESIGNATED ELEMENTS ARE INCLUDED IN THE ELEMENTS}

The Multiple Elements Sūtra mentions that there are sixty-two elements.[361] From among those, the eighteen elements such as the eye were explained previously. {The tally of the forty-four elements other than those eighteen are: (1–18) three sets of six, (19–22) one set of four, (23–40) six sets of three, and (40–44) two sets of two.[362]} Then the first set of six elements is explained: (1–4) the four primary elements such as earth are included in the element of tactility and so forth, and these were previously explained.

Cavities are called the “element of space.” Some say it is light and darkness. Contaminated consciousness is the element of consciousness that is the support of birth. (1:28)

nam mkha' dang rnam shes kyi khams ma bshad pas sgo dang skar khung la sogs pa'i bu ga ni nam mkha'i khams su shes par bya ste/{ bye brag tu smra ba rnams ni phyi nang gi dbye ba gsungs pa'i phyir nam mkha'i khams ni nam mkha' las tha dad de mdo las nang gi nam mkha' gang zhe na/ lus 'di'i nam mkha' gang zhig nang la brten pa nam mkhar gyur pa mi gsal ba/ khrag dang lpags pas ma khyab pa ste dper na mig gi bu ga lta bu ste zhes pa la sogs pa dang*/ phyi'i nam mkha' gang zhe na/ phyi'i nam mkha' gang zhig nam mkhar gyur pa/ mi gsal ba/ gzugs su gyur pa las ma khyab pa zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs so/ / gzhan yang gzugs kyi 'dod chags dang bral ba la nam mkha'i khams yangs par gsungs pa'i phyir te mdo las/ gang gi phyir de'i sems khams lnga rnams las 'dod chags dang bral bar rnam par grol bar 'gyur la/ de nas de'i rnam par shes pa nyid lhag mar lus par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs la/ zag med ni spang bya ma yin no zhes gsungs so zhes zer ro/ /} de yang nyin mo snang ba dang mtshan mo mun pa'i rang bzhin dag yin pa'i phyir gzugs kyi khams kyis bsdus so lo/ / 'di ni bye brag tu smra ba'i 'dod pa ste{ rtsig pa la sogs pa'i thogs bcas kyi nye 'khor na yod pa} thogs bcas nye 'khor ba{ 'i gzugs} yin no zhes zer ro/ / mdo sde pa na re 'di ni mdo'i dgongs pa ma yin te/ snang ba dang mun pa ni 'dus byas yin pa'i phyir dang*/ nam mkha'i khams kyang 'dus ma byas su bshad pa'i phyir thogs med nye 'khor ba yin no zhes zer ro/ / 'di ltar na nam mkha'i khams chos kyi khams su 'dus so/ /

Since the elements of space and consciousness were not [63] previously explained, first (5) the cavities (chidra) of doors and windows and so on are called the “element of space” (ākāṣadhātu). {Vaibhāṣikas state that the element of space is distinct from space because it has internal and external classifications. A sūtra states: What is internal space? It is space dependent on the internal space of the body that is imperceptible and not pervaded by blood or skin, such as the eye socket and so on.[363] And: What is external space? It is space that is external, imperceptible, and not pervaded by form.[364] Again, the state free from attachment to form is called “the expansive element of space.” A sūtra mentions: You are liberated when your mind is free of attachment to the five elements and your consciousness is left as remainder.[365] Uncontaminated states are not objects of abandonment.} Some say that the element of space is included in the element of form because the day possesses the essence of light (āloka) and the night possesses darkness (andhakāra). Vaibhāṣikas assert this, for they say it is {form} that is enclosed and impeded {for it exists within an enclosure of impeding walls and so on}. Sautrāntikas say that this is not the intention of the sūtras because light and darkness are conditioned states and the element of space is described as an unconditioned phenomenon. In that case, it is an enclosed unimpeded state. Thus the element of space is included in the phenomena element.

rnam shes thams cad ni rnam shes kyi khams ma yin gyi 'on kyang zag pa dang bcas pa'i rnam par shes pa'i khams yin par 'dod de/{ zag med srid pa gcod par byed pa yin pa la/} khams drug po de dag bcom ldan 'das kyis srid par skye ba dang rga ba dang na ba dang 'chi 'pho ba'i rten du gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / mdo las/ dge slong dag skyes bu 'di ni khams drug pa yin no zhes bya ba dang*/ khams drug la brten nas ma'i mngal du 'jug par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / des na rnam shes kyi khams ni sems kyi khams bdun du 'dus so/

(6) Not all consciousnesses are the element of consciousness; however, contaminated consciousness (sāsravavijñāna) is asserted to be the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu), and the Bhagavan stated that the six elements are the support of birth (janmaniśraya), aging, sickness, and death in saṃsāric existence {whereas uncontaminated phenomena disrupt [or sever] existence}. A sūtra declares: Monks, this being is the six elements.[366] And: You enter your mother’s womb in dependence on the six elements.[367] Therefore the element of consciousness is included in the seven mental elements.

{ khams drug po de dag las srid pa skyed pa yin te rnam shes ni srid par nying mtshams sbyor ba'i sa bon no/ / de gos bar byed pa ni 'byung ba bzhi ste rten du gyur pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / 'phel bar byed pa ni nam mkha' ste go 'byed pa'i phyir ro de ltar na 'di dag ni yang srid rgyas pa'i sa bon gyi don gyis na khams so/ / de dag las 'dir gnyis kho na 'chad pa ni la la bshad zin cing la la 'chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir de/ khams ni bco brgyad 'byung ba bzhi/ / dus gsum tshor ba la sogs bzhi/ / zag bcas zag med 'dus byas dang*/ / 'dus ma byas dang 'gog khams te/ / bshad zin so bzhi'o/ / sa sogs las gzhan drug tshan dang*/ dus gsum 'gog pa las gzhan pa'i gsum tshan 'chad 'gyur nyer drug /ces gsungs la/ yang na 'phro lus pa 'di gnyis kyis kha bskang ba'am/ log rtog bzlog pa'i phyir ro/}

{Existence is generated from the six elements because consciousness is the seed that links to existence; when it is awakened, the four primary elements act as its support, and when it develops, space accommodates it. Thus they are elements since they are the seeds of extensive rebirth. From among those six, only two are explained here because some were explained before and some are yet to be explained. The thirty-four elements already explained include (1–18) the eighteen elements, (19–22) the four primary elements, (23–25) the three times, (26–29) the four feelings and so on, (30) contaminated phenomena, (31) uncontaminated phenomena, (32) conditioned phenomena, (33) unconditioned phenomena, and (34) the element of cessation. The twenty-six yet to be explained include (1–12) the sets of six other than the earth and so on and (13–26) the sets of three that are other than the three times and cessation. Again, the two left as remainder either supplement these or stop wrong conception.}

de'i rjes la 'dod pa dang gnod sems dang rnam par 'tshe ba dang nges par 'byung ba dang gnod sems med pa dang rnam par mi 'tshe ba'i khams zhes bya ba drug bshad pa ni chos kyi khams kyis bsdus te/ dang po gsum ni 'dod pa'i 'dod chags dang sems can la zhe sdang ba dang*/ sems can la tho 'tsham pa'i rang bzhin spang bar bya ba'i sems byung dang*/ phyi ma gsum ni ma chags pa dang zhe sdang med pa dang snying brtse ba'i rang bzhin gnyen po'i sems byung yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i rjes la bde ba dang sdug bsngal dang yid bde ba dang yid mi bde ba dang btang snyoms dang ma rig pa'i khams zhes bya ba drug gsungs pa'ang chos kyi khams kyis bsdus te/ dang po lnga ni tshor ba dang drug pa ni 'du byed kyi nang du 'dus pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i rjes la tshor ba dang 'du shes dang 'du byed dang rnam par shes pa'i khams bzhi gsungs pa ni dang po gsum chos kyi khams dang bzhi pa sems kyi khams bdun gyis bsdus so/ / de'i rjes la 'dod pa dang gzugs dang gzugs med pa'i khams gsum gsungs pa ni rim pa bzhin khams bco brgyad dang dri ro dang sna lce'i rnam shes ma gtogs pa bcu bzhi dang khams tha ma gsum gyis bsdus so/ / de'i rjes la gzugs dang gzugs med pa dang 'gog pa'i khams gsum gsungs pa na khams bcu bzhi dang tha ma gsum dang chos kyi khams kyis bsdus te/ 'dir 'gog pa'i khams ni so sor brtags pa dang brtags min gyi 'gog pa yin no/ / de nas 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar byung ba'i khams gsum gsungs pa ni khams bco brgyad po thams cad kyis bsdus so/ /

Now the explanation of the second set of six. The elements of (1) attachment, (2) malice, (3) violence, (4) renunciation, (5) nonmalice, and (6) nonviolence are included in the phenomena element because the first [64] three are the mental factors of desire-realm attachment, aversion to sentient beings, and scorn for sentient beings. The second three are their antidotes, which are mental factors by nature: nonattachment, nonaversion, and altruism. Then the third set of six elements includes (1) pleasure, (2) pain, (3) mental satisfaction, (4) mental dissatisfaction, (5) equanimity, and (6) ignorance — which are included in the phenomena element — because the first five are feelings and the sixth is included in formation. Then the set of four elements includes (1) feeling, (2) discernment, (3) formation and (4) consciousness, where the first three are included in the phenomena element and the fourth is included in the seven mental elements. Then the first set of three includes the (1) desire realm, (2) form realm, and (3) formless realm, which are respectively included in (1) the eighteen elements, (2) the fourteen elements except for smell and taste and nose and tongue [consciousness], and (3) the latter three elements [namely, the mental element, the phenomena element, and the mental consciousness element]. Then the second set of three includes the (1) form realm, (2) formless realm, and (3) the element of cessation, which are respectively included in (1) the fourteen elements, (2) the latter three elements, and (3) the phenomena element, because here the element of cessation is analytical and nonanalytical cessation. Then the third set of three includes (1) the past, (2) present, and (3) future elements, which are included in all eighteen elements.

de'i rjes la ngan pa dang bar ma dang gya nom pa'i khams gsum gsungs pa ni 'dod pa'i khams la sogs pa gsum po nyid yin no/ / de'i rjes la dge ba dang mi dge ba dang lung du ma bstan pa'i khams gsum gsungs pa'i dang po gnyis ni gzugs dang sgra dang chos dang sems kyi khams bdun gyis bsdus so/ / tha ma ni khams bco brgyad kyis bsdus so/ / de'i rjes la slob pa dang mi slob pa dang gnyis ka ma yin pa'i khams gsum gsungs pa'i dang po gnyis ni yid dang chos dang yid kyi rnam par shes pa'i khams gsum gyis bsdus so/ / gsum pa ni khams bco brgyad du bsdus so/ / de'i rjes la zag pa dang bcas pa dang zag pa med pa'i khams gnyis gsungs pa las dang po ni khams bco brgyad kyis bsdus la/ phyi ma ni yid dang chos dang yid kyi rnam par shes pa'i khams{ tha ma gsum} gyis bsdus so/ / de'i rjes la 'dus byas dang 'dus ma byas kyi khams gnyis gsungs pa las dang po ni khams bco brgyad kyis bsdus la/ phyi ma ni chos kyi khams kyis bsdus te/ de ltar na de dag ni khams drug cu rtsa gnyis te de dag la mkhas na mkhas pa khams la mkhas pa zhes gsungs so/ / yang stong chung ngu'i 'jig rten gyi khams dang*/ stong gnyis bar ma'i 'jig rten gyi khams dang*/ stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams zhes gsungs pa ni bye brag med par khams bco brgyad kyis bsdus te/ de yang 'dod par gtogs pa ni bco brgyad po thams cad dang*/ bsam gtan dang po ni bcu bzhis bsdus so zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Then the fourth set of three includes (1) inferior, (2) intermediate, and (3) superior elements, which are included in the three realms — the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Then the fifth set of three includes (1) virtuous, (2) nonvirtuous, and (3) neutral elements, where the first two are included in form, sound, phenomena, and the seven mental elements; and the third is included in the eighteen elements. Then the sixth set of three includes (1) the learner element, (2) the nonlearner element, and (3) the element that is neither of those, for the first two are included in the mental element, the phenomena element, and the mental consciousness element, and the third is included in the eighteen elements. Then the first set of two is (1) contaminated elements and (2) uncontaminated elements. The first is included in the eighteen elements, and the second is included in {the last three:} the mental element, the phenomena element, and the mental consciousness element. Then the second set of two is (1) conditioned elements and (2) unconditioned elements. The first is included in the eighteen elements, and the second is included in the phenomena element. Thus there are sixty-two elements. If you are learned in them, you are called “a scholar learned in the elements.” Again, the world systems of the small chiliocosm, the world systems of the intermediate dichiliocosm, and the world systems of the great trichiliocosm are included in the eighteen elements without subcategories [65] because all eighteen elements pertain to the desire realm and the first absorption is included in the fourteen elements [of the form realm].

['di] la brgyad na
rab dbye nyi shu rtsa gnyis yod kyang
THERE ARE TWENTY-TWO CLASSIFICATIONS.

brjod bde ba'i dbang du byas nas bstan yod la sogs pa lnga dang*/ rtog bcas dpyod bcas la sogs pa'i rnam pa'i rab dbye dang*/ dmigs bcas la sogs pa lnga dang*/ byung ba gsum gyi rnam pa'i rab dbye dang*/ rdzas dang ldan pa la sogs pa lnga dang*/ mthong spang la sogs pa'i rnam pa'i rab dbye dang*/ lta ba dang lta ba ma yin pa'i rnam pa'i rab dbye dang*/ gnyis kyis shes par bya ba la sogs pa gsum bshad pa dang brgyad du bsdu bar bya'o/ /

From the perspective of the ease of expression, they are subsumed in eight: five that are demonstrable and so on; the investigative and analytical; five possessing a focal object and so on; the three types of derivation; the five such as substantial existence; objects to be eliminated by the path of seeing; view and nonview; and three such as those known by two and so on.
de la dang po ni [bstan yod la sogs pa lnga/]
Five that are demonstrable and so on
bstan yod 'dir ni gzugs gcig pu/ / thogs dang bcas pa gzugs can bcu/ / lung ma bstan brgyad de dag nyid/ / gzugs sgra ma gtogs gzhan rnam gsum/ / 29
The form element alone is demonstrable. The ten physical elements are impeded. Eight are undeclared: those except for form and sound. (1:29)
khams bco brgyad po de dag las bstan du yod pa rnams ni du/ bstan du med pa rnams ni du zhe na zhe pa la sogs pa'i dri ba ni 'og ma rnams la'ang shes par bya'o/ /
Question: How many of the eighteen elements are demonstrable? How many are undemonstrable?

de'i lan du bstan du yod pa ni 'dir gzugs kyi khams gcig pu yin te/ de ni 'di ni 'di na'o/ / pha gi ni pha gi na'o zhes{ sgras bstan pas} mig gi dbang po{ 'i shes pa bskyed cing mig shes} la bstan du yod pa'i phyir ro/ / des na slob dpon rgyal po'i sras kyis yang na tshig gis gzhan gyi mig gi rnam{ par} shes{ pa} skyed pa ni bstan pa yin la de dang lhan cig 'jug pa ni bstan yod de/ de yang gzugs kyi khams gcig pu yin no zhes bshad do/ / khams bcu bdun ni de lta ma yin pas bstan du med pa zhes bya ba yin no/{ mdo las kyang dge slong gzugs ni phyi'i skye mched yin te 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag rgyur byas pa gzugs dang ba/ gzugs can bstan du yod la thogs pa dang bcas pa'o zhes pa dang*/ dge slong mig ni nang gi skye mched yin te 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag rgyur byas pa gzugs dang po gzugs can bstan du med la thogs pa dang bcas pa'o zhes lus kyi bar du gsungs so/ / dge slong chos rnams ni phyi'i skye mched de skye mched bcu gcig gis ma bsdus pa bstan du med pa thogs pa med pa'o zhes gsungs so/ /}

Reply: The form element alone is demonstrable (sanidarśana) because {the words demonstrating} “this and that are here, the other is over there” {generate} eye sense {consciousness}, and such objects are demonstrable to {eye consciousness}. Thus Master Jinaputra explains that generating eye consciousness in another due to uttering words is demonstration, and those objects simultaneously engaged [by those words] are demonstrable.[368] This applies to the element of form alone, and the remaining seventeen elements are undemonstrable (anidarśana) since they are not like that. {Also a sūtra states: Monks, form is an external base since it is form derived from the four great elements that is physically demonstrable and impeded. Monks, eyes are an internal sense base because they are subtle organs caused by the four great elements that are physically undemonstrable but impeded.[369] And: Monks, phenomena are external bases because they are not included in the eleven bases, and they are undemonstrable and impeded.[370]}

yang khams bco brgyad las gcig tu{ sgrib pa'i} thogs pa dang bcas pa ni mig la sogs pa'i gzugs can bcu yin te/ de la thogs pa ni rdugs pa yin te/{ yul la thogs pa de dag sgrib pa la thogs sam zhe na mu bzhi ste/ dang po yul thogs sgrib mi thogs ni sems kyi khams bdun dang chos khams kyi mtshungs ldan no/ / gnyis pa ni yul lnga'o/ / gsum pa ni dbang po lnga'o/ / bzhi pa ni chos khams kyi mtshungs ldan ma gtogs pa'o/ / yul thogs dag dmigs pa la thogs sam zhe na tshig phyi ma dang sbyar te/ dmigs pa la thogs pa de dag yul la'ang thogs te yul med par mtshungs ldan rnams mi skye bas so/ / yul la thogs la dmigs pa la mi thogs pa ni dbang po lnga'o/} de yang rnam pa gsum ste/ sgrib pa la thogs pa dang*/ yul la thogs pa dang*/ dmigs pa la thogs pa'o/ /

From among the eighteen elements, the ten physical (rūpiṇa) elements such as the eyes are {obstructed} impeded (sapratighā) phenomena, for being impeded is to be hindered. {Question: Are those that are impeded to [accessing] object fields (viṣaya) impeded through being [physically] obstructed (āvaraṇa)? Reply: There are four possibilities: (1) Those impeded to [accessing] object fields but not impeded through being [physically] obstructed are the seven mental elements and concomitant states of the phenomena element. (2) Those impeded through being [physically] obstructed but not impeded to becoming object fields are the five objects. (3) Those impeded to both are the five sense faculties. (4) Those impeded to neither are those of the phenomena element except concomitant states. Question: Are those that are impeded to [accessing] object fields impeded to [accessing] focal objects (ālambana)? Reply: [A pervasion] applies to the latter because those that are impeded to [accessing] focal objects are also impeded to [accessing] object fields, since concomitant states would not arise without object fields. Those that are impeded to [accessing] object fields but not impeded to [accessing] focal objects [66] are the five sense faculties.} Impeded phenomena have three types: (1) those impeded through being [physically] obstructed (āvaraṇapratighāta), (2) those impeded to [accessing] object fields (viṣayapratighāta), and (3) those impeded to [accessing] focal objects (ālambanapratighāta).

de la dang po ni rang gi yul du gzhan skye ba'i gegs byed pa ste gzugs can dag gcig gi go sar gcig rdugs{ nas gzugs can gnyis pa mi 'byung} pa'o/{ rdul rdzas brgyad ces bya ba'ang rang rang go sar rtsib ma bzhibs nas gnas pa yin no/} gnyis pa ni mig la sogs pa rnams rang gi yul la 'jug gi gzhan la mi 'jug pa'o/ gsum pa ni sems dang sems byung rnams rang gi yul la 'dzin gyi gzhan la mi 'dzin pa'o/ / de la 'dir ni dang po'i dbang du byas pa yin te/ mig la sogs pa'i rdul phran rnams gcig gi go sar gcig 'ong ba la gegs byed par gnas pa'i phyir ro/ / khams lhag ma brgyad ni de lta ma yin pa'i phyir thogs pa med par grub bo/ / 'o na 'dir yul dang dmigs pa la khyad par ci yod ce na/ dbang po lnga'i yul gang yin pa de ni yul yin la/ gang zhig sems dang sems byung gis 'dzin pa de ni dmigs pa dang yul gnyis ka yin no/ /

(1) The first stops another arising in its spatial location, since one physical object prevents another taking its own spatial location {so that a second physical object does not occur there. For example, each of the eight substantial particles exist in their own discrete spatial location}. (2) The eyes and so on engage their own object fields and do not engage other object fields. (3) Minds and mental factors apprehend their own focal object and do not apprehend other focal objects. In this context, those that are impeded are explained from the perspective of the first because the atoms of the eyes and so on stop the entry of one atom to the spatial location of another. The remaining eight elements are established as unimpeded (apratigha) since they are not like this. Question: In this context, what is the difference between object fields and focal objects? Reply: Any object of the five sense faculties is an object field, but those that are apprehended by minds and mental factors are both object fields and focal objects.

'dir 'grel ba las yul thogs kyi skabs su gdags pa las gsungs pa'i mig la chu dang skam la thogs mi thogs kyi mu bzhi dang*/ mtshan mo dang nyin par thogs mi thogs kyi mu bzhi dang*/ gzhan yang yul dang sgrib thogs kyi mu bzhi dang*/ yul dang dmigs thogs kyi mu gnyis kyang bshad do/ / de nyid kyi phyir slob dpon blo gros brtan pas kyang bstan du yod la thogs pa dang bcas pa ni mig gi dbang po'i yul lo/ / bstan du med la thogs pa dang bcas pa ni mig la sogs pa lnga dang sgra dang dri dang ro dang rig bya bzhi'o zhes bshad do/ /

Here the Autocommentary explains: In the context of being impeded to object fields, the Prajñapti states that there are four possibilities for wetness and dryness being an impediment or not to the eyes, and four possibilities for night and day being an impediment or not to the eyes. Also, there are four possibilities for being impeded to object fields and impeded through [physical] obstruction, as well as two possibilities for being impeded to object fields and impeded to focal objects.[371] Therefore Master Sthiramati also notes: Demonstrable-impeded objects are objects of the eye sense faculty. And undemonstrable-impeded objects are the five sense organs, as well as the four elements of sound, smell, taste, and tactile objects.[372]

yang khams bco brgyad las dge ba dang mi dge ba'i ngo bor lung bstan du med pa'i phyir gcig tu lung du ma bstan pa ni brgyad de/ gang zhe na/ thogs bcas su bshad pa'i gzugs can bcu po gang dag yin pa de dag nyid las gzugs dang sgra{ gnyis ni dge mi dger yang 'gyur bas de gnyis} ma gtogs pa dbang po lnga dang dri ro reg bya rnams so/ / gzugs sgra ma gtogs pa ni de dag dge mi dger yang 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / kha cig na re rnam par smin pa'i phyir lung bstan du med pa ni lung ma bstan yin no zhes zer ba ni mi rigs te/ zag med 'dus byas kyang der thal ba'i phyir ro/ / des na de'i mtshan nyid kyang de nyid yin te/ bye bshad las kyang*/ dge ba dang mi dge ba'i dngos por lung bstan du med pas lung du ma bstan pa'o zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / kha cig de'i mtshan nyid blang dor du ma grub pa yin no zhes 'chad pa ni mi rigs te/ mig gsal ba la sogs pa blang bya dang*/ 'dod pa'i lta ba dang po gnyis mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa dang*/ khams gong ma gnyis kyi nyon mongs pa rnams dor bya ma yin par 'gyur ba'am/ yang na de dag lung ma bstan ma yin par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ /

Again, from the eighteen elements there are eight that are undeclared (avyākṛta) [or neutral] because their nature was not declared [by the Buddha] to be virtuous or nonvirtuous. Question: What are they? Reply: From those ten physical elements that are said to impede, they are the five sense faculties plus smell, taste, and tactility, except for {both} form and sound. Form and sound are omitted because they can be virtuous or nonvirtuous. Some say: Those whose karmic maturation is not declared are “undeclared.” Reply: That is illogical because it would absurdly follow that uncontaminated conditioned phenomena would be undeclared [or neutral]. Therefore their characteristics are just as described in the Great Treatise on Differentiation: They are undeclared since they are not declared in the way that [the karmic maturation of] virtuous or nonvirtuous things [is declared].[373] Some say: Those possessing such characteristics [i.e., those whose karmic maturation is not declared] are not established as something to be practiced or rejected. Reply: That is illogical because then cleaning the eyes and so on would not be something to be practiced, and the first two views of the desire realm and their concomitant states, [67] as well as the afflictions of the two higher realms, would not be something to be rejected, and if they were, they would not be undeclared.
'dod khams gtogs pa thams cad do/ / gzugs kyi khams na bcu bzhi'o/ / dri dang ro dang sna dang ni/ / lce yi rnam shes khams ma gtogs/ / 30
The others have three types. All exist in the desire realm. Fourteen exist in the form realm, except the elements of smell, taste, nose, and tongue consciousness. (1:30)

khams gzhan bcu po dag ni dge mi dge lung ma bstan rnam pa gsum yin te/ de la gzugs sgra ni lus ngag gi rig byed kyis bsdus pa sems dge mi dges kun nas bslang bas kun slong gis dge mi dge dang*/ sems lung ma bstan gyis kun nas bslang ba dang*/{ rgyud kyis bsdus kyang*/} rig byed kyis ma bsdus pa {rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa thams cad }ni ngo bo nyid kyi lung ma bstan yin no/ / sems kyi khams bdun ni grogs ma chags pa dang*/ chags pa la sogs pa dang mtshungs par ldan pas dge mi dge dang lung ma bstan kyang yin no/ /

The other ten have three types: virtuous, nonvirtuous, or neutral. Thus form and sound are virtuous or nonvirtuous by motivation when included in indicative [actions of] body and speech and motivated by virtuous or nonvirtuous minds. They are by nature neutral when motivated by neutral minds and not included in indicative form {though conjoined with the mindstream, or they are any form and sound not conjoined to the mindstream}. The seven mental elements are virtuous, nonvirtuous, or neutral through being concomitant with beneficial nonattachment, or attachment, and so on.
chos kyi khams ni
THE PHENOMENA ELEMENT

kha cig ngo bo nyid kyis dge ba dang*/ kha cig mtshungs ldan gyis dge ba dang*/ kha cig kun slong gis dge ba dang*/ kha cig don dam par dge ba'ang yod do/{ de dag gi mtshan nyid thob pa dang bcas pa'ang dge ba'o/} / mi dge ba dang lung ma bstan la'ang de bzhin du shes par bya'o/ / dge mi dge'i mtshan nyid ni rim pa ltar dam pas bsngags shing gnod med kyi 'bras bu skyed pa dang*/ de las bzlog pa'o/ / kha cig dge ba'i mtshan nyid yun du bde ba dang 'bras bu yid du 'ong ba skyed pa'o zhes 'chad pa ni mi rigs te/ bsam gtan bzhi pa yan chad kyi tshor ba skyed byed dge ba ma yin par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ /

Some say: The phenomena element is virtuous by nature. Some say: It is virtuous by concomitance. Some say: It is virtuous by motivation. Some say: That which is virtuous in an ultimate sense also exists. {Response: It is virtuous through obtaining those characteristics.} But it should also be understood to be nonvirtuous and neutral in the same way. The definition of virtue and nonvirtue is, respectively, (1) “that which is praised by pure beings and produces resultant states free of harm” and (2) that which is the opposite of that.[374] Some say: The definition of virtue is “that which produces pleasure and resultant pleasant states for a long period.” Reply: This is illogical because then virtue would not generate feeling on and above the fourth absorption.
gal te btang snyoms kyang yid du 'ong ba yin no zhe na/ ma yin te/ yid 'ong yid du mi 'ong dang zhes yid du 'ong ba ni bde ba la bshad pa'i phyir ro/ /
Objection: That equanimity is also pleasant! Reply: That is not so, because “pleasant,” as described in “Those possessing pleasant or unpleasant feeling” (6:3a), is explained as pleasure.

yang khams bco brgyad las 'dod pa'i khams su gtogs pa{ ste ma bral ba} ni bco brgyad po thams cad do/{ de'i sred pas bdag gir byas pa'i phyir ro}/ gzugs kyi khams na ni bcu bzhi'o/ / gang zhe na dri dang ro dang sna'i rnam shes dang lce'i rnam shes kyi khams ma gtogs pa rnams so/ / dri ro gnyis ni gzugs khams na med de/ de dag ni kham gyi zas yin {bsnam pa dang myang ba las gzhan pa'i dri ro la longs spyod pa med la des na } la de las 'dod chags dang bral ba dag der skye ba'i phyir ro/ / 'o na ni reg bya'ang med par 'gyur ro zhe na/ de la ni kham gyi zas dang zas ma yin pa gnyis yod pas kham zas su gyur pa'i reg bya med kyang dbang po la sogs pa'i gzugs kyi rten 'byung ba dang{ khang pa la sogs pa'i gzhi dang} gos kyi reg bya la sogs pa yod pa'i phyir ro/ / dri ro la ni kham zas ma yin pa med do/ / gal te yod du chug kyang gzugs khams na dgos pa med pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir sna lce'i rnam shes gnyis kyang med de/ / de dag gi yul med pa'i phyir dang*/ gzugs sgra 'dod pa na yod pa dag kyang de pa'i dbang pos 'dzin mod kyi dri la sogs pa ni phrad nas 'dzin pa'i phyir 'dod pa na yod pa'ang de'i yul ma yin pa'i phyir ro zhes bye brag tu smra ba rnams zer ro/ /

Regarding the eighteen elements, all eighteen {without exception} exist in the desire realm {because all are taken as mine there through craving}. Fourteen exist in the form realm. Question: What are they? Reply: They are those eighteen elements except for the elements of smell, taste, nose consciousness, and tongue consciousness. Neither smell nor taste exist in the form realm because they are oral food[375] (kavalīkāra) {and since there is no enjoyment of smell and taste other than that detected and experienced; therefore} those who are free of attachment to oral food are born in the form realm. Question: Do tactile objects also not exist in the form realm? Reply: From among either oral food and nonfood, oral food that is a tactile object doesn’t exist there. However, the primary elements supporting the form of the sense faculties and so on, {supportive bases such as houses and so forth,} and the tactile objects of clothes do exist there. Vaibhāṣikas say that there are no smells and tastes that are not oral food and if they existed in the form realm there would be no need for them. As such, there is no nose or tongue consciousness there because they have no objects. Although form and sound that exist in the desire realm are indeed apprehended by sense faculties of the form realm, smell and so on that exist in the desire realm are not objects of those sense faculties because such objects are apprehended through contact.

gal te dgos pa med pas mi 'byung na sna lce'i dbang po dag kyang med par 'gyur ro zhe na/ de ni{ dgos pa dang bcas te} lus mdzes par bya ba'i phyir ro/ / mdzes pa ni dbang rten gyis bya bar nus shing*/{ dbang po rten med yin pa'i phyir dang*/} dgos pa yod kyang rgyu med na mi 'byung la/{ dgos pa'i dbang gis 'byung ba ma yin gyi/} dbang po'i rgyu yang de la sred pas las bsags pa yin zhing*/{ de yod pas rgyu med ma yin pas rgyu'i dbang gis yin pa'i phyir dang*/} gang zhig yul la sred pa dang bral ba de ni yul can dbang po las kyang sred pa dang bral ba yin pa'i phyir rgyu med pas mi 'byung bar rigs so zhes slob dpon skyon brjod par byed do/ / bye brag tu smra ba ni dbang po med pa'i rten mi srid la/ skye bo rnams kyang dbang po dang bcas pa'i lus la sred pa dang bcas pas las gsog pa'i phyir dang*/ mdo las kyang gzugs na spyod pa'i dbang du mdzad nas dbang po rnams ma tshang ba med cing med ma yin no zhes gsungs{ pa dang 'gal lo zhe na der dbang po gang dag srid pa de dag ma tshang ba med pa la dgongs kyi/ gzhan du na pho mo'i dbang po'ang yod par thal lo/ / des na rang rgyud kyi sgo nas mig la sogs pa'i skye mched drug la sred pa kun tu spyod kyi yul dmigs pa'i sgo nas ma yin pas yul la chags pa dang bral yang dbang po la bral ba ma yin no/ / des na rgyu yod pas sna dang lce'i dbang po yod do/ / pho mo'i dbang po'i ni rgyu yul la rag pa'i sgo nas sred pa kun tu spyod pas yul gyi sgo nas sred pa spyod pa yin pas de la 'dod chags bral bas de na med la gang ma bral de dag ma spangs} pa'i phyir sna lce'i dbang po ni yod do zhes 'dod do/ /

Objection: If smell and so on don’t occur [68] because there is no need for them, then also the nose and tongue sense faculties should not arise. Reply: They {are required} to beautify the body. Vasubandhu raises the criticism that the supportive sense faculty is capable of beautifying the body, but even if such a need exists, beautification will not occur {when there is no supportive sense faculty} if no cause for it exists. {Though it does not occur due to the power of need,} karma is accumulated through craving beauty, and that is the cause of the sense faculties. On the other hand, to arise causelessly is illogical, {because they occur due to the power of causation since they exist and they are not causeless, and} because those who are free of craving for objects are also free of craving for the sense faculties possessing those objects. The Vaibhāṣikas assert that an object that lacks its corresponding sense faculty is impossible but that the nose and tongue sense faculties exist in the form realm because beings accumulate karma [that produces them] through craving for a body with just those sense faculties. A sūtra also states: From the perspective of engaging in activity in the form realm, there are no incomplete or nonexistent sense faculties.[376] {Objection: But you contradict this passage. Reply: The intention of that passage is that sense faculties that actually exist in the form realm are not incomplete; otherwise it would follow that male and female faculties would also exist there. Therefore form-realm beings are free from attachment to objects [of smell and taste] but not free of attachment to sense faculties, since they actively crave the six sense bases related to their mindstreams but not through focusing on their objects. That is, they have nose and tongue sense faculties since they possess the causes for them, but they are free of attachment to their objects [i.e., smell and taste]. Since the cause of male and female faculties is actively craving for contact with sensual objects, it is active craving in terms of an object. But since they are free of attachment to such objects, they do not possess those sense faculties. What they are free of they do not need to abandon.} Therefore the nose and tongue faculties are asserted to exist.
gzugs med gtogs pa yid dang ni/ / chos dang yid kyi rnam shes khams/ / de gsum zag bcas zag pa med/ / lhag ma rnams ni zag bcas so/ / 31
The mental element, phenomena element, and mental consciousness element exist in the formless realm. These three are contaminated or uncontaminated. The remainder are contaminated. (1:31)

gzugs med pa'i khams su gtogs pa ni yid dang chos dang yid kyi rnam par shes pa'i khams gsum yin te/ gzugs las 'dod chags bral ba dag der skye bas de na gzugs can gyi khams bcu med cing de dag med pas de dag gi{ brten pa dang dmigs pa'i} 'bras bu rnam shes kyi khams lnga'ang med pa'i phyir ro/ /

Three — the mental element (manodhātu), phenomena element (dharmadhātu), and mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) — exist in the formless realm. (1–10) The ten physical elements do not exist there since those free of attachment to material form are born there. (11–15) The five resultant consciousnesses do not exist there since those ten {the five supportive sense bases and five focal objects} do not exist there.

yang khams bco brgyad las gang dag bshad ma thag pa yid dang chos dang yid kyi rnam shes kyi khams de gsum la ni zag pa dang bcas pa dang zag pa med pa dag kyang yod de/ lam gyi bden par gtogs pa'i de gsum dang 'dus ma byas ni zag med yin la/ gzhan ni zag bcas yin pa'i phyir ro/ / lhag ma gzugs can gyi khams bcu dang de dag gi 'bras bu rnam shes kyi khams lnga ste bco lnga po rnams ni gcig tu zag pa dang bcas pa yin te/ sgom spang yin pa'i phyir dang*/ zag pa rnams rgyas par 'gyur ro/ / dpes ston pa rnams ni dgra bcom pa'i gzugs kyi phung po dang snod kyi 'jig rten ni zag pa'i gnyen po ma yin pa dang zag pa'i rten ma yin pas zag bcas zag med gnyis ka yin no zhes 'dod pa ni ma yin te/ de dag rnam par gcod pa'i 'gal ba yin pas phung po gsum pa mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ / gnas brgyad pa'i bsam gtan gyi yan lag 'chad pa'i skabs las ni dpes ston pas lus shin tu sbyangs pa byang chub kyi yan lag gis bsdus pa'i reg bya dang lus kyi rnam shes kyang zag med du 'dod par bshad do/ /

These three — (16) the mental element, (17) the phenomena element, and (18) the mental consciousness element, which were just explained from among the eighteen elements — are either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava) because their aspects that pertain to the truth of path and unconditioned phenomena are uncontaminated and their remaining aspects are contaminated. The remainder — the fifteen elements that include (1–10) the ten physicals elements and (11–15) their resultant five elements of consciousness — are together contaminated because they are objects abandoned by the path of meditation and they increase the contaminants. Dārṣṭāntikas assert that the form aggregate of arhats and physical world systems are both contaminated and uncontaminated since they are not the antidote to contaminants and also not the basis of contaminants. Reply: That is not so because a third alternative is impossible, since contaminated and uncontaminated states form a dichotomy. In the context of explaining the branches of absorption in part 8, [69] Dārṣṭāntikas assert that physical pliancy is a tactile object included in the requisites of enlightenment, and body consciousness is uncontaminated.
gnyis pa rtog bcas dpyod bcas la sogs pa'i rnam pa'i rab dbye ni
The investigative and analytical
rtog dang dpyod dang bcas pa ni/ / rnam par shes pa'i khams lnga yin/ / tha ma gsum ni rnam gsum mo/ / lhag ma rnams ni gnyis ka spangs/ / 32
The five consciousness elements are investigative and analytical. The latter three have three types. The remainder lack both. (1:32)

yang khams bco brgyad las gcig tu rtog pa dang bcas shing dpyod pa dang bcas pa ni mig la sogs pa'i rnam par shes pa'i khams lnga po yin te/ kha phyir bltas shing {rtog dpyod kyi sas bsdus pa rnam shes yin la/ } rtsing zhib dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / des na 'di la 'brel rnam gcod yin pas{ 'chad pa na 'di skad du/} rnam par shes pa'i khams lnga po/ / rtog dang dpyod dang bcas kho na zhes gdon par bya ste/{ TIka byed dag gis ni zhes bya ba'i sgra ni rtog pa dang dpyod pa dang bcas pa kho na'o zhes nges pa gzung ba yin no zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/} tha ma yid dang chos dang yid kyi rnam shes kyi khams gsum ni rtog pa dang bcas shing dpyod pa dang bcas pa dang*/ rtog pa med la dpyod pa tsam dang*/ rtog pa yang med dpyod pa yang med pa rnam pa gsum yin te/ 'di ltar 'dod pa dang bsam gtan dang po'i dngos gzhi{ tsam po} na yod pa'i yid dang yid kyi rnam shes kyi khams dang*/ rtog dpyod las gzhan pa'i chos kyi khams sems las byung ba rnams ni rtog pa dang bcas shing dpyod pa dang bcas pa yin te/ de dag dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir ro/ /

From among the eighteen elements, the five consciousness elements of eye consciousness and so on are investigative (savitarka) and analytical (savicāra) because they view external objects and because they are {consciousnesses associated with the levels of investigation and analysis and} concomitant with coarse and fine examination. Therefore, since they are exclusively related to coarse and fine examination, {it is said that} the five consciousness elements alone are called “investigative” and “analytical.” {Pūrṇavardhana’s commentary explains that the [Sanskrit] particle hi means that the five consciousnesses are definitely investigative and analytical alone.[377]} The three latter elements — the mental element, the phenomena element, and the mental consciousness element — have three types (prakāra): (1) those that are investigative and analytical, (2) those merely analytical and not investigative, and (3) those neither investigative nor analytical. (1) The mental element and the mental consciousness element that exist in the desire realm and in the {ordinary} actual basis of the first absorption, and the mental factors of the phenomena element that are other than investigation (vitarka) and analysis (vicāra), are analytical and investigative because they are concomitant with analysis and investigation.
