Those possessing the faculty of mental satisfaction also possess five because they possess equanimity, life force, the mental faculty, pleasure, and mental satisfaction itself. {Further, pleasure arises in the retinue of the five sense consciousnesses in the desire realm; in the first absorption it arises in the retinue of three; and in the third absorption it is mental bliss arising in the retinue of the mental faculty.}

gal te bsam gtan gnyis pa na{ byis pa la} yid bde yod kyang bde ba ni med de/ lus kyi bde ba ni dang po man chad pa'i sa pa yin pas{ sa 'phos pas/} spangs pa'i phyir dang*/ sems kyi bde ba ni gsum pa'i sa pa yin pas de ni ma thob pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ gsum pa'i bde ba nyon mongs can gyis thob pa ni de na'ang yod pa'i phyir dang*/ {sa gong ma'i nyon mongs can ma spangs pa de dang ldan na zhes pa ni grub pa'i mtha'o/ }

Objection: Though {childlike beings} have mental satisfaction in the second absorption, [physical] pleasure has been abandoned, since physical pleasure belongs to the level of the first absorption and below; they also do not obtain mental bliss since mental bliss belongs to the level of the third absorption. Reply: Obtainment of afflicted pleasure of the third absorption also exists there. {But the assertion that they possess unabandoned afflicted states of a higher level reflects a specific tenet position.}

gal te kun shes pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa'i 'phags pa phyir mi 'ong dang dgra bcom la zhugs pa ni khams gsum char du 'thob pa srid pas bsam gtan gsum pa man chad na bcu gcig dang ldan par rigs na bsam gtan bzhi pa dang gzugs med du skyes pa'i 'phags pa slob pa kun shes pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa de dag la ji ltar bde ba dang yid bde'i dbang po dang ldan te/ rang sa na med cing*/ bsam gtan gtogs pa'i dge ba ni/ / sa 'phos nyams pa dag gis gtong*/ / zhes sa 'phos pas 'og sa'i de gnyis spangs pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ zag bcas kyi bde ba dang yid bde spangs pas mi ldan med kyi zag med kyi de gnyis dang ldan te/ 'di ltar 'phags pas ni 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba na nges par bsam gtan dang po'i yid bde'i dbang po 'thob cing*/ bsam gtan gnyis pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba na bsam gtan gsum pa'i bde ba'i dbang po 'thob la/ de dag ni sa 'phos pas mi gtong ste/ 'di ltar sa 'phos pas zag bcas gtong gi zag med kyi gtong rgyur ma bshad la/ zag med ni/ 'phags pa/ 'bras bu thob sbyangs nyams pa las/ zhes bshad mod kyi 'bras bu thob pa dang dbang po sbyangs pa na'ang zhugs pa'i lam dang dbang po rtul po'i lam gyis bsdus pa'i zag med gtong yang 'bras bu dang dbang po rnon po'i lam gyis bsdus pa'i bsam gtan dang po dang gnyis pa'i yid bde dang gsum pa'i bde ba'i dbang po zag med kyi thob pa 'byung ste/ gang las chags bral bya phyir gang*/ / 'thob pa der yang 'og ma'ang 'thob/ / ces 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ /

Question: It is logical that ārya nonreturners and enterers to the state of arhat who possess the faculty of complete knowledge [106] possess eleven faculties on or below the third absorption, since it is possible that they obtain [complete knowledge] in the three realms. But how do ārya learners born in the fourth absorption or the formless realm, who possess the faculty of complete knowledge, also possess the faculty of pleasure or mental satisfaction, since those two faculties do not exist on their own level and are abandoned by changing level, for the Abhidharmakośa states, “Virtue belonging to the absorptions is relinquished by changing level or degeneration” (4:40ab)? Reply: Since they abandon contaminated pleasure and mental satisfaction, indeed they do not possess them, but they do possess the two uncontaminated pleasures. For āryas free from attachment to the desire realm definitely obtain the faculty of mental satisfaction of the first absorption, and if free from attachment to the second absorption, they obtain the faculty of pleasure of the third absorption. And these are not relinquished by changing level because relocation relinquishes contaminated states, but it is not said that it relinquishes uncontaminated states. Indeed, regarding uncontaminated states the Abhidharmakośa declares, “[The uncontaminated virtue of] the ārya [is relinquished] by obtaining the result, upgrading, or degeneration” (4:40d). Therefore, although uncontaminated states subsumed by the path of entry and the path of dull faculty are relinquished when the result is obtained or the intellectual capacity is upgraded, āryas obtain the uncontaminated faculties of mental satisfaction of the first and second absorptions and the pleasure of the third [absorption] subsumed by the resultant path, and the path of sharp faculty, since the Abhidharmakośa suggests, “In order to be free from attachment to any level, one obtains that and also one obtains lower level” (7:26ab).

de'i phyir bsam gtan bzhi pa dang gzugs med du skyes pa'i 'phags pa'i bde ba dang yid bde'i dbang po zag med ni sa 'phos pas mi gtong pas na gang zhig kun shes pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa de ni nges par dbang po bcu gcig dang ldan no zhes bya bar grub bo/ / de bzhin du kun shes pa dang ldan pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa la'ang dbang po bcu gcig nges par ldan pa'i tshul yang shes par bya'o/{ des na bzhi pa yan chad pa'i 'phags pa la bde ba gnyis zag med dang gsum pa man chad la zag bcas zag med gnyis ka ldan no/} dbang po gzhan mi ldan pa ni snga ma bzhin no/ /

Therefore, since the uncontaminated faculties of pleasure and mental satisfaction of āryas born in the fourth absorption or the formless realm are not relinquished by changing levels, those who possess the faculty of complete knowledge definitely possess eleven faculties. Similarly, you should understand that obtaining the faculty possessing complete knowledge is the method for definitely possessing eleven faculties. {Therefore āryas on the fourth absorption and above possess both uncontaminated faculties of pleasure and both contaminated and uncontaminated pleasure of the third absorption and below.} The faculties not possessed are as before.

kun shes par byed pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa ni 'dod khams kyi rten can gyi mthong lam pa yin la/ de la ni nges par rang nyid dang yid dang srog dang lus kyi dbang po dang yid bde dang bde ba dang sdug bsngal dang btang snyoms dang dad sogs lnga ste bcu gsum dag dang ldan pa yin no/ / gal te{ de lta na} gong na mthong lam med/ / mi skyo lung las 'dir rtsom zhing*/ / der mthar phyin ces 'byung phyir ro/ / zhes 'byung ba'i phyir kun shes byed pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa ni 'dod par skyes pa'i mthong lam pa kho na yin la/ de la ni pho mo'i dbang po gang rung zhig dang nges par ldan dgos te/ pho mo'i dbang po dang mi ldan pa dang rnam par nyams pa la sdom pa dang 'bras bu 'thob pa dang 'dod chags dang bral ba mi srid pas pho mo'i dbang po gang rung zhig ma tshang na mthong lam mi skye ba'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir pho mo'i dbang po gang rung zhig bsnan te dbang po bcu bzhi dang nges par ldan par 'gyur ro zhe na/ 'di'i lan la kha cig na re/ bcu bzhir mi 'gyur te/ sngar pho mo'i dbang po gang rung zhig ldan pa'i tshe sdom pa blangs te/ sdom pa dang ldan pa des phyis lam bsgoms te 'bras bu thob pa'i rjes la pho mo'i dbang po nyams te mtshan gnyis pa la sogs par gyur na/ mtshan gnyis byung bas so so thar pa'i sdom pa gtong gi 'bras bu thob pa ni mi gtong bas 'bras bu thob pa la mtshan gnyis pa la sogs pa'ang srid pa'i phyir ro/ /

Those who possess the faculty producing complete knowledge (ājñāsyāmīndriya) are desire-realm beings on the path of seeing. They definitely possess thirteen: (1) itself, (2) the mental faculty, (3) life force, (4) body, (5) mental satisfaction, (6) pleasure, (7) pain, (8) equanimity, and (9–13) the five such as faith. Objection: Only those beings on the path of seeing who are born in the desire realm possess the faculty producing complete knowledge, because the Abhidharmakośa mentions, “The path of seeing does not exist in higher realms because they [i.e., beings of higher realms] are not disgusted [with saṃsāra] and scripture declares that they commence here but finish there” (6:55b–d). But then they must possess either a male or a female faculty, because if either a male or a female faculty is missing, the path of seeing does not arise, since it is impossible for those who do not possess a male or a female faculty or [for one] whose organ has degenerated [107] to obtain vows or their result, freedom from attachment. Therefore they definitely possess fourteen faculties through adding either the male or the female faculty. Some say in response: They don’t possess fourteen because they took vows when they previously possessed either a male or a female faculty, and while possessing vows they meditated on the path and subsequently obtained that result. Later, when the male or female faculty degenerated or two organs and so on arose, pratimokṣa vows were relinquished since two organs arose. But since the obtainment of the result was not relinquished, it is possible that even those with two organs and so on can obtain that result.

de'i phyir thog mar mthong lam ma thob pa 'thob pa'i rten du pho mo'i dbang po gang rung zhig dgos kyi thob zin gnas pa'i rten du ni mi dgos te/ mthong lam thob nas pho mo'i mtshan ma tshang yang mthong lam mi gtong ba'i phyir dang*/ thog mar mthong lam 'thob pa'i dus na pho mo gang rung gi mtshan ma tshang bar yod kyang phyis mtshan ma tshang ba srid pa'i phyir ro/ / yang na 'dod khams pa nges 'byed cha mthun goms par byas pa zhig rim gyis 'chi ba na dbang po gzugs can rnams rim gyis 'gag pas 'chi kar pho mo'i dbang po 'gags ma thag mthong lam skye ba srid pas de'i phyir dbang po bcu gsum dang ni nges par ldan gyi pho mo'i dbang po ni 'chi kar pho mo'i dbang po dang mi ldan pa la mthong lam skyes pas kun shes byed pa'i dbang po dang ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes zer ro/ / gzhan dag na re de ni mi rigs te/ mnyam par ma bzhag par mthong lam mi skye zhing*/ mnyam gzhag dge ba sbyor byung la gnas bzhin du 'chi ba mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ / des na 'dir ni gang zag spyi'i dbang du byas nas nges par ldan pa'i tshul bshad pa yin gyi pho mo gcig kho na'i nges par ldan tshul bshad pa ma yin pas pho la brtsis na mo dbang dang mi ldan la/ mo la brtsis na pho dbang dang mi ldan pas mtha' gcig tu ma nges pas de gnyis nges ldan du ma brtsis so{ de gnyis gang yang min pa'i de gnyis gang rung mi srid do} zhes zer ba nyid rigs so/ / tshor ba'i dbang po bzhi ni dus gcig la mngon gyur mi srid kyang thob pa dang ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag las gzhan mi ldan pa ni snga ma bzhin no/{ de yang yid mi bde dang 'dod chags dang bral na mi ldan la mig sogs nyams pa la'ang mi ldan pa sogs so/ /} de dag gis ni dbang po gang zhig ldan pa de la gzhan nges par ldan pa'i tshul bshad pa yin no/ / da ni{ srid ldan la} nang na nyung ba dag dang ldan na du dang ldan zhe na/

Therefore, those who have not already obtained the path of seeing require either a male or female faculty as the basis for that obtainment, but that is not required for beings who maintain obtainment, because those who have already obtained the path of seeing but who lack a male or female organ do not relinquish the path of seeing, and it is possible that when they first obtain the path of seeing, they have either a male or female organ but later they may lack such an organ. Again, if desire-realm beings who have cultivated factors conducive to penetrative insight die in stages, then their physical faculties cease in stages, and they definitely possess thirteen faculties since it is possible that the path of seeing arises at the time of death, just before the male or female faculty ceases. Those who possessed male or female faculties but who do not possess them at the time of death possess the faculty of complete knowledge, since the path of seeing arises. Others say: That is illogical because the path of seeing does not arise without equipoise, and death is impossible while abiding in equipoise derived from virtuous preparation. Here the system by which one definitely comes to possess the faculties is explained from the perspective of the general person, but how one definitely comes to possess male or female faculties themselves has not been explained. As such, if the male faculty is counted then the female faculty is not possessed, or if the female faculty is counted then the male faculty is not possessed. Therefore it is logical that, since there is no absolute certainty, neither is counted as definitely possessed. {If it is neither, it is impossible it is either.} Though it is impossible that the four faculties of feeling manifest at the same time, their obtainment may be possessed. And the nonpossession of faculties other than those accords with the previous explanation. {Further, if one is free of mental dissatisfaction and attachment, they are not possessed; and if the eyes and so on degenerate, they are not possessed; and so on.} Therefore these instances explain how some faculties are definitely possessed when other faculties are possessed. Question: Now, from among those faculties {that may be} possessed, what is the minimum number that can be possessed?
dge med nang na nyung ldan pa/ / lus tshor srog yid brgyad dang ldan/ / gzugs med byis pa'ang de bzhin te/ / btang snyoms srog yid dge rnams dang / / 20

Those lacking virtue possess a minimum of eight: the body, feelings, life force, and mental faculty. So too childlike beings of the formless realm: equanimity, life force, mental faculty, and virtuous faculties. (2:20)

dge ba'i rtsa ba med pa ni 'dod pa pa kho na ste/ de la ni nang na nyung ba dang ldan pa ni lus dang{ 'chi kha lta bu na de la chags bral mi srid pas} tshor ba lnga dang srog dang yid kyi dbang po ste brgyad dang ldan gyi de dag las gzhan ni yod par nges pa med la/ de dag gi thob pa ni nges par yod pa'i phyir ro/ / ji ltar dge ba med pa nang na nyung ba dbang po'i grangs brgyad dang ldan pa ltar gzugs med pa'i byis pa so so'i skye bo'ang de bzhin du grangs brgyad dang ldan te gang zhe na/ btang snyoms dang srog dang yid dang dad pa la sogs pa'i dbang po dge ba lnga po rnams dang ldan no/ / de dag pas nyung ba dang ldan pa'i gang zag ni mi srid do/ /

Those lacking the root of virtue (niḥśubha) are desire-realm beings alone. From among them, those who possess the minimum possess eight: the faculties of body, the five feelings (vid), life force, and the mental faculty (manas). Though there is no certainty that they possess other faculties, [108] it is certain they obtain these. Just as those without virtue possess a minimum of eight faculties, so too ordinary childlike beings (bāla) of the formless realm possess eight. Question: What are they? Reply: They possess equanimity, life force, the mental faculty, and five virtuous faculties such as faith. A person possessing fewer is impossible.
mang por ldan la bcu dgu ste/ / dri ma med rnams ma gtogs so/ / mtshan gnyis 'phags pa chags bcas te/ / mtshan gcig dri med gnyis ma gtogs/ / 21
A maximum of nineteen are possessed, except the stainless faculties by those with both organs. Or āryas with attachment, except for one organ and two stainless faculties. (2:21)

yang dbang po nang na mang por ldan pa la bcu dgu dang ldan pa{ 'i byis pa} srid de/ gang zhe na dri ma med pa'i dbang po gsum po rnams ma gtogs pa rnams so/ / de yang 'dod pa pa'i gang zag dbang po rnams tshang zhing mtshan gnyis pa la yin no/ / de ni so so'i skye bo la yin gyi der ma zad gzhan yang 'phags pa chags bcas{ rgyun zhugs lan cig phyir 'ong yang dbang po bcu dgu dang ldan pa srid pa yin} te/ rgyun zhugs dang lan cig phyir 'ong 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang ma bral ba'ang grangs bcu dgu dang ldan pa srid de/ gang zhe na

Again, it is possible that from among those faculties a maximum of nineteen are possessed {by childlike beings}. Question: What are they? Reply: They are those faculties except for the three stainless faculties that are possessed by desire-realm beings with complete faculties and both organs (dviliṅga). [Nineteen are possessed] not only by ordinary beings but also by āryas with attachment (rāga), because it is possible that stream enterers and once returners not free from attachment to the desire realm possess nineteen. Question: What are they?

{ 'phags pa la mtshan gnyis pa mi srid cing chags bral la yid mi bde mi ldan la 'phags pa chags bcas slob par nges pas} pho mo'i mtshan gang yang rung ba gcig ma gtogs pa dang*/ kun shes par byed pa dang ldan pa{ 'i rgyun zhugs} la{ pho mo gang rung gcig} dri ma med pa'i dbang po phyi ma gnyis ma gtogs pa rnams dang ldan la/ kun shes pa dang ldan pa{ 'i phyir 'ong} la dri ma med pa'i dbang po snga phyi gnyis{ dang pho mo gang rung gcig} ma gtogs pa rnams dang ldan pa'i phyir/ / 'phags pa la mtshan gnyis pa mi srid pa'i phyir mtshan gcig ma gtogs zhes bya ba dang*/ 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba'i 'phags pa rnams ni yid mi bde mi ldan pa'i phyir chags bcos smros pa yin no/ / de dag gis ni dbang po rnams bshad zin to/ /

Reply: They possess all faculties except for one male or female organ (liṅga) and two stainless faculties, {since it is impossible that āryas have two organs, those freed from attachment do not possess mental dissatisfaction, and āryas with attachment are definitely learners}. {A stream enterer with either a male or female organ} possesses the faculty producing complete knowledge. {A once returner} who has complete knowledge [possesses all faculties] except both the former and latter stainless faculties {and one male or female organ}. “Except for one organ” (2:21d) is stated because it is impossible that āryas have two organs. “With attachment” (2:21c) is mentioned because āryas free from attachment to sense objects do not possess mental dissatisfaction. This completes the explanation of faculties.
7. The Generation of Conditioned Phenomena
da ni 'dus byas kyi skye tshul rgyas par bshad pa
ELABORATION OF HOW CONDITIONED PHENOMENA ARISE
['di] la don dngos dang*/ zhar la rgyu dang rkyen 'bras bu dang bcas pa bshad pa gnyis kyi
This has two headings: actual meaning and in addition, the explanation of cause, condition, and result.
dang po 'chad pa na
ACTUAL MEANING
This has two: synopsis and the real meaning.
'dir spyi'i don ni
Synopsis

shes bya thams cad gzhi lngas bsdus pa yin te/ gzugs dang*/ sems dang*/ sems las byung ba dang*/ mi ldan pa'i 'du byed dang 'dus ma byas so/ / de la bye brag tu smra ba ni de thams cad rdzas su yod par 'dod de/ thams cad yod par smra ba yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de la gzugs ni gzugs kyi phung po ste rdul phra rab dang rags pa dang*/ de gnyis ka ma yin pa'o/ /

All objects of knowledge are subsumed within the four or five basic categories: (1) form, (2) mind, (3) mental factors, (4) nonassociated formative factors, (5) unconditioned states. Vaibhāṣikas who assert that all five substantially exist are Sarvāstivādins. [The basic category of] (1) form is the form aggregate consisting of subtle particles, coarse form, and that which is neither.
rdul phra rab rnams ni
SUBTLE PARTICLES

cha shas med pa'i phyir phan tshun reg pa ni med kyi gcig la du mas bskor ba'i bar dang bcas pa yin te/ rig na ni phyogs thams cad kyis reg na phan tshun 'dren par 'gyur la/ phyogs res reg na cha bcas su thal ba'i phyir ro zhes 'dod de/ phyi rol don grub las/ rdul phran phyogs cha tha dad phyir/ / med ces smra gang de ma 'brel/ / 'ga' yis khyad par dang bcas pa'o/ / rdul la phyogs kyi sgrar bstan bya/ / de phyir phyogs cha'i khyad par gyis/ / de ni mang pos yongs bskor bar/ / brjod par zad kyi rdul de ni/ / cha shas bcas pa'i bdag nyid min/ / zhes bya ba dang*/ phan tshun bdag nyid ma reg par/ / cha shas med par rnam gnas te/ / de phyir sa yi dkyil 'khor sogs/ / bsags pa las ni byung ba yin/ / zhes gsungs pa bzhin no/ /

[Sarvāstivādins] assert that because subtle particles do not make contact with each other they have no spatial parts, but many [subtle particles] can surround a single [subtle particle]. However, if they do make contact they would make contact on all sides, and in consequence [109] they would merge. Alternately if they make contact at a single spatial location, in consequence they would have spatial parts. Proof of External Objects states: Some say atoms do not make contact nor interact because their spatial dimensions would be differentiated. Some apply the term spatial location to particles that are differentiated. Therefore, due to their difference in spatial location, it is said that many can surround [one.] But such particles themselves are not things that possess parts.[459] And: Due to not making mutual contact entitites abide without their parts being differentiated. In turn the earth maṇḍala and so on arise from the accumulation [of such entities].[460]

gal te bsags par gnas pa 'di dag gis rdul phra rab rnams ma reg na zhig par 'gyur ro zhe na/ mi 'gyur te/ rlung gis bzung ba'i phyir dang*/ rdzas kyi mthus kyang 'brel par byed pa'i phyir te/ de nyid las/ phan tshun du ni phan 'dogs pa'i/ / bye brag gis na brgyus pa bzhin/ / rdo rje la sogs rdul phran rnams/ / de dag chad par mi 'gyur te/ / ji ltar sngags kyi mthu yis ni/ / 'dre sbrul la sogs 'dzin pa bzhin/ / rdzas kyi mthu yis phan tshun du/ / 'dzin pa lu gu rgyud bzhin du/ / zhes gsungs pa yin no/ /

Objection: If entities arise due to the accumulation of particles, and those particles do not contact each other, those entities would disintegrate. Reply: That does not occur because the subtle particles are sustained by the wind element, and they also interact by the power of substance.[461] Proof of External Objects declares: The atoms of a diamond and so on are like a thread [whose components] specifically benefit each other; they do not separate. Just as spirits or snakes and so on are restrained by the force of mantra, so lambs in a line are restrained as one by the power of substance.[462]

'o na tsha reg gis grang reg la gnod pa byed pa dang*/ snang bas mun pa la gnod pa dang*/ mun pas gzugs can la sgrib pa dang*/ snang bas gsal byed du'ang mi 'gyur te/ de dag phan tshun phrad pa med pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ ma yin te tsha reg dang snang ba'i rdul la sogs pa nye bar gnas pa na grang reg dang mun pa la sogs pa rdul gyi 'gros 'gag pas gnod pa dang sgrib pa la sogs par brjod kyi cha gzhan phrad pas ni ma yin te/ de nyid las/ gang zhig dang ni nye ba las/ / 'gros ldan gang gi 'gros 'gag pa/ / des de'i sgrib par rab tu bshad/ / cha shas gzhan gyis ma yin no/ / zhes gsungs pa yin no/ / gal te rdul phran phrad pa med na rnga la sogs pa la dbyug gu bsnun pa la sogs pa las sgra mi 'byung bar 'gyur ro zhe na/ ma phrad kyang de dag shin tu nye ba dang rlung 'dus pa las sgra 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / kha cig rdul phra rab zlum po cha shas med pa zhes zer ba de ni ma yin te/ rdul phra rab la dbyibs med pa'i phyir te/ gnyis gzung 'gyur de rdul la med ces 'chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / rdul phra rab kyi tshad dang lhan cig tu gnas pa'i tshul ni 'og tu ston par 'gyur ro/ /

Objection: But then hot sensation would not harm cold sensation, light would not harm darkness, darkness would not obscure physical states, and light would not illuminate, because they would not mutually contact each other. Reply: That is not so, because if particles of heat, light, and so on abide near cold, darkness, and so on, they are said to harm or impair them since they stop the approach of those particles. But that is not through making contact because Proof of External Objects remarks: That which stops the progression of anything that approaches is said to obstruct [the other] but not by [contacting] the other part.[463] Objection: If there were no contact between particles, then sound would not occur from, say, striking a drum with a stick. Reply: Though there is no contact, sound is produced from their near approach and the compression of wind. Some say: Subtle particles are spherical and partless. Reply: That is not so. Subtle particles have no shape because it has been explained that “[A single form] would be apprehended by both [sense faculties]. [Shape] does not exist as a particle.” (4:3c) The dimensions of subtle particles and their mode of simultaneous abidance is taught below.
COARSE FORM

rags pa ni dbang po lnga dang don lnga yin te/ dbang po lnga ni mig gi dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni mig gi 'bras bu la go snyod nag po'i me tog bzhin du gnas te/ de dag so so sil bur gnas kyang kha dog dang bas bkab pas na so sor 'gyes par mi 'gyur ro/ / kha cig na re gong bu bzhin du ril ril por bla 'og tu gnas kyang shel bzhin du dang bas dbus dang mtha' na gnas pa rnams phan tshun mi sgrib bo zhes zer ro/ / rna ba'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni rna 'brug ces bya ba gro ga'i 'dzer bu lta bu'i nang na gnas so/ / sna'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni zangs kyi mo khab lta bu ste mtshul pa'i nang sna'i rgyud na gnas te/ dbang po dang po gsum po de dag ni phreng ba bzhin du kor kor por gnas so/ / lce'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni zla ba bkam pa lta bu ste/ lce'i dbus na skra'i rtse mo'i khyon tsam zhig lce'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab dag gis ma khebs par gnas so/ / lus kyi dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni lus bzhin du gnas so/ / lus kyi dbang po'i bye brag mo'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni rnga'i sbubs lta bu yin no/ / pho'i dbang po'i rdul phra rab rnams ni mthe bong lta bu yin no zhes bstan bcos las gsungs pa'i phyir dang*/ 'grel pa las/ dbang po'i rdul phra rab bam yul gyi rdul phra rab gcig gis rnam shes skyed pa ni med de/ rnam par shes pa'i tshogs lnga po dag gi rten dang dmigs pa ni bsags pa yin pa'i phyir ro zhes bya ba dang*/ dbu ma'i rgyan las/ rnam shes lnga'i khams rnams ni/ / bsags la dmigs pa'i rnam pa yin/ / zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ /

Coarse form consists of the five sense faculties and the five objects. The five sense faculties are, for instance, the molecular structures (paramāṇu) of the eye sense faculty that exist in the resultant eye, like black cumin flowers, which are partially separated but not fully so, and imbued with translucent color. Some say: Though they exist in a sphere above and below like a round mass, those abiding in the center or extremes do not mutually obscure each other, [110] since they are translucent like glass. The treatise[464] mentions that the molecular structures (paramāṇu) of the ear sense faculty exist internally, shaped like the protrusions in birch bark known as “ear thunder.” Those of the nose sense faculty exist in rows in the inner nostril, like fine copper needles. Moreover, those of the first three sense faculties exist coiled like rosaries. The molecular structures (paramāṇu) of the tongue sense faculty are like a full moon, where the subtle particles of tongue sense faculty exist in the center of the tongue, each covering an area less than the tip of a hair. Those of the body sense faculty are like the body itself. Those of the female faculty, which constitute a subset of the body sense faculty, are shaped like cymbals. Those of the male faculty are shaped like the thumb.[465] The Autocommentary states: One subtle particle of an object or one subtle particle of a sense faculty does not generate consciousness, for it is the accumulation [of such particles] that are the supportive basis or the focal objects of the fivefold collection of sense consciousness.[466] The Ornament of Madhyamaka states: [Objective] elements of the five sense consciousnesses are accumulations and aspects of focal objects.[467]
THAT WHICH IS NEITHER

rdul phra rab dang rags pa gnyis ka ma yin pa ni rig byed ma yin pa'i gzugs so/ / sems kyi gzhi ni rnam par shes pa'i tshogs drug ste/ de dag gis yul 'dzin pa ni yul gyi rnam pa ma shar bzhin tu 'dzin pa yin gyi rnam pa dang bcas pa ni ma yin te/ snang ba 'di don ma yin na mi snang ba'i don yod pa la sgrub byed med pa'i phyir dang*/ rags snang shes pa yin na rags pa rdul phran bsags pa ma yin par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / rnam par shes pa rnams kyang yul gzhan yongs su gcod pa yin phyi rang nyid gcod pa ni ma yin te/ bdag nyid la bcad bya gcod byed gnyis med pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar yang phyi rol don grub las/ gang gi tshe na rnam shes don/ / yongs gcod tsam du 'dod de'i tshe/ / shes pas ji ltar rang gi yul/ / rig par 'gyur zhes smras ma 'brel/ / rnam shes de yi byed po min/ / dam pa'i don du bya ba'ang min/ / rig pa tsam du zad mod kyi/ / byed pa nyid du sgro btags gsungs/ / zhes 'byung ba ltar ro/ / sems las byung ba dang*/ mi ldan pa'i 'du byed kyi gzhi ni 'og tu ston par 'gyur la/ 'dus ma byas ni bshad zin to/ / mdo sde pa rnams ni rdul phra rab rnams bar med par gnas pa la reg par 'du shes pa yin gyi reg pa ni ma yin te/ cha bcas su thal ba'i phyir ro/ / bar dang bcas na'ang bar der rdul gzhan 'jug pa la sus gegs byed de/ nyin mo snang ba dang mtshan mo mun pa'i rdul ni de dag gi bar du gnas par rigs pa'i phyir dang*/ mi gnas na de dag snang byed dang sgrib byed du ma grub par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir 'grel pa las kyang*/ btsun pa na re reg pa ni med kyi 'dab chags pa la reg go snyam du 'du shes par zad do zhes zer te/ btsun pa'i lugs 'dod par bya'o/ / de lta ma yin na ni rdul phra rab bar dang bcas pa rnams kyi bar stod pa dag tu 'gro ba la su zhig 'gog na 'di ltar thogs pa dang bcas pa dag tu 'dod ces bshad do/ /

That which is neither a subtle particle nor coarse form is nonindicative form. The basic category of (2) mind consists of the sixfold collection of consciousness. If these [consciousnesses] apprehend their objects without — and not with — the aspects of their objects appearing, and if [subtle] appearance is not their object, there is no proof that [subtle] objects that don’t appear, exist. But if they are aware of coarse appearance then it follows that such coarse [appearance] is not an accumulation of atoms. Also such consciousnesses determine objects other [than themselves], and they do not determine [or ascertain] themselves because [consciousness] itself is not both the object determined and the determining agent. Thus Proof of External Objects mentions: When consciousness is asserted to be something that merely determines its object, then the question arises, “How does consciousness cognize its object?” It is not related [to its object], consciousness is not its agent, and it does not even engage objects that are pure. Indeed it consists of mere cognition, and in terms of function, it is said to superimpose [reality].[468] The basic categories of (3) mental factors and (4) nonassociated formative factors will be explained below. (5) Unconditioned phenomena have been explained already. Sautrāntikas assert that subtle particles that abide without interstice are discerned to make contact but they do not make contact, because it would then follow they possess parts. If an interstice existed, then particles of illumination in the day and darkness at night would logically exist in that interstice and impede the entry of other particles; if they didn’t exist then it would follow that such particles would not illuminate or obscure. [111] Therefore the Autocommentary explains: The Bhadanta says they do not make contact and rejects any discernment that holds they make mutual contact. You should accept this system of the Bhadanta. If it were not true [and they possessed interstice], who could refute that subtle particles would enter the empty interstices? Thus accept they are obstructed.[469]

des na bar med cing ma reg pa zhes bya bar 'gyur ro/ / rags snang ni shes pa'i bdag nyid yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rdul phra rab 'dus pa zhes bya ba'ang rdul du ma bar med par gnas pa la brjod pa'i phyir rags pa ni rdzas su med do/ / shes pa rnam pa dang bcas pa ma yin na shes pa gcig gis don thams cad rig par thal ba'i phyir don gyi rnam par skye pa la don rig pa zhes brjod de/ dbu ma'i rgyan las/ shes pa rnam bcas phyogs la ni/ / dngos su de gnyis tha dad kyang*/ / de dang gzugs brnyan 'dra bas na/ / gdags pa tsam gyis tshor bar rang*/ / zhes bshad do/ /

Therefore they say subtle particles exist without interstice and do not make contact. Coarse objects are not substantially existent (dravyasat) because coarse appearance is [due to] the state of the mind itself and because “the assembly of subtle particles” is said to be many particles abiding without interstice. If consciousness were not aspected [that is, did not possess an aspect] it would follow that one consciousness would cognize all objects. Therefore cognizing an object is called “arising in the aspect of the object,” since the Autocommentary on the Ornament of Madhyamaka states: For aspected consciousness,[470] those two are in direct opposition. However, since it is like a reflection, it is experienced through mere imputation.[471]

de bzhin du shes pa rnams kyang rang nyid rang gis rig pa yin te/ rang ma rig na gzhan rig byed du ma grub par 'gyur te/ rang nyid ma grub pa'i phyir dang*/ gzhan gyis dmigs na'ang thug med du thal ba'i phyir te/ rnam nges las/ dmigs pa mngon sum ma yin na/ / don mthong rag tu 'grub mi 'gyur/ / zhes bshad pa yin no/ / mi ldan pa'i 'du byed ni gzugs la sogs pa gsum las gzhan du med la/ 'dus ma byas kyang rdzas su med do zhes bya bar 'dod do/ / rnal 'byor spyod pa pa rnams ni don du snang ba ni shes pa la dngos su gsal ba'i phyir dang*/ mi snang ba'i rdul phran la sgrub byed med pa dang*/ bar dang bcas na'ang rags pa gcig tu mi snang ba dang*/ bar med na'ang rdul phra rab rnams phan tshun reg par 'gyur la/ de lta na'ang phyogs thams cad kyis reg na rdul rnams 'dres pa dang*/ phyogs res reg na cha bcas su thal ba'i phyir rdul cha med ni rdzas su med do/ / rags pa'ang don du med de/ rdul phra rab bsags pa yin pa'i phyir dang*/ cha dang bcas pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir bag chags kyi stobs kyis rnam par shes pa nyid gzung 'dzin gnyis su snang ba yin te/ ji skad du nyi shu pa las/ rang gi sa bon gang las su/ / rnam rig snang ba gang byung ba/ / de dang de yi skye mched ni/ / rnam pa gnyis su thub pas gsungs/ / zhes 'byung ba lta bu'o/ /

So too, consciousness also cognizes itself. If it did not cognize itself, it would not cognize others, since consciousness itself would not be established. And if another consciousness had to focus on it to establish it, there would be the fallacy of an infinite regress. Thus Ascertainment of Valid Cognition declares: If [any consciousness] focusing [on suchness] is not [established by self-] perception, [then consciousness] that sees its object would not be perfectly established.[472] They assert that nonassociated formative factors do not exist as something other than the three basic categories of form and so on, and unconditioned states are not substantially existent. Yogācāras assert that appearance as an object directly manifests for consciousness and that there is no proof for atoms that do not appear [to consciousness]. If there were an interstice between particles, then gross objects would not appear as single objects. If there were no interstices, then subtle particles would mutually contact each other, and if that were so, all sides would contact and particles would merge. Alternately, if each side contacted other particles, it would follow that particles would have parts. Therefore partless particles are not substantially existent. Also they assert that gross objects do not exist as objects because they would then be the accumulation of subtle particles, and they would then possess parts. As such, consciousness appears as both the object and the subject due to the power of imprints. Twenty Verses says: Any appearance occurring to cognition related to karma and any of its seeds is stated by the Sage to have two aspects, that and its base.[473]

de bas na yang dag par na gzung 'dzin gnyis med pa'i rang gsal ba ni rdzas su yod de/ gsal bar nyams su myong la gnyis la gnod pa yod pa'i phyir te/ rnam par nges pa las/ gzung dang 'dzin pa med pa'i phyir/ / de ni de ltar rang nyid gsal/ / zhes gsungs pa lta bu'o/ / mi ldan pa'i 'du byed rnams ni gnas skabs la btags pa yin pas gzugs dang mtshungs ldan rnams las de nyid dang gzhan du brjod du med par 'dod de/ phung po lnga pa las/ sems dang ldan pa ma yin pa'i 'du byed rnams gang zhe na/ gang dag gzugs dang sems dang sems las byung ba'i gnas skabs la gdags pa ste/ de nyid dang gzhan du mi gdags so zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir sems dang sems las byung ba'i gzhi rdzas su yod kyi gzhan ni ma yin no zhes bya bar 'dod do/ /

Therefore, the perfect self-clarity of the nonduality of subject and object is substantially existent because duality is harmed through experiencing clarity. Ascertainment of Valid Cognition notes: It is self-clarified in that way because the object and subject do not exist.[474] Yogācāras assert that nonassociated formative factors are those states distinct from form and concomitant [or associated] states, since they are imputed in that way according to [112] circumstances and not given another name. Treatise on the Five Aggregates states: What formative factors do not possess mind? Those designated in the context of form, mind, and mental factors, and they are not designated as states other than those.[475] Therefore the basic categories of minds and mental factors are substantially existent, and the others are not.

How physical states arise
'dod na dbang po med pa dang / / sgra med phra rab rdul rdzas brgyad/ / lus dbang ldan la rdzas dgu'o/ / dbang po gzhan ldan rdzas bcu'o/ / 22

The eight substantial particles that arise in the desire realm are not associated with the sense faculties nor with sound. Those that possess the body sense faculty possess nine substances. Those that possess the other faculties possess ten substances. (2:22)
{ de la rdzas kyi rdul phran ni shar la sogs pa'i cha med pa'o/ / bsags pa'i rdul phran ni de las phra ba'i 'dus pa gzhan du med pa'o/ /}
{The substantial particle has no parts such as an eastern part, and regarding the aggregated atom there is no composite matter smaller than it.}

'dod pa'i khams na lus sogs kyi dbang po med pa dang sgra med pa'i bsags pa'i rdul phra rab nyi zer gyi rdul chung ngu lta bu la bsags pa ma yin pa'i rdul cha shas med pa'i rdzas 'byung ba bzhi dang gzugs dri ro reg bya ste brgyad nges par lhan cig skye'o/ / bsags pa'i rdul smos pa ni rdus phra rab cha med pa ni gcig pur gnas pa'i phyir rdzas gzhan 'dus pa med do snyam du bsam pa'o/ / gal te snga ba la sogs pa dang ldan pa la tsha ba la sogs pa ma dmigs pa'i phyir nges par lhan cig skye ba ma yin no zhe na/

The eight substantial partless particles (dravya) — (1–4) the four primary elements, (5) form, (6) smell, (7) taste, and (8) tactility — like minute particles of light, are not an aggregation. They are aggregating particles (paramāṇu) that definitely arise simultaneously in the desire realm and that are not associated with the sense faculties such as the body nor with sound. I think that the term “aggregating particles” refers to partless subtle particles that are not composed of other particles because they abide as discrete entities.[476] Objection: It is uncertain that they arise simultaneously, for heat and so on is not observed for those that possess solidity and so forth.

bye brag tu smra ba na re dper na khab dang sdong bu'i tshogs la reg pa dang*/ phye dang lan tsha'i ro ltar dmigs ma dmigs ni shas che chung yin gyi thams cad la'ang tshang bar yod de/ 'dzin pa dang sdud pa dang smin pa dang g.yo ba'i byed pa dang ldan pa'i phyir dang*/ rkyen dang phrad na lcags la sogs pa'i sra ba'ang gsher ba la sogs par mngon sum du snang ba'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ / bye bshad las kyang*/ phan tshun tha dad du mi 'jug par cis mngon zhe na/ las las mngon te zhes pa dang*/ de dag gi rang gi ngo bo mi dmigs kyang rdo la sogs pa la yod par las las ji ltar rjes su dpog ce na/ 'di ltar rdo la sogs pa la 'dus pa dang skam pa g.yo ba rnams yod pa las chu dang me dang rlung rnams sa'i khams dang lhan cig 'jug par mngon no/ / chu la yang shing 'degs pa dang pad ma'i 'dab ma rgyas pa dang chu g.yo ba rnams yod pa las sa dang me dang rlung rnams chu'i khams dang lhan cig 'jug par mngon no/ / me la'ang me lce 'degs pa dang 'dus pa dang g.yo ba rnams yod pa las sa dang chu dang rlung rnams me dang lhan cig 'jug par mngon no/ / rlung la'ang 'degs pa dang mi 'gyes pa dang gos la sogs pa skam par byed pa yod pa las sa dang chu dang me rnams rlung gi khams dang lhan gcig 'jug par mngon no zhes bshad do/ / las dang ngo bo'i khyad par yang de nyid las/ rang gi ngo bo grub tsam nyid na dngos po gzhan thams cad la mi ltos par gnas pa ni ngo bo yin la/ bya ba la ltos nas gzhag dgos pa ni las yin te/ 'byung bzhi'i las rten 'dzin pa dang sdud pa dang smin pa dang g.yo ba rnams ni gzung bya dang bsdu bya dang smin bya dang 'phel{ ba'am g.yo} bya'i dngos po gzhan la ltos nas 'jog pa'i phyir ro zhes bshad do/

Vaibhāṣikas say: For example, for one to observe whether one is touching a collection of needles or sticks, or is tasting sand or salt, depends on the quantity of each. Therefore each exists because it possesses the attributes of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving, and if the conditions arise, iron and so on will appear to perception as solid or as liquid and so forth. The Great Treatise on Differentiation also states: How do they manifest when they do not appear to be mutually distinct? They manifest from karma. How is their existence in stones and so on inferred from karma when their individual natures are not observed? Water, fire, and wind are inferred from the existence of compaction, dryness, and movement in stones and so on, which simultaneously manifest with the element of earth. Earth, fire, and wind are inferred from the existence of water that supports wood, the growth of lotus petals, and the movement of water and so on, which simultaneously manifest with the element of water. In terms of fire, earth, water, and wind are inferred from the existence of the support, the contraction and movement of tongues of flame, which simultaneously manifest with the element of fire. Earth, water, and fire are inferred from the existence of the support, nondispersal, and the drying of clothes and so on, which simultaneously manifest with the element of wind.[477] [113] Also, regarding the difference between nature and function, the Great Treatise on Differentiation declares: Its nature is its mere identity, which endures without reference to any other thing. Its function is necessarily posited in reliance on its activity because the functions of the four primary elements, such as supporting, condensing, maturing, and moving, are posited in reliance on other things that are supported, condensed, matured, and increased {or moved}.[478]
{ yang na bye brag tu smra ba ltar na ngo bo ni dus gsum pa dang las ni da lta bas bsdus pa kho na yin no zhes slob dpon gang spel 'chad do/ /}
{Again, according to Vaibhāṣikas: Its nature is the three times, and its function is subsumed by the present alone. This is explained by Master Pūrṇavardhana.[479]}

mdo sde pa na re byed pa'i las thams cad nges par lhan cig tu dmigs pas khyab pa med pa'i phyir dang*/ 'ga' zhig tu srid kyang des 'byung bzhi lhan cig pa srid par dpag par nus kyi khyab par ni ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rkyen dang phrad na mngon sum du 'gyur ba ni de dang der gsar du skyes pa yin pa'i phyir nges par lhan cig tu skye ba ni ma yin gyi 'on kyang rang gi ngo bor ni med cing sa bon gyi sgo nas thams cad yod la/ gang la gang dmigs pa de mngon gyur gyi sgo nas kyang yod de/ bcom ldan 'das kyis shing gi phung po 'di la khams rnam pa sna tshogs yod do/ / zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes zer ro/ / rnal 'byor spyod pa pa rnams ni kun las btus las 'dus pa gang la 'byung ba gang dmigs pa de ni de na yod do/ / zhes brjod par bya'o/ / 'byung ba gcig las gyur pa'i 'dus pa'ang yod/ / 'byung ba gnyis las gyur pa'ang yod pa nas 'byung ba thams cad las gyur pa'ang yod do/ / rgyur byas pa'i gzugs la'ang rgyur byas pa'i gzugs gang 'dus pa gang la dmigs pa de ni de na yod pa zhes rig par bya'o zhes 'byung bas 'byung ba gcig las gyur pa'i gzugs bong ba skam po lta bu dang*/ gnyis las gyur pa de nyid gsher ba dang*/ gsum las gyur pa de nyid dro ba dang*/ bzhi las gyur pa de nyid g.yo ba lta bu'o/ / de bzhin du 'bras bu'i gzugs kyang gzugs gcig pu dang ldan pa 'od dang*/ gnyis dang ldan pa sgra dang dri dang ldan pa'i rlung dang*/ gsum dang ldan pa gzugs dang dri dang reg bya yang ba dang ldan pa'i du ba dang*/ bzhi dang ldan pa a ka ru'i gong bu dang*/ lnga dang ldan pa de nyid sgra dang bcas pa lta bu'o zhes 'dod do/ /

Sautrāntikas say: There is no logical pervasion that all their functions are certain to be observed simultaneously; there is no pervasion that one can ascertain four primary elements simultaneously, though it is possible in some circumstances; and when the conditions assemble, they manifest and newly arise here and there. Therefore, though they are not certain to be simultaneous, all exist due to their seed not their nature, for whatever is observed in relation to anything else exists through becoming manifest. The Bhagavan has said: Various elements exist in the aggregate of wood.[480] Yogācāras say: The Compendium of Abhidharma records: Any primary element observed in any composite state exists within it.[481] A composite derived from one primary element exists, a composite from two primary elements exists, and a composite from all primary elements exists. Also, in terms of derivative form, one should recognize that when one observes any composite derivative form, [the primary elements] exist there. There is form derived from one primary element, such as a dry soil, and form derived from two primary elements, such as wet soil, and form derived from three primary elements, such as warm soil, and form derived from four primary elements, such as moving soil. So too in terms of resultant form, there is light that possesses form alone; that which possesses two, such as wind that possesses sound and smell; that which possesses three, such as smoke that possesses form, smell, and light tangible sensation; that which possesses four, such as a lump of aguru resin;[482] and that possessing five, such as just that [lump of agura resin] which possesses sound.

'o na mdo las gzugs gang yin pa ci yang rung ste/ de dag thams cad 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag dang 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag rgyur byas pa'o zhes gsungs pa ji lta bu zhe na/ de ni bzhi ga tshang ba srid pa la dgongs nas gsungs pa yin no zhes 'dod do/ / de la bye brag tu smra ba'i rdzas brgyad lhan cig tu skye ba la skye mched la rdzas su 'dod na mangs par smras te/ 'byung ba bzhi ni reg bya'i skye mched du 'dus pa'i phyir ro/ / rdzas la rdzas su 'dod na ni 'di nyungs par smras pa yin te/ der ni dbyibs dang yang ba la sogs pa gzhan yang yod pa'i phyir ro/ / 'byung ba ni rdzas kho na la rdzas su gzung la gzhan ni skye mched la rdzas su gzung ngo zhes bya ba'ang ma yin te/ 'bras bu'i gzugs phal cher 'byung ba bzhi tshan la rten pa'i phyir rdzas du mar thal bar 'gyur ro zhes brjod par bya'o/ / yang 'dir dpyad pa 'di yod de/ gal te rdzas brgyad po de dag go sa gcig tu 'byung ba lhan cig gi don yin na rdul phran rnams thogs bcas ma yin par 'gyur ro/ / gal te 'dab 'byor du gnas pa nyid de'i don du 'dod na bum pa lta bu la rdul phran grangs med pa 'dab 'byor du gnas pa'i phyir brgyad la sogs par nges pa med do zhe na/ kha cig 'dir go sa gcig pa nyid la 'dod de/ rdul phran rnams thogs bcas su bshad pa ni rigs mthun pa rnams yin gyi rigs mi mthun pa rnams ni thogs bcas ma yin te/ gzugs kyi go sa na reg bya dang*/ reg bya'i go sa na dri la sogs pa'ang yod pa'i phyir ro zhes 'dod do/ / { de mi 'thad de thogs bcas ma yin par thal bas so} {rags pa mi rtsom par yang thal lo }

Question: Why does a sūtra state: “Anything that is suitable to be form consists of the four great elements or it is derived from the four great elements”?[483] Reply: That is stated with the intention that it is possible for the four primary elements to be complete. Vaibhāṣikas assert that the eight substances simultaneously arise. But if they assert them to be substance in terms of sense bases (āyatana), they would advocate too many bases, because the four primary elements are included in the base of tactility. If they assert them to be substance in terms of substance alone, then they would advocate too few substances, because others, such as shape and lightness, [114] also exist there. It is not that the primary elements are held as substance in terms of substance alone and the others are held as substance in terms of the sense bases, because resultant form mostly depends on the four divisions of primary elements and it would then follow that there would be many substances. Objection: This should be analyzed further, because if those eight substances simultaneously occupy the same spatial location, atoms would not impede [each other]. If it is asserted that this is the meaning of abiding together, they could not be determined as eight and so on because, for example, the countless atoms of a vase also abide together. Some assert: “The same spatial location” is asserted here because the explanation that particles impede is for those of similar class. Those of dissimilar class do not impede [each other] because tactile objects exist at the spatial location of visible form, smell exists at the spatial location of tangible objects, and so on. {Reply: That is unacceptable because it would then follow that [even those of similar class] would not impede [each other]. Also, in consequence, coarse form could not be created.}

kha cig ni rigs mi mthun rnams kyang thogs pa dang bcas te/ gal te gzugs kyi rdul gyi go sa na reg bya la sogs pa yod na tha dad med par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir 'dab 'byor du gnas pa nyid la lhan cig gi don du 'dod de/ bum pa la sogs pa'i rdul mang po rnams ni nges par lhan cig tu skye ba ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ brgyad la sogs pa ni nges par lhan cig tu skye ba'i dbang du byas nas bshad pa'i phyir 'gal ba med do/ / de nyid kyi phyir 'grel pa las/ thams cad pas phra ba'i gzugs ni bsags pa'i rdul phra rab ces bya ste/ de las ches chung ba ni mi mngon no/ / de 'dod pa'i khams na sgra yang med dbang po yang med pa zhig yin na ni rdzas brgyad dang ldan par skye ste/ gang yang rung ba zhig med par ni ma yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes zer te de nyid dgongs pa yin{ rlung la kha dog ji ltar yod ce na de la de yod de dri yod pa'i phyir/ rna ma'i me tog bzhin no no/ /}

Some say: Particles of dissimilar class impede [each other] because if tangible objects and so on occupy the same spatial location as particles of visible form, it would follow that they would be nondistinct. Therefore it is asserted that abiding together means coexistent, because there is no certainty that the many particles of a vase and so on arise simultaneously and because this is explained from the perspective of the eight definitely arising simultaneously. Thus there is no contradiction. With that intention the Autocommentary states: The subtlemost form is called the aggregating subtle particle; nothing smaller than it exists. In the desire realm it arises with eight substances that are not associated with the sense faculties and sound and that are not lacking any one substance.[484] {Question: How does wind have color? Reply: It has color because it has smell, just like the nama flower.[485]}
rdzas brgyad las mang ba dang mi ldan nam zhe na/
Question: Does it possess more than eight substances?

lus kyi dbang po dang ldan pa la ni sngar gyi brgyad dang lus kyi dbang po nyid dang rdzas dgu ldan te/ dbang po'i tshogs pa na brgyad po ni nges par yod cing dbang po ni de dag las rdzas gzhan yin pa'i phyir ro/ / yang mig la sogs pa'i dbang po gzhan dang ldan pa la ni rdzas bcu ste/ sngar gyi dgu dang mig la sogs pa gang yang rung ba zhig go /de bzhin du brgyad dang dgu dang bcu dang ldan pa de dag sgra dang bcas par skye na ni dgu dang bcu dang bcu gcig dang ldan par 'gyur te/ de dag dang sgra gzhan du bgrang ba'i phyir ro/ / gzugs khams na ni dri ro med pa'i phyir dbang po med pa ni drug dang*/ lus kyi dbang po dang ldan pa bdun dang*/ dbang po gzhan dang ldan pa brgyad dang*/ sgra dang bcas na dgu lhan cig skye ba yin la/ gzugs med na ni spyir gzugs tsam med pas gzugs can lhan cig skye ba med do zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Reply: Those which possess the body sense faculty (kāyendriya) possess nine substances — (1–8) the previous eight plus (9) the body faculty — because eight substances definitely exist in the collection of the sense faculties and the body sense faculty is distinct in substance from them. Those which possess the other sense faculties of the eyes and so on possess ten substances because they possess the former nine and any other sense faculty such as the eyes. Similarly, if those which possess eight, nine, or ten substances arise with sound, they possess nine, ten, or eleven substances because they are enumerated separately from sound. In the form realm those without sense faculties possess six substances because there is no smell and taste. If they possess the body sense faculty, they have seven. If they possess another sense faculty, they have eight. And if they have sound, nine arise simultaneously. In the formless realm there is no simultaneous arising of [115] physical states, since in general form does not exist there.
8. The Generation of Mental Factors

SUMMARY
sems dang sems byung nges lhan cig / thams cad 'dus byas mtshan nyid dang / / thob pa'am...
Mind and mental factors, and all characteristics of conditioned states, definitely arise simultaneously, and sometimes obtainment. (2:23ab)

sems dang sems las byung ba rnams ni nges par lhan cig tu skye ste/ phan tshun med na mi 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / 'dus byas thams cad ni 'dus byas kyi mtshan nyid skye ba la sogs pa bzhi dang nges par lhan cig tu skye'o zhes bya ba ni bye brag tu smra ba'i grub pa'i mtha'o/ / rang gi rgyud kyis bsdus pa'i thob pa{ dus mnyam pa lus dang grib ma lta bu} dang thob bya'i chos lhan cig skye ba dang*/ 'gog pa gnyis kyi lta bu thob pa skyes kyang thob bya mi skye ba'ang yod pa'i phyir ram zhes rnam par brtag pa'i sgra mdzad do/ /

It is a tenet of the Vaibhāṣikas that the mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta) definitely arise simultaneously (sahāvaśya) because they don’t arise if they don’t coexist. Also all conditioned states and the four characteristics (lakśaṇa) of conditioned states, such as arising, definitely arise simultaneously. You should investigate obtainment (prāpta), for sometimes it arises simultaneously with the object obtained, {such as the body and its coexistent shadow,} and sometimes obtainment arises but the object obtained does not arise, such as the obtainment of the two cessations.

ELABORATION OF CONCOMITANCE

Mental factors have five types because universal mental states and so on are distinct. (2:23cd)

sems byung zhes pas mdor bstan pa yin te/ sems las byung ba nges pa rnams ni sde tshan rnam pa lnga ste/ sems kyis mang po pa dang*/ sogs pa'i sgras gzung ba dge ba'i sa mang po pa rnams dang*/ nyon mongs pa'i sa mang po pa rnams dang*/ mi dge ba'i sa mang po pa rnams dang*/ nyon mongs pa chung ngu'i sa pa zhes bya bar sde tshan tha dad pa'i phyir ro/ /

The words “mental factors” (2:23a) constitute the abbreviated teaching. Those ascertained to be mental factors have five types, or categories, because (1) universal mental states (cittamahābhūmika), (2) virtuous mental states (kuśalamahābhūmika), (3) afflicted mental states (kleśamahābhūmika), (4) nonvirtuous mental states (akuśalamahābhūmika), and (5) specific-afflicted mental states (parīttakleśamahābhūmika) are distinct categories. It has two headings: general meaning and the meaning of the text.

mtshan nyid dang rdzas dang btags pa'i khyad par dang*/ khams dang sa'i rnam par bzhag pa dang*/ rnam shes gang gi 'khor du gang 'byung ba dang*/ sgra'i don lnga las

This has five headings: definition [of minds and mental factors], substantial versus nominal, the presentation of realms and levels, which [mental factors] occur in the retinue of which consciousness, and the meaning of the term.

The definition of a mental factor is “that which is similar to the mind through being concomitant with it in five ways.” (1) Similar focal object means [minds and mental factors] focus on the same essential nature of the object. (2) Similar aspect means they take the same attribute of that object as their aspect. (3) Similar support means they arise in dependence on the same sense faculty. (4) Similar time means they exist at the same time. (5) Similar substance means that the substance of each is similar. Explanatory Commentary on Differentiating the Middle and Extremes explains: Since they have similar support, focus, time, and substance, they are concomitant. But they do not have a similar aspect, since otherwise it would follow that mental factors would not be different from consciousness.[486] This says that minds and mental factors do not have similar aspects, and the meaning of this has been explained. One asserts: A mental factor apprehends the attributes of its object by its own power, and it apprehends the nature of its object by the power of a separate mind. So too, the mind apprehends the nature of its object by its own power, and it apprehends [116] the attributes of its object by the power of mental factors.

Vaibhāṣikas assert that there are seventy-seven mental factors — {thirty-eight in five divisions:} (1–10) ten universal mental states, (11–20) ten virtuous mental states, (21–26) six afflicted mental states, (27–28) two nonvirtuous mental states, and (29–38) ten specific-afflicted mental states. Plus (39–46) eight that are indeterminate. Plus seven, including: (47) the nondeluded root of virtue, (48) root afflicted view, and the five afflicted mental states that occur in Abhidharma — (49) nonintrospection, (50) forgetfulness, (51) distraction, (52) inappropriate attention, and (53) wrong resolution.[487] Plus twenty-four derived from the Kṣudraka Chapter: [mental factors associated with] (54) dislike, {(55) yawning, (56) mental lassitude, (57) anguish, (58) uneven consumption of food, (59) discriminating difference, (60) inattentiveness, (61) physical dysfunction, (62) hostility, (63) abuse, (64) stench, (65) nonstench, (66) not abiding naturally, (67) thought of desire, (68) thought of violence, (69) thought of kin, (70) thought of neighbors, (71) thought of human death, (72) thought of contempt, (73) arrogant sense of class, (74) sorrow, (75) pain, (76) mental dissatisfaction}, and (77) disturbance.

From among those seventy-seven, seventy are substantially existent: forty-six of the (1–38) five divisions, plus (39–46) eight indeterminate mental factors, and (47–70) twenty-four from the Kṣudraka Chapter.[488] The remaining seven are nominally existent.[489] The first three are wisdom and the latter four are designated as mindfulness, concentration, attention, and resolution, respectively, because (1) wisdom is nondelusion that is virtuous alone, (2) afflicted wisdom alone is view, and (3) wisdom that is concomitant with afflicted minds and mental factors is nonintrospection. Afflicted (4) mindfulness, (5) concentration, (6) attention, and (7) resolution alone are forgetfulness, {distraction, inappropriate attention, wrong resolution.} Indeed, this is explained by past scholars and should be well analyzed. {It is permissible to designate the two, nonviolence and violence, as nonaversion and anger. Nonaversion is also said to be love as well as compassion, while nonviolence is altruism and violence is the desire for others to suffer. Therefore I think it is acceptable that the Vaibhāṣikas assert nine to be nominally existent.} Further, there is no contradiction in explaining dislike, mental lassitude, inattentiveness, sorrow, association with suffering, mental dissatisfaction, and disturbance, which occur in the Kṣudraka Chapter, to be feeling, laziness, afflicted wisdom, anger, and so on.

The former are mental factors, of which there are fifty-one: (1–5) the five omnipresent mental factors of feeling, discernment, intention, attention, [117] and contact; five object-determining mental factors: (6–10) aspiration, resolution, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; eleven virtuous mental factors: (11–21) faith, shame, embarrassment, the three of nonattachment and so on, effort, pliancy, diligence, equanimity, and nonviolence; and six root afflictions: (22–27) attachment, anger, pride, ignorance, view, and doubt. Branch afflictions have two sets of ten: (28–47) wrath, resentment, concealment, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, guile, arrogance, violence, shamelessness, nonembarrassment, lethargy, excitation, faithlessness, laziness, negligence, forgetfulness, nonintrospection, and distraction. There are four variables: (48–51) sleep, regret, investigation, analysis.[490] Both the Thirty Verses and the Five Aggregates state: The omnipresent, those determining specific states, virtuous mental factors, and similarly the afflictions and branch afflictions.[491] Regret and sleep also are similar because a treatise indicates: Investigation and analysis, and both branch afflictions, have two aspects.[492]

The first five mental factors are omnipresent since they are concomitant with all minds. (1) Aspiration only engages objects (bhāva) that have been contemplated. (2) Resolution only engages objects that have been ascertained. (3) Mindfulness only engages objects that are familiar. (4) Concentration and (5) wisdom only engage objects for which the faults and qualities have been investigated. These five such as aspiration individually determine their objects since they don’t engage other objects that have not been contemplated and so on. The eleven such as faith are virtue. The six such as attachment are the root of all affliction, and since they afflict the mind they are called root afflictions. The remaining twenty such as wrath are associated with the root afflictions, and they are called branch afflictions since they are close to the root afflictions and afflict the mind. Four mental factors constitute two divisions of two: sleep and regret, and investigation and analysis. They are not determined as branch afflictions for they have two aspects, afflicted or unafflicted; or three aspects, since unafflicted states can be either virtuous or unobscured-neutral; or four aspects, since afflicted states can be either nonvirtuous or obscured-neutral. Therefore they are variable. From the six categories, twenty-two mental factors are substantially existent: (1–10) the first two divisions; (11–17) the remaining seven of the third division except for the four — diligence, equanimity, nonviolence, and nondelusion; and (18–22) the five root afflictions other than view, because they are objects of awareness that do not rely on expressions, terms, or other reasons. The remaining twenty-nine mental factors are nominally existent since they do not comform with those reasons. {Some say: Something whose nature is separately established is substantially existent, and something whose function and essence are not separately established — but distinct in name — is nominally existent.}

Thus the three mental factors of nondelusion, view, and nonintrospection belong to wisdom alone. [118] Diligence and equanimity belong to the three roots of virtue along with effort. Nonviolence belongs to nonaversion. The five mental factors of wrath, resentment, spite, envy, and violence belong to anger. The three mental factors of avarice, arrogance, and excitation belong to attachment. The four mental factors of concealment, lethargy, faithlessness, and laziness belong to delusion. The two mental factors of guile and deceit belong to attachment and delusion. The three mental factors of shamelessness,[493] nonembarrassment, and distraction belong to the three poisons. Negligence belongs to the three poisons along with laziness. But [Vasubandhu’s] Exposing the Hidden Meaning explains that it pertains to attachment and delusion {and that violence pertains to anger}. Exposing the Hidden Meaning explains that forgetfulness is afflicted mindfulness. Sleep and regret are subsumed by the branch afflictions, for when afflicted they are imputed as delusion but when virtuous or unobscured-neutral they are imputed as wisdom. It is asserted that both investigation and analysis belong to intention and wisdom. Here twenty-nine nominally existent [mental factors] occur in the Compendium of Abhidharma and so on, but they are not explicitly set out from among the fifty-one mental factors.[494] Twenty-four mental factors occur in the Kṣudraka Chapter and these are also explained in [Asaṅga’s] Compendium of Bases. Therefore one should realize that there are seventy-five mental factors and so on since there are {fifty-three} that are nominally existent.

THE PRESENTATION OF REALMS AND LEVELS

Thirty mental states belong to the nine levels of the three realms: (1–26) mental states of the first three divisions, plus (27) the specific-afflicted mental state of arrogance, plus the indeterminate mental states of (28) attachment, (29) pride, and (30) doubt. Twelve belong to the desire realm alone: (1–2) both nonvirtuous mental states, plus (3–9) seven specific-afflicted mental states except for the three mental states of guile, deceit, and arrogance, plus the indeterminate mental states of (10) regret and (11) sleep, plus (12) anger. Four exist in the desire realm and the first absorption alone: the specific-afflicted mental states of (1) guile and (2) deceit, plus the indeterminate mental states of (3) investigation and (4) analysis. This is understood through textual reference supplemented with logical proofs.

Thirty-two mental states occur in the retinue of any of the six types of consciousness: (1–28) mental states of the first four divisions, the indeterminate mental states of (29) investigation and (30) analysis, plus (31) attachment and (32) aversion. Fourteen occur as retinue of mental consciousness alone: (1–10) specific-afflicted mental states plus the indeterminate mental states of (11) regret, (12) sleep, (13) pride, and (14) doubt. Those who assert the eightfold collection of consciousness assert that {seventeen} occur in the retinue of foundation consciousness: (1–5) five omnipresent mental factors {including the feeling of equanimity alone, for Thirty Verses declares: Contact, attention, feeling, discernment, and intention are always possessed.[495] And: Since its feeling is equanimity, foundation consciousness is an unobscured-neutral state.[496]} and (6–9) four root afflictions — the obscured-neutral mental factors of the afflicted view of the self, ignorance, pride, and attachment — {plus eight [119] branch afflictions which are afflicted mental states: the five explained in the Compendium of Abhidharma — (10) lethargy, (11) excitation, (12) faithlessness, (13) laziness, and (14) negligence[497] — plus the three explained in the Compendium of Ascertainment: (15) forgetfulness, (16) distraction, and (17) nonintrospection.[498] [Foundation consciousness] is concomitant with equanimity alone, since the Explanation of the Thirty Verses states: Further, it has the feeling of equanimity, which is an obscured-neutral state.[499]} The reason for this can be comprehended through reference to various texts. The difference between minds and mental factors and the analysis of one or distinct has thus been explained.
