nyon mongs gsum mo las gnyis so/ / gzhi bdun de bzhin 'bras bu yin/ /
Three are afflictions, and two are karma. Seven are the supportive basis, and so too, they are results. (3:26ab)

rten 'brel de dag las nyon mongs pa ni ma rig pa dang sred pa dang len pa gsum mo/ / las ni 'du byed dang srid pa gnyis so/ / las dang nyon mongs pa'i rten yin pa'i phyir gzhi ni rnam shes la sogs pa{ gzhan} lnga dang skye ba dang rga shi gnyis te bdun no/ / ji ltar yan lag bdun po gzhi yin pa de bzhin du 'bras bu'i yan lag kyang yin no/ / las dang nyon mongs pa de dag ni rgyu'i yan lag kyang yin pas thams cad kyang rgyu dang 'bras bu'i yan lag gnyis su 'gyur ro/ / de'i phyir slob dpon klu sgrub kyis kyang rten 'byung las bcu gnyis chos ni gsum du 'dus/ / dang po brgyad pa dgu nyon mongs/ / gnyis dang bcu pa las yin te/ / lhag ma bdun yang sdug bsngal yin/ / zhes bshad do/ /

From among the links of dependent origination, three are afflictions: (1) ignorance, (8) craving, and (9) grasping. Two are karma: (2) formation and (10) existence. Seven are the supportive basis (vastu) because they support karma and affliction: the five (3–7) such as consciousness, and the {remaining} two — (11) birth and (12) aging and death. Just as seven links are the supportive basis, so too they are also results (phala). Since those karmas and afflictions are also causal links, all twelve are either causal or resultant links. Therefore Master Nāgārjuna explained in Essence of Dependent Origination that the twelve phenomena are subsumed in three divisions: The first, the eighth, the ninth are affliction. The second and tenth are karma. The remaining seven are also suffering.[777]

des na rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba ni rnam pa gnyis te/ sngon gyi mtha' pa dang*/ phyi ma'i mtha' pa'o/ / de dag re re la yang rgyu dang 'bras bu gnyis gnyis yod pa las ma rig pa dang 'du byed ni sngon gyi mtha' pa'i rgyu dang*/ rnam shes nas tshor ba'i bar ni 'bras bu yin la/ sred len srid pa gsum ni phyi ma'i mtha' pa'i rgyu dang*/ skye ba rga shi ni 'bras bu yin no/ / kun las btus las ni/ 'du byed gang yin pa dag dang*/ rnam par shes pa gang yin pa dang*/ srid pa gang yin pa 'di ni las kyi kun nas nyon mongs par bsdu'o zhes kun gzhi rnam shes las kyi bag chags 'dzin pa'i cha nas lus su bshad do/ / de bzhin du de nyid las/ 'phen pa'i yan lag dang*/ 'phangs pa'i yan lag dang*/ mngon par 'grub par byed pa'i yan lag dang*/ mngon par grub pa'i yan lag dang bzhir bshad de/ de la ma rig pa dang 'du byed dang rnam shes gsum ni 'phen pa'i yan lag yin te/ ma rig pas kun nas bslang ba'i las kyi bag chags sems la bsgos nas ming gzugs la sogs pa 'phen pa'i phyir ro/ / ming gzugs nas tshor ba'i bar bzhi ni 'phangs pa'i yan lag yin te/ de dag ni las kyi bag chags las skyes pas rnam shes kyis dngos dang snga ma gnyis kyis brgyud nas 'phangs pa'i phyir ro/ / sred len srid pa gsum ni mngon par 'grub par byed pa'i yan lag yin te/ skye ba dngos su 'grub par byed pa'i phyir ro/ / skye ba dang rga shi gnyis ni mngon par grub pa'i yan lag yin te/ sred len srid pa gsum las grub pa'i phyir ro/ /

Thus dependent origination has two types — (1) the initial phase and (2) the latter phase — and each has both causal and resultant aspects. Ignorance and formation are causes of the initial phase, and from consciousness to feeling are its results. Craving, grasping, and existence are causes of the latter phase, and birth and aging and death are its results. The Compendium of Abhidharma declares: All formation, consciousness, and existence are subsumed in karmic affliction.[778] This explains karma from the perspective of foundation consciousness holding the imprint of karma. Also the Compendium of Abhidharma explains: There are four: (1) projecting links, (2) projected links, (3) establishing links, and (4) established links.[779] Three links — ignorance, formation, and consciousness — are (1) projecting links because karmic imprints laid down on the mind motivated by ignorance project name and form and so on. Four links, from name and form to feeling, are (2) projected links because they are directly projected by consciousness generated by karmic imprints, and indirectly [projected] by the former two. Three links — craving, grasping, and existence [233] — are (3) establishing links because they act to directly establish birth. Both birth and aging and death are (4) established links because they are established from craving, grasping, and existence.
gsum pa rgyu dang 'bras bu'i dbye ba ni
Classification of cause and effect

gal te rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba rgyu dang 'bras bur 'brel ba la khyad par med bzhin du sngon gyi mtha' pa'i rgyu ni gnyis su bsdus shing 'bras bu ni lngar phye la/ phyi ma'i mtha' pa'i rgyu ni gsum du phye la 'bras bu ni gnyis su bsdus she na/ sngon gyi mtha' pa'i 'bras bu ni rnam pa lngar phye zhe na/

Question: Given that dependent origination is not differentiated in terms of cause or effect, if the cause of the initial phase is included in two links and its result is classified in five, and the cause of the latter phase is classified in three and its result is included in two, then how is the result of the initial phase classified in five?
gnyis kyi rgyu 'bras mdor bsdus pa/ / bar ma'i rjes su dpag pa las/ / 26
Cause and effect are briefly taught according to both, and the middle phase is inferred from that. (3:26cd)

skye ba snga phyi gnyis kyi go rim bzhin du rgyu dang 'bras bu mdor bsdus te bstan pa ni bar ma 'dir 'bras bu la rnam pa lngar phye ba dang rgyu la gsum du phye ba'i rjes su dpag pa las phyi ma'i skye ba dang rga shi yang rnam pa lngar rjes su dpag par nus la/ snga ma'i ma rig pa dang 'du byed kyang rnam pa gsum du rjes su dpag par nus pa'i phyir ro/ / de bzhin du snga ma'i rgyu dang phyi ma'i 'bras bu mdor bsdus te bstan pa'i rjes su dpag pa las bar ma'i 'bras bu dang rgyu mdor bsdu bar yang rjes su dpag par nus so/ / de'i phyir rgyu dang 'bras bu mdor bsdu ba dang dbye ba rgyas par rtogs pa'i don du de ltar bstan pa yin gyi don la ni khyad par med do zhes shes par bya'o/ / gal te de lta na'ang ma rig pa la rgyu yod cing rga shi la 'bras bu yod na ni rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba bcu gnyis su nges par mi 'gyur la/ med na ma rig pa rgyu med pa dang*/ rga shi don byed pas stong pa dang*/ 'khor ba thog mtha' can du'ang 'gyur ro zhe na/

Reply: Cause (hetu) and effect (phala) are briefly taught in accordance with the order of links of both earlier and later lives, while the classification of effects in five types and the classification of causes in three types of the middle phase is inferred from that. Therefore birth and aging and death may be inferred to have five types, and ignorance and formation may be inferred to have three types. So too, the abbreviated cause and effect of the middle phase may be inferred from the abbreviated teaching of the earlier cause and later effect. Therefore it should be understood that dependent origination is taught in this way for the purpose of comprehending abbreviated cause and effect and its extensive classification, but there is no difference in meaning. Objection: If ignorance has a cause and aging and death have a result, dependent origination would not be fixed in number as twelve links. If not, ignorance would have no cause, aging and death would be empty of function, and saṃsāra would possess a beginning and end.
nyon mongs pa las nyon mongs dang / / bya ba nyid do de las gzhi/ / de las gzhi dang nyon mongs skye/ / 'di ni srid pa'i yan lag lugs/ / 27

From the afflicted the afflicted, and from them actions. From them the supportive basis, and from them the supportive basis. From them afflictions arise. This is the system of the links of existence. (3:27)

bshad pa nyon mongs pa sred pa las nyon mongs pa len pa 'byung ba dang*/ nyon mongs pa len pa dang ma rig pa las bya ba ste las srid pa dang 'du byed 'byung ba nyid do/ / las srid pa dang 'du byed de{ bya ba} de las ni gzhi 'byung ste/ 'du byed las rnam shes dang srid pa las skye ba 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / gzhi de dag las kyang gzhi 'byung ste/ rnam shes las ming dang gzugs nas reg pa las tshor ba 'byung ba'i bar dang skye ba las rga shi 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / gzhi de dag las kyang nyon mongs pa skye ste/ tshor ba las srid pa dang*/ tshor ba'i bar ni rga shi yin la sred pa ma rig pa yin pas rga shi las ma rig pa 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / de lta na de lta bu 'di ni srid pa'i yan lag bcu gnyis kyi lugs rnam par bzhag pa yin pas/ de'i phyir skyon gnyis ka las grol te/ ma rig pa'i rgyu ni rga shi yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rga shi'i 'bras bu'ang ma rig pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir sngon dang phyi ma'i mtha' med par rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba yan lag bcu gnyis nyid 'khor ba yin te/ rten 'byung las/ gsum po dag las gnyis 'byung ste/ / gnyis las bdun 'byung bdun las kyang*/ / gsum 'byung srid pa'i 'khor lo de/ / nyid ni yang dang yang du 'khor/ / 'gro kun rgyu dang 'bras bu ste/ / 'di las sems can gzhan ci'ang med/ / ces pa dang*/ rin po che'i phreng ba las kyang*/ lam gsum thog mtha' dbus med par/ / 'khor ba'i dkyil 'khor 'gal me yi/ / 'khor lo lta bur phan tshun gyi/ / rgyu can 'di ni 'khor bar 'gyur zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: From afflicted craving arises afflicted grasping. And from afflicted grasping and ignorance arise the actions of karmic existence and formation. From {the actions of} karmic existence and formation arise the supportive basis (vastu) because consciousness arises from formation and birth arises from existence. Also from the supportive basis, the supportive basis arises because from consciousness name and form arises, from those contact arises, from contact feeling arises, and from birth aging and death arise. Also from the supportive basis arise afflictions because from feeling craving arises, and since the links up to feeling correspond to aging and death, and craving corresponds to ignorance, ignorance arises from aging and death. Therefore this is the system of the twelve links of existence (bhavāṅga). Since it is posited in such a way, it is free from those two errors because the cause of ignorance is aging and death and also the result of aging and death is ignorance. Thus the twelve links of dependent origination, which have no earlier or later limit, are saṃsāra because the Essence of Dependent Origination states: From those three, two occur. From two, seven occur. Also from seven, three occur. This wheel of existence cycles again and again as the cause and effect of all reincarnating beings, [234] and there are no sentient beings other than these.[780] Also the Precious Garland notes: Those who possess the mutual causes of these three paths without beginning, middle, or end cycle in the wheel of saṃsāra like the wheel of a firebrand.[781]

de ltar na rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i rgyu ni lnga dang 'bras bu ni bdun yin no/ / kun las btus las ni/ rnam shes ni sa bon gyi kun gzhi yin pas rgyu yin pa'i phyir rgyu drug dang 'bras bu drug tu bshad la/ rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i mdo'i 'grel par ni ming gzugs la sogs pa bzhi yang sa bon gyi kun gzhi yin pa'i phyir rgyu bcu dang 'bras bu gnyis yin par bshad mod kyi/ 'dir rgyu ni las dang nyon mongs pa yin la 'bras bu ni sdug bsngal gyi gzhi'i dbang du byas pa yin pas na ming gzugs la sogs pa ni gzhi nyid du nges pa'i phyir rgyu'i yan lag ma yin no/ / gal te 'bras bu bskyed pa tsam gyis de dag rgyu'i yan lag tu smra na ni skye ba dang rga shi'ang de ltar thal ba'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir snga ma kho na legs so/ / gal te nyon mongs pa'i yan lag tu ma rig pa dang*/ sred len kho na smros kyi khong khro la sogs pa ci'i phyir ma smros she na/ ma rig pa ni nyon mongs pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba yin pa'i phyir de smros na gzhan dag kyang mon par 'gyur ba'i phyir te/ don ni skye ba snga ma'i nyon mongs pa thams cad rgyu yin pa'i phyir ro/ / sred len ni skye ba'i srid par nying mtshams sbyor ba'i gtso bo yin pa'i phyir de dag bstan pas gzhan thams cad kyang mtshon pa'i phyir yin no/ /

Thus the causes of dependent origination are five and the results are seven. The Compendium of Abhidharma explains that there are six causes and six results because consciousness is a cause since it is the supportive basis of the seed.[782] The Commentary on the Dependent Origination Sūtra indeed explains that there are ten causes and two results because the four links from name and form and so on are also the supportive basis of the seed.[783] Here since the cause is taken to be karma and affliction and the result is taken to be the supportive basis of suffering, therefore name and form and so on are not causal links since they are identified with the supportive basis. Objection: They are causal links since they generate results. Reply: It would then follow that birth and aging and death would also be causal links. Therefore just the former statement is correct. Objection: Only ignorance, craving, and grasping are said to be afflicted links. Why aren’t anger and so on mentioned? Reply: When ignorance is mentioned it represents the other afflictions because ignorance is the root of all afflictions, and it is really the cause of all afflictions of past births. Craving and grasping also represent all other afflictions because they are the main links to birth existence.
bzhi pa mdo'i don bshad pa ni
Explaining the meaning of the sūtras
mdo las/ dge slong dag khyed la rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba dang*/ rten cing 'brel par byung ba'i chos rnams kyang bstan par bya'o zhes gsungs pa'i don ci zhe na/
Question: A sūtra declares: Monks, I will teach you phenomena that arise dependently and phenomena that have arisen dependently.[784] What is the meaning of this passage?
'dir ni 'byung ba rgyu yin te/ / byung ba 'bras bu yin par 'dod/ /
It is said in this sūtra that that which arises is the cause and that which has arisen is the effect. (3:28ab)

bstan bcos las ni gnyis ka rang 'dus byas kyi chos thams cad kyi rnam grangs yin par khyad par cung zad kyang med par bshad mod kyi 'on kyang gang la ltos nas rgyu yin par de de la ltos nas 'bras bu ma yin la/ gang la ltos nas 'bras bu yin pa de de la ltos nas rgyu ma yin pas mdo las/ de ltar gsungs pa 'dir ni rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba ni phyi ma skyed pa'i rgyu{ 'i yan lag lnga} yin te 'di las 'bras bu 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / rten cing 'brel par byung ba ni snga ma las skye pa'i 'bras bu yin par 'dod de/ rgyu las byung ba'i phyir ro/ / ci'i phyir de dag la rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba zhes bya zhe na/ 'dir saM skr-i ta'i skad la pra tI t+ya sa mud bA da zhes 'byung ste/ de la nyer bsgyur pra ti ni phrad pa dang rten pa'o/ / skad kyi dbyings i ti ni 'gro ba yin kyang nyer bsgyur pra ti dang 'brel pa na nas dang cing la sogs par yongs su 'gyur ba'i phyir phrad nas dang phrad cing zhes bya ba yin te/ sgra pa dag gis/ skad kyi dbyings ni stobs ldan yang*/ / nye bar bsgyur bas zil gnon 'gyur/ / gang+gA'i chu ni mngar mod kyi/ / rgya mtsho'i chu yis ji bzhin no/ / zhes bshad pa lta bu'o/ /

Reply: Indeed a treatise[785] explains that there is not the least difference since both are equivalent to all conditioned phenomena. However, if something is a cause of a specific entity it is not its result, and if something is a result of a specific entity it is not its cause. Therefore it is said in accordance with this sūtra that that which arises (samutpāda) dependently is {the five links of} the cause generating future rebirth because effects arise from them. That which has arisen (samutpanna) dependently is the effect arisen from past states because it arose from causes. Question: Why is it called dependent origination? Reply: In Sanskrit the term is pratītyasamutpāda. The prefix prati means “to meet” and “to depend on.” Although the root word iti means “to go,” if joined to the prefix prati it also has the connotation of “from” or “through” and so on, signifying “from meeting” or “through meeting.” As such, grammarians argue: Though the root word is potent, it is dominated by its prefix, just as the water of the Gaṅga is sweet, yet the water of the ocean makes it salty.[786] [235]

skad kyi dbyings pA da yod pa yin yang nyer bsgyur sa mud gong na yod pa ni 'byung ba la 'jug pa'i phyir rgyu rkyen dang 'bras bu phrad nas yang dag par 'byung ba yin no/ / phrad pa'i don yang bar ma chad par 'byung ba yin la/ phrad nas 'byung ba'ang phrad pa nyid kyi tshe 'byung ba yin te kha gdangs nas nyal lo zhes brjod pa bzhin no/ / de'i phyir brda sprod pa pas med pa phrad par mi rung ba'i phyir dang*/ yod pa phrad na'ang de'i rjes la 'byung ba mi 'thad de/ grub zin pa'i phyir dang*/ phrad nas 'byung ba'ang rim gyis pa'i sgra yin pa'i phyir phrad nas 'byung ba'i sgra ni skyon dang bcas so zhes smras pa'ang bsal ba yin no/ / kha cig gis 'dir rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i sa mtshungs dpyad mod kyi/ 'di'i lugs ni tshe gsum dang cha gsum du bstan pa nyid kyi shugs la shes pa'i phyir dang*/ rnam par dpyad pa de yang gzhan gyi lugs yin pa'i phyir bdag gis ma byas so/ /

Though the verbal root pāda means “exists,” it is modified by the prefix samut, such that the compound means “arises” in the sense of “correctly arising from meeting causes and conditions.” “Meet” also means “arising without interruption,” and since “arising from meeting” means “arising at the time of meeting,” it is similar to the expression “Yawning, he lay down.” Therefore grammarians state that interpreting it to mean “arising after meeting” is flawed because meeting a nonexistent entity is untenable. Even if something met an existent entity, it is not acceptable that it arises after [meeting that entity] since it is already established as existent and “arising after meeting” is a term indicating serial development. Thus they reject this interpretation. One says: Indeed here one should analyze what is common in the presentation of dependent origination. This is not something fabricated by me, for one may indirectly infer the teaching on three lives and three phases from this system, and its analysis may be inferred from the systems of others.

yang mdo las/ 'di yod na 'di 'byung*/ 'di skyes pas 'di skye'o zhes rnam grangs gnyis gsungs pa ni ma rig pa la sogs pa 'di yod na 'du byed la sogs pa 'di 'byung gi med na ni mi 'byung la/ de bzhin du 'di skyes na 'di skye'i 'di ma skyes na ni 'di mi skye'o zhes nges par gzung ba'i don dang*/ ma rig pa 'di yod na 'du byed 'di 'byung la/ 'du byed 'di skyes pas rnam par shes pa 'di skye'o/ / zhes bya ba la sogs pa yan lag brgyud par bstan pa'i phyir ram/ sngon gyi mtha' 'di yod na da ltar gyi mtha' 'di 'byung la/ da ltar gyi mtha' 'di skyed pas phyi ma'i mtha' 'di skye'o zhes tshe brgyud pa gnyis bstan pa'i phyir ram/ de dag gnyis ka ltar na yang dngos dang brgyud pa'i rgyu dang 'bras bur bstan pa'i phyir te/ ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed ces bya ba la sogs pa ni rgyas par bshad pa yin no/ / rnam pa gcig tu 'di yod na 'di 'byung bas ni sems pa med pa'i rgyu la ltos pa dang*/ 'di skyes pas 'di skye bas ni mi rtag pa'i rgyu la ltos pa dang*/ ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed la sogs pas ni nus pa'i rgyu la ltos par bstan pa'i phyir ro/ / rnam pa gcig tu na lhan cig pa dang de ma thag pa dang 'gags nas yun ring du lon pa'ang rgyur 'gyur ro/ / zhes bstan pa'i phyir 'di yod na zhes pa la sogs pa gsungs pa yin no/ / thams cad kyi ltar na'ang rgyu med pa dang bdag rtag pa la sogs pa mi mthun pa'i rgyu dgag pa'i phyir gsungs pa yin no/ /

Again, a sūtra proclaims: If this exists then this occurs. By this having arisen then this arises.[787] This states two sequences: “If this” ignorance and so on “exists” then “this” formation and so on “occurs,” but if it doesn’t exist then [the other] will not occur. So too the words “If this has arisen then that arises, if this has not arisen then that does not arise”[788] corroborates this meaning. “If ignorance exists then formation occurs, and due to formation having arisen consciousness arises”[789] and so on teaches that the links arise in succession. Or “If the initial phase exists then the present phase occurs, and through the present phase having arisen then the last phase arises” teaches two lives in succession. Or through combining both it teaches direct and indirect causes and effects, because [such passages] extensively teach that due to the condition of ignorance then formation [arises] and so on. In one respect it teaches reliance on an unintentional cause: “If this exists, this occurs”; reliance on an impermanent cause: “By that having arisen, this arises”; and reliance on a potent cause: “Due to the condition of ignorance, formation and so on arises.” In another respect it states “If this exists, this occurs . . .” and so on because it teaches that “it acts as a cause of long duration through negating simultaneous and immediately preceding causes.” But all this is stated in order to refute impossible [forms of] causation such as [the assertion that] causation itself does not exist or that the self is permanent, and so on.
lnga pa rgyun chags pa'i rten 'brel 'chad pa ni
Continuous dependent origination

mdo sde pa la sogs pa na re ma rig pa la sogs pa gnas skabs phung po lnga pa ni ma yin te/ mdo las/ ma rig pa gang zhe na/ smras pa/ sngon gyi mtha' mi shes pa gang yin pa'o zhes pa la sogs pa ma rig pa ni mi shes pa'i sems las byung ba dang*/ 'du byed ni sems pa la sogs pa kho na la gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / ma rig pa la sogs pa gtso che ba'ang ma yin te/ rnam shes kho na gtso che ba'i phyir de 'ba' zhig ston par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / shas che ba la gtso bo'i sgras brjod na tshe snga ma la ma rig pa kho na shas che la 'di la sred len kho na shas che ba'i nges pa med pa'i phyir dang*/ rnam shes dang ming gzugs ni 'dod gzugs na khyad par med par yod pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir de ltar bstan pa 'di ni rgyu dang 'bras bu'i bye brag 'ba' zhig kho na ston pa yin gyi 'dus byas kyi rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba'i spyi ston pa ni ma yin te/ sa bon las myu gu 'byung ba la sogs pa phyi'i rten cing 'brel bar 'byung ba'ang ma bsdus pa'i phyir ro/ / des na ma rig pa dang 'du byed la sogs pa sgra ji bzhin pa kho na yin pa'i phyir de bshad par bya'o zhes zer ro/ / 'o na ma rig pa zhes bya ba'i don gang yin zhe na/

[Higher schools] such as the Sautrāntikas say that ignorance and so on are not the five aggregates arising in phases because a sūtra says: What is ignorance? It is any unknowing from the limitless past . . . and so on.[790] This sūtra indicates that ignorance is the mental factor of not knowing, and formation [236] is intention alone and so on. Also, it is not that ignorance and so on are primary, for consciousness alone is primary because it alone is said to be [a primary mind]. But if the term primary (prādhānya) means “dominant,” then there is no certainty that ignorance alone was dominant in past lives, or that craving and grasping alone are dominant in this life, and there is no difference between the links of consciousness and name and form in the desire and form realms. Therefore this presentation teaches specific causation alone, and not the general dependent origination of conditioned states, because it does not subsume the general dependent origination of sprouts arising from seeds and so on. This is explained because ignorance and formation and so on exist just as they are described. Question: But what is the meaning of ignorance?
rig pa'i mi mthun phyogs chos gzhan/ / ma rig mi mdza' rdzun sogs bzhin/ / 28
Ignorance is a separate mental factor that counters knowledge, like the malicious, lies, and so on. (3:28cd)

'di ltar yang dag par rig pa'i dngos kyi mi mthun phyogs su gyur pa bden pa dang las dang 'bras bu dang dkon mchog la sogs pa mi gsal ba'i sems las byung ba chos gzhan zhig ma rig pa yin gyi dngos med dang bem po'ang der 'gyur bas rig pa med pa dang ma yin par dgag pa tsam ni ma rig pa ma yin te dper na mi mdza' ba dang rdzun te mi bden pa dang*/ sogs pa'i sgras gzung ba chos ma yin pa dang don ma yin pa dang bya ba ma yin pa la sogs pa dgra dang rdzun dang mi dge ba dang log pa'i don dang ngan pa'i bya ba la sogs pa go ba bzhin no/ / gal te ma rig pa rig pa med pa tsam ma yin par gang las she na/

Reply: Ignorance (avidyā) is a separate mental factor — blind to the four truths, karmic causation, the Three Jewels, and so on — that directly counters authentic knowledge (vidyā). The mere absence or negation of knowledge is not ignorance, for then even nonthings or matter would become ignorance. For example, it is like those who are malicious (amitra), untruths that are lies (anṛta), and so on, which refers to immoral acts, meaningless acts, and inappropriate acts. These are understood [respectively] as enemies, lies, nonvirtue, perverted acts, evil acts, and so forth. Question: What is the source of that assertion that ignorance is not merely a lack of knowledge?
kun sbyor sogs tshig phyir gal te/ / shes rab ngan pa'o min lta phyir/ / lta ba de dang mtshungs ldan phyir/ / shes rab nyon mongs bstan phyir ro/ / 29
Because they proclaim the fetter and so on. Defective wisdom is not ignorance because it is view, because view is concomitant with it, because a sūtra teaches that ignorance afflicts wisdom. (3:29)

mdo las/ ma rig pa'i rkyen gyis 'du byed rnams 'byung ngo zhes rkyen gyis dngos por bstan pa'i phyir dang*/ gzhan yang mdo dag las ma rig pa'i kun tu sbyor ba dang sogs pas bsdus pa 'ching ba dang phra rgyas dang chu ba dang sbyar ba zhes bya ba'i tshig gis gsungs pa'i phyir te/ med pa ni de dag tu 'os pa ma yin no/ / de lta mod kyi gal te shes rab ngan pa ni ma rig pa yin te bu ngan pa la bu ma yin zhes brjod pa bzhin no zhe na/ de ni yang dag pa min te/ shes rab ngan pa ni lta ba yin pa'i phyir dang*/ lta ba dang ma rig pa rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa tha dad du gsungs pa'i phyir dang*/ chu bo la sogs pa'ang tha dad du gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te lta ba ma yin pa'i shes rab ma rig pa yin no zhes na/ de yang ma yin te/ lta ba ni ma rig pa de dang mtshungs par ldan par bshad pa'i phyir dang*/ lta ba'ang shes rab yin pas shes rab kyi rdzas gnyis mtshungs par ldan pa'ang mi srid pa'i phyir dang*/ mdo las/ 'dod chags kyis nye bar nyon mongs pa can du gyur pa'i sems ni rnam par mi 'grol lo/ / ma rig pas nye bar nyon mongs pa can du gyur pa'i shes rab ni rnam par mi 'dag go zhes ma rig pa ni shes rab kun nas nye bar nyon mongs par byed po nyid du bstan pa'i phyir dang*/ shes rab rang nyid ni rang nyid la nyon mongs par byed par 'gal ba'i phyir ro/ / 'di dag gis ni btsun pa dpal len ma rig pa nyon mongs pa spyi'i ming du 'dod pa dang*/ btsun pa chos skyob nga'o snyam du sems can la 'jug pa dang*/ slob dpon chos kyi grags pas/ nyes pa'i rnam pa ma lus pa/ / 'jig tshogs lta las skyes pa yin/ / de ma rig ces 'jig tshogs la lta ba ma rig par bzhed pa'ang bsal bar lta'o/ / de'i rjes la ming dang gzugs kyi gzugs ni bshad zin la/

Reply: A sūtra declares: Through the condition of ignorance, formation occurs . . .[791] This teaches that ignorance is a thing [or functional entity] since it is a condition. Again, it is inappropriate that ignorance is a lack of knowledge because the sūtras proclaim the fetter (saṃyojana) of ignorance, the tie of ignorance, the negative tendency of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the bond of ignorance, and so on.[792] Objection: Defective wisdom (kuprajñā) is ignorance as in the statement “A bad son is not a son.” Reply: That is not correct because defective wisdom is view, and view and ignorance are said to be distinct root afflictions, distinct floods,[793] and so on.[794] Objection: Wisdom that is not view is ignorance. Reply: That also is incorrect because view (dṛṣṭi) is said to be concomitant (saṃprayukta) with ignorance, view is wisdom, and it is impossible for two wisdoms with distinct substance to be concomitant. A sūtra says: The mind that is afflicted with attachment is not liberated. Wisdom that is afflicted with ignorance is not pure,[795] [237] This teaches that ignorance is the agent that fully afflicts wisdom and that it would be contradictory for wisdom to afflict itself. Bhadanta Śrīlāta asserts that ignorance is the common name of the afflictions.[796] Bhadanta Dharmatrāta asserts that it exists for sentient beings who possess the thought “I.”[797] Also Master Dharmakīrti asserts that the afflicted view of the self is ignorance. He writes: All faults without exception arise from the afflicted view of the self. That is ignorance.[798] However, these assertions should be scrutinized with clarity.
ming ni gzugs can min phung po/ / reg drug 'dus te byung ba yin/ / lnga ni thogs pa'i reg pa yin/ / drug pa bla dgas tshig ces bya/ / 30
Name refers to the nonmaterial aggregates. Contact of six types arises through union. Five are impeding contact. The sixth is called “contact through designation.” (3:30)

ming ni tshor ba la sogs pa gzugs can min pa'i phung po bzhi yin te/ de dag ni{ lhas byin zhes sogs kyi} ming gi dbang gis don la 'jug pa'i phyir dang*/ ming ltar thogs pa med pa'i phyir de skad du brjod do/ /

After that are name and form. Form has already been explained. Name (nāma) refers to the four nonmaterial aggregates of feeling and so on because they engage their objects due to the power of names, {such as the label Devadatta,} and like names they are unimpeded.

de'i rjes la reg pa ni mig gi 'dus te reg pa nas yid kyi 'dus te reg pa'i bar drug ste/ de dag kyang{ dbang po dang yul dang} mig gi dbang po dang gzugs dang mig gi rnam shes gsum 'dus te yul yongs su gcod pa 'byung ba yin no/ / de bzhin du rna ba'i 'dus te reg pa la sogs pa la'ang shes par bya'o/ / 'di la sngon gyi slob dpon kha cig ni mdo las/ de ltar na chos gsum po 'di dag 'brel zhing 'dus la tshogs pa gang yin pa de ni reg pa yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir reg pa gsum 'dus pa la btags pa yin gyi gzhan ni med de zhes zer ro/ / kha cig ni drug tshan drug gi mdo las/ chos kyi rnam grangs drug tshan drug gang zhe na/ nang gi skye mched drug dang*/ phyi'i skye mched drug dang*/ rnam par shes pa'i tshogs drug dang*/ reg pa'i tshogs drug dang*/ tshor ba'i tshogs drug dang*/ sred pa'i tshogs drug go zhes gsungs pa'i phyir reg pa ni gsum 'dus pa las byung ba'i yul yongs su gcod pa'i sems las byung ba gzhan zhig yin te/ gal te gsum 'dus pa tsam yin na phyi nang gi skye mched bcu gnyis dang rnam shes drug las logs su gsung bar mi rigs pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

After that is contact (sparśa), which has six types, from the union with the eye up to the union with the mental faculty, and determination of the object arises through the union (saṃnipāta) of three states: (1) the eye sense faculty, (2) form, and (3) eye consciousness. Understand contact through union with the ear and so on in the same way. A past master says: Contact is imputed to the union of these three and not to anything else because a sūtra states: Any assembly that connects and unites these three phenomena is contact.[799] Some say that because the Six Times Six Sūtra declares: What are the six times six synonyms of phenomena? The six internal bases, the six external bases, the sixfold collection of consciousness, the sixfold collection of contact, the sixfold collection of feeling, the sixfold collection of craving.[800] Therefore contact is a separate mental factor that discerns its object through union of the three states. If it were the mere union of these three states, it would be illogical to state it separately from the twelve internal and external bases or the sixfold collection of consciousness.

reg pa'i tshogs drug po de dag las mig gi 'dus te reg pa la sogs pa{ dang po} lnga ni thogs pa'i reg pa yin te/ thogs bcas kyi dbang po la rten pa'i phyir ro/ / drug pa yid kyi 'dus te reg pa ni tshig bla dwags kyi reg pa zhes bya ste/ tshig bla dwags ni ming yin la/ yid ni gtso bor ming la dmigs pas yul gyis yul can la btags pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir mdo las kyang*/ mig gi rnam par shes pas ni sngon po rnam par shes kyi sngon po'i zhes bya bar ni rnam par mi shes so/ / yid kyi rnam par shes pas ni sngon po'ang rnam par shes la sngon po'o zhes bya bar yang rnam par shes so zhes gsungs so/{ yang na tshogs pa snga mas phyi ma skyed pa tsam la dus mnyam du gzhag go /}des na thogs pa'i reg pa ni rten gyis rab tu phye ba yin la/ gnyis pa ni dmigs pas rab tu phye ba yin no/ / kha cig na re sgo lnga'i rnam shes ni tshig la ma ltos par don la 'jug gi yid shes ni tshig gi dbang du byas nas don la 'jug pas na tshig bla dwags yin la de dang mtshungs ldan gyi reg pa la'ang tshig bla dwags kyi reg pa zhes bya ste/ des na 'di ni mtshungs ldan grogs kyis rab tu phye ba yin no zhes zer ro/ /

From among the six types of contact, the {first} five — contact through union with the eyes and so forth — are impeding contact (pratisaṃsparśa) because they are supported by an impeding sense faculty. Contact through union with the sixth, the mental faculty, is called “contact through designation” (adhivacana) because “designation” refers to names and the mental faculty mainly focuses on names. Therefore it is a case of the mind being named after its object. Also, a sūtra declares: Eye consciousness is conscious of blue but not conscious of the term “blue.” Mental consciousness is conscious of blue and also conscious of the term “blue.”[801] {The five types occur at just the same time that the latter [i.e., the mental faculty] is generated.} Thus impeding contact is differentiated by its support, and the second [i.e., contact through designation] is differentiated by its [238] focal object. Some say: Consciousnesses of the five sense doors engage their objects without relying on words, but mental consciousness engages its object through the power of words. Therefore consciousness “engages through designation,” and contact concomitant with it is called “contact through designation.” Thus consciousness is said to be differentiated by its concomitant companion.
rig dang ma rig dang gzhan reg / dri med nyon mongs can lhag ma/ / gnod sems rjes su chags pa'i reg / bde ba myong 'gyur la sogs gsum/ / 31
The contact of knowledge, ignorance, and others is stainless, afflicted, and the rest. It is contact with malice or attachment. Or three: experience of pleasure and so on. (3:31)

yang reg pa ni gsum ste/ rig pa'i reg pa dang*/ ma rig pa'i reg pa dang*/ de gnyis las gzhan rig pa'ang ma yin ma rig pa'ang ma yin pa'i reg pa ste/ de dag kyang rim pa bzhin du dri ma ste zag pa med pa'i reg pa dang*/ nyon mongs pa can gyi reg pa dang*/ lhag ma dge ba zag bcas dang ma bsgribs lung ma bstan dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i reg pa'o/ / ma rig pa'i reg pa'ang gnyis te/ gnod sems dang rjes su chags pa dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i reg pa'o/ / yang reg pa thams cad bsdu na gsum ste/ bde ba myong bar 'gyur ba dang*/ de la sogs pa sdug bsngal myong bar 'gyur ba dang*/ btang snyoms myong bar 'gyur ba'i reg pa dang gsum yin no/ / de ltar na reg pa bcu drug go /

Again, contact has three types: (1) the contact of knowledge (vidyā), (2) the contact of ignorance (avidya), and (3) the contact of states other than knowledge and ignorance. They are, respectively, (1) stainless (amala) or uncontaminated contact, (2) afflicted contact, and (3) the rest, which are contact concomitant with contaminated virtue or unobscured-neutral states. The contact of ignorance has two types: contact concomitant with malice (vyāpāda) and that concomitant with attachment. Again, if all contact is summarized, there are three types: (1) contact inducing the experience of pleasure and so on, meaning (2) contact inducing the experience of pain and (3) contact inducing the experience of equanimity. Thus there are sixteen types of contact.[802]
de las byung ba'i tshor ba drug / lnga ni lus kyi'o sems kyi gzhan/ / de yid nye bar rgyu ba las/ / rnam pa dag ni yang bco brgyad/ / 32
Six feelings arise from those. Five are physical. Mental feeling differs. Those that initiate movement of the mind are also eighteen types. (3:32)

de'i rjes la tshor ba ni{ dbye na} reg pa de dag las byung ba'i tshor ba{ ni mig gi 'dus te reg pa las byung ba la sogs pa} drug{ yin pa} ste mig gi 'dus te reg pa las byung ba'i tshor ba la sogs pa'o/ / tshor ba'i mtshan nyid ni bshad zin pa'i phyir 'dir dbye ba tsam zhig smros so/ / tshor ba drug po de dag las dang po lnga ni dbang po gzugs can la rten pa'i phyir lus kyi tshor ba ste/ lus ni gzugs la brjod par 'dod pa'i phyir ro/ / sems kyi tshor ba ni mig la sogs pa las gzhan pa'i yid la rten pa ste/ de ni bdag po'i rkyen sems tsam la rten pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te reg pa las tshor ba dus mnyam du'am de'i rjes su 'byung*/ dus mnyam pa ni ma yin te/ gnyis ka grub pa ngag la bskyed bya skyed byed gnyis mi 'thad pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i rjes su 'byung ba yin na reg pa dang ldan pa'i sems la tshor ba med par 'gyur na/ de lta na'ang tshor ba sems kyi sa mang po pa ma yin par 'gyur ro zhe na/ bye brag tu smra ba ni lhan cig 'byung ba'i rgyu yin pa'i phyir dus mnyam du 'byung ste mar me las 'od dang myu gu las grib ma bzhin no/ / mdo las kyang*/ mig dang gzugs rnams la brten nas mig gi rnam par shes pa dang*/ gsum 'dus pa'i reg pa dang*/ lhan cig skyes pa'i tshor ba dang*/ 'du shes da nga*/ sems pa skye'o zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes 'chad do/ /

After that is feeling. {If classified,} there are six feelings (vedanā) that arise from contact, such as feeling arising from contact through union with the eye and so on. Here just the classification of feeling is mentioned because its definition has already been explained. Because the first five of those six feelings are supported by the physical sense faculties, they are physical (kāya) feelings because the body is termed “physical.” Mental feeling is supported by the mental faculty and that differs from the [feeling of] eye [consciousness] and so on, for it is supported by the mind alone as its dominant condition. Objection: If feeling arises from contact, either it arises (1) at the same time or (2) later. (1) They do not arise at the same time because if both are established at the same time, it would be unacceptable for them to be related as the generator and that generated. (2) If feeling is established after contact, then the mind concomitant with contact would not have feeling, and if that is so, feeling would not be a universal mental state. Vaibhāṣikas assert that they are coemergent causes because they occur at the same time, like the flame of a butter lamp and its light, or a sprout and its shadow. A sūtra also explains: In dependence on the eye and form, then eye consciousness, contact of the union of the three — feeling, formation, and intention — are generated.[803]

mdo sde pa ni reg pa'i rjes su tshor ba yin te/ dus mnyam pa'ang rgyu 'bras yin na phan tshun rgyu dang 'bras bur 'gyur na mdo las/ mig gi 'dus te reg pa la brten nas mig gi 'dus te reg pa las byung ba'i tshor ba skye'i mig gi 'dus te reg pa las byung ba'i tshor ba la brten nas mig gi 'dus te reg pa skye ba ni ma yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / tshor ba la sogs pa sa mang po par bshad pa ni rtog pa dang bcas shing dpyod pa nang bcas pa'i sa dang*/ rtog pa med la dpyod pa tsam gyi sa dang*/ rtog pa'ang med dpyod pa'ang med pa'i sa dang*/ dge ba'i sa dang*/ mi dge ba'i sa dang*/ lung du ma bstan pa'i sa dang slob pa'i sa dang*/ mi slob pa'i sa dang*/ gnyis ka ma yin pa'i sa thams cad na yod pa'i phyir sa mang po par bshad kyi sems thams cad la khyab pa ni ma yin no zhes 'dod do/ / 'di la btsun pa dpal len na re reg pa dang ldan pa'i sems la reg pa'i skad cig snga ma la skyes pa'i tshor ba yod pa'i phyir tshor ba la sogs pa sems thams cad la khyab pa ma yin par mi 'gyur ro zhes zer ba ni ma yin te/ sems med las langs ma thag pa'i sems la de med par 'gyur ba'i phyir dang*/ mig gi rnam shes kyi rjes thogs nyid du rnam shes gzhan 'byung ba la reg pa dang tshor ba med par 'gyur te/ gzhan la dmigs pa'i rnam shes kyis gzhan la dmigs pa'i reg pa dang tshor ba bskyed pa'i mi rigs pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir 'di dag sems thams cad la khyab par smra na dus mnyam pa'i rgyu 'bras khas blangs bar bya'o/ /

Sautrāntikas assert that feeling occurs after contact because if cause and effect occurred at the same time, they would become mutual causes and effects of each other. A sūtra states: Feeling arising from contact through union with the eye is generated in dependence on contact through union with the eye, but contact through union with the eye is not generated in dependence on feeling arising from contact [239] through union with the eye.[804] Feeling and so on are explained to be universal mental factors because they exist on all levels, including the level of investigation and analysis, the level without investigation but with analysis, the level with neither investigation nor analysis, the level of virtue, the level of nonvirtue, the neutral level, the learner level, and the nonlearner level. But they do not pervade all sentient beings. Bhadanta Śrīlāta asserts that because feeling arising from earlier moments of contact exists in the mind possessing contact, it is not that feeling and so on do not pervade all minds. Reply: That is not so, because feeling does not exist for minds immediately before waking from mindless states, and contact and feeling do not exist when another consciousness arises immediately after eye consciousness. It is illogical that consciousness focusing on one object generates contact and feeling focusing on another object. Therefore if it is said that they pervade all minds, one must accept that cause and effect occur at the same time.
yid nyer rgyu bshad pa/

yang sems kyi tshor ba de nyid{ ngo bo las yid bde mi bde btang snyoms gsum dang dmigs pa las gzugs sogs yul drug la dmigs pa dang*/ mtshungs ldan las yid dang mtshungs par ldan pas} yid nye bar rgyu ba'i bye brag las rnam pa dag ni{ yid bde ba'i nye bar rgyu ba drug /yid mi bde ba'i nye bar rgyu ba drug btang snyoms kyi nye bar rgya ba drug ste/ sngar drug tu dbye ba la ltos nas} yang bco brgyad du dbye zhing*/ gang zhe na/ yid bde ba'i nye bar rgyu ba drug dang*/ yid mi bde ba'i nye bar rgyu ba drug dang*/ btang snyoms kyi nye bar rgyu ba drug go /gal te de dag ngo bo nyid dam/ mtshungs ldan nam/ dmigs pa gang las gzhag /dang po ltar na ni yid bde mi bde btang snyoms gsum kho nar 'gyur zhing*/ gnyis pa ltar na ni yid dang mtshungs par ldan pas gcig kho nar 'gyur la/ gsum pa ltar na ni yul drug la dmigs pa'i phyir drug kho nar 'gyur ro zhe na/ gsum ga las gzhag ste/ ngo bo nyid las ni yid bde mi bde btang snyoms gsum dang*/ mtshungs ldan las ni yid kyi nyer rgyu dang*/ dmigs pa las ni gsum po re re'ang drug drug tu 'gyur te/ gzugs la sogs pa yul drug yod pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag kyang bco lnga ni gzugs sogs yul so sor nges pa la dmigs pa'i phyir ma 'dres pa la dmigs pa yin la/ chos la dmigs pa'i nyer rgyu gsum ni 'dres pa dang ma 'dres pa gnyis ka la dmigs pa yin no/ / nye bar rgyu ba ni yid la brten nas tshor ba bde ba la sogs pa yul la rgyu ba'i phyir ram/ tshor ba la brten nas yid yul la rgyu ba'i phyir ro/ / lus kyi tshor ba ni yid nyer rgyu ma yin te/ yid nyer rgyu ni rtog bcas kyi yid la rten pa yin pa la lus tshor ni dbang po gzugs kho na la rten pa'i rtog med yin pa'i phyir ro/ / bsam gtan gsum pa'i bde ba'ang yid nyer rgyu ma yin te/ brtan par gnas pa'i phyir ro/ / { de yang bye brag tu smra ba yid la brten nas tshor ba yul la rgyu bar 'dod la/ mdo sde pa tshor ba'i dbang gis yid yul la rgyu bar 'dod do} de rnams khams gang na du yod ce na/

Moreover, {since in terms of essential nature there are three: mental satisfaction, mental dissatisfaction, and equanimity; since in terms of focal object there are six objects, form and so on; and since in terms of concomitance there is concomitance with the mind (manas),} then the feelings of the mind that specifically initiate movement of the mind (manopavicāra) are also classified as eighteen types. Question: What are they? Reply: (1–6) Six types of mental satisfaction that initiate movement, (7–12) six types of mental dissatisfaction that initiate movement, (13–18) six types of equanimity that initiate movement. Question: Are those posited from the perspective of (1) nature, (2) concomitance, or (3) focal object? (1) According to the first, they are mental satisfaction, mental dissatisfaction, and equanimity. (2) According to the second, they constitute just one type since they are concomitant with the mind (manas). (3) According to the third, they constitute six types because they focus on the six objects. Reply: They are posited from the perspective of all three because from the perspective of nature they are the three: mental satisfaction, mental dissatisfaction, and equanimity. From the perspective of concomitance they initiate movement of the mind. From the perspective of the focal object there are six for each of the three because there are six objects such as form. Also, because fifteen definitely focus on objects such as form, they focus on unmixed states. The three that initiate movement through focusing on the phenomena element focus on both mixed and unmixed states. They “initiate movement” (3:32c) because the feeling of pleasure and so on initiates movement to the object in dependence on the mind, or because the mind initiates movement to the object in dependence on feeling. Physical feeling does not initiate movement of the mind because initiating movement of the mind depends on the mind that possesses discursive investigation, but physical feeling lacks discursive investigation because it depends on the physical faculties alone. [240] Also the pleasure of the third absorption does not initiate movement of the mind because it abides stably. {Vaibhāṣikas assert that feeling initiates movement to the object in dependence on the mind. Sautrāntikas assert that the mind initiates movement to the object due to the power of feeling.} Question: In what realms do they exist and how many exist?
'dod na thams cad rang dmigs can/ / spyod yul gzugs can bcu gnyis so/ / gong ma gsum gyi bsam gtan ni/ / gnyis na bcu gnyis 'dod 'gro rnams/ / 33
All exist in the desire realm, focusing on their own. Twelve take form as their object field. Three above. Twelve exist in both absorptions and are attracted to desire-realm objects. (3:33)

'dod pa na ni yid nye bar rgyu ba{ bco brgyad po} thams cad yod de/ de dag kyang 'dod pa{ 'i khams} rang nyid la dmigs pa'i yul can yin gyi gzugs dang gzugs med{ khams gong ma gnyis} la dmigs pa la ni bco brgyad mi tshang ba'i phyir ro/ / 'dod pa'i yid nyer rgyu'i spyod yul te dmigs pa gzugs can gyi khams pa yin na ni/ de na dri ro med pas de gnyis la dmigs pa drug ma gtogs pa bcu gnyis so/ / 'dod gzugs kyi gong ma gzugs med ni de na yul lnga med pas chos la dmigs pa'i 'dod pa'i yid bde mi bde btang snyoms gsum gyi spyod yul du 'gyur ro/ / de dag ni 'dod pa'i dbang du byas pa yin no/ /

Reply: All {eighteen} [mental feelings] that initiate movement of the mind exist in the desire realm because they engage objects through focusing (alambanā) on their own desire{-realm} objects. Not all eighteen focus on form and formless objects {in the two higher realms}. Twelve that initiate movement of the mind in the desire realm also take the form realm as their object field (gocara) or focal object. Excluded are the six focusing on smell and taste, since such objects do not exist there. Three [mental feelings] take the formless realm, which is above the desire and form realms, as their object field: mental satisfaction, mental dissatisfaction, and equanimity of the desire realm. These three focus on the phenomena [element], since the five sensory objects do not exist in the formless realm. These [eighteen feelings] are from the perspective of the desire realm.

gzugs khams kyi bsam gtan dang po dang gnyis pa gnyis na ni bcu gnyis yod do/ / de dag na yid mi bde ba drug med pa'i phyir ro/ / bcu gnyis po de dag kyang 'dod pa'i khams la yid 'gro zhing dmigs pa rnams yin gyi rang dang gong ma la dmigs pa ni ma yin te/ de dag ni dri ro med pa'i phyir ro/ /

Twelve exist in both the first and second absorptions (dhyāna) of the form realm because the six types of mental dissatisfaction do not exist there. Those twelve are also attracted to the desire realm, where [smell and taste] are focal objects. They do not focus on [the smell and taste of] their own or higher realms because smell and taste do not exist there.
rang la dmigs brgyad gzugs med pa/ / gnyis kyi'o bsam gtan gnyis na drug / drug gi 'dod pa'o rang ni bzhi'i/ / gong ma gcig gi dmigs pa yin/ / 34

Eight focus on their own realm. Two focus on the formless. There are six in both absorptions. The focal object of those six is desire-realm objects. The form realm is the focal object of four, the higher realm, one. (3:34)

de'i phyir gzugs kyi khams rang la dmigs na brgyad de/ dri ro'i ma gtogs pa gzugs dang sgra dang reg bya dang chos la dmigs pa'i yid bde dang btang snyoms dag yod pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs med pa ni chos la dmigs pa'i bde ba dang btang snyoms gnyis kyi dmigs pa yin no/ /

Therefore eight [feelings] focus on their own form realm because mental satisfaction and equanimity focus on form, sound, tactility, and the phenomena element but not on smell and taste. Two focus on the formless realm: pleasure and equanimity, which focus on phenomena.

bsam gtan gsum pa bzhi pa gnyis na ni{ btang snyoms kyi} yid nye bar rgyu ba drug yod de de dag ni yid bde med pa'i phyir dang*/ sems bde ni yid nyer rgyur mi 'gyur ba'i phyir btang snyoms kyi drug go /drug po de dag gi dmigs pa ni 'dod pa'i khams yin te/ yul drug la dmigs pa'i btang snyoms drug yod pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs kyi khams rang nyid ni btang snyoms kyi nyer rgyu bzhi'i dmigs pa yin te/ dri ro la dmigs pa gnyis med pa'i phyir ro/{ gzugs khams kyi/} gong ma gzugs med pa ni chos la dmigs pa'i btang snyoms kyi yid nye bar rgyu ba gcig gi dmigs pa yin no/ /

There are six {equanimities} that initiate movement of the mind in both the third and fourth absorptions because on those levels mental satisfaction does not exist, and mental bliss does not initiate movement of the mind. The focal object of those six is desire-realm objects because there are six equanimities focusing on six objects. The form realm itself is the focal object of four equanimities that initiate movement of the mind because the two that focus on smell and taste do not exist. The formless realm, which is higher {than form,} is the focal object of one equanimity focusing on the phenomena element that initiates movement of the mind.
gzugs med nye bar bsdogs na bzhi/ / gzugs 'gro gong mar 'gro ba gcig / dngos gzhi na gcig rang yul can/ / bco brgyad thams cad zag dang bcas/ / 35
There are four in the access concentrations to the formless realm. One proceeds higher to the formless realm. One in the actual bases takes itself as its object. All eighteen are contaminated. (3:35)

gzugs med pa nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched kyi nye bar bsdogs na ni btang snyoms kyi nyer rgyu bzhi yod de/ de ni nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched dang bsam gtan bzhi pa la zhi ba dang rags par lta ba yin pa ni dmigs pa gzugs khams {kyi bzhi } pa la yid nye bar 'gro ba'i phyir dang*/ {bzhi pa } de na'ang yul bzhi yod pa'i phyir ro/ / de yang yul bzhi po so so la dmigs pa ltar na bzhir 'gyur gyi gang dag gi ltar na yul bzhi po bzlums te dmigs pa de dag gi ltar na ni de na chos la nye bar rgyu ba 'dres pa la dmigs pa gcig kho na yod do/ / gzugs khams las gong ma gzugs med par 'gro ba ni nyer bsdogs yin yang gcig ste/ chos 'ba' zhig las med pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs med kyi dngos gzhi bzhin yang yid nyid nye bar rgyu ba gcig ste/ de dag ni gzugs med dngos gzhi dge rnams kyi/ / spyod yul zag bcas 'og ma min zhes 'byung bas 'dod gzugs la mi dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ rang sa na chos gcig pu las med pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir rang yul can zhes smros so/ /

There are four equanimities that initiate movement of the mind in the access concentrations to the base of infinite space of the formless realm, because form-realm beings {of the fourth absorption} view the base of infinite space as refined and the fourth absorption as coarse, and they are attracted to the four [formless] objects. In accordance with those that focus on objects individually, there are four. In accordance with others that focus on the four objects together, there is just one [equanimity] focusing on mixed phenomena that initiates movement of the mind. [241] One access concentration proceeds higher from the form realm to the formless realm because there is nothing but the phenomena [element in the formless realm]. So too, there is just one [equanimity] that initiates movement of the mind in the four actual bases (maula) of the formless realm; it does not focus on the desire or form realms, since [the Abhidharmakośa] notes: “The object fields of those virtuous, formless, actual bases are not contaminated lower levels” (8:21ab). Therefore it takes itself as its object (svaviṣaya) because there is just one phenomenon on its level and no others.

de dag thams cad kyi don bsdu ba ni yid nye bar rgyu ba bco brgyad po de dag thams cad ni zag pa dang bcas pa yin te/ {srid pa 'phel bar byed pa'i phyir dang*/ 'phags lam ni srid pa la rgyab kyis ltos pa'i phyir } de dag gi yid yul la zhen pa dang bcas pas nye bar rgyu ba'i phyir ro/ / 'di ni bye brag tu smra ba'i lugs yin la/ slob dpon zag bcas thams cad kyang yid nyer rgyu ma yin te/ 'di ni zhen pa la rten pa'i bde pa la sogs pa la bshad pas na de ni nyon mongs pa can kho na yin pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes 'chad do/ / gal te rten 'brel ston pa na 'dir ma rig pa dang ming dang reg pa dang tshor ba rnams kho na ston gyi gzhan ni ma yin zhe na/

In summary, all eighteen [mental feelings] that initiate movement of the mind are contaminated (sāsrava) because they initiate movement of the mind through longing for those mental objects, {they enhance existence, and the ārya path turns its back on existence}. This is the system of the Vaibhāṣika. Vasubandhu mentions that not all contaminated states initiate movement of the mind. Only those that are afflicted — pleasure and so on — do that, since they depend on longing.[805] Objection: Here in elucidating dependent origination, only ignorance, name, contact, and feeling are taught and not the others.
bshad dang 'chad par 'gyur ba gzhan/ /
The others have been explained or will be explained. (3:36a)

gzugs dang rnam shes dang skye mched drug ni khams bstan par bshad zin pa'i phyir dang*/ 'du byed dang srid pa dang sred len ni gnas bzhi pa dang lnga par 'chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir {de dag gis ni rgyun chags pa'i rten 'brel bshad zin to } gzhan dag ni ma bshad do/ /

Reply: The others are not explained here because form, consciousness, and the six bases have already been explained when presenting the elements; and formation, existence, craving, and grasping will be explained in parts 4 and 5 {and this part has explained continuous dependent origination}.
drug pa rten 'brel mtshon pa'i dpe bshad pa ni
Metaphors for the links
'dir ni nyon mongs sa bon bzhin/ / klu bzhin bzhin ljon shing bzhin/ / de bzhin shun pa bzhin du 'dod/ / 36
In this context afflictions are asserted to be like a seed, like a nāga, like a root, like a tree. Similarly, they are like a husk. (3:36bcd)

rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba nyon mongs pa dang las dang gzhi gsum du bsdus nas bstan pa'i skabs 'dir nyon mongs pa rnams ni sa bon la sogs pa 'di dag dang 'dra ba yin te/ ji ltar zhe na/ dper na sa bon las sdong bu la sogs pa 'byung ba bzhin du nyon mongs pa las kyang nyon mongs pa dang las dang gzhi rnams 'byung ba'i phyir dang*/ klu gnas pa'i mtsho mi skam pa bzhin du nyon mongs pa'i klu gnas pa'i skye ba'i mtsho yang mi skam pa'i phyir dang*/ nags tshal sogs rtsa ba nas ma phyung na bcad kyang slar skye ba bzhin du nyon mongs pa'i rtsa ba ma phyungs na 'gro ba rnams kyi skye ba'ang slar skye ba'i phyir dang*/ ljon shing gi dus dus su me tog dang 'bras bu skyed pa bzhin du nyon mongs pas kyang lan cig ma yin par nyon mongs pa dang las dang gzhi'i me tog dang 'bras bu rnams skyed pa'i phyir ro/ /

Dependent origination has been taught briefly in three parts: (1) afflictions, (2) karma, and (3) the supportive basis. In this context afflictions (kleśa) are similar to seeds and so on. Question: In what way? Reply: For example, afflictions, karma, and the supportive basis are asserted to be like shoots arising from the seed (bīja) of the afflictions. And like a lake where a nāga abides that never dries up, the lake of nāga-like afflictions does not dry up. And like a forest that is cut down without removing the roots (mula) and so regenerates, if the afflictions are not removed from the root, beings again take rebirth. And like a tree (vṛkṣa) that generates flowers and fruit season after season, afflictions also generate the flowers and fruit of the afflictions, karma, and the supportive basis again and again. Similarly, like the husk (tuṣa) of rice, just as rice grows with a thick husk without which it cannot grow, so too, karma must possess the husk of the afflictions to generate the sprouts of existence.
las ni shun bcas 'bras dang 'dra/ / de bzhin sman dang me tog bzhin/ / gzhi ni bza' btung grub pa bzhin/ /
Karma is like rice with its husk. So too, it is like an herb and like a flower. The supportive basis is like food and drink. (3:37abc)

de bzhin du 'bras kyi shun pa bzhin du 'dod de dper na shun pa dang bcas pa'i 'bras thug po che rnams skye bar nus kyi shun pa med par skye mi nus pa ltar nyon mongs pa'i thob pa'i shun pa dang bcas pa'i las kyis srid pa'i myu gu bskyed pa'i phyir ro/ / de bzhin du las ni shun pa dang bcas pa'i 'bras dang 'dra ste/ nyon mongs pa'i shun pa dang bcas pa'i las ni srid pa'i myu gu skyed pa'i nyer len yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de bzhin du sman dang yang 'dra ste/ sman gyis nad gcig bsal nas nus pa zhi ba ltar las kyis kyang rnam par smin pa gcig phyung nas gnyis pa mi 'byin pa'i phyir ro/ / de bzhin du me tog 'bras bu'i nye ba'i rgyu yin pa bzhin du las kyang rnam smin gyi nye ba'i rgyu yin pa'i phyir ro/ / sdug bsngal gyi gzhi{ bdun po} rnams ni bza' ba dang btung ba grub zin pa ni longs spyad bya 'ba' zhig yin pa bzhin du longs spyad nas yang{ sa bon du mi rung bas nying} mtshams mi sbyor ba'i phyir ro/{ des na rnam smin las tshe rabs gzhan du rnam smin 'byung ba med de/ 'byung na ni dgra bcom pa'ang rnam smin yod pas 'khor ba las thar bar mi 'gyur ro/ / de ltar srid pa la bzhi las mi 'da' bas so/}

Similarly, karma is like rice with its husk (tuṣitaṇḍula), because karma possessing the husk of the afflictions is the substantial cause (upādānahetu) generating the sprouts of existence. So too, it is also like an herb (oṣadhi), because just as the potency of a herb declines as it removes an illness, when karma [242] has produced a single karmic maturation, it does not produce a second. Similarly, it is like a flower (puṣpa) that is the direct cause of its fruit, because karma also is the direct cause of karmic maturation. The {seven types of} supportive basis (vastu) of suffering are like food and drink that are utilized once and once consumed cannot be used again {since they do not survive in a seed state}. {Therefore that which has matured does not again produce karmic maturation in other lives. If it did arhats would experience further karmic maturation, they would not be emancipated from saṃsāra, and thus they would not have transcended the four types of existence.}
14. Birth, Food, and Death
gsum pa srid pa bzhi bshad pas don bsdu ba ni
The four types of existence
srid pa bzhi po de dag las/ / 37 skye ba'i srid pa nyon mongs can/ / rang gi sa pa'i nyon mongs kun/ / gzhan rnam gsum mo gzugs med gsum/ /
From those four existences, (3:37d) birth existence is afflicted with all the afflictions of one’s own level. Others have three types. Three in the formless realm. (3:38abc)

skye srid la sogs pa srid pa bzhi po de dag las gcig tu skye ba'i srid pa ni nyon mongs pa can kho na yin te/{ las kyi rnam smin skyed pa nyon mongs la ltos par yang yang bshad do/ / de yang sa gzhan gyi nyon mongs kyis sa gzhan gyi mtshams mi sbyor bas des na/} nyon mongs pa gang gis she na/

The abbreviated meaning is that from those four existences (bhava), birth existence (upapattibhava) is only afflicted (kliṣṭa). {It is frequently explained that the maturation of karma relies on affliction and that the afflictions of one level do not link to other levels.} Question: What is it afflicted by?

rang gi sa pa'i nyon mongs pa kun gyis skye ba len pa srid de/ 'on kyang kun dkris chig rkyang thub pa ma rig pa tsam dang mtshungs par ldan pa phrag dog dang ser sna dang khro ba dang 'chab pa bzhi dang slob dpon gang spel gyis 'gyod pa dang lnga bshad de de rnams kyis ni ma yin no/ / de bzhin du bar srid du nying mtshams sbyor ba'ang nyon mongs can kho nar nges so/ / skye srid las gzhan bar srid dang sngon dus kyi srid pa dang 'chi ba'i srid pa gsum ni nyon mongs pa can dang dge ba dang ma bsgribs lung ma bstan rnam pa gsum mo/ / theg chen pa ni sa'i dngos gzhi las/ dge ba'i sems dang ldan par 'chi 'pho ba ji lta bu zhe na/ kha cig 'chi ba'i tshe dge ba'i chos sngon du bsten pa rnams dran nam gzhan gyis dran par byas kyang rung ste de'i tshe dad pa la sogs pa dge ba'i chos gang dag sems la kun tu spyod pa de dag ji srid du 'du shes rags pa 'byung ba'i bar du'o/ / 'du shes cha phra mo rgyu bar gyur pa'i tshe ni dge ba'i sems ldog cing lung du ma bstan pa'i sems nyid du gnas te/ 'di ltar des de'i tshe sngon goms par byas pa'i dge ba la rang gis brtsal par yang mi nus la gzhan dag gis kyang dran par byed mi nus so/ / de bzhin du mi dge ba la'ang sbyar ro zhes pa dang*/ don gsang rnam par phye ba las kyang*/ theg pa chen po las ni 'chi ba'i sems thams cad ma bsgribs la lung du ma bstan pa yin par brjod na zhes 'byung bas 'chi ba'i sngon rol gyi sems gsal ba'i tshe dge mi dge 'byung yang 'chi sems ni lung ma bstan kho na yin par bzhed do/ /

Reply: It is possible to take birth [i.e., to be conceived] with all the afflictions of one’s own level (svabhūmika). However, rebirth may be taken with just a solitary entanglement (paryavasthāna) but not with the four — envy, avarice, wrath, [and] concealment, plus a fifth, regret, explained by Master Pūrṇavardhana — that are concomitant with ignorance alone. So too, linkage to the intermediate existence is definitely solely afflicted. The three states that are other than birth existence — intermediate existence, prior existence, and death existence — have three types: afflicted, virtuous, and unobscured-neutral. A Mahāyānist asserts that in this context Yogācāra Levels notes: How does death occur for those possessing the mind of virtue? Some say that at the time of death, those who have previously relied on virtue should recall it or be reminded of it. At that time, for as long as coarse discernment arises, they should mentally practice any virtue such as faith and so on. When discernment becomes subtle, virtuous minds stop and the mind abides in a neutral state. At that time one cannot make exertion in virtuous practices one has previously cultivated, nor can others remind one of them. This also applies to nonvirtuous practices.[806] And Exposing the Hidden Meaning declares: In the Mahāyāna all minds of death are unobscured-neutral states.[807] Therefore, though virtuous or nonvirtuous minds occur prior to death, the mind of death is neutral alone.

yang srid pa bzhi po de dag las 'dod gzugs gnyis na ni bzhi ga yod la/ gzugs med na ni gsum ste/ de na bar srid med pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir kun las btus las kyang*/ bar ma do'i srid pa ni 'dod pa'i khams dang gzugs kyi khams su skye ba na'o/ / gzugs med pa nas ni 'pho ba na'o zhes 'byung ste/ de ni gzugs med nas shi nas khams 'og ma gnyis su skye ba'i dbang du byas pa ste/ de'i bar srid ni khams 'og ma gnyis su gtogs pa'i phyir ro/ /

Again, from among these four existences, all four occur in both the desire and form realms. There are three in the formless realm because the intermediate existence does not exist there. Therefore the Compendium of Abhidharma states: The intermediate existence is born in the desire realm and the form realm. It transfers from the formless realm.[808] [243] This is from the perspective of taking birth in the two lower realms from the formless realm, since their intermediate existences belong to the two lower realms.
da ni gang gis gnas pa'i zas bshad pa ni
Foods that sustain life
'gro ba zas kyis gnas pa yin/ / 38
Reincarnating beings abide due to food. (3:38d)

'gro ba rnams ni zas kyis gnas pa yin no zhes yang dag par ldan pa'i lung las/ bcom ldan 'das nyid kyis mngon par mkhyen cing mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas nas chos gcig bka' stsal pa 'di lta ste sems can thams cad zas kyis gnas pa'o zhes gsungs so/ /

It is said that “reincarnating beings abide due to food (āhara).” The Connected Discourses reveals: The Bhagavan stated with perfect comprehension: “If I were to state one thing, having attained complete enlightenment, it would be that all sentient beings abide due to food.”[809]
kham gyi zas ni 'dod pa na/ / skye mched gsum gyi bdag nyid do/ / gzugs kyi skye mched ma yin des/ / rang dbang grol la mi phan phyir/ / 39
Oral food exists in the desire realm and consists of the three bases. The form base is not oral food because it does not benefit its sense faculty nor those liberated. (3:39)

zas kyang bzhi ste/ rags pa dang phra ba'i khams gyi zas dang*/ reg pa'i zas dang*/ yid la sems pa'i zas dang*/ rnam par shes pa'i zas so/ / de dag las dang po kham gyi zas ni{ gong ma gnyis 'dod chags dang bral bas} 'dod pa'i khams kho na na yod de/ de yang dri {sna lce lus gsum gyis kham du bcad cing mid pas de dang 'dod pa'i } ro reg bya'i skye mched gsum gyi bdag nyid do/ / ci ste na/ de dag sna lce lus gsum gyis kham du bcad cing mid nas za ba'i phyir ro/ / kham zas la'ang phra rags gnyis las dang po ni bar srid pa dang 'dod lha dang bskal pa dang po'i mi rnams kyi yin te/ dri za ba'i phyir dang*/ bye ma la til mar blugs pa ltar yan lag gi nang du 'ju bas rgyu mthun med pa'i phyir ro/ / yang na byis pa dang drod gsher skyes la sogs pa sems can phra mo rnams kyis ni phra ba dang*/ de dag las gzhan ni rags pa'o/ / de bzhin du khrus dang bsku mnye la sogs pa gang dag mi mid la lus gnas par byed pa de dag kyang zas phra mo yin no/ / 'o na grib ma dang nyi ma dang me la sogs la yod pa'i reg bya de dag ji ltar zas yin zhe na/ 'di ni phal che ba'i dbang du byas pa yin pas de dag ni ma yin no zhes kha cig 'dod do/{ 'dis ni skye mched gsum phal cher zas su bstan la nyi grib la sogs pa kha cig kham du byed par me ston no/} gal te 'bras chen la sogs pa la yod pa'i gzugs kyi skye mched kyang kham du byas nas mid pas ci'i phyir kham zas ma yin zhe na/

There are four foods: coarse and subtle oral food, the food of contact, the food of mental contemplation, and the food of consciousness. From among those, the first, oral food (kavalīkāra), exists only in the desire realm, {since the two higher realms are free of attachment [to it],} and it consists of the three bases (āyatana): smell, taste, and tactility. Moreover, these are consumed through the nose, tongue, and body, through dividing it into portions and ingesting it. Oral food has two types: (1) subtle and (2) coarse. (1) The first is the food of intermediate beings, desire gods, and humans of the first eon because they eat smells and because they ingest food through their limbs, like sesame oil poured onto sand, without producing excrement. The food of fragile sentient beings such as infants and those born from heat and moisture and so on is subtle. (2) Foods other than those are coarse. Also washing, massage, and so on, which act to maintain the body without requiring ingestion, are also regarded as subtle food. Question: How are tactile objects such as shadow, sunlight, fire, and so on food? Some assert: This claim is from a general perspective, but they are not [actual] food. {Others assert: This indicates that the three bases are food in a general sense, but sunlight, shade, and so on are not taught to be oral food.} Question: Why are instances of the form base such as cooked rice and so on, which are swallowed in portions, not oral food?

Reply: The [visible] form base is not oral food because food benefits the sense faculty and the elements that support it, but the form base does not benefit (anugraha) its eye sense faculty, nor does it benefit the elements that are the support of its sense faculty. If it does not benefit its sense faculty and the elements supporting it when swallowed, how could it benefit other sense faculties and elements? Objection: If tortured by hunger, won’t merely seeing food be of benefit? Reply: Mental satisfaction arises through merely seeing food, and the contact producing that experience of pleasure acts as food. But visible form does not benefit, [244] because if benefit arose by merely seeing form, then nonreturners and arhats who are free from attachment to desire-realm objects would be satisfied by merely seeing food. But it does not benefit those liberated from desire-realm afflictions {because even those without hope for food at present do not benefit from seeing it}. At that time just the {afflicted} contact {or intention} that craves food is asserted to be food. {Pūrṇavardhana says that coarse form is not food because it is not an object of the sense faculties apprehended through contact.[810] This statement is sound. Again, he mentions that since the mental faculty and the phenomena element are not physical, and since the five sense faculties are translucent like light and sound lacks a continuum, they are not food.}

reg dang sems pa rnam shes ni/ / zag bcas zas yin gsum dag na/ / yid las byung dang srid tshol dang / / dri za srid pa bar ma dang / / 40
'grub pa'o 'di la gnas dang ni/ / rten pa rgyas pa'i don du gnyis/ / srid gzhan 'phen dang 'grub pa yi/ / don du gnyis te go rims bzhin/ / 41

Contact, intention, and consciousness that are contaminated are food in the three realms. Mentally created, seekers of existence, smell eaters, intermediate beings, (3:40)
those who establish existence. Two are for supporting and developing minds and mental factors in this life. Two are for the purpose of serially projecting another existence and establishing that existence. (3:41)

bye brag tu smra ba rnams na re zas kyi don ni srid pa gso bar byed pa yin pas reg pa dang sems pa dang rnam par shes pa ni zag bcas kho na zas yin gyi zag med ni srid pa zad par byed pas srid pa'i gnyen po yin pa'i phyir {reg sogs zag med gsum yang } zas ma yin no zhes zer ro/ / {des na khams dang sa skal ba mi mnyam pa'i zag bcas kyis rgyas par byed kyang zas ma yin no/ } de dag gi ngo bo ni bshad zin to/ / de dag khams gsum po dag na yod do/ / 'o na mdo las zas rnams ni sems can byung ba rnams gnas par byed pa dang 'tsho bar byed pa dang*/ srid pa 'tshol ba rnams la phan par byed pa yin no/ / zhes gsungs pa'i{ phyir de'i} byung ba ni skyes pa yin na srid pa 'tshol ba gang zhe na/

Vaibhāṣikas say that food refers to that which nourishes existence, and therefore contact (sparśa), intention (saṃcetanā), and consciousness (vijñā) are food (āhāra) only when contaminated. Uncontaminated states {such as the three states of uncontaminated contact} are not food because they are antidotes to existence; they end existence. The nature of these foods has already been explained, and they exist in the three realms. Question: {Because} a sūtra states: Food sustains and nourishes sentient beings and assists those seeking existence.[811] if those who exist have already been born, who are those seeking existence?

yid kyis rdzus te skyes pa'i phyir pha ma'i mi gtsang ba la mi ltos pas yid las byung ba dang*/ {sngon dus sam } skye ba'i srid pa 'tshol ba'i ngang tshul can yin pa'i phyir srid pa 'tshol ba dang*/ zas su dri phra ba za ba'i phyir dri za dang*/ 'chi ba dang skye ba'i bar na gnas pa'i phyir srid pa bar ma dang*/ skye ba la mngon du phyogs pa'i phyir mngon par 'grub pa'i srid pa zhes bya ba ni rnam grangs su lta'o/ / des na mdo las/ mngon par 'grub pa'i kun sbyor spangs la skye ba'i kun sbyor ma spangs pa la sogs pa mu bzhi gsungs pa'i mu dang po ni phyir mi 'ong khams 'og ma gnyis las 'dod chags dang bral ba dang*/ gnyis pa bar ma dor mya ngan las 'da' ba dang*/ gsum pa dgra bcom pa dang*/ bzhi pa de dag ma gtogs pa'o/ / {bdag cag la sogs pa } yang na byung ba ni dgra bcom pa yin la/ srid pa 'tshol ba ni srid pa dang bcas pa rnams so/ / yang ci'i phyir zas bzhir bstan zhe na/

Reply: They are called mentally created (manomaya) because they are born supernaturally through the mental faculty without relying on the unclean substances of a mother and father; they are called seekers of existence (sambhavaiṣī) because they possess the means of seeking birth existence {or prior existence}; they are called smell eaters (gandharva) because they eat subtle smell as food; they are called intermediate beings (antarābhava) because they abide between death and birth; and they are called beings who establish existence because they manifest birth. These terms are taken to be synonyms. A sūtra declares that there are four possibilities regarding (1) those who abandon the fetter that establishes existence and (2) those who do not abandon the fetter of birth and so on.[812] The first possibility is a nonreturner who is free of attachment to the two lower realms. The second is one attaining nirvāṇa as an intermediate being. The third is an arhat, and the fourth is anyone not belonging to those categories {such as ourselves}. “Mentally created” also refers to arhats, and “seekers of existence” refers to those possessing existence. Question: Again, why are four foods taught?

Reply: (1) Oral food[813] is for developing the body along with its sense faculties, which are the basis for supporting the minds and mental factors supported in this life. (2) Contact is for the purpose of developing just those supported minds and mental factors. Thus two — oral food and contact — are taught first, since their primary [function] is to nourish the birth existence already arisen, like a nursemaid. (3) The food of the mind is for the purpose of projecting (kṣepa) another future existence (bhava). (4) Consciousness is for the purpose of actually [245] establishing future existence through consciousness projected by karma. Thus the latter two are taught serially since they are the main generators of [birth] existence not yet arisen, like a mother. Therefore there are definitely four foods. But this is from a general perspective; oral food and contact also indirectly generate future existence because from them afflicted states arise, and from afflicted states karma is accumulated. A sūtra also declares: Monks, these four foods are the root of illness, tumors, and aching pain. They are the conditions of aging and death.[814] Also sentient beings survive through intention and consciousness. As long as those afflicted by famine have the intention of opening a bag of dust, they will not die,[815] {and as long as they exist near a mass of foam, they will not die}, for it is well known that without hope they will die. And when conjoined with consciousness, the body and mental factors supported by it will develop. {It is often said that if the mother has the intention not to forget the egg she laid on a beach, it does not perish, but if she does forget it, it perishes. However, Vasubandhu says that if that were so, it would follow that the intention of one [being] would become another’s food. Therefore the valid example is that if the [being in the] egg recalls its mother it will not perish, but if it does not recall its mother it will perish.[816] Again, the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra records: Those born from eggs, alligators, and so on survive on the food of mental intention, for if the mother or father is mindful of their offspring, that memory satisfies. Then having grown and survived, they engage in actions to obtain food.[817]}

THE MIND AT THE MOMENT OF DEATH

Severing, linking, free from attachment, degenerating, death, and rebirth are asserted to be mental consciousness alone, and death and rebirth are equanimity. (3:42)

The mind of death has six varieties: (1) the mind severing (cheda) the root of virtue {through wrong view}, (2) the mind linking (saṃdhāna) with that, (3) the mind free from attachment (vairāgya) to realms and levels, (4) the mind degenerating (hāni) from that {through inappropriate attention}, (5) the mind of death (cyuta), {which stops the sense faculties,} and (6) the mind taking rebirth (upapatti) as an intermediate existence and birth existence. Different schools assert the mind of death to be mental consciousness alone, saying it is solely conceptual, while others assert that it is a state of equipoise alone, and still others assert that it is an unclear state.

Master Pūrṇavardhana explains that because of that the minds of birth and death in the [first] three absorptions are access concentrations alone and not actual bases of absorption because those [absorptions] do not possess equanimity.[821]

Also birth and death do not exist in mental equipoise coursing in single-pointed (aikāgra) concentration because {equipoise and} a mind of a different type would then manifest simultaneously; {equipoise is clear, since} it arises from a preparatory state that applies concentration; and it benefits the body {through pliancy}. {Therefore birth and death do not exist in the minds of equipoise of the two higher realms.} Also {the minds of death and rebirth} do not exist {in the three} mindless (acitta) {states, because while abiding there one cannot be harmed}, and because the minds of death and birth relocate and link with other minds, but there is no mind in mindless states. When beings devoid of discernment[822] are born or die, it is said that the mind arises. {Again, they are not born without afflictions.}

Despite those who say death existence has three types, arhats entering nirvāṇa have either of two [neutral] minds that are not declared to be virtuous or afflicted. {If it is asserted that [the arhat] has neutral karmic maturation in the desire realm, then either} the mind governing emanation or that arisen from karmic maturation [is his mind of death]. {If he has no [such karmic maturation], then the mind governing demeanor} [is his mind of death]. These are special cases because these two minds permit severence of the mindstream, since they possess little strength, while other minds possess great strength. Master Pūrṇavardhana observes in his commentary: Some say: Arhats do not attain nirvāṇa through abandoning nonvirtuous {and afflicted states} or through clarifying uncontaminated states. They do not attain nirvāṇa through virtuous minds since contaminated virtue possesses karmic maturation [247] and arhats turn their back on future karmic maturation.[823] Others say: They abandon saṃsāra sequentially: they abandon nonvirtue since they are free of attachment to desire-realm objects, they abandon obscured-neutral states since they are free of attachment to the summit of existence, they abandon virtuous minds since they manifest the unobscured-neutral mind of nirvāṇa, and they abandon unobscured-neutral states by entering the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder.[824]
