Question: In what part of the body does consciousness cease when one dies? Reply: There are those entering the first three birth processes who will take rebirth by proceeding to the three evil lower rebirths, or human or god rebirths, and those not taking rebirth, such as arhats who attain nirvāṇa. If they die gradually (kramacyuta), then, respectively, the minds (manas) of those of lower rebirth depart at death from the feet, humans from the navel, [and] gods and arhats from the heart (hṛdaya). But there is no certainty for those born supernaturally {since the mind and body and all faculties cease instantly when death is instantaneous}. Some say: [The minds of] arhats depart from the crown. Further, since consciousness is formless and undemonstrable, indeed it does not abide in a place. However, when dying, the body faculty subsides in the feet of the body and so on, like the vaporization of water poured on hot stones, and this is called transference of mind. The Compendium of Abhidharma explains: The body of one who has [mainly] engaged in virtue first becomes cold at the feet. The body of one who has [mainly] engaged in nonvirtue first becomes cold at the head.[825] This text indicates only where heat [first] gathers [in the body after death]. Ultimately, however, all [heat] gathers at the heart, and from there foundation consciousness departs. Question: What {causes} sever the vital essence[826] at death?

Reply: That which severs the vital essence (marman) is water and so on, meaning the elements of water, fire, and wind, {which are respectively an excess of phlegm, bile, and wind}. Death occurs through the degeneration of any part of the body through the intense disturbing influence of any element. Further, severence is like the vital essence being struck by sharp weapons. It degenerates through one’s inability to bear that feeling, when that [vital] essence itself can no longer function. Severence is not like wood that is split by ghosts and spirits. Question: Why does the earth element not sever it? Reply: Sentient beings can have imbalances of wind, bile, and phlegm; there is no fourth imbalance. If wind is in excess, the vital essence is severed by wind. If bile is in excess, it is severed by fire. If phlegm is in excess, it is severed by water. Earth is omitted. Some say: This corresponds to the destruction of the physical cosmos. Master Pūrṇavardhana explains that those who perform virtue and do not harm others by oppressing them, as well as gods who die instantaneously, die without severing their vital essence.[827] Therefore death is possible without the vital essence being severed.

{Severence of the vital essence does not exist among gods. However, when devaputras (sons or daughters of the gods) die in the desire realm, [248] there are five possible signs of approaching death: (1) their clothes and (2) ornaments make unpleasant sounds, (3) their physical radiance diminishes, (4) drops of ablution water remain attached to their bodies, (5) and eyes that are open begin to close. There are five sure signs of death: (1) their clothes become dirty, (2) their flower garlands fade, (3) they perspire from both armpits, (4) their bodies emit a bad odor, and (5) the younger gods become dissatisfied with their status.[828] Master Pūrṇavardhana states in his commentary: It is uncertain that all sure signs of death will necessarily occur; indeed, none may occur. But if enumerated there are five signs of death, and these signs occur for five days of the gods.[829] Therefore, though the physical suffering in the hell of Avīci is great, the mental suffering of gods experiencing the signs of death is greater. The Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra records: What suffering is generated if one falls from the heavens? The suffering specific to hell beings does not match even one sixteenth part.[830] Once a god is struck by the signs of death, other younger gods distance themselves. Seated on a central branch of a flowering tree, they proclaim: “Son of the gods, from here you will die and be reborn in the human world of Jambudvīpa. With the plough of faith, you must sow the field of virtue.” He then collapses on the ground and wails: I am like a worm on hot sand! Alas, I will leave the grove of manifold chariots. Alas, I will leave the gently falling waters. Alas, I will leave the devas with their beautiful minds.[831]}

In the context of the birth, abidance, and death of sentient beings, a sūtra declares: The assemblies of sentient beings are stated to be three. What are they? The appropriate assembly, the inappropriate assembly, and the indeterminate assembly.[832]

Āryas and those who commit heinous actions comprise perfect and corrupt assemblies. (3:44cd)

From among sentient beings, āryas and those who commit heinous actions (ānantaryakārina) respectively comprise perfect (samyaṅ) and corrupt (mithyātva) assemblies. Āryas are born in high status and not in lower rebirths and are certain to be emancipated. Those who commit heinous actions are certain to be born in hell immediately after death. The remainder comprise the indeterminate assembly. This completes the explanation of the cosmos of beings.

15. The Physical Cosmos

IN EXPLAINING THE PHYSICAL cosmos, I cannot present every world system without exception here because countless presentations are taught in various sūtras: Some say: World systems are covered by a dome. Some say: World systems are randomly distributed. Some say: World systems lack a covering dome or mantle. Some say: World systems lack a sun and moon, {for example, the field of the array of jewels, activated by the jewel between the eyebrows of a buddha}. Some say: A trichiliocosm is circled by one sun and moon, {for example, the field of Samantabhadra}. Some say: The bodhi tree also is equal in measure to a trichiliocosm. [249]

{'jig rten rnams kyi dbyibs kyang sna tshogs yod de/ phal chen las/ phyogs rnams kun na zhing rnams rgya mtsho snang*/ / la la zlum po la la gru gsum ste/ / de dag la la phyogs na gru bzhir gnas/ / kun kyang las rnams rgya mtshos rnam par bris zhes so/ / 'jig rten 'di yang phal chen las/ gzhi dang snying po me tog gis brgyan pa'i 'jig rten na sangs rgyas rnam par snang mdzad kyi phyag mthil gyi nor bu rin po che'i nang na rnam par shes pa'i khams dang chos kyi dbyings dang nam mkha' dang me dang chu dang sa'i khams rgya mtsho dang me tog tshad med dang phyag mthil gyi rgyud la sogs pa 'jig rten khams ming can nyi shu rtsa lnga yod pa'i bcu gsum par bshad la mi mched 'di'i shar gyi 'dab chags pa na 'jig rten gyi khams khebs pa can dang*/ lho na lhag pa dang*/ nub na rdul bsam pa dang*/ byang na rnam par byung dang*/ byang shar na 'pho bar byed pa dang*/ shar lho na phan pa dang*/ lho nub na kun tu song ba dang*/ nub byang na yongs su dga' ba dang*/ 'og na mi che ba dang*/ steng na zhing khams dbyangs sgrogs zhes bya ba yod par bshad do/ / gling bzhi pa 'di ni bcom pa dang ldan pa zhes bya la/ 'di'i shar gyi 'dab chags pa na gling bzhi pa shin tu bsrungs pa dang*/ lho na bzod par dka' ba dang*/ nub na gnyen dang ldan pa dang*/ byang na seng ge yod pa dang*/ byang shar na rnam par brtsegs pa dang*/ shar lho na dga' ba dang*/ lho nub na snying po dam pa dang*/ nub byang na sa bzang po zhes bya ba yod par gsungs so }

{Also, there are various shapes of world systems because the Avataṃsaka proclaims: In all directions fields appear like an ocean; some are spherical, some triangular, and some have square sides, but all are fully created by an ocean of karma.[833] Also, regarding [Vairocana’s] world system the Avataṃsaka declares: In this world whose base and core are adorned with flowers, and in the precious jewel within the palm of Buddha Vairocana, there are twenty-five well-known world systems, such as the realm of consciousness, the expanse of reality (dharmadhātu), the realms of space, fire, water, and earth, immeasurable oceans and flowers, those in the region of his palm, and so on. When describing the thirteenth world system, then in the eastern sector of this chiliocosm (sahāloka) is the world of the Satisfied (khengs pa can), in the south is Surpassing (lhag pa), in the west is Subtle Contemplation (rdul bsam pa), in the north is Specific Arising (rnam par byung), in the northeast is Transformation (’pho bar byed), in the southeast is Benevolence (phan pa), in the southwest is Complete Pervasion (kun tu song ba), in the northwest is Complete Joy (yongs su dga’ ba), below is None Greater (mi che ba), and above is the buddha-field of Melodious Sound (zhing khams dbyangs sgrogs). The fourth continent is called Victorious (bcom pa dang ldan pa). On the petal to the east of this is the fourth continent Well-Guarded (shin tu bsrungs pa), in the south is Difficult to Bear (bzod pa dka’ ba), in the west is Abode of Friends (gnyen dang ldan pa), in the north is Lion’s Residence (seng ge yod pa), in the northeast is Specific Array (rnam par btsegs pa), in the southeast is Joy (dga’ ba), in the southwest is Holy Essence (snying po dam pa), and in the northwest is Good Ground (sa bzang po).}[834]
WORLD SYSTEM OF A CHILIOCOSM

de'i phyir 'dir bstan pa ni mi mjed kyi 'jig rten gyi khams 'di'i rnam par bzhag pa tsam zhig bstan to/ zhes shes par bya ste/ { 'jig rten gnyis yod pa'i/} sems can gyi 'jig rten bstan pa'i rjes de la snod kyi 'jig rten {te stong gsum } bstan par bya'o zhes mtshamde 'chad pa na snod kyi 'jig rten gyi rim pa dang tshad dang*/ sems can gyi 'jig rten dang*/ tshad nyid bshad pa gsum las s sbyar ba'o/ /

Therefore understand that what is taught here constitutes the principles of the world system of a chiliocosm. {There are two types of world:} the physical cosmos {of the three chiliocosms} is taught first, and then the cosmos of beings associated with it is taught. And in explaining this, there are three headings: the stages and dimensions of the physical cosmos, the cosmos of beings, and explaining its measurements.
dang po [snod kyi 'jig rten gyi rim pa dang tshad]
The stages and dimensions of the physical cosmos
de la snod kyi 'jig rten gyi/ / gnas par 'dod pa'i 'og dag gi/ / rlung gi dkyil 'khor rngams su ni/ / sa ya drug 'bum grangs med do/ / 45
Ābhidharmikas assert that the physical cosmos rests on a wind maṇḍala and that the height of this lower foundation is 1.6 million yojanas and its breadth immeasurable. (3:45)
['di] la'ang gsum yod pa'i
rten ni
THE BASIS

snod kyi 'jig rten rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi steng du gnas par 'dod pa'i mngon pa ba ltar na snod kyi 'og dag gi gzhir gyur pa'i rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi rngams te steng 'og tu ni dpag tshad sa ya {phrag gcig dang } drug 'bum yod la {stong gsum dang mnyam pas } rgyar grangs med pa dang ldan pa sems can spyi'i las kyi stobs kyis 'chags so/ / rlung gi steng du gnas so zhes bya bas khyab 'jug pa rus sbal gyi steng na gnas pa dang*/ dbang phyug pa dbang phyug gi 'dod pa las byung bar 'dod pa la sogs pa sel lo/{ phyogs rgyu kha dog dbyibs dang chad/ / yon tan byed las nges pa'i tshig /ces pa brgyad byas nges par bya'o/ /} rlung de'i ming ni 'jam po zhes bya ba dang*/ dbyibs ni zlum po'o/ / kha dog sna tshogs pa'am/ kha cig ni sngo skyar 'dod la/ yon tan ni tshan po che chen po'i rdo rjes kyang gzhig par mi nus pa{'i sra ba } dang*/ las ni brten pa rnams 'degs pa dang*/ ngo bo ni sa la sogs pa rdzas brgyad kyi rang bzhin yin yang rlung shas che ba'i phyir rlung gi dkyil 'khor zhes brjod do/ /

According to Ābhidharmikas who assert that the physical cosmos (bhājanaloka) rests on a wind maṇḍala, the height of this wind maṇḍala, which acts as the lower foundation of the environment, is 1.6 million yojanas, and its breadth is immeasurable {since it is equal in size to the trichiliocosm}. It is generated by the force of the overall karma of sentient beings. The statement “it rests on wind” refutes the followers of Viṣṇu, who assert that it rests on a turtle, and the followers of Īśvara, who assert it arises through the will of Īśvara. {[This wind] should be ascertained with eight attributes: direction, cause, color, shape, severance, quality, function, and etymology.[835]} The name of that wind is “the smooth one,” its shape is round, its color is varied though some assert it is pale green, its quality [250] is {solidity such that} many great vajras could not destroy it, its function is to raise up that which it supports, and its nature is the essence of the eight substances such as earth. However, since the wind element is dominant it is called “the wind maṇḍala.”
chu rngams 'bum phrag bcu gcig dang / / stong phrag dag ni nyi shu'o/ / phyis ni rngams su 'bum phrag brgyad/ / lhag ma dag ni gser du 'gyur/ / 46
The height of the water maṇḍala is 1,120,000 yojanas. Then a part remains as water 800,000 yojanas in height, and the remainder transforms into gold. (3:46)

de lta bu'i rlung de'i steng du nam mkha' la sprin gser gyi snying po can zhes bya ba 'khrigs pa las char gyi rgyun lo mang por bab pa las chu'i dkyil 'khor 'chags te chu{ 'i dkyil 'khor chags pa} de'i tshad ni rngams su dpag tshad 'bum phrag bcu gcig dang stong phrag dag ni nyi shu yod pa'o/ / {thad kar mi 'bo ba ni las las grub pa ste zas pa zhu ba long gar sdod pa bzhin no/ / yang gla na gnas pa'i rlung gis brten pa'o/ } de lta bu'i chu de{ yun ring por} rlung gis dkrugs pa las{ dus} phyis ni{ chu'i} rngams su dpag tshad 'bum phrag brgyad yod pa'i mtshor gyur te/ / de'i lhag ma {dpangs su } dpag tshad 'bum phrag gsum dang stong phrag nyi shu {khor yug tu sa ya phrag gsum drug 'bum khri dang sum brgya lnga bcu } dag ni mtsho'i steng du gser gyi dkyil 'khor du gyur to/ /

A cloud called “the essence of gold” collects in the space above the wind maṇḍala, and it rains continuously for many years forming a water maṇḍala. The height of the water {maṇḍala that is formed} is 1,120,000 yojanas. {Some say: The water doesn’t overflow since it is contained by karma, just as food that is being digested [temporarily] abides in the intestines. Others say: It is supported by wind like something resting in a basket.} Then the water maṇḍala is churned by the wind {for a long period}. Part of it remains as an ocean {of water} 800,000 yojanas in height, and the remainder transforms into a gold maṇḍala 320,000 yojanas {in height} above the water maṇḍala {3,610,350 yojanas in circumference}.
chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi/ / thad kar 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang / / stong phrag gsum dang brgya phrag ni/ / phyed dang lnga rnams kho na'o/ / 47
The diameter of the gold and water maṇḍalas is just 1,203,450 yojanas. (3:47)
chu de dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gnyis kyi dkyil gyi thad kar ni dpag tshad 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang stong phrag gsum dang brgya phrag ni phyed dang lnga rnams kho na'o/ /
The diameter of the disk of both the gold and water maṇḍalas is just 1,203,450 yojanas.

khor yug tu ni sum 'gyur ro/ / de la lhun po gnya' shing 'dzin/ / gshol mda' 'dzin dang seng ldeng can/ / de bzhin blta na sdug ri dang / / 48
rta rna dang ni rnam 'dud dang / / mu khyud 'dzin ri'o de nas ni/ / gling rnams yin no de dag gi/ / phyi rol na ni khor yug ste/ / 49

The circumference is three times that. Beyond Meru are Yugandhara, Īṣādhara, Khadiraka, as well as Sudarśana, (3:48)
Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, Nimiṃdhara. Beyond these are the continents and outside those is the outer ring. (3:49)

de dag gi khor yug ste mtha' skor du ni sum 'gyur du brtsi ste/ dpag tshad 'bum phrag sum cu rtsa drug dang stong phrag bcu dang brgya phrag phyed dang bzhi'o/ / gal te dkyil 'khor dag tshad mnyam pa ma yin nam ji ltar na rlung gi dkyil 'khor gyi thad kar dang mtha' mar tshad med la chu dang gser la yod ce na/ skyon med de/ rlung ni stong gsum gyi 'og gzhir gnas pa la tshad med par bshad pa yin la/ chu dang gser la tshad bshad pa ni gling bzhi'i 'og gzhir gyur pa'i tshad yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir gling bzhi'i 'og gzhir gyur pa'i rlung la'ang chu dang gser gyi tshad tsam {la bye ba phrag brgya chu zil ltar } yod la/ stong gsum gyi 'og gzhir gyur pa'i chu dang gser la'ang tshad med do zhes shes par bya'o zhes bya ba ni kha cig gi yin no/ / kha cig na re rlung ni stong gsum gyi 'og gzhi gcig tu 'dab chags par 'brel pa'i de la tshad med la/ chu dang gser ni de'i steng du gling bzhi'i 'og gzhir gyur pa zil pa'i thigs pa ltar dum bur chags pa'i phyir te de dag gi tshad bstan pa yin la/ de dag gi bar rnams na ni gling bar gyi mun pa yod de/ gdags pa las/ 'jig rten bar mtshams phan chad du/ / nyi zla de bzhin skar ma dang*/ / rgyu skar tshogs ni rgya chen kun/ / khor yug mi 'da' 'jig rten gyi/ / bar mtshams thams cad mun par 'dug /ces bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir slob dpon rgyal po'i sras kyis kyang khor yug gi phyi rol tu chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor gyi phyogs rer dpag tshad stong nyis brgya brgyad cu rtsa phyed dang brgyad lhag par bshad pa'i phyir dang*/ slob dpon gang ba spel bas kyang*/ gang dag gi re re'i tshad thad kar 'bum phrag bcu gnyis dang zhes bya ba la sogs par bshad pa chu dang gser gyi dkyil 'khor bye ba phrag brgyar gnas so zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes zer te de nyid rigs par blta'o/ / slob dpon 'phags pas ni dkyil 'khor gsum ga la tshad ma gsungs so/ / 'o na chu de dag ji ltar thad kar 'bo bar mi 'gyur zhe na/ kha cig na re sems can rnams kyi las kyi dbang gis mi 'bo ste zas ma zhu ba long du mi ltung ba bzhin no zhes zer ro/ / 'phags pa thogs med ni rlung de ni glo na gnas pa dang*/ 'og gzhir gnas pa gnyis yod pa'i phyir rlung gis brten pas 'bo bar mi 'gyur ro zhes bzhed do/ /

Their circumference or perimeter is calculated as three times that diameter, or 3,610,350 yojanas. Question: Aren’t the maṇḍalas equal in size? How do the water and gold maṇḍalas exist in relation to the wind maṇḍala, whose diameter and limits are immeasurable? Reply: There is no error because wind abides as the lower foundation of the trichiliocosm and that is explained to be immeasurable, while the water and gold maṇḍalas merely extend to the lower foundation of the four continents. Some say: Therefore one should understand that the wind maṇḍala acts as the foundation of the four continents and that is the extent of the {billion} water and gold maṇḍalas {which are like a spray of water}. Also the water and gold maṇḍalas that act as the lower foundation of the trichiliocosm are immeasurable. Others say: Those maṇḍalas related to the single lower foundation of the trichiliocosm are immeasurable. The water and gold maṇḍalas that act as the lower foundation of the four continents above them are measurable because they form spheres like drops of spray. A dark interspace exists between them since Presentation on the World states: The moon and sun and similarly the stars exist up to the interspace of the worlds. The collection of the constellations does not transcend the limit of the entire vastness, and darkness exists in all the interspaces between worlds.[836] Therefore Master Jinaputra also explains that outside the circumference on each side of the water and gold maṇḍalas there are an extra 2,875 yojanas.[837] Master Pūrṇavardhana explains that the diameter of each of those is 1.2 million yojanas [251] and so on. He explains that there are a billion water and gold maṇḍalas.[838] Reply: This assertion appears to be correct. Master Ārya Asaṅga did not state the dimensions of the three maṇḍalas.[839] Question: But why doesn’t the water maṇḍala overflow? Some say: It does not overflow due to the karma of sentient beings, just as food not yet digested does not descend in the intestines. Ārya Asaṅga asserts that the water maṇḍala does not overflow since it is supported by wind, for wind both abides in the lungs and it abides as the lower foundation.[840]
rten bshad pa
Mount Meru and the oceans
['di] la
There are three types [of basis]: the basis that is the mountains, the basis that is the oceans, and the basis that is the continents.
ri bshad pa ni/
THE BASIS THAT IS THE MOUNTAINS

de nas ni yang shar dang lho dang nub dang byang du khams tha ma sdud cing 'byed pa'i rlung gis khol bur dkrugs pas lus 'phags kyi gling la sogs pa rnams 'chags pa yin no/ / de dag thams cad kyi mtha' nas kun du bskor bas gling gi phyi rol na ni khor yug lcags ri ste/ {de'i phyi'i mtha' skor du dpag tshad sa ya phrag gsum dang drug 'bum nyis stong drug brgya nyi shu rtsa lnga yod pa } des ni gling bzhi khor yug tu bskor to/ /gling bzhi po thams cad kyang de lta bu'i tshul gyis dus mnyam du 'chags so/ /

Beyond these mountains, the continents (dvīpa) of Videha [Jambu, Godānīya, and Kuru] form in the east, south, west, and north through the condensing and separating winds churning the minor-level elements into minor material bodies. Outside those elements, beyond them and entirely surrounding them, is an iron mountain outer ring (cakravāḍa). That encircles the outer limit of the four continents {with an outer circumference of 3,602,625 yojanas}. The four continents all form simultaneously due to this method.

bdun ni gser yin de lcags so/ / lhun po rin chen bzhi'i rang bzhin/ / chu yi nang du brgyad khri dag / nub bo de bzhin steng du yang / / 50 dpag tshad dag ni brgyad khri'o/ / brgyad po 'phang du phyed phyed dbri/ / de dag rngams su'ang 'phang dang mnyam/ /

The seven mountains are gold, the outer ring is iron. Meru in essence is the four precious substances. Meru is immersed in water 80,000 yojanas. Also it rises above (3:50)
the water 80,000 yojanas. The height of the eight progressively decreases by half. Their depth is equal to their height. (3:51abc)

ri de dag las mu khyud 'dzin la sogs pa bdun ni gser gyi rang bzhin yin la khor yug de ni lcags kyi rang bzhin no/ {gdags pa las/ shar shel/ nub dngul du bshad do } lhun po ni shar dngul dang lho bai DUr+Ya dang nub shel dmar po dang byang gser te rin chen bzhi'i rang bzhin yin no/ / ri rab kyi ngos rin po che gang gi rang bzhin yin pa de'i 'od kyis de'i ngos kyi nam mkha'ang de'i kha dog tu snang la/ de'i 'od kyis ngos kyi rgya mtsho'ang de'i kha dog tu snang ste/ des na 'dzam bu'i gling gi ngos bai DUr+Ya yin pas de'i 'od kyis 'di'i nam mkha' dang rgya mtsho'ang bai DUr+Ya'i kha dog tu snang ngo*/ / tshad ni ri dgu po thams cad kyang chu'i nang du dpag tshad brgyad khri dag nub po zhes bya ste/ thams cad gser gyi sa gzhi la brten pa'i phyir ro/ / chu'i steng du yang ri rab ni dpag tshad dag ni brgyad khri 'phags pa'o/ / mdo phal cher las ni/ ri rab dpag tshad 'bum drug khri brgyad stong pa dang*/ rgya mtsho'ang dpag tshad brgyad khri bzhi stong par bshad mod kyi/ 'dir ni 'dul ba lung gzhi las/ ri'i rgyal po ri rab ni dpag tshad brgyad khri ni 'og tu gser gyi sa gzhi la thug par 'dug go /dpag tshad brgyad khri ni chu'i steng du byung ste de ltar dpag tshad 'bum drug khri yod do/ / zhes gsungs pa dang mthun par bshad do/ / ri phyi ma brgyad po'i 'phang gi tshad du ni ri rab kyi phyed phri ba gnya' shing 'dzin yin pa la sogs pa phyed phyed dbri bar bya ste/ 'di ltar gnya' shing 'dzin dpag tshad bzhi khri yin pa nas khor yug dpag tshad sum brgya dang phyed dang bcu gsum yin no zhes bya ba'i bar du sbyar te/ des na ri brgyad po'i chu mtshams yan chad kyi 'phang tshad bsdoms pas lhun po'i chu mtshams yan chad kyi 'phang la dpag tshad sum brgya phyed dang bcu gsum gyis ma sleb par shes par bya'o/ / ri de dag thams cad kyi rngams su ste zheng du'ang rang rang gi 'phang dang tshad mnyam ste/ de dag kyang chu'i steng yan chad kyi dbang du byas so/ / des na ri rab dpag tshad brgyad khri pa dang gnya' shing 'dzin bzhi khri pa la sogs pa'o/{ khams ngan pa rnams las ri rab kyi bang rim bzhi dang gling bcu gnyis dang khor yug gi ri rnams grub la gling bcu gnyis ni chu'i gling na gnas so/}

These seven mountains such as Nimiṃdhara and so on are gold [252] in essence, and the outer ring is iron. Meru in essence is made of the four precious substances: silver in the east, vaiḍūrya in the south, red crystal in the west, and gold in the north. {The Treatise on Designation explains that it is crystal in the east and silver in the west.} Each face of Meru radiates the light of the essence of its precious substance, and the space in front of that face appears with that color. Even the oceans appear with that color through that light. Therefore, since the side facing Jambudvīpa is vaiḍūrya, that light makes the sky and the oceans appear as the color of vaiḍūrya. It is said that from among all nine mountains,[843] Meru is immersed in water to a depth of 80,000[844] yojanas and that all [nine] are supported on the golden base. Also Meru rises above the water 80,000 yojanas. Indeed, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra explains that the supreme mountain is 168,000 yojanas [high], and also the ocean is 84,000 yojanas [deep].[845] Here, in [general] conformity with that, Chapters on Vinaya explains: Meru, the king of mountains, exists in contact with the golden base, with 80,000 yojanas below the water and 80,000 yojanas above the water. Thus it measures 160,000 yojanas.[846] The height of the eight outer mountains such as Yugandhara, which is half that of Meru, progressively decreases by half. Thus Yugandhara is 40,000 yojanas, and one applies this on up to the outer ring, which is 312.5 yojanas. Understand that the minimum height of these massifs above the water may not reach 312.5 yojanas when one collates the minimum height of these eight mountains above the water line. Also the depth and breadth of all those mountains is equal to the measure of their height above the water. Therefore Meru is 80,000 yojanas wide, Yugandhara is 40,000 yojanas, and so on. {The four tiers of Meru, twelve continents, and the mountains of the outer ring are created within the inferior realms (hīnadhātu), and the twelve continents exist as continents within the outer sea.}
gnyis pa mtsho bshad pa ni
THE BASIS THAT IS THE OCEANS
de dag bar bdun rol mtsho yin/ / 51
In the seven spaces between these mountains are the oceans. (3:51d)

ri rab nas mu khyud 'dzin la thug pa'i ri de dag gi bar bdun ni rol pa'i mtsho bdun yin te/ klu'i rgyal po rnams rol zhing rtse ba'i gnas yin pa'i phyir de skad du brjod do/ / de dag ni bsil dang zhim dang yang ba dang*/ / 'jam dang dwangs dang dri nga med/ / 'thungs na mgrin dang lto ba la/ / mi gnod yan lag brgyad ldan chu/ / zhes pa'i yan lag brgyad dang ldan pa'i chus gang {zhing*/ dga' bo nyer dga' rtas rgal dang*/ / btang gzung dang ni gzi can dang*/ / yul 'khor bsrung dang nag po che/ / e la'i 'dab ma phyi ma yin zhes pa'i klu chen brgyad rtse } ba'o/ / tshad ji tsam zhe na/

In the seven intervals between these eight mountains, from Meru to Nimiṃdhara, are the seven pleasure oceans. They are so called because they are the abodes of pleasure and sport of the kings of the nāgas. They are full of water that possesses eight qualities, since it is: “(1) cool, (2) delicious, (3) light, (4) smooth, (5) translucent, (6) fragrant, and when drunk (7) the throat and (8) stomach are not harmed, for this water possesses eight qualities”[847] {where eight great nāgas sport: “Nanda, Upananda, Aśvaśīrṣa, Mucilinda, Manasvin, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mahākāla, Elapatra”}. [253] Question: What is their measure?
dang po stong phrag brgyad cu'o/ / de ni nang gi rgya mtsho yin/ / de yi ngos la sum 'gyur ro/ / rol mtsho gzhan ni phyed phyed do/ / 52
The first is 80,000 yojanas. These are inner oceans. The shore of that ocean is three times the breadth. The others are each half of the former. (3:52)

de dag thams cad zabs su ni dpag tshad brgyad khri par mtshungs shing dang po ri rab dang gnya' shing 'dzin gyi bar gyi rol mtsho la kha zheng du dpag tshad stong phrag brgyad cu'o/ / de yang ri rab dang gnya' shing 'dzin gyi bar gyi tshad yin gyi shar nub tu ni{ zhing} dpag tshad nyis 'bum bzhi khri yod pa'i phyir ro/ / nang gi rgya mtsho dang phyi'i rgya mtsho gnyis las rol mtsho bdun po de dag ni nang gi rgya mtsho chen po zhes bya ba yin te/ nang kho nar nges pa'i phyir dang*/ gza' skar la sogs pa'i gzugs brnyan 'char ba dang*/ chu'i gter yin pa'i phyir ro/ / mtsho de'i gnya' shing 'dzin gyi ngos la ni phyogs re re la'ang zheng gi gsum 'gyur ro ste/ dpag tshad ni nyis 'bum bzhi khri pa re re yod la/ rol mtsho gzhan drug ni snga ma snga ma'i phyed phyed kyi tshad de/ rim pa ltar dpag tshad bzhi khri dang nyi khri dang khri dang lnga stong dang nyis stong lnga brgya dang stong nyis brgya lnga bcu yod do/ / de dag gi ngos kyi tshad ni snga ma snga ma bas ches che bar shes par bya'o/ /

Reply: The depth of all those oceans is the same: 80,000 yojanas. The first ocean, between Meru and Yugandhara, is 80,000 yojanas wide. That is the distance from Meru to Yugandhara, but from east to west it is 240,000 yojanas. In general there are both inner and outer oceans, and from among them these seven oceans are called great inner oceans because they are solely ascertained as enclosed oceans. Moreover reflections of the planets and stars and so on appear in them, and they are repositories of water. The shore of that ocean bordering Yugandhara is three times the breadth, or 240,000 yojanas. The other six oceans are in measure each half of the preceding one, because in order they are 40,000, 20,000, 10,000, 5,000, 2,500, 1,250 yojanas. The faces of the preceding are greater than [those of] the later [oceans].
lhag ma phyi yi mtsho chen yin/ / 'bum phrag gsum dang stong phrag ni/ /
The remaining body of water is the great outer ocean, 322,000 yojanas. (3:53ab)

lhag ma mu khyud 'dzin dang khor yug gi bar gyi chu rnams ni phyi'i rgya mtsho chen po yin te/ de'i tshad ni mu khyud 'dzin gyi thel nas khor yug gi thel gyi bar du dpag tshad 'bum phrag gsum dang stong phrag nyi shu rtsa gnyis so/ / mtha' skor gyi tshad ni dpag tshad sa ya phrag gsum dang drug 'bum bdun brgya lnga bcu yod do/ / de ltar brtsis pas khor yug lcags ri'i phyi'i mtha' skor du ni dpag tshad sa ya phrag gsum drug 'bum nyis stong drug brgya nyi shu rtsa lnga yod do/ / phyi'i rgya mtsho de ni ba tshwa can gyi chus gang ngo*/ /

The remaining body of water, from Nimiṃdhara to the outer ring, is the great outer ocean, which measures 322,000 yojanas from the limit of Nimiṃdhara to the limit of the outer ring. Its circumference measures 3,600,750 yojanas, while the outer circumference of the outer iron mountain ring is calculated as 3,602,625 yojanas. The outer ocean is full of salt water.

{The Avataṃsaka declares: From this continent into the outer ocean descends 2,500 streams.[848] And the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra states: They descend like drops falling from the midst of 10 trillion waterfalls. In the northern continent 10,000 descend, in the western continent 5,000, and in the eastern continent 7,500. Still, the body of water arising from the cloud of the nāga king Daśaraśmi is greater. But the body of water that arises from the cloud of Jambudvaja, the son of the nāga Haimavata, is greater than the body of water that arises from the cloud of the nāga king that combines 8 trillion of those. But the body of water that arises from the cloud emanated by Haimavata himself is greater. Yet from all these the river descending from the abode of Haimavata called Vaiḍūrya is vastly greater. But none of them are free from the pollutants of the great ocean.[849] Again, the outer ocean is not moved by waves, it does not accommodate human corpses even for a day, it is a source of inexhaustible elements and precious substances, and one is never satisfied by viewing it because the Sūtra Requested by Brahmaviśeṣacinti declares: A jewel called “that subsuming all precious substances” exists in [the outer ocean]. If it is not moved to other worlds, then the fire of the eon of destruction cannot diminish the great ocean in the least.[850]}

Objection: If that is so, then the statement “The diameter of the gold and water maṇḍalas is just 1,203,450 yojanas”[851] (3:47) would be unacceptable because the distance from the mountains to the ocean up to the outer ring is calculated as just 1,200,875 [254] yojanas. Reply: There is no error because Master Jinaputra asserts that the outer ring is smaller and the gold and water maṇḍalas are larger, since the gold and water maṇḍalas extend beyond each face of the outer ring by 1,287.5 yojanas. That is so for one side, and if both sides are added together it would increase by 2,575 yojanas, making 1,203,450 yojanas.[852] Other earlier masters say: All these mountains exist like mounds of grain, and the height and depth of Meru is equal when calculated from the water line because they do not differ (viśiṣṭa). Also these measurements do not contradict the dimensions previously explained since the basis of the outer ring extends beyond the water and gold maṇḍalas.[853]
The continents

This has two headings: outline, and detailed explanation of the features of Jambudvīpa.

OUTLINE

nyi shu gnyis so de la ni/ / 'dzam bu'i gling ste ngos gsum la/ / 53 stong phrag gnyis so shing rta'i dbyibs/ / gcig la dpag tshad phyed dang bzhi/ / shar gyi lus 'phags zla kham 'dra/ / ngos gsum 'di dang 'dra gcig la/ / 54 dpag tshad sum brgya lnga bcu'o/ /

Jambudvīpa is in that ocean, 2,000 yojanas on three sides (3:53cd) and 3.5 yojanas on one side, the shape of a chariot. Videha is to the east like a half moon with three sides like Jambudvīpa and one that is 350 yojanas. (3:54)

mtsho de la ni{ thog mar lho de nas shar dang nub dang byang dang khor yug rnams rim pa ltar 'grub pa las} ri rab kyi lho na shing 'dzam bus mtshon pa dang mtha' chus 'khor zhing rang gi ngo bo skam sar gnas pas 'dzam bu'i gling ste tshad ni ngos gsum la dpag tshad stong phrag gnyis gnyis yod la ngos gcig ste khor yug la bstan pa la ni dpag tshad phyed dang bzhi yod do zhes sbyar ro/ / ngos dag tshad mnyam pa ma yin nam zhe na ma yin te/ gling 'di ni shing rta'i dbyibs su yod pa'i phyir te/ mtha' skor na dpag tshad stong phrag drug dang phyed dang bzhi yod do/ / de'i dbus su gser gyi sa gzhi la gang du byang chub sems dpa' bzhugs nas rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin bskyed par mdzad pa'i rdo rje'i gdan mngon par 'grub ste/ ting nge 'dzin de ni lus dang sa phyogs gzhan gyis bzod par mi nus so/ /

{Initially, the southern continent is established, then, in order, the eastern, western, and northern continents and the outer ring.} Jambudvīpa is in the ocean to the south of Meru, marked by the rose-apple tree, surrounded by water, and by nature dry ground. Its perimeter is said to measure 2,000 yojanas on three sides and 3.5 yojanas on one side. Question: Those sides are not equal in measure? Reply: No, they are not equal. This continent has the shape of a chariot with a perimeter of 6,003.5 yojanas. At the center [of the continent] there is a golden base where the Bodhisattva actualizes the vajra seat (vajrāsana) through the act of engaging in vajra-like concentration. Such concentration cannot be borne by other bodies or sites.

'di nas shar phyogs kyi ri rab kyi ngos na lus 'phags po zhes bya ba'i gling yod de/ dbyibs ni zla kham 'dra ste bcad kham ni ri rab la bstan pa'o/ / tshad ni de'i ngos gsum la ni 'dzam bu'i gling 'di dang 'dra bar stong phrag gnyis gnyis yod do/ / ngos chung shos{ nang du bstan yang gsung} khor yug la bstan pa gcig la dpag tshad sum brgya lnga bcu'o/ / mtha' skor na dpag tshad stong phrag drug stong dang phyed dang bzhi brgya'o/ / gling de ni gzhan pas shing ta la bdun srid kyis 'phags pa'am der skyes pa'i mi rnams 'di pa bas lus che ba'i phyir lus 'phags po'o/ /

Then the continent called Videha exists to the east of Meru. It has a shape like a half moon measuring 2,000 yojanas on each of three of its sides, like Jambudvīpa, with the straight segment facing Meru.[854] One side, the smallest {said to face outward}, has a length of 350 yojanas, making the circumference 6,350 yojanas. This continent is called “superior body” because humans born there are taller than others by seven tala trees or simply because they have bodies greater in size.

The continent of Godānīya is round, 7,500 yojanas in circumference and 2,500 yojanas in diameter. Kuru is a square with a perimeter of 8,000 yojanas. (3:55)

Then, facing the western side of Meru, there is a continent called Godānīya. It has a completely round shape, with a circumference of 7,500 yojanas and a diameter of 2,500 yojanas. It is called Godānīya (“Utilizing Cattle”) because beings on this continent mainly utilize cattle and make use of its precious substances.

Opposite Meru’s northern face [255] is the continent of Kuru. It measures 2,000 yojanas on each side, 8,000 yojanas in perimeter, with the shape of a square. It is called “unpleasant sound” because for one week prior to their death, sentient beings there hear an unpleasant voice from the sky intoning “You will die,” or else it is because they speak the demonic language of the piśāca. Further, the faces of the humans {as well as the birth existence of females} of any particular continent are similar in shape to that continent. Regarding their dimensions Yogācāra Levels explains: The measure of the western and northern [continents] accord. But the southern and eastern [continents] are, respectively, 6,500 and 7,000 yojanas.[855] {The Throwing Stones Sūtra explains that the [continent] in the east is 8,000, west is 9,000, and north is 10,000 yojanas.[856]}
de yi bar gyi gling brgyad ni/ / lus dang lus 'phags sgra mi snyan / / sgra mi snyan gyi zla dang ni/ / 56 rnga yab dang ni rnga yab gzhan/ / g.yo ldan dang ni lam mchog 'gro/ /
There are eight intermediate continents: Dehas and Videhas, Kurus and Kauravas, Cāmaras and Avaracāmaras, Śāṭhas and Uttaramantrins. (3:56)

gling bzhi po de'i bar gyi gling phran brgyad po rnams ni lus 'phags po'i lho na lus dang byang na lus 'phags zhes bya ba ni lus 'phags po'i gling g.yog yin no/ / sgra mi snyan gyi shar na sgra mi snyan dang nub na sgra mi snyan gyi zla dang*/ gnyis ni sgra mi snyan gyi gling g.yog go /'dzam bu'i gling gi nub na rnga yab dang shar na rnga yab gzhan gnyis ni 'dzam bu'i gling gi gling g.yog yin no/ / ba lang spyod kyi byang na g.yo ldan dang lho na lam mchog 'gro{ zhes bya ba gnas so} gnyis ni ba lang spyod kyi gling g.yog yin no/ /

There are eight minor intermediate continents (antaradvīpa) associated with the four continents. To the south and north of Videha are the companion continents Dehas and Videhas. Then to the east of Kuru is Kurus and to the west is Kauravas. Both are companion continents of Kuru. To the west of Jambudvīpa is Cāmaras and to the east is Avaracāmaras. Both are companion continents of Jambudvīpa. To the north of Godānīya is Śāṭhas and to the south is Uttaramantrins. Both are companion continents of Godānīya.

Some say: Rākṣasas abide in Cāmaras. Reply: However, because they are human [abodes], humans abide in all. These continents are supported on the golden base. Their shape is similar to the main continent, and their measure is not stated in Abhidharma. In Kālacakra it is stated that their measure is half that of their main continents, but it does not state the measure of the main continents nor the distance between them.[857]

To the north of Jambudvīpa there are three black (kīṭa) mountains, then to their north there are another three black mountains, and to their north are three more black mountains, making nine. Beyond them are the glorious snow mountains (himavat). Beyond the snow mountains {on their northern side} is the fragrant (gandhamādana) mountain.[858] Beyond the snow mountains but ten yojanas before the fragrant mountain is the deep-water abode of the nāga king Anavatapta called Lake Anavatapta (“that which never heats up”),[859] which is fifty yojanas wide. It is square in shape, with a circumference of two hundred yojanas. When viewed it is beautiful and handsome and full of water possessing the eight qualities. It is covered with flowers [such as] utpalas, lotuses, kumutas, and white lotuses. The water of Lake Anavatapta rotates to the right and issues from the lake through the four great rivers such as the Gaṅga and five hundred smaller tributaries. Thus its water emerges via the eastern gorge, which is like the mouth of an elephant, from the southern gorge like the mouth of a bull, from the western gorge like the mouth of a horse, and from the northern [256] gorge like the mouth of a lion, and proceeds to the eastern, southern, western, and northern oceans. Presentation on the World observes: The Gaṅga, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Sītā rivers, garlanded with waves and foam, descend rapidly. All are clear water arising from the surrounding four directions. The Gaṅga proceeds to the eastern ocean. The Sindhu proceeds to the southern ocean. The Vakṣu proceeds to the western ocean. The Sītā proceeds to the northern ocean. These four supreme rivers are supremely pure, descend individually, and convey the water of five hundred separate streams to the great ocean.[860]

'grel pa las/ der ni rdzu 'phrul dang mi ldan pa'i mis bgrod par dka'o/ / zhes bshad la/ lung sman gyi gzhi las kyang*/ gnod sbyin gtum po mi bzad gnas pa yid 'ong zhing*/ / me tog sna tshogs shing gis rnam par mdzes byas pas/ / de las rgya mtsho dug can dag tu 'gro ba yi/ / chu bo bzhi po 'di dag phyogs bzhir 'bab/ / gang+gA sin+d+hu de bzhin pak+Shu dang*/ / si ta de la rdzu 'phrul stobs thob pa/ / ma gtogs mi rnams kyis ni mi bgrod pa/ / der ni thob pa dge 'dun bcas pa bzhugs/ / zhes gsungs so/ /

The Autocommentary explains: It is difficult for humans who do not possess supernatural powers to proceed there.[861] Also the Chapter on Medicine remarks: From the appealing abode of fierce, unbearable yakṣas, beautified with various flowering trees, the four rivers of the Gaṅga, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Sītā, descend in the four directions and proceed to poisonous [or salty] seas. Humans cannot proceed there without obtaining supernatural powers. But [Śākya]muni with his Saṅgha abides there.[862]

The Avataṃsaka states: The waters of Anavatapta circle seven times to the right before descending as the four rivers through the elephant gorge and so on, which are colored silver, gold, blue vaiḍūrya, and diamond-like (vajra), before coursing through silver, gold, vaiḍūrya, and diamond sands before finally proceeding to the oceans of the four directions. Those lands that the water touches while it circles are also beautified by various flowers of divine nature, and the bed of Anavatapta is covered with precious stones and ornamented with various jewels, while various jewels are set in its shore as in a wall.[863] Thus it is the source of all the rivers of Jambudvīpa, and all the flowers, fruit, medicinal plants, and forests, as well as all the jewels of the ocean, arise through its might. The Collection of Verses on the Perfection of Wisdom states: In whatever way the rivers descend in Jambudvīpa, the flowers, fruit, medicine, and forests are generated in reliance on the powerful lord nāga abiding in Anavatapta, who is called the glorious mighty lord of the nāgas.[864] And: For example, if there were no lord nāga abiding in Anavatapta, {how could the rivers descend to Jambudvīpa? If there were no rivers, no fruit would arise, and there would be no precious materials in the ocean.}[865] {When the world was formed, a single great tree arose from the condensation of the winds of supreme essential elements to the right [or east] of this lake.} This tree grew on the banks of the lake and was called Jambu (Rose Apple) because it produced sweet fruit [257] that ripened and fell into the water producing the sound jambu. The lords of nāgas emanated as fish and ate the fruit, while the fruit that fell into the water of Anavatapta and remained uneaten turned to gold through contact with the water. Because this tree or its fruit symbolized this continent, it was called Jambu. {The Treatise on Designation explains that it was in the vicinity of the snow mountains.}

Twenty yojanas to the north of the fragrant mountain, there is a golden monolith called Asurapārśva (Face of the Asura). Each face is fifty yojanas, and it is two hundred yojanas in circumference. Extending three and a half yojanas above it is a rock mantle with eight thousand {rock shelters. It is twenty yojanas long and one and a half yojanas wide.} Twenty yojanas to the north of that rock is the king of sāla trees called Airāvata surrounded by seven rings of sāla trees. The roots of the king of the sālas penetrate forty armspans, while the roots of the first row of the seven rings of the garland of trees penetrate thirteen spans, outward to the roots of the seventh [ring], which penetrate seven spans. {The first ring of trees is thirteen yojanas high, outward to the seventh, which is seven yojanas high.} The branches, leaves, and petals of the king of sālas reach the first ring of sālas, and so on outward, until and the branches, leaves, and petals of the sixth ring reach the seventh ring of sālas. Therefore they fully cover the sky.

Twenty yojanas to the east of that tree is a lake called Gently Cascading Pool, each side fifty yojanas wide, making a circumference of two hundred yojanas, and it is surrounded by eight thousand companion pools. The elephant Airāvata, fearless in Indra’s battles, is accompanied by eight thousand companion elephants. They live for the four months of winter at the golden monolith called Asurapārśva, for the four months of spring near the king of sāla trees called Airāvata, and for the four months of summer at Gently Cascading Pool. {His body measures two and a half yojanas long, a yojana wide, and one and a half yojanas tall, and he is ringed by seven rows of elephants. His body is white and head blue, with six red tusks. When he proceeds to other places, he emanates either an ordinary or divine supernatural being, who is mounted upon the supreme elephant, and proceeds with a great fanfare of cymbals and so on. When he abides at [his destination], his retinue faces inward, and he eats lotus roots to a depth of seven layers.}

Again, in the west of this continent, vidyādharas live in the palace of Uḍḍiyāna Mahāvajra. In the land of the southern ocean, Ārya Avalokiteśvara is seated at the summit of the Potala, at its base is the residence of Venerable Tārā, and the residence of Ārya Mañjuśrī is Wutaishan. The buddhas of the three times [258] take their seats in the central region of Vajrāsana, which is not destroyed by fire, water, or wind, {and there are six great cities[866]}. Again, in Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great regions {in the outer regions: China (rgya yul), Mongolia (hu na), Persia (phu na), Kāmpoche (kam po rtse), Kāśmīr (sha kha), Southern Mongolia (sbal kha), Land of the Dog-Faced (khyi gdong), Land of the Fox-Faced (wa gdong), Land of the Pox-Faced (grib sha’i gdong), Land of the Sky-Faced (gnam gdong), Land of Those Who Turn Their Faces Away (phyir phyogs gdong), Land of the Cleaved Obstacle (gshog thogs), Land of the Naked (gcer bu), Land of Those Who Travel Deceptively (sgyus te ’gro ba), Land of the Small Nosed (sna med), and Land of Wool (klag kra)}, 1,000 smaller regions, 360 different races of men, and 720 different languages.

ngan song gi gnas ni

Twenty thousand yojanas below Jambudvīpa is Avīci, with uniform dimensions. Above it are the seven hells. All eight have sixteen additional hells. (3:58)
THE DOMAINS OF HELL BEINGS

Regarding the evil abodes, 20,000 yojanas below Jambudvīpa is the upper limit of the great hot hell of Avīci. Because this abode is 20,000 yojanas {in each direction} and square, it is said to have the uniform dimensions. {Question: How can it exist within this continent? Reply: The continents are not immeasurable but abide like a mass of grain;} therefore the lower foundation exists 40,000 yojanas below this continent. {Jñānaśrī says it is below Meru.} It is called Avīci (Incessant Torment) because the sentient beings abiding there suffer continuously since their suffering is without respite. Seven hells exist above Avīci: Pratāpana (Intensely Burning), Tapana (Burning), Mahāraurava (Great Wailing), Raurava (Wailing), Saṃghāta (Crushing), Kālasūtra (Black Line), and Sañjīva (Reviving), stacked one above the other. Some say: The seven hells exist adjacent to Avīci. {This is stated in a commentary on Abhidharma.[867]}

Also all eight hot hells have sixteen {surrounding hells}, each {differentiated as} additional hells according to their direction. Question: What are they?
de dag gi ni ngos bzhi na/ / me ma mur dang ro myags dang / / 59 spu gri'i lam sogs chu bo yin/ / chu bur can sogs grang brgyad gzhan/ /
There are four in the four directions: Kukūla, Kuṇapa, Kṣuramārga, and so on. Beyond is Vaitaraṇī. Arbuda and so on are the eight distinct cold hells. (3:59)

Reply: There are four in each of the four directions outside the hot hells. {The four are, respectively:} (1) When beings escape from the actual sufferings of the hot hells, they sink up to their knees in the trenches of Kukūla (Burning Embers). The beings who proceed there lose the skin, flesh, and blood of their legs, and only the bones remain. But if they raise their legs, the flesh grows back again. (2) When they cross those trenches they then sink up to their waists in the mire of feces called Kuṇapa (Rotting Mire). For those hell beings who proceed there, worms with white bodies and black heads called “sharp beaks” [260] remove the flesh down to the bone with their iron beaks. (3) Those who escape from there then proceed on the path full of extremely sharp {razors} called Kṣuramārga (Razor Path), which is also known as the Śastracakra (Weapon Wheel.) When they put their feet down, the flesh and blood is stripped from their feet but it is regenerated when they raise them. The “and so on” refers to the forest of sword-leaves that sever the major and minor limbs when the sharp sword-leaves fall. It also refers to the dogs with iron fangs {who drag beings down and rip open [their flesh] exposing their spines}. When sentient beings climb the iron śalmalī trees, sharp thorns sixteen finger-widths long turn downward, and when they descend, those thorns turn upward, piercing their bodies. Above, crows with iron beaks called “wings of terror” pick out sentient beings’ eyes and eat them. These are counted as one “wheel of weapons.” Therefore, Pūrṇavardhana writes in his Commentary: Dogs exist in the sword forest; birds with iron beaks exist in the śalmalī forest.[869]

de'i pha rol na thal tshan gyi chu bo rab med pa yod de der dmyal ba dag 'bras 'tshed pa bzhin du 'tshed pa yin no/ / {lcags kyi drwa bar bcug nas lcags bsregs kyis gzhi la gan rkyal du bzhag nas srung ma dag gis ci 'dod dris pa na/ bdag cag gis kyang mi shes mi mthong ste/ 'on kyang bdag bkres so zhes zer ba dang thu lum 'bar dang zangs zhun khar blug pas kha lkog rgyu ma bsreg pa'i sdug bsngal myong ste/ 'di dag gi rgyu yang rim pa bzhin bslab pa nyams pa dang log 'tsho spyad pa dang*/ chos kyi stegs 'jig pa dang*/ bag phab la gnod pa byed pa dang*/ chu la gnas pa gsod pa la sogs pa'o/ / srung ma de dag sems can yin min zhe na bye brag smra ba/ sems can yin te des byas pa'i las de yang dmyal ba de nyid du smin no zhes 'dod do/ / de dag dmyal mes mi 'tshig pa ni las kyis mtshams bcad pas so zhes so/ / mdo sde pa las kyi dbang gis 'byung ba nyid sems can ltar snang bas gzugs su 'dod do/ / sems tsam pa rang gi sems su 'dod pa nyid legs so }

Beyond that is the (4) Vaitaraṇī (Unfordable River). It consists of boiling water and ashes, where hell beings are cooked like rice. {Hell guardians trap the hell beings in iron nets, burn them with iron, place the beings on hearths on their backs, and question the hell beings as to what they want. When the hell beings reply “We do not know, we do not see, but we are hungry,” the guardians pour blazing iron balls and melted copper into their mouths, and the hell beings experience the pain of burning mouths, stomachs, and intestines. The cause of these sufferings is casting aside ethical training, engaging in wrong livelihood, destroying the ford of Dharma, harming those who slacken their effort, killing those who abide in water, and so on. Question: Are these guardians sentient beings or not? Vaibhāṣikas assert that they are sentient beings since the karma committed by them will mature on them as hell beings. They are not burned by the fires of hell since their karma places a limit on those fires. Sautrāntikas assert that they are form appearing as sentient beings and arising through the power of karma. Cittamātrins assert that they are the minds of each being. This assertion is best.}

de ltar na phyogs re na bzhi bzhi'i bye brag gis bcu drug tu bgrang ngo*/ / de dag ni gnod pa lhag pa'i gnas yin pa'i phyir lhag pa zhes bya ste/ dmyal ba chen po dag tu gnod pa byas na yang 'di dag tu gnod pa byed pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag la ni nye 'khor ba'i dmyal ba zhes kyang bya ste/ yongs su gdung ba dang bcas pa dang yongs su gdung ba med pa bstan pa'i mdo las/ yang sos dang ni thig nag dang*/ / bsdus 'joms ngu 'bod gnyis dang ni/ / tsha ba rab tu tsha ba dang*/ / mnar med pa zhes bya ba ste/ / de ltar de dag dmyal ba ni/ / brgyad ces bya ste rgal bar dka'/ / drag po'i las kyis kun tu gang*/ / re re la yang lhag bcu drug /rtsig pa bzhi dang sgo bzhi ste/ / rnam phye ris su chad pa yin/ / lcags kyi rwa bas kun tu bskor/ / lcags dag gis ni gang ba yin/ / de na lcags 'bar sa gzhi ste/ / 'bar ba'i me dang ldan pa yin/ / dpag tshad brgya phrag du mar ni/ / me lce dag gis khyab par gnas/ / zhes gsungs pa yin no/ /

Thus these hells are sixteen in number since there are four each for each direction. They are called “additional hells” because they are abodes of additional harm: beings are harmed in the great hells and they are harmed again in these [adjacent] abodes. They are also called “surrounding hells” because the Sūtra Teaching the Tormented and Untormented states: The abodes of Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, both Rauravas, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci are called the eight hells. They are difficult to cross and continuously full due to the strong negative karma of beings. There are sixteen additional hells with four walls and four doors open to the unfortunate. They are completely surrounded by an iron fence and pervaded by the iron of the blazing iron ground that is engulfed in blazing flames spreading [261] tongues of fire for many hundreds of yojanas.[870]

The cold hells are (1) Arbuda (Blistering), where the body is tormented by extreme cold. “And so on” refers to (2) Nirarbuda (Bursting Blisters), which is even colder than Arbuda. (3) Aṭaṭa (Chattering Teeth) is where beings endure the chattering of teeth through the torment of extreme cold. (4) Hahava (Wailing and Sneezing) is colder than Aṭaṭa. (5) Huhuva (Wailing and Lamenting) is still colder. (6) Utpala is where physical wounds open like the petals of an utpala flower that crack due to the extreme cold. (7) Padma (Lotus) is even colder than Utpala, where one’s wounds open like the petals of a lotus. (8) Mahāpadma (Great Lotus) is even colder than Padma, where one’s wounds open more widely, like the petals of a lotus that crack due to the extreme cold. Thus the eight cold hells are distinct from the hot hells. The names of five of the hells — the first two and last three — correspond to the physical form that [hell beings] take, and the remaining three correspond to the cries they make. Such beings live within the dark frozen wastes directly to the north of the hot hells beneath Jambudvīpa. Master Pūrṇavardhana asserts that the eight cold hells exist as if surrounding the outer edge of the Sañjīva hell and so on. His commentary states: Some say: They are cold since they exist near the great ocean. Some say: The abodes of the cold hells exist together in darkness outside the outer ring of mountains surrounding the four continents.[871] Yogācāra Levels declares: The Arbuda hell exists forty thousand yojanas directly beyond the Sañjīva hell. The other seven cold hells each exist in stages two thousand yojanas below that.[872]

{'di dag tu skye ba'i rgyu ni rten gsum gyi na bza' bshus pa dang chos 'chud pa'i mdun khang bshig pa dang pha ma dang sdug bsngal ba'i gos bshus pa la sogs pa yin no/ / grang dmyal las tsha dmyal sdug bsngal che la/ spyir dmyal ba'i sdug bsngal la bshes spring las/ 'di na nyin gcig mdung thung sum brgya yis/ / rab tu drag btab sdug bsngal gang lags pa/ / de yis dmyal ba'i sdug bsngal chung ngu yis/ / 'ol yang mi bgyid char yang mi phod do/ / zhes bshad do }

{The cause of being born there is stripping the robes from the three beings, destroying abodes for practicing Dharma, stripping the clothes from one’s parents and those who are suffering, and so on. The hot hells have greater suffering than the cold hells. In general, regarding the sufferings of hell, Letter to a Friend says: The suffering that arises in one day from being fiercely stabbed by three hundred spears does not match nor resemble the least suffering of hell.[873]}

de ltar na tsha grang gi dmyal ba de dag so so'i las gang las byung ba ni dran pa nyer gzhag la sogs pa'i mdo las shes par bya ste yi ge mangs su dogs nas ma bris so/ / nyi tshe ba'i sems can dmyal ba ni mi'i yul gyi mya ngam gyi thang stong pa la sogs pa{ dang rgya mtsho'i 'gram dang 'og na'ang yod pas} na{ nges pa med cing} nyin zhag re la dmyal ba dang mtho ris kyi bde ba 'dren mar myong ba ste/ lung ko lpags kyi gzhi las/ nyin par gzhan gyi srog gcod cing*/ / nub mo tshul khrims yon tan ldan/ / las de'i 'bras bya bzang po dang*/ / sdig to 'di ni myong ba yin/ / zhes pa dang*/ mtshan mo byi ba byed la chags/ / nyin par tshul khrims yon tan ldan/ / las de'i 'bras bu bzang po dang*/ / sdig to 'di ni myong ba yin/ / zhes nyi tshe ba dag gis tshong dpon gro zhun skyes la smras pa bzhin no/ / de dag gis ni dmyal ba bshad zin to/ /

The karma from which each of these sufferings of the hot and cold hells arises may be understood from sūtras such as the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra and so on,[874] but for fear of being long-winded, I have not written them down here. Sentient beings of the occasional hells each day and night experience alternately the suffering of the empty desolation of the plains, {ocean shores, or underground} of human realms and the pleasure of higher rebirth, {but there is no certainty}. The Chapter on Hides declares: Those who take the lives of others during the day but possess ethics after sunset experience benefit and harm as the results of that karma.[875] And also: Those who are attached to the act of rape at night but possess ethics during the day experience benefit and harm as the results of that karma.[876] The lives of the beings of the occasional hells are illustrated by stories of the trader Śroṇa [Koṭikarṇa]. This [262] completes the explanation of the hells.
yi dwags kyi gnas bshad pa/
THE DOMAINS OF GHOSTS

yi dwags kyi gnas kyi rtsa ba { ni rgya mtsho chen po yin la de dag gi} rgyal po'i khab ni 'dzam bu'i gling 'di nyid kyi 'og dpag tshad lnga brgya 'das pa na yi dwags kyi grong khyer ser skya zhes bya ba yod de/ de na yi dwags kyi gtso bo chos kyi rgyal po gshin rje zhes bya ba 'phen byed mi dge bas byas shing rdzogs byed dge bas byas pa lha'i dpal lta bu myong ba zhig yod de/ {kha 'thor ba ni lha mi'i gnas na'ang yod de/ thang dang chu dang nam mkha'i spyod yul pa dag yin no/ / rgyal po } de'i 'khor na yi dwags kyi ris sum cu rtsa drug yod par dran pa nyer gzhag las bshad de/ 'di ltar/ lto gug kha khab ltar phra dang*/ / bshang za kun ston dri za dang*/ / chos za sbyin pa za ba dang*/ / chu 'thung bsam pas 'tsho ba dang*/ / mchil ma za dang phreng ba za/ / khrag za sha za bdug pa za/ / drag shul spyod dang glags lta dang*/ / sa 'og gnas dang mthu bo che/ / mtshan mo lus 'bar mi glags lta/ / 'dod gzugs gling bar gnas pa dang*/ / gshin rje'i dbyug pa byis pa za/ / tshangs srin 'bru yi shun pa za/ / mi gtsang za dang lam chen gnas/ / mang du za dang me 'dag za/ / dug za dgon par gnas pa dang*/ / dur khrod gnas dang shing la gnas/ / lam gyi bzhi mdor gnas pa dang*/ / bdud kyi sde ste sum cu drug / ces bya ba dag yin no/ /

The root abode of ghosts is {the great ocean}. The city of ghosts is called Kapila and exists five hundred yojanas below Rājagṛha in Jambudvīpa. The principal ghost is the Dharma king called Yāma, born there through nonvirtuous projecting karma but whose experience is like that of a glorious god through virtuous completing karma. {Various wandering ghosts also live in the abodes of humans and gods and inhabit the plains, waters, and sky.} There are thirty-six types of ghosts in the retinue {of the king} explained in the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra, which states: (1–2) Those whose gullets or mouths are narrow like a needle, (3) those who eat feces, (4) those who reveal all, (5) those who eat odors, (6) those who partake of Dharma, (7) those who eat offerings, (8) those who survive thinking they are drinking water, (9) those who eat saliva, (10) those who eat garlands, (11) those who drink blood, (12) those who eat flesh, (13) those who eat incense, (14) those who engage in fierce practices, (15) those who seek opportunity, (16) those who live underground, (17) those who engage in black magic, (18) those whose bodies blaze at night, (19) those who do not seek opportunity, (20) those who live in desire lands, (21) those who live in form lands, (22) those who live in sanctuaries, (23) those who are the cudgels of Yāma, (24) those who eat children, (25) those who are Brahma rākṣasas, (26) those who eat husks of grain, (27) those who eat what is unclean, (28) those who live on highways, (29) those who eat frequently, (30) those who eat charcoal, (31) those who eat poison, (32) those who live in forests, (33) those who live in cremation grounds, (34) those who live in trees, (35) those who live at crossroads, (36) the class of māras. These are the thirty-six.[877]

sa'i dngos gzhi las ni bkres skom gyis gdungs nas chu klung la sogs par phyin pa na skyes bu mtshon cha sna tshogs thogs pas srung ba dang*/ chu la sogs pa'ang rnag khrag tu mthong ste longs spyad du mi rung bar 'gyur ba zas skom la phyi rol gyi sgrib pa yod pa dang*/ gzhan gyis gegs ma byas par zas skom rnyed kyang kha dang mgrin pa dang rkang lag phra zhing lto che ba la sogs pas longs spyad par mi nus pa zas skom la nang gi sgrib pa yod pa dang*/ yi dwags me lce'i phreng ba can dang*/ ljan ljin za ba la sogs pa kha cig gi zas skom gyis lus 'tshig pa dang*/ bshang gci la sogs par 'gyur ba dang*/ kha cig rang gi sha bcad cing za ba tsam las bza' btung bsod pa longs spyad par mi nus pa zas skom la sgrib pa yod pa zhes bya ba yi dwags kyi rigs gsum bshad do/ kha 'thor ba ni de dag las 'phros pa ste/ mkha' la rgyu ba'i yi dwags rdul khrod kyi sha zar bgrang ba la sogs pa rnams yin no/ / yi dwags kha 'thor ba ni mya ngam gyi thang la'ang yod par bshad de/ ko lpags kyi gzhi de nyid las/ bdag cag ngag rtsub khro ldan zhing*/ / bdag cag ser snas 'jungs pas na/ / sbyin pa cung zad ma btang des/ / bdag cag yi dwags 'jig rten lhags/ / zhes pa dang*/ nad med rgyags pas myos pa dang*/ / lang tsho longs spyod dregs myos ste/ / sbyin pa cung zad ma btang des/ / bdag cag yi dwags 'jig rten lhags/ / zhes gro zhun skyes rgya mtsho'i 'gram du 'khyams pa la yi dwags rnams kyis smras pa yin no/ /

Yogācāra Levels mentions three types of ghost: (1) Those who have external obstructions to food and drink are those tormented by hunger and thirst who proceed to places such as rivers but cannot consume food they find since it is guarded by beings brandishing various weapons, or the water and so on appears to them as pus and blood. (2) Those who have internal obstructions to food and drink are those who find food and drink offered to them by others but who cannot consume it since their mouths, throats, feet, and hands are tiny but their stomachs large and so on. (3) Those whose tongues are garlanded by fire and those who eat filth and so on are obstructed from food and drink and cannot consume it since food and drink burns their bodies, or it turns into feces, and so on. Some cut off their own flesh to eat, for they cannot make use of pleasant food and drink since they are obstructed from such solid and liquid nourishment.[878] Supplementary to these ghosts are beings who wander, such as ghosts who fly, spirits who wear rags and eat meat, and so on. Wandering ghosts are said to also exist in the desert plains. The Chapter on Hides states: Due to our harsh words, wrath, avarice, and miserliness, we did not give in the least and now languish as ghosts in mundane realms.[879] And: Intoxicated with pride in our health and intoxicated with youth, resources, and haughtiness, we did not give in the least and now languish [263] as ghosts in mundane realms.[880] This was related to Śroṇa by ghosts when he wandered on the shores of the ocean.

bye brag tu smra ba ni dmyal ba na'ang yod par 'dod de/ dmyal bsrungs gshin rje rnams yi dwags kyi sder gtogs pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir slob dpon chos ldan rab 'byor gyis 'gro ba drug gis tshig le'ur byas pa las kyang*/ gang dag khro zhing gtum las dang*/ / sdig la mngon par dga' ba dang*/ / sdug bsngal ba la dga' de dag gshin rje'i srin por skye bar 'gyur/ / zhes bshad do zhes 'dod do/ /

Vaibhāṣikas assert that they also exist in the hells because māras guarding the hells belong to the realm of ghosts. Therefore Master Dhārmika Subhūtighoṣa also explains in his Verses on the Six Types of Reincarnation: Those who take joy in fierce and wrathful deeds as well as immorality, and who take joy in inflicting pain, are born as rākṣasas of Yamarāja.[881]

mdo sde pa na re de na dmyal ba min pa'i sems can ni med de/ mi dge ba'i dbang 'bras phyi rol gyi don nyid gshin rje'i skyes bu dang lcags kyi khyi dang khwa ta 'dab 'jigs la sogs par snang ba'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

Sautrāntikas say that sentient beings who are not hell beings do not exist in the hells. As such, external phenomena that appear as māras, iron dogs, crows called “wings of terror,” and so on do so through the power of [the hell beings’] nonvirtue.

rnal 'byor spyod pa pa dang dbu ma pa rnams ni de ltar gnas la sogs pa nges par bstan pa ni sems can de dag gi bsam pa dang mthun par bshad pa yin gyi/ de dag na dmyal ba ma gtogs pa'i sems can gzhan dag kyang yod pa ma yin la/ phyi rol gyi don yang ma yin gyi/ rang gi sems nyid mi dge ba'i stobs kyis gshin rje'i srin po dang*/ lcags bsregs kyi sa gzhi dang me 'bar ba dang 'jigs pa'i snang bar skyes nas gdung bar byed do zhes 'dod de/ spyod 'jug las/ sems can dmyal ba'i mtshon cha rnams/ / su zhig gis ni ched du byas/ / lcags bsregs sa gzhi su yis byas/ / me tshogs de dag ci las byung*/ / de 'dra de dag thams cad ni/ / sdig sems byung bar thub pas gsungs/ / zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/ /

Yogācāras and Mādhyamikas explain that such abodes and so on are said to exist to conform with the ideas of sentient beings, but only hell beings exist in the hells and no other sentient beings, and even these have no external reality, for hell beings are tormented by the fearful appearance of the rākṣasas of Yamarāja, and by the burning iron grounds and blazing fires that are generated by the power of their nonvirtuous minds. Engaging in the Deeds of a Bodhisattva states: Who created the beings and the weapons of hell for such purposes? Who created the burning iron ground? From where do the billowing flames arise? The Sage has stated that all these arise from an evil mind.[882]
THE DOMAINS OF ANIMALS

The main abode of animals is the external ocean,[883] but dispersed populations live in the abodes of humans and gods. Vaibhāṣikas assert that animals exist even in hell.
