rgyal chen ris bzhi pa dang sum cu rtsa gsum pa gnyis ni dbang po gnyis sprad pas lha'i bu dang bu mo gnyis 'khrig pa spyod de 'on kyang sa{ de dag gi zas la mi gtsang ba'i rgyu mthun med pas} bon 'byung ba ni med de rlung rgyu bas gdung ba dang bral bar gnas so/ / 'thab bral ba ni 'khyud pa tsam dang*/ dga' ldan pa lag pa bcangs pa dang*/ 'phrul dga' ba rgod pa tsam dang*/ gzhan 'phrul dbang byed pa bltas pa tsam gyis 'khrig pa spyod pa yin no/ / bye brag tu smra ba rnams na re ji tsam du yul shas che ba de tsam du 'dod chags shas che ba'i phyir thams cad kyang gnyis kyis gnyis spras nas 'khrig pa spyod pa yin te/ dbang po gzugs can rnams ni yul so sor nges pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / gdags pa las bshad pa ni/ dus kyi tshad bstan pa yin no zhes zer ro/ /

Reply: In the two heavens, Cāturmahārājika and Trāyastriṃśa, gods engage in sexual union through both sons and daughters of the gods joining both organs. However, {since their food is not the compatible cause of feces,} there is no emission of semen, and they quell their passion through the release of winds. In the Yāma heaven, they engage in sexual union through merely embracing; in Tuṣita, through holding hands; in the heaven of Nirmāṇarati, through laughter; and in the heaven of Paranirmitavaśavartin, by merely observing each other. Vaibhāṣikas say that the more pleasurable the object, the more intense the attachment. Therefore all the gods engage in sex through both gods joining both organs, where the physical organs are ascertained as separate pleasurable objects. The explanation in Presentation on the World is in terms of duration of the act.[938]
gal te sa bon 'byung ba med na lha'i bu dang bu mo zhes ji ltar brjod ce na/
Question: If no semen is produced, how can they be called sons or daughters of the gods?
byis pa lo lnga lon pa nas/ / lo bcu lon pa lta bu'i bar/ / 70 de dag tu skye gzugs can rnams/ / kun rdzogs gos dang bcas pa nyid/ /
Progeny similar to children five to ten years old are born in those heavens. Form-realm gods are born with complete bodies, fully clothed. (3:70)

{rgyal chen rigs bzhir } bong tshod byis pa lo lnga lon pa nas{ sum cu rtsa gsum dang 'thab bral dang dga' ldan dang 'phrul dga' dang gzhan 'phrul dbang byed rnams su rim pa ltar lo drug dang bdun dang brgyad dang dgu dang} lo bcu lon pa lta bu'i bar gyi lha'i bu dang bu mo dag rgyal chen ris bzhi la sogs pa de dag tu lha dang lha mo'i pang du rdzus te myur bar skye ste/ de'i phyir gang zhig gang dag gi pang du skyes pa de de dag gi lha'i bu dang bu mo zhes brjod do/ / de la rgyal chen ris bzhir ni lo lnga lon pa dang*/ sum cu rtsa gsum du lo drug dang*/ 'thab bral du lo bdun dang*/ dga' ldan du brgyad dang*/ 'phrul dgar dgu dang*/ gzhan 'phrul dbang byed du bcu lon pa lta bu'o/ / gzugs can gyi lha rnams ni bongs tshod lus kun rdzogs pa dang*/ {ngo tsha khrel med spangs pas } gos dang bcas pa nyid du skye'o/{ 'chi ba na'ang gos bcas su 'chi'o/} gzugs khams pa'i lha thams cad kyang rdzun spangs pa'i phyir bden par smra bas 'phags pa'i skad du smra ba yin no/ /

Reply: Sons or daughters of the gods, similar in size to children five to ten years old, are instantly and supernaturally born in the laps of the daughters of the gods in those heavens such as Cāturmahārājika. Because they are born in the laps of the gods, [278] they are called sons or daughters of the gods. In the heaven of Cāturmahārājika, they are like children five years old; in the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa, they are like children six years old; in Yāma, they are like children seven years old; in Tuṣita, they are like children eight years old; in the heaven of Nirmāṇarati, they are like children nine years old; and in the heaven of Paranirmitavaśavartin, they are like children ten years old. The form gods are born with complete, full-sized bodies that are fully clothed {since they have abandoned shamelessness and nonembarrassment. Also when they die, they die fully clothed.} Moreover, because all gods of the form realm abandon lying and speak the truth, they speak the language of the āryas.
sems can gyi khyad par la 'dod pa skye ba ni
The arising of desire differentiates sentient beings.
'dod pa skye ba gsum po ni/ / 'dod pa'i lha dang mir bcas rnams/ / 71 bde ba skye ba gsum po ni/ / bsam gtan gsum la sa dgu yin/
Three types of desire arise among desire gods and humans. Three types of pleasure arise as nine since there are three for each absorption. (3:71)

A sūtra explains the arising of three types of desire,[939] and these three types of desire arise among desire gods and humans: (1) desire-realm humans and the four types of god up to Tuṣita abide with desire and generate desire for objects controlled by Īśvara. {Further, they utilize whatever arises from the maturation of their karma.} (2) Gods of Nirmāṇarati generate the desire to control their emanations. {Further, they utilize their emanations in accordance with their desire.} (3) Gods of Paranirmitavaśavartin generate the desire to control others’ emanations. {Further, they control both theirs and others’ emanations in accordance with their desire.}

bde ba skye ba ni/ mdo las/ { gsungs pa'i/} dben pa las skyes pa'i bde ba dang*/ ting nge 'dzin las skyes pa'i dga' ba'i bde ba dang*/ dga' ba med pa'i bde ba skye ba gsum bshad pa'i bde ba skye ba gsum po ni bsam gtan dang po gsum re re las gsum gsum yod pas sa dgur bshad pa rnams yin te/ de la bsam gtan dang po'i gsum ni 'dod pa las dben pa las skyes pa'i bde ba dang*/ gnyis pa'i gsum ni { rtog dpyod spangs pa'i} ting nge 'dzin las skyes pa'i dga' ba'i bde ba dang*/ gsum pa'i gsum ni dga' ba med pa'i bde ba yin/{ pa'i phyir ro 'dod pa'i mi ni de lta ma yin no/} gal te de lta na dang po'i bsam gtan khyad par can skyes pa de bde ba skye ba ma yin par 'gyur te/ btang snyoms kyi sa pa yin pas dga' ba de med pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ bye brag tu smra ba rnams na re 'di ni phal che ba bstan pa yin te/ dper na mdo{ rab tu byed pa} las/ mngon par shes pa gang zhe na/ shes rab dge ba{ yin no} 'o/ zhes 'byung ba bzhin no zhes zer ro/ / gal te 'di nas rgyal chen ris bzhi la sogs pa gong ma rnams brtsegs te gnas na {gang dag lha'i gnas nyi shu rtsa gnyis bshad pa } de dag gi bar thag gi tshad ji tsam zhe na/

A sūtra explains the arising of three types of pleasure: (1) pleasure arising from absence, (2) joyful pleasure arising from concentration, (3) and pleasure free of joy.[940] The types of pleasure (sukha) that arise are explained as nine since there are three for each of the first three absorptions (dhyāna). The three of the first absorption are pleasure arising from the absence of desire, the three of the second absorption are the pleasure of joy arising from concentration {abandoning investigation and analysis}, and the three of the third absorption are pleasure free of joy. {Desire-realm humans do not [naturally] possess such pleasure.} Objection: Thus those born in the special first absorption do not generate pleasure because they have no joy, since that is the level of equanimity. Vaibhāṣikas say this is a general presentation, for example, it is like the statement of the sūtras {or Topic Divisions}: What is higher perception? It is virtuous wisdom.[941] Question: If higher abodes such as Cāturmahārājika {that are explained as the twenty-two abodes of the gods} exist in layers, what is the distance between them?
gnas nas gnas 'og ji srid pa/ / de nas de yi gong de srid/ / 72 rdzu 'phrul gzhan rten ma gtogs pa/ / de dag gong ma mthong ba med/ /

The distance from its own abode to the lower abode is as far as the distance from its abode to the higher abode. Those of lower level cannot see higher levels except through supernatural power or in dependence on others. (3:72)

rang rang gi gnas nas gnas 'og ma'i gnas kyi bar thag ji srid pa de rang gi gnas de nas de'i gong ma'i gnas su'ang de srid de/ 'di ltar gnas rgyal chen ris bzhi{ 'i rtsa ba'i gnas bang rim bzhi pa} nas 'og 'dzam bu'i gling du dpag tshad bzhi khri yin pa de bzhin du sum cu rtsa gsum du'ang de srid{ de bzhi khri} yin no/ / gnas sum cu rtsa gsum nas gnas 'og 'dzam bu'i gling du brgyad khri yin pa de bzhin du 'thab bral du'ang brgyad khri yin pa la sogs pa'o/ / sa las ni shin tu mtho dman tshad dpag tshad bzhi khri bzhi khri dang de nas 'og min la dpag tshad 'bum drug khri yod par bshad do/ / de dag tu bgrod par byed pa ji ltar zhe na/

Reply: The distance from its own abode to the lower abode is the distance from its abode to the higher abode. Thus the distance from the abode of Cāturmahārājika {of the fourth tier of the root abode} to the lower abode of Jambudvīpa is 40,000 yojanas, and so too the distance to the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa [279] is also {40,000 yojanas}. The distance from the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa down to Jambudvīpa is 80,000 yojanas, and so too the distance to the Yāma heaven is 80,000 yojanas and so on. Yogācāra Levels explains that below Sudarśana it is 40,000 yojanas each, and from there to Akaniṣṭha it is 160,000 yojanas. Question: How does one proceed to them?

rdzu 'phrul dang ldan pa'am rdzu 'phrul dang ldan pa gzhan la brten pa ma gtogs pa khams dang sa 'og ma pa de dag gis gong mar bgrod pa dang gong ma pa dag mthong ba'ang med do/ / de'i phyir gang dag{ 'og ma bas gong ma} mthong ba de dag ni sprul pa'i gzugs yin gyi dman pa'i yul mchog ma yin pas 'og mas gong ma'i gzugs mthong ba ma yin no/ / 'o na gong ma de dag gi gnas kyi rgya'i tshad ji tsam zhe na/ 'thab bral la sogs pa bzhi ni sum cu rtsa gsum dang tshad mnyam mo/ / kha cig na re nyis 'gyur gyis gong ma gong ma che ba yin no zhes zer ro/ / bsam gtan bzhi'i tshad ni rim pa ltar gling bzhi dang stong chung ngu dang stong gnyis bar ma dang stong gsum dang mnyam mo/ / kha cig na re bsam gtan dang po la sogs pa gsum ni stong chung ngu la sogs pa gsum dang mnyam la bzhi pa la{ 'og gzhi gcig tu 'bral ba med pas} tshad med do zhes zer ro/ /

Reply: Those of lower realms and levels cannot go to or see higher levels except through possessing supernatural power or in dependence on others. Therefore that which is seen {by beings of lower levels who see higher levels} is emanated form. [Eyes] of lower levels do not see higher form since [such eyes are] inferior and they do not see superior objects. Question: What are the dimensions of those higher abodes? Reply: The four heavens such as Yāma are equal in size to the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa. Some say: The higher are twice as large, increasing as one goes higher.[942] The four absorptions are equal in measure, respectively, to the four continents, the small chiliocosm, the dichiliocosm, and the trichiliocosm. Some say: The first three absorptions are equal in measure to the small chiliocosm, the dichiliocosm, and the trichiliocosm, and the fourth is immeasurable[943] {since it is entirely separate from the lower bases}.
stong gsum bshad pa ni
EXPLANATION OF THE TRICHILIOCOSM
gling bzhi pa dang nyi zla dang / / ri rab dang ni 'dod lha dang / / 73 tshangs pa'i 'jig rten stong la ni/ / stong ni spyi phud yin par 'dod/ /
One thousand times the four continents, the sun, moon, Meru, the desire-god abodes, and the heaven of Brahma are asserted to be a chiliocosm. (3:73)

gling bzhi pa dang nyi ma dang zla ba dang dbus kyi ri rab dang gser gyi ri rnams dang mtsho rnams dag khor yug gi lcags ri'i bar dang 'dod pa'i lha drug dang tshangs pa'i 'jig rten stong la ni stong spyi phud kyi 'jig rten gyi khams zhes bya ba yin par 'dod la/

One thousand times the four continents (dvīpa), the sun (arka), moon (candra), central Meru, the golden mountains, the oceans up to the iron mountain at the circumference, the six desire-god abodes, and the heaven of Brahma (brahmaloka) are asserted to be the region of world systems of a small chiliocosm (sāhasracūḍika).
de stong la ni stong gnyis pa/ / bar ma'i 'jig rten khams yin no/ / 74 de stong la ni stong gsum mo/ / mnyam du 'jig cing 'byung ba yin/ /
One thousand of those is a dichiliocosm intermediate region of world systems. One thousand of those is a trichiliocosm. They are destroyed and arise together. (3:74)

stong spyi phud de stong la ni stong gnyis pa bar ma'i 'jig rten gyi khams zhes bya ste de la ni gling bzhi nas tshangs pa'i 'jig rten gyi bar sa ya phrag gcig yod do/ / stong gnyis pa de stong la ni stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams te/ de la ni gling bzhi nas tshangs pa'i 'jig rten gyi bar bye ba phrag brgya yod do/ / stong chung ngu la sogs pa gsum yang khor yug gi lcags ri re res bskor te gnas so/ / {de ci'i phyir stong gsum zhes bya zhe na }

One thousand small chiliocosms make a dichiliocosm (dvisāhasra), which is an intermediate region of world systems consisting of a million times the four continents up to the heaven of Brahma. One thousand dichiliocosms make a trichilochosm (trisāhasra), which is a great region of world systems consisting of a billion times the four continents up to the mundane heaven of Brahma. The three chiliocosms from the small chiliocosm and so on are also surrounded by iron rings. {Question: Why is it called a trichiliocosm?

de lta bu'i stong gsum de ni mthar mnyam du 'jig cing dang po mnyam du 'byung ba ste 'chags pa yin no/ / des na bsam gtan gnyis pa yan chad ni stong gsum du ma 'dus te/ tshangs pa'i 'jig rten man chad kho na la der bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir slob dpon gang spel gyis kyang*/ tshangs pa'i 'jig rten stong la ni zhes smros pas bsam gtan gnyis pa la sogs pa rnams ni stong chung ngu'i 'jig rten gyi khams kyis bsdus pa ma yin no zhes bshad do/ / rgya che rol pa'i mdo las ni/ gling bzhi bye ba phrag brgya nas 'og min gyi bar bye ba phrag brgya la stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams gcig ces bya ste yangs shing rgya che ba'o zhes 'og min man chad stong gsum du gsungs so/ /

Reply:} Such trichiliocosms are ultimately destroyed together and initially form through arising together, but this is explained only for the heaven of Brahma and below. Therefore Master Pūrṇavardhana also mentions: Since it is called the chiliocosm of the heaven of Brahma, the second absorption and so on are not subsumed by the world systems of a small chiliocosm.[944] The Extensive Display Sūtra states that the trichiliocosm consists of Akaniṣṭha and below: One billion times the four continents, up to a billion heavens of Akaniṣṭha, is called a region of world systems of the trichiliocosm that is light and extensive.[945] [280]
lus kyi tshad bstan pa/
Physical measure and lifespan of beings
'dzam bu gling pa rnams kyi tshad/ / khru bzhi pa dang phyed dang bzhi/ / 75 shar dang ba lang spyod dang ni/ / byang zhes bya ba nyis 'gyur bskyed/ /
The size of human bodies of Jambudvīpa is four or three and a half cubits. Eastern Videha, Godānīya, and northern Kuru grow to twice the former. (3:75)

lus kyi tshad bstan pa la ngan song gsum gyi lus tshad ni ma nges pa'i phyir 'dir ma bstan to/ / {sa'i dngos gzhi las kyang*/ sems can dmyal ba chen po dag gi tshad ni nges pa med de/ gang gis sdig pa mi dge ba'i las shin tu drag po byas shing bsags pa de'i lus ni ches che bar 'grub par 'gyur la/ gzhan dag gi ni gzhan du 'gyur ro/ / sems can dmyal ba chen po dag gi ji lta ba bzhin du grang ba'i sems can dmyal ba rnams dang*/ nye tshe ba'i sems can dmyal ba rnams dang*/ nye 'khor pa'i sems can dmyal ba rnams dang*/ dud 'gro dang*/ yi dwags rnams kyang de dang 'dra'o/ / zhes mi dge ba che chung gi lus che chung du 'gyur bar bshad do }

mi rnams las 'dzum bu'i gling pa'i mi rnams kyi lus tshad ni che ba rnams khru bzhi pa dang chung ba rnams phyed dang bzhi pa yin no/ / khru ni thams cad du 'og nas 'chad pa'i phra rab rdul la sogs pa bsags pa'i tshad dang ldan pa yin gyi rang rang gi khru ni ma yin no/ / {sa'i dngos gzhi las ni/ /'dzam bu'i gling gi mi rnams ni lus kyi tshad ni nges pa med de/ res 'ga' ni chen por 'gyur ro/ / res 'ga' ni chung ngur 'gyur te/ de yang rang rang gi khru tshad phyed dang bzhi'o zhes bshad do } shar lus 'phags po dang nub ba lang spyod pa dang byang sgra mi snyan pa zhes bya ba rnams ni rim pa ltar snga ma snga ma nyis 'gyur gyis bskyed pa khru brgyad dang bcu drug dang sum cu rtsa gnyis pa yin no/ / de dag kyang 'dzam bu'i gling pa'i khru'i dbang du byas kyi{ sa'i dngos gzhi las shar gyi lus 'phags pa rnams kyi lus kyi tshad ni nges pa yin te/ de dag kyang rang gi khru tshad phyed dang bzhi pa ste lus shin tu che ba'o/ / shar gyi lus 'phags pa ji lta ba bzhin du nub kyi ba lang spyod pa rnams dang*/ byang gi sgra mi snyan pa rnams kyang lus shin tu che'o/ / zhes 'byung bas} rang rang gi ni khru bzhi pa{ 'am phyed dang bzhi} kho na yin no zhes gsung ngo*/ / gling phran rnams kyi mi rnams ni gtso bo'i gling gi mi'i lus kyi phyed phyed dang ldan no zhes grag go /slob dpon gang spel gyis kyang bar gyi gling brgyad po de dag thams cad ni las ngan pa'i dbang gis grub pa zhig ste/ de'i phyir de na gnas pa'i mi rnams ni lus chung ba yin no zhes bshad do/ /
'dod dang ldan pa'i lha yi lus/ / bzhi cha nas ni rgyang grags dag/ / 76 phyed dang gnyis kyi bar du bskyed/ / gzugs can dang po dpag tshad phyed/ /
The bodies of desire-realm gods increase from one fourth krośa to a krośa and a half. The first form-realm gods are half a yojana. (3:76)

'dod pa dang ldan pa'i lha drug po'i lus tshad ni rgyal chen ris bzhi pa rgyang grags bzhi cha gcig yin pa nas sum cu rtsa gsum pa rgyang grags phyed dang*/ 'thab bral ba bzhi gsum dang*/ dga' ldan pa gcig dang*/ 'phrul dga' ba gcig dang bzhi cha dang*/ gzhan 'phrul dbang byed pa rgyang grags dag phyed dang gnyis kyi bar du bskyed par bya'o/ / {sa'i dngos gzhi las ni sum cu rtsa gsum pa rnams kyi tshad ni rgyang grags kyi bzhi cha gcig pas lhag go /lha'i dbang po brgya byin gyi tshad ni rgyang grags phyed do/ / 'thab bral ba rnams kyang rgyang grags phyed do/ / de yan chad ni bzhi cha re re lhag par blta bar bya'o zhes pa dang*/ lha ma yin rnams kyi lus ni sum cu rtsa gsum pa'i lha'i tshad bzhin du rnam par bzhag rig par bya'o zhes bshad do } lha ma yin rnams ni sum cu rtsa gsum pa'i lha rnams dang lus tshad mnyam par sa las bshad do/ /

The dimensions of bodies of the six desire-realm gods increase from the gods of Cāturmahārājika, who are one fourth of a krośa, to the gods of Trāyastriṃśa, who are half a krośa, to the gods of Yāma, who are three fourths of a krośa, to the gods of Tuṣita, who are one krośa, to the gods of Nirmāṇarati, who are one and one fourth krośa, to the gods of Paranirmitavaśavartin, who are a krośa and a half. {Yogācāra Levels declares: The size of the gods of Trāyastriṃśa exceeds a quarter of a krośa. The size of Śakra, the lord of the gods, is half a krośa, as well as gods of Yāma. The gods above them increase by a quarter krośa each. And: The bodies of demigods should be understood to be similar to gods of Trāyastriṃśa.[950]} The demigods are explained to be equal to the gods of Trāyastriṃśa. This is stated in Yogācāra Levels.
gzugs can gyi lha rnams kyi dang po tshangs ris pa'i lus kyi tshad ni dpag tshad phyed pa yin no/ /
The size of the bodies of the first form-realm gods of Brahmakāyika is half a yojana. [281]
de yi gong ma phyed phyed bskyed/ / 'od chung rnams kyi ltag yan chad/ / 77 lus ni nyis 'gyur nyis 'gyur te/ / sprin med dpag tshad gsum dor ro/ /
Those above increase by half each. Those above, that are beyond Parīttābha, increase twofold. In Anabhraka they are reduced by 3 yojanas. (3:77)

tshangs ris pa de'i gong ma tshangs pa'i mdun na 'don dang*/ tshangs chen pa dang*/ 'od chung ba rnams kyi lus ni rim pa ltar dpag tshad phyed phyed kyis bskyed pa dpag tshad gcig dang*/ phyed dang gnyis dang gnyis yin no/ / 'od chung ba rnams kyi ltag chad med 'od yan chad kyi na lus nyis 'gyur nyis 'gyur gyis che ste/ 'on kyang sprin med pa nyis 'gyur gyis bskyed pa las dpag tshad gsum dor ro zhes bya ba ni khyad par yin te/ 'di ltar tshad med 'od pa dpag tshad bzhi dang*/ 'od gsal ba brgyad dang*/ dge chung ba bcu drug dang*/ tshad med dge ba sum cu rtsa gnyis dang*/ dge rgyas pa drug cu rtsa bzhi dang*/ sprin med pa dpag tshad brgya nyi shu rtsa brgyad la gsum dor ba'i brgya nyi shu rtsa lnga dang*/ bsod nams skyed pa phyed dang sum brgya dang*/ 'bras bu che ba lnga brgya dang*/ mi che ba stong dang mi gdung ba nyis stong dang*/ gya nom snang ba bzhi stong dang*/ shin tu mthong ba brgyad stong dang*/ 'og min pa khri drug stong ngo*/ / gzugs med pa ni lus can ma yin pa'i phyir lus kyi tshad med la/ de na sprul pa'i gzugs yod par 'dod pa ltar na'ang tshad nges pa med phyir ro/ /

The bodies of the gods of Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, and Parīttābha that are above Brahmakāyika increase by half a yojana each and are, respectively, one yojana, one and a half yojanas, and two yojanas. The bodies of the gods of Apramāṇābha and above, which are beyond Parīttābha, increase twofold. However, there is an exception since in Anabhraka they are reduced by three yojanas even though they increase twofold. Therefore gods of Apramāṇābha are four yojanas, Ābhāsvara is eight, Parīttaśubha is sixteen, Apramāṇaśubha is thirty-two, Śubhakṛtsna is sixty-four. But gods of Anabhraka are three yojanas less than 128, making 125 yojanas. Those of Puṇyaprasava are 250 yojanas; Bṛhatphala, 500; Avṛha, 1,000; Atapa, 2,000; Sudṛśa, 4,000; Sudarśana, 8,000; and Akaniṣṭha are 16,000 yojanas. Because beings of the formless realm have no bodies, their bodies cannot be measured. Still, in accordance with the assertion that emanated form exists there, their measure is not fixed.
tshe'i tshad bstan pa ni
TEACHING THE MEASURE OF LIFESPAN
sgra mi snyan na tshe stong ste/ / gnyis na phyed phyed spangs pa'o/ / 78 'di na ma nges tha mar ni/ / lo bcu dang po dpag tu med/ /
In Kuru the lifespan is a thousand. In two continents it decreases by half. In Jambudvīpa lifespan is not fixed, ten years at the end and immeasurable in the beginning. (3:78)

byang gi sgra mi snyan na ni tshe lo stong thub ste/ nub dang shar gyi gling gnyis na ni rim pa bzhin snga ma snga ma'i phyed phyed spangs pas lnga brgya dang phyed dang sum brgya'o/ / 'dzam bu'i gling 'di na tshe'i tshad ma nges te/ tha ma thung ngur gyur pa na ni tshe'i tshad lo bcu pa dang dang po ni tshe dpag tu med pa dang de dag gi bar du'ang 'phel 'grib du ma yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

In the northern continent of Kuru the lifespan (āyus) is 1,000 years. In two continents, the western and eastern, the lifespan decreases by half of the former, to 500 and 250 years, respectively. In Jambudvīpa the measure of lifespan is not fixed because the lifespan is short, at ten years at the end of the eon and immeasurable (amita) in the beginning, with many periods of increase and decrease between.
'dod pa'i lha rnams kyi tshe tshad ni
THE MEASURE OF THE LIFESPAN OF DESIRE GODS
mi rnams kyi lo lnga bcu la/ / 'dod pa dag gi lha rnams las/ / 79 'og ma dag gi nyin zhag gcig / des na tshe lo lnga brgya'o/ /
For the lowest desire gods fifty human years is one day and night. Their lifespan is five hundred years. (3:79)

mi rnams kyi lo lnga bcu la 'dod pa dag gi lha rnams las thams cad kyi 'og ma rgyal chen ris bzhi pa'i lha dag gi nyin zhag gcig tu brtsis pa'i zhag sum cu la zla ba gcig dang zla ba bcu gnyis la lo gcig yin pa des na tshe'i tshad rang gi lo lnga brgya'o/ /

For the gods of Cāturmahārājika, the lowest of all desire gods, fifty human years is calculated as one day and night. The measure of their lifespan is five hundred years, where thirty such days make one month and twelve such months make one year.
gong ma gnyis ka nyis 'gyur ro/ / gzugs can nyin mtshan med tshe ni/ / 80 rang lus gzhal ba'i bskal pa yis/ /
Those above have double both. Form-realm gods have no day and night. The measure of their lifespan is calculated in eons according to the dimensions of their bodies. (3:80)

rgyal chen ris bzhi'i gong ma sum cu rtsa gsum pa las sogs pa ni zhag dang lo gnyis ka nyis 'gyur ro ste/{ snga ma'i bzhi 'gyur phyi ma'i tshe tshad yin pas/} 'di ltar sum cu rtsa gsum pa rnam ni mi'i lo brgya la zhag gcig tu brtsis pa'i rang lo stong thub pa nas gzhan 'phrul dbang byed pas mi'i lo stong drug brgya la zhag gcig tu brtsis pa'i rang lo khri drug stong thub pa'i bar du'o/{ de dag la mi'i lo ni rim pa ltar dang po la sa ya phrag dgu dang*/ gnyis pa la sa ya phrag sum cu rtsa drug dang*/ gsum pa la dung phyur dang bye ba bzhi dang sa ya bzhi dang*/ bzhi pa la dung phyur lnga dang bye ba bdun dang*/ sa ya drug dang*/ lnga pa la ther 'bum gnyis dang*/ dung yur gsum dang sa ya bzhi dang*/ drug pa la ther 'bum dgu dung phyur gnyis bye ba gcig sa ya drug yod do/}

The gods above Cāturmahārājika, such as the gods of Trāyastriṃśa, have double both the days and years {since the measure of the lifespan of the latter is four times the former.} Thus in the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa, a hundred human years is calculated as one day and night and they live a thousand years, up to the heaven of Paranirmitavaśavartin, where 1,600 human years is calculated as one day and night and they live 16,000 years. {In terms of human years, those are, respectively, 9 million years for the first, 36 million for the second, 144 million for the third, 576 million for the fourth, 1,152 million for the fifth, and 2,304 million for the sixth.}

gal te sum cu rtsa gsum yan chad na nyi zla med pas nyin mtshan med pa'i phyir zhag la sogs pa rnam par bzhag pa dang snang ba'i bya ba yod par mi 'gyur ro zhe na/ nyi zla med kyang nyin mtshan yod de/ dus kyi dbang gis me tog kha zum pa dang bya skad mi 'byin pa dang gnyid bro ba na mtshan mo dang*/ me tog kha bye ba dang*/ bya skad 'byin pa dang gnyid sangs pa ni nyin mo yin pa'i phyir ro/ / snang ba'i bya ba ni rang gi lus la 'od yod pas byed do/ / lha ma yin gyi tshe tshad ni sa{ 'i dngos gzhi} las sum cu rtsa gsum pa rnams dang 'dra'o zhes bshad la/ dran pa nyer gzhag las ni mi lo lnga brgya la nyin zhag gcig tu byas pa'i rang lo lnga stong sgra gcan gyis thub cing*/ mi lo drug brgya la nyin zhag gcig tu byas pa'i rang lo drug stong mgul phreng dang brten pas thub la/ mi lo bdun brgya la nyin zhag gcig tu byas pa'i rang lo bdun stong me tog phreng gis thub par gsungs shing*/ thags bzang ris kyi tshe tshad ni ma gsungs so/ /

Objection: The gods of Trāyastriṃśa and above have no day or night because they have no sun or moon. Therefore they would have no system of days and so on, nor would there be illumination and so forth. Reply: Though they have no sun nor moon, they have day and night [282] because through the influence of time it is night when flowers close, birds stop singing, and gods feel sleepy, and it is day when flowers open, birds sing, and gods awaken from sleep. Illumination occurs through the light of their bodies. The measure of the lifespan of the demigods is explained in {Yogācāra} Levels to be similar to the gods of Trāyastriṃśa.[951] The Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra states: Five hundred human years is taken as one day and night, and Rāhu lives six thousand such years.[952] Six hundred human years is taken as one day and night, and Kaṇṭhābharaṇa and Balin live six thousand such years.[953] Seven hundred human years is taken as one day and night, and Mālyā is able to live seven thousand such years.[954] However, it does not state the measure of lifespan of Vemacitra.

gzugs can rnams la ni nyin mtshan med de/ nyin mtshan gyi rnam par 'jog byed med pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs can de dag gi tshe tshad ni rang gi lus kyi tshad gzhal ba'i dpag tshad kyi grangs kyi tshad kyi bskal pa yis 'jal pa yin te/ 'di ltar gzugs can dang po skal pa phyed/ / de yi gong ma phyed phyed bskyed/ / 'od chung rnams kyi ltag yan chad/ / tshe ni nyis 'gyur nyis 'gyur te/ / sprin med bskal pa gsum dor ro/ / zhes 'don pa bsgyur ro/ / rgyal ba'i yum la sogs pa mdo kha cig las ni gya nom snang dang shin tu mthong go rim bsnor nas gya nom snang gi rjes la 'og min bshad cing*/ slob dpon zhi gnas lhas mdo drangs pa las kyang*/ shin tu mthong dang gya nom snang ba'i tshe tshad rim pa ltar bskal pa bzhi stong dang*/ brgyad stong du bshad do/ /

Form-realm gods have no day and night because there is nothing to establish day and night. The measure of the lifespan of form-realm gods is calculated in eons according to the dimensions of their bodies. Thus it is said: The first form realm is half an eon and those above increase by half for each. Above and beyond Parīttābha the lifespan increases twofold. But Anabhraka is reduced by three eons.[955] Some say: The Mother of the Conquerors Sūtra and so on explain Akaniṣṭha after Sudṛśa through confounding the order of Sudṛśa and Sudarśana. Master Śamathadeva, quoting from the sūtras, also explains that the measure of the lifespan of gods of Sudarśana and Sudṛśa are four thousand and eight thousand eons, respectively.[956]
gzugs med bskal pa stong phrag ni/ / nyi shu lhag pas lhag pa yin/ / 'od chung nas bzung bskal chen te/ / 81 de yi 'og ma phyed yin no/ /
Each of the formless exceeds the former by 20,000 eons. They are great eons from Parīttābha, and that below is half a great eon. (3:81)

gzugs med pa rnams ni bskal pa stong phrag nyi shu nyi shu lhag pa yin zhes bya ba ni nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched{ la sogs pa bzhi rim pa ltar} bskal pa stong phrag nyi shu dang*/ rnam shes mtha' yas skyes mched bzhi bcu dang*/ ci yang med pa'i skye mched drug cu dang*/ srid pa'i rtse mo bas brgyad cu thub bo zhes bya ba'i don to/ / 'o na de dag thams cad bar bskal lam bskal chen yin zhe na/

It is stated that the lifespan of beings in the formless realm exceeds the former by 20,000 eons. This means that the base of infinite space is 20,000 eons, the base of infinite consciousness is 40,000 eons, the base of nothingness is 60,000 eons, and the summit of existence is 80,000 eons. Question: Are all those lifespans intermediate eons or great eons?

'od chung nas gzung nas bskal pa chen po yin te/ 'od chung de'i 'og ma tshangs chen man chad ni bskal pa chen po'i phyed bar bskal bzhi bcu la bskal par btags pa yin no/ / de lta ma yin na tshangs chen pa ma shi bar snod 'jig pa'i me 'bar bar 'gyur ba dang*/ stongs nas kyang yod par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / des na tshangs ris pa bar bskal nyi shu dang tshangs pa mdun na 'don pa bar bskal bzhi bcu dang tshangs chen pa bar bskal drug cur bar bskal gnyis kyis chad pa yod de/ snod 'jig 'chags la bar bskal re re yod la snod 'chags pa ma rdzogs pa'i tshe tshangs pa ma skyes shing snod 'jig pa'i gong du tshangs pa shi ba'i phyir ro/ / 'on kyang bskal pa bzhi gsum thub par bshad pa ni de dang nye ba'i phyir ro/ / des na tshangs chen dang 'od chung gi che tshad kyi bar na bar bskal brgya yod do/ / sa'i dngos gzhi las ni bar bskal nyi shu dang bzhi bcu dang drug cu la bskal pa{ 'i re re} tha snyad du mdzad nas tshangs ris pa la sogs pa gsum gyi tshe tshad bskal pa re rer bshad do/ /

Reply: They are great eons from Parīttābha, and the lifespan of gods of Mahābrahma who exist below Parīttābha is half a great eon and designated as forty intermediate eons. If that were not so, then the blazing fire that destroys the environment would occur without the gods of Mahābrahma dying, and though those realms would be empty, those gods would still exist. Therefore Brahmakāyika is twenty intermediate eons, Brahmapurohita is forty, and Mahābrahma is sixty. Two intermediate eons are omitted because the destruction and formation of the environment take an eon each, Brahma does not take rebirth when the formation of the environment is incomplete, and he dies before the environment is destroyed. Now the explanation that four eons endure for three is close to this explanation. Therefore, between the measure of the lifespan of the gods of Parīttābha and Mahābrahma, [283] there are a hundred intermediate eons. Yogācāra Levels notes: Having applied the term intermediate eon at twenty, forty, and sixty eons {respectively}, the measure of the lifespan of the three types of god from Brahmakāyika and so on is an eon each.[957]
yang sos la sogs drug rim bzhin/ / 'dod lha'i tshe dang nyin zhag mnyam/ / des na de dag rnams kyi tshe/ / 82 'dod pa'i lha dang 'dra ba yin/ /
The lifespan of the six hells such as Sañjīva is that a day and night equals the lifespan of the desire gods. Therefore their lifespan corresponds to the desire gods. (3:82)
ngan song gi tshe'i tshad la

yang sos la sogs pa tsha ba'i dmyal ba drug gi tshe tshad ni rim pa bzhin du 'dod pa'i lha rgyal chen ris bzhi la sogs pa drug po'i tshe'i tshad ji tsam bshad pa dang yang sos la sogs pa drug gi nyin zhag mnyam par shes par bya ste/ {dang po drug snga ma'i brgyad 'gyur phyi ma'i tshe tshad yin pas } 'di ltar rgyal chen ris bzhi pa'i tshe tshad rang lo lnga brgya la yang sos pa'i{ nyin} zhag{ gcig} tu brtsi ba la sogs pa'o/ / de lta bu'i zhag sum cu la zla ba dang zla ba bcu gnyis la lo gcig yin pa des na yang sos la sogs pa de dag rnams kyi tshe tshad ni rang gi lo lnga brgya dang stong dang nyis stong dang bzhi stong dang brgyad stong dang khri drug stong thub par 'dod pa'i lha drug po rnams dang lo'i grangs 'dra ba yin no zhes shes par bya'o/{ 'dir yang yang sos kyi nyin zhag gcig la mi lo sa ya phrag dgu dang*/ rang lo lnga brgya la mi'i lo phrag khrig bcu drug dang ther 'bum chen po gnyis yod pa nas tsha ba'i rang lo khri drug stong la mi'i lo gtams gsum gtams chen po lnga rab bkram brgyad dang rab bkram chen po brgyad/ phrag khrig dgu ther 'bum chen po gnyis yod pa'i bar du sbyar pa'o/ /}

Also, regarding the measure of the lifespan of the lower rebirths, the lifespan of beings of the six hot hells, such as the Sañjīva hell and so on, is that one of their days and nights is equal to the lifespan of the six desire gods such as the gods of Cāturmahārājika. Thus the five-hundred-year lifespan of gods of Cāturmahārājika is calculated as {one} day {and night} of the Sañjīva hell and so on {since the measure of lifespan of each subsequent [god realm] is eight times the earlier for the first six [god realms]}. Therefore, since thirty such days is a month and twelve such months is a year, the measure of the lifespan (āyus) of the Sañjīva hell and so forth corresponds to the life expectancy of the six desire gods who live 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000, 16,000 years, respectively.[958] {Moreover, one day and night of the Sañjīva hell is 9 million human years, and five hundred such years are 20,001,600,000 human years, up to 16,000 years of the Tapana hell being, which is 8.02 trillion human years.}
rab tu tsha phyed mnar med ni/ / bar gyi bskal pa'o dud 'gro rnams/ / mchog ring bskal pa'o yi dgas rnams/ / 83 zla ba nyin zhag gi lnga brgya/ /

Those of Pratāpana live half and those of Avīci one intermediate eon. Animals with extremely long lifespan, one eon. One human month is one day and night of a ghost, and they live five hundred years. (3:83)
rab tu tsha ba'i dmyal bas ni bar gyi bskal pa phyed thub bo/ / mnar med pas ni bar gyi bskal pa gcig thub pa'o/ /
Beings in the Pratāpana hell live half an intermediate eon, and those in Avīci live for one intermediate eon.

dud 'gro rnams kyi tshe thung ba la nges pa med pas tshe mchog tu ring bas ni bar gyi bskal pa gcig thub ste/ lus las/ dge slong dag klu brgyad po 'di dag ni klu chen po ste/ bskal par gnas pas 'dzin pa bya'i rgyal po nam mkha' lding gis mi phyin pa lha dang lha ma yin gyi g.yul yang nyams su myong zhing so sor nyams su myong ba yin no/ / de dag kyang gang zhe na/ 'di lta ste/ klu'i rgyal po dga' bo dang*/ nyer dga' bo dang*/ rta mgo dang*/ btang bzung dang*/ yid las byung dang*/ yul 'khor srung dang*/ nag po chen po dang*/ e la'i 'dab bo zhes gsungs pa lta bu'o/ / shin tu thung ba ni yud tsam re'i tshe'i cha dang bcas pa dag kyang yod do/ /

The lifespan of animals is short and not fixed, but those with supremely long lifespan live for one intermediate eon. A scripture declares: Monks, these eight nāgas are great nāgas. Since they live for an eon, even the king of birds, the garuḍa, cannot go there. They experience the battle of the gods and demigods and experience it individually. Who are they? They are the nāga kings Nanda, Upananda, Aśvaśira, Mucilinda, Manomaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mahākāla, Elāpattra.[959] Extremely short lifespans also exist for those who live just a fleeting moment.

yi dwags rnams ni mi'i zla stod la nyin mo dang*/ zla smad la mtshan mor byas nas mi rnams kyi zla ba gcig la yi dwags kyi nyin zhag gcig gi grangs su brtsis pa'i rang lo lnga brgya thub pa yin la/ bshes spring las/ bar chad med par sdug bsngal bsten gyur pa/ / nyes par spyad pa'i las kyi zhags pa yi/ / drwa bas bcings pa'i lus can kha cig lo/ / lnga stong dag dang khrir yang 'chi mi 'gyur/ / zhes 'byung ba ni mi'i lo'i dbang du mdzad pa'o/ / dran pa nyer gzhag las ni mi'i lo bcu la yi dwags kyi nyin zhag gcig tu brtsis pa'i rang lo lnga brgya thub par gsungs te/ {de'i ltar na rang lo lnga brgya la mi lo sa ya phrag gcig dang dgu 'bum du 'gyur ro/ / sa'i dngos gzhi las ni dud 'gro dang yi dwags rnams kyi tshe'i tshad ni nges pa med do zhes pa dang*/ de bzhin du nye 'khor gyi sems can dmyal ba dang*/ nye 'tshe ba'i sems can dmyal bar skyes pa'i sems can rnams kyi tshe'i tshad ni nges pa med do zhes bshad do }

Since ghosts take the waxing moon as the day and the waning moon as the night, one human month is calculated as one day and night of a ghost (pretā), and they live for five hundred such years. Letter to a Friend notes: Some are caught fast in continuous suffering, their bodies bound by the net of the karmic snare of evil behavior, deprived of death for five or ten thousand years.[960] This is from the perspective of human years. The Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra says that one day and night of a ghost is calculated as ten human years and they live five hundred such years.[961] {Therefore, in accordance with that sūtra, five hundred such years would be 10.9 million human years. Yogācāra Levels mentions: Thus the measure of the lifespan of animals and ghosts is not fixed. [284] And: Similarly, the measure of the lifespan of sentient beings who are born in the surrounding hells or occasional hells is not fixed.[962]}
til sbyangs nang nas lo brgya zhing / / til gcig phyung bas zad gyur pa/ / chu bur can gyi tshe yin te/ / 84 gzhan gyi tshe ni nyi shus bsgyur/ /
The lifespan of Arbuda is the time taken to exhaust a cart full of sesame by removing one sesame grain every hundred years. The lifespan of others is twenty times longer. (3:84)
grang dmyal gyi tshe tshad ni
THE MEASURE OF LIFESPAN OF THE COLD HELLS

til gyi sbyangs pa ma ga d+ha'i bre'i til khal brgyad cus gang ba'i nang 'ga' zhig gis lo brgya brgya zhing til gcig ste re re phyung bas til de dag zad par gyur pa ni chu bur can gyi tshe tshad yin te/ chu bur rdol pa can la sogs pa gzhan gyi tshe ni nyi shur bsgyur ba'i 'gyur gyis phyi ma phyi ma ring{ sa'i dngos gzhi las ni grang ba'i sems can dmyal bar skyes pa'i sems can rnams kyi tshe'i tshad ni sems can dmyal ba chen por skyes pa'i sems can rnams las phyi ma phyi ma phyed phyed zhugs par rig par bya'o zhes 'byung ste/ de'i don kha cig tsha dmyal rnams kyi phyed phyed thub par 'chad mod kyi/ tshe'i mtha' mdo ltar na tsha dmyal dang po drug pas grang dmyal dang po drug ring bar mngon no} ngo*/ / ci sngar smros pa'i sems can de dag bar ma dor mi 'chi bar tshe tshad ltar nges pa kho na yin nam zhe na/

The lifespan (āyus) of beings of the Arbuda hell is the time taken to exhaust eighty bushels (khāri), a Magadhan cart (vāha) full, of sesame by removing one sesame grain every hundred years. The lifespan of others, such as the hell of Nirarbuda and so on, is progressively twenty times longer for each of the latter. {Yogācāra Levels states: For the measure of the lifespan of sentient beings born in the cold hells, understand that they live half [the lifespan] of the latter — that is, sentient beings born in the great hells.[963] Regarding the meaning of that text, some say: Indeed, this explains that they each live for half of those of their corresponding hot hell. The End of Life Sūtra also confirms that the lifespans in the first six hot hells are longer than those in the first six cold hells.} Question: From those discussed above, what beings do not die an untimely death but definitely live out the measure of their lifespan?
sgra mi snyan ma gtogs par 'chi/ /
With the exception of Kuru, there is [untimely] death. (3:85a)

sgra mi snyan pa dag ni stong du nges te/ bar ma dor 'chi ba med pa'i phyir ro/ / sgra mi snyan pa ma gtogs pa rnams la bar ma dor 'chi ba yod pa'i phyir nges pa ni ma yin gyi spyi'i tshe tshad smros pa yin no/ / de ltar tshe tshad la sogs pa rgyas par bstan nas 'dir ma smros pa gdags pa las 'byung ba ni/ bkres skom gling bzhi 'dod lha na/ / gong ma na med gling gsum na/ / 'bras chan zan phye sha 'khur ba'i/ / zas za sgra mi snyan pa rnams/ / ma rmos {ma btab pa'i } 'bras kyi {sa lu'i } 'bru dag za/ / 'dod lha {kha dog bzhi pa'i } dri dang{ dang sbrang sogs chang} bdud rtsi'o/ / gong na kham zas rnam par spangs/ / bshang gci gling bzhi dag na yod/ / yan chad na med char ba dag /'bab nyes pa dang legs pa dang*/ / lo nyes lo legs mu ge dag gling gsum na yod sgra mi snyan/ / 'dod lha yan chad de dag med/ / 'jigs dang yid bde res 'jog ni/ / gling gsum dag dang 'dod lha la/ / sgra mi snyan dang gong na med/ / nor 'bru gser dngul nyo tshong dag gling gsum na yod sgra mi snyan/ / lha rnams kun la yod ma yin/ / bzhin mdog dkar nag sngo sangs dang*/ / skya snar{ bzhi ka gling} gsum { dang} 'dod lha rnams/ / sngo sar dkar dmar{ bzhi ka dang} sgra mi snyan/{ dang gzugs khams pa} tshangs ris yan chad dkar por gnas/{ kha dog dkar po kho na'o/ /}

Reply: Those of Kuru definitely live for a thousand years, and they do not die an untimely death. With the exception of Kuru human lifespan is not fixed, and just the general lifespan is mentioned because untimely death exists there. An extensive presentation of lifespan and so on is not given here but does occur in Presentation on the World, which states: Hunger and thirst exist on the four continents and among the desire-realm gods but not in the higher realms. Beings in the three continents eat cooked rice, flour, meat, and pastry, but the humans of Kuru eat unploughed {unplanted wild} rice and grains. Desire-realm gods eat smells {of four colors} and nectar {of honey and beer}, but in the higher realms there is no oral food. Beings on the four continents produce feces but not those in higher abodes. There are good and bad rains and good and bad harvests, and famines in the three continents. But these do not exist in Kuru, among the desire-realm gods, and above. Fear and mental happiness alternate on the three continents and among the desire-realm gods, but not in Kuru and the higher realms. Wealth, grain, gold and silver, and buying and selling exist on the three continents, but these do not exist in Kuru and all the god realms. Complexion {is of four types} on the three continents and among the desire-realm gods: black, white, blue-tinged, and brown. Blue, yellow, white, and red occur in Kuru. {In the form realm} it is white in Brahmakāyika and above {where their complexion is white alone}.

ched du byas dang ma byas pa'i/ / khang pa gling gsum 'dod lha na/ / sgra mi snyan dang gzugs khams pa/ / ched du byas pa ma yin nges/ / bal gos ras dang zab dar sogs/ / {lci yang gnyis ka } gling gsum na yod sgra mi snyan/{ sgra mi snyan pa srang gcig dang*/ 'dod lha drug pa'o/ /} 'dod lha drug po srang gcig nas/ / drug cu rtsa bzhi cha yi bar/ / ches yang sngo ser dkar dmar dag /dpag bsam shing las 'byung bar bshad/ / gzugs khams gos dang bcas par skye/ / rang lus tshad las nyis 'gyur gyis/ / lhag pa'i gos dag gon par bshad/ / bag ma len dang gtong ba ni/ / gling gsum 'dod lha rnams la yod/ / sgra mi snyan dang gong na med/ / lus la tsha dang grang ba ni/ / gling gsum dag na sgra mi snyan/ / lha rnams rnam par spangs pa yin/ / dgun dpyid dbyar dang ston rnams ni/ / gling bzhi 'dod lha rnams na yod/ / gong ma na med nyin mtshan dang*/ / pha ma rnams kyang de bzhin no/ / rje bran gling gsum 'dod lha rnams/ / sgra mi snyan dang gong na med/ / nor dang 'bru yod gling gsum na'o/ / 'bru yod nor med sgra mi snyan/ / nor yod 'bru med 'dod lha rnams/ / gnyis ka med pa gong ma yin/ / pha ma nas ni 'bru 'i bar/ / kun la zhen pa gling gsum na/ / 'bru ma gtogs la zhen pa ni/ / 'dod lha'o sgra mi snyan dang ni/ / gong ma'i lha rnams zhen pa med/ / zla mtshan sbrum ma bu btsa' ba/ / gling bzhi na yod lha rnams ni/ / rdzus skyes khu ba 'byung ba yang*/ / mi rnams 'dod lha rlung dag rgyu/ / tshe dang lus dang 'khrig pa spyod/ / rtsa bar bshad phyir 'dir ma bris/ / mtho ris kyi ni longs spyod dag /lung bzhin du ni bsdebs pa yin/ / zhes shes par bya'o// //

Owned and unowned houses exist on the three continents and among the desire-realm gods. Homes of Kuru and the form realm are definitely not owned. Woolen cloth, cotton, silk, and so on, {both heavy and light,} exist on the three continents. {Those of Kuru weigh one ounce.} Garments of the six types of desire-realm god weigh from one to sixty-four ounces (srang), are predominantly blue, yellow, white, and red, and are said to arise from wish-fulfilling trees. Beings of the form realm are born with clothes twice the measure of their bodies, and it is said that [285] they wear extra clothes. Taking and divorcing a wife exists on the three continents and among the desire gods but not in Kuru or the higher abodes. The body feeling hot or cold exists in the three continents, but it doesn’t exist in Kuru or among the gods. Winter, spring, summer, and autumn exist on the four continents and among the desire-realm gods but not in the higher abodes. Days and nights and having a mother and father are similar. Rulers and subjects exist on the three continents and among the desire gods but not in Kuru or the higher abodes. Both wealth and grain exist on the three continents. Grain exists in Kuru but not wealth, wealth exists for the desire-realm gods but not grain, but neither exist in the higher abodes. Craving for all, from parents to grain, exists on the three continents. Craving for all those except grain exists for the desire gods and in Kuru. Higher gods do not crave them. Menstruation, pregnancy, and nursing babies exist on the four continents. Gods have supernatural birth. Emission of semen exists for humans. For desire gods the winds move in life and in the body, and when engaged in sex.[964] Because this is explained in the root sources, I have not written it down here. The enjoyments of the higher rebirths are described in accordance with the scriptures.
17. Units of Measurement and Other Matters
da ni de dag 'jal byed kyi tshad bshad
EXPLAINING THEIR DIMENSIONS
['di] pa la don dngos dang*/ zhar las byung ba gnyis kyi
This has two headings: actual meaning and additional meaning.
dang po
ACTUAL MEANING
['di] la'ang gnyis las
This also has two headings: the measure of matter and the measure of time.
gzugs can gyi tshad bstan pa ni
The measure of matter

gzugs ming dus mtha' rdul yig dang / / skad cig phra rab rdul dang ni/ / 85 rdul phran dang ni de bzhin du/ / lcags chu ri bong lug dang glang / / nyi zer rdul dang sro ma dang / / de las byung dang de bzhin du/ / 86 sor tshigs zhes bya gong bdun bsgyur/ /

The smallest unit of matter is a particle; names, a letter; time, a moment. Seven subtle particles equal an atom. So too (3:85bcd) iron, water, rabbit, sheep, ox, light-ray particle, egg of a louse, [and the louse] derived from that; and similarly one finger joint, the latter seven times the former. (3:86)

The smallest unit (paryanta) of matter (rūpa) is the subtle particle; the smallest unit of names (nāma) is {one} letter (akṣara) {because there is no component smaller than that}; and the smallest unit of time (adhva) is a moment (kṣaṇa), {which is one sixty-fifth part of the duration of a finger snap}.

Seven subtle particles (paramāṇu) equal one atom (aṇu), and just as seven subtle particles equal one atom, so too seven atoms equal one iron particle, and seven of those equal one water particle, and seven of those equal one rabbit particle, and seven of those equal one sheep particle, and seven of those equal one ox particle, and seven of those equal one light-ray particle, and seven of those equal one louse egg, and seven of those equal one louse derived from that egg; and just as seven of those eggs equal one louse, similarly seven lice equal one barley seed, and seven of those equal one finger joint {because when destroyed or separated nothing smaller than those is observed}. Therefore each of the latter is seven times the former. Presentation on the World does not include either iron or water [particles] but explains that each of the latter is seven times the former: There is a subtle particle, an atom, a light-ray particle, a rabbit particle, and an ox particle, {which are designated as collections of particles but do not measure even the tip of a hair of a living being}, a louse egg, an abagana,[965] a batika,[966] a finger-joint, [286] and so on. Each of the latter is seven of the former.[967] Indeed, the Extensive Display Sūtra declares: There is a subtle particle (paramāṇu), an atom (aṇu), a minute particle, a light-ray particle, a rabbit particle, a sheep particle, an ox particle, a louse egg, a mustard seed, a barley seed, and a finger joint, where the size of each is seven times the preceding.[968] Though they have distinct names, subtle particles have no discernable size.

Twenty-four finger widths are a cubit (hasta), four cubits are one full armspan (dhanu), five hundred of those spans are a krośa, and one krośa beyond the village is considered the site for a monastery.
de brgyad dpag tshad ces bya'o/ /
Eight krośa are called a yojana. (3:88a)

Eight krośa are called a yojana. The Extensive Display Sūtra explains that: One thousand spans are a Magadha krośa, and four krośa are a yojana.[969] These cover all the dimensions of the physical cosmos and its inhabitants.

EXPLAINING YEARS

Indeed, the previously explained smallest moment is illustrated by the time taken for a subtle particle to change course or the period when the potency of a cause is not impeded. But if that is too difficult to understand, then Ābhidharmikas say: A moment lasts one sixty-fifth part of the duration of a finger snap of a strong person.[970]

One hundred and twenty such moments are a second. Sixty of those are one minute. (3:88bcd)
de lta bu'i skad cig ma brgya nyi shu la ni de'i skad cig dang*/ de'i skad cig ma de dag drug cu la thang gcig go /
One hundred and twenty such moments (kṣaṇa) are a second (tatkṣaṇa). Sixty of those seconds are one minute (lava).

The three periods of hours, days and nights, and months are each progressively thirty times the former. Twelve months with six omitted days make one year. (3:89)

Thirty minutes is an hour (muhūrta), thirty hours is one day and night, and thirty of those is one month. Thus these three periods are progressively thirty times the former. All months are not fixed at thirty days

because the Autocommentary has previously said: When one and a half months of winter, spring, and summer have passed scholars discard the omitted day in the half months that remain.[971] {The Vinaya Sūtra states: It climaxes after one day. The seasons leave out half a month.[972]} Also, the Vinaya Verses states: {In the decreasing phase of the second and fourth months of the summer season, those possessing vows make confession on the fourteenth.} Through the passing of all these periods, [a day] is eliminated after each of the three half-months. In one year, six months are said to lose a day.[973] This is calculated from the sixteenth day of the last month of autumn. Therefore for each period of two half-months, a day to be omitted occurs at the end of the second half-month. Also, it is said that for the middle summer month and the middle winter month there are no omitted days, but for the middle autumn month and the middle spring month there are omitted days for each. Therefore for the six periods: (1) the first winter month, (2) the last winter month, (3) the middle spring month, (4) the first summer month, (5) the last summer month, and (6) the middle autumn month, the month finishes on the fourteenth of the decreasing phase, and confession is held on the fourteenth. The meaning of “omitted” is that the sky month omits the surplus of an earth month. The reason the sky month omits days [287] is due to the logic of the reality of things as they are, but there is no absolute certainty since it is beyond reckoning. I have not analyzed this, and though others have analyzed it, they have not made the meaning clear. Thus twelve months with six omitted days added the following year make one year. Objection: If that is so, an intercalary [or extra] month would occur every five years. But this would contradict the statement “An intercalary [month] occurs in the horse, bird, rat, and rabbit [years]. Two middle [months] in autumn, winter, spring, summer.” This mentions that [the intercalary month] should be allocated every third year.

The Vinaya Sūtra explains: When allocating the intercalary month, follow the system of the king.[975] Also, the Vinaya Verses notes: [The system for] allocating years, months, and the intercalary month is extolled when it accords with the king’s instruction. Those who enforce his orders, the famous, the wise, and generals should follow this.[976] {So too that scripture affirms: The monks did not concur with the astronomers; they did not follow them and censured the astronomers. The monks requested advice from the Master, who said: “Monks, censuring the astronomers is boastfulness. Instead you should follow those astronomers.[977] The Vinaya Sūtra also mentions: In terms of the lunar mansions follow the astronomers.[978] Further, one should adhere to the following: if a proper month is not omitted, the extra month also is not omitted; if it is omitted, omit the extra month also.} Such a year gives the measure of the lifespan by which desire-realm gods, humans, beings of the six hot hells, and ghosts are assessed.

Many types of eons are explained. (3:89e) The eon of destruction is from the disappearance of the hells to the annihilation of the physical cosmos. Formation occurs first from the wind maṇḍala up to the existence of hell beings. (3:90)

Many types of eons (kalpa) are explained. The eon of destruction (saṃvartakalpa) begins from the disappearance of the hells (naraka) up to the annihilation of the physical cosmos (bhājana). Thus, after existing in the mundane cosmos for twenty intermediate eons {and attaining a lifespan of 80,000 years}, sentient beings are no longer newly born as hell beings. {At this time abidance is completed, and destruction begins.} Those previously born in the hells take birth in higher abodes through the exhaustion of their karma, or if their karma is not exhausted, they take birth as hell beings in other world systems, and the hells gradually empty. {This is the destruction of the hells.} Then the ghost and animal realms empty in just this way. Then humans of the southern continent of Jambudvīpa are born in the first absorption, obtained spontaneously, {but this is without scriptural source}. {Twice the words “Listen, joy and pleasure that are generated from nonattachment are blissful” are proclaimed, and that sound pervades Jambudvīpa with little difficulty. All humans of Jambudvīpa hear it and spontaneously obtain meditative attainment in the first absorption}. They die and are reborn in the first absorption. So too, the human abodes of the eastern and western continents become empty in just that way.

{Yogācāra Levels explains that all desire-realm humans and gods obtain the second absorption spontaneously, die from the desire realm, and take birth in Ābhāsvara.[980]} Then, as below, the external physical cosmos is destroyed in one intermediate eon {through the exhaustion of karma that projects that environment}. {Presentation on the World explains: At the end of time, water clouds do not rain in the least in this sustaining world system. One sun annihilates roots, trunks, medicinal plants, and seeds. A second sun dries up the various smaller pools and similarly the smaller rivers. A third sun [289] evaporates the water of the various larger pools and the larger rivers. A fourth sun dries up the great lakes and the abodes of nonhumans, such as the extremely attractive lake called Anavatapta, completely filled with pure water. A fifth sun scorches and entirely evaporates the great jewel-filled oceans, in which a great collection of beings abide. A sixth sun completely scorches the ground, the snow, and similarly Kailash and the seven mountains such as the golden monolith. They collapse completely with utter finality. When the seventh sun shines the array of light fully radiates, and from that time all the mountains completely and fully blaze. Those seven suns, possessing the annihilating array of light, move, and this ground, and so too the golden foundation, the eight hells containing sentient beings, all the mountains, and the mansions of the desire gods, though universal objects of desire, are incinerated, separating desire gods from their beautiful mansions and completely incinerating the abodes of Brahma. All those states without exception are incinerated. Even the destructive power of the brilliant suns comes to an end at the end of time, and they are annihilated due to disintegration through impermanence. Thus, pure beings rely on the fact that the monolith, the great oceans, the grounds, as well as high rebirth states will be destroyed and constantly place their trust in the abodes of the āryas.[981] That level also subsumes the fire that destroys the first absorption. But the fire of the desire realm is unable to harm other levels since they are established from different karma.

Water of the desire realm is related to water of the first absorption, and this is related to the water of the second absorption, and such water causes the environment to cease simultaneously.

FORMATION

Formation (vivarta) occurs after the void state following destruction by fire, first from the commencement of the formation of the wind maṇḍala as the lower basis of the first absorption, up to the existence of one sentient being in the hell of Avīci. Formation of the physical cosmos takes one eon, and the formation of sentient beings takes nineteen eons, making twenty eons. Now, the method of formation of the physical cosmos has for the most part been explained already. However, according to the Autocommentary[982] and the system of the Subcommentary[983] of Jinaputra, whatever initiates the prior destruction determines the next formation. Therefore {if destroyed by fire,} at first the mansion of Brahma arises, then those {not related to that level} serially arise from the mansions of Paranirmitavaśavartin up to the mansions of Yāma. Then after the formation of the mansions of Yāma, the wind maṇḍala and so on {of the lower basis} develop. From the first absorption to the heaven of Yāma but prior to the formation of the four continents is called “descending formation,” and this differs from what was said before. [290] So too, when destroyed by water, the environment of the second absorption is formed {first}, and when destroyed by wind, the third absorption is formed {first}.

THE INHABITING SENTIENT BEINGS

{After destruction by fire,} at first one god alone of Ābhāsvara dies through the exhaustion of lifespan, karma, and merit and is born in an empty mansion of the first absorption. Since he is born alone, he prays, “May others with fortunes similar to mine be born here.” Though other gods of the second absorption are not born there through his prayer, still they die through the exhaustion of their lifespan, karma, and merit and are reborn there due to chance {as a crow landing in a tāla tree}.[984] Because the first born has a large body and thinks he has initiated the entry of others, he is called Mahābrahma, “ancestor,” and “chief.” Tīrthikas proclaim him to be “one possessing the heart of gold” and “one born from a lotus” because he is born from the heart of a golden lotus. {He is definitely an ordinary being since āryas are not born in lower levels.} Those who are born later have smaller bodies, and because they think they are born from his wish they become his retinue. So too, the gods of Brahmapurohita and the desire realm, such as Paranirmitavaśavartin, serially develop, and then serially the humans of the northern, western, eastern, and southern continents develop. Then, through beings engaging in small, medium, and great nonvirtue in the three continents, they are serially born as animals, ghosts, and hell beings. When sentient beings are first born in Avīci, formation is complete {and the eon of endurance commences. Nineteen intermediate eons [remain]}. This system applies to the formation of the second and third absorptions {and to birth in lower states from Śubhakṛtsna and the fourth absorption and so on}.

An intermediate eon is from an incalculable lifespan to ten years. From there the remaining eons of increase and decrease are eighteen. (3:91)

In the eon of endurance there are twenty intermediate eons. An intermediate eon (antaḥkalpa) is measured from the incalculable (amita) lifespan of humans of Jambudvīpa through serial decrease to 80,000 years within the eon of formation, and from the decrease from 80,000 to the measure of human lifespan of Jambudvīpa of ten years [within the eon of endurance]; this constitutes the first {intermediate} eon. Also, from there the remaining eons of increase {to 80,000} and decrease {to ten} are eighteen. Each of those is calculated to have periods of both increase and decrease.

There is increase for one intermediate eon. The lifespan in those eons increases to 80,000. Thus this formation of mundane states lasts twenty intermediate eons. (3:92)

Then, starting from a lifespan of ten years, there is increase for one intermediate eon, {the twentieth}. Thus there are twenty intermediate eons. Question: Up to what lifespan do they live? Reply: The lifespan in those intermediate eons increases to 80,000 years, but it does not increase above that. The first intermediate eon consists of decrease {alone}, and the last [291] increase {alone}. The eighteen intermediate eons between them comprise periods of both increase and decrease, but [the eighteen] are of equal length to the first and last because [the first] slowly decreases and [the last slowly] increases, {since they proceed at a slower pace,} while the other [eighteen] proceed more quickly. Therefore Master Pūrṇavardhana also writes: Why are the first and last intermediate eons of increase and decrease equal in length to the other eighteen? The difference is whether they proceed quickly or slowly: the first and last eons proceed slowly, and the eighteen intermediate proceed quickly. Therefore all take the same time.[985] The quickness or slowness of those is a consequence of the nature of reality. Yogācāra Levels explains: The twenty periods of decrease and the twenty periods of increase make forty periods that constitute an intermediate eon. The periods of increase alone and decrease alone constitute two periods each.[986]
de ltar na 'jig rten sngar chags pa 'di bar gyi bskal pa nyi shu gnas pa yin no/ /
Thus this early formation of mundane states (lokavivṛtta) lasts twenty intermediate eons (antarakalpa).
'chags pa dang ni 'jig pa dang / / zhig nas 'dug pa dag mnyam mo/ / 93 de dag brgyad cu la bskal chen/ /
Formation, destruction, and the aftermath of destruction are equal in duration. Eighty of those make a great eon. (3:93abc)

'chags pa dang 'jig pa dang zhig nas 'dug pa stongs pa'i bskal pa dag ni gnas pa dang dus mnyam kho na ste thams cad la bar bskal nyi shu nyi shu yod do/ / de ltar na bar gyi bskal pa de dag brgyad cu la ni bskal pa chen po gcig tu byed{ bskal pa ni phung po lngas bsdus so} do/ /

The eons of formation (vivarta), destruction (saṃvṛtta), and the void eon in the aftermath of destruction (saṃvartate) are equal in duration to the eon of endurance alone; therefore all are twenty intermediate eons each. Eighty of those intermediate eons make one great eon (mahākalpa). {Eons are subsumed within the five aggregates.}[987]

In terms of what is explained as a great eon, the term “for” (la) in the statement “for three countless eons” that is enumerated [in the sequence] from one then two [and so on] should be taken as “over” (du) since it accords with how [the particle] du engages [its object]. As the Door of Speech declares: [Grammatical particles] such as “over” (du) and so on accord with [the particle] “for” (la).[988] Therefore buddhas arise from the collection of merit and pristine wisdom over three countless eons (asaṃkhyakalpa).

Objection: It is unacceptable to posit meditation on the path for three countless eons because three cannot be asserted to be countless! Reply: It is not absolutely countless because it is called “countless” if it reaches sixty decimal places. The figure of sixty decimal places occurs in the Miscellaenous Discourses, which is summarized in the Compendium: (1) One (ekam), (2) ten (daśa), (3) hundred (śatam), (4) thousand (sahasram), (5) ten thousand (prabheda), (6) hundred thousand (lakṣa), (7) million (atilakṣa), (8) ten million (koṭi), and (9) hundred million (madhya) should be known as a complete round. (10) Ayuta, (11) mahāyuta, (12) nayuta, (13) mahānayuta, (14) prayuta, (15) mahāprayuta, (16) kaṅkara, (17) mahākaṅkara, (18) bimbara, (19) mahābimbara, (20) akṣobhya, (21) mahākṣobhya, (22) vivāha, (23) mahāvivāha, (24) utsaṅga, (25) mahotsaṅga, (26) vāhana, (27) mahāvāhana, (28) tiṭibha, (29) mahātiṭibha, (30) hetu, (31) mahāhetu, (32) karabha, (33) mahākarabha, (34) indra, (35) mahendra, (36) samāpta, (37) mahāsamāpta, (38) gati, (39) mahāgati, (40) nimbaraja, (41) mahānimbaraja, (42) mudrā, (43) mahāmudrā, (44) bala, (45) mahābala, (46) saṃjñā, (47) mahāsaṃjñā, (48) vibhūta, (49) mahāvibhūta, (50) balākṣa, (51) mahābalākṣa, where “great” (mahā) qualifies every second number, and (60) countless (asaṃkhya) is the final number. The eight numbers between [51 and 60] have been lost. Therefore the numbers below one hundred million (madhya) are applied to these eight where appropriate.[990]
