Bodhisattva Levels explains: A countless eon should be recognized as having two types. (1) A great eon is termed “countless” when it cannot be measured in terms of days, nights, months, and half-months. And: (2) A great eon is also termed “countless” when it is beyond enumeration by any form of calculation whatsoever. The first countless eon implies that enlightenment is obtained in no less than a countless eon. The last countless eon implies that enlightenment is obtained only after three countless eons but not more.[991] One great eon cannot be counted in terms of days, nights, and so on, so therefore it is called a “countless eon.” But also a great eon that can be enumerated from one to sixty decimal places is also called “countless.”[992] Therefore, statements in the sūtras that enlightenment is obtained after many countless eons are from the perspective of the first “countless.” Statements that enlightenment is obtained after three countless eons are from the perspective of the last “countless.” Vaibhāṣikas assert that one obtains the stages up to and including the path of accumulation after three countless eons. A Commentary on the Eight Thousand Verses and so on indeed explains that as many as thirty-three countless eons are required to establish the path.[993] Bodhisattva Levels explains that the first level “Joyous,” the seventh level, and buddhahood are obtained, respectively, in the first, second, and the third countless eon.[994] {The Lotus Sūtra explains that the buddha Nakṣatra [293] appeared when the lifespan was ten years in the world system of beings the size of a thumb.[995] Other sūtras explain that buddhas appeared when the lifespan was immeasurable or the lifespan was eight years}. Thus how many countless eons buddhas depend on has been explained.

{sangs rgyas mi bzhugs pa'i zhing du 'byung ba ni } rang sangs rgyas rnams ni bskal pa yar 'phel ba dang*/ mar 'grib pa gnyis ka la 'byung zhing*/ / de yang bse ru lta bu dang tshogs na spyod pa gnyis yin no/ / de la tshogs na spyod pa ni nyan thos sngon du 'gro ba'i rang rgyal lo/ / kha cig na re so so'i skye bo sngon du 'gro ba'ang yod do zhes zer ro/ / de dag las bse ru lta bu ni bskal pa chen po brgyar bden pa dang rten 'brel dang dge ba bcu la goms pa'i rgyus 'thob pa yin no/ / de yang slob dpon med par rang nyid gcig pu'i don du byang chub pa'i phyir rang sangs rgyas zhes bya ba yin la/ sgra med par chos ston pa dang 'gro ba rnams kyi bsod nams kyi zhing mdzad pa'i sgo nas sems can gyi don byed do/ / tshogs na spyod pa ni bskal pa 'di srid cig na zhes ma nges pa'i phyir ro/ /

Pratyekabuddhas {who occur in lands where buddhas do not reside} appear in both the increasing and decreasing phases of the eon. There are two types: (1) rhinoceros-like, and (2) those who interact with communities. Those who interact with communities are pratyekabuddhas who were initially śrāvakas. Some say: There are also those who were initially simply ordinary beings. From among those, the state of the rhinoceros-like (khaḍga) is caused by meditation on the four truths, dependent origination, and the ten virtues over one hundred great eons. Further, they are called pratyekabuddhas (“solitary buddhas”) because they have no preceptor and they become enlightened for their own ends alone. They advance the interests of sentient beings by teaching Dharma without words and by acting as a field of merit for reincarnating beings. It is uncertain whether those who interact with communities can exist in this eon.
Universal monarchs
'khor los sgyur ba 'byung ba ni/ / stong phrag brgyad cu las mi 'phyi/ / 95 gser dngul zangs lcags 'khor lo can/ / de dag gling gcig gling gnyis dang / / gsum dang bzhi las mas rim bzhin/ /
Cakravartins do not appear when it is shorter than 80,000. They possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron. They rule in reverse order one, two, (3:95) three, or four continents. (3:96a)

'khor los bsgyur ba'i rgyal po 'byung ba ni mi rnams kyi tshe lo stong phrag brgyad cu las mi 'chi ba ni snga ba ste de yan chad tshe lo dpag tu med pa nas brgyad khri'i bar du zhes bya ba'i don to/ / {stobs kyi 'khor los bsgyur ba ni 'byung ste ka ni ka la sogs pa'o } de man chad du ni ma yin te/ bsod nams mi chud pa'i phyir ro/ / ci'i phyir 'khor los bsgyur ba zhes bya zhe na/ de dag la 'khor lo rin po che dag yod la des rgyal srid la mnga' bsgyur ba'i phyir ro/ / 'khor los bsgyur ba de yang gser dang dngul dang zangs dang lcags kyi 'khor lo can bzhi yin no/{ 'khor los bsgyur ba de dag kyang 'dzam bu gling pa'i rten can du nges so/ /} de rnams kyang rdo 'phangs pa'i mdo las/ rim pa ltar khor yug tu rgyang grags bzhi pa dang gsum pa dang gnyis pa dang gcig pa can du gsungs so/ / de dag kyang 'dzam bu'i gling gcig dang lho dang shar gyi gling gnyis dang byang ma gtogs pa gsum dang bzhi char la mas rim bzhin du mnga' bsgyur ro zhes gdags pa las bshad do/ / mdo las ni gser gyi 'khor lo can kho na gsungs so/ /

Cakravartin kings do not appear when human lifespan is shorter than 80,000 years. This means they appeared in ancient times when the lifespan was between incalculable and 80,000 years. They do not appear in times less than that because human merit is insufficient, {but those turning the wheel of power such as King Kaniṣka do appear.} Question: Why are they called cakravartins? Reply: Because they possess a precious wheel (cakra) with which they rule their empires. Further, there are four types of cakravartins: those who possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron. {Such cakravartins are definitely beings of Jambudvīpa.} The Throwing Stones Sūtra states: The wheels are, respectively, four, three, two, and one krośa in circumference.[996] Also, Presentation on the World explains that they rule, in reverse order, one continent of Jambudvīpa, two continents of southern Jambudvīpa and eastern Videha, three except for northern Kuru, and four continents.[997] One sūtra declares they possess a golden wheel alone.[998]
lhan cig gnyis min sangs rgyas bzhin/ / 96 phas bsu rang 'gro g.yul bshams dang / / mtshon brtsams pas rgyal gnod pa med/ /
Like buddhas, two cakravartins do not appear simultaneously. They conquer by welcoming, himself advancing, preparing for battle, displaying weapons, without harming beings. (3:96bcd)

'khor los bsgyur ba de dag gling bzhi gcig tu { gang gis dbang byed pa'i gling du} dus lhan cig tu gnyis la sogs pa 'byung ba ni min te/ 'gran zla med pa'i las can yin pa'i phyir dper na sangs rgyas gnyis 'jig rten gyi khams gcig tu dus gcig la mi 'byung ba bzhin no/ / 'di yang bye brag tu smra ba dag ni 'jig rten gyi khams thams cad du sangs rgyas gcig las mi 'byung ste/ gang dag sangs rgyas gcig gis 'dul bar mi nus pa'i sems can de dag ni gzhan gyis kyang 'dul bar mi 'os pa'i phyir te/ sangs rgyas rnams mkhyen pa dang thugs rje dang mthu thogs pa dang bcas par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / khams mang po pa'i mdo las kyang*/ gang de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas gnyis snga phyi med par 'jig rten du 'byung ba ni gnas ma yin zhing go skabs med de 'di ni gnas med kyi gcig gang yin pa de ni gnas yod do/ / de bzhin gshegs pa dag ji lta ba de ltar 'khor los bsgyur ba dag kyang de bzhin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes 'dod do/ / phal chen sde pa la sogs pa gzhan dag ni mdo'i dgongs pa ni 'jig rten gyi khams gcig gi dbang du mdzad nas gsungs pa yin gyi mdo gzhan las shar la sogs pa'i 'jig rten na'ang sangs rgyas du ma yod par gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes 'dod pa nyid rigs pa yin no/ /

Two or more cakravartins do not appear together, simultaneously, in the four continents {or continents they control} because they rule without a rival, like two buddhas not appearing at the same time in the same world system. Vaibhāṣikas assert that no more than one buddha occurs in all world systems because those sentient beings who cannot be tamed by one buddha cannot be tamed by another buddha, since it would follow that the realization, compassion, and might of that buddha would be impeded. The Multiple Elements Sūtra states: The appearance at the same time of two tathāgatas, arhats, [294] completely enlightened buddhas in one world system is not possible nor viable. But if just one instance of this impossible state existed, it would then be possible. Cakravartins exist in just the way tathāgatas exist.[999] The Mahāsāṃghika school and so on assert that this sūtra intends just one world system. In other sūtras it is stated that many buddhas exist in other world systems, such as those in the east and so on. This assertion is logical.
'khor los bsgyur ba bzhi po de dag gis phyogs las rgyal bar byed pa'i tshul ni
HOW THE FOUR CAKRAVARTIN KINGS CONQUER ALL

(1) The holder of the golden wheel conquers {vassal kings of the realm} by welcoming (pratyudyāna) opponents. (2) The possessor of the silver wheel conquers by himself advancing (svayaṃyāna) [alone]. (3) The possessor of the copper wheel conquers by merely preparing for battle (kala). (4) The possessor of the iron wheel conquers by merely displaying weapons (hāstra). Due to that the adversaries bow, and victory is won without harming any sentient being because [cakravartins] have abandoned the ten nonvirtuous actions. {Further, among those who simultaneously generate the awakening mind and accumulate merit, some become buddhas and some [become cakravartins] and none can oppose them. Therefore such beings don’t appear in the same world at the same time, but they do appear in other worlds. The [Multiple Elements] Sūtra intends a single world, otherwise more than one cakravartin would not appear anywhere. The cause of taking birth as a cakravartin is having formerly constructed stūpas, printed volumes of texts, turned the wheel of Dharma, and so on.} So too, cakravartin kings have six other excellent precious articles: a precious elephant, horse, jewel, queen, treasurer, and minister. Thus they have seven precious possessions in their empire. The Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra records they have seven secondary precious possessions: Sword, hide, bedding, grove, residence, clothes, and shoes.[1000]

lus phun sum tshogs pa skyes bu chen po'i {mdzod spu dang gtsug tor ma gtogs pa} mtshan sum cu yang yod de 'on kyang rin po che'i phreng ba las/ 'khor los bsgyur ba thams cad la/ / 'di dag yod par 'dod mod kyi/ / dag dang mdzes dang gsal ba ni/ / sangs rgyas rnams kyi char mi phod ces dang*/ nyi ma rnams kyis 'od byed pa/ / me khyer rnams dang bag 'dra ltar/ / sangs rgyas rnams kyi mtshan dang ni/ / 'khor los bsgyur rnams bag tsam 'dra/ / zhes 'byung ba ltar

Also, they possess the thirty excellent marks of the body of a great being {excluding the spiral hair between the eyebrows and the crown protrusion.} The Precious Garland says: Indeed, it is asserted that all cakravartins have these. But their purity, beauty, and clarity are no match for the features of the buddhas.[1001] And: Just as the radiance of a firefly is minute compared to the radiance of the sun, the marks of a cakravartin are infinitesimal compared to the marks of a buddha.[1002]
thub mtshan yul na gnas pa dang / / gsal la rdzogs pas 'phags pa yin/ / 97
The marks of a sage are superior in placement, radiance, and completion. (3:97ab)
thub pa sangs rgyas kyi mtshan sum cu rtsa gnyis ni shin tu yul na gnas pa dang gsal la rdzogs pas khyad par du 'phags pa yin la 'khor los bsgyur ba'i ni de lta ma yin no/ /
Thus the thirty-two marks (lakṣaṇa) of a sage buddha are superior in placement (deśatha), radiance (uttapta), and completion (pūrṇatva). The marks of the cakravartins cannot compare.
'jig rten 'grib pa'i tshul ni
The destruction of world systems

'jig rten 'di 'chags nas ring po ma lon pa na shing rta'i srog shing tsam gyi char bab pas sa chen po 'di chus gang bar gyur pa rlung gis bsdus shing 'thas par byas pas sa'i steng du sa'i ro'am bcud kha dog mar gsar 'dra ba ro sbrang rtsi ma bskol ba lta bu dri phun sum tshogs pa chags par gyur to/ / de nas sems can tshe dang las dang bsod nams zad pa dag 'od gsal gyi lha'i ris nas shi 'phos nas 'dir skyes par gyur te de dag la ni bskal pa dang po pa zhes bya'o/ / de'i tshe ni nyi zla dang rgyu skar dang dus tshigs dang lo zla dang nyin mtshan dang skad cig thang cig yud tsam dang skyes pa dang bud med kyi dbang po tha dad dang bshang gci dang khang khyim dang ming dang rigs dang mdog dbyibs tha dad kyang med de gzhan du na sems can sems can zhes bya'o/ / yang ci bskal pa dang po'i mi rnams kyang rgyal po dang bcas pa yin nam zhe na ma yin te/

Not long after the formation of this world system, rain falls, covering this great earth with water to the depth of a chariot pole. Then the wind condenses it, [295] making it solid. The residue or essence of the earth congeals on the surface with a color like fresh butter, a taste like unboiled honey, and an excellent smell. Then sentient beings whose lifespan, karma, and merit are exhausted die as gods of Ābhāsvara and are born here. They are called “beings of the first eon.” At that time there was no sun nor moon, nor constellations, nor divisions of time (years, months, days, nights, moments, seconds, hours). There were no different male or female faculties, nor feces or urine, nor different houses, language, caste, color, or physical shape. Still, sentient beings of this era were called sentient beings. Question: Did humans of the first eon have a king or not?
sngar byung sems can gzugs can bzhin/ / de nas rim gyis ro la chags/ /
In ancient times sentient beings were like form gods. Then, in time, one being desired tastes. (3:97cd)

sngar byung ba'i sems can bskal pa dang po pa'i mi rnams ni gzugs can gyi lha bzhin du rdzus te skyes pa dbang po tshang ba mdzes pa kha dog bzang ba lus la 'od yod pa rdzu 'phrul gyis nam mkha' la 'gro ba bsam gtan gyi dga' ba zas su za ba tshe dpag tu med pa dang ldan pa yin no/ / de nas rim gyis sems can ro la brkam zhing chags pa'i rang bzhin can zhig gis sa'i ro 'dzub mos blangs te bsnams shing zos la sems can gzhan gyis kyang mthong nas zos te khams gyi zas de dag zos pas lus lci zhing rtsub la 'od kyang 'gags te mun par gyur pa na chos nyid kyis nyi zla dang rgyu skar dang dus tshigs la sogs pa byung ste nyi ma dang zla bas gling bzhir snang ba'i bya ba byas so/ / {de'i tshe shar phyogs nas nyi ma shar ba na sems can de dag 'di skad du lha'i 'od de nyid 'di re zhes pas nyin mo byung ngo*/ / de nub pa na lha'i 'od de dmar por gyur pa 'di re zhes pa la mtshan mo byung ngo*/ / de nas zla ba shar ba mthong ste mun pa bkra bar byed do/ / zhes pas zla ba zhes chags so/ / yang nyi ma shar ba na lha'i 'od de nyid 'khor ba 'di re zhes brjod pas nyi ma zhes chags so }

Reply: They did not, because in ancient times sentient beings, humans of the first eon, were born supernaturally, possessing complete faculties, handsome, pure in color, with bodies radiating light, capable of flying due to their supernatural powers, consuming the joy of the absorptions as food, with inestimable lifespans like the form gods. Then, in time, one being was born who naturally desired and craved tastes, and he took and held some of the earth with his fingers and ate it. Others, seeing this, also ate it, and through eating oral food, their bodies became heavy and gross and their radiance faded. In the darkness the sun, moon, constellations, and the divisions of time arose spontaneously, and the sun and moon shone on the four continents. {At that time, when the sun dawned in the east, sentient beings said, “This is the light of the divine,” and the day came to exist. When it set they said, “The divine light has reddened,” and the night came to exist. Then when they saw the dawning of the moon, they said, “It shines in the darkness,” and the moon came to exist. And when the sun dawned, they said, “This is the return of the divine light,” and the sun came to exist.}

de nas gang kha zas mang du za ba de ni kha dog ngan zhing lus lci la gang nyung du za na de ni kha dog bzang bas kha dog sna tshogs kyang byung zhing kha dog bzang ba'i nga rgyal can dag gis ngan pa rnams la brnyas pa dang mi dge ba spyad pas sa'i ro de nub par 'gyur to/ / de nas sa'i ro'am bcud zad nas mya ngan byas pa dang sa'i zhag dri ro snga ma dang 'dra ba kha dog dong ka'i me tog lta bu byung ba zos pas de yang snga ma ltar nub bo/ / de zad pa na myu gu'i tshal dri ro sngar dang 'dra ba kha dog ka dam yu ka'i me tog lta bu zhig byung ba zos so/ / sa'i bcud dang zhag dang myu gu'i tshal rnams ni rim pa ltar sor bcu drug dang bcu gnyis dang brgyad yin par gzhan dag 'chad do/ / snga ma ltar de yang zad pa na ma rmos ma btab pa'i 'bras sa lu sor bzhi tsam pa nang brngas na nub skye nub brngas na nang skye ba phub shun med pa byung ba zos so/ / de ni kham gyi zas ches rags shing rtsub pa yin pas mi gtsang 'byung ba'i lam pho mo'i dbang po dang dbyibs tha dad pa dag kyang byung bar gyur to/ / de nas de dag phan tshun du bltas pa na sngon goms pa'i tshul bzhin ma yin pa yid la byed pas 'dod chags skyes te log par zhugs pa na gzhan dag gis {blun po bya ba ma yin pa byed pa sems can sun 'byin pa zhes brjod cing } sa rdul la sogs pa gtor zhing smad pas de'i ched du khang {bya ba min pa de bya ba'i phyir } khyim dag byas so/ / {de ni khyim gyi dang po'o }

Then the complexion of those who ate more declined, and their bodies became heavy, while the bodies of those who ate less retained their pure and diverse complexions. Those with pride in having a pure complexion despised those who did not, and through such nonvirtue, the taste of the earth deteriorated. Then when the residue or essence of the earth was depleted, they grieved and ate the flowers of the kantikara[1003] tree that had a similar smell, taste, and color to the nectar of the earth. But as before the taste declined, and when depleted, they ate the flowers of the kadamyuka[1004] tree, which had a smell and taste like a grove of reeds. Others explain that the essence of the earth, the nectar of the earth, and the grove of reeds are, respectively, sixteen, twelve, and eight fingers in length. Also, when these early foods were depleted, beings harvested unploughed, unplanted wild rice (śāli) four fingers in height. And through harvesting in cycles of decline, growth, and decline, it grew without a husk, and beings ate it. Since this oral food was extremely coarse and rough, beings developed an anus through which feces could pass, male and female organs, and distinct body shapes. [296] Then when they looked at each other, attachment arose through past karmic habits, and they engaged in sexual union. Others cursed them, {saying, “Don’t act stupidly; other beings will criticize you,”} and threw dust on them and so on. Therefore they built houses {so that they could engage in such actions [in private]. These were the first householders}.
le los sog 'jog byas nas ni/ / 'dzin bcas rnams kyis zhing dpon bstabs/ / 98 de nas las kyi lam lhag pas/ / tshe thung lo ni bcu yin no/ /

Through laziness they hoarded the harvest. To protect their interests, they appointed a leader. Then, through the excessive [practice of nonvirtuous] karmic paths, their lifespan decreased to ten years. (3:98)

ma rmos ma btab pa'i 'bras sa lu de dag kyang nam 'dod pa na len pa na le lo can rnams kyis {nang par za rgyu nub mo bslangs nas gzhan yang de la 'gran nas } gsog 'jog byas pa na phub shun kyang byung la de brngas pa'i shul du yang mi skye bas de nas ni sems can de dag ma mthun par so sor yongs su 'dzin pa dang bcas pa rnams kyis zhing bgos te gnas pa ni phan tshun{ du lan gsum du} rku 'phrog tu gyur pa na{ de la brtsad par gyur te tshar bcad pa'i phyir tshogs nas bcos shing} de dgag pa'i phyir skye bo rang bzhin bzang po zhig zhing dpon du bstabs shing bskos nas lo thog gi drug cha ster ba byas pa ni rgyal po mang pos bkur ba zhes bya ba yin te/ de yang chos dang tshul khrims kyi kun spyod dang shes rab kyi tshul kun tu spyod pas 'khor mgu bar byed pas rgyal po dang zhing rnams kyi bdag por gyur cing phongs pa las skyob pas na rgyal rigs zhes bya ste rgyal po rnams kyi dang po ni de yin la/ {de ni bdag cag gi ston pa yin no } de'i khyim la'ang rgyal po'i khab ces bya'o/ / de'i tshe gang dag 'dod pa chung zhing khyim las yid phyir phyogs te dgon pa dang nags su gnas pa de dag la ni bram ze dang*/ rku ba la sogs pa mi byed pa la rje'u'i rigs dang*/ byed pa la dmangs rigs dang gdol pa'i rigs zhes bya ba'i ming du gyur te rigs tha dad kyang byung ngo*/ / mang pos bkur ba'i bu 'od mdzes dang*/ de'i bu dge ba dang*/ de'i bu dge mchog dang*/ de'i bu gso sbyong 'phags te/ de dag la ni bskal ba dang po'i rgyal po lnga zhes zer ro/ / de'i rjes la nga las nu dang mdzes pa dang nye mdzes dang mdzes can dang mdzes ldan rnams ni 'khor los bsgyur ba lnga zhes zer ro/ /

They took the unploughed, unplanted wild rice when they desired. But through laziness they hoarded the harvest, {collecting it at night while fending off others, to eat in their houses}. Then husks began to appear, and rice would not grow in the wake of the harvest. Sentient beings fell into disagreement, and to protect their interests they divided up the fields and lived there. But then beings began to mutually plunder each other’s crops. {After this had occurred three times, dispute arose, and} to end it {they formed a group to settle the issue}. A being with a good nature was appointed leader, and he was called Mahāsaṃmata (“great one honored by many”) and allocated one-sixth of the harvest. He gladdened his companions through his practice of Dharma, ethics, and wisdom, and he became king and lord of all the fields. He was called a kṣatriya due to protecting his subjects from poverty, and he became the first king; {that being was our Master,} and his household was called Rājagṛha. At that time those who had little desire, who directed their minds (manas) beyond the duties of the householder and lived in solitude in the forests, were called brahmans. Those who did not steal were called vaiśya. Those who did steal were called śūdra or low caste (caṇḍala). Thus the castes arose. Mahāsaṃmata, his son called Rocana, his son called Kalyāṇa, his son called Varakalyāṇa, and his son called Upauṣadha are known as the five kings of the first eon. Then Māndhātṛ, Cāru, Upacāru, Cārumat, and Abhirūpa are called the five cakravartins.

de dag las rgyal po'i brgyud pa ji ltar byung ba'i tshul ni gdags pa dang*/ lung gzhi dang*/ mngon par 'byung ba'i mdo dag tu blta bar bya'o/ / {de'i bu 'od mdzes te/ de'i tshe sems can rnams kyi ming cha stod ces bya'o/ / de'i bu dge ba ste/ de'i tshe mi rnams kyi ming til skyes zhes bya'o/ / de'i bu dge mchog ste/ de'i mi rnams kyi ming sprin mgrin zhes bya'o/ / de'i bu gso sbyong 'phags te/ de'i tshe mi rnams kyi ming ta la'i rje dar zhes bya'o/ / de dag ni bskal pa dang po'i rgyal po lnga yin no/ / gso sbyong 'phags kyi spyi bo las skyes pa ni 'khor los bsgyur ba'i rgyal po nga las nu ste gling bzhi dang*/ sum cu rtsa gsum gyi phyed la dbang byas so/ / de'i mi rnams kyi ming spyod pa can dang*/ sems pa can dang*/ nyer rtogs pa can dang*/ shed las skyes pa zhes pa bzhi bshad de/ ming gi rnam grangs tha dad 'di nas byung bar gsal lo/ / de'i brla g.yas las skyes pa mdzes pa ste gling gsum la dbang ngo*/ / de'i brla g.yon las skyes pa nye mdzes te gling gnyis la dbang ngo*/ / de'i bol las skyes pa mdzes can te/ gling gcig la dbang byas so/ / de'i rkang mthil las skyes pa mdzes ldan te/ gling gcig la dbang ngo*/ / 'di man chad kyi 'khor lo bsgyur ba rnams ni gling gcig la dbang ba sha stag tu bshad cing mthar sgra gcan zin gyis mang pos bkur ba'i rgyal brgyud mthar thug par bshad do/ / khams kyi rgyal phran ni ma ga d+ha'i gzugs can snying po/ ko sa la'i gsal rgyal/ bad sa la'i 'char byed/ 'phags rgyal gyi rab snang la sogs pa'o }

You should consult the Presentation on the World,[1005] the Chapters on Vinaya,[1006] and the Sūtra on Going Forth[1007] to understand how the lineage of kings arose from them. {At the time of his son Rocana, men were called “the ancient ones” (pūrva); at the time of his son Kalyāṇa, men were called “cultivators of sesame” (tilakāṣika);[1008] at the time of his son Varakalyāṇa, men were called “cloud necks” (meghagrīva); at the time of his son called Upauṣadha, men were called “palmyra legs” (tālajaṅgha); and these were the five kings of the first eon. The cakravartin king Māndhātṛ was born from the crown of Upauṣadha, and he ruled half of the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa. The name of humans of that time was fourfold: “those who act,” “those who think,” “those who realize,” and “those born from Manu” (manuja), and other synonyms arose from these. Cāru was born from Upauṣadha’s right thigh, and he ruled three continents. Upacāru was born from his left thigh, and he ruled two continents. Cārumat was born from his ankle, [297] and he ruled one continent. Abhirūpa was born from the sole of his foot, and he ruled one continent. It is said that the cakravartins after them ruled one continent only and that Rāhula was the final king in the lineage of King Mahāsaṃmata.[1009] The vassal kings of this realm were King Bimbisāra of Magadha, King Prasenajit of Kosala, King Udayin of Vaiśālī, King Pradyota of Ujjayanī, and so on.}

gang gi tshe mang pos bkur ba la sogs pa rgyal por bskos pa de'i tshe sems can gcig la gcig log par spyod pa'i 'dod log dang ma byin par len pa dang srog gcod pa dang rdzun du smra ba la sogs pa mi dge ba du ma byas so/ /de nas{ mi dge ba'i} las kyi lam de dag lhag par spyad pas tshe dang gzugs dang longs spyod rnams 'gribs te tshe shin tu thung bas lo ni{ ring shos kyang} bcu pa'i bar du mar 'grib pa{ yin pas des na phung krol gyi rtsa ba ro la chags pa dang le lo} yin no/{/de'i tshe na bu mo ni lo lnga nas bag mar gtong ngo*/ / gos kyi mchog skra'i la ba/ zas kyi mchog ko tra ba/ rgyan gyi mchog mtshon cha/ ro kha ba min pa lnga nub bo/ / mar til mar sprang rtsi bu ram lan tshwa lnga yang nub bo/ / mtshon gyi dus su bsam pa rtsub pa mthong tshad la sdang ba'i gnod sems drag po/ mtshon cha rtsub pa ci bslangs mtshon du gyur te/ rngon pas ri dwags mthong ba bzhin/ gcig gis gcig gsod pa zhag bdun 'byung la des shi ba thams cad dmyal bar skye'o/ / ma shi ba kha cig 'dus nas srog gcod spangs pas/ tshe dang kha dog dang stobs dang bde ba dang longs spyod 'phel te de dag gi bu bu mo rnams kyis lo nyi shu thub bo/ / de bzhin du mi dge bcu spangs pas brgyad khri bar 'gyur ro/ / de nas yang mi dge ba spyad pas bcu par gyur pa na mi ma yin rnams 'khrugs nas nad gsor mi rung ba zla ba bdun btang bas phal cher 'chi ste des shi ba rnams kyang dmyal bar skye'o/ / de'i lhag ma tshogs na 'bring du skyes nas mi dge bcu spangs pas brgyad khrir 'phel lo/ / de las yang 'gribs nas lhas char ma phab pas mu ge lo bdun/ zla ba bdun/ zhag bdun 'byung bas phar cher 'chi la/ lhag ma lus nas cher skye bas de chad nas brgyad khrir 'phel lo/ / des shi ba rnams yi dwags su skye bar bshad do//}

When Mahāsaṃmata and so on were appointed kings, sentient beings did not engage in nonvirtuous actions such as the sexual misconduct of engaging in perverse acts with each other, taking what was not given, taking life, or uttering lies. But then, through strongly engaging in {nonvirtuous} karmic paths, their lifespan, bodies, and enjoyment declined, and through that decline, their lifespan decreased to {a maximum} of ten years. {Thus the root of dissatisfaction is attachment to tastes, and laziness.} {At that time, females were given in marriage from the age of five years, the best clothing was hair cloth, the best food was millet, and the best ornaments were weapons. The five tastes that were not bitter declined along with the five foods of butter, sesame oil, honey, molasses, and salt. Then, in the era of weapons, the thoughts of beings become coarse, and when they see another, a strong impulse to harm arises. Whatever they pick up becomes a crude weapon, just like a hunter who [uses anything as a weapon] when he sees a deer. Then they kill each other for seven days, and all those who die are reborn in hell. Those who survive assemble together and vow to stop taking life, and due to that their lifespan, complexion, strength, pleasure, and enjoyment increase and their sons and daughters obtain a lifespan of twenty years. Through abandoning the ten nonvirtuous actions, the lifespan of beings gradually increases to 80,000 years. Then again, through practicing nonvirtue, it again decreases to ten years. Due to the disturbance of nonhuman spirits, a mortal illness afflicts beings, and after seven months most die, and those who die are born in hell. The remainder assemble, develop a medium degree of virtue, and through abandoning the ten nonvirtues their lifespan increases to 80,000 years. Thereafter it decreases to ten again, and through the gods withholding rain, there is famine for seven years, seven months, and seven days, and most beings die. Those remaining generate great virtue, and lifespan increases to 80,000. Those who die are born as ghosts.}
bskal pa mtshon dang nad dang ni/ / mu ge dag gis tshar phyin to/ / 99 zhag rnams dang ni zla ba dang / / lo bdun dag tu go rims bzhin/ /
That eon ends with weapons, sickness, and famine. They last, respectively, seven days, seven months, or seven years. (3:99)

de'i tshe bar gyi bskal pa de mtshon gyi bskal pa dang*/ nad kyi bskal pa dang*/ mu ge'i bskal pa dag gis tshar phyin par gyur to/ / de la mu ge ni {'bru gab cor kung pa } gab co dang*/ {rus pa snum dang bral ba } rus gong dkar po dang*/ {'brur tsam gyi } thur mas 'che ba zhes bya ba gsum yin no/ / mtshon la sogs pa'i bskal pa de dag ni zhag bdun po rnams dang*/ zla ba bdun dang zhag bdun dang*/ lo bdun dang zla ba bdun dang zhag bdun dag tu mtshon chas gsod pa dang nad dang mu ge gsum dang go rim bzhin du sbyar ro/ / bar bskal de dag las thar pa'i rgyu ni nyin re tsam srog gcod spong ba dang dge 'dun la sman dang zhal zas 'bul ba rnams yin te/ khang bu brtsegs pa'i mdo las/ kun dga' bo gsum po 'di dag ni bar gyi bskal pa dag yin no/ / gsum po gang zhe na/ mtshon gyi bar gyi bskal pa dang*/ nad kyi bar gyi bskal pa dang*/ mu ge'i bar gyi bskal pa'o/ / kun dga' bo de la gang gis nyi ma gcig srog gcod pa spong zhing yang dag par blangs te gnas par byed na de mtshon gyi bar gyi bskal par mi skye bar 'gyur ro/ / gang zhig gis a ru ra gcig tsam yang dge 'dun la 'bul bar byed na de nad kyi bar gyi bskal par mi skye bar 'gyur ro/ / gang zhig gis zas nal ze gang tsam dge 'dun la phul na de mu ge'i bar gyi bskal par mi skye bar 'gyur ro zhes gsungs so/{ sa las sum cu pa la mu ge dang*/ nyi shu pa la nad dang*/ bcu pa la mtshon 'byung bar bshad do/ / de dag gi dus su gling gnyis su gnod sems lhag pa dang*/ kha dog ngan pa dang*/ nyams chung ba dang*/ bkres pa dang*/ skom pa tsam du 'gyur la/ byang na ni cung zad kyang mi 'byung ngo*/ / snod rags pa chags pa'i sa bon ni 'jig pa'i rtse mo'i rlung gi dkyil 'khor las byung ngo yang na rlung gi 'jig rten gzhan nas khyer nas 'ongs pa las 'byung ngo zhes so/ /}
'jig pa'i nges pa bshad pa ni
THE CERTAINTY OF DESTRUCTION
me dang chu dang rlung dag gis/ / 'jig pa dag ni yang gsum yin/ / 100 bsam gtan gnyis sogs gsum po ni/ / de dag gi rtse go rims bzhin/ /
There are three destructions by fire, water, and wind. Three absorptions from the second and so on are, respectively, peak stages. (3:100)

me dang chu dang rlung dag gis snod 'jig pa dag ni yang gsum yin te/ 'di ltar mes 'jig pa ni nyi ma bdun gyis 'jig ste/ gang gi tshe bar bskal bcu dgur sems can gyi 'jig rten zhig ste bsam gtan dang po man chad du sems can gcig kyang ma lus par gyur pa de'i tshe nam mkha' la sprin med cing nyi ma 'di nyid bzhi 'gyur gyis tsha bar gyur pas ni chu las gyur pa'i rtsi shing dang nags tshal rnams skem par byed do/ / de bzhin du gnyis pas ni chu phran dang lteng ka che chung rnams dang*/ gsum pas ni chu bo chen po bzhi dang*/ bzhi pas ni mtsho chen po ma dros pa dang*/ lnga pas ni phyi'i rgya mtsho'ang skem par byed do/ / drug pas ni sa chen po dang mchog tu sra ba'i ri rab la'ang du ba 'thul bar byed do/ / bdun pas ni thams cad me lce gcig tu 'bar te me de yang rang zhi bar 'gyur ro/ / chus 'jig pa ni 'od gsal gyi gnas su sprin 'khrigs pa las char chen po babs nas lan tshwa chu'i nang du zhu ba ltar 'gyur ro/ / rlung gis 'jig pa ni las kyi rlung gis ri rab kyang gtor yad du byed na gzhan rnams lta ci smros pa'i rlung gis 'jig par byed do/ / kha cig na re rlung gis ma par byed pa yin te mi rlung nad can skam pa bzhin no zhes zer ro/ / de dag gis gang 'jig ce na/

There are three destructions of the environment: by fire (agni), water (ambu), and wind (vāyu). (1) Thus destruction by fire is destruction by seven suns, where the cosmos of beings is destroyed over nineteen intermediate eons, leaving not even one sentient being on or below the first absorption. At that time it becomes extremely hot, and fruit trees and forests dependent on water dry up through the appearance of four suns in a cloudless sky. So too, through the appearance of two suns, small rivers and small and large pools dry up. Through the appearance of three suns, the four great rivers dry up. Through the appearance of four suns, the great lake of Anavatapta dries up. Through the appearance of five suns, even the great outer ocean dries up. Through the appearance of six suns, the great earth and even Meru, supreme in solidity, turns to smoke. Through the appearance of seven suns, everything blazes in one tongue of fire. But even that fire dies out and is pacified. (2) Destruction by water: In the abode of clear light, from the gathering clouds a great rain falls, and the realm dissolves like salt dissolves into water. (3) Destruction by wind: By the action of wind, if even the supreme mountain is destroyed, what need to mention the others that are destroyed by wind? Some say: Wind acts to dry up because it is like a human with wind illness who becomes thin.[1013] Question: What do those destroy?

me dang chu dang rlung gsum gyis 'jig pa na rim pa ltar bsam gtan dang po gnyis pa gsum pa man chad 'jig go /de'i phyir bsam gtan gnyis pa la sogs pa bsam gtan gsum pa dang bzhi pa gsum po ni me dang chu dang rlung gis 'jig pa de dag gi ma zhig par lus pa'i rtse mo yin par go rim bzhin du sbyar te shes par bya'o/ / de yang ci'i phyir zhe na/

Reply: The three states of fire, water, and wind destroy the environment up to the first, second, and third absorptions, respectively. Therefore the three absorptions — the second, third, and fourth absorptions — should be known as the peak stages of the undestroyed remaining environment that is not destroyed, respectively, by fire, by water, or by wind. Question: Why?
de yi skyon dang chos mthun phyir/ / bzhi pa na med mi g.yo'i phyir/ / 101 mi rtag de yi gzhal med khang / / sems can bcas te 'byung 'jig phyir/ /

Because their errors correspond to them. In the fourth there is no destruction because it is not affected. They are impermanent because the mansions possess sentient beings who arise and perish. (3:101)
de dag ni mi rtag ste bzhi pa{ 'di yan chad na rlung la sogs pa 'og gzhi gcig tu 'brel ba ni med la} de'i gzhal med khang ni sems can dang bcas te 'byung ba dang 'jig pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: Those are impermanent because the fourth absorption {and above, which have no direct relationship to the lower bases of wind, water, and fire,} and the mansions of this level possess sentient beings who arise and perish.
me yis bdun no chu yis gcig / de ltar chu bdun thal nas kyang / / 102 me yis bdun no de nas ni/ / mjug tu rlung gis 'jig pa yin/ /
It is destroyed by fire seven times, then by water. Thus, following destruction by water seven times, it is destroyed by fire seven times. Then at the end of those it is destroyed by wind. (3:102)

go rim ni me yis lan bdun btud de 'jig pa yin no/ / de'i 'og tu chu yis 'jig pa lan gcig yin no/ / de nas me bdun bdun btud de 'jig pa'i 'og tu chus 'jig pa re re ste de ltar chus 'jig pa lan bdun thal nas kyang yang me yis lan bdun 'jig pa yin no/ / mes bdun zhig pa'i rjes de nas ni de'i mjug tu rlung gis 'jig pa yin te/ {de lta na gdags pa las dge rgyas pa rnams kyi tshe tshad bskal chen drug cu re bzhi yin no zhes pa yang legs par drangs pa yin no zhes so/ / 'dir tshangs chen gyi tshe tshad bar bskal drug cur bshad kyang snod 'chags 'jig gi bar bskal gnyis kyis ma tshang ngo*/ / gal te snod 'chags ma thag skyes la/ 'jig khar 'chi 'pho bas tshang ngo zhe na/ de lta na snod 'chags 'jig la bar bskal re re dang*/ sems can 'chags 'jig la bar bskal bcu dgu bcu dgu bshad pa dang 'gal lo/ / de bzhin du 'od gsal ba'i tshe tshad bskal chen brgyad du bshad pa'ang bar bskal nyi shu rtsa gnyis kyis ma them la/ dge rgyas ba'i drug cu re brgyad bshad pa'ang de dang 'dra mod kyi/ 'od kyang de dang nye bas de skad bshad do/ / gal te chus 'jig pa ni dus ring po na 'byung la/ rlung gis 'jig pa de bas kyang ring ba na 'byung zhe na/ rgyu snyoms 'jug gi khyad par las te/ dang po bas gnyis pa snyoms 'jug khyad par 'phags la/ gnyis pa las gsum pa khyad par du 'phags pas lus gnas pa'ang yun ring la snod kyang de dag gi tshe dang mthun par gnas pa'i phyir ro} de ltar na bsam gtan dang po man chad ni 'chags pa dang gnas pa dang 'jig pa dang stongs pa thams cad bsdoms pa la bskal pa chen po gcig tu byed cing*/ bsam gtan gnyis pa ni bskal pa chen po brgyad na 'jig la/ bsam gtan gsum pa ni bskal pa chen po drug cu rtsa bzhi na 'jig go zhes bya ba yin no/ /

The order of destruction is that the environment is destroyed by fire seven times. Then it is destroyed by water once. Then it is destroyed by fire seven times. Then it is destroyed by water. Thus, following destruction by water through seven cycles, it is destroyed again by fire seven times. Then, at the end of those seven destructions by fire, it is destroyed by wind. {Thus Treatise on Designation expounds: It is properly stated that the measure of the lifespan in Śubhakṛtsna is sixty-four great eons.[1014] Still, the measure of the lifespan of gods of the heaven of Mahābrahma is said to be sixty intermediate eons, less the two intermediate eons of formation and destruction of the environment. Objection: If beings are born just at the formation of the environment and die just at its destruction, it would be complete. Reply: Thus it would contradict the assertion that there is an intermediate eon each for the formation and destruction of the environment, and there are nineteen intermediate eons each for the formation and destruction of sentient beings. So too, the measure of the lifespan of Ābhāsvara is explained as eight great eons less twenty-two intermediate eons, and indeed the way Śubhakṛtsna is explained to be sixty-eight eons is similar to this. Moreover, this is stated since they are analogous. Question: If destruction by water occurs over a long time, is destruction by wind even longer than that? Reply: There is a difference in causal meditative attainment since the second [absorption] excels the first in meditative attainment and the third excels the second. Thus the bodies [of the gods] survive [progressively] longer [in the three absorptions], and the environment itself survives [progressively] longer, matching the lifespan of their inhabitants.} In that case, destruction of the first absorption and below occurs over one great eon comprising formation, endurance, destruction, and void periods. Destruction of the second absorption occurs over eight great eons, and the destruction of the third absorption occurs over sixty-four great eons.
khams gsum 'gro lnga skye gnas rten 'brel dang*/ / srid zhi zas dang snod bcud tshad rnams dang*/ / 'jal byed bskal pa'i rnam dbye la sogs pa/ / rtogs par 'dod pas gnas 'di mnyan par gyis/ /

Those who desire to comprehend the three realms, five types of reincarnating being, birth processes, dependent origination, existence, peace, food, the measure of the physical cosmos and its inhabitants, dimensions, classifications of eons, and so on should study this part.
chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi tshig le'ur byas pa las/ /'jig rten bstan pa zhes bya ba ste gnas gsum pa'o// //
chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi 'grel pa mngon pa'i rgyan las 'jig rten bstan pa zhes bya ba ste gnas gsum pa'i bshad pa'o// ! //
This has been part III, the “Exposition of Cosmology,” from Ornament of Abhidharma: A Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa. [300]
gnas bzhi pa las bstan pa/
18. The Theory of Action
da ni las bstan pa 'chad pa na 'o na {sdug bden gyis bsdus pa'i } snod bcud kyi 'jig rten sna tshogs bshad pa gang yin pa de dag sus byas she na/
QUESTION: WHO HAS CREATED the various physical world systems and their inhabitants {that are subsumed by the truth of suffering}?
las las 'jig rten sna tshogs skyes/ / de ni sems pa dang des byas/ / sems pa yid kyi las yin no/ / des bskyed lus dang ngag gi las/ / 1
Various mundane states arise from karma. That karma is intention and what is produced by it. Intention is mental karma. It induces physical and verbal karma. (4:1)

dbang phyug la sogs pa sus kyang blo sngon du btang ste byas pa ma yin gyi 'on kyang sems can rnams kyi las dge mi dge sna tshogs las snod bcud kyi 'jig rten bde sdug dang bzang ngan la sogs pa sna tshogs skyes zhes bya bas mtshams sbyar nas/ las dngos ston pa la las kyi rang bzhin dang*/ mdo las gsungs pa'i las rgyas par bshad pa gnyis las/

Reply: It is not the case that a creator such as Īśvara has created them through the prior projection of his thought. Instead, it is said that various types of outer or inner mundane states — whether pleasant or unpleasant, attractive or repulsive — arise from the diverse virtuous and nonvirtuous karma of sentient beings. At this stage in the actual presentation of karma there are two divisions: the nature of karma, and the elaboration of karma expressed in the sūtras.
[dang po] las kyi rang bzhin/
The nature of karma
['di] la'ang
This has two headings: overview and elaboration.
mdor bstan pa ni
OVERVIEW
'o na de lta bu'i 'jig rten skyed byed kyi las de yang gang zhe na/
Question: What is this karma that acts to generate such mundane states?

smras pa/ {thun mong dang so so'i } las de ni sems pa'i las dang sems pa des byas pa{ ste des kun nas bslang ba} bsam pa'i las gnyis las sems pa'i las ni yid shes dang mtshungs ldan{ yid yul la g.yo bar byed pa} lus ngag gi las mngon par 'du byed pa'i sems byung yin pa'i phyir/ yid kyi las yin no/ / yid ni 'dir skye mched kyi yid yin no/ / {yid kyang rig byed min par 'gyur ro zhe na/ rig byed min pa ni rten 'byung ba la ltos la yid la mi ltos so/ / las kyang rkyen la ltos par smra bas kho na rgyur smra ba'i lta bar mi 'gyur de yang rnam smin kho na min gyi skyes bu byed 'bras gtso che'o/ / 'jig rten gnyis po de yang yul dang lus la chags pas 'grub bo } sems pa des bskyed pa'i{ bsam pa'i} las ni lus kyi las dang ngag gi las te/ de dag ni sems pas kun nas bslang ba'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: That {shared and unique} karma is both (1) the karma that is intention (cetanā) and (2) karma derived from intention, which is produced by that intention {through being motivated by it}. (1) Karma that is intention is the mental factor concomitant with mental consciousness {that moves the mental faculty to its object} and actually creates physical and verbal karma. Thus it is mental karma, and here “mental” refers to the mental base.[1015] {Objection: But the mental faculty would become nonindicative [form] (avijñapti). Reply: Nonindicative [form] relies on dependent origination; it does not rely on the mental faculty. But since karma relies on conditions, it should not be spoken of in terms of causes alone. Further it is not just karmic maturation but primarily a result of conscious effort. Also both types of mundane states are established through attachment to objects and the body.} That intention induces the karma {that is the outcome of intention}: specifically, physical (kāya) karma and verbal (vāk) karma are the karma motivated by intention.
de dag rnam rig rnam rig min/ / lus rnam rig byed dbyibs su 'dod/ / 'gro min gang phyir 'dus byas ni/ / skad cig ma yin 'jig phyir ro/ / 2
These are indicative or nonindicative. Some assert that the indicative aspect of the body is shape. It cannot travel. Why? Because conditioned states are momentary states that disintegrate. (4:2)

yang lus kyi las ni lus la brten pas de'i las dang*/ ngag ni ngag gi rang bzhin nyid las dang*/ yid kyi las ni yid kyis kun nas bslangs pa'i phyir las su 'dod do/ / lus ngag gi las de dag ni rnam par rig byed dang rnam par rig byed min pa gnyis yin no/ /

Physical karma is karma supported by the body; verbal karma is karma that is, by nature, speech itself; and mental karma is fully motivated by the mental faculty. Thus they are all asserted to be karma. These physical and verbal karmas are either (1) indicative (vijñapti) or (2) nonindicative (avijñapti).
rgyas par bshad pa
ELABORATION
['di] la rig byed dang*/ rig byed ma yin pa dang*/ de dag gi khyad par bshad pa gsum las
This has three headings: indicative form, nonindicative form, and explaining their difference.
dang po
Indicative form
['di] la lus kyi rig byed dang ngag gi rig byed gnyis las
This has two headings: indicative form of the body, and indicative form of speech.
lus kyi rnam par rig byed ni
INDICATIVE FORM OF THE BODY

bye brag tu smra ba 'gro ba dang phyag 'tshal ba dang srog gcod pa la sogs pa rnam smin gyi lus dang{ rgyas byung gi lus} las tha dad pa'i{ lus de lta bu'i} dbyibs su{ rdzas grub tu} 'dod de/ 'di ltar rnam smin gyi lus nyid yin na ni rig byed dge mi dge mi srid par 'gyur te/ de ni lung ma bstan yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir phyar 'chol ba la sogs pa'i tshe lus kyi rig byed dbyibs su grub pa zhig spyi bo'i gtsug nas rkang pa'i bar du yod la/ de ni rig byed 'od ltar dang ba'i phyir dang*/ rnam smin gyi lus kyi gseb tu tshud pa'i phyir che bar yang mi 'gyur lci bar yang mi 'gyur zhes 'dod de nags la me zhugs pa bzhin no zhes zer ro/

Vaibhāṣikas assert that the indicative aspect of the body is {the substantially established} shape (saṃsthāna) {of the body} when walking, prostrating, killing, and so on but it is distinct from the maturational body {and enhanced body}. It is impossible for the maturational body itself [301] to reveal virtue or nonvirtue because it is neutral. Vaibhāṣikas assert that the indicative aspect of the body is established as shape when prostrating and so on and exists from the crown to the feet. Because the indicative aspect of the body is translucent like light and penetrates the interstices of the maturational body, it does not grow in size and weight but is like a fire that enters a forest.

{ 'o na rnam smin gyi lus las rdzas tha dad cing de dang mnyam pa'i rig byed kyi lus dbyibs su skye na rnam smin gyi lus sngar bas che bar 'gyur ro/ / rnam smin gyi lus gseb dang bcas pa de la thad ka thad kar thim pas so zhe na/ 'o na rnam smin gyi lus sngar pas 'khregs shing lcir song bar thal lo zhe na/ rig byed kyi lus 'od ltar dang bas mi 'gyur zhes so mtshan nyid ni de la dmigs pa'i sems pas kun nas bslang ba'i dbyibs so/ / de smra ba na mchu 'gul ba dang*/ 'gro ba na yan lag g.yo ba dang*/ ston pa'i mchu bim pa ltar dmar ba sogs bsal te/ rim pa ltar mchu lag 'gul ba ni 'gul bar bya'o snyam du de la dmigs pa'i sems bskyed pa min gyi zhar byung yin la/ phyag 'tshal ba sogs ni 'gul bar bya'o snyam pa'i sems skyes pas so/ / ston pa'i mchu ni smon lam gyis bskyed pa yin la/ de la dmigs pa'i sems bskyed pa min pas so/ / zhes 'dod do/ /}

{Objection: If the indicative aspect of the body is distinct in substance from the maturational body but arises with the same shape, it would be greater in size than [the maturational body] since the maturational body would precede it and it would immediately dissolve into the interstices of the maturational body. Since the maturational body would precede it, it would be hard and heavy. Reply: That would not occur since the indicative aspect of the body is translucent like light. [Vaibhāṣikas] define it as “the shape motivated by the intention that focuses on it.” Reply: If that is said, then (1) the movement of the lips, (2) the movement of the limbs when walking, and (3) the redness of the red lips of the Buddha would not be [indicative form] because, respectively, movement of the lips and limbs is not generated by intention focusing on them thinking “move” but instinctively, unlike prostrations and so on that occur due to the intention thinking “move,” and the lips of the Buddha are generated by prayer and not through intention focusing on them.}

don 'di la gnas ma'i bu'i sde pa ni yul gzhan na yod pa'i lus kyi rig byed nyid ma nyams par yul gzhan du {sems pas ji ltar dmigs lus kyang de ltar 'gyur bas lus nyid } 'gro bar{ rig byed du} 'dod de/{ lus kyi las ni lus kyi bya ba yin na de ni lus g.yo ba la rigs kyi mi g.yo ba la min pas des na/ /} 'dis sems sems byung dang sgra dang me lce dang glog dang 'bab chu las gzhan skad cig mar mi 'dod {kyi 'jig rgyu dang phrad nas mi rtag par 'dod } pa'i phyir dngos po gzhan yang de bzhin du 'dod do/ /

Regarding the meaning of this, the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that the indicative aspect of the body that exists in one place may travel {as indicative form} to another place without transforming {since the body changes according to the way intention focuses on it}. {If physical karma is physical action, then it is logical that it is the movement of the body and not nonmovement. Therefore} they do not assert states to be momentary other than minds and mental factors, sound and flames, and lightning and waterfalls. {They assert them to be impermanent due to meeting their causes of destruction}, and they assert other functional entities to be similar.

de ni 'thad pa ma yin te/ lus kyi dbyibs ma nyams par yul gzhan du 'gro ba ni min te/ gang gi phyir zhe na/ 'dus byas rnams ni grub ma thag 'jig pa'i skad cig ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de yang rgyu gzhan med par 'jig pa'i gtan tshigs kyi phyir ro/ / phyogs snga ma na re rgyu med par 'jig pa ni ma yin te/ bum pa 'jig pa tho ba dang grang ba 'jig pa tsha ba la sogs pa la ltos so zhe na/ 'jig pa zhes bya ba 'di bum pa la sogs pa med pa'am/ de las gzhan pa'i dngos po'am/ de'i bdag nyid kyis 'jig pa yin/ phyogs dang po thob ni thob la sogs pas byed pa ma yin te/ med pa bya bar 'gal ba'i phyir ro/ / gnyis pa'ang ma yin te bum pa la sogs pa 'jig pa'i rgyu ma yin par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / phyogs gsum pa'ang ma yin te/ 'jig pa'i bdag nyid du rang gi rgyu las grub pa'i phyir ro/ / ma grub na 'jig pa bum pa la sogs pa'i bdag nyid ma yin par thal ba'i phyir ro zhes bya ba'i skyon rigs pa mkhyen pa rnams kyis brjod mod kyi

Reply: This is unacceptable because if the shape of the physical body does not transform, the body cannot travel to other places. Question: Why? Reply: Because conditioned states are momentary (kṣaṇika) entities that disintegrate (vyavāt) as soon as they are established. Moreover reasoning demands that they disintegrate without requiring any other cause for their destruction. One holding that previous position says: It is not disintegration without other causes because the destruction of a vase relies on hammers and so on, and the destruction of cold relies on heat and so forth. Reply: This “destruction” you refer to is either (1) the nonexistence of a vase and so on, (2) a thing other than it, or (3) destruction by its own state itself. The first position, where destruction is instigated by a hammer and so on, is not established because the vase’s nonexistence would exclude the act of destruction. The second position is not established because in consequence the vase and so on would not be the cause of its destruction.[1016] The third position also is not established because the state of destruction is established from the very cause of that thing itself. If these refutations are not established, then indeed those who understand logic would highlight the error that, in consequence, disintegration would not be the very state of the vase itself and so on.
rgyu med pa las 'ga' mi 'byung / / rgyu yang 'jig pa por 'gyur ro/ / gnyis gzung 'gyur te rdul la med/ /
[Disintegration] would never occur in those lacking the causes. The cause would also act as the agent that destroys. It would be apprehended by both. Shape does not exist as a particle. (4:3abc)

'on kyang 'dir bye brag tu smra bar rang gi grub pa'i mtha' la gnod par dogs nas skyon gzhan brjod par byed de/ 'di ltar 'jig pa rgyu gzhan la ltos pa yin na blo dang sgra dang me lce dang glo la sogs pa 'jig pa'i rgyu gzhan med pa rnams las 'jig pa 'ga' yang mi 'byung bar 'gyur te/ rgyu med pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag dang gis 'jig par 'dod na{ spyir 'jig pa phyis} rgyu la ltos par 'dod pa nyams pa yin no/ /

However, Vaibhāṣikas now equivocate on the issue, anxious that this may harm their own tenet system: [302] If disintegration relies on other causes, then disintegration would never occur in phenomena such as awareness, sound, flames, and lightning that lack other causes of disintegration, because they have no separate cause of disintegration. Reply: But if you assert that they disintegrate in that way, then your assertion that, {in general, disintegration} relies on {subsequent} causes would fail.
bye brag pa blo yang blo phyi mas 'jig la/ sgra yang sgra phyi mas 'jig go zhes bya bar 'dod pa'ang ma yin te/ de dag {cig car mi 'byung bas } phrad pa med pa'i phyir ro/ /

Vaiśeṣikas assert that awareness is destroyed by subsequent awareness and sound is destroyed by subsequent sound. Reply: This is not the case, because the former and latter [instances] do not meet {since they do not occur at the same time}.

gzhan yang {phyi ma phyi mas snga ma snga ma 'jig par byed na 'o na } me la sogs pas 'bras chan la sogs pa 'tshed pa na ma tshos pa tshos pa dang ches tshos pa dang ches cher tshos par byed pa na phyi ma phyi mas snga ma snga ma 'jig par byed pa'i phyir skyed par byed pa'i rgyu yang 'jig par byed pa po'i rgyur 'gyur ro/ / de lta na skyed pa'i rgyu de nyid 'jig pa'i rgyu yin na ni{ 'bras bu 'gal ba gnyis byed pa'am} skyes tsam nyid na 'jig pa'i phyir 'dus byas rnams{ mi 'jig par} yul gzhan du 'pho ba ma yin pa dang*/ {phyis } rgyu gzhan la ltos pa med par yang grub bo/ / bye brag tu smra bas lus kyi rig byed kha dog las rdzas tha dad pa'i dbyibs su 'dod pa la mdo sde pa na re

Again, {if the latter destroys the former, then} when fire and so on cooks rice and so forth, the latter would destroy the former: cooked rice would destroy uncooked rice, fully cooked rice would destroy semi-cooked rice, and the cause that generates would also act as the causal agent that destroys. Thus if just that cause of generation were the cause of destruction, then {it would produce two contradictory results}: (1) conditioned states would not move to other places {without destruction} because they would be destroyed through merely arising, and (2) disintegration would be established without reliance on other {subsequent} causes. Vaibhāṣikas assert that the indicative body is shape that is distinct in substance from color. Regarding that, Sautrāntikas say:

dbyibs gcig po de nyid mig shes kyis kyang mthong la lus kyi dbang pos reg pa na lus kyi rnam shes kyis kyang shes pa'i phyir skye mched kyi gzugs gcig dbang po gnyis kyi gzung bar 'gyur na de lta bu ni med de/ de'i phyir kha dog gi rdul phra rab bkod pa la kha dog gi dbyibs dang reg bya'i rdul phra rab bkod pa la reg bya'i dbyibs su 'dogs pa'i phyir de gnyis las rdzas gzhan pa ni med do/ { gal te ring po la sogs pa'i dbyibs mig dang mig shes kyis 'dzin na/ de tsam du lus kyis reg na'ang ring po la sogs par 'dzin pa'i blo skye bar myong bas grub pa'i phyir dbyibs de nyid dbang po gnyis kyis gzung bar thal ba las mi 'dzin pas so/ / des na kha dog dang reg bya'i rdul rags pa mig shes dang lus shes la snang ba'i bkod pa'i khyad par la yid shes rtog pas dbyibs su sgro btags pa yin gyi dbyibs mig shes dang lus shes gnyis kas 'dzin pa med kyi/ lus kyis 'dzin zhes pa'ang mig gis 'dzin na rgyu mtshan mtshungs zhes dgag pa'o/ / gzhan yang dbyibs du ma yul gcig na gnas par thal dkyil 'khor la sogs gru bzhi'am zlum po lta bu gcig la kha dog sna tshogs su snang ba'i phyir 'dod na/ go sa gcig tu dbyibs du ma mi 'byung bar 'dod pa nyams so/ / dbyibs kyi gzugs rags pa mi srid par 'gyur te sogs de'i byed rdul phran la dbyibs med pas so/} gzhan yang dbyibs rdzas su yod na rdul phra rab la dbyibs yod par 'gyur te/ gzugs can rdzas su grub pa ni rdul phra rab kho na yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

Eye consciousness sees shape itself, but if [that shape] can be touched by the physical body faculty, then body consciousness also would be aware of it, and one form base would be apprehended by both sense faculties; but such a state cannot exist. Therefore shape does not exist as a substance that is different from both [color and tactility] because the shape of color is imputed to the configuration of subtle particles of color, and the shape of tactility is imputed to the configuration of subtle particles of contact. {If the eye and eye consciousness were to apprehend a shape such as “long” and so on, and if just that shape were touched by the body, then it would follow that just that shape would be apprehended by two sense faculties because it would be established by tactile experience generating awareness that apprehends “long” and so on. But that is not apprehended. Therefore mental conception that conceives the different configurations of the coarse particles of color and tactility appearing to eye consciousness and body consciousness, imputes them to be shape. But shape is not apprehended by either eye consciousness or body consciousness, and shape being apprehended by the body or by the eye is also refuted since that reason equally applies. Again, some assert that it follows that many shapes exist in one object because one square or round maṇḍala, for instance, appears with various colors [possessing associated shapes within the maṇḍala]. Reply: But if that were so, then to assert many shapes do not occur in a single spatial location would fail. Moreover, the course shape of form would also be impossible, since the atoms that accrete to form it have no shape.} Again, if shape substantially exists, then subtle particles would have shape because substantially established physical objects consist of subtle particles alone.

rdul phra rab la dbyibs yod pa de lta'ang ma yin te/ cha dang bcas par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / gang gi phyir dbyibs de rdul phra rab la med pa de'i phyir yang dbyibs rdzas su med do zhes zer mod kyi de lta na kha dog dang reg bya'ang med par 'gyur te/ dbyibs ni de dag gi bdag nyid yin la de rdzas su med pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag gi bdag nyid kyang ma yin de las don gzhan du'ang med na dngos por ma grub pa'i phyir dbang po'i shes pa ma 'khrul ba la mi snang bar thal ba la lan med pa nyid yin no/ / de'i phyir dbyibs rdzas su gtan nas kyang ma grub bo zhes bya ba ni don smra ba la legs par ma mthong ngo*/ /

However, subtle particles can have no shape because it would then follow that they possessed parts. Indeed, they say that shape is not substantially existent because shape does not exist as a subtle particle. But color and tactility would also not be substantially existent because shape, which is not substantially existent, consists of just those. And if shape didn’t consist of those, or any other object, [303] then it would not be established as a thing, and it would follow that it would not appear to nonmistaken sense consciousness. To this [Vaibhāṣikas] have no reply. Therefore the statement “Shape is never substantially established” is not seen to be correct by exponents of external objects.
[ngag gi rnam par rig byed]
INDICATIVE FORM OF SPEECH
ngag rnams rig byed ni ngag sgra/ / 3
Indicative speech is the sound of speech. (4:3d)

ngag gi rnam par rig byed ni ngag gi rang bzhin gyi sgra nyid yin no/ / ngag gi sgra smros pa ni spyi la thal ba spang ba'i phyir ro/ / rig byed ni rang kun nas slong ba'i bsam pa rig par byed pa'i phyir yin no/ / mdo sde pa rnams ni lus ngag gi rang bzhin ni las ma yin gyi 'on kyang de dag gi dus su'ang sems pa nyid las yin te/ sems pa dge mi dge bar gyur na lus ngag mi dge ba dang dge bar snang yang don dge ba dang*/ sdig par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / 'o na sems pa dang bsam pa'i las gnyis gsungs pa ma yin nam zhe na/ sems pa dang bsam pa'i las ni rim pa ltar rgyu dang dus kyi kun slong gi dbang du mdzad nas gsungs pa yin la/ lus ngag las su gsungs pa ni/ sems pa de mthar phyin par byed pa'i phyir las su btags nas gsungs pa yin gyi thams cad du'ang sems pa nyid las yin no zhes bya bar 'dod la/ don 'di ni theg pa gong ma pa thams cad kyang bzhed pa yin no/ /

Indicative speech (vāgvijñapti) is sound (dhvani) that is the essence of speech (vāc). “Sound of speech” is stated to eliminate general [unwanted] consequences. “Indicative” means indicating [or revealing] the thought motivating the action. Sautrāntikas assert that the essence of physical and verbal action is not karma, for the intention that exists at the same time as them is karma, because if the intention is virtuous or nonvirtuous, then the action will be virtuous or sinful, even though the body and speech may appear to be [the opposite, that is,] nonvirtuous or virtuous. Question: Weren’t both karma that is intention and karma derived from intention stated? Reply: Karma that is intention and karma derived from intention were stated from the perspective of the causal motivator and concurrent motivator. Body and speech are said to be karma because they bring intention to fruition, and intention itself is asserted to be karma in every instance. This point is also asserted in all higher vehicles.
gnyis pa rig byed ma yin pa bshad pa ni/
Nonindicative form
rnam gsum dri med gzugs gsungs dang / / 'phel dang ma byas lam sogs phyir/ / 'dod gtogs rnam rig min skad cig/ / phyin chad 'das pa'i 'byung las skye/ / 4

Scripture declares three types, stainless form, increase, and the path not committed and so on. Nonindicative form of the desire realm arises in the first moment. After that it arises from past elements. (4:4)

'o na rig byed ma yin pa'i ngo bo ni bshad zin na de yod par gang gis shes she na/ lung gis shes te/ mdo las gnas gsum gyi gzugs kyis gzugs thams cad bsdus pa yin te/ bstan du yod la thogs pa dang bcas pa'i gzugs kyang yod/ bstan du med la thogs pa dang bcas pa'i gzugs kyang yod/ bstan du yang med la thogs pa yang med pa'i gzugs kyang yod do zhes gzugs rnam pa gsum gsungs pa'i phyir te/ bstan du yang med la thogs pa yang med pa'i gzugs ni rig byed min pa las gzhan med pa'i phyir dang*/ gzhan yang zag pa med pa'i chos rnams gang zhe na/ gzugs 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar byung ba gang la rjes su chags pa'am khong khro ba mi skye ba 'di dag ni zag pa med pa'i chos rnams zhes bya'o zhes bya ba nas rnam par shes pa'i bar du dri ma med pa'i gzugs gsungs pa'i phyir te/ zag pa med pa'i gzugs ni zag med kyi sdom pa las gzhan med pa'i phyir dang*/

Question: The nature of nonindicative form has been explained, but how do we know of its existence? Reply: This may be understood through [eight] scriptural passages: (1) A sūtra states that form of the three domains subsumes all form: Demonstrable and impeded form exists, undemonstrable and impeded form exists, and undemonstrable and unimpeded form exists.[1017] This sūtra declares three types of form, where undemonstrable and unimpeded form is nothing other than nonindicative form. (2) Again, a sūtra states: What are uncontaminated phenomena? They are any form occurring in the past, present, or future in relation to which attachment or anger is not generated; these are uncontaminated phenomena . . . [up to] . . . consciousness.[1018] This sūtra mentions stainless form (āmalarūpa), where uncontaminated form is nothing other than the uncontaminated vows.[1019]

gzhan yang lung rnam 'byed las/ bcom ldan 'das yul ko'u sham bi na dbyangs len gyi kun dga' rwa ba na bzhugs so/ / de nas tshe dang ldan pa skul byed bcom ldan 'das ga na ba der song ste phyin nas/ bcom ldan 'das kyi zhabs la mgo bos phyag 'tshal nas phyogs gcig tu 'dug ste/ bcom ldan 'das la tshe dang ldan pa skul byed kyis 'di skad ces gsol to/ / btsun pa rdzas las byung ba'i bsod nams bgyi ba'i dngos po 'bras bu che ba phan yon che ba gzi brjid che ba rgya che ba gdags pa mchis lags sam/ bcom ldan 'das kyis de la skul byed yod do zhes bka' stsal te/ skul byed bdun po 'di dag ni rdzas las byung ba'i bsod nams bya ba'i dngos po 'bras bu che ba phan yon che ba gzi brjid che ba rgya che ba yin te/ de dag dang ldan pa'i dad pa'i rigs kyi bu'am/ rigs kyi bu mo ni rgyu yang rung 'dug kyang rung nyal yang rung mi nyal yang rung ste rtag tu rgyun mi chad par bsod nams mngon par 'phel ba kho nar 'gyur ro/ / bdun gang zhe na skul byed 'di ni dad pa'i rigs kyi bu'am bu mo phyogs bzhi'i te/ de dang ldan pa'i dad pa'i rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo ni rgyu yang rung 'dug kyang rung nyal yang rung mi nyal yang rung ste rtag tu rgyun mi chad par bsod nams mngon par 'phel ba kho nar 'gyur zhing bsod nams nye bar skye ba kho nar 'gyur ro zhes bya ba nas de bzhin du kun dga'i rwa ba de nyid du gtsug lag khang rtsig pa dang*/ mal cha dang stan 'bul ba dang*/ 'tsho ba nar ma 'bul ba dang*/ mgron bu glo bur du 'gro 'ong byed pa la sbyin pa gtong ba dang*/ nad pa dang nad g.yog la sbyin pa gtong ba dang*/ rlung dang char pa la sogs pa yul ngan pa'i tshe gtsug lag khang gi nang du bsod snyoms 'bul ba zhes bya ba drug la'ang sbyar nas rgyas par gsungs so/ / de bzhin du rdzas las byung ba ma yin pa'i bsod nams 'phel ba bdun yang lan gnyis kyi bar du yang bcom ldan 'das la/ tshe dang (3) Moreover, Vinaya Divisions states: Once, when the Bhagavan was in the region of Kauśāmbī, he stayed at the grove of Ghoṣila. Venerable Cunda went to the residence of the Bhagavan, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. Then Cunda said to the Bhagavan: [304] “Venerable, are things that generate merit from material generosity, held to have a great result, great benefit, great splendor, and great magnitude?” The Bhagavan said: “Cunda, they are. Cunda, seven things that generate merit from material generosity have great result, great benefit, great splendor, and great magnitude. A son or daughter of good lineage with faith who possesses these, whether moving or seated, asleep or awake, always, without break, only increases in merit.” Cunda asked: “What are the seven?” The Bhagavan replied: “Cunda, they are when a son or daughter of good lineage with faith (1) offers groves to the fully ordained Saṅgha of the four directions. Cunda, this is the first thing generating merit from material generosity that has great result, great benefit, great splendor, and great magnitude because a faithful son or daughter of good lineage who possesses them, whether moving or seated, asleep or awake, always, without break, only increases in merit and only generates merit. So too, in that grove (2) building a temple, (3) offering beds and mattresses, (4) offering regular sustenance, (5) giving to guests who unexpectedly arrive, (6) giving to the sick and those nursing the sick, and (7) offering alms within the temple when conditions decline in that region due to storms and floods and so on.”[1020] These are extensively explained by applying the formula of the first to the remaining six.

btsun pa rdzas las byung ba ma lags pa'i bsod nams bgyi ba'i dngos po'i 'bras bu che ba nas rgya che ba'i bar gdags su mchis pa lags sam bcom ldan 'das kyis de la skul byed yod do zhes bka' stsal te/ skul byed bdun po 'di dag ni rdzas las byung ba ma yin pa'i bsod nams bya ba'i dngos po yin te/ de dag dang ldan pa'i dad pa'i rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo ni zhes bya ba nas bsod nams nye bar skye ba kho nar 'gyur ro zhes bya ba'i bar du gsungs nas/ bdun gang zhe na/ skul byed 'di ni dad pa'i rigs kyi bu'am/ rigs kyi bu mo de bzhin gshegs pa'am de bzhin gshegs pa'i nyan thos grong ngam zhing che ge mo zhig na rten cing bzhugs so zhes thos shing thos nas kyang*/ dga' ba dang*/ rab tu dga' ba rgya che ba dge ba nges par 'byung ba dang ldan pa thob ste/ skul byed 'di ni rdzas las byung ba ma yin pa'i bsod nams bya ba'i dngos po dang po yin no zhes bya ba nas bsod nams nye bar skye ba kho nar 'gyur ro zhes bya ba'i bar snga ma bzhin du gsungs so/ / de bzhin du de bzhin gshegs pa'am de'i nyan thos tshur gshegs pa brtsom pa dang*/ lam du zhugs pa dang*/ nye ba'i grong dang grong khyer du phyin pa dang*/ lta ba'i phyir 'gro zhing mthong ba dang*/ chos thos pa dang*/ dkon mchog gsum la skyabs su 'gro ba dang*/ bslab pa'i gnas 'dzin pa na dga' ba dang*/ rab tu dga' ba rgya che ba dge ba nges par 'byung ba dang ldan pa thob ste/ skul byed 'di ni rdzas las byung ba ma yin pa'i bsod nams bya ba'i dngos po 'bras bu che ba bdun pa yin no/ / zhes bsod nams rnam par 'phel ba rdzas las byung ba dang rdzas las byung ba ma yin pa'i bsod nams bdun tshan gnyis rgyas par gsungs te/ de dag la mkhas pa dag gis/ / kun dga' rwa ba gtsug lag khang*/ / mal stan tshor ba nar ma dang*/ / glo bur nad pa nad g.yog dang*/ / yul ngan tshe na sbyin pa ni/ / rdzas las byung ba'i bsod nams bdun/ / bzhugs dang gshegs rtsom lam zhugs dang*/ / phyin pa thos dang mthong ba dang*/ / chos thos bslab pa'i gzhi 'dzin las/ / dga' dang dad pa bskyed pa ni/ / rdzas la ma ltos bsod nams bdun/ / zhes sdom du mdzad do/ /

Venerable Cunda then said twice to the Bhagavan: “So too, are there seven generating merit not derived from material generosity? Venerable, are there things generating merit not derived from material generosity that are held to be of great result, great benefit, great splendor, and great magnitude?” The Bhagavan replied: “Cunda, there are. Cunda, seven things generate merit not derived from material generosity. A son or daughter of good lineage with faith who possesses them, whether moving or seated, asleep or awake, always, without break, only increases in merit and only generates merit.” Cunda asked: “What are the seven?” The Bhagavan replied: “Cunda, they are when a son or daughter of good lineage with faith obtains virtuous renunciation that is joyous and supremely joyous from (1) hearing that a tathāgata or śrāvakas of a tathāgata reside and live in a particular town or field. Cunda, this is the first thing generating merit not derived from material generosity that only generates merit. So too, it is when they obtain virtuous renunciation that is joyous and supremely joyous from (2) inviting tathāgatas and their śrāvakas, (3) going to where they take the path to proceed to nearby towns and cities, (4) going to look at them and see them, (5) listening to their Dharma, (6) taking refuge in the Dharma, and (7) maintaining the state of training. Cunda, these are the seven ways of generating merit not derived from material generosity that bring great result and so on.”[1021] This sūtra extensively explains the two divisions of seven types of increase of merit from substance and without substance. [305] The Compendium states: In that respect, scholars should offer groves, temples, beds and mattresses, regular sustenance, gifts to unexpected guests, alms and nurses to the sick, and charity when conditions decline in that region. These are the seven merits from material generosity. Generating joy and faith from residing, inviting, taking to the path, going, hearing and seeing, listening to Dharma, and maintaining the basis of training: these are the seven merits not derived from material generosity.[1022]

de dag kyang bar ma dge ba'i rig byed ma yin pa yin gyi rig byed dang sems pa yin na nyal ba la sogs pa'i gnas skabs su mi 'byung bar thal ba las 'byung ba'i phyir dang*/ de bzhin du rang nyid kyis ma byas pa'i las kyi lam la sogs pa gsungs pa'i yang phyin te/ 'di ltar 'ga' zhig gis gzhan dag bskul te/ 'ga' zhig gsod pa dang ma byin par len pa la sogs pa byed du bcug na pha rol po'i srog chad pa dang*/ nor thob pa la sogs pa'i tshe bskul bar byed pa po lus ngag gi rigs byed dang sems pa dge bar gnas pa'i tshe'ang srog gcod pa dang ma byin par len pa la sogs pa'i mi dge ba'i las kyi lam gyi dngos gzhi 'byung bar gsungs pa'i phyir de ni rig byed ma yin pa yin te/ rig byed dang sems pa ni dge bar yod pa'i phyir ro/ / sogs pa'i sgras bcom ldan 'das kyis skye mched bcu gnyis ston pa na/ dge slong mig ni nang gi skye mched yin te/ 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag rgyur byas pa gzugs can bstan du med pa thogs pa dang bcas pa'o zhes bya ba nas lus kyi bar dang*/ dge slong gzugs dag ni phyi'i skye mched yin te/ 'byung ba chen po bzhi dag rgyur byas pa gzugs can/ bstan du yod pa thogs pa dang bcas pa'o zhes bya ba nas reg bya'i bar du gsungs la/ dge slong chos ni phyi'i skye mched yin te/ skye mched bcu gcig gis ma bsdus pa bstan du med pa thogs pa med pa'o zhes gsungs te/ 'di la rig byed ma yin pa gzugs su med na gzugs can ma yin pa zhes gsungs par rigs pa las/ de skad du ma gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / gzhan yang 'phags pa'i lam yan lag brgyad par yang mi 'gyur te/ mnyam par bzhag pa na lus ngag gi rig byed dag med pa'i phyir yang dag pa'i ngag dang las kyi mtha' dang 'tsho ba rnams med par 'gyur pa las lam yan lag brgyad par bshad pa'i phyir/ yang dag pa'i ngag la sogs pa ni spong ba bdun gyi bdag nyid kyi rig byed ma yin par bzhed pa yin no/ /

These are intermediate virtuous nonindicative states. But if they were indicative and intentional, it would follow that they would not occur when asleep and so on. (4) Similarly, the sūtras also state that the karmic path not committed by oneself [is nonindicative,] because when some induce others to act by making them kill and steal and so on, the agent inducing the act is said to incur the actual basis of the karmic path of nonvirtue, such as killing and stealing when the life of another is taken, the wealth is obtained, and so forth. They are nonindicative because the indicative form and intention of such a person may be virtuous. (5) Regarding the meaning of “and so on,” the Bhagavan remarks when teaching the twelve bases: “Monks, the eyes are internal bases because the four great elements act as their cause and they are undemonstrable and impeded physical objects,” and this applies to the other sense bases up to the body. “Monks, form is an external base because the four great elements act as its cause and it is a demonstrable and impeded physical object,” and this applies up to tactile objects. “Monks, phenomena are external bases because they comprise undemonstrable and unimpeded states not subsumed by the other eleven bases.”[1023] If these twelve bases did not exist as nonindicative form, then it would be logical for the Bhagavan to state that they are not physical states, but he did not say this. (6) Again, the eight branches of the ārya path would cease to exist because physical [306] and verbal indicative forms do not exist in equipoise. But because eight branches of the ārya path are delineated — which include right speech, right action, and right livelihood — therefore right speech and so on are explained as nonindicative states [opposing] the seven [verbal and physical] actions to be abandoned.

gzhan yang rig byed ma yin pa med na so so thar pa'i sdom pa rgyun chags par yang mi 'gyur te/ rig byed dang spong ba'i sems pa dag yid gzhan la g.yengs pa'am/ sems med pa'i gnas skabs su med pa'i phyir ro/ / gzhan yang mdo las spong ba ni 'chal ba'i tshul khrims kyi gegs byed pa'i phyir chu lon du'ang gsungs na med pa ni chu lon du mi rigs pa'i phyir ro/ / dran pa nyer gzhag las kyang*/ gang gi tshe chos thams cad kyi byed pa dang ldan pa gang sdom pa nyid blangs pa de phan chad gnyid log gam myos sam rab tu myos kyang dge ba'i chos kyi rgyun nyid rab tu 'jug ste/ dper na chu bo'i rgyun bar chad med par rtag tu 'bab pa de bzhin du skyes bu gnyid log gam rab tu myos pa'i 'jug pa yang de bzhin no/ / de ltar rnam par rig byed ma yin pa'i gzugs bstan du med pa thogs pa med par 'dod do zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir rig byed ma yin pa gzugs su yod do zhes zer ro/ / don 'di la mdo sde pa la sogs pa ni rig byed ma yin pa gzugs rang gi mtshan nyid pa ni ma yin te/ thogs pa dang bcas pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa gzugs su rung ba'i mtshan nyid med pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te gzugs las skyes pas gzugs su 'dod na/ mig gi rnam shes la sogs pa'ang thal bar 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / mdo'i dgongs pa'ang don la mi gnas pa kho nar gsal bar shes te/ bstan med thogs med kyi gzugs ni bsam gtan pa rnams kyi ting nge 'dzin la zad par zil gnon dang mi sdug pa la sogs par snang ba chos kyi skye mched pa'i gzugs kyi dbang du mdzad nas gsungs pas gzugs su btags pa yin la/ de nyid la zag pa med pa'i gzugs su'ang gsungs so/ / chos kyi skye mched la gzugs can ma yin pa mi gsungs ba'i rgyu yang de nyid yin no/ / dpes ston pa ni zag med kyi gzugs gsungs pa ni/ dgra bcom pa'i gzugs dang de dag la snang ba'i phyi rol gyi gzugs yin te/ zag pa'i rten ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

(7) Further, if there is no nonindicative form, there would be no breakage of pratimokṣa vows, because indicative form and the intention to abandon nonvirtue do not exist when distracted by another mental faculty or when there is no mind. (8) Again, if ethics are nonexistent, it would be illogical for the sūtras to state that ethics are like a dam that blocks the unethical behaviors that are to be abandoned.[1024] Also, the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra proclaims: When one takes vows to practice any virtuous Dharma, then after that, even if one is asleep, addled, or insane, one fully enters the stream of virtuous Dharma. For example, just as a stream always descends without interruption, so too, such a being enters virtue whether asleep or insane.[1025] In that way nonindicative form is asserted to be undemonstrable and unimpeded. Thus [Vaibhāṣikas] say that nonindicative form exists. Sautrāntikas and so on say that nonindicative form is not actual form because it lacks the appropriate characteristics of form, such as being impeded and so on. Moreover, if it is asserted to be form since it is generated from form, then it would follow that even eye consciousness and so on would be form. It may be clearly understood that [Vaibhāṣikas] have not found the point or meaning of the sūtras at all. Undemonstrable and unimpeded form, such as states of subjugation and repulsiveness,[1026] is imputed to be form since it arises in the context of mental-object form[1027] that appears only to the concentration of those engaged in the absorptions. It is also said to be uncontaminated form. Further, it is the very reason that the phenomena base is not described as physical.[1028] Dārṣṭāntikas assert that calling it uncontaminated form is a reference to the form of an arhat and the external form appearing to arhats because arhats are not a basis for the contaminants.

'o na mdo las/ zag pa dang bcas pa'i chos rnams gang zhe na/ mig ji snyed pa dang gzugs ji snyed pa dag yin no zhes gsungs she na/ de ni zag pa'i gnyen po ma yin pa'i dbang du mdzad nas zag bcas su gsungs so zhes 'chad do/ / bsod nams rnam par 'phel ba dag kyang yul dang bsam pa dang dngos po'i khyad par gyis bag chags bsgos pa'i rgyud 'gyur ba'i dbang du mdzad nas gsungs pa yin la/ ma byas pa'i las kyi lam yang byed du 'jug pa'i sems pa dang*/ lus ngag gi rig byed dang gzhan gyis byas pa'i rkyen las sdig pa'i bag chags brtan pa thob pa chos nyid do/ / zhes dgongs pa ni de yin no/ /

Objection: But a sūtra states: What are contaminated phenomena? They are any eye and any form . . .[1029] Reply: They are contaminated from the perspective of not being the antidote to the contaminants. This is stated from the perspective of those seeking to enhance their merit by transforming their mindstreams with the imprints of objects, thoughts, and special things. Stable imprints of immorality are obtained due to the intention to induce others to engage in karmic paths of inaction [by not committing virtuous deeds] or [inducing] others to engage in [nonvirtuous] indicative [actions] of body [307] and speech.
THE EIGHT BRANCHES OF THE ĀRYA PATH
