When the Master was a brahman youth, he saw Buddha Puṣya in a mountain cave abiding in equipoise focusing on fire. He raised one foot and completed the perfection of effort by praising the buddha for seven days with the verse: Lord of beings, none among the great practitioners of virtue is your equal: none in the abodes of gods, none in this world, none in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, none even in the supreme abodes of the divine celestial palaces nor in the cardinal directions and subdirections. How, then, could there be anyone among these extensive lands with their mountains and forests?[1272] By circumambulating the buddha as he praised him, he reduced the period of collecting merit by nine eons. As it says in the Chapter on Medicine: When Buddha Puṣya dwelt in a cave of various jewels, I praised him with one verse and reduced my period of [collecting] merit by nine eons.[1273] Another sūtra notes: When I was the brahman Uttama I praised the Tathāgata with strength and effort, and nine eons were subtracted.[1274] Thus, through great effort and skill in means, the bodhisattva reduced many eons to a short period, but he could not reduce it by a countless eon, because Bodhisattva Levels declares: From among those who apply themselves with the greatest of the great effort, some reduce the period of merit by many intermediate eons, some reduce a great eon to an intermediate eon, but none can reduce that period by a countless eon.[1275] The Great Perfection of Wisdom Commentary records: Just as many eons up to trillions of eons can be transcended if one strives with extremely great effort, so too our Master, Bhagavan Śākyamuni, reduced the period by nine eons through pleasing Buddha Puṣya when a bodhisattva.[1276]

byang chub pa'i sngon rol gyi de ma thag la ste rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gyi tshe ni ting nge 'dzin bsam gtan dang blo'i ste shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdzogs te/ de dag ni rang rang gi phun sum tshogs pa'i pha rol tu phyin pas na pha rol tu phyin pa zhes bya'o/ /

Thus, by striving with extremely great effort, many trillions of eons can be transcended, but none can transcend a countless eon. Immediately before enlightenment, while engaged in vajra-like concentration, he completed the perfection of absorption that is concentration (samādhi), and the perfection of wisdom that is intelligence (dhī). They are called perfections since they perfect specific excellent qualities.

Merit, action, and basis
gsum po bsod nams bya ba dang / / de'i gzhi dper na las lam bzhin/ / 112
The three are merit, action, and the basis of that. For example, it is like calling all “karmic paths.” (4:112cd)

A sūtra says: The three: merit, action, and basis [407] are derived from generosity, ethics, and meditation.[1277] These three [i.e., generosity, ethics, and meditation] are (1) merit (puṇya), since they have pleasant results, (2) action (kriyā), since they are by nature karma, and (3) the basis of that (tadvastu) merit and action, because the motivating intention supporting those three is also the basis of engagement. For example, it is like calling all ten actions karmic paths (karmapathā), since the seven actions of body and speech are both karma and karmic paths and the three mental actions are karmic paths alone. Here the term “basis” means cause. While physical and verbal karma derived from generosity are all three — merit, action, and the basis — the motivating intention is merit and action {but not the basis, since it is not the support of action.} Further, other concomitant phenomena such as feeling are merit alone. Those derived from ethics are all three since they are physical and verbal karma alone. Regarding those derived from meditation, love is both merit and the basis of merit and action because it makes manifest the intention concomitant with it by means of love. The intention and the absorption and uncontaminated vows simultaneously arising with it are both merit and action. {It is not the basis, since it does not engage in dependence on these intentions.} Other states derived simultaneously with love — feeling and so on — are merit alone. Again, if one practices merit in order to establish these three, these three are called “the basis of merit and action.” One {Sautrāntika} says: If merit and action are ultimately virtuous intention, then generosity, ethics, and meditation are the basis of that virtuous intention.
THE OUTCOME OF GENEROSITY
sbyin pa las byung ba gang zhe na/
Question: What is that “derived from generosity”?
gang gis sbyin byed de sbyin pa/ / mchod dang phan gdags 'dod pa yis/ / lus dang ngag las slong dang bcas/ / de 'bras longs spyod chen po can/ / 113

The act of giving by any is generosity. It is giving with the desire to worship or benefit concomitant with the intention motivating physical and verbal karma. The result of that is possessing great resources. (4:113)

skyes bu gang gis bsam pa dge bas bdog pa'i dngos po gzhan la sbyin par byed pa de ni sbyin pa yin te/ drang srong rgyas pas zhus pa las/ drang srong chen po dad pas gang cung zad cig byin pa de dag thams cad ni sbyin pa zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / kun nas slong ba gang zhe na/ yul bzang po la mchod par 'dod pa dang*/ rang dang snyoms pa dang*/ dman pa la phan gdags par 'dod pa yis gtong ba sbyin pa yin gyi 'jigs pa dang lan la re ba la sogs pas ni ma yin no/ / las de yang lus ngag gi las kun nas slong ba'i sems pa mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa yin no/ / sbyin pa las byung ba zhes bya ba ni sbyin pa'i rang bzhin yin pa'i phyir de skad du brjod de lo ma las byung ba'i spyil po zhes bya ba bzhin no/ / 'og ma dag la'ang de bzhin du shes par bya'o/ / de nyid kyi phyir 'grel pa las/ gang tshe skyes bu dge yid kyis/ / rang gi rdzas dag sbyin byed pa/ / de tshe dge ba'i phung po rnams/ / sbyin pa zhes ni brjod pa yin zhes 'byung ngo*/ / des na lus ngag gi las kun slong mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa yin pas phung po lnga yin no/ / de nyid kyi phyir kun las btus las kyang*/ sbyin pa'i las gang zhe na/ de'i gzhi dang*/ kun nas slong ba dang*/ dngos po dang*/ ngo bo nyid kyis kyang rig par bya ste/ gzhi ni ma chags pa dang zhe sdang med pa dang gti mug med pa'o/ / kun nas slong ba ni de dag dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i sems pa'o/ / dngos po ni sbyin par bya ba'i dngos po'o/ / ngo bo nyid ni gtong ba na lus dang ngag gi las so zhes bshad do/ /

Reply: The act of giving by any being with virtuous intention who gives something of value to another is generosity (dāna), because the Sūtra Requested by Rishi Vyāsa declares: All those acts of giving to the Great Rishi [i.e., the Buddha] by those with faith, however small, are generosity.[1278] Question: What is the motivation? Reply: Giving with the desire to worship (pūja) pure objects or giving to benefit those who are equal or inferior to oneself is generosity, but giving out of fear, hope of return, and so on is not. Also it is concomitant with that karma that is the intention motivating physical and verbal karma. “Derived from generosity” is stated because it is the essence of generosity, like a hut derived or made from leaves. Also that which follows should be understood in this way. Therefore the Autocommentary states: When a being with a virtuous mind gives away his property, then his virtuous aggregates [408] are said to be generous.[1279] Therefore, since it is physical and verbal karma concomitant with motivation, it is the five aggregates. Because of that the Compendium of Abhidharma also notes: What is the karma of giving? It is to be understood through its basis, motivation, object, and nature. Its basis is nonattachment, nonaversion, and nondelusion. Its motivation is the intention concomitant with those. Its object is the object that is given. Its nature is the physical and verbal karma of giving.[1280] The result of that generosity is possessing great resources (mahābhogya).
bdag gzhan don phyir gnyis don phyir/ / gnyis ka'i don du min phyir sbyin/ / de yi khyad par sbyin bdag dang / / dngos dang zhing gi khyad pa las/ / 114
It is for the purpose of self, others, for the purpose of both, for the purpose of neither. Excellent generosity is excellence of the giver, object, and field. (4:114)

sbyin pa de'i 'bras bu ni longs spyod chen po can yin no/ / dbye ba ni bdag gi don gyi phyir sbyin pa ni{ 'phags pa} 'dod chags dang ma bral ba'am/ so so'i skye bo 'jig rten pa'i lam gyis 'dod chags dang bral bas mchod rten la sbyin pa'o/{ bdag la phan la mchod rten la mi phan pas so/} gzhan gyi don gyi phyir sbyin pa ni mthong chos la myong ba ma gtogs pa 'phags pa 'dod chags dang bral bas sems can gzhan la sbyin pa'o/ / {de yang kho 'dod pa las 'das la sbyin pa'i rnam smin gyi sa ni 'dod pas bsdus pas gzhan la phan rang la mi phan pas so } gnyis ka'i don gyi phyir sbyin pa ni 'phags pa 'dod chags dang ma bral ba'am so so'i skye bo 'dod chags dang bral bas sems can gzhan la sbyin pa'o/ / {de yang rang dge ba bsags pa'i phyir dang gzhan gyi 'byung ba la phan btags pa'i phyir ro } gnyis ka'i don du min pa'i phyir gyi sbyin pa ni mthong chos la myong ba ma gtogs pa 'phags pa 'dod khams las 'dod chags dang bral bas mchod rten la 'bul ba yin te/ {phyi mar rang dang mchod rten la phan pa med pas de la 'bul ba ni } de ni bkur sti dang byas pa gzo ba 'ba' zhig gis 'bul ba'i phyir ro/ / {mthong chos la myong bar ni mi 'gal lo }

If generosity is classified, there are [the following types]: (1) Generosity for the purpose of self is {an ārya} free of attachment, or an ordinary being free of attachment due to the mundane path, giving to a stūpa {since it benefits oneself, not the stūpa}. (2) Generosity for the purpose of others is an ārya free of attachment giving to other sentient beings, with the exception of karma to be experienced in the current life. {Again, this benefits others, it does not benefit the giver, since the level of the karmic maturation of generosity is subsumed by the desire-realm level but that being has transcended the desire-realm level.} (3) Generosity for the purpose of both is an ārya not free from attachment or an ordinary being not free from attachment giving to other sentient beings {because this accumulates virtue for oneself, and it benefits the primary elements of other sentient beings.} (4) Generosity for the purpose of neither is an ārya free of attachment to the desire realm making offerings to a caitya, with the exception of karma to be experienced in the current life, {since making offerings to that caitya brings no subsequent benefit to oneself or the caitya. An ārya making offerings to the caitya} is making offerings with respect while conscious of the act, {and it is not contradictory that it is generosity to be experienced in this current life}.
sbyin pa de'i khyad par du 'phags pa ni sbyin bdag dang dngos po dang zhing gi khyad par gsum las yin no/ /
Excellent generosity is the three: (1) excellence of the giver (dātṛ), (2) the object (vastu), and (3) the field (kṣetra).
sbyin bdag khyad 'phags dad sogs kyis/ / gus la sogs pas sbyin par byed/ / de phyir bkur sti rgya chen dang / / dus dang bar chad med par rnyed/ / 115
An excellent giver is one with faith and so on. Because he gave with respect and so forth, he receives respect and abundant resources, when required, without obstacles. (4:115)

de la re zhig sbyin bdag khyad par du 'phags pa ni dad pa dang sogs kyis gzung ba tshul khrims dang gtong ba dang thos pa dang ngo tsha shes pa dang khrel yod pa dang shes rab ces bya ba'i 'phags pa'i nor bdun dang 'dod chen chung ba dang ldan pas so/ /

Now, an excellent giver is one with faith and so on who possesses the seven jewels of the āryas: (1) ethics, (2) giving, (3) hearing, (4) shame, (5) embarrassment, (6) wisdom, and (7) minimal attachment.

HOW TO GIVE

mdo las/ dge slong dag skyes bu dam pa'i sbyin pa ni rnam pa lnga ste/ lnga gang zhe na/ dad pas sbyin pa sbyin par byed pa dang*/ gus par byas te dang*/ rang gi lag nas dang*/ dus su dang*/ gzhan la mi gnod par sbyin pa sbyin par byed do zhes pa dang*/ mkhas pas gus dang rang lag nas/ / dus su mi gnod sbyin byed na/ / sbyin bdag sbyin pa yangs shing che/ / skal ba chen po 'byung bar 'gyur zhes 'byung la/ 'grel pa las ni/ gus pa dang*/ sogs pa bsdus pa rang gi lag gis ster ba dang*/ nye bar mkho ba'i dus dang*/ gzhi des gzhan la {brkus pa dang*/ shan pa la lug byin pa lta bu byin bya dang*/ dug mi 'phrod pa'i zas lta bu zhing la gnod pa ma yin par gzhan la } mi gnod par sbyin par byed pa'o/ / zhes dad pa las gzhan bzhi bshad do/ /

A sūtra declares: Monks, the generosity of a pure being has five aspects. What are those five? Giving with faith, with respect, with one’s hands, in a timely way, without harming others.[1281] And: Scholars say if one gives with respect, with one’s own hands, in a timely way, without harming, it is generosity of the giver that is extensive and great and produces great fortune.[1282] The Autocommentary explains the four aspects other than faith: The terms “respect” and “and so on” refer to giving with one’s own hands, giving necessities to others when required, giving objects without harming others {without stealing them from others, not giving such things as sheep to butchers, not giving inappropriate foods such as those that are poisonous, giving without harming fields of benefit}.[1283] [409]

THE RESULT

gus pa la sogs pas byin pa de'i phyir gus par byin pas skye ba phyi ma la rang la 'khor gyis bkur sti byed pa dang*/ rnyed par 'gyur ba dang*/ rang gi lag gis byin pas ni longs spyod rgya chen po la dad pa ste rang dbang 'byor bar 'gyur ba dang*/ nye bar mkho ba'i dus su byin pas ni rang la dgos pa'i dus su rnyed par 'gyur ba dang*/ gzhan la gnod pa med par byin pas ni rang gi longs spyod la dgra dang mes 'tshig pa la sogs pa'i bar chad med par rnyed pa ste/ 'dir gzhan la gnod pa ni pha rol la ma byin par blangs nas ster ba la sogs pa'o/ /

Because he gave with respect (śrāddhya) and so forth, in the future he receives respect from his retinue, he acquires property, he becomes independently wealthy with abundant resources since he gave with his own hands with faith, he receives articles when required through having given to others when they required necessities, and he receives resources without obstacles — such as enemies or fire incinerating them and so on — since he gave without harming others. Here “harming others” is giving to others that which is stolen.
kha dog la sogs phun sum dngos/ / de las gzugs bzang grags ldan dang / / dga' dang shin tu gzhon sha dang / / dus su reg na bde lus 'gyur/ / 116
From giving objects with excellent color and so on, one will possess a pure form, fame, joy, a very youthful body, and a body blissful when touched. (4:116)

'thob pa yin zhes gsungs so/ /

The Five Times Five Sūtra states: If one gives articles with many excellent qualities, without defects, that action matures in the form of receiving articles with many excellent qualities. Rely on each of these.[1284] From giving the finest objects with excellent color and so on — such as excellent smell, taste, and texture — then in one’s future lives one will come to possess respectively a pure form, fame, mental joy, a very youthful body, and a body blissful when touched, since jewel-like females warm one’s body when it is cold, cool it when it is hot, and maintain it in equilibrium when it abides in equilibrium. The Compendium of Abhidharma explains: What is excellent giving? Giving to external fields, giving without bias, giving that fulfills desires, giving without lingering, giving extensively, giving with joy, giving to vessels of the teachings, and giving through properly distinguishing old companions from recent acquaintances should be known as excellent giving. How does one know that the object to be given is excellent? The object to be given should not injure, it should not be stolen, decaying, or stained but appropriate, fit for the purpose of establishing Dharma.[1285] Bodhisattva Levels mentions: Since a gift infested with insects is inappropriate, it should not be given.[1286] The Sūtra Requested by Sāgaramati states: There are four that obstruct the Mahāyāna: giving with the hope of receiving in return, with aversion, with delusion, and with fear. There are four others: giving for fame and for the expressions, words, and verses [of praise]. There are another four: giving with an eye to wealth, on a trivial occasion, through borrowing, and not giving by hand. There are a further four: giving [410] with an evil mind, through killing humans, without respect, and with higher pride. There are a final four: giving weapons, poison, that which is inappropriate, and that which is not permitted.[1287] Therefore giving with an inferior intention, preparation, or gift will be an obstacle to enlightenment. The Sūtra Requested by Sumati advises: Give in a timely way, without regret. Give what is pleasant and without hope of karmic maturation. Those who are brave act in this way and always obtain great resources.[1288]
zhing khyad par du 'phags pa ni/
EXCELLENT FIELDS OF GENEROSITY
'gro dang sdug bsngal phan 'dogs dang / / yon tan rnams kyis zhing khyad 'phags/ / mchog ni grol bas grol ba'am/ / byang chub sems dpa' yis brgyad pa/ / 117
A field is excellent due to rebirth, suffering, benefit, qualities. Supreme generosity is the liberated giving to the liberated or a bodhisattva who gives anything. The eighth is supreme. (4:117)

'gro ba bzang bas zhing khyad par du 'phags pa ni/ go'u ta ma'i mdo las/ kun dga' bo dud 'gro'i skye gnas su song ba la sbyin pa byin na slar rnam par smin pa brgya 'gyur du re bar bya'o/ / tshul khrims 'chal par gyur pa'i mi la sbyin pa byin na stong 'gyur du re bar bya'o zhes gsungs pa lta bu'o/ {/'gro ba bzang ba dang*/}sdug bsngal gyis zhing khyad par du 'phags pa ni rdzas las byung ba'i bsod nams bya ba'i gzhi'i nang nas nad pa dang nad g.yog dang grang ba la sogs pa'i dus su byin pa ni rdzas las byung ba'i bsod nams yin pas bsod nams tshad med par gsungs pa lta bu'o/{ sdug bsngal ba dang*/ /} phan 'dogs pas zhing khyad par du 'phags pa ni pha ma dang phan 'dogs pa gzhan yang rung ste dom dang ri dwags la sogs pa'i skyes pa'i rabs {lta bu rang la phan 'dogs pas dang } dper bya'o/ / yon tan gyis zhing khyad par du 'phags pa ni go'u ta ma'i mdo las/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa la byin na rnam par smin pa 'bum 'gyur du re bar bya'o/ / rgyun du zhugs pa'i 'bras bu la zhugs pa la byin na rnam par smin pa tshad med do/ / de bas kyang rgyun du zhugs pa la byin na ches tshad med do zhes gsungs pa lta bu'o/{ yon tan dang ldan pa ste bzhi po de rnams kyis zhing khyad par du 'phags so/ /} legs nyes kyi rgyu dang 'bras bu bstan pa'i mdo las ni/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa'i dge slong la sbyin pa btang na rnam par smin pa khrir 'gyur snyed 'thob par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs so/ / rnams zhes bya ba ni mang po'i tshig ste zhing bzhi po de dag go /

A field is excellent due to producing good rebirth (gati) since, for example, the Gautama Sūtra says: Ānanda, if one gives to those born as animals, then one may hope for a hundredfold karmic maturation. If one gives to humans with unethical conduct, one may hope for a thousandfold karmic maturation.[1289] A field is excellent due to {producing good rebirth and} [alleviating] suffering (duḥkha), since from among the bases of merit derived from material generosity, it is giving to the sick, giving to nurses, giving to those when they are cold, and so on. Since this is merit from material generosity, it is said to be immeasurable merit. A field is excellent due to its {alleviating suffering and} [creating] benefit (upakāritva), since it consists of one’s father, mother, and others who have benefited oneself. It is like the jātaka of the Buddha’s past lives as a bear[1290] and a deer[1291] {since such stories edify.} A field is excellent due to its qualities (guṇa), for as the Gautama Sūtra observes: If one gives to those with ethical conduct, one may hope for a hundred-thousandfold karmic maturation. If one gives to one who is entering the result of stream entry, the karmic maturation is immeasurable. If one gives to a stream enterer, the immeasurable karmic maturation is even greater.[1292] {These four fields are excellent since they possess those qualities.} The Sūtra Revealing the Results of Good and Bad Causes declares: If one gives to a fully ordained monk with ethical conduct, one obtains a ten-thousandfold karmic maturation.[1293] The Tibetan pluralizing term rnams refers to the four fields.

sbyin pa thams cad kyi nang na mchog tu gyur pa ni khams gsum las grol bas grol ba la byin na khyad par du 'phags te/ de la skyon gang yang med pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir go'u ta ma'i mdo las ni/ gang zhig lus ngag bsdams bdag nyid/ / lag brkyang bsod snyoms spyod pa yi/ / 'dod chags bral la chags bral gyis/ / sbyin na zag zing sbyin pa'i mchog ces gsungs so/ /

That which is supreme from among all instances of generosity is the generosity of a being who is liberated from the three realms giving to another who is liberated. This is excellent generosity because there are no faults in this action at all. Therefore the Gautama Sūtra states: If one free of attachment gives to one free of attachment, a being restrained in body and mind who extends his hands for alms, it is supreme worldly giving.[1294]

lung las kyang*/ 'dod chags dang bral bas 'dod chags dang bral ba la sbyin pa byin pa gang yin pa de ni zag zing gi sbyin pa rnams kyi nang na mchog yin no zhes gsungs so/ / yang sbyin bdag byang chub sems dpa' yis sems can thams cad la phan par bya ba'i phyir gang ci byin pa de ni ma grol bas ma grol ba rnams la byin yang rdzogs pa'i byang chub dang sems can thams cad kyi don du byin pas mchog yin te/ sems can thams cad kyi mgon du 'gyur pa'i sbyin pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

A scripture also mentions: If any being free of attachment gives to one free of attachment, it is supreme among wordly giving.[1295] Again, if a bodhisattva benefactor gives anything in order to benefit all sentient beings, it is supreme generosity even though it is the generosity of one who is not liberated [411] giving to others who are not liberated. It is supreme generosity that protects all sentient beings since it is giving in order to attain complete enlightenment and for achieving the purposes of all sentient beings.

yang mdo las/ nye ba la sbyin pa dang*/ 'jigs pas sbyin pa dang*/ bdag la byin pas sbyin pa dang*/ bdag la sbyin par 'gyur bar sbyin pa dang*/ sngon bdag gi pha dang mes po dag gis sbyin pa byin pa sbyin pa dang*/ mtho ris kyi don du sbyin pa dang*/ grags pa'i don du sbyin pa dang*/ sems kyi rgyan gyi don dang sems kyi yo byad kyi don dang rnal 'byor gyi tshogs kyi don dang don gyi mchog thob par bya ba'i phyir sbyin pa byin pa'o zhes sbyin pa rnam pa brgyad gsungs pa dag gi nang na ni brgyad pa sems kyi rgyan la sogs pa'i phyir sbyin pa mchog yin no/ / de la nye ba la sbyin pa ni slob dpon snga ma dag na re nam nye bar gyur cing nye bar lhags pa dag la sbyin par byed pa'o zhes zer ro/ / 'jigs pas sbyin pa ni med par byed pa mngon sum du mthong nas dam pa sbyin no zhes sbyin par byed pa'o/ / bdag la byin pas sbyin pa ni 'dis sngon bdag la byin no snyam nas sbyin pa'o/ / gzhan ni go sla'o/ / sems kyi rgyan ni rdzu 'phrul lo/ / sems kyi yo byad ni 'phags pa'i lam yan lag brgyad pa'o/ / rnal 'byor gyi tshogs ni zhi gnas dang lhag mthong ngo*/ / don gyi mchog ni dgra bcom pa'ang mya ngan las 'das pa mthong ba'o zhes rgyal po'i sras grags pa'i bshes gnyen 'chad do/ / slob dpon gang spel ni sems kyi rgyan gyi don la sogs pa bzhi ni go rim bzhin du dad pa la sogs pa'i nor 'dren pa dang*/ ser sna'i dri ma dang 'gal ba dang*/ snyoms 'jug gi bde ba skyed pa dang*/ mya ngan las 'das pa 'dren pa'i phyir ro zhes 'chad do/ / sa las ni zang zing med pa'i sems kyis don gyi mchog mya ngan las 'das par bsngos pa dang rnal 'byor gyi tshogs myang 'das kyi rgyu tshogs su 'gyur ba dang*/ sems kyi rgyan bde 'gror 'gro ba dang*/ sems kyi yo byad longs spyod chen por yang 'gyur ba'o zhes bshad do/ / yang na sems kyi rgyan la sogs pa bzhi rim pa ltar tshogs sbyor dang*/ mthong lam dang*/ sgom lam dang*/ myang 'das sam/ yang na tshogs sbyor dang*/ sa dang po bdun dang*/ dag pa'i sa gsum dang*/ sangs rgyas kyi sa rnams dang sbyar ro/ / 'o na ci'i phyir sbyin pa snga ma bdun po dman zhe na/

Again, a sūtra states: (1) Giving to those who are close, (2) giving out of fear, (3) giving since another gave to me, (4) giving since another will give to me, (5) giving since my father and grandfather gave, (6) giving for high rebirth, (7) giving for fame, (8) giving to adorn one’s mind, for mental qualities, for amassing yogic practices, or to obtain the supreme purpose.[1296] This mentions the eight aspects of giving. The eighth, giving to adorn one’s mind and so on, is supreme. Past masters say: Giving to those who are close is giving to others when they are near and when they approach. Giving out of fear is giving what is excellent when one sees that death is near. Giving since another gave to me is giving through thinking, “He was generous to me before.” The others are easy to understand. That which adorns the mind is supernatural powers. Mental qualities are the eight branches of the noble path. The amassing of yogic practices is calm abiding and insight. The supreme purpose is becoming an arhat or seeing nirvāṇa. This is explained by Jinaputra Yaśomitra. Master Pūrṇavardhana explains: The four that start with “giving to adorn one’s mind” respectively induce precious states such as faith, exclude the stain of avarice, generate the bliss of meditative attainment, and induce nirvāṇa.[1297] Bodhisattva Levels declares: With a mind not immersed in worldly things, directed to nirvāṇa, the supreme purpose, one accumulates the causes of nirvāṇa that are the assembly of yogas, adorns one’s mind through proceeding to blissful rebirths, and attains great resources that are mental qualities.[1298] Again, the four of giving to adorn one’s mind and so on should be applied respectively to (1) the paths of accumulation and preparation, (2) the path of seeing, (3) the path of meditation, and (4) nirvāṇa; or, again, (1) accumulation and preparation, (2) the first seven levels, (3) the three pure levels, and (4) the level of a buddha. Question: Why are the first seven generosities inferior [to the eighth]?

Reply: Yogācāra Levels states: The first seven are respectively explained as inferior: (1) giving that degenerates through laziness, (2) offering worldly objects to others out of fear or since Īśvara wishes it, (3) giving that is conscious of past generosity, (4) giving that seeks future return, (5) giving with contempt for the receiver, (6) giving desiring resources of higher births, (7) giving with the fault of desiring fame.[1299] [412] Again, the Sūtra Requested by Rishi Vyāsa declares that one should establish special pure generosity through abandoning the thirty-two types of impure generosity: Great rishis, though one may engage in these thirty-two types of generosity, they are not fully pure: (1) giving through the giver having distorted view or lacking faith, (2) giving because one is returning the benefit of those who previously benefited oneself, (3) giving inferior objects, (4) giving to fire or flame or (5) giving to water to achieve one’s desires, and (6) giving to the king so that he is aware of you, (7) giving to thieves and so on out of fear, (8) giving poisons, (9) giving weapons, (10) giving the flesh of beings that have been slaughtered, (11) giving alcohol to the indolent, (12) giving to obtain followers, reflecting, “May they become my followers; may they assist me in my rites and offerings,” (13) giving in order to hear words and verses [of praise], (14) giving to musicians for the purpose of dancing, singing, laughter, play, stories, and frivolity, (15) giving to astrologers for the purpose of divining the signs of continents and stars,

(16) giving the jewels of others to loved ones, (17) giving others’ fields and stores of grain to wild animals and birds to eat for their enjoyment, (18) giving to benefit artisans, (19) giving to doctors out of fear of becoming sick, (20) giving to beggars due to their angry reproof, (21) giving through doubting whether the maturational result of giving exists, (22) giving that is tormented giving, tormented by regret, (23) giving with a mind reflecting “I will give so that all that is taken from me will be returned to me in future lives,” (24) giving with a mind reflecting “May the result of the merit of my giving not manifest for any other sentient being,” (25) being made to give when young, (26) those afflicted with age, sickness, and approaching death being goaded to give to worthy objects by friends and relatives when they lack faith in Buddhism, (27) giving to become famous through thinking “I will become famous as a benefactor in other lands,” (28) giving food due to seeing that the world does not like those who are not generous, with the thought that the world tolerates the faults of those who are generous, (29) giving riches such as jewels, gold, and silver to the family, kinsmen, and relatives of a woman one finds attractive for the purpose of seeking that female’s hand in marriage, and rejoicing in that, (30) giving through reflecting, “I will give from my property whatever is appropriate to have a woman,” (31) giving thinking, “I will give in this life so that I attain property in my next life,” (32) giving to the very rich through offering them any desired flower, fruit, or worldly object but disregarding those who are destitute, [413] enslaved, ugly, or wearing ragged and smelly clothes.[1300]

{These are restated in verse: (1) Giving without faith, (2) giving in return for benefit, (3–6) giving to fire, to water, and to satisfy the king,[1301] (7) giving out of fear, (8) giving poisons, (9) weapons, (10) meat from slaughter, (11) giving alcohol to the indolent, (12) giving to attract followers. (13) Giving for praise, (14) giving to astrologers, (15) giving to musicians, (16) giving others’ property to loved ones, (17) giving others’ grain to birds and so on, (18) giving to artisans, (19) giving to doctors out fear of illness. (20) Giving in response to reproof, (21) giving with doubt about maturation, (22) giving with subsequent regret, (23) giving thinking “This will be returned to me,” (24) giving thinking “May this mature for me alone.” (25) Being made to give when young, (26) giving when old, when sick, and at the time of death through being goaded by others when one has no faith, (27) giving for fame in other lands, (28) giving to instill generosity. (29) Giving to court females, (30) giving while reflecting “I have no woman,” (31) giving to attain property in a future life, (32) giving to the rich while disregarding the poor. These are called the thirty-two impure types of generosity.}

Great rishis, their karmic maturation is like the bad sprouts that are generated from planting bad seeds in salt-encrusted fields. Indeed, the karmic maturation of such generosity is not nonexistent, but it is like a harvest or fruit that is impeded due to faulty fields and seed. Great rishis, it is like, for example, some person planting the specific seeds of a desired harvest in an unploughed, unweeded field, and as the seeds lie in that field it rains, and they are soaked, but even though the seeds are capable of sprouting, a harvest or fruit will not arise. Great rishis, similarly, since these divisions of generosity arise from afflicted intention and preparation, their maturational result is not potent. Therefore they are called the thirty-two impure types of generosity.[1302] Some say: Giving to fire, giving to water, and giving to the king should be taken as one, and when old, sick, or dying are three generosities. The four generosities through being goaded by others when lacking faith are enumerated as four, but discarding giving to doctors thus makes thirty-two. However, the system of this sūtra is to take giving inferior objects when good-quality objects exist, giving to fire, giving to water, and giving to kings as four separate {types of generosity; and to take giving through being goaded by others when old, sick, and dying as one [single generosity]. From the perspective of practicing proper generosity, this same sūtra states: Great rishis, anyone who gives out of fear of the next world, who does not speculate or entertain [opinons] about the recipient, whether they are ethical or unethical, but who generates faith and gives with eyes open, with a mind unbiased toward sentient beings — this, rishis, is a benefactor. And the special benefactor: Anyone who generates faith and, while focusing on sentient beings, [414] gives to them with love, respectfully, and with a mind of discipline has thoroughly pure generosity. Giving the five special objects: Giving Dharma, giving worldly objects, giving abodes, giving butter lamps, and giving incense and garlands.[1303]

From the perspective of superior fields: Giving when there are (1) guests, (2) the sick, (3) nurses, (4) teachers of Dharma, and (5) those traveling to other places is to fulfill the five types of generosity.[1304] And the five highest objects of generosity: It is the highest giving if one gives to tathāgatas, the Saṅgha, Dharma teachers, the sick, and one’s parents.[1305] And the nine great generosities: The great generosities are (1) giving to kings who have lost power in their kingdoms, those tortured by kings, those without protectors, and the sick; (2) healing those in despair of being abandoned by the king and those meeting death; (3) giving medicine to the sick; giving in a timely way to the Saṅgha who possess (4) excellent ethics, (5) concentration, (6) wisdom, and (7) the seeing of liberated transcendent wisdom; (8) giving without fear to those reincarnating in the birth states of animals such as crows, owls, wild animals, and so on; and (9) fulfilling the desires of any who lack possessions for any specific requirements.[1306] It is said that by encouraging generosity in others and rejoicing in it, one obtains equal merit: If one encourages other sentient beings to act in that way, they generate faith and clear faith, and in coming to rejoice in this pure giving, one becomes similar to those who generate all such merit. Thus all who rejoice in such actions or who encourage others to do so generate merit and become benefactors who are similar to them.[1307] Again, the same sūtra declares: Great rishis, the contributor, having given the gift, inspires others to give through generating faith and inspires others to give in other lands. If contributors give their wealth, they are benefactors due to [giving] that property. One who gives through encouraging others to give is a contributor but not a benefactor. If one gives any of one’s own property, one is a benefactor and a contributor.[1308] Thus there are four possibilities for benefactor and contributor.

The Bodhisattva Levels explains ten pure types of generosity: (1) Giving without obstruction is giving without delay to a begger as soon as he arrives. (2) Giving without clinging to wrong view as supreme is giving through not adhering to wrong view as the supreme cause of mundane and transcendent states. (3) Giving without offering that which is accumulated is giving what one has at hand when requested but not giving instantly what one has accumulated over a long period. [415] (4) Giving without an inflated mind is giving that abandons the mind of conceit that considers beggars as inferior and that vies with others, praising oneself and faulting others. (5) Giving without reliance is not giving for the purpose of fame, pleasant words, or laudatory verses, since fame arises from false conceptions and depends on mere empty words that are like dry leaves. (6) Giving without discouragement is giving without despising oneself or feeling discouraged, thinking, “I cannot make large offerings,” but with a clear mind giving the actual gift with mental joy as preparation, and after making the offering being free of regret. (7) Giving that is not inferior is not giving inferior gifts or those too few in number but giving through assembling many excellent offerings. (8) Giving without bias is giving equally with compassion to all without differentiating friends, enemies, and strangers. (9) Giving without seeking return is giving with compassion alone, without hope for the return of gifts in later lives. (10) Giving without seeking karmic maturation is giving without hope for a fine body or resources in future since they have no essence, since all conditioned states are impermanent.[1309]

Again, from a general perspective, one should stop misinformed giving that is inappropriate for mendicants, such as giving leftover food and drink to renunciates who strive in purity, or giving that which is polluted by feces and urine or that which is spoiled. And similarly, one should stop giving garlic, onions, meat, or alcohol to those who do not consume them. In certain cases, one should directly or indirectly give poison, fire, weapons, or alcohol when beneficial. Precious Garland states: For whomever poison is beneficial, give poison to that person.[1310] Again, Bodhisattva Levels notes: For any action committed by oneself alone, the result of that merit is great. For any action one makes others do, the result of that merit is very great. For any action committed in common, the result of that merit is extremely great, for it should be known as the highest.[1311] Actions committed by oneself alone, those one has made others commit alone, those committed jointly by both self and others, and those joint actions one has initiated are explained to increase in merit from the first of these to the last.

the offerings given to {fields of benefit such as} one’s father and mother though not āryas, {the field of suffering of} the sick, Dharma teachers, and bodhisattvas in their last birth are incalculable merit because [416] the Sūtra Revealing the Results of Good and Bad Causes declares: Again, if one gives to three types of persons — tathāgatas, parents, and the sick — one cannot measure the results of karmic maturation. It is equal to the merit of giving to the tathāgatas.[1313] Further, the Dārṣṭāntika school asserts that though one makes offerings to the Buddha, making offerings to the Saṅgha has greater result, since the Buddha is included within the Saṅgha. The Dharmagupta school asserts that though one makes offerings to the Saṅgha, making offerings to the Buddha has much greater result, since the Buddha is not included within the Saṅgha. This is stated in the Detailed Presentation of Textual Systems.[1314] In this context Vaibhāṣikas assert that the final birth [of a being] is the final existence in which one attains enlightenment and that being is an ordinary being. Moreover, since Dharma teachers benefit sentient beings by giving the Dharma, they are a supreme field. The Autocommentary declares: To which of the four fields of excellence do Dharma teachers belong? They belong to the field of benefit because they give the eye of wisdom to people blinded by ignorance, they teach what is fit and unfit, and they actually establish the uncontaminated Dharma body; since, in brief, they engage in all the actions of the Buddha, they are great spiritual friends.[1315] The Sūtra Revealing the Results of Good and Bad Causes states: If one gives to a Dharma teacher who proclaims without error the many wheels of the secret essence of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna, opening the eyes of sentient beings, the maturational result is immeasurable.[1316] The others are easily understood.

HEAVY AND LIGHT KARMA
mjug dang zhing dang gzhi dang ni/ / sbyor dang sems pa bsam pa ste/ / de dag chung dang che ba las/ / las kyang chung dang che ba nyid/ / 119
Conclusion, field, basis, application, intention, thought. If these six are weak or potent, then karma is weak or potent. (4:119)

(1) That which is potent in terms of conclusion (pṛṣṭha) is continued engagement in an action after the actual basis of the karmic path [has been established]. (2) That which is potent in terms of the field (kṣetra) is that which benefits or harms a field, for instance, that benefits or that possesses qualities. (3) That which is potent in terms of the basis (vastu) is actions such as the potent physical karma of taking life, the potent verbal karma of lying, and the potent mental karma of wrong view. Taking life is potent through killing an arhat and so on, since one falls to Avīci. It is medium through killing those on the path, and it is light through killing animals and those lacking ethical conduct. This is stated in the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra. The Compendium of Ascertainment explains: Killing an animal of large dimension, and killing a human, or human fetus, or one’s parents, or brothers, or one’s guru, friends, students, bodhisattvas, or arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, or spilling the blood of a Tathāgata motivated by an evil mind and the thought to kill, are heavy in terms of [417] the basis.[1317] (4) That which is potent in terms of application (prayoga) is karma directly applied through body and speech. The Compendium of Ascertainment states: Taking mental delight and joy in preparing to commit, committing, and having committed killing, inducing others to commit killing like oneself, praising killing, rejoicing when one sees similar actions, over a long period thinking about killing, repeatedly committing killing, venerating killing, killing many beings at once, killing with an afflicted mind through bad temper, killing through making others commit improper acts through immorality, killing the weak, killing those who suffer, killing those wailing with torment, killing those with hunger and thirst, and killing those who plead for compassion are heavy in terms of application.[1318]

(5) That which is potent in terms of intention (cetanā) is karma with the potent intention to complete {or fulfill} that karma. (6) That which is potent in terms of thought (āśaya) is karma with a potent motivating thought. If these six of conclusion and so on are weak or potent, then the karma that arises is weak or potent. If all six are complete, it should be known as extremely heavy karma. The Compendium of Bases states: Karma is heavy in three ways: (1) Karma is heavy by means of thought when committed through the intense cultivation of the six entanglements (paryavasthāna),[1319] through taking delight in seeing similar actions, and through later reinforcing it through investigation and analysis. (2) Karma is heavy by means of application when that karma is continuously committed and accumulated and through praising it and making others do it. (3) Karma is heavy by means of the field when one acts to benefit or harm those who benefit oneself, those who correctly enter those paths, and those who emphatically establish those paths.[1320] Therefore the Foundations of Mindfulness Sūtra explains: Stealing due to hunger, though there is danger of punishment from the king or from one’s guru, the sick, pratyekabuddhas, stream enterers, and so on has a small result. Similarly, those who steal who have not taken vows against stealing, those who having once stolen, regret and confess and do not repeat the act, and those who do not complete the preliminary stages or conclusion of that karma have a small result because it is not definite that the result will be experienced.[1321] Engaging in the Deeds of a Bodhisattva states: Constantly motivated by great aspiration or motivated to apply appropriate remedies, if I give to fields of excellence, benefit, and those in distress, great merit will arise.[1322] This explains four factors that enhance karma — namely, the time, the motivation, the elimination of opposing states, and the field.

Letter to a Friend says: There are five types of potent virtuous and nonvirtuous karma: karma arising from continuous engagement, manifest longing, lack of antidote, the field of qualities, and the primary sentient basis. From among those, one should make exertion in virtuous conduct.[1323] Thus this text explains a fifth potency supplementary to the four: namely, the potency of the sentient basis acting with youth and strength. The Compendium of Abhidharma explains: A person employing strong antidotes converts karma that would otherwise be [418] experienced as birth in hell and so on into something to be experienced in this life, and karma that would be experienced in this life into something not to be experienced at all. Nonvirtue committed by desire-realm beings has greater strength than virtue since such nonvirtue has many associated root and branch afflictions. Habitual nonvirtue is stronger than that which is not habitual, and it endures . . .[1324] Nonvirtue committed by those with youthful minds and bodies is stronger than that of children and elders. Nonvirtue committed by those who have severed their lineage is stronger than that committed by those who possess a lineage. It is strong karma if committed in relation to superior fields such as the Three Jewels, one’s mother or father, and so on. It is stronger when committed with a strong application of mind such as the act of producing the mind awakening to the motivation of the three vehicles.

Again, one should know that strong karma has nine aspects: (1) Field, (2) object, (3) nature, (4) basis, (5) attention, (6) thought, (7) assistance, (8) frequency, (9) multiple agents.[1325] (1) Karma committed with respect to ethical beings who are fields of merit is stronger than to those without ethical conduct. (2) When given, objects with more good qualities and fewer bad qualities produce stronger karma. (3) Karma committed in later stages is by nature stronger than that committed in earlier stages, in terms of the three bases for creating merit,[1326] the six perfections, and so on. (4) Karma committed by a sentient person free of attachment is stronger than that committed by one with attachment. (5) Karma committed with full clarity or intense affliction is stronger than that committed with ordinary attention. (6) Karma committed with the thought of producing the cause or result of liberation is stronger than that committed for the purpose of producing the cause or result of saṃsāra. (7) Generosity committed with the assistance of ethics and so on or accompanied by subsequent rejoicing is stronger than generosity committed without these. (8) Karma committed frequently is stronger than karma committed once. (9) Karma committed by multiple agents — by oneself and others inspired by oneself — is stronger than that committed by oneself alone. Some say: Karma committed by many beings is karma committed by an assembly of many beings. The opposite of such karma is weak karma.[1327]
bsams bzhin pa dang rdzogs pa dang / / mi 'gyod gnyen po med pa dang / / 'khor dang rnam par smin pa las/ / bsags pa'i las shes bya ba yin/ / 120
Karmas that are said to be accumulated are committed intentionally through completing the branches, without regret, without antidote, with associates, with karmic maturation. (4:120)
yang mdo las/ las byas la bsags pa dang byas la bsags pa ma yin pa zhes bya ba gsungs pa la
Again, a sūtra declares: There is karma that is committed and accumulated, and karma that is committed but not accumulated.[1328]

blo sngon du ma btang ba dang bab col du byas pa ma yin par 'di nges par bya'o snyam du ched du bsam bzhin byas pa dang*/ las kyi yan lag {gang gis skye ba 'grub par 'gyur ba ste }rdzogs par byas pa dang*/ byas pa la phyis mi 'gyod pa dang 'chags pa sogs/ las de la gnod byed kyi gnyen po med pa dang / rjes su yi rang sogs/ 'khor dang bcas pa dang*/ rnam par smin pa myong bar nges pa zhes bya ba drug las ni byas la bsags pa'i las zhes bya ba yin la/ las gzhan dag ni gang gis skye ba 'grub par ste byas la bsags pa ma yin pa'i las zhes bya'o/ / de bzhin du bsags la ma byas pa dang*/ gnyis ka ma yin pa'ang shes par bya'o/ / de la rdzogs pa ni las kha cig ni nyes par spyad pa dang legs par spyad pa gcig gis ngan 'gro dang bde 'gror 'gro la/ kha cig ni lus dang ngag dang yid gsum gyi las bcu char gyis ngan 'gro dang bde 'gror 'gro ba yod do/ / de'i las dag rdzogs par byas pa'o/ /

Six karmas are said to be committed and accumulated: (1) karma committed intentionally (saṃcetanā) while purposefully thinking “I will definitely commit this” and not committed impulsively, without premeditation; (2) karma committed through completing the branches of karma, {where whatever arises is accomplished}; (3) karma committed without later regret; (4) karma committed without applying an antidote to that karma that would harm it, such as confession; (5) karma committed with associates such as rejoicing and so on; and (6) karma with maturation certain to be experienced. [419] Karmas other than those are karmas committed but not accumulated or are those accumulated but not committed and those neither accumulated nor committed. Some say: “Completing the branches” means proceeding to an evil or blissful rebirth through committing a single negative or positive action. Some say: One proceeds to evil or blissful rebirths through committing the ten branches of physical, verbal, and mental karma. That is completing the branches of karma.

gnyen po med pa ni log lta dang 'gyod pa la sogs pa dang bshags pa dang bsdam pa la sogs pa med pa'o/ / rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba las/ gnyen po med pa ni srog gcod la sogs pa'i mi dge ba byed la/ bslab pa'i gnas 'ga' yang mi len pa dang*/ tshes brgyad dang bcu bzhi dang bco lnga la bsnyen gnas la gnas par mi byed pa dang*/ dus dus su sbyin pa dang bsod nams dang mngon du smra ba dang phyag 'tshal ba dang ldang ba dang thal mo sbyor ba dang 'dud pa la sogs pa mi byed pa dang*/ dus dus su ngo tsha khrel yod dang 'gyod pa shas chen po mi 'thob pa dang*/ 'jig rten pa'i 'dod chags dang bral ba dang*/ chos mngon par rtogs pa la mi rig pa'o zhes bshad do/ / 'khor ni dge ba'i las la ni 'khor yang dge ba dang*/ mi dge ba'i las la ni 'khor yang mi dge ba ste gang zhig byas nas rjes su yi rang byed pa'o zhes TI kar bshad mod kyi 'dir 'khor ni sbyor ba dang mjug gnyis ka yin no/ / gzhan dag ni shes par sla'o/ / gzhi bsdu ba las ni mi shes bzhin du byas pa dang*/ rmi lam du byas pa dang*/ ma bsgribs lung ma bstan dang*/ mi dge ba la 'gyod pa dang*/ gnyen pos zin pa dang*/ rgyud dag par byas pa'i las ni ma bsags pa'o zhes bshad do/ /

“Without antidote” means being without confession, restraint, regret, and so on for wrong view and so on. The Compendium of Ascertainment reads: “Without antidote” means that, having committed the nonvirtues of taking life and so on, one does not take up any form of training; nor does one take one-day vows on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth; nor does one frequently engage in generosity, merit, [virtuous] speech, prostration, standing up, placing one’s palms together, bowing, and so on; nor does one frequently generate shame, embarrassment, and regret; nor does one comprehend Dharma as it is.[1329] “With associates” means that the associated factors are virtuous for virtuous karma, and the associated factors are nonvirtuous for nonvirtuous karma, such as rejoicing in whatever karma was committed. Indeed, this is explained in the Ṭikā. Here “associates” refers to both preparation and conclusion. The others are easy to understand. The Compendium of Bases mentions: Karma committed unconsciously, karma committed in a dream, karma that is an unobscured-neutral state, karma where the nonvirtue is regretted, karma that is offset by the antidote, and karma committed in a pure mindstream is not accumulated.[1330]

de bzhin du las rnam par 'byed pa'i mdo las kyang*/ byas la ma bsags pa'i las gang zhe na/ las gang byas nas ngo tsha ba dang 'dzem pa dang 'gyod pa dang smod pa dang 'thol ba dang 'dor ba dang spong ba dang ma 'ongs pa na sdom par byed pa'o/ / bsags la ma byas pa'i las gang zhe na/ las gang lus kyis yongs su rdzogs par bya ba de sems kyis yongs su rdzogs par byas shing tshig tu'ang las 'di bya'o zhes smras la las de ma byas pa'o/ / byas la bsags pa'i las gang zhe na/ las gang byas nas ngo mi tsha ba nas ma 'ongs pa na mi sdom pa'i bar ro/ / ma byas pa la ma bsags pas las gang zhe na las gang ched du ma bsams par byas pa'o zhes pa dang*/ de bzhin du las gang sems can dmyal ba'i tshe yongs su rdzogs par byas nas 'chi ba'i las gang zhe na/ 'ga' zhig dmyal bar skye ba'i las byas shing bsags nas de ngo mi tsha ba nas ma 'ongs pa na mi sdom pa'i bar te dper na lhas byin lta bu'o/ / sems can dmyal ba'i tshe phyed zad nas 'chi ba'i las gang zhe na/ 'ga' zhig gis dmyal bar skye ba'i las byas nas ngo tsha ba nas ma 'ongs pa na sdom par byed pa'i bar ro/ / sems can dmyal bar skyes ma thag tu 'chi ba'i las gang zhe na/ 'ga' zhig gis dmyal bar skye ba'i las byas shing bsags nas des ngo tsha ba nas sdom pa'i bar du byed cing shin tu yid la gcags pa yin yang des las de sel bar mi nus pa ste dper na rgyal po ma skyes dgras pha bsad pa lta bu'o zhes gsungs so/ / de'i phyir nyan thos sde pa ltar na 'gyod pa dang bshad pa dang phyis mi byed par bsdam pa byas kyang sdig pa rtsa ba nas dag par mi 'dod de/ de nyid las/ shin tu mi bzad las rnams byas pa ni/ / bdag la smod dang rab tu bshags pa dang*/ / sdom par byed pas de dag bsrabs 'gyur gyi/ / shin tu rtsa nas phyin ces mi smra'o zhes gsungs so/ / de'i rgyu mtshan ni gnyen po stobs bzhi ma tshang ba'i phyir ro zhes dam pa rnams gsung ngo*/ /

Similarly, Divisions of Karma states: What karma is committed but not accumulated? Karma committed with shame, humiliation, regret, reproach, confession, rejection, abandonment, and future restraint. What karma is accumulated but not committed? Karma meant to be completed by the body but never committed except by the mind or by verbally stating, “I intend to commit this karma.” What is karma committed and accumulated? It is any karma committed without shame and without future restraint. What karma is neither committed nor accumulated? Karma committed without the thought to do so. Similarly, what is the karma at death of a sentient being that is to be completed in the life of a hell being? That is committing any karma that generates birth in hell and, having accumulated it, generating no shame for it and not restraining oneself from it in the future. An example is the karma of Devadatta. What is the karma of a sentient being who dies having partially exhausted the karma of life in hell? That is the karma [420] of those who commit karma that generates birth in hells but who develop a sense of shame for it and restrain themselves from committing that action in the future. What is the karma of a sentient being who dies immediately after birth in hell? That is the karma of those who, having committed and accumulated karma for birth in hell, cannot fully eliminate that karma even though they practice shame and future restraint and intensely confess the act. An example is Ajātaśatru, who killed his father.[1331] Therefore śrāvaka schools assert that regret and restraint for committing that action in future cannot purify root immorality, since that sūtra says: Unbearable karmas that have been committed are lessened through blaming oneself, fully confessing them, and applying future restraint. But that is not called “removal from the root.”[1332] The reason for that, say holy beings, is that the four opponent powers are not complete.

gzhan yang de nyid las/ sngar bde la phyis sdug bsngal bar 'gyur ba'i las gang zhe na/ 'ga' zhig sbyin pa byin pa na yid rab tu dga' zhing yid bde ba skyes la/ byin nas phyis 'gyod pa yin te/ de ni tshe stod la bde bar spyod la phyis longs spyod nyams shing zad pas sdug bsngal du 'gyur ba'o/ / sngar sdug bsngal la phyis bde bar 'gyur ba'i las gang zhe na/ sbyin pa sbyin pa na sdug bsngal bar 'jug cing sbyin pa byin nas mi 'gyod par dga' ba dang yid bde ba ste/ de ni mi rnams kyi nang du skyes pa na sngar dbul la phyis longs spyod 'phel nas bde ba'o/ / sngar yang bde la phyis kyang bde ba'i las gang zhe na/ sbyin pa sbyin pa na de yid dga' bzhin du byin la byin nas kyang mi 'gyod pa'o/ / sngar yang sdug bsngal la phyis kyang sdug bsngal bar 'gyur ba'i las gang zhe na/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang bral bas sbyin pa cung zad kyang ma byin zhing sdig pa'ang cung zad kyang ma byas pa'o/ / yang phyug por gyur la gtong ba dang ldan pa'i las gang zhe na/ zhing bzang po la sbyin pa dpag tu med pa byin pa'o/ / phyug la ser sna can du 'gyur ba'i las gang zhe na zhing bzang po la sbyin pa cung zad tsam byin pa ste/ des zhing bzang po la phul bas ni skyid par gyur la/ gtong ba la goms par ma byas pas ni ser sna can du gyur to/ /

Again, that sūtra states: What karma is initially blissful but later becomes painful? That is the karma of those who, when giving, generate mental joy and mental satisfaction but later generate regret. At the beginning of that life they give with joy, but later, through their resources declining and being used up, they experience suffering. What karma is initially painful but later pleasurable? That is the karma of one who suffers when giving but, having given, does not regret it and generates joy and mental satisfaction, and when born among humans, though initially poor, he later experiences a blissful increase in wealth. What karma is initially blissful and later blissful? That is the karma of giving with mental joy and, having given, not regretting it. What karma is initially painful and later painful? That is the karma of those who lack a spiritual friend and do not give in the least, even though they commit not even the slightest immorality. Again, what is the karma of giving to become wealthy? That is the immeasurable generosity of giving to superior fields of merit. What is the karma of having greed for wealth? That is giving a mere slight amount to superior fields of merit, being satisfied with such offerings to superior fields, and having greed through not giving habitually.

dbul la gtong ba dang ldan pa'i las gang zhe na/ zhing ngan pa la sbyin pa mang du byin pa yin te/ de'i bsod nams zad pas ni dbul por gyur la sngon goms par byas pas ni gtong phod par gyur to/ / dbul la ser sna can du 'gyur ba'i las gang zhe na/ sngon dge ba'i bshes gnyen dang bral bas sbyin pa cung zad kyang ma btang ba'o zhes 'byung ngo*/ / gzhan yang kun las btus las/ thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'i las gnyis kyang bshad de/ de la dang po ni snod kyi 'jig rten 'grub par byed pa yin la/ gnyis pa ni sems can gyi 'jig rten 'grub par byed pa'o/ / de bzhin du bsam gyis mi khyab pa dang mi khyab pa'i las gnyis kyang bshad de/ de la dang po ni las dge ba zag bcas kyis bde 'gro 'thob pa dang*/ mi dge bas ngan song gsum du skye ba la sogs pa'o/ / gnyis pa ni las 'di kho nas sems can gyi lus sna tshogs su 'grub pa dang*/ phyi'i dngos po sna tshogs 'grub bo zhes pa dang*/ nor bu dang sngags dang sman gyi nus pa dang*/ 'khyud spyad kyi las dang rnal 'byor pa rnams kyi mtha'i las dang*/ byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi dbang gi las dang*/ sangs rgyas rnams kyi mdzad pa sgrub pa'i 'phrin las rnams te/ de dag ni phal cher sangs rgyas ma gtogs pas bsam par mi nus pa'i phyir ro/ / phal chen sde'i bye brag shar nub kyi ri bo'i sde pa la sogs pa na re 'dod chags dang bcas pas mchod rten la phul na de bdag gi don gyi phyir sbyin pa yin no zhes pa ni mi rigs te/ mchod rten la phul ba la bsod nams 'byung bar ga la 'gyur te/ len pa dang longs spyod pa med pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ba ni mi rigs te/

What is the karma of giving to the poor? That is giving frequently to inferior fields of merit. Through exhausting that merit one becomes poor, and due to the prior habit of giving one is able to give. What is the karma of having greed for giving? That is, due to being separated from a past spiritual friend, not giving in the least.[1333] Again, the Compendium of Abhidharma explains two karmas: shared and unshared.[1334] The first establishes the physical cosmos and the second establishes the cosmos of beings. So too, it explains another two karmas: conceivable and [421] inconceivable. The first is obtaining pleasant rebirth through contaminated virtuous karma and birth in the three lower states through nonvirtue. The second is the various bodies of sentient beings established by this karma alone and the various external things that are established. This includes the potency of jewels, speech, and medicine, the karma of embrace, the mighty karma of yogis, the powerful karma of bodhisattvas, and the enlightened actions accomplishing the deeds of buddhas, which are inconceivable except by buddhas. The Pūrvaśaila and Aparaśaila subschools of the Mahāsāṃghika sect say: It is illogical to say, “Those with attachment who make offerings to stūpas give for their own benefit,”[1335] because how does merit arise from making offerings to a stūpa, given that there is no receiver or being who enjoys the offering?
mchod rten la btang rgyus byung ba'i/ / bsod nams len med byams sogs bzhin/ / rgyu las 'bras bu mi 'khrul phyir/ / ngan pa'i zhing la'ang 'bras yid 'ong / / 121

Though there is no receiver, merit arises from the cause of giving to a stūpa, like love and so on. Because it is unmistaken that pleasant results arise from virtuous causes, even giving to inferior fields produces pleasant results. (4:121)

de dag la len pa dang longs spyod pa las byung ba'i bsod nams med kyang{ sems kyi mthus }mchod rten la btang ba'i rgyu las byung ba'i bsod nams 'byung ste/ dper na sems can thams cad bde bar gyur cig snyam pa sogs pa'i byams pa tshad med pa la sogs pa dang*/ yang dag pa'i lta ba sgom pa la len pa dang gzhan la dngos su phan pa med kyang rang gi sems kyi mthus bsod nams tshad med pa 'byung ba bzhin no/ / de'i phyir sbyin pa las byung ba la ni bsod nams gnyis te/ longs spyad pa las byung ba dang*/ btang ba'i rgyu las byung ba'o/ / de la mchod rten la phul ba la sogs pa la ni btang ba'i rgyu las byung ba'i bsod nams gcig pu yod do/ / 'dod chags dang bcas pa'i 'dod chags dang bral ba'i 'phags pa 'dod pa'i khams su skyes pa la byin pa la ni gnyis ka yod do/ / gal te phan 'dogs pa la sogs pa'i zhing bzang po la byin pa'i 'bras bu ni rnam smin yid du 'ong bar rigs na dud 'gro la sogs pa zhing ngan pa la byin pas ni rnam smin yid du 'ong bar mi 'gyur ro zhe na/

Reply: It is illogical to say that because there is no receiver or being enjoying the offering, no merit is accrued. Merit arises from the {force of mind that is the} cause of giving to a stūpa. For example, it is like meditation on immeasurable love, thinking, “May all sentient beings be happy” and so on. Likewise, though no receiver or being is directly benefited from meditation on correct view, immeasurable merit arises from the force of this mind. Therefore there are two types of merit that arise from giving: merit arising from a gift being enjoyed and merit arising from the cause of giving. In making offerings to stūpas and so on, only merit derived from the cause of giving exists. Both exist when those with attachment give to an ārya who is free of attachment who takes birth in the desire realm. Question: If it is logical that giving to superior fields of merit such as fields of benefit results in pleasant karmic maturation, then giving to inferior fields such as animals should result in unpleasant karmic maturation.

rgyu dge ba las 'bras bu rnam smin yid du 'ong ba 'byung ba ni thams cad du mi 'khrul ba'i phyir ngan pa'i zhing la byin pa la'ang rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu ni yid du 'ong ba kho na 'byung ba yin no/ / 'on kyang zhing ngan pa'i stobs kyis rnam smin chung ba'am med par 'gyur te zhing ngan pa la btab pa'i 'bras bu dus su mi smin pa dang chung ba la sogs par 'gyur ba bzhin no/ / de dag gis ni sbyin pa las byung ba'i bsod nams bya ba'i gzhi bshad zin to/ /

Reply: Because it is completely unmistaken that pleasant results of karmic maturation arise from virtuous causes, even giving to inferior fields produces only pleasant results of karmic maturation. However, due to the power of an immoral field, the karmic maturation may be small or nonexistent. It is similar to planting inferior fields where the harvest does not mature on time or is small and so on. This completes the explanation of the basis of merit derived from giving.
tshul khrims las byung ba'i bsod nams bya ba'i gzhi bshad pa la
THE BASIS OF MERIT AND ACTION
'chal pa'i tshul khrims mi dge'i gzugs/ / de spong tshul khrims rnam gnyis so/ / sangs rgyas kyis ni bcad pa yang / / rnam dag yon tan bzhi ldan no/ / 122
Unethical conduct is nonvirtuous form. Ethics abandons that. It has two types. Abandoning that proscribed by the Buddha is also ethics. Pure ethics possesses four qualities. (4:122)

'chal ba'i tshul khrims ni mi dge ba'i rig byed dang rig byed ma yin pa'i gzugs te {srog gcod sogs lus ngag gi las dang }sdom pa ma yin pa yin la/ 'chal ba'i tshul khrims de spong bar byed pa'i tshul khrims ni tshul khrims las byung ba'i dge ba yin no/ / tshul khrims de yang spangs bya rig byed dang rig byed ma yin pa gnyis kyi gnyen po yin pas rig byed dang rig byed ma yin pa rnam pa gnyis so/ / rang bzhin gyis sdig pa ma yin yang dus ma yin pa'i kha zas spong ba la sogs pa sangs rgyas kyis ni bcad pa ste bkag pa de spong ba'i rig byed dang rig byed ma yin pa yang tshul khrims yin no/ / tshul khrims de yang rnam par dag pa ni yon tan bzhi dang ldan pa yin no/ / bzhi gang zhe na/

Unethical conduct (dauḥśīlya) is nonvirtuous indicative and nonindicative form that is {mental and physical karma, including such things as taking life and} perverse [422] ethics. Ethics that abandons that unethical conduct is virtue derived from ethics. Further, since ethics is the antidote of both indicative and nonindicative form to be abandoned, it has two types: indicative and nonindicative. Abandoning actions that are not natural immoral acts but are proscribed by the Buddha, such as taking food at the wrong time, is also ethics that is indicative and nonindicative form that abandons and stops such actions. Also pure ethics possesses four qualities. Question: What are those four?
'chal khrims de'i rgyus 'phen ma byung / / de gnyen po dang zhi la rten/ /
It is not affected by unethical conduct nor by its causes. It is dependent on the antidote to that and on peace. (4:123ab)

'chal pa'i tshul khrims kyis 'phan te skyon ma phyung ba dang*/ de'i rgyu 'dod chags la sogs pa nyon mongs pa dang nye ba'i nyon mongs pas 'phan ma byung ba dang*/ 'chal ba'i tshul khrims de'i gnyen po byed pa'i dran pa nyer gzhag la brten pa dang*/ thar par bsdos pas zhi ba la brten pa'o/ / gzhan dag na re tshul khrims rnam par dag pa ni rgyu lnga dang ldan pa yin te/ srog gcod pa la sogs pas ma gos pas las kyi lam dngos kyis rnam par dag pa dang*/ srog gcod pa la sogs pa'i sbyor bas kyang ma gos pas nyer bsdogs dag gis rnam par dag pa dang 'dod pa'i rnam rtog la sogs pas ma gos pas rnam par rtog pa rnams kyis 'phan ma phyung ba dang*/ lus dran pa nyer gzhag gis brtan par byas pa'am/ dran pas zin pas dran pas yongs su bzung ba dang*/ mya ngan las 'das par yongs su bsdos pa yin no zhes zer ro/ / gzhan dag ni tshul khrims ni bzhi ste/ 'tsho ba med pa dang tshigs su bcad pa med pa dang chad pa dang ngan 'gros 'jigs nas srung ba 'jigs pa'i tshul khrims dang*/ srid pa dang longs spyod dang bkur sti la chags nas srung ba legs su smon pa'i tshul khrims dang*/ sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa la zhugs pa yang dag pa'i lta ba can rnams thar pa'i don du srung ba byang chub kyi yan lag gi rjes su mthun pa'i tshul khrims dang*/ dri ma med pa'i phyir zag pa med pa'i tshul khrims ni yongs su dag pa'i tshul khrims so zhes 'chad do/ /

Reply: (1) It is not affected by the error of unethical conduct (dauḥśīlya). (2) It is not affected by decline due to its causes: root afflictions and branch afflictions such as attachment. (3) It is dependent on the close placement of mindfulness that acts as the antidote to that unethical conduct. (4) It is dependent on peace (śama), since it is directed to liberation. Others say: Pure ethics possesses five causes. (1) It is pure in terms of the actual karmic path, since it is not sullied by taking life and so on. (2) It is pure in terms of the preliminary stages, since it is not sullied by preparing to take life and so on. (3) It is not projected by conception, since it is not sullied by desire-realm conception and so on. (4) It is stabilized by close placement of mindfulness on the body or fully held by mindfulness through prior mindfulness. (5) It is fully directed to nirvāṇa.[1336] Others explain that there are four types of ethics: (1) Ethics through fear guards sentient beings who fear having no livelihood, having no verses [of teachings], incurring punishment, or taking bad rebirth. (2) Ethics from authentic prayer guards those attached to existence, resources, and respect. (3) Ethics conforming to the requisites of enlightenment guards those possessing correct view who enter the Buddha’s teachings for the purpose of liberation. (4) Uncontaminated ethics is for the purpose of the stainless state. All these are thoroughly pure ethics.[1337]
bsgoms pa las byung ba'i dge ba bshad pa ni
VIRTUE DERIVED FROM MEDITATION
mnyam par bzhag pa'i dge ba ni/ / bsgom pa'o sems la sgo phyir ro/ / 123
Virtue derived from meditation is from equipoise [and is so called] because it lays down imprints on the mind. (4:123cd)

mnyam par ma bzhag pa dang nyon mongs can sgom byung ma yin pas sems dmigs pa la mnyam par bzhag pa las byung ba'i dge ba ting nge 'dzin mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa ni bsgoms pa las byung ba'o/ / ci'i phyir de la sgom pa zhes bya zhe na {til mar dang me tog gi dri ltar } sems la dge ba'i bag chags bsgo zhing goms pa dang dbang du byed pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na tshul khrims dang bsgoms pa las byung ba de dag gang gtso zhe na/

Virtue derived from meditation is not derived from either nonequipoise or afflicted states but is concomitant with concentration derived from equipoise and focuses on the mind. Question: Why is it called meditation? Reply: Because it lays down imprints of virtue on the mind, {like the smell of sesame oil and flowers,} and makes the mind familiar with its object. Question: What is more important, keeping ethics or being derived from meditation?
mtho ris don du tshul khrims dang / / 'bral ba'i don du bsgom gtso'i phyir/ / bskal par mtho ris dga' gnas phyir/ / bzhi yi tshangs pa'i bsod nams yin/ / 124

For the purpose of higher rebirth, ethics is more important; for the purpose of freedom, meditation is more important. It is the merit of Brahma of the four because they abide in the joy of higher rebirth for eons. (4:124)

bzhi brgya pa las/ tshul khrims kyis ni mtho ris 'gro/ / lta bas go 'phang mchog tu 'gro zhes 'byung ba ltar mtho ris thob pa'i don du tshul khrims gtso che ba'i phyir dang*/ bar chad med pa'i lam gyi spang bya dngos su spong bas na nyon mongs pa dang 'bral ba'i don du sgom pa gtso che ba'i phyir de dag 'dod pas de bzhin du bsten par bya'o/ / tshul khrims la brten nas zhi gnas lhag mthong 'byung bas gtso chung ba ni gnyis ka'ang gnyis ka'i rgyu yin no/ / de'i phyir lha'i bu rab rtsal sems kyis zhus pa'i mdo las/ longs spyod chen po'i rgyu sbyin pa mi spong ba dang*/ mtho ris su skye ba'i rgyu tshul khrims mi spong ba dang*/ shes rab chen po'i rgyu thos pa mi spong ba dang*/ 'bral ba'i rgyu sgom pa mi spong ba ste zhes pa dang*/ longs spyod che rgyu sbyin pa mi spong de'i 'bras de/ / mtho ris skye rgyu tshul khrims mi spong de'i 'bras de/ / shes rab nyon mongs 'joms rgyu thos pa de'i 'bras de/ / rnam grol reg rgyu sgom par byed cing de'i 'bras de/ / rgyu bzhi de la rtag brtson mkhas pa de dag ni/ / byang chub snying por dbang bskur 'bras phyir nyin mtshan spyod ces pa dang*/ rgyud bla ma las kyang*/ gang phyir sbyin pas longs spyod dag ni sgrub byed cing*/ / khrims kyis mtho ris bsgoms pas nyon mongs spong byed la/ / shes rab nyon mongs shes bya kun spong de yi phyir/ / 'di mchog nyid de de yi rgyu ni 'di thos yin zhes bshad do/ /

Reply: This accords with Four Hundred Stanzas, which mentions: Through ethics one proceeds to higher rebirth; through view one proceeds to the supreme state.[1338] Therefore, for the purpose of obtaining higher rebirth (svargāya), ethics (śīla) [423] is more important. For the purpose of freedom (visaṃyoga) from affliction through directly abandoning objects to be abandoned by the uninterrupted path, meditation (bhāvana) is more important. Therefore one should rely on them in accordance with what one desires. Of lesser importance is that each one acts as the cause of the other, since calm abiding and insight arise in dependence on ethics. Therefore the Sūtra Requested by Suvikrānta states: Do not abandon giving, the cause of great resources. Do not abandon ethics, the cause of birth in higher states. Do not abandon study, the cause of great wisdom. Do not abandon meditation, the cause of freedom. The result of not abandoning giving is having great resources. The result of not abandoning ethics is higher rebirth. The result of study is wisdom that annihilates affliction. The result of that meditation is attaining higher status. Those skilled in always striving in the four causes practice day and night to attain the essence of enlightenment.[1339] Sublime Continuum observes: Why does generosity establish resources, ethics establish higher rebirth, and meditation abandon afflictions? Because wisdom abandons all afflicted objects of knowlege. The cause of this supreme state is study.[1340]

'o na mdo las/ gang zag bzhi ni tshangs pa'i bsod nams skyed de/ ma byas pa'i sa phyogs su de bzhin gshegs pa'i sku gdung gi mchod rten byed pa 'di ni gang zag tshangs pa'i bsod nams skyed pa dang po yin no zhes bya ba dang*/ de bzhin du phyogs bzhi'i dge 'dun la kun dga' ra ba 'bul zhing de nyid du gtsug lag khang rtsig pa dang*/ de bzhin gshegs pa'i nyan thos bye ba sdum pa dang*/ byams pa tshad med sgom pa la yang sbyar nas gsungs so/ /

Now, a sūtra notes: Four persons generate the merit of Brahma. They are those who erect a relic stūpa of the Tathāgata in a vacant place. This is the first person who generates the merit of Brahma.[1341] And: Similarly, they are those who offer groves to the Saṅgha of the four directions, build temples for them, mend divisions of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata, and meditate on immeasurable love.[1342]
de lta bu'i tshangs pa'i bsod nams ni
Regarding the merit of Brahma,

tshangs pa'i mdun na 'don gyi tshe dang mnyam par{ bar gyi} bskal par {bzhi bcu } mtho ris su dga' bar gnas pa'i phyir sngar smros pa'i ma byas pa'i sa phyogs su sku gdung gi mchod rten rtsig pa la sogs pa byed pa'i gang zag bzhi'i tshangs pa'i bsod nams yin no zhes bya ste/ 'dir tshangs pa ni tshe bskal par thub pa tshangs pa'i mdun na 'don la 'dod do/ / sde pa gzhan gyi lus las kyang*/ tshangs pa'i bsod nams skyed pa ni/ / bskal par mtho ris dga' bar gnas zhes 'byung ste/ 'di ni sngon gyi slob dpon gyi yin no/ / de'i phyir slob dpon rgya mtsho sprin gyis kyang*/ tshangs pa'i bsod nams kyi tshad ni bsod nams gang gis bskal pa gcig tu mtho ris su 'gro bar 'gyur ba ste/ yang dang yang du rgyun mi chad par rnam par smin par 'jug par 'gyur ba'i bsod nams la tshangs pa'i bsod nams zhes brjod de/ bsam gtan dang po'i sems can gyi bsod nams dang mtshungs pa la bya'o zhes pa dang*/ tshigs su bcad pa gzhan dag las ni/ dge 'dun mthun par byas na ni/ / bskal par mtho ris bde ba thob ces bshad do/ /

it is called “the merit of Brahma” of the four persons who build relic stūpas of a Tathāgata on unclaimed vacant places and so on because through it they abide in joy in higher rebirths for {forty intermediate} eons, which is equal to the lifespan of the gods of Brahmapurohita.[1343] Here Brahma is asserted to refer to gods of Brahmapurohita, who live for forty intermediate eons. Scriptures of other schools also declare: By generating the merit of Brahma, one abides with joy for eons in high rebirth.[1344] This is stated by past masters. Therefore Master Sāgaramegha states: The measure of the merit of Brahma is any merit by which one comes to migrate to a high rebirth for one eon. Merit producing continuous unbroken karmic maturation is called “the merit of Brahma” because it is similar to the merit of the sentient beings of the first absorption.[1345] Other verses confirm: [424] If one acts in conformity with the Saṅgha, one obtains the bliss of higher rebirth for eons.[1346]

Vaibhāṣikas say: The merit of Brahma is the karma that matures as a mark of a buddha because it produces as its result the resources of all sentient beings except bodhisattvas who have attained certainty.[1347] It is the merit of Brahma because it corresponds to the merit of Brahma or the merit generating birth as Brahma, greatly prolongs higher rebirth in the desire realm, and generates the experience of bliss for forty [intermediate] eons.[1348] Some say: Great merit is called “the merit of Brahma.”

THE GIVING OF DHARMA
chos sbyin nyon mongs can min pas/ / mdo sogs yang dag ji bzhin ston/ /
The giving of Dharma is teaching discourses and so on without afflicted motivation, but correctly just as it is. (4:125ab)

chos kyi sbyin pa ni bsam pa kun slong rnyed pa dang bkur sti la sogs pa 'dod pa'i nyon mongs pa can min pas bstan bya mdo'i sde la sogs pa {dbyangs bsnyad lung bstan tshigs bcad dang*/ / ched brjod gleng gzhi rtogs brjod dang*/ / de lta bu skyes shin tu rgyas/ / rmad byung gtan la dbab pa'i sde/ / zhes pa }gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis sam sde snod gsum po dag sbyor ba yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin ma nor bar ston pa yin no/ / de la gsum las

The giving of Dharma is teaching the subject matter of the twelve branches of scripture such as the category of discourses, {chants, predictions, stanzas, sayings, ethical precedents, stories, former events, former lives, extensive discourses, marvelous events, instruction,} and so on, or teaching the twelve branches of scripture, or the three piṭakas, without afflicted motivation such as the desire for property and respect and so on, but teaching it just as it is with correct preparation and without error. Such teachings have three types: (1) classification in the twelve branches of scripture, (2) subsuming those in three or two piṭaka baskets, and (3) equivalent terms.
