TWELVE BRANCHES OF SCRIPTURE

gdul bya mdor bsdus pa la dga' ba rnams kyis rnam par bzhag sla ba dang bshad sla ba dang*/ bzung sla bas chos la gus pas tshogs rdzogs pa dang*/ myur du chos nyid rtogs pa dang*/ dkon mchog gsum la shes nas dad pa 'thob pa dang*/ mthong ba'i chos la bde bar reg par gnas pa dang*/ 'bel gtam la mkhas par bya ba'i dgos pa bcu'i phyir gdul bya'i nyon mongs pa'i spyod pa la brtsams nas mdor bstan pa'i tshul gyis phung po dang khams dang skye mched dang rten 'brel dang zas dang bden pa dang theg pa gsum dang mi sdug pa dang dbugs 'byung rngub dang bslab pa gsum dang shes nas dad pa dang byang chub kyi phyogs kyi chos sum cu rtsa bdun la sogs pa rkyang pas gsungs pa mdo'i sde dang*/ gang gi dbus dang mthar tshigs su bcad de gsungs pa dang drang don gyi mdo sde gang yin pa de ni dbyangs kyis bsnyad pa'i sde dang*/ gang las nyan thos 'das te shi 'phos pa dang ma 'ongs pa na 'byung ba lung ston pa dang nges don gyi mdo sde ni lung bstan pa'i sde dang*/ rkyang pas gsungs pa ma yin pa rtsa ba gnyis pa dang*/ rtsa ba gsum pa dang*/ rtsa ba bzhi pa dang*/ rtsa ba lnga pa dang*/ rtsa ba drug par bsdebs nas gsungs pa tshigs su bcad pa'i sde dang*/

(1) The category of discourse (sūtra) consists of prose works on the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, substance, the truths, the three vehicles, repulsiveness, inhalation-exhalation, the three higher trainings, faith through knowledge, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, and so on. These consist of abbreviated statements composed to counter the afflicted conduct of disciples who like abbreviated teachings, and to address ten needs. These ten are to complete the collection of merit through teachings that are (i) easily presented, (ii) easily explained, (iii) easily grasped, and (iv) engender respect for Dharma; through Dharma that is (v) swiftly comprehended; or is obtained (vi–viii) due to faith through knowledge of the Three Jewels; (ix) due to attaining bliss in this current life; and (x) due to becoming learned in the teachings (sāṃkathya). (2) The category of chants (geya) [i.e., hymns and praises] consists of verses occurring in the middle or end of a work. It includes interpretive sūtrānta. (3) The category of predictions (vyākaraṇa) consists of predictions of the death and future rebirth of śrāvakas. It includes definitive sūtrānta. (4) The category of stanzas (gāthā) consists of works not in prose but in verse comprising two, three, four, five, or six lines (pada).

gang zag gi ming dang rigs ma brjod par dam pa'i chos dang bstan pa yun ring du gnas par bya ba'i phyir yi rang nas gsungs pa ched du brjod pa'i sde dang*/ gang zag gi ming dang rigs brjod nas bstan cing bshad pa dang gang gi ched du gsungs pa dang 'dus pa dang ldan pa'i byung ba dang bcas gleng gzhi dang bcas pa'i so so thar pa gsungs pa gleng gzhi'i sde dang*/ dpes don gsal bar byed pa dpe dang bcas par gsungs pa rtogs pa brjod pa'i sde dang*/
sngon gyi gtam rgyud kyi sbyor ba dang ldan par gsungs pa de lta bu byung ba'i sde dang*/ 'das pa'i dus la brten te bcom ldan 'das kyis skye mched de dang de dag tu byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa dang dka' ba spyad pa bstan pa skyes pa'i rabs kyi sde dang*/ gang las bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub dang stobs bcu la sogs pa dang sgrib pa med pa'i ye shes sgrub par byed pa byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi lam stan pa shin tu rgyas pa'i sde dang*/ gang las sangs rgyas dang byang chub sems dpa' dang nyan thos rnams kyi thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'i yon tan gzhan las khyad par du 'phags pa ngo mtshar rmad du byung bar grags pa bstan pa rmad du byung ba'i chos kyi sde dang*/ chos thams cad kyi rang dang spyi'i mtshan nyid phyin ci ma log par bstan pas mdo sde'i don 'chad cing gsal bar byed pa dang gtan la 'bebs par byed pa ma lta bu'i chos mngon pa thams cad ni gtan la dbab par bstan pa'i sde zhes bya'o/

(5) The category of sayings (udāna) consists of hortative works made for the continued existence of the holy Dharma and the teachings, without expressing the names of persons or castes. (6) The category of ethical precedents (nidāna)[1349] consists of works of pratimokṣa that explain the reason why a rule was declared, [425] the names and castes of those involved, and the assemblies that occurred. (7) The category of stories (avadāna) consists of works with narratives clarifying the meaning of Dharma through illustration.
(8) The category of former events (itivṛttaka) consists of works expressing the circumstances of former teachings. (9) The category of former births (jātaka) consists of works in which the Buddha taught the various circumstances under which he engaged in bodhisattva practices and austerities in past lives. (10) The category of extensive discourses (vaipulya) consists of works teaching how highest perfect complete enlightenment, the ten powers, stainless transcendent wisdom, and the paths of bodhisattvas are established. (11) The category of marvelous events (adbhutadharma) consists of works teaching amazing, famous, and extraordinary stories of the shared and unshared qualities of buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas. (12) The category of instruction (upadeśa) consists of all the works of Abhidharma that clearly explain and settle the meaning of the sūtras through correctly teaching the real and abstract nature of all phenomena.

Śrāvaka Levels mentions: The ten, such as the category of discourses and so on are the Sūtra Piṭaka, the category of ethical precedents is the Vinaya Piṭaka, and the category of instruction is the Abhidharma Piṭaka.[1350] The Compendium of Abhidharma states: The first five [(1) discourses, (2) chants, (3) predictions, (4) stanzas, and (5) sayings] are the śrāvaka Sūtra Piṭaka. The four (6–9) from the category of narratives to the category of former births are the Vinaya Piṭaka. (10–11) Both the categories of extensive discourses and marvelous events are the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka. (12) Instruction is the Abhidharma Piṭaka of both the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.[1351] If you well investigate them, it does not appear that they are absolutely fixed in just these categories because the category of discourses, chants, stanzas, and so on also appear in the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka, stories and so on appear in the other two, and it is logical that the śrāvaka category of marvelous events is the śrāvaka category of discourses.[1352]

THE NEED FOR TEACHING THEM IN THREE PIṬAKAS
rgyu dgus gzhag ste/ de la gsum mtshan gsum las

There are nine reasons, posited in three sets of three: 1. They are taught to abandon the three afflictions to be abandoned. 2. They are taught to present and establish {the subject matter of} the three trainings. 3. They are taught {to show the functions of} Dharma and meaning.
dang po spang bya nyon mongs pa gsum spang ba'i ched du bstan pa ni
THEY ARE TAUGHT TO ABANDON THE THREE AFFLICTIONS TO BE ABANDONED

las 'bras la sogs pa la the tshom za ba'i gnyen por ni mdo sde'i sde snod bstan te/ gang zhig gang la the tshom za ba de de la nges par bya ba'i ched du gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / spyod pa mtha' gnyis la sbyor ba'i gnyen por ni 'dul ba'i sde snod bstan te/ 'dod yon la chags pas gsog 'jog byed pa la sogs pa kha na ma tho ba dang bcas pa rab tu byung ba la yongs su dpyad pa dgag pa'i sgo nas 'dod pa bsod nams kyi mtha' spong la/ brgya stong ri ba'i gos dang khang bzang dang kha zas ro brgya pa la sogs pa kha na ma tho ba med pa'i yongs su spyad pa rjes su gnang ba'i sgo nas don med pa'i dka' thub bdag nyid dub pa la sbyor ba'i mtha' spong ba'i phyir ro/ / rang gi lta ba mchog tu 'dzin pa'i gnyen por ni mngon pa'i sde snod bstan te/ chos rnams kyi rang dang spyi'i mtshan nyid phyin ci ma log par bstan pas lta ba ngan pa rnams spong ba'i phyir ro/ / yang na bstan pa la ma zhugs pa 'jug pa'i gegs the tshom dang*/ zhugs pa'i spyod pa dang lta ba phyin ci log spong ba la gsum po rim pa bzhin no/ /

(1) The Sūtra Piṭaka is taught as the antidote to doubt about cause, result, and so on because it is stated for the purpose of ascertaining [426] that which one doubts. (2) The Vinaya Piṭaka is taught as the antidote to engaging in the two extremes of conduct because it abandons the extreme of overindulgence in sensory objects through ceasing to analyze [the actions of] ordained beings who commit offensive acts and accumulate karma through attachment to sense objects and so on. Also it abandons the extreme of engaging in wearisome meaningless austerities through assenting to practice nonoffensive acts such as utilizing expensive cloth, fine houses, and foods with hundreds of flavors. (3) The Abhidharma Piṭaka is taught as the antidote to clinging to one’s [false] views as supreme because false views are abandoned through teachings that correctly posit the real and abstract nature of all phenomena. Again, they are respectively the three that abandon: (1) doubt impeding entry to the teachings and the path, (2) conduct engaging [extremes], and (3) incorrect view.
gnyis pa{ brjod bya} bslab pa gsum ston cing sgrub pa'i dbang du byas te bstan pa ni
THEY ARE TAUGHT TO PRESENT AND ESTABLISH THE THREE TRAININGS

mdo sdes ni bslab pa gsum gyi ngo bo rgyas par ston la/ 'dul bas ni bslab pa dang po gnyis sgrub pa yin te/ lhag pa'i tshul khrims ma thob pa thob par byed pa dang*/ thob pa mi nyams par bsrung ba dang*/ nyams na phyir bcos pa'i sgo nas tshul khrims kyi bslab pa sgrub la/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa ni 'gyod pa med cing*/ 'gyod pa med pas ni sems las su rung la/ de la brten nas dmigs pa la mnyam par bzhag pa'i rim gyis ting nge 'dzin 'thob pas lhag pa'i sems kyi bslab pa sgrub pa'i phyir ro/ / chos mngon pas ni lhag pa'i shes rab kyi bslab pa sgrub pa yin te/ des mi rtog pa'i ye shes skye ba'i thabs bstan pa la brten nas thos bsam byas te bsgoms pas 'jig rten dang de las 'das pa'i sgom byung gis shes bya'i don phyin ci ma log par rab tu 'byed pa'i phyir ro/ /

(1) Sūtra extensively teaches the nature of all three trainings. (2) Vinaya establishes the first two trainings. The training of ethics is established by means of those who have not yet obtained higher ethics obtaining it, guarding that obtained from degenerating, and restoring it when it degenerates. Those possessing ethics have no regrets, and since they have no regrets, their minds are serviceable. Thus they establish the higher training of mind [or concentration] since, in dependence on ethics, they gradually obtain concentration engaged in meditative equipoise on its focal object. (3) The higher training in wisdom is established through Abhidharma because by hearing, contemplating, and meditating on the teachings on how nonconceptual transcendent wisdom arises, wisdom derived from meditation that transcends the world correctly and fully differentiates the meaning of all objects of knowledge.
gsum pa{ byed las} chos dang don gyi dbang du byas te bstan pa ni
THEY ARE TAUGHT {TO SHOW THE FUNCTIONS OF} DHARMA AND MEANING

mdo sdes ni rjod byed sgra'i chos dang brjod bya don gyi chos la byang bar byed pas na de gnyis bshad la/ 'dul bas ni chos dang don 'grub ste/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa la brten nas nyon mongs pa 'dul ba la rab tu brtson pas mnyam par bzhag na chos dang don mngon sum du rtogs par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / chos mngon pas ni chos dang don 'bel ba'i gtam rnam par gtan la dbab pa la mkhas par byed de/ des shes bya'i chos kyi rang spyi'i mtshan nyid phyin ci ma log par shes pas tshig don gtan la 'bebs pa la mi 'jigs pa thob pas bde ba la reg par gnas pa 'thob pa'i phyir ro/ / des na 'dir chos dang don ni sgra dang don nyid yin par shes par bya'o/ /

(1) Both the “attributes of words that express” and the “attributes of the meaning expressed” are explained, since they clarify the category of Sūtra. (2) Through Vinaya one establishes Dharma and meaning, because by striving to tame afflictions in dependence on possessing ethics, one comes to directly realize the Dharma and its meaning in equipoise. (3) Through Abhidharma, one becomes learned in interpreting discourses in terms of their doctrine and meaning. That is, one attains a blissful state through gaining fearlessness in settling the meaning of the words and correctly understanding phenomena in terms of their real and abstract nature. Therefore, here Dharma and meaning should be understood as “words” and their “meaning.”

SUBSUMING THOSE IN TWO PIṬAKAS

byang sa las/ gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis las shin tu rgyas pa'i sde ni byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod do/ / lhag ma ni nyan thos kyi sde snod yin par rig par bya'o zhes 'byung bas bcu gnyis dang gsum pa de dag nyid theg pa dman pa dang mchog gi bye brag gis nyan thos kyi sde snod dang*/ byang chub sems dpa'i sde snod gnyis su 'gyur ro/ / de ltar na rang rgyal gyi sde snod dang gsum du 'gyur ro zhe na/ mi 'gyur te/ de ni nyan thos kyi sde snod las logs su med pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir chos mngon pa kun las btus pa las kyang rang sangs rgyas kyi theg pa'i skabs su nyan thos kyi sde snod nyid la dmigs nas chos kyi rjes su mthun pa'i chos sgrub pa dang zhes nyan thos kyi sde snod kho na la dmigs par bshad do/ /

Bodhisattva Levels declares: Extensive discourses (vaipulya) are the Mahāyāna Piṭaka. The remainder should be known as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.[1353] [427] Since the twelve or the three are subsets of the individual and supreme vehicles [respectively], there are two piṭakas: the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Objection: There would be three with the Pratyekabuddha Piṭaka. Reply: There would not, because that is not separate from the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. The Compendium of Abhidharma also explains that a practitioner of the pratyekabuddha path focuses on the Śrāvaka Piṭaka alone: He accomplishes Dharma appropriate to him through focusing on the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.[1354]

ETYMOLOGY

ci'i phyir sde snod ces bya zhe na/ shes bya'i don thams cad bsdus pa'i phyir sde snod ces bya ste/ de skad du yang mdo sde'i rgyan las/ sde snod dag ni gsum mam gnyis kyang rung*/ / bsdus pa'i phyir te rgyu ni dgus 'dod do zhes bshad do/ /

Question: Why are they called piṭakas? Reply: Because they contain the meaning of all objects of knowledge, they are called piṭakas. The Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras declares: Because they are subsumed in two or three piṭakas, they are asserted to arise through nine causes.[1355]

EQUIVALENT TERMS

gsung rab dang*/ sde snod dang*/ bka' dang*/ lung dang*/ gtsug lag dang*/ bstan bcos zhes kyang bya ste/ lung phran tshegs las/ 'phags pa 'od bsrungs chen pos/ kye ma stobs bcu mnga' ba'i gsung ni tshad med pa/ / 'gro la phan phyir chos kyi bstan bcos 'di bsdus pas/ / gang na 'jig rten blo ngan mun byed chud zos pa'i/ / blo gros rab rib bsal nas sgron mar yang dag ldan zhes pa dang*/ 'dul ba la bstod pa las kyang*/ rgyal ba ston pa de'i bstan bcos dag /mdo dang chos mngon yin gsung 'dul ba ni/ / ston dang bstan pa dngos yin de yi phyir/ / gnyis gyur phyag bya sangs rgyas chos gcig bzhin zhes pa dang*/ {byang sa las kyang*/ sangs rgyas kyi gsung rab ni nang gi bstan bcos zhes bya ste zhes pa dang } rnam bshad rigs pa las kyang*/ don dam par na sangs rgyas kyi gsung kho na bstan bcos yin no zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / 'dis ni brjod bya mtshungs pa'i phyir de'i don 'grel byed kyi bstan bcos ston pa'ang chos kyi sbyin par bstan pa yin no/ / de lta bu'i chos kyi sbyin pa de yang kun slong gi bsam pa rnyed pa la sogs pa la chags pas ston pa ni bdag nyid bsod nams chen po las nyams par byed pa yin la/ sbyor ba nor bar ston pa'ang chos kyi sbyin pa ma yin te/ 'grel pa las/ de'i phyir gang dag chos log par 'chad par byed pa'am/ sems nyon mongs pa can rnyed pa dang bkur bsti dang grags pa 'dod pas 'chad pa de dag ni bdag nyid kyi bsod nams chen po nyams par byed pa yin no zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / de las bzlog ste bsam pa bzang pos chos phyin ci ma log par bstan na ni bsod nams 'phel ba'i rgyur 'gyur te/ bslab pa kun las btus pa las/ chos kyi sbyin pa zang zing med/ / bsod nams 'phel ba'i rgyu yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ /

They are called scripture, canonical works, speech, transmissions, literature, or treatises. The Kṣudraka Collection notes: The great ārya Kaśyapa said: “Listen: speech that possesses the ten powers is immeasurable because it benefits reincarnating beings, and through treatises on Dharma one comes to correctly hold the lamp of Dharma that eliminates minds confused and degraded by the darkness of evil mundane states.”[1356] Praise of Vinaya observes: Sūtra and Abhidharma are said to be the treatises of the Conquering Master. Vinaya is revelation and the actual teachings. Therefore both the Buddha and Dharma are revered as one and the same.[1357] {Bodhisattva Levels notes: The scriptures are Buddhist treatises.[1358]} Rational System of Exposition declares: Ultimately, only the Buddha’s speech constitutes a treatise.[1359] Teaching treatises that comment on Dharma’s meaning also is taught to be the giving of Dharma because the subject matter is the same. If one gives Dharma motivated by attachment to property, one’s great merit degenerates. And teaching with inadequate preparation is not the proper giving of Dharma, because the Autocommentary states: Therefore explaining Dharma wrongly or giving explanations with an afflicted mind desiring property, respect, or fame will cause the degeneration of one’s great merit.[1360] Conversely, if one teaches Dharma correctly with pure thought, one’s merit increases. As the Compendium of Training explains: Giving Dharma is not a worldly act. It causes merit to increase.[1361] [428]
bcu bzhi pa cha mthun gyi dge ba gsum bshad pa ni
The three conducive factors
bsod nams mya ngan 'das pa dang / / nges 'byed cha mthun dge rnam gsum/ / 125
Those which are conducive to merit, nirvāṇa, and penetrative insight are the three virtues. (4:125cd)
mdo las/ bsod nams kyi cha dang mthun pa dang*/ thar pa'i cha dang mthun pa dang*/ nges par 'byed pa'i cha dang mthun pa'i dge ba gsum gsungs pa la/
A sūtra mentions three virtues: virtue that is conducive to merit, virtue that is conducive to liberation, and virtue that is conducive to penetrative insight.[1362]

'khor bar rnam smin yid du 'ong ba can ni bsod nams cha mthun no/ / tshogs lam du mya ngan las 'das par bsdos pa'i dge ba ni mya ngan las 'das pa thar ba'i cha dang mthun pa ste gang skyes na yongs su mya ngan las 'da' ba'i chos su 'gyur ba'o/ / dge ba de yod par ni 'khor 'das kyi nyes dmigs dang yon tan brjod pa na dad pa'i shugs kyis ba spu ldang ba la sogs pa'i rtags las shes so/ / nges par 'byed pa'i cha dang mthun pa'i dge ba ni dro ba la sogs pa bzhi yin te/ de ltar na cha mthun gyi dge ba rnam pa gsum mo/ /

(1) Virtue possessing pleasant karmic maturation in saṃsāra is conducive to merit (puṇyabhāgīya). (2) Virtue directed to nirvāṇa on the path of accumulation is conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) or nirvāṇa (nirvāṇabhāgīya), for whatever arises becomes the state of nirvāṇa. One will come to know if one has this virtue when the disadvantages of saṃsāra and qualities of nirvāṇa are expressed, for goosebumps and so on will arise by the power of faith. (3) Virtue that is conducive to penetrative insight (nirvedhabhāgīya) is the four stages of heat and so on. These are the three aspects of virtue that are conducive factors.
rigs pas rab tu bcug pa'i las bshad pa/
The three karmas engaged by cognition
rigs pas rab tu bcug pa'i las/ / rnam gsum kun slong bcas pa ni/ / yig 'bru brgya dang bgrang bcas pa'i/ / snyan ngag grangs ti go rims bzhin/ / 126
Karma that is properly performed is the three types and their concomitant motivations. They are, respectively, syllables, sculpting images, poetry that recounts, and calculation. (4:126)
bco lnga pa{ 'jig rten pa'i las gsum gyi rnam grangs bstan pa ni}
{PRESENTING THE CLASSES OF THE THREE MUNDANE KARMAS}

Karma that is properly performed (rigs pas rab bcug) refers to the three types of physical, verbal, and mental karma that are performed with appropriate methods of training. These along with their concomitant motivations constitute the essential nature of the five aggregates. Writing syllables such as ka and sculpting images of deities are physical karma. Poetry that recounts specific events and so on is verbal karma. Calculation such as “ten times ten is one hundred” {along with its motivation} is mental karma {related to four aggregates}.[1363] They should be understood in this order.
bsgribs ngan kha na ma tho bcas/ / nyan mongs can chos dri med dge/ / gya nom 'dus byas dge bsten bya/ / thar pa bla na med pa yin/ / 127
Afflicted phenomena are obscured, evil, and offensive acts. Unstained virtue is sublime purity. Cultivate conditioned virtuous Dharma. Liberation is highest. (4:127)

gzhan yang yig 'bru la sogs pa bstan pa'i zhar la byung ba'am/ yang na 'di chos mngon pa bsdus pa yin pas chos kyi phung po'i rnam par bshad pa las 'byung ba'i rnam grangs 'ga' zhig brjod par bya ste/
Again, some say these synonyms are derived from the explanation of the aggregate of Dharma, since syllables and so on are supplementary to the teachings or they are subsumed within Abhidharma.

nyon mongs pas{ kun slong dang bcas pas} bkab pas na bsgribs pa dang*/ nyon mongs dang bcas pas gnag cing 'phags pa rnams kyis bor bas na ngan pa dang*/ nyon mongs pa dang lhan cig 'dug pas na kha na ma tho ba dang bcas pa zhes bya ba ni nyon mongs pa can gyi chos zag bcas kyi ming gi rnam grangs so/ /

Afflicted phenomena synonymous with contaminated states are obscured (nivṛtā), since they are covered by affliction {along with its motivation}; evil (hīna), since they are black through motivation and discarded by āryas; and offensive (savadhya), since they exist simultaneously with affliction.

dri ma med pa'i dge ba ni dag pa rab kyi mthar phyin pas na gya nom pa zhes bya ste/ des na gya nom pa zhes bya ba ni dge ba zag med kyi rnam grangs so/ / nyon mongs pa ni ngan pa kho na yin la/ dge ba zag med ni gya nom pa kho na yin pas na ngan pa dang gya nom pa las gzhan pa {dge ba zag bcas dang ma bsgribs lung ma bstan } ni bar ma zhes bya'o/ / rgyud la skyed pa'i sgo nas gus par bsten par bya ba zhes bya ba ni 'dus byas kyi chos dge ba zag bcas zag med thams cad kyi rnam grangs so/ / de las gzhan pa 'dus ma byas dang mi dge ba dang bsgribs la lung ma bstan rnams ni bsten par bya ba ma yin no/ / ci'i phyir 'dus ma byas bsten bya ma yin zhe na/ 'dus ma byas ni bsten bya ma yin te/ bskyed pa dang*/ yang dang yang du rgyud la goms par byar mi rung ba'i phyir dang*/ 'bras bu'i don du bsten pa yin na de la 'bras bu'ang med pa'i phyir ro/ / mi dge ba dang*/ bsgribs la lung ma bstan dang*/ 'dus byas ma bsgribs lung ma bstan dang*/ dge ba zag bcas dang*/ 'dus byas zag med dang*/ 'dus ma byas ma bsgribs lung ma bstan nam mkha' brtags min dang*/ thar pa so sor brtags 'gog rnams ni snga ma snga ma phyi ma phyi mas bla ma dang bcas pa yin te/ rim pa ltar rnam smin yid du mi 'ong ba med pa'i phyir dang*/ nyon mongs can ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rnam smin gyi 'bras bu yid du 'ong ba can yin pa'i phyir dang*/ zag bcas ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rtag pa'i phyir dang*/ rtag cing dge ba'i phyir ro/ /

Unstained (amala) virtue is called sublime (praṇīta) since it fully accomplishes purity (śubhā). Therefore sublime is a synonym of the uncontaminated state. Since afflicted states are solely evil and uncontaminated virtue is solely sublime, that which is other than evil or sublime is called an “intermediate state” — {that is, contaminated virtue or [429] an unobscured-neutral state.} “States to be respectfully cultivated within one’s mindstream” is a synonym for all uncontaminated and contaminated conditioned virtuous Dharma. Unconditioned, nonvirtuous, and obscured-neutral states other than those are not to be cultivated. Question: Why are unconditioned states not to be cultivated? Reply: Unconditioned states are not to be cultivated because they cannot be generated or frequently cultivated in one’s mindstream, and if one relies on them for a result then they have no result. (1) Nonvirtue, (2) obscured-neutral states, (3) conditioned unobscured-neutral states, (4) contaminated virtue, (5) conditioned uncontaminated states, (6) unconditioned unobscured-neutral space, (7) nonanalytical cessation, and (8) liberation that is analytical cessation are each progressively superior to the preceding state because, respectively, (1) it has no pleasant karmic maturation, (2) it is afflicted, (3–4) they possess a pleasant maturational result, (5) it is not contaminated, (6–7) they are permanent, and (8) it is permanent and virtuous.

des na chos gzhan thams cad ni bla ma dang bcas pa yin la/ thar pa myang 'das so sor brtags 'gog ni de las phul du phyin pa dang khyad par du 'phags pa gzhan med pas bla na med pa yin te/ mdo las/ dge slong dag chos 'dus byas sam/ 'dus ma byas gang ji snyed pa de dag gi nang na mchog ni 'dod chags dang bral ba yin par brjod do zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / thar pa'i rnam grangs kun las btus las ni/ ma lus par spangs pa dang*/ nges par spangs pa dang*/ byang bar gyur pa dang*/ zad pa dang*/ 'dod chags dang bral ba dang*/ 'gog pa dang*/ rnam par zhi ba dang*/ nub pa la sogs pa dang*/ sa'i dngos gzhi las ni rtag pa dang*/ brtan pa dang*/ ther zug pa dang*/ mi 'gyur ba'i chos can dang*/ gnas dang*/ gling dang*/ skyob pa dang*/ skyabs dang*/ dpung gnyen dang*/ bde ba dang*/ zhi ba dang*/ legs pa'i gzhi dang*/ bde legs su 'gyur ba dang*/ mi g.yo ba dang*/ mi gzhal ba dang*/ bltar dka' ba dang*/ 'chi ba med pa dang*/ mya ngan med pa dang*/ 'chi 'pho med pa dang*/ rims nad med pa dang*/ yongs su gdung ba med pa dang*/ nad med pa dang*/ g.yo ba med pa dang*/ mya ngan las 'das pa dang*/ spros pa med pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa bshad do/ /

Therefore all other phenomena are inferior, but the liberation (mokṣa) of nirvāṇa that is analytical cessation is highest (anuttara), since with respect to the others it is complete and unexcelled. That is because a sūtra observes: Monks, supreme among all those phenomena that exist, both the conditioned and the unconditioned, is freedom from attachment.[1364] The Compendium of Abhidharma gives these synonyms of liberation: . . . abandonment without exception, definite abandonment, purified, exhausted, free of attachment, cessation, complete pacification, subsided, and so on.[1365] Yogācāra Levels notes: Permanent, stable, constant, unchanging subject, abode, continent, protection, refuge, defender, bliss, peace, excellent basis, attained excellent bliss, invariable, inestimable, difficult to view, deathless, free of sorrow, free of death, free of disease, free of violence, free of illness, free of variance, nirvāṇa, free of proliferation.[1366]

Those who desire perfect realization should study well this section that includes the karma of intention and the karma derived from intention that establish the world, indicative and nonindicative form, vows, negative commitments, interim precepts, and the classifications of karmic causation.

22. The Nature of Negative Tendencies
da ni gnas lnga pa phra rgyas bstan pa 'chad pa la phra rgyas kyi rang bzhin dang*/ de ji ltar spong ba'i tshul dang*/ spangs pa'i 'bras bu yongs shes bshad pa gsum las/
IN EXPLAINING THE PRESENTATION of part V, there are three headings: the nature of negative tendencies, how they are abandoned, and the thorough understanding of the result of abandonment.
dang po [phra rgyas kyi dbye ba]
THE NATURE OF NEGATIVE TENDENCIES
['di] la'ang phra rgyas kyi dbye ba dang*/ rnam pa'i rab dbye bshad pa gnyis kyi
This has two headings: the classification of negative tendencies and the classification of aspects.
dang po ni
THE CLASSIFICATION OF NEGATIVE TENDENCIES

srid pa'i rtsa ba phra rgyas drug / 'dod chags de bzhin khong khro dang / nga rgyal ma rig lta ba dang / / the tshom yin te de drug kyang / / 1 'dod chags dbye bas bdun du bshad/ / khams gnyis las skyes srid 'dod chags/ / kha ni nang du bltas phyir der/ / thar pa'i 'du shes bzlog phyir bshad/ / 2

The root of existence is the negative tendencies. There are six: attachment as well as anger, pride, ignorance, view, and doubt. Those six are also (5:1)
explained to be seven through dividing attachment. Those arising in both realms are attachment to existence because they are similar in viewing internal states. These are explained to stop discriminating them as liberation. (5:2)

gnas bzhi par las las 'jig rten sna tshogs skyes zhes gang bshad pa'i las de dag kyang phra rgyas kyi dbang gis bsags{ shing rnam smin 'phen nus} par 'gyur gyi phra rgyas med par ni zag bcas kyi las mi gsog cing las med par yang srid mi 'grub ste/ {gzhan du na ma nges pa'i las yod pas dgra bcom la'ang yang srid yod par thal bas des na }

Karma, which is explained in part IV in the statement “Various mundane states arise from karma” (4:1a) is accumulated {and capable of projecting karmic maturation} through the power of negative tendencies (anuśaya). Thus, without negative tendencies, contaminated karma is not accumulated, and also, without karma, rebirth is not established. {Otherwise, it would follow that rebirth would even exist for arhats, since they have indeterminate karma. Therefore}

srid pa'i rtsa ba ni phra rgyas yin par rig par bya'o/ / de la slob dpon gang spel ni/ skye ba'i shing rta skye bo byis pa yis/ / zhon zhing nyon mongs las kyi 'phang lo can/ / 'di ni nyon mongs 'phang lo gcig nyams na/ / las kyi 'phang lo gcig pu 'khor ma yin zhes las kyis yang srid 'phen par byed pa dang mngon par 'grub par byed pa'i rtsa ba phra rgyas yin no zhes srid pa ni yang srid nyid la 'dod cing de'i rtsa ba ni phra rgyas yin no zhes 'chad la/ slob dpon rgyal po'i sras ni srid pa ni 'dir yang srid phyi ma dang*/ de'i rgyu las kyi srid pa gnyis ka yin par 'dod la/ de'i rtsa ba ni phra rgyas yin te/ nyon mongs pa 'jug pa na bya ba bcu byed pa'i phyir ro zhes 'chad do/ /

the root (mūla) of existence (bhava) should be recognized as the negative tendencies. Master Pūrṇavardhana writes: The chariot of birth, driven by childlike beings, possesses the wheels of affliction and karma. But if the wheel of affliction breaks, the wheel of karma cannot turn.[1367] This states that karma projects rebirth, and the root that actually establishes karma is the negative tendencies. It explains that existence is the desire for rebirth and the root of existence is the negative tendencies. Master Jinaputra explains: Existence is asserted to be both one’s future rebirth and its cause, karmic existence. Its root is the negative tendencies because if one enters afflicted states, one activates the ten processes.[1368]
de la bya ba bcu ni/
The ten processes

{rgyun mi chad pas } rtsa ba brtan byed thob pa'i rgyun/ / {yang yang rgyun mi chad du bskyed pas } rgyud gnas byed pa phra rgyas rgyun/{/lus kyi lo thog skyed pas/}zhing ni rang rgyud phra rgyas gzhir/ / rgyu mthun sgrub pa nye nyon skyed/ / las kyi srid pa sgrub par byed/ / rang tshogs 'dzin pa tshul bzhin min/ / dmigs la kun rmongs mi shes nyid/ / rnam shes rgyun 'khrid srid par 'phen/ / dge las g.yo ba nyams pa yin/ / 'ching ba khams las mi 'da' ba/ / {yin nyon mongs gang zhig khams su gtogs pa des ni de las 'da' ba'i gegs byed pa'i phyir ro de ltar } rnam pa bcu ni gnas 'dir yang*/ / rab tu bstan pa yin par 'dod ces bya'o/ /
The six main negative tendencies

phra rgyas de yang dbye na re zhig rnam pa drug ste/ gang zhe na/ 'dod chags dang de bzhin du khong khro dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa dang lta ba dang the tshom yin te {nyer len gyi phung po la bdag tu chags pa'i 'dod chags kyis gzhan lnga yang dmigs pa la rgyas par 'gyur te bdag lta dang sred pas bdag gir byas pa las rgyas pa'i phyir/ zag med dang skal ba mi mnyam pa'i khams la mi rgyas so/ / grangs nges ni/ stod 'grel las bza' bya yul tshor ba gsum gyi dug za ba po sems can la log par zhugs pa nga rgyal dang*/ phyin ci log spong ba la log zhugs lta ba dang*/ the tshom ste/ log par nges pa dang ma nges pa'o }

If those negative tendencies are classified, there are six types. Question: What are they? Reply: They are attachment (rāga) as well as anger (pratigha), [431] pride (māna), ignorance (avidya), view (dṛṣṭi), and doubt (vicikitsā). {Attachment, which is attached to a self as [or within] the appropriated aggregates, also increases the other five due to this focal object, because the view of the self and craving increases through grasping [the aggregates] as “mine,” but the other five do not increase in relation to uncontaminated states and aggregates of different realms. Regarding the certainty of number, Detailed Explanation of Yogācāra Levels declares: The pride that wrongly engages the being or agent who eats poison from the three: the act of eating, the object, and the feeling; view that wrongly engages distorted states to be abandoned; and doubt — these are either certain to wrongly engage or not certain to wrongly engage their object.}[1369]
de ltar rnam pa de drug kyang bdun du bshad ces 'brel lo/ /
Those six types are also explained to be seven.

ji ltar byas nas zhe na/ mdo las 'dod chags la 'dod pa'i 'dod chags kyi phra rgyas dang*/ srid pa'i 'dod chags kyi phra rgyas zhes gnyis su dbye ba byas nas so/ / {phra rgyas ni bye brag smra ba kun dkris dang gnas ma bu pa thob pa dang*/ mdo sde pa sa bon la 'dod pa yod pas } skabs 'dir dpyad pa 'di bya ste gal te gzhi mthun pa'i drug pa/ 'dod pa'i 'dod chags nyid phra rgyas yin pas 'dod chags kyi phra rgyas sam/ 'on te {gzhi tha dad pa'i drug pa }'dod pa'i 'dod chags las tha dad pa'i phra rgyas{ yin pas 'dod chags kyi phra rgyas} yin par 'dod/ phyogs dang po ltar na{ lung bar ma'i} mdo las 'di na la la 'dod pa'i 'dod chags kyi kun nas dkris pa'i sems kyis lan mang du mi gnas la/ 'dod pa'i 'dod chags kyi kun nas dkris pa byung na'ang phyis nges par 'byung ba yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin rab tu shes shing de'i 'dod pa'i 'dod chags kyi kun nas dkris pa de mthus yang dag par shin tu kun nas 'joms shing phra rgyas dang bcas par spong bar byed do zhes kun nas dkris pa dang phra rgyas tha dad par bshad pa dang 'gal lo/ /

Question: How? [Reply:] Through dividing attachment in two, for a sūtra states that there is: the negative tendency of attachment to desire-realm objects (kāmarāga) and the negative tendency of attachment to existence (bhavarāga). {Vaibhāṣikas assert that negative tendencies are entanglements (paryavasthāna). Vātsīputrīyas assert that negative tendencies are obtainments (prāpti). Sautrāntikas assert that negative tendencies are seeds (bīja).} This will now be analyzed here. Question: It may be asserted that (1) the sixth[1370] that is not distinct is the negative tendency of attachment since it is the negative tendency of attachment to desire-realm objects, or it may be asserted that {(2) the sixth that is distinct} is the negative tendency {of attachment since it is} a negative tendency distinct from attachment to desire-realm objects. (1) The first position contradicts a sūtra {from the Medium-Length Discourses} that explains that entanglements and negative tendencies are distinct: Here, for some the entangled mind of desire-realm attachment does not frequently manifest, and though the entanglement of desire-realm attachment arises, later they come to know renunciation properly as it is, and due to the might [of renunciation] they correctly and fully annihilate the entanglement of desire-realm attachment, and they abandon that which is associated with this negative tendency.[1371]

phyogs gnyis pa ltar na phra rgyas ni thob pa yin par 'gyur na de ni mi ldan pa'i 'du byed yin pa'i phyir chos mngon pa las/ 'dod pa'i 'dod chags kyi phra rgyas ni dbang po gsum dang mtshungs par ldan pa yin no/ /

(2) If, according to the second position, negative tendencies are obtainments, they would be nonassociated formative factors. But this contradicts Abhidharma, which declares: The negative tendency of desire-realm attachment is concomitant with three faculties.

gsum gang zhe na/ bde ba dang yid bde ba dang*/ btang snyoms kyi dbang po dag dang mtshungs par ldan no zhes gsungs pa dang 'gal lo/ / de mtshungs ldan du bshad pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ der bye brag tu smra ba rnams na re 'dod pa'i 'dod chags nyid phra rgyas yin pa'i phyir chos mngon pa las{ nyon mongs la} bshad pa ni mtshan nyid pa yin te/ mdo las phra rgyas dang bcas pa'i sgra ni 'dod chags la sogs pa dang rjes su 'brel ba'i nyon mongs pa gzhan nam/ yang na thob pa la btags nas gsungs pa'i phyir 'gal ba med do/ / zhes zer ro/ / de'i phyir/ sems ni nyon mongs byed phyir dang*/ / sgrib phyir dge dang 'gal phyir dang*/ / dge ba'ang dmigs pa'i phyir na 'dir/ / phra rgyas ldan pa ma yin min zhes 'grel par gsungs so/ /

What are the three? It is concomitant with the faculties of pleasure, mental satisfaction, and equanimity.[1372] That is because here negative tendencies are explained to be concomitant with feeling. Vaibhāṣikas say: Because desire-realm attachment itself is a negative tendency, the explanation in Abhidharma {that it is an affliction} is correct. This does not contradict the sūtra that mentions that the term “that which is associated with that negative tendency” refers to affliction related to attachment and so on, or otherwise that it is designated as obtainment.[1373] Therefore the Autocommentary asserts: Because they afflict the mind, because they obscure it, because they prevent virtue, and because they also focus on virtue, negative tendencies are not disassociated from the mind.[1374]

mdo sde pa rnams na re phra rgyas ni thob pa'ang ma yin kun nas dkris pa'ang ma yin gyi 'on kyang bag la nyal yin no/ / de'i phyir kun nas dkris pa ni phra rgyas mngon du gyur pa yin la bag la nyal ni phra rgyas sa bon yin no/ / de'i phyir mdo las gsungs pa ni mtshan nyid pa yin la bstan bcos ni kho bo cag mi 'don no zhes zer ro/ / gnas ma'i bu'i sde pa ni phra rgyas ldan pa ma yin pa thob pa la 'dod do/ / gal te 'dod chags ni zag bcas la sred pa yin la de la gnyis las 'dod pa'i 'dod chags ni 'dod pa'i khams kyi 'dod chags yin na srid pa'i 'dod chags gang zhe na khams gong ma gnyis las skyes pa'i 'dod chags ni srid pa'i 'dod chags yin te/ de dag 'dod pa la 'dod chags dang bral zhing yang srid par 'phen pa'i 'dod chags yin pa'i phyir ro/ / yang ci'i phyir khams gnyis po'i 'dod chags bsdoms nas srid pa'i 'dod chags su byas she na/

Sautrāntikas say: Negative tendencies are neither obtainments nor entanglements but dormant states. Therefore entanglements are manifest negative tendencies, and dormant afflictions are the seeds [432] of negative tendencies. Thus the statement in the sūtra is the actual explanation, but we [Sautrāntikas] do not accept that stated in the treatises.[1375] The Vātsīputrīya school asserts: Negative tendencies are obtainments that are not possessed. Question: If attachment is craving for contaminated objects, such attachment has two types. If desire-realm attachment is attachment to desire-realm objects, then what is attachment to existence? Reply: The attachments arising in both higher realms are attachment to existence (bhavarāga) because such attachment projects a rebirth free from attachment to desire-realm objects. Question: Why are the attachments to both [higher] realms together taken as attachment to existence?
REASON

rgyu mtshan ni de dag gzhal med khang sogs la chags pa yod kyang / phal cher snyoms 'jug la sred pas kha ni nang du bltas te 'jug pa dang*/ gcig tu bsgribs la lung ma bstan pa dang mnyam par bzhag par 'dra ba'i phyir dang*/ dang de lung ma bstan kha nang bltas/ / mnyam gzhag sa pa'i phyir gcig byas zhes 'byung bas gnyis ka'ang gcig tu bsgribs la lung ma bstan yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: The reason is that though attachment to celestial mansions and so on exists in both realms, [together they are taken as attachment to existence,] because they are similar (1) in engaging their objects by viewing internal states (antarmukhatva) through craving meditative attainment foremost, (2) in being obscured-neutral states, and (3) in being equipoise. Both are obscured-neutral states, since it is said, “They are taken as one because they are neutral, they view internal states, and they are levels of equipoise” (5:36ab).
dgos pa ni
NEED

de ltar na mnyam gzhag yin pas khams gnyis po der te de dag la {bsam gtan bzhi thob pa la 'bras bu bzhi thob bo snyam nas de dag } thar pa yin no snyam pa 'byung ba la/ thar pa 'dod pa ni dge ba'i chos la 'dun pa yin na khams gong ma gnyis dang de dag gi rgyu snyoms 'jug gnyis la thar par sred pa ni srid pa'i 'dod chags yin gyi thar pa ni ma yin no zhes yang dag pa'i thar pa yin no snyam pa'i 'du shes bzlog pa'i phyir de gnyis srid pa'i 'dod chags su bshad do zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'dod do/ / slob dpon ni sems can de dag 'dod pa la 'dod chags dang bral ba'i phyir dang*/ snyoms 'jug rten lus dang bcas pa kho na la sred pa'i phyir dang*/ lus ni srid pa yin pa'i phyir dang*/ 'dod yon la dmigs pa ma yin pa'i phyir srid pa'i 'dod chags zhes gcig tu bsdoms so zhes shes par bya'o zhes bzhed do/ /

They are explained as attachment to existence to stop discriminating those two realms as perfect liberation (mokṣa). The thought may arise that they are liberation {through reflecting that one obtains the four results when one obtains the four absorptions.} But craving the two higher realms and both their causal meditative attainments as liberation is attachment to existence and not to liberation, since the desire for liberation is the aspiration for virtuous Dharma. This is asserted by Vaibhāṣikas. Vasubandhu explains that together they are called “attachment to existence” because sentient beings of these realms are free of attachment to desire-realm objects; because they crave meditative attainment and its supportive body alone, that body which is existence; and because they do not focus on desire-realm objects.[1376]
lta ba lnga ste 'jig tshogs dang / / log dang mthar 'dzin lta ba dang / / lta ba dang ni tshul khrims dang / / brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin dang bcu/ / 3
There are ten through dividing view into five: afflicted view, wrong view, extreme view, clinging to views as supreme, and clinging to rules and ritual as supreme. (5:3)
yang phra rgyas drug po de dag chos mngon pa las bcur yang bshad do zhes sbrel lo/ / ji ltar zhe na
Moreover, it should be added that these six negative tendencies are explained in Abhidharma as ten. Question: How?

lta ba la 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang*/ skur pa 'debs pa/ log par lta ba dang*/ {khyad par du sgro 'dogs pa} mthar 'dzin par lta ba dang*/ lta ba mchog tu 'dzin pa dang*/ tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa dang lngar phye ste bsnan pa'i phyir ro/ / 'jig tshogs la lta ba'i rjes la mthar 'dzin pa'i lta ba yin yang 'dir tshigs bcad bsdebs pa'i ngor de'i rjes la log lta bshad do/ / gal te lta ba la dbye ba byed na rgyu mtshan mtshungs pas nga rgyal la'ang byed par 'gyur ro zhe na/ mi mtshungs te/ lta ba la rnam pa dang byed las tha dad yod la nga rgyal la khengs pa'i rnam pa gcig las med cing byed las kyang gcig las med pa'i phyir ro/

Reply: They are expanded through dividing view into five: (1) the afflicted view of the self[1377] (satkāyadṛṣṭi), (2) wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) that underestimates, (3) extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) that specifically overestimates, (4) clinging to those views as supreme (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and (5) clinging to rules and ritual as supreme (śīlavrataparāmarśa). Though extreme view [normally] follows afflicted view of the self, in this formulation of the verse wrong view is explained after [afflicted view of the self].[1378] Objection: If view is subdivided, pride should also be subdivided for similar reasons. Reply: They are not similar because different views have distinct aspects [or apprehended objects] and functions, but different types of pride do not have distinct aspects or functions. [433]

{kha cig lta ba nyes pa che bas spang dgos la de la shes pas khyab pas du mar phye zhes pa ni ma rig pa la'ang ha cang thal bas mi 'thad do/ / kha cig nga rgyal la bdun yod kyang spyi mtshan dang sems khengs pa'i byed pa gcig las med pas gcig tu bzhag ces pa'ang lta ba la'ang sems phyin ci log tu byed pa'i byed pa gcig las med pas zhes mtshungs so/ / rog na re dngos po la lta ba la sngar byung bas dang*/ nga rgyal la dngos po la gcig las ma byung bas lnga dang gcig tu bzhag la/ da ltar 'ong ba'i rgyu yang bzhin gyi kha mig gi grangs ltar dngos po'i che ba yin no/ / zhes zer ba ni rgyu mtshan ma rnyed par zad do/ / des na zla cog na re 'di dag dmigs rnam gyis tha dad du 'jog pa na lta ba la 'dzin stangs kyi rnam pa tha dad lnga yod pas dang*/ nga rgyal la bdun yod kyang 'dzin stangs kyi rnam pa gcig las med pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ / kha cig na re 'dzin stangs la ni gnyis ka la'ang tha dad yod do/ / de na 'dir dbye ba srid tshad la dbye ba byed pa ni ma yin te/ 'dod chags dang ma rig pa la sogs pa la'ang yod pa'i phyir ro/ / 'on kyang dgos pa'i dbang gis te mu stegs byed lta ba de dag la yang dag par rtog ste/ de ni ma yin gyi mthong spang yin no zhes bstan pa'i phyir mdo las de ltar du gsungs pa yin no zhes gsungs so/ }

{Some say: View must be abandoned since it has greater fault. Therefore it is differentiated into many types so that it may be pervasively understood. Reply: That is unacceptable since it would follow that this would also apply to ignorance. Some say: Though pride has seven types it is posited as a single type since it has just the single generic characteristic and function of inflating the mind. View is similar in that it has just the single function of distorting the mind. Rok[1379] says: Five views and one pride may arise with respect to one object, therefore they are posited as five or one, like objects that arise in the present where mouths and eyes outnumber them. Reply: This assertion can be discounted since no source can be found. Therefore Dachok[1380] says: If they are separately posited by focal object and aspect, then view has five different aspects according to its mode of apprehension, and pride has just one aspect according to its mode of apprehension though it has seven types. Some say: The apprehended object is distinct for both. Therefore here classification is not made regarding the modes of possible classifications because that exists also for attachment, ignorance, and so on. Instead, it is made due to need, since tīrthikas conceive such views to be correct view. But that is not so, for as stated in the sūtras, these are taught to be objects abandoned by the path of seeing.}

'o na lta ba la'ang nges par rtog pa'i rnam pa gcig las med pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ de ni rnam pa ma yin te/ lta ba la bdag dang bdag gi rtag tshad dang zhes pa la sogs pa rnam pa'i dbye ba yod la/ nga rgyal la ni rnam pa'i dbye ba med de/ thams cad khengs pa'i rnam pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / 'o na nga rgyal bdun du mi 'byed par 'gyur ro zhe na/ de dag ni yul la ltos pa'i yin gyi rnam pa'i dbye ba ni ma yin no/ / yang chos mngon pa'i bstan bcos las/ phra rgyas bcu po de dag dgu bcu rtsa brgyad du'ang 'chad de/ ji ltar zhe na/

Objection: There is just one aspect of view or decisive conception. Reply: That is not so, because view is classified as the views of “I,” “mine,” permanence, annihilation, and so on. Pride has no such classification because it is inflated toward all objects. This is explained in Purṇavardhana’s Commentary.[1381] Objection: Why then classify pride as sevenfold? Reply: The seven are classified in reliance on the focal object but not the aspect. Again the treatise (Attainment of Knowledge)[1382] explains that these ten negative tendencies have ninety-eight types.[1383] Question: How?
de dag bcu dang bdun bdun brgyad/ / lta ba gsum gnyis ma gtogs pa/ / 'dod na sdug bsngal la sogs pa/ / mthong bas rim bzhin spong bar byed/ / 4
Ten, seven, seven, and eight, because three or two views are excluded. They are serially abandoned by seeing suffering in the desire realm and so on. (5:4)

phra rgyas bcu po de dag 'dod pa'i khams na lta ba dang po gnyis kyang 'bras bsdus kyi nyer len gyi phung po la log par 'jug pas sdug bsngal mthong spang bcu po thams cad dang*/ kun 'byung mthong spang bdun dang*/ 'gog pa mthong spang bdun dang*/ / {'jig mthar gnyis nyer len gyi phung po lnga la dmigs pa ni sdug bsngal mthong spang kho na yin la/ phung po de dag la dag grel nges 'byin du lta ba'i tshul khrims mchog 'dzin yang bden pa dang po tha ma la dmigs pa yod kyi 'di gnyis la med pas so } lam mthong spang ni brgyad yin te/ dngos dang brgyud nas log par mi 'jug pas kun 'byung dang 'gog pa la lta ba dang po gnyis dang lnga pa gsum ma gtogs pa'i phyir dang*/ lam la lta ba dang po gnyis ma gtogs pa'i phyir ro/ / des na phra rgyas bcu dang bdun dang bdun dang brgyad po de rnams bden pa bzhi so so la dngos dang brgyud nas log par 'jug pas{ so gnyis po dag ni} 'dod pa'i sdug bsngal la sogs pa'i bden pa bzhi so so'i rang mtshan mthong bas spang bya de rnams rim pa bzhin du spong bar byed do/{ de ltar na 'jig mthar ni spang bya rigs gcig gi sgo can dang*/ log lta lta ba mchog 'dzin the tshom ni bden pa bzhi la dmigs pas bzhi'i dang*/ tshul khrims mchog 'dzin bden pa dang po dang tha ma la dmigs pas gnyis kyi sgo can te de dag ni mthong spang yin no/ / 'dod chags khong khro nga rgyal ma rig pa bzhi ni mthong spang sgom spang gnyis su 'gyur bas ris lnga lngar 'gyur ro/ /} des na 'dod pa na phra rgyas mthong spang{ de dag ni bden pa mthong ba tsam gyis spong pas mthong spang yin no} ni sum cu rtsa gnyis so/ /

Reply: Regarding the ten negative tendencies of the desire realm, all ten are abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering, since the first two views also wrongly engage the appropriated aggregates that constitute the result. Seven are abandoned by seeing the truth of origin, and seven are abandoned by seeing the truth of cessation, {since afflicted view of the self and extreme view, which focus on the five appropriated aggregates, are abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering alone, and clinging to rules and ritual as supreme, which views those aggregates as the pure state of definite release, focuses on the first and last truths but not on these two [intermediate] truths}. Eight are abandoned by seeing the truth of path because, respectively, three views are excluded — the first two [afflicted view and extreme view] and the fifth [clinging to rules and ritual as supreme], since they do not directly or indirectly wrongly engage the truths of origin and cessation — and for the truth of path, the first two views are omitted. These {thirty-two}: ten, seven, seven, and eight negative tendencies that directly or indirectly engage each of the four truths wrongly are serially abandoned by seeing the specific characteristics of each of the four truths, such as the truth of suffering in the desire realm and so on. {Thus afflicted view of the self and extreme view are susceptible to one type of abandonment. Wrong view, supreme view, and doubt are susceptible to four, since they focus on the four truths. [434] Clinging to rules and ritual as supreme is susceptible to two, since it focuses on the first and last truths. Four — attachment, anger, pride, and ignorance — are each susceptible to five [types of abandonment], through being objects abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of meditation.} Therefore there are thirty-two objects abandoned by the path of seeing that are negative tendencies of the desire realm. {They are objects abandoned by the path of seeing since they are abandoned by merely seeing the truth}.
bzhi ni bsgom pas spang bya yin/ / khong khro ma gtogs de dag nyid/ / gzugs khams gzugs med de dang 'dra/ / de ltar dgu bcu brgyad du 'dod/ / 5
Four are abandoned by meditation. Just those except for anger exist in the form realm, and the formless realm is similar to that. Thus ninety-eight are asserted. (5:5)

'dod chags dang khong khro dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa bzhi ni bsgom pas spang bar bya ba'ang yin pas spang bya ris lngar 'gyur te/ 'dod chags la sogs pa bzhi'i lhan skyes ni bden pa rnams mthong ba tsam gyis mi spong ba'i phyir dang*/ kun brtags ni spang ba'i phyir rnam pa gnyis ka yin na/ lta ba lnga dang the tshom ni bden pa rnams mthong ba tsam gyis spong ba'i phyir mthong spang kho na yin te/ de ltar na 'dod pa na spyod pa'i phra rgyas ni sum cu rtsa drug yin no/ /

Four — attachment, anger, pride, and ignorance — have five types of abandonment since they are also abandoned by the path of meditation. They have two aspects because the innate[1384] states of the four negative tendencies such as attachment are not abandoned by the path of seeing alone, but their mentally fabricated[1385] states are abandoned by the path of seeing. The five views and doubt are abandoned by the path of seeing alone because they are abandoned by merely seeing the four truths. Thus there are thirty-six negative tendencies that exist in the desire realm.

gang dag 'dod khams su bshad pa las khong khro ma gtogs pa'i nyon mongs pa de dag nyid gzugs kyi khams na yod kyi khong khro ni ma yin te/ {rten dang bas sdug bsngal gyis tshor ba med pa'i phyir rgyas pa'i gzhi med pas dang } rgyud zhi gnas kyis brlan pas kun nas mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu med pa'i phyir ro/ /

From among those negative tendencies explained for the desire realm, just those [four] afflictions except for anger exist in the form realm. Anger does not exist there because the nine states of the tormented mind do not exist within a mindstream moistened by calm abiding, {and a being possessing clear [faith] does not have that experience of pain since he does not have the complete basis for such experience}.
kun nas mnar sems kyi dngos po dgu ni
THE NINE STATES OF THE TORMENTED MIND

bdag la gnod pa byas so/ /byed do/ /byed par 'gyur ro zhes bya ba gsum dang*/ bdag gi mdza' bo la gnod pa byas so/ /byed do/ /byed par 'gyur zhes bya ba gsum dang*/ bdag gi dgra la phan btags so/ /'dogs so/ /'dogs par 'gyur ro zhes bya ba gsum ste dgu'o/ /

There are nine: three exemplified by the statements (1) “I was harmed,” (2) “I am being harmed,” and (3) “I will be harmed”; three exemplified by the statements (4) “My friends were harmed,” (5) “My friends are being harmed,” and (6) “My friends will be harmed”; and three exemplified by the statements (7) “My enemies were benefited,” (8) “My enemies are being benefited,” and (9) “My enemies will be benefited.”[1386]

des na gzugs na ni mthong spang dang sgom spang gi phra rgyas sum cu rtsa gcig yod de/ khong khro lnga ma gtogs pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs med pa'i khams na'ang gzugs kyi khams de dang 'dra bar sum cu rtsa gcig yin pas de dag dgu dang drug drug bdun/ khong khro lta ba sum gnyis dag /ma gtogs gzugs na sdug bsngal sogs/ / mthong bas rim bzhin spong bar byed/ / gsum ni bsgoms pas spang bya yin/ / zhes pa dang*/ gzugs med la'ang sbyar te shes par bya'o/ /

Therefore thirty-one negative tendencies that are abandoned by the paths of seeing and meditation exist in the form realm, excluding the five of anger. Also the formless realm is similar to the form realm in having thirty-one. It is said: Nine, six, six, and seven, because three or two types of anger and view are excluded. They are serially abandoned by seeing suffering and so on in the form realm. Three are abandoned by meditation.[1387] And this should also be applied to the formless realm.

de ltar na bye brag tu smra ba ltar na khams gsum na mthong spang brgyad cu rtsa brgyad dang sgom spang bcu ste dgu bcu rtsa brgyad du 'dod la/ de dag khams dang sa dang rnam pa'i sgo nas phye na nyis brgya lnga bcu rtsa gnyis su 'gyur ro/ /

Thus, in accordance with the Vaibhāṣikas, ninety-eight are asserted in the three realms: eighty-eight objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing, and ten objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation. If these are classified by means of realm, level, and aspect, there are 252.

chos mngon pa ba gzhan dag ni phung po lnga pa las/ nyon mongs pa de la 'dod chags dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa ni bco lnga bco lnga'o/ / khong khro ni lnga'o/ / the tshom ni bcu gnyis so/ / lta ba ni sum cu rtsa drug go /de dag las lta ba 'og ma gsum dang the tshom ni kun tu brtags pa'o/ / lhag ma ni lhan cig skyes pa dang kun brtags pa'o/ / zhes 'byung bas 'dod chags la sogs pa bzhi dang lta ba dang po gnyis te drug ni lhan skyes sgom spang dang kun brtags mthong spang yin pas gnyis ka dang*/ lta ba phyi ma gsum dang the tshom ni kun brtags kho na yin pa'i phyir mthong spang nyid du nges so/ / nyon mongs pa bcu po de dag kyang sdug bsngal la sogs pa'i bden pa bzhi la khyad par med par log par 'jug pa'i phyir 'dod pa na mthong spang bzhi bcu dang*/ khams gong ma gnyis na khong khro med pa'i phyir sum cu rtsa drug drug ste/ brgya dang bcu gnyis dang*/ sgom spang ni 'dod pa na drug dang*/ khams gong ma gnyis na lnga lnga ste bcu drug yin la/ de dag kyang{ rnam pa dang} khams dang sa'i sgo nas phye na bzhi brgya dang bcu bzhir 'gyur ro zhes zer ro/ / rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba las ni 'dod pa'i sdug bsngal la ni bcu po thams cad log par 'jug go /bden pa phyi ma gsum la ni 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang mthar 'dzin par lta ba gnyis ma gtogs pa brgyad brgyad log par 'jug go /khams gong ma gnyis kyi bden pa la ni khong khro ma gtogs pa snga ma bzhin du dgu dang bdun bdun log par 'jug go zhes mthong spang 'dod pa na sum cu rtsa bzhi dang*/ gong ma gnyis na sum cu sum cu ste dril bas dug bcu rtsa bzhi dang*/ sgom spang ni 'dod pa'i khong khro dang*/ khams gsum gyi 'dod chags dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa'o/ / de dag la ni lam mchog tu goms pas spong bas na sgom spang zhes bya'o zhes 'di dang mthun par bshad do/ / 'di dag la grang ti na re 'dir bshad pa ni bye brag tu smra ba dang*/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu bar bshad pa ni mdo sde pa dang*/ kun las btus las bshad pa ni sems tsam pa'i lugs yin no zhes zer{ la bla cog gi TI kar yang mthong bas spang bya'i phra rgyan las/ grub mtha' smra ba gsum gyis ni/ / brgyad cu brgyad dang dgu bcu bzhi/ / brgya rtsa bcu gnyis dgu cu 'dod ces 'byung} mod kyi/

Other Ābhidharmikas assert that Five Aggregates states: From among those afflictions, attachment, pride, and ignorance have fifteen types each, anger has five, doubt has twelve, and view has thirty-six. From those, the three latter views and doubt are mentally fabricated, and the rest are both innate and mentally fabricated.[1388] Therefore six — the four negative tendencies of attachment and so on and the first two views — are both [innate and mentally fabricated], since the innate are objects abandoned by the path of meditation and those mentally fabricated are objects abandoned by the path of seeing. The latter [435] three views and doubt are mentally fabricated alone because they are ascertained to be objects abandoned by the path of seeing. Further, there are forty objects abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm because those ten afflictions wrongly engage the four noble truths without distinction, and thirty-six in each of the higher realms because anger does not exist there, making 112. There are six objects abandoned by the path of meditation in the desire realm and five in each of the higher realms, making sixteen. Moreover, if those are classified by means of realm, {aspect}, and level, there are 414. The Compendium of Ascertainment observes: All ten wrongly engage the truth of suffering in the desire realm. Eight, excluding the afflicted view of the self and extreme view, wrongly engage the three latter truths. Nine, seven, and seven, except for anger, wrongly engage the truths of the two higher realms, as before.[1389] There are thirty-four objects abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm and thirty in each of the two higher realms, making ninety-four in total. Anger of the desire realm and attachment, pride, and ignorance of the three realms are objects abandoned by the path of meditation. They are called “objects abandoned by meditation” since they are abandoned through becoming familiar with the supreme path. This is explained in conformity with that text. Indeed, Bangti[1390] says: Here this is the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika system. The explanation of the Compendium of Ascertainment is that of the Sautrāntika system, and the explanation of the Compendium of Abhidharma is that of the Cittamātra system. {Also, Dachok’s Commentary[1391] says: The three tenet systems assert eighty-eight, ninety-four, one hundred and twelve, and ninety negative tendencies that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing.}

'on kyang lugs phyi ma gnyis ni rnam pa 'gal tsam dang dngos su 'gal ba'i dbang du byas nas bshad pa yin no zhes mchims gsung ngo*/ / gal te mthong spang gi nyon mong pa de dag mthong lam kho nas spang bar bya ba yin nam zhe na/

However, Chim[1392] mentions that the two later systems explain this from the perspective of aspects that are solely excluded or directly excluded. Question: Are these afflictions that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing objects abandoned by the path of seeing alone?
srid rtse las skyes bzod pa yis/ / gzhom bya mthong bas spang bya nyid/ / lhag skyes mthong dang bsgom gnyis kyis/ / bzod pas gzhom min bsgom kho nas/ / 6

Those that arise at the summit of existence are eliminated by perseverance. They are just objects abandoned by seeing. Those arising on other levels, by both seeing and meditation. Those not eliminated by perseverance, by meditation alone. (5:6)

khyad par yod de srid pa'i rtse mo las skyes pa'i sdug bsngal mthong spang la sogs pa'i phra rgyas gang dag sdug bsngal la rjes su shes pa'i bzod pa bzhi yis gzhom par bya ba de dag ni bden pa mthong bas spang bar bya ba nyid yin te/{ de dag ni mthong lam kho nas spang bar nges pa'i phyir} nyid ces bya ba ni{ kho na'i} nges par gzung ba'o/ / 'di ltar mthong spang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i sgom lam gyis spong ba mi srid pa'i phyir dang*/ srid rtse ba'i mthong spang de la spong byed 'jig rten pa'i lam yang med pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: There is a difference. Any negative tendencies such as objects abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering and so on that arise at the summit of existence (bhavāgra) are eliminated by the four aspects of perseverance for subsequent knowledge of the truth of suffering (duḥkhe’nvaya jñānakṣānti).[1393] They are just objects abandoned by seeing the truth, where “just” definitely means {“only” because they are certainly abandoned by the path of seeing alone}. This is because it is impossible that the transcendent path of meditation abandons objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing, and neither do the mundane paths abandon objects of the summit of existence that are abandoned by the path of seeing.

srid rtse las gzhan pa'i mthong spang sa lhag ma ci yang med pa'i skye mched man chad las skyes pa'i mthong spang rnams ni mthong{ lam chos bzod rjes bzod ci rig} ba dang sgom pa'i lam gnyis kyis ci rigs par spong ste/ 'phags pa rnams ni mthong lam dang*/ so so'i skye bo rnams ni sa gong ma la zhing dang 'og ma la rags par lta ba'i 'jig rten pa'i sgom lam gyis kyang spong ba'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir bstan bcos las/ bcom ldan 'das kyis nyan thos ni mthong ba'i lam gyis spong la/ so so'i skye bo ni sgom pa'i lam gyis spong ngo zhes gsungs so/ / sa thams cad na'ang phra rgyas bzod pas gzhom par bya ba min pa'i sgom spang{ du bshad pa'i lta min bzhi pa} gang dag shes pas gzhom par bya ba de dag ni{ bden pa la log par ma zhugs pa'i spang yin pas skye 'phags gnyis kas kyang} sgom pa'i lam kho nas spang bar bya ba yin te/ mthong lam gyis sgom spang spong ba mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ / sgom lam ni 'jig rten pa dang 'jig rten las 'das pa gnyis kas yin no/ / des na mthong lam ni 'jig rten las 'das pa kho na yin la/ sgom lam ni 'jig rten pa dang 'jig rten las 'das pa gnyis ka yod do zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Objects other than those of the summit of existence that are abandoned by the path of seeing are objects abandoned by the path of seeing arising on other levels, those on or below the base of nothingness. They are abandoned by both the path of seeing {that is either perseverance for Dharma knowledge of the truth of path or perseverance for subsequent knowledge of the truth of path} and meditation because āryas [436] abandon them by the path of seeing and ordinary beings abandon them by the mundane path of meditation that views higher states as peaceful and lower states as coarse. Therefore a treatise[1394] notes: The Bhagavan has stated that śrāvakas abandon those by the path of seeing and ordinary beings abandon those by the [mundane] path of meditation.[1395] On every level {the four nonview} negative tendencies are not eliminated by perseverance (kṣānti) but {are said to be} objects abandoned by meditation and eliminated by knowledge. {Since they are objects to be abandoned that do not wrongly engage the four truths, both ordinary beings and āryas} abandon them by the path of meditation alone, because it is impossible that the path of seeing abandons objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation. The path of meditation is both mundane and transcendent; therefore it should be understood that the path of seeing is transcendent alone and the path of meditation is both mundane and transcendent.

'di la mdo sde pa dang rnal 'byor spyod pa pa la sogs pa rnams na re so so skye bo rnams kyis mthong spang spong ba ni mi srid de/ de ni 'jig rten pa'i sgom lam gyis spong bar 'dod pa yin na mdo las 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba bsam gtan gyi sems dang ldan pa'i byis pa so so'i skye bo phyi rol pa'i dge sbyong dang bram ze la sogs pa la 'dod pa la dmigs pa'i log lta dang*/ rtag par lta ba dang*/ kha cig rtag par lta ba dang*/ rgyu med par lta ba la sogs pa 'byung bar gsungs pa'i phyir dang*/ de dag kyang 'dod khams kyi mthong spang yin pa'i phyir ro/ / ji ltar gsungs she na/ las rnam par 'byed pa chen po'i mdo las/ kun dga' bo 'di na la la srog gcod pa spong ba nas log par lta ba spong ba'i bar du yin la/ 'di la'ang mi dga' zhing so sor mi dga' la lus zhig nas shi ba'i 'og tu ngan song ngan 'gro log par ltung ba dmyal ba dag gi nang du skye bar 'gyur ro/ / de phyi rol gyi mu stegs pa dge sbyong ngam bram ze yang rung*/ rdzu 'phrul dang ldan pa lha'i mig dang ldan pa gzhan gyi sems shes pa gang zhig gis mthong nas de 'di snyam du lus kyis legs par spyad pa yang med la/ lus kyis legs par spyad pa'i rnam par smin pa yang med do/ / ngag dang yid kyis legs par spyad pa yang med la/ ngag dang yid kyis legs par spyad pa'i rnam par smin pa yang med do snyam du sems so zhes bya ba la sogs pa rgyas par 'byung ba'i log lta 'di ni 'dod khams la dmigs pa yin te/ las de dag 'dod pa na spyod pa yin pa'i phyir dang*/ dmyal ba'ang 'dod pa kho na na yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

The Sautrāntikas, Yogācāras, and so on say that it is impossible that an ordinary being abandons objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing. If it is asserted that they are abandoned by the mundane path of meditation, then a sūtra states: Childlike ordinary beings — non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, brahmans, and so on — who possess the mind of absorption free from attachment to desire-realm objects have wrong view focused on desire-realm objects and possess the view of permanence, and some have the view of permanence with the view that there is no cause and so on.[1396] These [views] are objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing that belong to the desire realm. Question: How are [such views] depicted? Reply: Divisions of Karma declares: Ānanda, some abandon actions from taking life up to wrong view and dislike such actions and dislike them specifically, yet after death and the destruction of the body, they fall to lower rebirths and are born among hell beings. Non-Buddhist tīrthikas, śramaṇas, or brahmans who possess supernatural powers and the divine eye see this through the knowledge of others’ minds and speculate that there is no positive physical action and there is no karmic maturation of positive physical action, there is no positive verbal or mental action, and there is no karmic maturation of positive verbal or mental action . . . and so on.[1397]
Such statements are common. This wrong view focuses on the desire realm because these actions are committed in the desire realm and hell beings only exist in the desire realm.

de bzhin du tshangs pa'i drwa ba'i mdo las/ 'di na dge sbyong ngam bram ze la la dgon pa na 'dug kyang rung*/ shing drung na 'dug kyang rung ste/ kun du sbyangs pa'i rgyu dang*/ spong ba'i rgyu dang*/ bsgoms pa'i rgyu dang*/ lan mang du byas pa'i rgyu dang*/ legs par yid la byas pa'i rgyus sems mnyam par bzhag pa ji lta bus 'jig pa dang 'chags pa'i bskal pa nyi shu yang dag par rjes su dran par 'gyur ba de lta bu'i sems kyi ting nge 'dzin zhi ba la reg par 'gyur zhing*/ de 'di snyam du bdag dang 'jig rten 'di ni rtag pa yin no snyam du sems par 'gyur ro zhes bya ba la sogs pa rgyas par 'byung ba 'di dag kyang bdag dang 'jig rten la dmigs pas 'dod khams la dmigs pa yin no/ / sgom spang sa bon 'jig rten pa'i lam gyis spong ba ni med de/ nyon mongs pa'i mngon gyur 'das pa ni 'gags pa'i phyir dang*/ ma 'ongs pa ma skyes pa'i phyir dang*/ da ltar ba dang gnyen po lhan cig tu mi gnas pa'i phyir dang*/ sa bon 'jig rten pa'i lam gyis spong na 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba'i so so'i skye bo rnams la phyis nyon mongs pa skye ba dang*/ 'dod par skye ba mi srid par thal ba'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

So too, the Brahma Net Sūtra declares: Some śramaṇas or brahmans capable of living in solitude and abiding under trees attain equipoise through the causes of thorough purity, abandonment, meditation, frequent practice, and proper attention. [437] Through such equipoise, they correctly recall twenty eons of destruction and formation, and thinking that due to such mental concentration they have attained peace, they reflect, “In this mundane world I am eternal.”[1398]
Such statements are common, and since such views focus on the self and the world, they focus on the desire realm. But just because past manifest afflictions have ceased, future manifest afflictions do not arise, and present manifest afflictions and their antidotes do not coexist does not mean that the mundane path abandons objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation and their seeds. For if the mundane path did abandon seeds, it would be impossible for ordinary beings who are free of attachment to desire-realm objects to subsequently generate desire-realm afflictions or be born in the desire realm.

de'i phyir rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba las kyang*/ 'jig rten pa'i lam 'ba' zhig gi bag la nyal yang dag par 'joms pa ni med de/ 'jig rten pa ni 'dris pa'i phyir dang*/ mtshan ma la mngon par zhen pas 'jug pa'i phyir ro/ / de ni ji ltar mtshan ma la mngon par zhen pas 'jug pa de ltar mtshan ma rnam par 'jig par 'jug par mi 'gyur la/ ji ltar mtshan ma rnam par 'jig par mi 'jug pa de ltar gnas ngan len yang dag par 'joms par yang mi 'gyur bas/ des na des bag la nyal yang dag par 'joms pa med do zhes pa dag so so'i skye bos 'jig rten pa'i lam gyi sa bsam gtan dang po thob pa dang*/ dang por skyes pa de'i 'dod pa'i nyon mongs can gyi sa bon de dag ni nyams pa yin gyi yang dag par bcom pa ni ma yin te/ de ting nge 'dzin de las yongs su nyams nas yang 'dod pa'i nyon mongs pa mngon du byed pa dang*/ dang po nas shi nas yang 'dod par skye ba'i phyir ro/ / des na sa bon de ni zhi gnas kyis re zhig nyams par byas pa yin te dper na nas la sogs pa'i sa bon rlan dang bral ba rnams re zhig mi skye yang sa bon nyid med pa ni ma yin pa bzhin no/ / 'phags pa nyan thos 'jig rten las 'das pa'i lam gyis 'dod chags dang bral ba thob pa ni nyon mongs pa'i sa bon thams cad yang dag par bcom pa yin te dper na sa bon mes bsregs pas gtan med pa bzhin no zhes pa dang*/ gzhan yang de nyid las sa bon yang dag par bcom pa dang*/ sa bon nyams pa bzhi bshad de/ de la yang dag par bcom pa ni 'phags pas spangs pa yin la/ nyams pa bzhi ni gnyen po'i sgo nas 'dod yon la sems mi 'jug cing des de la dmigs pa'i nyon mongs mi skye ba yongs su spong bas nyams pa dang*/ tshul bzhin yid la byed pas 'dod pa la nyes dmigs su lta ba sun 'byin pas nyams pa dang*/ 'jig rten pa'i 'dod chags dang bral ba zhi gnas kyis nyams pa dang*/ dgra bcom pa'i dge ba dang lung ma bstan ni grogs nyon mongs spangs pas de dag gis phyi mar rnam smin dang rang nyid skyed mi nus pa grogs yang dag par bcom pas nyams pa'o/ / de las 'dir ni nyams pa gsum pa'o/ /

Therefore the Compendium of Ascertainment also states: The mundane path alone does not actually destroy dormant states because it is accustomed to mundane states, and it engages them since it conceives the marks [of entities]. Just as it engages dormant states through conceiving marks, so too it does not facilitate the destruction of marks. Just as it does not destroy marks, so too it does not come to actually destroy dysfunctional tendencies. Therefore it does not actually destroy dormant states.[1399] And: When an ordinary being obtains the first absorption through the mundane path, at first the seeds of desire-realm affliction become inactive, but they are not actually destroyed. They become inactive due to that concentration, but when afflicted states manifest and that being dies from the first absorption, he is born in the desire realm. In other words, through calm abiding, those seeds become inactive, but they do not cease to exist. It is like barley seeds and so on that, through lack of water, do not immediately sprout. But the transcendent path of an ārya śrāvaka who obtains freedom from attachment actually destroys all seeds of affliction, just as seeds seared by fire are no longer viable.[1400] This text goes on to explain actual destruction of seeds and the four inactive seed states: Full destruction is abandonment by an ārya. The four inactive states are: (1) Seeds that are inactive due to the mind not engaging desire-realm objects through applying their antidotes and not generating afflictions focusing on desire-realm objects by abandoning them. (2) Seeds that are inactive due to appropriate attention that views desire-realm objects as disadvantageous and repudiates them. (3) Seeds that are inactive due to calm abiding that is free of mundane attachment. (4) Seeds that are inactive due to the virtuous or neutral states of an arhat that abandon supportive afflictions (Tib. grogs nyon mongs). Supportive [afflictions] [438] are completely destroyed, since they cannot generate either karmic maturation or themselves in the future.[1401] The three degenerations are derived from them.

bye brag tu smra ba ni dper na lung dbyen gyi gzhi las/ lhas byin bsnyen bkur gyi zil gyis mnan te dge slong gi dge 'dun 'khor du bya ba'i phyir bcom ldan 'das la thugs las chung ngur bzhugs par gsol lo snyam du sdig pa'i bsam pa skyes pa dang rdzu 'phrul las nyams pa dus mnyam du byung bar bshad pa ltar mdo de dag ni bsam gtan gyi sems nyams pa dang dus mnyam du lta ba skye ba la dgongs nas gsungs pa'i phyir dang*/ nyon mongs pa'i sa bon ni thob pa la 'dod na de ni 'jig rten pa'i lam gyis spong ba yin yang phyis nyon mongs pa skye ba dang 'dod par skye ba ni 'das pa'i nyon mongs pa rdzas su yod pa las skye ba'i phyir ro zhes bya bar 'dod do/ / de ltar rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa'i phra rgyas drug las 'dod chags dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa ni bshad zin cing*/ the tshom ni bden pa dang las 'bras dang dkon mchog la sogs pa rnams la dmigs nas rnam pa yid gnyis za ba'am dmigs pa la rnam pa gnyis su 'jug pa dge ba'i phyogs rnams la mi 'jug pa'i rten byed pa'i las can yin par 'chad par 'gyur la/ khong khro ni yul drug la dmigs nas rnam pa sems khong nas 'khrug pa ste bde ba la reg par mi gnas pa dang nyes spyod kyi rten byed pa'i las can no/ /

Vaibhāṣikas, for example, quote the Chapter on Dissension: When the negative thought to invite the Bhagavan to sit in a lower place and to demonstrate that he [Devadatta] surpassed the Buddha in deserving veneration and respect, and thus to create his own retinue of monks, arose in Devadatta’s heart, his supernatural powers instantly degenerated.[1402] They assert that such statements were made in the sūtras to show that the mind of absorption degenerates the instant afflicted view arises. They also assert that though the mundane path abandons the obtainment of seeds of affliction in the desire realm, future generation of affliction and rebirth in the desire realm arise from past affliction that is substantially existent. Thus, from the six negative tendencies that are root afflictions, (1) attachment, (3) pride, and (4) ignorance have already been explained. (5) Doubt focuses on the four truths, karmic causation, the Three Jewels, and so on, wavers with regard to its aspect or engages two aspects of its focal object, and hinders entry into virtuous states. (2) Anger focuses on the six objects, the mind engaging that aspect is deeply agitated, it does not maintain contact with happiness, and it functions to support negative action.
bdag dang bdag gi rtag chad dang / / med dang dman la mchog lta dang / / rgyu min lam min der lta ba/ / de dag lta ba lnga yin no/ / 7
That which views them as a self and mine, as permanent or annihilated, as nonexistent, that which views inferior states as supreme, and views them as causes and the path, are the five views. (5:7)

[Afflicted] view is ascertained to be an object to be abandoned by the path of seeing alone. Though it possesses a nature similar to realization, it is classified as realization in name only and not in terms of its nature, since its aspect and function are different from realization. In terms of its aspect and nature, in general all views focusing on the person are indeed {afflicted} views of the self. But here a general name is imputed to a specific case. Just the view possessing the aspect of a self (ātma) and mine (ātmīya) that focuses on objects that are impermanent and multiple and views them as a self and mine — and does not focus on a single, permanent self asserted by non-Buddhists — is taught to be the afflicted view of the self [or the view of the perishable composite] (satkāyadṛṣṭi). A sūtra states: Monks, if those training in virtue and brahmans view the self correctly, all such correct views of the self view those five appropriated aggregates alone.[1403] Therefore (6) [the afflicted view of the self] focuses on the five impermanent appropriated aggregates that perish each moment and exist as a composite of many particles and parts, and views the aggregate of consciousness as the self, or controller, and the remaining four aggregates as mine, or states to be controlled. Or it views the four aggregates of name to be the self and the aggregate of form to be mine. (7) [Extreme view] focuses on just that basis [439] actually imputed to be the self, and views or apprehends it to be utterly permanent (dhruva) or annihilated (ucchedanā). All afflicted views are (8) wrong view to the extent that they wrongly engage or conceive their focal object and aspect. If, however, we interpret [“wrong view”] in its strict [or narrow] sense, then all wrong views must underestimate their object. In this sense the component of extreme view that apprehends its object as annihilated [or nonexistent] and underestimates its object [is wrong view], and the component of extreme view that apprehends its object as permanent and does not underestimate its object [is not wrong view]. Still [all afflicted views including extreme view are called wrong view] in the same way that all rancid butter has a bad smell but rancid butter with an extremely bad smell is still just called rancid butter with a bad smell. As such wrong view sees the four truths that do in fact exist as nonexistent (nāsti).
