'o na thams cad rang gi yul la dmigs pas rgyas sam zhe na/ zag med dang sa gong ma'i yul can gyi nyon mongs pas de dag la dmigs kyang{ dmigs pa'i sgo nas} rgyas pa min te/ zag med dang sa gong ma ba dag 'og mas bdag tu lta ba dang sred pas bdag gir ma byas pa'i phyir{ te de dag la de dag gis dmigs mi nus pa'i phyir} dang nyon mongs pa de dag gi gnyen po yin pa'i phyir dang*/ rgyas pa ni rgyun 'phel ba yin na de dag la 'phel bar 'os pa ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir slob dpon gang spel gyis kyang*/ phra rgyas la kun 'gro dang kun 'gro ma yin pa gnyis las dang po la'ang rang gi khams dang sa skal ba mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa gnyis so/ / kun 'gro ma yin pa la'ang zag bcas dang zag med la dmigs pa gnyis so/ / de la kun 'gro rnams ni yul spang bya ris lnga char la dmigs pa yin la kun 'gro ma yin pa ni rang rang gi ris kho na la dmigs so/ / de la zag med dang skal ba mi mnyam pa'i khams dang sa gong ma la dmigs pa rnams ni mtshungs ldan gyis rgyas 'gyur yin gyi dmigs pas rgyas 'gyur ni ma yin te/ ser dang bcas pa'i zhing la myu gu skye ba ltar gang la bdag lta dang sred pa 'jug pa de la gzhan dag kyang rgyas par 'gyur ba yin na zag med dang sa gong ma la ni bdag lta dang sred pa mi 'jug ste/ de gnyis ni rang nyid kyi nyer len gyi phung po la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na 'dod pa na gnas pa zag med dang sa gong ma don du gnyer ba de ji ltar sred pa ma yin zhe na/ de ni dge ba'i chos la 'dun pa yin no zhes bshad do/ / {kha cig phra rgyas kyi don ni rjes su mthun pa'i don yin pa la zag med dang sa gong ma ni de dag gi rjes su mthun pa ma yin te rlung nad can la kha zas rtsub po bzhin no/ / de'i phyir zag med la dmigs pa'i log ltas dge rtsa gcod mi nus so zhes gsung ngo }

Reply: Afflictions possessing objects (viṣaya) that are uncontaminated states or of higher level do focus on those objects, but they do not increase {due to focusing on them}. This is because the view of the self and the craving of lower levels do not take uncontaminated states and higher levels as “mine,” {because afflicted states cannot focus on actual uncontaminated states}, and because uncontaminated states are antidotes to them. And if “increase” means to enhance the stream of afflictions, uncontaminated states cannot enhance them. Thus Pūrṇavardhana also explains that negative tendencies are either pervasive or not pervasive. The first also is divided into those of the same realm and level and those that are not. Those that are not pervasive focus on either contaminated or uncontaminated states. The pervasive focus on the five types of object to be abandoned, and those not pervasive focus on their own type. Those that focus on uncontaminated states, different realms, and higher levels are increased through concomitance, but they are not increased through taking them as focal objects. Other afflictions increase when the view of self and craving engage any object like sprouts growing in a polluted field, but the view of self and craving do not engage uncontaminated states and higher levels because both [the view of self and craving] focus on one’s own appropriated aggregates. Objection: How is seeking uncontaminated states and higher levels in the desire realm not craving? Reply: That is because it is aspiration for virtuous Dharmas.[1433] {Some say: The meaning of negative tendency is “that which conforms with negative tendencies” but uncontaminated states and higher levels do not conform with negative tendencies, just as food appears rancid to one with a wind imbalance. Therefore wrong view focusing on uncontaminated states cannot sever the root of virtue}.

phra rgyas gang zhig sems dang sems byung gi sa mang po ba la sogs pa gang dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phra rgyas de dag ni grogs der te de dag la ma spangs kyi bar du mtshungs par ldan pa'i sgo nas rgyas par 'gyur te/{ dug dang 'dres pa'i chang gis dug gi nus pa 'phel ba bzhin no/ /} de ltar na phra rgyas dgu bcu rtsa brgyad las zag med la dmigs pa bcu gnyis ni mtshungs ldan kho nas rgyas 'gyur dang*/ 'gog lam mthong spang gi ma rig pa drug dang*/ khams 'og ma gnyis kyi kun 'gro bco brgyad de nyi shu rtsa bzhi ni dmigs yul zag bcas zag med dang rang sa dang gong sa la ltos nas ci rigs dmigs pa dang mtshungs ldan gyis rgyas 'gyur gnyis ka ci rigs pa dang*/ lhag ma drug cu rtsa gnyis ni rgyas 'gyur gnyis kar nges la/ dmigs pas rgyas pa la mtshungs ldan gyi rgyas pas khyab pas{ dmigs pas} rgyas 'gyur kho na yin pa ni med do/ /

Those negative tendencies that are concomitant with minds and mental factors like the universal mental states and so on are assisted and increased by means of that concomitance until they are abandoned, {like beer when mixed with poison enhances the potency of the poison}. Thus, from among the ninety-eight negative tendencies, twelve that focus on uncontaminated states increase through concomitance. Twenty-four — the six ignorances abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and path and the eighteen pervasive negative tendencies of both higher realms — increase due to both their focal object and their concomitance; they focus on distinct focal objects through relying on contaminated and uncontaminated states of their own level and higher levels. The remaining sixty-two definitely increase due to both. Since it is necessary that any increase due to the focal object is increase through concomitance, they are not increased solely {due to their focal object}. [454]
bzhi pa mi dge ba dang lung du ma bstan par dbye ba ni
Those that are nonvirtuous or neutral
gong ma thams cad lung ma bstan/ / 'dod na 'jig tshogs lta ba dang / / mthar 'dzin lhan cig ma rig pa/ / lhag ma rnams 'dir mi dge ba'o/ / 19
All higher afflictions are neutral. Afflicted view of the self, grasping an extreme, and coexistent ignorance are neutral in the desire realm. The remainder are nonvirtuous in this realm. (5:19)

khams gong ma gnyis kyi nyon mongs pa thams cad ni bsgribs la lung du ma bstan pa yin te/{ ting nge 'dzin gyis btul bas rnam smin 'byin mi nus pa'i phyir} nyon mongs can yin la/ gong na mi dge ba med pa'i phyir dang*/ gal te mi dge ba yod na de'i rnam smin ni sdug bsngal yin na sdug bsngal de yang khams gong ma gnyis na med de/ pha rol la gnod pa'i rgyu gnod sems la sogs pa med pa'i phyir dang*/ nyon mongs pa dge ba dang ma bsgribs par 'gyur ba'ang mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ /
slob dpon 'phags pa ni khams gong ma gnyis kyi nyon mongs la zhi gnas dang ldan pas nye bar zhi bas lung du ma bstan pa zhes bzhed de/ kun las btus las/ nye bar zhi bas lung du ma bstan pa gang zhe na/ gzugs dang gzugs med pa na spyod pa'i nyon mongs pa ste/ zhi gnas dang ldan pa'i phyir ro zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/

All afflictions of the two higher realms are obscured-neutral states (avyākṛta) {in that they are incapable of producing karmic maturation; this is because they are subdued by concentration,} they are afflicted, and there is no nonvirtue in the higher realms. If nonvirtue existed there, then pain that is karmic maturation would exist there. Pain, however, does not exist in the two higher realms because malice and so on that are the cause of harming others do not exist there, and it is impossible for affliction to become virtuous or unobscured.
Master Ārya Asaṅga asserts that since afflictions of the two higher realms possess calm abiding and are fully pacified, they are neutral. The Compendium of Abhidharma says: What are neutral states that are pacified? They are afflicted states that possess calm abiding in the two higher realms.[1434]

'dod pa'i khams na 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang mthar 'dzin par lta ba dang de dag gnyis dang lhan cig mtshungs par ldan pa'i ma rig pa gsum ni bsgribs la lung ma bstan yin no/ / ji ltar zhe na/ 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang rtag par lta ba ni sbyin pa gtong ba dang tshul khrims srung ba la sogs pa dge ba dang mi 'gal bar 'jug pa'i phyir ro/ / bdag 'jig rten pha rol tu bde bar bya ba'i don du sbyin pa dang*/ tshul khrims la 'jug pa'i phyir ro/ / chad par lta ba'ang thar pa dang mthun pa'i phyir te/ mchog tu gdags pa bcu ston pa'i mdo las/ phyi rol pa'i lta bar gyur pa rnams kyi nang na 'di lta ste/ bdag med par gyur cig /bdag gi med par gyur cig /bdag 'byung bar ma gyur cig /bdag gi 'byung bar ma gyur cig ces lta ba 'di mchog yin no zhes gsungs pa yin no/ /

In the desire realm three views — the afflicted view of the self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view grasping an extreme (antagrāha), and coexistent ignorance concomitant with them — are obscured-neutral states. Question: How? Reply: The afflicted view of the self and the view of permanence engage their objects without excluding virtues such as giving and protecting ethics and so on, because one engages in giving and ethics in order to spread joy to other worldly beings. Even the view of annihilation is compatible with liberation, because the Sūtra Teaching the Ten States Designated as Supreme states: Among the views of outsiders, the views that the self does not exist, “mine” does not exist, the self does not occur, and “mine” does not occur are supreme.[1435]

gzhan yang lta ba 'di gnyis ni rang gi rgyud du gtogs pa'i nyer len gyi phung po la kun tu rmongs pas rang gi rdzas la rmongs pa'i phyir dang*/ gzhan la gnod par ma zhugs pas mi dge ba ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / dge ba'ang ma yin te/ nyon mongs pa can yin pa'i phyir ro/ / gtan tshigs de dag ni de gnyis dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i ma rig pa la'ang mtshungs so/ / sngon gyi slob dpon dag ni de lta na mtho ris la sred pa'i 'dod chags dang nga'o snyam pa'i nga rgyal yang lung ma bstan du thal bar 'gyur te/ rgyu mtshan de dag mtshungs pa'i phyir ro/ / des na lta ba de gnyis lhan cig skyes pa ri dwags dang bya rnams la'ang yod pa ni bsgribs la lung ma bstan yin te/{ bab col du sgra thos pas skrag pa'i rgyur 'gyur ba lta bu'o/ /} ser skya dang gzegs zan la sogs pas kun tu brtags pa ni mi dge ba yin par bzhed de/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba las/ 'jig tshogs la lta ba ni gnyis te/ lhan cig skyes pa dang kun brtags pa'o/ / de la dang po ni byis pa so so'i skye bo thams cad dang tha na bya dang ri dwags rnams kyi'ang yin no/ / gnyis pa ni gzhan mu stegs can rnams kyi yin par lta 'o/ / mthar 'dzin par lta ba la'ang gnyis las rtag ltas bsdus pa'i mthar 'dzin gyi lta ba ni lta ba'i rnam pa drug cu rtsa gnyis las sngon gyi mthar rtog pa rtag par smra ba rnams dang*/ la la rtag par smra ba rnams dang*/ phyi ma'i mthar rtog pa 'du shes can du smra ba rnams dang*/ 'du shes med par smra ba rnams dang*/ 'du shes yod med gnyis ka ma yin par smra ba rnams kyi yin la/ chad ltas bsdus pa'i mthar 'dzin gyi lta ba ni dngos po bdun gyis chad par smra ba'i dge sbyong dang bram ze rnams kyi yin te/ de dag gi mthar 'dzin gang de ni kun brtags kho na'o zhes pa dang 'dod pa'i 'jig tshogs la lta ba lhan cig skyes pa de ni lung ma bstan yin te/ rtag tu dang yang du 'byung ba'i phyir dang*/ bdag dang gzhan la shin tu gnod pa'i gnas ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / rtog pas mngon par zhen pa de ni mi dge ba yin no zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / de lta na 'dod pa'i 'dod chags dang nga rgyal dag kyang lhan skyes bsgribs la lung ma bstan dang kun brtags mi dge bar 'gyur zhing khams gong ma na'ang mi dge ba yod par 'gyur te/ 'jig tshogs la lta ba la sogs pa kun du brtags pa yod pa'i phyir ro/ / med na ni mthong spang med par thal ba 'di spang dgos so/ /

Again, the afflicted view of the self and the view of permanence [i.e., extreme view] are confused about the substance of self, since they are fully confused about the appropriated aggregates belonging to one’s mindstream. They are not nonvirtuous since they don’t harm others, and they are not virtuous because they are afflicted. These logical proofs should also be applied to ignorance that is concomitant with these two. Earlier masters assert that if that were so, then it would follow that attachment craving for higher rebirth and the pride thinking “I” would be neutral because those reasons similarly apply. Therefore these two views, which arise innately even in wild animals and birds, are obscured-neutral states, {such as the experience of fear through hearing the sounds of senseless babble,} but followers of Kapila and Kanada assert that conceptual fabrications [455] are nonvirtuous. The Compendium of Ascertainment observes: The afflicted view of the self is twofold: innate and mentally fabricated. The first exists for childlike ordinary sentient beings, including birds and wild animals. The second exists for others, such as tīrthikas. Also, the view grasping extremes is twofold: (1) extreme view comprising the view of permanence, which, from the sixty-two extreme views, refers to advocating permanence through conceiving the past, advocating permanence for some, advocating discernment through conceiving the future, advocating nondiscernment, and advocating neither discernment nor nondiscernment. (2) Extreme view comprising the view of annihilation exists for śramaṇas and brahmans who advocate annihilation due to seven things. Any of these extreme views is only mentally fabricated.[1436] It is also said that “The innate afflicted view of the self of the desire realm is neutral because it occurs continuously or frequently and because it is not a state that intensely harms self or others. But that actively conceived by thought is nonvirtuous.”[1437] In that case, even desire-realm attachment and pride that are innate would be obscured-neutral states, while mentally fabricated states would be nonvirtuous. Not only that, but in higher realms nonvirtue would exist, because fabricated conceptions that are afflicted views of the self and so on would exist there. If they don’t exist there, it would follow that objects abandoned by the path of seeing do not exist there, and this must be refuted.

'dod chags la sogs pa'i phra rgyas 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang mthar 'dzin par lta ba'i{ lta ba dang po gnyis mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa ma gtogs pa'i phra rgyas} lhag ma rnams ni 'dod pa'i khams 'dir mi dge ba yin par shes par bya'o/ / de nyid kyi phyir rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba las kyang*/ mang dang nyon mongs can dang ni/ / spyod dang sdug bsngal nyid dang yang*/ / kha na ma tho bul 'bras dang*/ / ting nge 'dzin dang skye ba'o zhes 'dod pa dang khams gong ma'i nyon mongs pa la khyad par brgyad dam bcu bshad do/ /

It should be known that the remaining negative tendencies such as attachment and so on {which are negative tendencies excluding} the afflicted view of the self and the view grasping extremes {and those concomitant with the first two views}, are nonvirtuous in this desire realm. Therefore the Compendium of Ascertainment notes: Multiple, afflicted, and conduct, suffering itself, as well as offensive acts, desired results, concentration, and birth.[1438] This explains the eight or ten differences between afflictions of the desire and higher realms.
lnga pa mi dge ba dang lung ma bstan gyi rtsa ba bshad pa ni
The roots of nonvirtuous and neutral states
'dod na 'dod chags khong khro dang / / rmongs rnams mi dge'i rtsa ba yin/ / lung ma bstan pa'i rtsa ba gsum/ / de ne srid dang ma rig blo/ / 20
In the desire realm, attachment, anger, and confusion are the roots of nonvirtue. The three roots of neutral states are craving, ignorance, and discernment. (5:20)

'dod pa'i khams na spang bya ris lnga char gyi 'dod chags dang khong khro ni rtsa ba gnyis dang*/ 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang mthar 'dzin par lta ba dang po gnyis dang*/ mtshungs par ldan pa'i gti mug ma gtogs pa'i kun tu rmongs pa rnams ni mi dge ba'i rtsa ba yin te/ mi dge ba thams cad gsum po de las 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / 'dod na zhes bya bas khams gong ma'i de dag mi dge ba'i rtsa ba yin pa sel bar byed do/ / mi dge ba'ang yin la rtsa ba'ang yin pas gsum po de dag kho na mi dge ba'i rtsa ba'o/ / gsum po ma gtogs pa ni mi dge ba'i rtsa ba ma yin no/ / slob dpon gang spel ni nyon mongs pa gang zhig phra rgyas rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa yin pa dang*/ spang bya ris rnam pa lnga'i rang bzhin yin pa dang*/ lus ngag gi las kun nas slong ba dang*/ rnam shes tshogs drug car dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ dge rtsa gcod pa la stobs dang ldan pa'i rgyu yin pa de kho na mi dge ba'i rtsa ba yin te/ phra rgyas rnam pa lnga'i rang bzhin/ / lus ngag bya ba kun slong byed/ / rnam shes lngar rten dkar po'i rtsa/ / kun gcod 'dren pa mi dge'i rtsa'o zhes 'chad do/ / sa'i dngos gzhi las ni/ mi dge ba'i rten du gyur pas na rtsa ba rnams so zhes 'byung ngo*/ /{ lhag ma ni rtsa ba ma yin no}

In the desire realm, the two root afflictions of attachment (rāga) and anger (pratigha), which are components of the five types of abandonment, plus complete confusion (mūḍha), except for delusion (amoha) concomitant with the first two views — the afflicted view of the self and the view grasping an extreme — are the roots of nonvirtue because all nonvirtue arises from these three. “In the desire realm” is stated to refute afflictions of higher realms being roots of nonvirtue. These three alone are the roots of nonvirtue since [456] they are nonvirtuous as well as roots, and states other than these three are not the roots of nonvirtue. Master Pūrṇavardhana writes: Only those afflicted states that are (1) afflicted root negative tendencies, (2) by nature the five types of abandonment, (3) motivators of physical and verbal karma, (4) concomitant with the six types of consciousness, and (5) strong causes that sever the roots of virtue are the roots of nonvirtue, because by nature they possess these five aspects of negative tendencies, they are motivators of physical and verbal action, and they are the roots of nonvirtue that sever the basic white roots of the five consciousnesses.[1439] Yogācāra Levels notes: Since they act as the support of nonvirtue, they are roots; {the remainder are not roots}.[1440]

lung du ma bstan pa'i rtsa ba ni gsum mo/ / gang zhe na/ lung ma bstan gyi rtsa ba gsum po de dag ni khams gong ma gnyis kyi ro myang ba dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ gzhal med khang la sogs pa la sred pa{ sogs khams gong ma gnyis kyi srid pa thams cad} dang ma rig pa khams gsum gyi sgrib pa thams cad dam yang na/{ 'dod pa'i lta ba dang po gnyis dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang} blo ni shes rab ste/{ de'i ngo bo nyon mongs can ma yin yang lung ma bstan gyi rtsa bar 'dod de/ /} de yang 'dod pa na rnam smin skyes la sogs pa ma bsgribs lung ma bstan gyi sems bzhi dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ bsgribs la lung ma bstan gyi lta ba{ dang po} gnyis dang*/ khams gong ma gnyis na nyon mongs pa dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ ma bsgribs lung ma bstan rnam smin skyes la sogs pa'i sems dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i shes rab thams cad yin no/ / 'di yang lung ma bstan yang yin la rtsa ba'ang yin pas lung ma bstan gyi rtsa ba ste/ mi dge ba dag ni lung ma bstan gyi rtsa bar mi 'os pa'i phyir ro/ /

The roots of neutral states are three. Question: What are they? Reply: The three roots of neutral states are (1) craving (tṛṣṇā) concomitant with the experience of the taste of the two higher realms {and all craving that exists in the two higher realms, such as craving for celestial mansions and so on}, (2) ignorance (avidya) that is all obscuration of the three realms {or ignorance concomitant with the first two desire-realm views}, and (3) intelligence (mati) that is wisdom. {Though its nature is not afflictive, intelligence is asserted to be a root of neutral states} since it is (1) any wisdom concomitant with the four unobscured-neutral minds of maturational birth in the desire realm and so forth, or (2) concomitant with the {first} two obscured-neutral views and afflicted states of the two higher realms, or (3) concomitant with the minds of those possessing unobscured-neutral maturational birth and so on. Further, since these three are neutral and roots, they are the roots of neutral states because nonvirtuous states cannot be the roots of neutral states.
rnam gnyis mthor 'jug phyir de las/ / gzhan min bzhi zhes nyi 'og pa/ / de dag sred lta nga rgyal rmongs/ / bsam gtan pa gsum ma rig las/ / 21

Those other than these are not roots because doubt engages two aspects and pride engages an inflated mind. Aparāntakas assert four — craving, view, pride, and confusion — that are three absorptions arising from ignorance. (5:21)

gsum po de dag las gzhan pa'i the tshom ni lung ma bstan gyi rtsa ba min te/ rnam pa gnyis su 'jug pas mi brtan pa'i phyir te rtsa ba ni brtan pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / nga rgyal yang ma yin te/ sems mtho ba'i rnam par 'jug pa'i phyir dang*/ rtsa ba ni gting na gnas pa'i phyir ro/ / khong khro ni khams gong ma na med pa'i phyir dang*/ 'dod pa na yod pa dag ni mi dge ba yin pa'i phyir ro zhes bya bar kha che bye brag tu smra ba 'dod de/ brtan pa dang gting na gnas pa tsam ni 'dir rtsa ba'i don ma yin gyi 'on kyang 'dir gtso bo'i rgyu la brjod par 'dod pas na de ma yin pa'i phyir ro zhes brjod do/ /

Doubt that is other than these three is not a root of neutral states because it engages two aspects, making it unstable, and roots are stable. Also, pride is not a root because it engages the aspect [or object] of an inflated [or superficial] mind, whereas a root abides in the depths of the mind. Kāśmīri Vaibhāṣikas assert that anger does not exist in higher realms and that that which exists in the desire realm is nonvirtuous. They say that merely being stable or abiding deeply is not the meaning of “root” here and that those are not roots since “root” refers to the main cause.

lung du ma bstan pa'i rtsa ba ni bzhi yin no zhes nyi 'og pa bye brag tu smra ba rnams 'dod de/ nyi 'og pa ni rgya gar ba rnams sam kha che ba'i yul las gzhan na gnas pa rnams yin no/ / bzhi po de dag kyang gang zhe na/ khams gong ma gnyis kyi sred pa dang lta ba thams cad dang*/ 'dod pa na lung ma bstan gyi lta ba dang po gnyis dang*/ khams gong ma gnyis kyi nga rgyal dang*/ sngar bshad pa'i rmongs pa rnams yin no/ / ci'i phyir zhe na/ {nga rgyal shas che ba'i bsam gtan pa ni bsam gtan des khengs par 'gyur ba'i phyir/ sred pa shas che ba'i bsam gtan pa ni/ bsam gtan dag la ro myang bar byed pa'i phyir ro/ / lta ba shas che ba'i bsam gtan pa ni bsam gtan la brten nas rtag pa la sogs par lta ba 'byung ba gang yin pa'o/ / the tshom shas che ba'i bsam gtan pa ni bsam gtan la brten nas ci 'di mya ngan las 'das pa'i lam yin nam/ 'on te gzhan zhig yin snyam pa dang*/ ci bdag 'das pa'i dus na byung ba'am/ 'on te ma byung snyam pa la sogs pa'o/ / nyon mongs pa rgyu ba'i gnas skabs 'di dag kyang bsam gtan la snyoms par zhugs pa 'di dag kho na la 'byung ngo*/ / zhes rnam bshad rigs pa'i 'grel pa las 'byung ba ltar }

Aparāntaka Vaibhāṣikas assert that there are four types of roots of neutral states. Aparāntakas are Indian Buddhists who abide in places other than Kāśmīr. Question: What are these four? Aparāntakas say: These are (1) all craving (tṛṣṇa) and view of both higher realms, (2) the first two neutral views (dṛga) of the desire realm, (3) pride (māna) of the two higher realms, and (4) confusion (moha) that was previously explained. Question: Why? [457] {Commentary on Rational System of Exposition: Absorption with strong pride inflates that absorption. Absorption with strong craving experiences the taste of that absorption. Absorption with a strong sense of view is the view of permanence and so on that arises in dependence on that absorption. Absorption with strong doubt is the thought, “What is this absorption? Is it the transcendent path or something else?” or, “What self arises at the time of transcendence?” and so on. Entering such meditative attainment of the absorptions only occurs when affected by afflicted states.}[1441]

ro myang ba dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i bsam gtan sgom pa sred pa shas che ba dang*/ bsam gtan la brten nas rtag lta la sogs pa skyed dang byed pa lta ba shas che ba dang*/ bdag ni bsam gtan thob pa yin gyi gzhan dag ni de lta ma yin no snyam du rlom pa nga rgyal shas che ba'i bsam gtan pa gsum ni bsgribs la lung ma bstan yin la/ de gsum yang ma rig pa las byung ba'i phyir ro zhes 'dod do/ / 'o na lung ring po las/{ bsam gtan ni mtshon pa ste gzugs med kyi snyoms 'jug lung ma bstan dang 'dod pa'i bsgribs pa la sogs pa gzhan yang yod ces gsungs so/ /} bdag dang 'jig rten rtag gam mi rtag gam gnyis ka'am gnyis ka ma yin nam mtha' dang ldan nam mi ldan nam gnyis ka'am gnyis ka ma yin nam de bzhin gsher ba grongs phan chad 'byung ngam mi 'byung ngam gnyis ka'am gnyis ka ma yin nam/ lus de nyid srog yin nam srog kyang gzhan la lus kyang gzhan yin nam zhes pa lung du ma bstan pa'i dngos po bcu bzhi gsungs pa rnams dge mi dger lung ma bstan pa'i lung du ma bstan pa yin naM zhe na/ ma yin te/ de ni dri ba la lan mi gdab par gzhag par bya ba'i lung du ma bstan pa yin no/ / ji ltar zhe na/

Thus [Aparāntakas] assert that the three absorptions (dhyāna) — (1) absorption with strong craving concomitant with the experience of the taste, (2) absorption possessing a strong sense of view that generates the view of permanence and so on in dependence on that absorption, and (3) absorption possessing strong pride that is the conceit thinking “I have obtained absorption; others are not like me” — are obscured-neutral states. And these three absorptions also arise from (4) ignorance (avidya). It is said in the Longer Discourses: Such absorptions exemplify neutral formless meditative attainments, other desire-realm obscured states, and so on.[1442] Question: Now, there are the fourteen undeclared states: (1) the self and the world are permanent, or (2) impermanent, or (3) both, or (4) neither; or they (5) possess a limit, or (6) do not possess a limit, or (7) both, or (8) neither; or so too, they are (9) born from moisture and above, or not (10), or (11) both, or (12) neither; or (13) just the body is life force, or (14) life force is one thing and the body is something else. Are they called “undeclared” because they are not declared to be virtuous, nonvirtuous, or neutral? Reply: No, it is because they are posited as undeclared answers to questions. Question: In what way?
mgo gcig dang ni rnam phye dang / / dri dang gzhag par lung bstan pa/ / 'chi dang skye dang khyad par 'phags/ / bdag gzhan la sogs lta bu yin/ / 22
Stated categorically, through qualifying, through questioning, through remaining silent. For example, they die, they are reborn, they are superior, and is the self other and so on. (5:22)

dri ba'i lan ni mgo gcig tu lung bstan pa dang rnam par phye ste lung bstan pa dang dris te lung bstan pa dang*/ gzhag par lung bstan pa bzhi yod pa las/ dang po ni dper na ci sems can skyes pa thams cad 'chi bar 'gyur ram zhes 'dri na 'chi'o/ / zhes lan gdab pa lta bu dang*/ gnyis pa ni dper na ci 'chi ba thams cad skye'am zhes 'dri na nyon mongs pa med pa rnams mi skye la nyon mongs pa dang bcas pa rnams skye'o zhes lan gdab pa lta bu dang*/ gsum pa ni dper na ci mi 'di khyad par du 'phags pa yin nam/ 'on te dman pa yin zhes 'dri na lha la ltos nas sam ngan song la ltos nas 'dri zhes kho nyid la dris te lha la ltos nas zhes zer na ni dman la ngan song la ltos nas 'dri na ni khyad par du 'phags so zhes lan gdab pa lta bu dang*/ bzhi pa ni dper na ci bdag phung po las gzhan yin nam gcig pa yin zhes bya ba dang*/ de dag la sogs pas bzung ba gnyis ka'am gnyis ka ma yin pa gang yin zhes 'dri na gang du'ang lan mi gdab pa lta bu yin te/ de ltar na dri ba'i lung bstan pa bzhi las bcu bzhi po de dag ni mi dge ba yin yang mtha' gcig tu lung bstan par bya ba ma yin pas na lung ma bstan zhes bya'o/ / des na de dag ni bcom ldan 'das kyis kyang lung du ma bstan te/ thams cad bdag la brtsams nas smra ba na de ma grub pa'i phyir dang*/ med do zhes bstan na'ang de dag skrag par 'gyur bas de dag bstan pa la rim gyis bzhugs pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na lung bstan par 'gal lo zhe na/ de dag tu lung mi bstan to zhes gzhag par lung bstan pa'i phyir 'gal ba med do/ / de'i phyir mdo las kyang dris pa lung bstan pa ni rnam pa bzhi ste/ bzhi gang zhe na/ mgo gcig tu dris pa lung bstan pa dang*/ rnam par phye ste dris pa lung bstan pa dang*/ dri ba dris te lung bstan pa dang*/ rnam par bzhag pa lung bstan pa'o zhes pa dang*/ mgo gcig lung bstan nyid dang ni/ / rnam par phye ba de bzhin gzhan/ / dris pa lung bstan gsum pa ste/ / rnam par bzhag pa bzhi pa'o/ / dris pa lung bstan bzhi po dag /de dang de la go rim bzhin/ / 'di ltar shes shing smra ba dag /dge slong de nyid rig pa yin zhes rnam par bzhag pa'ang lung bstan pa nyid du gsungs so/ /

Reply: Answers to questions are (1) stated (vyākaraṇa) categorically (ekāṃśata), (2) declared through qualifying (vibhajya), (3) declared through questioning (paripṛcchya), and (4) declared through remaining silent (sthāpya). (1) The first is, for example, if it is asked, “Do all sentient beings who are born die?” it is answered, “They die.” (2) The second is, for example, if it is asked, “Are all those who die, reborn?” it is answered, “Those free of afflictions are not reborn, but those with afflictions are reborn.” (3) The third is, for example, if it is asked, “Are those who are humans superior or inferior?” it is answered, “Regarding gods they are inferior, but regarding animals they are superior.” (4) The fourth is, for example, if it is asked, “Is the self other than the aggregates or are they one?” where “so on” refers to “Are they both?” or “Are they neither?” [458] then there is no possible answer. Thus those fourteen [answers] to the four declared questions are termed “undeclared,” since though they are nonvirtuous, that was not absolutely declared by the Buddha. He did not declare them because if he said “I have composed an answer,” it would not be accepted. He did address them serially, for if he said “there is no answer,” others would be afraid. Objection: This contradicts that they are declared! Reply: By positing them to be “undeclared” they were declared, and thus there is no contradiction. Because of that a sūtra states: Declaring answers to questions has four types. What are those four? Declaring an answer to a question categorically, declaring an answer to a question through qualifying, declaring an answer to a query through questioning, and declaring an answer to a question through remaining silent. And: Declaring an answer to a question categorically, through qualifying, and through questioning like the others are the three declared answers. Remaining silent is the fourth. Monks, you should recognize the four declared answers to questions respectively in terms of understanding the question and to whom the answer was addressed.[1443]
drug pa ldan pa'i tshul 'chad pa ni/
How one possesses them

{ phra rgyas ldan tshul la'ang*/ yang zag gang gi phra rgyas dmigs pa gang la rgyas pa'i gang zag de ni/ phra rgyas des bcings shing de'i yul dang yang ldan no/ / sgo lnga'i shes pa'i phra rgyas kyis ni dmigs pa'i sgo nas rang gi yul dang ldan par byed do/ / yid kyi phra rgyas kyis ni dmigs pa'i sgo nas skye mched bcu gnyis dang ldan par byed do/ / kun 'gro rnams kyis ni dmigs pa'i sgo nas ris lnga dang ldan par byed la/ kun 'gro ma yin pas ni rang ris kho na dang ngo*/ / de dag dang mtshungs ldan gyis ni mtshungs ldan gyi sgo nas ldan par byed pa thams cad la 'dra'o/ /} nyon mongs pa la rang gi mtshan nyid pa dang*/ spyi'i mtshan nyid pa gnyis las dang po ni 'dod chags dang khong khro dang nga rgyal te/ yul rang gi mtshan nyid la dmigs pa'i phyir te/ 'dod chags dang nga rgyal ni bde ba myong bar 'gyur ba'i yul la dmigs nas skye zhing khengs la khong khro ni sdug bsngal myong bar 'gyur ba'i yul la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / gnyis pa ni lta ba dang the tshom dang ma rig pa ste bye brag med par bde ba myong bar 'gyur ba dang sdug bsngal myong bar 'gyur ba dang btang snyoms myong bar 'gyur ba la sogs pa'i yul gsum ga la ci rigs par dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ /

{Regarding how negative tendencies are possessed, those whose negative tendencies increase toward specific focal objects are bound by such negative tendencies and possess their objects. Negative tendencies of the five doors of sense consciousness possess their objects by means of focal object. Negative tendencies of the mental faculty possess the twelve bases by means of focal object. Pervasive negative tendencies possess the five types of abandonment by means of focal object. Those negative tendencies that are not pervasive possess their own type alone. Those concomitant with them are all similar in actively possessing them by means of concomitance.} Afflicted states are of two types, real and abstract. The first is attachment, anger, and pride, because they focus on real objects. Attachment arises and pride inflates the mind through focusing on objects that give rise to the experience of pleasure. Anger focuses on objects that give rise to the experience of pain. The second — abstract afflicted states — are view, doubt, and ignorance, which focus on any of the three objects without dividing them into those that give rise to the experience of pleasure, those that give rise to the experience of pain, those that give rise to the experience of equanimity, and so on.
'das dang nyer gnas 'dod chags dang / / khong khro nga rgyal dag gis ni/ / gang la de skyes ma spangs pa'i/ / dngos po de dang ldan pa yin/ 23

One who possesses them is bound by attachment, anger, and pride that arose in the past and abide in the present toward the objects of those arisen and unabandoned [afflictions focusing] on any of the five. (5:23)

de la 'das pa dang nye bar gnas pa da ltar byung ba'i 'dod chags dang khong khro dang nga rgyal skyes la ma spangs pa dag gis ni rnam shes{ drug gi sa pa yin pas rnam shes drug} gang gi 'khor du byung yang rung ste/ yul spang bya ris lnga po dus gsum pa'i dngos po gang la dmigs nas nyon mongs pa de dag skyes la ma spangs pa'i yul gyi dngos po de dang thag pas glang bu phur pa la btags pa ltar gang zag de ldan{ par byed} pa yin no/ / {'di dag gi yul thams cad la dmigs mi nus la spangs na yul la mi rgyas so } de yang sgo lnga'i rnam shes kyi 'khor du ni chags sdang gnyis 'byung gi nga rgyal ni yid shes kho na'i 'khor du 'byung ngo*/ / skyes zhes bya ba ni nyon mongs pa de dag rang gi mtshan nyid pa yin pas 'ga' zhig la mi skye ba srid pa'i phyir ro/ / ma spangs pa zhes bya ba ni skyes kyang spangs na mi ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / des na de dag bcad pa'i phyir tshig gnyis po de smros so/ / ldan pa zhes bya ba'ang yul de dag la dmigs pa'i tshul gyis gang zag la{ spang byar} ldan pa yin gyi yul gyi{ thob pa} ldan pa ma yin te {'gog pa gnyis ma gtogs pa }rgyud du ma gtogs pa la{ thob pa} ldan pa med pa'i phyir ro/ {/des ni rang gi ris kho na ldan par 'gyur ro/ / des mtshon nas mi rgyas pa'i yul kun mi ldan la/ nyon mongs pa'i thob pa rgyud gang la yod pa'i yul de gang zag de dang ldan no gsung ngo*/}/

A person who possesses them is bound by attachment, anger, and pride that have arisen and have not been abandoned. These arose in the past and abide in the present and occur in the retinue of any {of the six consciousnesses, since they exist on the level of the six types of} consciousness. They are directed toward the objects of those arisen and unabandoned afflictions that focus, like a calf tied to a peg by a rope, on any of the five types of object of abandonment of the three times. [459] {They cannot focus on all these objects, and when abandoned, the objects do not increase}. Further, both attachment and aversion occur in the retinue of consciousness of the five sense doors, and pride occurs in the retinue of mental consciousness alone. “Arisen” means actual manifest afflictions, since it is possible that some do not arise. “Unabandoned” means the affliction has already arisen and is not yet abandoned. These two terms are stated in order to refute [unintended connotations]. “Possesses” means that a person possesses those objects {as objects of abandonment} by means of focal object, but does not possess {the obtainment of} the object because {apart from the two cessations} there is no possession {of the obtainment} of that which does not belong to the mindstream. {Thus he comes to possess [objects] of this type alone. This means he does not possess any [afflicted] objects that do not increase, and it states that the obtainment of affliction is possessed by that person, as an object existing in his mindstream.}
yid kyi de dag ma 'ongs pas/ / kun dang gzhan gyis rang dus pa/ / mi skye rnams kyis thams cad dang / / lhag ma kun gyis kun dang ldan/ / 24

Those in the retinue of mental consciousness possess all since they engage future objects. Others possess objects of their own time. Unarisen instances possess all objects. Those remaining possess all in all. (5:24)
de ltar 'das pa dang da ltar byung ba'i 'dod chags la sogs pa la ni khyad par med pas spyir bshad la/ ma 'ongs pa la dbye ba yod pas de bshad pa'i phyir

Thus [objects of] attachment [and likewise anger and pride] that arise in the past and present are explained as a general group without distinction. But those of the future are differentiated and explained as follows.

yid kyi rnam shes kyi 'khor du byung ba'i 'dod chags la sogs pa gsum po de dag ni ma 'ongs pas 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar byung ba'i yul kun dang dmigs pa'i tshul gyis ldan te/ yid kyi yul du dus gsum pa'i chos 'gro ba'i phyir ro/ / de yang gang la ma spangs pa de dag ces bya ba yin no/ / yid las gzhan pa sgo lnga'i rnam shes kyi 'khor du byung ba'i 'dod chags dang khong khro ma 'ongs pa dag gis ni yul rang gi dus pa ma 'ongs pa'i dngos po kho na dang ldan te/ rnam shes de dag 'das pa{ dang ma 'ongs pa} la mi dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / skye ba'i chos can rnams kyi de lta bu yin gyi mi skye ba'i chos can rnams kyis ni sgo lnga'i rnam shes kyi 'khor du byung ba'i 'dod chags dang khong khro gnyis kyis kyang{ ma spangs na} dus gsum pa'i dngos po thams cad dang dmigs pa'i tshul gyis ldan no/ / {de yang de dag mang bas dmigs rung du ldan gyi dngos su dmigs pa ni ma yin no } rang gi mtshan nyid pa de dag gi lhag ma{ spyi'i mtshan nyid pa gsum po} lta ba dang the tshom dang ma rig pa ste de dag 'das pa la sogs pa dus gsum po kun gyis kyang yul dus gsum gyi dngos po ris lnga po kun dang ldan te/ de dag ni nyer len gyi phung po lnga char la dmigs pas spyi'i mtshan nyid la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / de yang ji srid du ma spangs kyi bar du'o/ / gal te 'das ma 'ongs rdzas su yod na ni dus thams cad du yod pa'i phyir 'dus byas rtag par 'gyur la/ med na dus gnyis kyi dngos po de dag dang phra rgyas des ldan pa dang bral bar ji ltar 'gyur zhe na/

Those three — attachment, anger, and pride — can engage future objects since they occur in the retinue of mental consciousness. They possess all objects occurring in the past, present, and future as focal objects since phenomena of the three times function as mental objects for them. Moreover, it is those [afflictions] that are not abandoned that are known thus. Future attachment and anger occurring in the retinue of the five sensory consciousnesses that are other than mental consciousness possess only future objects of their own time [i.e., when they exist in future]. But these [sensory] consciousnesses do not focus on the past {and future}. Arisen instances of attachment and anger are like this, but unarisen instances of both attachment and anger {if not abandoned} that occur in the retinue of the five sensory consciousnesses possess all objects of the three times through those being their focal object. {Further, many of these are possessed as potential focal objects, not as actual focal objects}. Those remaining real entities of view, doubt, and ignorance {are actually three abstract entities that} possess all five types of object of the three times in all the three times of past, present, and future. That is because they focus on abstract entities — the five appropriated aggregates. This applies up to the point that they are abandoned. Question: If the past and future exist substantially, then conditioned states would be permanent because they would exist in all three times. If they do not exist substantially, how could negative tendencies come to possess, or be free of, the objects of those two times?
dus rnams kun tu yod gsungs phyir/ / gnyis phyir yul yod phyir 'bras phyir/ / de yod smra ba'i phyir thams cad/ / yod par smra bar 'dod de dag / 25

Times exist in all three times because he stated it, because it depends on both, because the object exists, because the result exists. They are said to be Sarvāstivādins because they advocate the existence of the three times. (5:25)

bye brag tu smra ba rnams ni dus de dag 'dus byas kyi mtshan nyid skye sogs bzhi dang ldan pa'i phyir rtag par ni mi 'dod kyi 'das pa la sogs pa'i dus rnams rang rang gi dus kun tu rdzas su yod par ni gsal bar dam 'cha'o/ / ci'i phyir zhe na/ bcom ldan 'das kyis yod par gsungs pa'i phyir te/ ji ltar zhe na/ dge slong dag gzugs 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa'ang mi rtag na da ltar byung ba lta ci smros/ 'phags pa nyan thos thos pa dang ldan pa de ltar lta ba ni 'das pa'i gzugs la lta bar mi 'gyur/ ma 'ongs pa'i gzugs la mngon par dga' bar mi 'gyur gyi da ltar byung ba'i gzugs la yid byung bar bya ba dang*/ 'dod chags dang bral bar bya ba dang*/ 'gog par bya ba'i phyir zhugs pa yin no/ / dge slong dag gal te 'das pa'i gzugs shig yod par ma gyur na 'phags pa nyan thos pa dang ldan pa 'das pa'i gzugs la mi lta bar yang mi 'gyur ba zhig na/ gang gi phyir 'das pa'i gzugs yod pa de'i phyir 'phags pa nyan thos thos pa dang ldan pa 'das pa'i gzugs la mi lta ba yin no/ / gal te ma 'ongs pa'i gzugs shig yod par ma gyur na 'phags pa nyan thos thos pa dang ldan pa thos ma 'ongs pa'i gzugs la mngon par dga' ba med par yang mi 'gyur ba zhig na/ gang gi phyir ma 'ongs pa'i gzugs yod pa de'i phyir 'phags pa nyan thos thos pa dang ldan pa ma 'ongs pa'i gzugs la mngon par dga' ba med pa yin no zhes dus gnyis yod par gsungs pa'i phyir te/ gal te 'das ma 'ongs med na de ltar gsung par ji ltar 'gyur/ yang mdo las/ mig nas yid kyi rnam par shes pa'i bar ni mig dang gzugs nas yid dang chos kyi bar gnyis la brten nas skye bar gsungs pa'i phyir te/ mig gi rnam par shes pa ni mig dang gzugs dang zhes bya ba nas yid kyi rnam par shes pa ni yid dang chos la brten nas skye'o zhes bya ba'i bar te/ 'di la yid kyi rnam shes yid dang chos gnyis la brten pa ni 'di'i shes par byed pa yin te/ yid 'das pa rdzas su med na rang nyid rang la brten par 'gal ba'i phyir ro zhes pa'i lung dang*/ yul med na dmigs pa med pa'i phyir de dag gi rnam shes kyang med par 'gyur na/ 'das ma 'ongs la dmigs pa'i rnam shes kyi yul yod pa'i phyir dang*/ las kyi rnam par smin pa'i 'bras bu yod pa'i phyir

Vaibhāṣikas do not assert these times to be permanent because they possess the four characteristics [460] of conditioned states such as arising. They clearly assert that the times of past, present, and future substantially exist in all three times separately. Question: Why? Reply: That is because the Bhagavan stated that they exist in this way. Question: How? Reply: A sūtra declares: Monks, if past as well as future form were impermanent, then it goes without saying that present form would be as well. Learned ārya śrāvakas do not see past form, nor are they attracted to future form because they enter [meditation] generating disappointment with present form, and they are freed from and sever attachment to present form. Monks, if a single past form did not exist, then learned ārya śrāvakas not seeing past form would not arise. Because past form exists, learned ārya śrāvakas do not see past form. If future form did not exist, then learned ārya śrāvakas’ aversion to future form would not arise. Because future form exists, learned ārya śrāvakas’ aversion to future form arises.[1444] Here the Bhagavan states that those two times exist. Why would he say that if the past and future did not exist? Again, a sūtra states: Eye consciousness up to mental consciousness arise [respectively] in dependence on both the eye and form, up to both mental consciousness and phenomena.[1445] This scripture explains that because eye consciousness refers to “that arisen in dependence on both the eye and form” and mental consciousness refers to “that arisen in dependence on both mental consciousness and phenomena,” it should be understood that mental consciousness depends on both the mental faculty and phenomena. If the past mental faculty did not substantially exist, then [mental consciousness] would depend on itself, and that would be contradictory.
If the object did not exist, then the consciousness of it would not exist because that consciousness would have no focal object. However, the past and future substantially exist because the object of a consciousness that focuses on the past and future exists and because the maturational result of karma exists.

yang 'das ma 'ongs rdzas su yod de/ de dag rdzas su med na las yod pa'i tshe rnam par smin pa med la rnam par smin pa yod par 'dod pa'i tshe las 'gags nas med pa'i phyir ro zhes bya ba'i rigs pas kyang grub bo/ / thams cad yod par smra ba yin phan chad gdon za bar dus gsum{ dang gzhi lnga po} dngos por yod pa 'di khas blang dgos te{ gzhi dang lnga} dus gsum po de thams cad yod par smra ba'i phyir thams cad yod par smra bar 'dod kyi/ da ltar ba dang 'bras bu ma bskyed pa'i las 'das pa cung zad cig ni yod la ma 'ongs pa dang 'bras bu bskyed zin pa'i 'das pa cung zad cig ni med par smra ba ni rnam par phye ste smra bar 'gyur ba'i phyir ro zhes bye brag tu smra ba rnams 'dod do/ / de'i phyir slob dpon gang spel gyis kyang*/ dus gsum ga yod par smra ba dang*/ da ltar dang 'das pa 'bras bu ma bskyed pa yod par smra ba dang*/ da ltar byung ba yod par smra ba rnams ni go rim bzhin du thams cad yod par smra ba dang*/ rnam par phye ste smra ba dang*/ mdo sde pa yin no zhes bshad do/ /

Again, the past and future substantially exist because if they did not substantially exist, then logically, when karma exists maturation would not exist, and when maturation is asserted to exist karma would no longer exist, since the karma would have ceased. This is asserted by Sarvāstivādins. Both those and higher schools necessarily accept unreservedly that the three times are things {subsumed within the five basic categories}.[1446] They are asserted to be Sarvāstivādins because they advocate the existence of all three times. Those who advocate the existence of some past ungenerated results in the present and the nonexistence of some past already generated results in the future are Vibhajyavādins. This is asserted [461] by Vaibhāṣikas. Therefore Master Pūrṇavardhana explains that (1) those advocating the existence of the three times, (2) those advocating existence of the nongeneration of results in the present and past, and (3) those advocating existence occurring in the present are, respectively, Sarvāstivādins, Vibhajyavādins, and Sautrāntikas.[1447]
rnam bzhi dngos dang mtshan nyid dang / / gnas skabs gzhan gzhan 'gyur zhes bya/ gsum pa bzang ste bya ba yis/ / dus rnams rnam gzhag gegs su byed/ / 26
They are four: the transformation of state, characteristics, context, and mutual reliance. The third is best because the three actions represent the three times. What acts to hinder action? (5:26)

gang dag dus gsum rdzas su yod par 'dod pa'i thams cad yod par smra ba de dag kyang dbye na rnam pa bzhi yin te/ dngos po gzhan du 'gyur ba dang*/ mtshan nyid gzhan du 'gyur ba dang*/ gnas skabs gzhan du 'gyur ba dang*/ gzhan dang gzhan du 'gyur ba zhes bya ba'o/ / de la dngos po gzhan du 'gyur bar smra ba ni btsun pa chos skyabs yin te/ de ni shes pa dang brjod pa 'jug pa'i khyad par la ltos nas tha dad de dngos po gcig nyid dus rnams su 'jug cing 'pho ba na gzugs la sogs pa'i rdzas kyi rang gi mtshan nyid ni mi 'gyur gyi ma 'ongs pa da ltar du 'gyur ba na ma 'ongs pa'i dngos po 'dor zhing da ltar byung ba'i dngos po 'thob la/ da ltar ba 'das par 'gyur ba na'ang da ltar gyi dngos po 'dor zhing 'das pa'i dngos po 'thob pas dus de dang der 'das pa'i dngos po dang ma 'ongs pa'i dngos po dang da ltar byung ba'i dngos po zhes bya ba'i ming thob ste dper na gser gyi snod bcom nas snod gzhan du bsgyur ba na gser gyi rang bzhin dang kha dog la 'gyur ba med kyang snod kyi dbyibs tsam zhig gzhan du 'gyur ba dang*/ 'o ma zhor 'gyur ba na ro nus la sogs pa'i yon tan tsam zhig 'dor gyi rdzas dang kha dog mi 'dor ba lta bu'o zhes zer ro/ /

Those who assert the three times substantially exist are Sarvāstivādins, and they in turn are classified as four types: those who advocate (1) the transformation of state (bhāva), (2) the transformation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa), (3) the transformation of context (avasthā), and (4) the transformation through mutual reliance (anyathā).[1448] (1) Bhadanta Dharmatrāta advocates the transformation of state and asserts that time is differentiated in reliance on a thing’s attributes that are engaged by word and concept, and when one single thing enters the three times and progresses [from one time to another], the specific substance of its visible form and so on does not transform. Instead, when the future transforms into the present, the future state is destroyed, and a state occurring in the present is obtained. When the present transforms into the past, the present state is destroyed and a state occurring in the past is obtained. It therefore obtains at those times the names “a state that is past,” “a state that is future,” and “a state presently occuring.” An example is when one melts down a golden vessel and transforms it into other vessels where merely the shape of the vessel transforms but the essence of gold and its color does not transform. Another is when milk becomes curd and the qualities of its taste and potency are destroyed but its substance and color are not.[1449]

mtshan nyid gzhan du 'gyur bar smra ba ni btsun pa dbyangs sgrogs yin te/ de ni mtshan nyid 'jug pa thob pa la ltos nas tha snyad byed de/ dngos po gcig nyid 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar byung ba'i mtshan nyid dang ldan pa'i phyir mtshan nyid tha dad pa'i sgo nas dus gsum du gzhag gi de dag la dus gzhan gyi mtshan nyid gtan med pa dang rdzas tha dad pa ni ma yin te dper na chags can bud med cig la chags pa dang bcas pa de gzhan la chags pa dang bral ba ma yin pa bzhin no zhes zer ro/ / gnas skabs gzhan du 'gyur bar smra ba ni btsun pa dbyig bshes yin te/ de ni gnas skabs tha dad la ltos nas {te dper na 'das pa'i mtshan nyid gtso che ba na 'das par bzhag pas/ des na } tha snyad byed de dngos po gcig nyid dus rnams su 'jug pa na chos de bya ba mi byed pa dang*/ bya ba byed pa dang*/ bya ba byas nas 'gags pa'i gnas skabs gsum la rim pa ltar ma 'ongs pa dang da ltar dang 'das pa zhes brjod pas dngos po gcig nyid dus de dang de'i gnas skabs su phyin pa na de dang de'i ming 'thob pas na 'das pa la sogs pa'i gnas skabs su ming tsam zhig gzhan du 'gyur gyi rang mtshan gyi rdzas gzhan du 'gyur ba ni ma yin te dper na ri lu gcig nyid gcig gi shod mig tu bzhag na gcig dang*/ brgya'i shod mig tu bzhag na brgya dang*/ stong gi shod mig tu bzhag na stong zhes brjod pa bzhin no zhes zer ro/ /

(2) Bhadanta Ghoṣaka advocates the transformation of characteristics and asserts that such terms [as “past” and so on] are applied in reliance on activating their characteristics. One single thing possesses the characteristics of the past, the future, and the present and the three times are posited by means of their distinct characteristics. But it is not that each of the three times never possesses the characteristics of the other times or is distinct in substance. It is like one who is attached to one woman and yet is not free of attachment to other women.[1450] (3) Bhadanta Vasumitra advocates the transformation of context and asserts that those terms are applied in reliance on distinct contexts. {For example, if the characteristics of the past are predominant, it is posited as “past.”} If one single thing enters the [three] times, then that phenomenon has three contexts — not yet engaging in action, engaging in action, and having ceased engaging in action — and these are called, respectively, the future, the present, and the past. Therefore, when a single thing functions in a specific context, it obtains a specific name, and just that name [applied] in the context of the past and so on transforms, but the real substance does not transform. For example, in an abacus, [462] if the bead is placed in the first slot it is one, in the hundred slot it is one hundred, and in the thousand slot it is one thousand.[1451]

gzhan dang gzhan du 'gyur ba smra ba ni btsun pa sangs rgyas lha yin te/ de ni snga phyi gnyis la ltos nas tha snyad byed de/ dngos po gcig po de nyid dus rnams su 'jug pa na snga ma 'das da ltar gnyis la ltos nas ma 'ongs pa dang*/ phyi ma da ltar dang ma 'ongs pa gnyis la ltos nas 'das pa dang snga ma 'das pa dang phyi ma ma 'ongs pa gnyis la ltos nas da ltar bar bzhag ste dper na bud med gcig nyid bu mo la ltos nas ma dang ma la ltos nas bu mor 'gyur ba bzhin no zhes zer ro/ /

(4) Bhadanta Buddhadeva advocates the transformation of mutual reliance and asserts that those terms are applied in reliance on both earlier and later states. If a single thing engages those times, the future is posited in reliance on both the past and the present that precede it, the past is posited in reliance on both the present and the future that occur later, and the present is posited in reliance on both the preceding past and the subsequent future. For example, an individual woman is a mother in reliance on her daughter and a daughter in reliance on her mother.[1452]

de la{ de dag la slob dpon gyis} dngos po gzhan du 'gyur ba ni { dang po} rnam par 'gyur bar smra ba'i grangs{ rdzas gnas la chos 'dor len byed par 'dod pa'i phyir} can gyi nang du 'dus par 'gyur ro/ / mtshan nyid gzhan du 'gyur bar smra ba la ni dus re re la'ang dus gsum ga'i mtshan nyid dang ldan pa'i phyir dus 'chol bar 'gyur ba dang*/ dpe don mi mtshungs pa'i skyon du 'gyur ro/ / gzhan dang gzhan du 'gyur ba la ni 'das pa'i dus la'ang snga phyi dbus gsum yod pas de dag rim pa ltar 'das ma 'ongs da ltar gsum du 'gyur bas 'das pa gcig pu la'ang dus gsum cig car 'byung bar 'gyur ba'i skyon yod pa'i phyir

In this respect {Master Vasubandhu observes that the first position,} advocating the transformation of state, should be included within the views of the Sāṃkhya, {who assert that substance endures [without change]}. For those advocating transformation of characteristics, time would become confused, because each of the three times would possess the characteristics of the three times, and there is the error that the example and meaning are not in accord. For those advocating transformation through mutual reliance, past time would then have three phases — former, latter, and intermediate — that respectively would be past, future, and present, and there would be the error that in the past the three times would occur at the one time.

gsum pa gnas skabs gzhan du 'gyur bar smra ba nyid bzang ste/ bya ba ma skyes nas mi byed pa dang byed pa dang byas nas 'gags pa gsum po yis dus gsum po rnams rnam par bzhag pa byed pa'i phyir ro zhes gsungs mod kyi bzhi ka la ming tha dad pa ma gtogs pa khyad par ci yang yod par ma mthong ngo*/ / 'o na dus gsum du ji ltar 'gyur te/ thams cad da ltar rdzas su yod pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ bye brag tu smra ba na re/ bya ba 'gags pa ni 'das pa'o/ / bya ba ma skyes pa ni ma 'ongs pa'o/ / bya ba skyes la ma 'gags pa ni da ltar ba yin pas dus gsum bya bas gzhag go zhes bshad zin pa ma yin nam zhes zer ro/ / slob dpon gyis de lta na da ltar ba'i mig de mtshungs rang gi bya ba gzugs la mi blta bas da ltar bar mi 'gyur ro zhes brjod pa na bye brag tu smra ba na re mig de mtshungs de blta ba'i bya ba mi byed kyang rang gi rgyu mthun dang skyes bu byed 'bras 'dzin pa dang 'byin pa'i bya ba byed pas na da ltar ba yin no zhes zer ro/ / slob dpon gyis 'o na ni da ltar gyi dang 'das pa dag gcig ni 'das pas 'byin par 'gyur zhes 'byung bas skal mnyam dang kun 'gro dang rnam smin gyi rgyu 'das pa dag kyang da ltar bar 'gyur te de dag la 'bras bu 'byin pa'i bya ba yod pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te 'bras bu 'dzin pa dang 'byin pa'i bya ba gnyis ka yod pa la da ltar bar brjod pa na de dag la 'bras bu 'byin pa yod kyang 'dzin pa med pas da ltar bar mi 'gyur ro zhe na/

The third, transformation of context, is best because the three actions — that which is not active since it is unarisen, that which is active, and that which has ceased having been active — represent the three times. But though this statement is true, nevertheless, there is no difference in these four positions whatsoever, other than a difference in name. Question: Now, how do the three times arise, given that all are substantially existent in the present? Vaibhāṣikas say: The three times are posited by action: action that has ceased is the past, action not arisen is the future, and action arisen and not ceased is the present. But hasn’t this been explained already? Vasubandhu suggests: If that is so, the eye of the present would not exist in the present, since [eyes] that are partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga) do not see form.[1453] Vaibhāṣikas say: Though that eye that is partially homogeneous does not see, it exists in the present since it holds and produces a result of natural outflow and a result of conscious effort.[1454] Vasubandhu states that the past homogeneous cause, past omnipresent cause, and past cause of karmic maturation would also become present states because they would possess the production of results. As the Abhidharmakośa mentions, “Two produce results as present and past causes. One produces its result in the past alone” (2:59cd).[1455] Objection: If something is called “present” since it is something that both bears a result and something that is productive activity,[1456] then it follows it cannot exist in the present; it does not bear a result even though it is productive of a result. [463]

de lta na'ang dus gsum du bya bas bzhag pas na de dag la 'bras bu 'dzin pa'i bya ba 'gags pa'i cha nas 'das par 'gyur la/ 'byin pa'i bya ba dang ldan nas da ltar bar 'gyur bas dus gsum mtshan nyid 'chol ba'i nyes par 'gyur ro zhes skyon brjod do/ /

Reply: If the three times are posited in that way due to their function in the three times, then the error would arise that the characteristics of the three times would become confused, since something would be past due to the cessation of the activity that bears a result, and present due to possessing productive activity.

gzhan yang 'di dgag pa'i phyir 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa rdzas su yod pa'i phyir de bya ba byed pa la bgegs su zhig byed de/ de dag gis kyang rtag tu bya ba byed par 'gyur ro/ / gal te rgyu rkyen ma tshogs pas bya ba mi byed do zhe na/ rkyen thams cad dus rtag tu yod par khas blangs pa na rtag tu yod pa la ma tshogs pa mi 'thad pa'i phyir ro/ / bya ba 'gags pa dang ma 'ongs pa yin na bya ba dang dngos po mi gcig par 'gyur la de lta na'ang dngos po bya ba med par 'gyur ro/ /

Further, because this is refuted, and because the past and future are substantially existent, what acts to hinder them from engaging in action, for they would always engage in action? Objection: If causes and conditions do not assemble, there is no engagement in action. Reply: If one accepts that all conditions always exist, it would be untenable that those that always exist do not assemble. If the action had ceased or exists in the future, the action and the thing would not be one, and as such, things would have no action whatsoever.
de yang ji ltar gzhan ma yin/ / dus su mi rung de bzhin du/ / yod na ci phyir ma skyes zhig / chos nyid dag ni zab pa yin/ / 27

Further, how is action past and so on? They are not separate. It is untenable to posit the three times by action. If they exist in that way, how could they be unarisen and destroyed? The reality of phenomena is profound. (5:27)

bya ba de yang ji ltar 'das pa la sogs pa yin nam/ 'on te ma yin/ phyogs dang po ltar na bya ba la'ang bya ba gzhan gnyis pa zhig yod par 'gyur te/ bya ba de yang bya ba 'gags pa dang byed pa dang ma skyes pas dus gsum par gzhag dgos pa'i phyir ro/ / phyogs gnyis pa ltar na bya ba 'dus ma byas su 'gyur te/ dus kyis ma bsdus pa'i phyir ro/ /

Further, how is action either (1) past and so on or (2) not past and so on? According to the first possibility, any action exists with the destruction of the other two actions because action must be posited with regard to the three times: action that has ceased, action now occurring, and action unarisen. According to the second possibility, they would be unconditioned because they would not be subsumed within time.

gal te bya ba dngos po las gzhan ma yin no zhe na/ de ltar na bya bas dus gsum po rnams su rnam par bzhag par mi rung ste/ dngos po dang bya ba gcig yin la 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa'i dngos po'ang da ltar yod pas bya ba'ang yod pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te da ltar ba ji ltar yod pa de bzhin du ma 'ongs pa dang 'das pa'i dngos po'ang yod na ci'i phyir ma skyes pa dang zhig pa yin te de dag yod pa'i phyir ro/ / gal te ma skyes pa dang zhig pa ni bya ba yin no zhe na/ de yang dngos po'i bdag nyid yin pa'i phyir dngos po bzhin yod par 'gyur ro zhes slob dpon gyis brjod do/ / gang yang 'dus byas kyi mtshan nyid dang ldan pas rtag par mi 'gyur ro zhes smras pa de yang tshig tsam yin te/ dngos po dus thams cad du yod pa la skye 'jig mi rung ba'i phyir ro/ / des na 'grel par/ rang bzhin yang ni rtag tu yod/ / dngos po yang ni rtag mi 'dod/ / rang bzhin las kyang dngos mi gzhan/ / dbang phyug tha snyad yin par gsal zhes bshad la/ / bcom ldan 'das kyis 'das ma 'ongs yod par gsungs pa ni 'das pa sngar byung ba nyid du yod pa dang ma 'ongs pa ni rgyu rkyen yod na 'byung bar 'gyur ba'i dbang du mdzad nas yod pa'i sgrar gsungs kyi rdzas kyi rang gi mtshan nyid du yod pa ni ma yin te dper na mar me shi ba yod do zhes bya ba la sogs pa bzhin no/ /

Objection: Actions are not separate from things. Reply: Thus it would be untenable to posit the three times by means of action because if things and action are the same entity, then just as past and future things exist, so too action would exist. If future and past things were to exist in the way that present states exist, how could they, being existent, be unarisen (ajāta) and destroyed (naṣṭa)? Question: What if “unarisen and destroyed” (5:27c) were actions? Vasubandhu mentions that they would come to exist like things because they are states of things.[1457] Further, statements such as “They are not permanent since they possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena” would be mere idle words, because it would be untenable that things that exist in all three times would arise and disintegrate. Therefore the Autocommentary explains: The essence [is posited to] exist as permanent, but things are not permanent, and since the essence is not separate from things, it is clear that Īśvara is just a convention.[1458] The Bhagavan stated that the past and future exist. He stated the term “exist” from the perspective of the past existing through having occurred previously and the future coming to occur when the causes and conditions exist. However, they do not exist as real substance for they are like the disintegrated flame of a butter lamp and so on.[1459]

yid kyi rnam shes chos dang yid gnyis la brten par bshad pa'i yid ni snga ma'i rjes thogs su 'byung ba'am/ nyon mongs pa can gyi yid kyi dbang du mdzad nas gsungs pa yin la/ yid kyi yul 'das pa dang ma 'ongs par bshad pa ni dmigs pa tsam du gsungs pa yin gyi dmigs pa'i rkyen ni ma yin no/ / gang yang dag par ldan pa'i lung las kun du rgyu dbyug thogs thor tshugs can rnams kyi dbang du mdzad nas/ las 'das pa dang*/ zad pa dang*/ 'gags pa dang*/ bral ba dang*/ rnam par 'gyur ba gang yin pa de ni yod do zhes gsungs pa de yang rgyud de la sngon gyi las des kun du drangs shing bzhag pa'i rnam smin skyed pa'i nus pa yod par bstan pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar ma yin na 'das par mi 'gyur te/ da ltar rang gi mtshan nyid du yod pa'i phyir ro/ /

Mental consciousness is said to depend on the mental faculty and phenomena, and the mental faculty arises immediately after earlier states, or it is explained from the perspective of afflicted intellect. Objects of the mental faculty that are explained as future or past objects are said to be merely focal objects and not objective conditions. Moreover, it is said [464] in the Connected Discourses: From the perspective of the Lāguḍaśikhīyaka, any karma that is past, exhausted, ceased, separated, or transformed exists.[1460] This indicates that past karma fully activated and deposited within that mindstream possesses the potency to generate karmic maturation. If that were not so, it would not become past because the present would exist as a real entity.

gzhan yang bcom ldan 'das kyis don dam pa stong pa nyid kyi mdo las/ dge slong dag mig ni skye ba na'ang gang nas kyang mi 'ong la 'gag pa na'ang gang du yang rtsogs par mi 'gyur ro/ / de lta bas na dge slong dag mig ni ma byung ba las 'byung zhing byung nas kyang slar 'jig par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs pa dang 'gal bar 'gyur ro/ /

Furthermore, this would contradict the Bhagavan, who has stated in the Ultimate Emptiness Sūtra: Monks, from the eyes arising, in future they cease and do not remain at all. Monks, in that way eyes arise from that which has not arisen, and having arisen, they are again destroyed.[1461]
'dir bye brag smra ba dag ni rnam par brtag pa de dag gis ni mi gnod de/ chos rnams kyi chos nyid dag ni zab pa yin pas rtog ge'i spyod yul ma yin pa'i phyir ro zhes lan 'debs so/ /
Here the Vaibhāṣikas answer that such analysis does not harm their assertion because the reality (dharmatā) of phenomena is profound, and therefore it is not the domain of dialectitions.
yang nyon mongs pa gang dag rang nyid spangs kyang ldan pa'ang yod de/ de la dmigs pa'i yul can spangs pas yul yang bral bar mi 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / de dag kyang gang zhe na/

Again, though one abandons afflicted states one still possesses them, because one is not separated from the object by abandoning the mind that focuses on it. Question: What are abandonment and separation?
sdug bsngal mthong spang bya spangs kyang / / kun 'gro lhag ma rnams kyis ldan/ / dang po'i rnam pa spangs kyang de'i/ / yul can dri ma lhag rnams kyis/ / 28

One abandons that to be abandoned by seeing suffering and possesses the remaining pervasive negative tendencies. Though one abandons any aspect of the first, one possesses the remaining stains of the mind focusing on it. (5:28)

{ spangs pa dang bral ba'i khyad par ni dngos po gang zhig spangs na de dang bral ba yin nam/ bral na spangs pa yin nam zhe na/ spangs pa ni thob pa chad pa dang*/ bral ba ni yul can spangs pa'o/ / de la gang dang bral na des dngos po de spangs pa yin la/ spangs kyang ma bral ba yod de/ sdug bsngal shes pa skyes la kun 'byung shes pa ma skyes pa'i tshe/} sdug bsngal mthong bas spang bar bya spangs kyang{ de dag yul du byas nas ldan te} sdug bsngal mthong spang la dmigs pa'i kun 'gro lhag ma kun 'byung mthong spang gi kun 'gro rnams kyis dmigs pa'i sgo nas ldan pa'i phyir dang*/ de bzhin du sgom spang dang po'i rnam pa chen po'i chen po{ pa ci rigs} spangs kyang de la dmigs pa'i yul can gyi dri ma lhag ma chen po'i 'bring po la sogs pa gang ma spangs pa rnams kyis dmigs pa'i tshul gyis ldan pa yin no/ / 'dir yul can de dag ldan no zhes ston pa ni ma yin te/ 'on kyang yul can ldan pas yul spangs kyang ldan no zhes bya ba ni grub pa'i mtha' yin te/ 'di la ngo bo spangs na ci zhig ldan thob pa rdzas su yod pa ni bsal zin to zhes brjod par bya'o/ /

Reply: {Regarding the difference between abandonment and separation, if a thing is abandoned, is one separated from it? Or if separated from it, is it abandoned? Abandonment is severing [or stopping] possession, and separation is abandoning the mind engaging it. Whoever separates from a thing abandons it. Yet abandoning but not separating from something does exist, because when the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe jñāna) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (samudaye jñāna) has not yet arisen} one abandons (prahīṇa) that to be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering, and one possesses (saṃyukta) the remaining pervasive negative tendencies focusing on suffering that are pervasive states abandoned by seeing the truth of origin, due to their being focal objects. {That is, one possesses them through taking them as one’s object}. Similarly, though one abandons {any} great-of-the-great aspect of the first object to be abandoned by the path of meditation, one possesses the remaining stains of the mind (viṣaya) focusing on it — the focal objects that are great-of-the-medium objects of abandonment and so on that are not yet abandoned. Here it is not suggested that “these minds possess them” but rather the philosophical position that “due to possessing such minds one possesses objects to be abandoned,” for it is said, “If an entity had been abandoned, that which it possesses and subsequently obtains is also eliminated.”
bdun pa chos {gang zhig sems } du'i yul du 'gyur ba bshad pa ni
How phenomena {and minds} become their objects

Here, all objects are included in the sixteen aspects because they include the five types of abandonment for each of the three realms and uncontaminated states, {where uncontaminated states are also unconditioned}. Also, all sentient beings who possess objects are included in these sixteen aspects. [465] Therefore, if one knows what phenomenon becomes the object of what mind, one will know what increases affliction by means of focal object. {Further, objects abandoned by the path of seeing are subsumed by four aggregates, and objects abandoned by the path of meditation are subsumed by five aggregates.}
sdug bsngal rgyu mthong goms pa yis/ / spang bya 'dod khams las skyes pa/ / rang gi gsum dang gzugs gtogs gcig / dri med rnam shes spyod yul lo/ / 29

That arisen in the desire realm that is abandoned by seeing suffering and its cause, and by meditation, are objects of five. Three of its level, one of the form realm, and one stainless consciousness. (5:29)

de la sdug bsngal dang sdug bsngal gyi rgyu kun 'byung mthong spang dang*/ lam goms pa yis spang bar bya ba 'dod pa'i khams las skyes pa {lhan cig 'byung ba rjes 'brang dang bcas pa } ni{ sems lnga'i dmigs pa yin te} 'dod pa rang gi sdug bsngal mthong spang la sogs pa gsum{ gyi yul du 'gyur te de yang kun 'gros ris gzhan la'ang dmigs la/ de ma yin pa'i nyon mongs can gyis rang gi ris la dmigs la/ sgom spang dag pas gsum char la dmigs pa'i phyir} dang gzugs su gtogs pa'i sgom spang {dge yul yod dgu yin zhes pas sgom spang dge ba } gcig{ gi yul du'ang 'gyur te gzugs su skyes pa 'dod pa'i sems la lta ba dang*/ 'dir skyes pa chags bral 'jig rten pa'i lam gyis 'dod khams la dmigs pa'ang yod pa'i phyir} dang dri ma med pa{ sdug kun la} chos shes phyogs dang mthun pa'i rnam shes dang lnga'i spyod yul du 'gyur ro/{ de dag las gzhan gyis dmigs mi nus pa ni 'gog lam mthong spang zag bcas la dmigs pa tsam ni rang ris la dmigs pa tsam dang*/ gong ma'i nyon mongs can gyis 'og ma la dmigs pa med la/ gzugs med kyi sgom spang dge ba yang 'dod pa la ring ba nyid bzhis ring ba'i phyir ro}

That arisen in the desire realm {occurring simultaneously and with complements} that is abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering and the truth of origin that is the cause of suffering, and that abandoned by meditation on the path, are objects (gocara) of five consciousnesses. There are three, such as (1) that to be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering of its desire-realm level and so on {including (2) pervasive states focusing on different types and (3) different afflicted states focusing on its own type. Thus they focus on three aspects by purifying objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation.} (4) One abandoned by the path of meditation belonging to the form realm {is a virtuous object abandoned by the path of meditation, since the Abhidharmakośa mentions, “The object of virtuous absorption is all objects” (8:20d)}. (5) And one is stainless consciousness compatible with Dharma knowledge {of the truths of suffering and origin}. {Minds other than those cannot focus on those objects because they are distant in four ways: (1–2) minds focusing on contaminated objects to be abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and path alone merely focus on their own type; (3) afflicted states of higher realms do not focus on lower states; and (4) virtuous states that are objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation in the formless realm are distant from the desire realm.}
gzugs khams las skyes rang gi dang / / 'og gsum gong gcig dri med kyi'ang / / gzugs med las skyes khams gsum gtogs/ / gsum dang zag med spyod yul lo/ / 30

Those arisen in the form realm are objects of its realm, three of its own and lower, one of higher, and stainless consciousness. Those arising in the formless realm are objects belonging to the three realms: three for each, and stainless consciousness. (5:30)

gzugs kyi khams las skyes pa'i sdug bsngal mthong spang la sogs pa gsum ni{ sems brgyad kyi dmigs pa yin te} gzugs khams rang gi de gsum dang*/ 'og ma 'dod pa'i khams kyi de {skal ba mi mnyam pa'i khams kun 'gro gnyis dang sgom spang dge ba de la dmigs pa'i thos bsam las byung dge ba'i chos la 'dun pa yang dag pa'i lta ba mtshungs ldan de } gsum dang*/ gong ma gzugs med pa'i sgom spang gcig dang*/ dri ma med pa rjes shes kyi phyogs mthun gyi rnam shes kyi'ang yul du 'gyur bas de ltar rnam shes brgyad kyi spyod yul du 'gyur ro/ / de la 'dod pa'i sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung mthong spang ni skal ba mi mnyam pa'i khams kun 'gro gong du dmigs pa rnams kyi yin la/ gzugs med pa'i ni nam mkha' mtha' yas skye mched kyi nyer bsdogs kyis{ rags par lta ba'i shes pa'i} yul yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

The three arisen in the form realm that are abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering and so on are objects (gocara) of eight consciousnesses: (1–3) three of its own form realm, (4–6) three of the lower desire realm {that are concomitant with correct view aspiring to virtuous Dharmas and derived from hearing and contemplation focusing on two pervasive negative tendencies of different realms}, (7) one abandoned by meditation in the higher formless realm, and (8) stainless consciousness compatible with subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna). The objects abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering and origin of the desire realm are those that focus on higher pervasive negative tendencies of different realms. Those of the formless realm are taken as objects {of knowledge viewing coarse states} through access concentration to the base of infinite space.

gzugs med pa las skyes pa'i sdug bsngal mthong spang la sogs pa gsum ni khams gsum du gtogs pa sngar bshad pa'i sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung mthong spang gnyis dang sgom spang dang gsum gsum ste dgu dang zag pa med pa rjes shes phyogs dang mthun pa'i rnam shes dang bcu'i spyod yul du 'gyur ro/ / de la 'dod gzugs kyi sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung mthong spang ni skal mi mnyam pa'i khams kun 'gro dang mtshungs ldan gyi sems yin no/ / de dag gi rgyu mtshan ni 'gog lam mthong spang zag med la dmigs pa'i sems rnams ni 'gog lam kho na la dmigs la/ zag bcas la dmigs pa rnams kyang kun 'gro ma yin pas 'gog lam mthong spang kho na la dmigs kyi khams dang ris gzhan la mi dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ sa gong ma'i bden pa dang po gnyis kyi mthong spang kun 'gro dag kyang sa 'og ma la mi dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ ring ba bzhis ring bas gzugs med kyi sgom spang dge ba'i sems kyis kyang 'dod pa la mi dmigs pa'i phyir rnam shes gzhan gyi spyod yul du ni mi 'gyur ro/ /

The three arising in the formless realm that are abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering and so on are the objects of ten consciousnesses that belong to the three realms: (1–9) three for each realm, including the two abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering and origin and the one abandoned by the path of meditation that were previously explained, making nine, and (10) uncontaminated consciousness compatible with the state of subsequent knowledge. Objects to be abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering and origin of the desire and form realms are minds concomitant with pervasive [negative tendencies] of different realms. The reason for this is that minds focusing on that which is to be abandoned by seeing the uncontaminated truths of cessation and path only focus on the truths of cessation and path. Since those that focus on contaminated states are not pervasive, they focus on that which is to be abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and path alone and do not focus on different realms and types. [466] Also, those pervasive negative tendencies to be abandoned by seeing the first two truths of the higher realms do not focus on lower levels. Formless-realm virtuous minds to be abandoned by the path of meditation do not focus on the desire realm, since they are distant through the four types of distance and do not become the objects of other consciousnesses.
'gog dang lam mthong spang bya kun/ / rang gis glags pa'i spyod yul lo/ / zag med khams gsum mtha' gsum dang / / zag pa med pa'i spyod yul lo/ / 31

All objects abandoned by seeing cessation and path are objects with their own categories. Uncontaminated states are objects of three each at the limit of the three realms, and the uncontaminated mind. (5:31)

'gog pa dang lam mthong bas spang bya{ khams gsum pa} kun ni sngar gyi de dag gi steng du rang rang gis glags te bsnan pa'i rnam shes kyi spyod yul lo/ / des na lnga'i spyod yul du 'gyur drug ni spyod yul yin pa la sogs pa'o/ / {de yang drug dgu bcu gcig yul lo } de la rang rang gis glags pa zhes bya ba'ang 'gog lam mthong spang zag bcas la dmigs pa 'dod chags la sogs pa dang mtshungs ldan gyi yin gyi/ med la dmigs pa log lta la sogs pa dang mtshungs ldan ni ma yin te/ de dag ni 'gog lam kho na la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ /

All objects abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and the path {of the three realms} are objects of consciousness that augment those former states with their own categories (adhika). Therefore those that are objects of five consciousnesses become objects of six and so on. {They are also six, nine, and eleven objects.} The statement “with their own categories” means they are concomitant with attachment and so on that focus on contaminated objects to be abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and path, but they are not concomitant with wrong view focusing on nonexistent states and so on because they focus on the truths of cessation and path alone.

zag med ni 'dod pa la sogs pa khams gsum gyi mtha' ma 'gog lam mthong spang gnyis dang sgom spang ste gsum gsum dang zag pa med pa'i sems rang nyid dang bcu'i spyod yul lo/ / de yang zag med so sor brtags 'gog dang lam bden ni khams gsum gyi log lta la sogs pa zag med la dmigs pa rnams dang mtshungs ldan dang*/ sgom spang dge ba zag bcas kyi sems dang*/ zag med chos shes rjes shes kyi dmigs pa yin la/ nam mkha' dang so sor brtags min gnyis ni sgom spang gi sems nyon mongs pa can ma yin pa kho na'i dmigs pa yin no/ / slob dpon yon tan blo gros dang dbyig bshes na re nam mkha' dang so sor brtags min gnyis sgom spang nyon mongs can dang nyon mongs can ma yin pa gnyis ka'i dmigs pa yin no/ / zhes zer ba ni mi rigs te/ drug ni zag med spyod yul can zhes brtags 'gog dang lam bden kho na nyon mongs can gyi dmigs par bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir 'grel par/ khams gsum sdug bsngal rgyu mthong dang*/ / sgom pas spang bya zag pa med/ / rnam shes lnga brgyad bcu dang ni/ / rnam shes bcu yi spyod yul te/ / 'gog dang lam mthong spang bya kun/ / rang gis glags pa'i spyod yul lo zhes 'byung ste/ de gnyis ni rnam shes drug dgu bcu gcig yul zhes bya bar 'gyur ro/ /

Uncontaminated states are objects of ten consciousnesses: (1–6) three each for the two objects abandoned by seeing the truths of cessation and path, (7–9) objects abandoned by the path of meditation at the limit of the three realms of desire and so on, and (10) the uncontaminated mind itself.
