Further, (a) uncontaminated analytical cessation and the truth of path concomitant with wrong view of the three realms and so on that focus on uncontaminated states and (b) minds of contaminated virtue that are objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation are focal objects of Dharma knowledge and subsequent knowledge. Both space and nonanalytical cessation are the focal objects of unafflicted minds that are objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation. Masters Guṇamati and Vasumitra say that both space and nonanalytical cessation are the focal objects of both afflicted and unafflicted states to be abandoned by the path of meditation. Reply: This is illogical because the Abhidharmakośa mentions, “[Six] possess uncontaminated objects” (5:14d), and this explains that only analytical cessation and the truth of path are focal objects of afflicted states. Therefore the Autocommentary states: Uncontaminated states that are objects abandoned through seeing and meditating on suffering and its cause in the three realms are five, eight, and ten consciousnesses. They are the objects of ten consciousnesses since all objects abandoned by cessation and path are objects with their own categories.[1462] Therefore these two are called the objects of six, nine, or eleven consciousnesses.

kun las btus las kyang*/ 'dod pa na spyod pa'i yid kyis khams gsum na spyod pa rnams dang zag pa med pa'i chos rnams kyang shes so/ / 'dod pa'i khams pa ji lta bar gzugs na spyod pa'ang de bzhin no/ / gzugs med na spyod pa'i yid kyis ni gzugs med rang sa'i chos rnams dang zag med kyi chos rnams kyang shes so/ / zag med kyi yid kyis ni khams gsum na spyod pa rnams dang zag med kyi chos rnams kyang shes so zhes bshad de/ gzugs med ni nam mkha'i nyer bsdogs las gzhan pa rnams kyi dbang du byas pa'o/ / de ltar na de dag la ci rigs par dmigs pa dang mtshungs ldan gyi sgo nas rgyas par 'gyur ro zhes shes par bya'o/ / des mtshon nas sems bcu drug po re re'i yul du chos bcu drug po du du 'gyur dpyad pa ni/ khams gsum bden bzhi mthong spang dang*/ / sgom spang sems kyi yul du ni/ / rim bzhin bco lnga gnyis bcu drug /bcu dang gnyis dang bcu drug dang*/ / lnga dang gnyis dang bcu gcig 'gyur/ / zag med yul du bcu drug 'gyur zhes pa'o/ /

Also, the Compendium of Abhidharma states: The mental faculty utilizing desire-realm objects knows phenomena utilized in the three realms and uncontaminated states. Objects are utilized in the form realm just as they are utilized in the desire realm. The mental faculty utilizing formless objects knows phenomena of its formless-realm level and uncontaminated states. The uncontaminated mental faculty knows those utilized in the three realms and uncontaminated states.[1463] The presentation of formless minds is from the perspective of states other than access concentration to infinite space. Thus it should be known that [467] they increase through either focal object or concomitance. Having presented this, we now examine how many of the sixteen phenomena are objects of each of the sixteen minds, since it is said: Objects of mind such as the four truths in the three realms, objects to be abandoned by seeing, and objects to be abandoned by meditation are respectively fifteen, two, sixteen, ten, two, sixteen, five, two, and eleven. There are sixteen that are uncontaminated objects.

de ltar yul dang yul can de rnams las yul gang la yul can phra rgyas du rgyas dpyad pa'i skabs 'dir yul de chos gang du gtogs pa dang*/ de sems du'i yul du 'gyur ba dang*/ yul can gyi sems de phra rgyas yin min dang*/ phra rgyas yin pa de yul de la rgyas mi rgyas dpyad pa bzhis shes par bya ba las gzugs kyi phung po la mtshon na de 'dod gzugs kyi sgom spang dang zag med gsum du gtogs la/ 'dod pa'i sgom spang gi gzugs rgyud kyis bsdus pa nyon mongs can yin na 'dod pa rang sa'i bden pa dang po gnyis kyi kun 'gro gnyis dang sgom spang dang bsam gtan dang de'i nyer bsdogs dang sgom lam zag med dang sems lnga'i yul du 'gyur la/ sems lnga las dang po gsum phra rgyas dang phyi ma gnyis sgom lam zag bcas zag med yin pa la phra rgyas ma yin pas bden pa dang po gnyis kyi kun 'gro bcu gcig dang sgom spang bzhi ste phra rgyas bco lnga rgyas par 'gyur zhing*/ rgyud kyis bsdus kyang nyon mongs can ma yin pa dang rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa thams cad la sgom spang bzhi po kho na rgyas so zhes shes par bya'o/

Thus from among such subjects and objects, here we analyze which negative tendency as a subject increases with respect to which object, through four types of analysis: (1) what object belongs to what phenomena, (2) what becomes the object of what mind, (3) whether or not those minds that are subjects are negative tendencies, and (4) whether or not those that are negative tendencies increase with respect to their object. (1) The form aggregate, for instance, belongs to three phenomena: (a) desire and (b) form-realm objects abandoned by the path of meditation and (c) uncontaminated states. (2) If desire-realm form to be abandoned by the path of meditation is an afflicted state conjoined to the mindstream, it is an object of five minds: (a–b) two omipresent negative tendencies focusing on the first two truths of its level, (c–d) absorption and its access concentration that are objects abandoned by meditation, and (e) the uncontaminated path of meditation. (3) From those five minds, the first three are negative tendencies, and the latter two are the contaminated and uncontaminated path of meditation. (4) Since they are not negative tendencies they increase fifteen negative tendencies: (a) the eleven pervasive states of the first two truths and (b) the four objects abandoned by the path of meditation. Though they are conjoined to the mindstream, they are not afflicted, and all that are not conjoined to the mindstream increase the four objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation alone.

{ kha cig rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa la lta ba dang po gnyis mi rgyas la/ nga rgyal rgyas mi rgyas bsam mo/ / khams gong ma'i gzugs la'ang khong khro bor ba'i khams de nyid kyi phra rgyas bcu bzhi rgyas so zhes 'chad pa ni mi rigs te/ rgyud kyis ma bsdus pa'i gzugs nyon mongs can ma yin pas kun 'gro thams cad mi rgyas shing*/ nga rgyal sgom spang kha phyir bltas rgyas pa mi 'gal ba'i phyir ro/ /}

{Some say: Regarding form not conjoined to the mindstream, the first two views are not increased. But investigate whether or not pride increases. Regarding form of higher realms that are realms where anger is discarded, fourteen negative tendencies increase. Reply: That is illogical, because nonconjoined form does not increase any pervasive negative tendency since it is not afflicted, and it is not contradictory that pride which is an object to be abandoned by the path of meditation increases, since it views external objects}.
sems phra rgyas dang bcas par bzhag pa ni
POSITING MINDS WITH NEGATIVE TENDENCIES
nyon mongs phra rgyas bcas rnam gnyis/ / nyon mongs can min rgyas 'gyur gyis/ /
An afflicted mind associated with negative tendencies has two types. Unafflicted states are increased by the focal object. (5:32ab)

'grel pa las/ phra rgyas gang dag gis sems phra rgyas dang bcas pa'i phra rgyas de dag sems de la rgyas par 'gyur ram zhe na/ rgyas pa 'gyur ba dag kyang yod de/ sems de dang mtshungs par ldan zhing ma spangs la dmigs pa yang ma spangs pa'i phra rgyas gang dag yin pa'o/ / rgyas par mi 'gyur ba dag kyang yod de/ sems de dang mtshungs par ldan pa spangs pa'i phra rgyas gang dag yin pa'o zhes 'byung ba la sems ni mtshon pa ste zag bcas mtshungs ldan dang de ma yin pa gnyis las

The Autocommentary states: Do negative tendencies that are negative tendencies associated with minds increase those minds or not? Those that increase those minds exist because there are negative tendencies that neither abandon concomitance with those minds nor abandon the focal object of those minds. Those that don’t increase those minds exist because they are negative tendencies that abandon concomitance with those minds.[1464] The mind represented here is either concomitant with contaminated states or not concomitant with them.

mtshungs ldan nyon mongs pa can phra rgyas dang bcas pa ni{ rgyas pa dang mi rgyas pa'i bcas pa} rnam pa gnyis las dang po ni so so'i skye bo'i sems nyon mongs can ni 'dod chags la sogs pa mtshungs ldan dang dmigs pa gnyis kas rgyas shing bcas pa yin la/ 'phags pa la mtshungs ldan spangs kyang dmigs pas rgyas pa dang bcas pa yod de/ sdug bsngal mthong spang bya spangs kyang*/ / kun 'gro lhag ma rnams kyis ldan/ / dang po'i rnam pa spangs kyang de'i/ / yul can dri ma lhag rnams kyis zhes bshad pa bzhin no/ / gnyis pa ni 'phags pa dgra bcom pa rnams la 'das pa'i sems nyon mongs can dang nyon mongs pa dang lhan cig gnas pa dang*/ ma 'ongs pa mi skye ba'i chos can gyi sems nyon mongs can mongs pa dang lhan cig gnas pa bzhin te/ de dag bcas pa yin la rgyas par mi 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / mi rgyas kyang phra rgyas dang bcas par 'jog pa ni sngar ma spangs pa'i dus na rgyas pa'i phyir ro zhes bye brag smra ba zer te/ 'di ni dus gsum rdzas su grub pa'i grub mtha' 'khrul pa la 'khrul ba 'thus pa yin no/ /

An afflicted mind concomitant with the contaminants that is associated with negative tendencies (anuśaya) has two types: {associated with the increase of negative tendencies or not associated with increase}. The first is the afflicted minds of ordinary beings that increase through both concomitance with attachment and so on and due to their focal object. Though āryas abandon increase through concomitance, they have increase due to focal objects. As the Abhidharmakośa (5:28) explains: One abandons that to be abandoned by seeing suffering and possesses the remaining pervasive negative tendencies. Though one [468] abandons any aspect of the first, one possesses the remaining stains of the mind focusing on it.[1465] The second is that ārya arhats abide with past afflicted minds and afflicted states and abide with future unarisen afflicted minds and afflicted states because they possess those states though do they not increase. Though they do not increase, they are posited as associated with negative tendencies since they did increase negative tendencies when not abandoned at an earlier time. This is stated by Vaibhāṣikas who seize such mistaken ideas by holding the mistaken tenet that the three times are substantially established.

{sems nyon mongs can phra rgyas dang bcas pa de yang rgyas pa dang mi rgyas pa rnam pa gnyis so/ / dang po ni nyon mongs dang mtshungs ldan dang de la dmigs pa ma spangs pa ste/ de'i thob pas sems de'i rgyud bzung zhing*/ rgyud de lam 'ongs pa'i rgyu mthun gyi rgyu bzhag pa de srid du'o/ / gnyis pa ni gnyen pos phra rgyas mtshungs ldan spangs pas de'i thob pa dang bral ba 'ga' zhig ste 'das pa kho na'o/ / spangs na sems de ji ltar phra rgyas dang bcas she na/ nyon mongs dang lhan cig pa'i phyir te/ gnyen po gang gis kyang mtshungs ldan la 'bral bar mi nus pa yin no/ / yang na rang rgyud kyi nyon mongs pa ma spangs pa 'ga' zhig gis dmigs pa'i phyir ldan no zhes brjod na legs so/ /}

{Further, afflicted minds with negative tendencies are of two types: those that increase and those that do not. The first is that concomitant with affliction that does not abandon what [that affliction] focuses on, for the continuum of that mind is robust since it obtains that [focal object] and it is possible that continuum is posited as the future cause of its natural outflow. The second refers to some that are free from the obtainment of the [focal object] since they abandon concomitant negative tendencies due to applying an antidote that is past alone. Question: But if [negative tendencies] have been abandoned, how could it possess negative tendencies? Reply: Because it is simultaneous with afflictions, and no antidote can separate it from being concomitant. But if you say “Because some unabandoned afflictions in one’s mindstream focus on it, it is possessed,” this is better.}

rang sa'i mtshungs ldan nyon mongs pa can min pa mtshungs ldan ma yin pa{ dge ba zag bcas dang ma bsgribs lung ma bstan} rnams ni dmigs pas rgyas 'gyur gyis phra rgyas dang bcas pa yin te/ de dag la rang sa'i nyon mongs kyi dmigs pa ma rgyas pa mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ / 'on kyang zag med ni phra rgyas kyis dmigs kyang rgyas pa gnyis ka ma yin no/ / zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Those that are concomitant with one’s own level but not concomitant with unafflicted {contaminated virtue and unobscured-neutral states} are associated with negative tendencies that are increased by focal objects because it is impossible that they are not increased by afflicted focal objects. However, negative tendencies that focus on uncontaminated states do not increase by either [concomitance or focal object].
brgyad pa go rim ni
The sequence of their arising
rmongs las the tshom de nas ni/ / log lta de nas 'jig tshogs lta/ / 32
From confusion, doubt; from that, wrong view; from that, the afflicted view of the self. (5:32cd)

bden pa bzhi'i dmigs pa la kun tu rmongs pa las bden bzhi yin nam ma yin snyam pa'i the tshom dang*/ the tshom gyi rjes de nas ni the tshom gyi log par thos shing bsam pa las bden pa med do zhes skur ba 'debs pa'i log lta dang*/ log lta skyes pa de nas phung po mi rtag du mar ma shes pas bdag tu zhen pa'i 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang*/

From confusion (mohā) focusing on the four truths, doubt arises to whether or not the four truths exist. From that doubt, through wrongly addressing and contemplating the basis of that doubt, wrong view arises that underestimates the four truths, conceiving them to be nonexistent. From that wrong view, the afflicted view of the self arises that conceives a self without recognizing the aggregates to be impermanent and multiple.
de nas mthar 'dzin de nas ni/ / tshul khrims mchog 'dzin de nas lta/ / rang gi lta la nga rgyal chags/ / gzhan la zhe sdang de ltar rim/ / 33

From that, extreme view; from that, clinging to rules and ritual as supreme; from that, clinging to those views as supreme; from that, attachment and pride in one’s own view and aversion toward others’ views. This is the order. (5:33)

de nas bdag rtag chad du lta ba'i mthar 'dzin par lta ba dang*/ mthar 'dzin skyes pa de nas ni gang la mthar bzung ba des 'dag par yid ches pa'i tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog 'dzin dang*/ de nas 'dag par yid ches pa de la mchog tu 'dzin pas lta ba mchog 'dzin dang*/ de nas rang gi lta ba la chags shing khengs pa'i chags pa dang nga rgyal dang gzhan gyi lta ba la zhe sdang skye ste/ de ltar na 'di ni skye ba'i rim pa yin no/ / sngon gyi slob dpon dag na re mthong spang rnams kyi dmigs pa ni rang gi rgyud la yod pa'i lta ba yin pa'i phyir zhe sdang yang gzhan gyi lta ba la zhe sdang ba ni ma yin gyi/ 'on kyang bdag gis sngar gyi lta ba ngan pa 'di lta bu bor ro zhes gzhan rang nyid kyis sngar bzung ba'i lta ba de la zhe sdang ba yin no zhes zer ro/ {gang gi 'jug tu gang skye ma nges pas 'di bzhin skye bar ma nges kyang bden pa'i dmigs nas 'di bzhin skye ba srid pas de'i dbang du byas so }

From that, extreme view arises that views the self as permanent or annihilated. From extreme view, clinging to rules and ritual as supreme arises, which believes in purification that adheres to extremes. From that, since believing in such purification adheres to [such purification] as supreme, clinging to those views as supreme arises. From that arise attachment and pride attached to one’s own view, which inflate the mind, and aversion toward others’ views. This is the order in which they arise. Past masters say: Because the focus of abandonment by the path of seeing is view existing in one’s own mindstream, [469] it is not aversion or aversion for others’ views. Likewise it is saying “I will discard such things as previous bad views” and “I have aversion for previously held views.” {This is stated from the perspective that, though it is uncertain what state will arise at the conclusion of another, it is possible that something like this will occur through focusing on the four truths.}
dgu pa skye ba'i rgyu ni
Causes giving rise to them
phra rgyas spangs pa ma yin dang / / yul ni nye bar gnas pa dang / / tshul bzhin ma yin yid byed las/ / nyon mongs rgyu ni tshang ba yin/ / 34
Afflictions arise from three causes when complete: not abandoning negative tendencies, closely abiding with conducive objects, and inappropriate attention. (5:34)

rgyu'i stobs dang rkyen rgyud la thob pa ma bcad cing gnyen po ma skyes pas phra rgyas spangs pa ma yin pa dang*/ yul gyi stobs dang dmigs rkyen 'dod chags la sogs pa skye ba dang mthun pa'i yul nye bar gnas par gyur pa dang sbyor ba'i stobs dang de ma thag rkyen tshul bzhin ma yin pa yid la byed pa gsum las nyon mongs 'byung bas na nyon mongs pa'i rgyu ni tshang ba yin no/ / bye brag tu smra ba na re dgra bcom pa yongs su nyams pa'i chos can gyi nyon mongs pa lta bu res 'ga' rgyu'i stobs med kyang yul gyi stobs kho na las skye'o zhes zer ba la 'grel bar grag go zhes smros te/ rgyu ma tshang ba'i 'bras bu skye ba ni yod pa ma yin no zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / 'di la phra rgyas spangs pa ma yin pa zhes bya ba ni mdo sde pa la sogs pa nyon mongs pa'i sa bon dang bye brag tu smra ba thob la 'dod do/ /

Afflictions arise from three causes when complete: (1) not abandoning negative tendencies (anuśaya) is due to the power of their cause, and neither eliminating the obtainment of their conditions nor generating their antidotes in one’s mindstream; (2) closely abiding with objects conducive to them is due to the power of their object, and the arising of focal objects of attachment and so on; and (3) inappropriate attention is due to the power of application and the immediately preceding condition. Vaibhāṣikas say: The afflicted states of arhats, which have temporarily degenerated and are causally ineffective, arise from the power of the object alone.[1466] This is well established in the Autocommentary. Reply: But Pūrṇavardhana’s commentary explains that “The result arising without complete causes” does not exist![1467] Sautrāntikas and so on assert that the statement “not abandoning negative tendencies” refers to the seeds of affliction, and Vaibhāṣikas assert that it refers to obtainment.
bcu pa mdo las gsungs pa'i zag pa la sogs pa'i dbye ba bstan pa
24. The Taxonomy of the Contaminants and So On in the Sūtras

['di] la zag pa dang*/ chu bo dang*/ sbyor ba dang*/ nyer len dang*/ phra rgyas la sogs pa'i ming don dang*/ kun sbyor dang*/ 'ching ba dang*/ nye ba'i nyon mongs dang*/ kun dkris dang*/ dri ma dang*/ de dag gi rnam pa'i rab dbye dang*/ sgrib pa lnga bshad pa dang bcu gcig las

THIS HAS ELEVEN HEADINGS: (1) contaminants, (2) floods and bonds, (3) appropriators, (4) the meaning of the name “negative tendency” and so on, (5) fetters, (6) ties, (7) branch afflictions, (8) entanglements, (9) stains, (10) their specific attributes, and (11) the five obscurations.
dang po [zag pa bshad pa] ni
Contaminants
phra rgyas de dag nyid mdo las/ 'dod pa'i zag pa dang*/ srid pa'i zag pa dang*/ ma rig pa'i zag pa'o zhes zag pa gsum du gsungs pa las

Regarding those negative tendencies, a sūtra declares: The contaminants of desire, the contaminants of existence, and the contaminants of ignorance.[1468] This passage declares the three contaminants.
'dod na gti mug ma gtogs pa'i/ / nyon mongs kun nas dkris bcas zag / gzugs dang gzugs ni med pa na/ / phra rgyas kho na srid pa'i zag / 35
In the desire realm, afflicted states except delusion, plus the entanglements, are contaminants. In the form and formless realms, just the negative tendencies are contaminants of existence. (5:35)

'dod khams na gti mug lnga ma gtogs pa'i nyon mongs pa lta ba bcu gnyis the tshom bzhi 'dod chags khong khro nga rgyal gsum po lnga lnga ste sum cu rtsa gcig dang kun nas dkris pa bcu dang bcas pa bzhi bcu rtsa gcig ni 'dod pa'i zag pa yin no/ / gzugs dang gzugs med pa'i khams na ni ma rig pa bcu ma gtogs pa'i phra rgyas nyi shu rtsa drug drug po rnams kho na gcig tu bsdoms pa lnga bcu rtsa gnyis ni srid pa'i zag pa yin no/ / 'o na srid zag lnga bcu rtsa drug tu 'gyur te/ gong ma gnyis na'ang rmugs rgod kyi kun dkris yod la/ rab tu byed pa las/ srid pa'i zag pa gang zhe na/ ma rig pa rnams ma gtogs pa de las gzhan pa gzugs dang gzugs med pa dang ldan pa'i kun tu sbyor ba dang*/ 'ching ba dang*/ phra rgyas dang*/ nye ba'i nyon mongs pa dang*/ kun nas dkris pa gang dag yin pa'o zhes bshad pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ kha che ba rnams na re khams gong ma'i rmugs rgod gnyis 'dod chags la sogs pa dang yang mtshungs par ldan pas rang dbang can ma yin pa'i phyir ma bshad do zhes zer ro/ / gal te de lta na 'dod pa'i ngo tsha med pa dang khrel med pa dang rmugs rgod rnams kyang 'dod pa'i zag pa ma yin par 'gyur te/ 'dod chags la sogs pa dang mtshungs par ldan pas rang dbang can ma yin pa'i phyir zhe na/ 'dir rang gi 'jug pa shas chung bas rang dbang can ma yin par 'dod kyi chags sogs dang mtshungs par ldan pas rang dbang can ma yin pa ni ma yin no zhes 'dod do/ /

In the desire realm, (1–12) the twelve afflicted views, except the five delusions (moha), with (13–16) four doubts, and (17–31) five times the three afflictions of attachment, anger, pride, making thirty-one, plus (32–41) the ten entanglements (paryavasthāna), constitute the forty-one contaminants (āsrava) of the desire realm. In the form and formless realm, just the twenty-six negative tendencies (anuśaya) for each realm, except for the ten ignorances, constitute the fifty-two contaminants of existence when combined. Objection: There should be fifty-six contaminants of existence because Topic Divisions declares that the entanglements of confusion and excitation exist in the two higher realms: What are the contaminants of existence? They are the fetters, ties, negative tendencies, branch afflictions, [470] and entanglements possessed in the form and formless realms minus the ignorances.[1469] Vaibhāṣikas say: They are not explained here. Both confusion and excitation of the higher realms are not autonomous, since they are concomitant with attachment and so on. Objection: Thus desire-realm shamelessness, nonembarrassment, confusion, and excitation would also not be contaminants of the desire realm because they are not autonomous, being concomitant with attachment and so on. Since their engagement in this desire realm is weak, they are not asserted to be autonomous. But since they are concomitant with attachment and so on, they are not asserted to be non-autonomous!
de lung ma bstan kha nang bltas/ / mnyam gzhag sa pa'i phyir gcig byas/ / rtsa ba ma rig yin pas na/ / logs shig tu ni zag par bstan/ / 36

They are taken as one because they are neutral, they view internal states, and they are levels of equipoise. They are separately taught to be a contaminant, since ignorance is the root of all affliction. (5:36)

khams gong ma gnyis kyi phra rgyas rnams gcig tu bsdoms nas srid pa'i zag pa gcig tu 'jog pa ni nyon mongs pa de dag bsgribs la lung du ma bstan pa dang*/ kha nang du bltas pa dang mnyam gzhag gi sa pa yin pa'i phyir gcig tu byas so/ / {dgos pa ni de la thar ba'i 'du shes bzlog pa'i phyir } khams gsum char gyi ma rig pa bco lnga po thams cad gcig tu byas pa ni ma rig pa'i zag pa'o/ / de gcig pu logs su ston pa ni nyon mongs pa thams cad kyi rtsa ba ma rig pa yin pas na nyes pa che bas logs shig tu ma rig pa'i zag par bstan te/ mdo las/ kun tu chags par byed pa'i rgyu ni ma rig pa'o zhes pa dang*/ 'jig rten 'di dang pha rol na/ / 'dod dang chags pas bslang ba yi/ / ngan 'gro gang dag ci yod pa/ / thams cad ma rig rtsa ba can zhes gsungs so/ /

The negative tendencies of the two higher realms are posited as one contaminant of existence through combining them as one. They are taken as one because they are both obscured-neutral states, they view internal states, and they are levels of equipoise (samāhita). {This presentation is necessary to prevent discriminating them as liberation.} All fifteen ignorances in the three realms are taken as one contaminant of ignorance. They are separately taught to be the contaminant of ignorance since ignorance is the root of all affliction and it has great fault. Further, the contaminant of ignorance is taught separately, since a sūtra states: The cause that always activates attachment is ignorance. And: One arises in this world and worlds beyond through desire and attachment. Any lower rebirth that exists possesses ignorance as its root.[1470]
gnyis pa chu bo dang sbyor ba bshad pa ni
Floods and bonds

yang mdo las/ chu bo ni bzhi ste/ 'dod pa'i chu bo dang*/ srid pa'i chu bo dang*/ lta ba'i chu bo dang*/ ma rig pa'i chu bo'o zhes bya ba dang*/ sbyor ba ni bzhi ste/ 'dod pa'i sbyor ba dang*/ srid pa'i sbyor ba dang*/ lta ba'i sbyor ba dang*/ ma rig pa'i sbyor ba'o zhes gsungs pa'i

A sūtra declares: Floods are four: the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of view, and the flood of ignorance. And: Bonds are four: the bond of desire, the bond of existence, the bond of view, and the bond of ignorance.[1471]
chu bo sbyor ba'ang de bzhin du/ / lha rnams gsal phyir logs shig bstan/ / zag par ma yin grogs med rnams/ / 'jog pa'i rjes su mi mthun lo/ / 37

Floods and also bonds in the same way. Those views are taught separately because they are sharply defined. View is said not to be a contaminant because those unassisted are not compatible with that posited as saṃsāra. (5:37)

chu bo dang sbyor ba'ang ji ltar zag pa bshad pa de kho na bzhin du rig par bya ste/ 'dod pa la sogs pa'i zag pa ni 'dod pa la sogs pa'i sbyor ba la sogs pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ /
'o na chu bo dang sbyor ba gsum du 'gyur ro zhe na/ khams gsum pa'i lta ba rnams ni nyon mongs pa gzhan las logs shig tu lta ba'i chu bo dang sbyor ba zhes bstan te/ lta ba rnams nyon mongs pa gzhan pas g.yo ba dang rnam pa gsal ba'i phyir ro zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'dod de/ de lta na ma rig pa rnam pa mi gsal ba'i phyir logs shig tu mi ston pa dang*/ khong khro dang 'dod chags la sogs pa'ang logs shig tu ston par thal ba'i skyon yod pas gdul bya'i bsam pa la ltos nas bshad do zhes shes par bya'o/ /

Floods (ogha) and also bonds (yoga) should be understood in the same way contaminants are explained because the contaminant of attachment and so on is the bond of attachment and so forth.
Objection: But if that were so, then floods and bonds would have three divisions [like the contaminants]. Vaibhāṣikas assert: Those views of the three realms are taught separately as the flood of view and the bond of view because views are moved by other afflicted states and their aspect is sharply defined (pāṭava). Reply: If that is so, the error would arise that ignorance should not be separately taught because its object is not sharply defined, but anger and attachment and so on should be separately taught. Therefore this is explained in reliance on the inclination of the disciple.

'o na zag pa'ang bzhir 'gyur te/ khyad par med pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ zag par ni lta ba rnams logs shig tu bstan pa ma yin te/ 'khor bar 'jog pa'i phyir zag pa zhes bya ba yin na 'dod chags la sogs pa'i nyon mongs pa gzhan gyi grogs med pa'i lta ba rkyang pa rnams ni 'khor bar 'jog pa'i ming gi don dang rjes su mi mthun pa'i phyir ro/ / lo'i sgra ni bye brag tu smra ba'i 'dod pa ste/ 'jog pa'i don 'khor bar dngos su nying mtshams sbyor ba la 'dod na ma rig pa'ang zag par mi 'gyur te/ dngos su sred pa kho nas nying mtshams sbyor ba'i phyir te/ rnam 'grel las/ sdug bsngal phyin ci log blo dang*/ / sred pa kun nas 'ching ba ni/ / skye rgyu gang la de med pa/ / de ni skye bar mi 'gyur ro/ / zhes bshad pa bzhin no/ / phyin ci log gi blo ni ma rig pa ma yin gyi lta ba yin pa'i phyir ro/ / kun nas slong ba tsam la 'dod na nyon mongs pa thams cad kyis 'khor bar 'jog par byed pas lta ba'ang der thal bar 'gyur ro/ / de'i phyir 'di yang gdul bya'i dbang gis bshad pa tsam du rig par bya'o/ /

Objection: Contaminants would also be four in number because they are not different from floods and bonds. Reply: View is not taught [471] to be a separate contaminant. Something is called a contaminant because it establishes saṃsāra, but those views alone, unassisted by any other afflicted state such as attachment, are not compatible with that which is nominally posited as saṃsāra. The “said” (kila) indicates that this is an assertion of the Vaibhāṣikas. If they assert that the meaning of “posited [as saṃsāra]” is that which directly links to saṃsāra, then even ignorance would not be a contaminant because it directly links to craving alone. That is because Exposition of Valid Cognition explains: One is completely tied by suffering, distorted awareness, and craving. If any of these causes of birth do not exist, one is not born there.[1472] Distorted awareness is not ignorance but view. But if one asserts that to be the motivation alone, then it would follow that view would also be saṃsāra, since saṃsāra is established by all the afflictions. Therefore understand this to be an explanation from the perspective of the disciple alone.
nyer len bshad pa/
Appropriators

gsum pa nyer len bshad pa ni mdo las/ nye bar len pa ni bzhi ste/ 'dod pa nye bar len pa dang*/ lta ba nye bar len pa dang*/ tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa nye bar len pa dang*/ bdag tu smra ba nye bar len pa'o zhes gsungs pa la/
A sūtra states: The appropriators are four: the appropriator of desire, the appropriator of view, the appropriator clinging to rules and ritual as supreme, and the appropriator advocating a self.
ji skad bshad nyid ma rig bcas/ / nyer len rnams te lta rnam gnyis/ / phye ba'i phyir ro ma rig pa/ / 'dzin par byed pa min phyir bsres/ / 38
Those previously explained plus ignorance are appropriators because view is divided in two. Ignorance that does not seize saṃsāra is mixed. (5:38)

'dod pa dang srid pa'i chu bo dang sbyor bar ji skad bshad pa nyid ma rig pa dang bcas pa ni rim pa ltar 'dod pa dang bdag tu smra ba nye bar len pa rnams yin te/ lta ba rnam pa lnga ni lta ba nye bar len pa dang*/ tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa nye bar len pa gnyis su phye ba'i phyir ro/ / de la tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog 'dzin nyer len tha dad du bstan pa ni grangs can la sogs pa'i lam gyis thar pa thob par lta bas yang dag pa'i lam gyi dgrar gyur pa'i phyir dang*/ zas mi za ba dang me dang chur 'jug pa la sogs pa dang yul yid du 'ong ba spangs pas dag par yid ches pas khyim pa dang rab tu byung ba'i phyogs gnyis ka bslu ba'i phyir logs shig tu byas so/ / ma 'dres pa'i ma rigs pa 'ba' zhig pas ni mi gsal bas 'khor bar 'dzin par byed pa min pa'i phyir dang*/ 'dres pa ni nyon mongs pa gzhan dang 'brel ba'i stobs kyis len par byed pa'i phyir lta ba las gzhan pa'i nyon mongs pa rnams dang bsres nas 'dod pa nye bar len pa dang*/ bdag tu smra ba nye bar len par bshad de/ nye bar len pa'i don ni 'khor bar len pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / 'di ni bye brag tu smra ba'i 'dod pa ste/ slob dpon ni 'dun pa'i 'dod chags kho na nyer len yin pas ma rig pa nyer len du ma bshad pa yin gyi 'dzin par byed pa ma yin pas ma rig pa nyer len du logs su ma bshad pa ni ma yin no/ / de la sbyor ba dang nyer len ni 'dun pa'i 'dod chags nyid yin gyi nyon mongs pa gzhan dag ni ma yin te/ sbyor ba dang nyer len gyi don dngos su 'khor bar sbyor ba dang len pa yin na nyon mongs pa gzhan gyis ni de lta ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ 'dod chags kyis dngos su 'khor sbyor ba dang nye bar len pa'i phyir ro zhes bzhed do zhes slob dpon gang spel 'chad do/ /

Those states previously explained as the flood and bond of desire and existence, plus ignorance, are respectively (1–2) the appropriators (upādāna) of desire and advocating a self, while the five aspects of view are divided in two: (3) the appropriator of view, and (4) the appropriator clinging to rules and ritual as supreme.[1473] Clinging to rules and ritual as supreme is taught as a distinct appropriator because the path of the Sāṃkhya and so on that views liberation as something already obtained acts as an enemy to the correct path, and it deceives both lay and ordained communities through fostering the conviction that fasting, entering fire or water and so on, or abandoning pleasant objects is a means of purification. Because unmixed ignorance alone does not sieze (grāhikā) saṃsāra, since its object is not sharply defined, it is explained as the appropriator of desire through being mixed (miśrita) with afflictions other than view. It is explained as the appropriator advocating a self because mixed ignorance clings through the power of being related to other afflictions. The meaning of “appropriator” is to cling to saṃsāra. This is asserted by Vaibhāṣikas. Vasubandhu holds that ignorance is not explained to be an appropriator since longing desire alone is an appropriator, and ignorance is not explained as a separate appropriator since it does not seize saṃsāra. Bonds and appropriators are longing desire, but other afflictions are not. The meaning of “bond” and “appropriator” is to bond and cling to saṃsāra directly, [472] but other afflictions are not like that, and attachment bonds and clings directly to saṃsāra.[1474] This is asserted by Master Pūrṇavardhana.

de'i phyir 'dod pa'i sbyor ba dang nye bar len pa ni 'dod pa la chags pa nyid yin la/ de bzhin du srid pa la chags pa nyid srid pa'i sbyor ba dang bdag tu smra ba nyer len yin te/ mdo las/ 'dod pa'i sbyor ba gang zhe na zhes pa nas rgyas par 'di'i 'dod pa rnams la { 'dod pa la} 'dod chags pa dang*/ 'dod pa la 'dun pa dang*/ 'dod pa la sred pa dang*/ 'dod pa la dad che ba dang*/ 'dod pa la 'dod pas brgyal ba dang*/ 'dod pa la zhen pa dang*/ 'dod pa la dga' ba dang*/ 'dod pa la 'chums pa dang*/ 'dod pa la lhag par chags pa yod pa gang yin pa des 'di'i sems yongs su gtugs te gnas pa 'di ni 'dod pa'i sbyor ba zhes bya'o zhes pa'i bar dang*/ lta ba'i sbyor ba gang zhe na 'di'i lta ba rnams la 'dod chags pa dang zhes pa nas gnas pa 'di ni lta ba'i sbyor ba zhes bya'o zhes pa'i bar dang*/ yang nye bar len pa'i dbang du byas te nye bar len pa gang zhe na/ 'di la 'dun pa'i 'dod chags gang yin pa'o zhes gsungs so/ /

Therefore the bond and appropriator of desire is desire-realm attachment, and similarly, attachment to existence itself is the bond of existence and the appropriator advocating a self. That is because a sūtra asks: What is the bond of desire? More extensively: For these desires there is attachment {to desire}, aspiration to desire, craving for desire, great faith in desire, fainting through desire, longing for desire, liking desire, trembling with desire, excessive attachment to desire[-realm objects]. It is the bond of desire since it maintains full contact with this mind. And: What is the bond of view? Attachment to those views of this . . . [up to] . . . this is the bond of view. And: From the perspective of the appropriators, what is an appropriator? It is any longing desire.[1475]
bzhi pa phra rgyas la sogs pa'i ming gi don ni
The meaning of the name “negative tendency” and so on
ci'i phyir nyon mongs pa de dag la phra rgyas la sogs pa zhes bya zhe na/
Question: Why are these afflictions called negative tendencies and so on?
gang phyir de dag phra ba dang / / rjes 'brel rnam gnyis rgyas 'gyur dang / / rjes su 'brang bas de yi phyir/ / phra rgyas dag tu bshad pa yin/ / 39
They are called negative tendencies because they are subtle and related to obtainment and because they increase in two ways and adhere. (5:39)

gang gi phyir nyon mongs pa de dag{ ni gzugs can yin zhing} sems las byung ba'i ngo bo nyid kyis rtogs par dka' bas 'jug pa phra ba'i phyir dang*/ thob pa dang rjes su 'brel ba'i phyir phra ba yin no/ / dmigs pa dang mtshungs ldan rnam pa gnyis kyi sgo nas rgyas par 'gyur ba dang*/ 'bad mi dgos par bzlog bzhin du rgyud la yang dang yang du mngon du 'gyur bas rgyun phyogs su rjes su 'brang ba'i phyir yang rgyas pa ste de'i phyir na phra rgyas dag tu bshad pa yin no/ /

Reply: They are called negative tendencies (anuśaya) because these afflictions {are nonphysical and} subtle (aṇava) in their engagement, since by nature they are mental factors that are difficult to comprehend; they are also subtle since they are related (anugata) to obtainment. [They are called negative tendencies], too, because they increase (anuśerate) in two ways — through focal objects and concomitance — and they continuously adhere (anubadhnat) to the mindstream through frequent manifestation without need for exertion, even when obstructed.
de dag 'jog byed zag byed dang / / 'khyer bar byed dang 'byar byed dang / / nye bar 'dzin phyir zag la sogs/ / de dag gi ni nges tshig yin/ / 40
They are contaminants and so on because they establish, they contaminate, they carry away, they adhere, they closely bind. These are their etymologies. (5:40)

khyad par du khams gsum las 'dod chags dang ma bral na nyon mongs pa de dag gis 'khor bar 'jog par byed pa'i phyir dang*/ srid rtse nas mnar med kyi bar du skye mched drug gi rma'i sgo nas zag par byed pa'i phyir dang*/ 'khor ba'i rgya mtshor khams dang 'gro ba dang skye gnas gzhan du 'khyer bar byed pa'i phyir ram/ rnam shes yul la 'jug par byed pa'i phyir dang*/ 'khor ba dang khams dang 'gro ba dang skye gnas su nying mtshams sbyor ba'am/ rnam shes yul gzhan la 'byor bar byed pa'i phyir dang*/ 'khor bar rnam shes nye bar 'dzin pa'i phyir rim pa ltar zag pa la sogs pa chu bo dang sbyor ba dang nyer len zhes bya ba de dag gi ni nges pa'i tshig yin no/ / slob dpon ni 'di dag gis rnam par shes pa'i rgyud yul la 'jog cing 'bo bar byed pas zag pa dang*/ chu bo ltar nyon mongs pa'i shugs chen pos 'khyer bas chu bo dang*/ skye ba la sogs pa'i sdug bsngal sna tshogs dang sbyor ba'am/ rgyud la yang dang yang du sbyor bas sbyor ba dang*/ 'dod pa la sogs pa nye bar len pas 'dun pa'i 'dod chags nyid nye bar len pa yin no zhes bya ba ni ches legs pa yin no zhes 'chad do/ /

In particular, for those beings not free of attachment to the three realms, they are respectively called contaminants, floods, bonds, appropriators, and so on because these afflictions establish (āsaya) beings in saṃsāra; because they contaminate (āsrava) through the wound of the six sense bases from the summit of existence to Avīci; because they carry beings away (hara) to other realms, rebirths, and birth states in the ocean of saṃsāra; or because they act to engage the objects of consciousness because they link saṃsāra, realms, reincarnating beings, and birth states; or because they adhere (śleṣaya) to other objects of consciousness; or because they closely bind (upagṛhṇa) consciousness to saṃsāra. These are their etymologies. Vasubandhu explains that these afflictions are contaminants since they cause the stream of consciousness to fixate on and move to its object. They are floods since strong afflictions carry beings away like a flood. They are bonds since they bind to various sufferings such as birth and so on, or since they frequently bind those states to the mindstream. They are appropriators [473] since longing desire appropriates objects of desire and so forth. This is an excellent explanation.[1476]
lnga pa kun sbyor bshad pa ni/
Fetters
de dag kun tu sbyor sogs kyi/ / dbye bas yang rnam lngar bshad do/ / rdzas dang mchog 'dzin 'dra ba'i phyir/ / lta gnyis kun tu sbyor gzhan no/ / 41
There are said to be five types through classifying them as fetters and so on. Both views are distinct fetters because the latter are similar in substance and in clinging to them as supreme. (5:41)

phra rgyas de dag nyid kun tu sbyor ba dang*/ sogs pas gzung ba 'ching ba dang*/ phra rgyas dang*/ nye ba'i nyon mongs pa dang*/ kun nas dkris pa rnams kyi dbye bas yang rnam pa lngar mdo dang*/ chos mngon pa las phye nas bshad do/ / de la phra rgyas ni bshad zin la/ gzhan dag ni rim pa bzhin 'chad do/ / de la mdo las/ kun tu sbyor ba ni dgu ste/ rjes su chags pa dang*/ khong khro ba dang*/ nga rgyal dang*/ ma rig pa dang*/ lta ba dang*/ mchog tu 'dzin pa dang*/ the tshom dang*/ phrag dog dang*/ ser sna'i kun tu sbyor ba rnams so zhes gsungs te yul dang skye ba dag la kun tu sbyor bar byed pa'am/ 'di dag yod na sdug bsngal gyi khyad par du ma dang kun tu sbyor bas na kun sbyor ro/ / de la rjes su chags pa dang nga rgyal dang ma rig pa dang the tshom gyi kun sbyor bzhi ni khams gsum ga'i dang*/ khong khro dang phrag dog dang ser sna gsum ni 'dod khams kho na'i dang*/ lta ba'i kun sbyor ni khams gsum pa'i lta ba dang po gsum dang*/ mchog tu 'dzin pa'i kun sbyor ni lta ba phyi ma gnyis yin no/ / kun sbyor dgu po de dag gis ni gnyen po dgu la sgrib ste/ khams gsum la chags na skye ba mi 'byung bas skyo ba la rjes su chags pa'i kun sbyor gyis sgrib cing*/ khong khro'i gzhi la btang snyoms su byed mi nus pas btang snyoms la khong khro'i kun sbyor gyis sgrib la/ lhag ma bdun gyis ni de kho na nyid mthong ba la sgrib ste/ de la mngon par rtogs pa'i dus na nga'o snyam pa'i nga rgyal 'byung bas 'jig tshogs su lta ba yongs su shes pa la nga rgyal gyi kun sbyor gyis sgrib bo/ / nyer len gyi phung po mi rtag du ma gzhan dbang can du mi shes pas ma rig pa'i sbyor gyis 'jig tshogs la lta ba'i gzhi yongs su shes pa la sgrib bo/ / lta ba dang po gnyis kyis de la skrag cing log ltas skur ba 'debs pas na lta ba'i kun sbyor gyis 'gog pa'i bden pa yongs su shes pa la sgrib bo/ / lam gzhan gyis mchog dang dag par 'dzin pas na mchog tu 'dzin pa'i kun sbyor gyis lam gyi bden pa yongs su shes pa la sgrib bo/ / dkon mchog gi yon tan la mngon par yid mi ches pa the tshom gyi kun sbyor gyis dkon mchog gsum yongs su shes pa la sgrib bo/ / rnyed bkur gyi nyes pa ma mthong bas phrag dog gi kun sbyor gyis rnyed pa dang bkur sti yongs su shes pa la sgrib bo/ / yo byad la lhag par zhen pas ser sna'i kun sbyor gyis yo byad bsnyungs pa yongs su shes pa la sgrib ste/

There are said to be five types of negative tendencies through classifying them as fetters (saṃyojana) and so on, which includes ties that bind, negative tendencies, branch afflictions, and entanglements. Negative tendencies have already been explained, but the others will be explained sequentially. A sūtra states: The fetters are nine: the fetters of attraction, anger, pride, ignorance, view, clinging to them as supreme, doubt, envy, avarice.[1477] They are fetters since they completely bind to objects or lives, or since when they are present, they completely bind to many different sufferings. The four fetters of attraction, pride, ignorance, and doubt exist in all three realms. Three — anger, envy, and avarice — exist in the desire realm alone. The fetter of “view” constitutes the first three views of the three realms, and the fetters of “clinging to them as supreme” refers to the latter two views. These nine fetters obscure their nine antidotes: (1) The fetter of attraction obscures disappointment, since if one is attracted to the three realms, disappointment with them does not arise. (2) The fetter of anger obscures equanimity, since one is unable to act with equanimity to the basis of anger. The remaining seven obscure seeing reality (tattva). (3) The fetter of pride obscures the full understanding of the afflicted view of the self, since pride thinking “I” occurs at the time of actually comprehending [suchness]. (4) The fetter of ignorance obscures the full understanding of the basis of the afflicted view of the self, since it does not understand that the appropriated aggregates are impermanent, multiple, and controlled by other states. (5) The fetter of view obscures the full understanding of the truth of cessation, since the first two views fear the truth of cessation and wrong view underestimates it. (6) The fetter of clinging to those views as supreme obscures the full understanding of the path, since that clings to other paths as purifying agents. (7) The fetter of doubt that lacks conviction in the qualities of the Three Jewels obscures the full understanding of the Three Jewels. (8) The fetter of envy obscures the full understanding of property and respect, since it does not see the faults of [seeking] respect and property. (9) The fetter of avarice obscures the full understanding of reducing one’s possessions, since it longs for an increase in possessions.

dbus mtha' las/ kun du sbyor rnams sgrib pa yin/ / skyo ba dang ni btang snyoms dang*/ / de kho na ni mthong ba dang*/ / 'jig tshogs lta dang de'i gzhi dang*/ / 'gog dang lam dang dkon mchog dang*/ / rnyed pa dang ni bkur sti dang*/ yo byad bsnyungs pa yongs shes la/ / sgrib bo zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / dgur grangs nges pa'ang de nyid yin no/ / yang ci'i phyir lta ba rnams las dang po gsum lta ba'i kun sbyor dang*/ phyi ma gnyis mchog tu 'dzin pa'i kun sbyor zhes gcig tu byas she na/

Differentiating the Middle and Extremes says: The fetters obscure because they obscure the perfect knowledge of (1) disappointment, (2) equanimity, (3) seeing suchness and the afflicted view of the self, (4) its basis, (5) cessation, (6) the path, (7) the Jewels, (8) property and respect, and [474] (9) reducing possessions, and they are fixed in number as nine.[1478] Question: From the five views, why are the first three views the fetter of view and the latter two the fetter of clinging to those as supreme?

lta ba dang po gsum dang phyi ma gnyis rdzas bco brgyad par 'dra ba'i phyir dang*/ lta ba phyi ma gnyis kyis lta ba snga ma gsum la mchog dang dag par 'dzin pas na snga ma gsum ni bzung ba dang phyi ma gnyis dman pa la mchog tu 'dzin par 'dra ba'i phyir lta ba dang po gsum dang phyi ma gnyis kun tu sbyor ba gzhan du gsungs pa yin no/ / de la rdzas bco brgyad par 'dra ba ni lta ba dang po gnyis 'dod pa na sdug bsngal mthong spang gnyis dang khams gong ma gnyis na gnyis gnyis te drug dang*/ log lta khams gsum na bden bzhi mthong bas spang bar bya ba bzhi gsum bcu gnyis te lta ba dang po gsum la rdzas bco brgyad dang*/ lta ba lnga pa 'dod pa na sdug bsngal dang lam mthong spang gnyis da nga*/ khams gong ma gnyis na'ang gnyis gnyis te drug dang*/ lta ba bzhi pa khams gsum na bden bzhi mthong pas spang bar bya ba bzhi gsum bcu gnyis te de ltar na mchog tu 'dzin pa gnyis kyang rdzas bco brgyad pa yin no zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'chad mod kyi 'on kyang logs shig tu ston pa ni mchog 'dzin du 'dra ba nyid yin no/ / gal te kun tu sbyor ba dag tu kun nas dkris pa brgyad las phrag dog dang ser sna kho na ston pa la rgyu mtshan ci yod ce na/

Reply: Both the first three views and the latter views are said to be distinct fetters because, while the first three views and the latter two are similar in having eighteen substances each, the former three are objects, and the latter two are similar in clinging to these inferior states as supreme. That is, the latter two views cling to the former three views as supreme states and as purifying agents. Being similar in having eighteen substances means that the first two views have six substances: (1–2) those abandoned by seeing suffering in the desire realm and (3–6) two for each of the two higher realms. Wrong view has twelve: (7–18) those abandoned by seeing the four truths in the three realms. Therefore the first three views have eighteen substances. The fifth view has six: (1–2) two abandoned by seeing suffering and path in the desire realm and (3–6) two for each of the two higher realms. The fourth view has twelve: (7–18) those abandoned by seeing the four truths in the three realms. Thus the two types of clinging to those views as supreme have eighteen substances. Indeed, the Vaibhāṣikas state this, but the latter two views are taught to be similar simply because they both cling to those views as supreme. Question: For what reason are only the fetters of envy and avarice taught from among the eight entanglements?
gang phyir gnyis ka'ang gcig tu ni/ / mi dge rang dbang de yi phyir/ / phrag dog ser sna de dag las/ / logs shig kun sbyor gnyis su bshad/ / 42
Envy and avarice are said to be fetters separate from those six because both are nonvirtuous alone, autonomous, and others are not like that. (5:42)

gang gi phyir phrag dog dang ser sna gnyis ka gcig tu mi dge ba dang*/ ma rig pa tsam dang mtshungs par ldan pas rang dbang can yin pa de'i phyir phrag dog dang ser sna ngo tsha med pa la sogs pa'i kun nas dkris pa drug po de dag las logs shig tu kun tu sbyor ba gnyis su bshad de/ kun nas dkris pa gzhan dag ni de lta ma yin pa'i phyir te/ ngo tsha med pa dang khrel med pa gnyis gcig tu mi dge ba yin yang rang dbang can ma yin te/ 'dod chags la sogs pa nyon mongs pa gzhan dang yang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / 'gyod pa rang dbang can yin yang mi dge bar ma nges te/ dge ba'ang yod pa'i phyir ro/ / rmugs rgod dang gnyid ni dge ba'ang yod cing lung ma bstan yang 'dod chags la sogs pa dang yang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir gcig tu mi dge ba dang ma rig pa tsam dang mtshungs ldan pa'i rang dbang can yang ma yin pa'i phyir ro zhes bstan bcos rab tu byed pa'i rjes su 'brang ba'i bye brag tu smra ba kha cig 'dod do/ / gzhan dag na re de lta na bye brag tu smra ba gang gi ltar na kun nas dkris pa bcur 'dod pa de'i ltar na khro ba dang 'chab pa'ang mi dge ba dang rang dbang can yin pa'i phyir kun tu sbyor bar 'chad par thal bar 'gyur ro zhes zer ro/ / 'di'i lan la slob dpon 'dun bzang na re kun dkris bcu yod kyang phrag dog dang ser snas bde 'gro na lhag par 'ching ba'i phyir te/ shin tu rno ba dang*/ yang dang yang 'byung ba'i phyir dang*/ de gnyis ni rim pa bzhin du dbang chung ba dang longs spyod chung ba'i rgyu yin pa'i phyir logs shig tu bstan te/ 'dod pa na kun sbyor gzhan mang po yod kyang mdo las/ ko'u shi ka lha dang mi rnams ni phrag dog dang ser sna'i kun tu sbyor ba can yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

Envy (īrṣya) and avarice (mātsarya) are said to be two fetters separate from those six entanglements such as shamelessness and so on because both envy and avarice are nonvirtuous alone, they are autonomous (svatantra) since they are concomitant with ignorance only, and other entanglements are not like that. Though both shamelessness and nonembarrassment are solely nonvirtuous, they are not autonomous because they are concomitant with other afflictions such as attachment. Though regret is autonomous, it is not definite that it is nonvirtuous because virtuous regret also exists. Because confusion, excitation, and sleep may be virtuous or neutral, or concomitant with attachment and so forth, they are not autonomous states that are nonvirtuous and concomitant with ignorance only. This is asserted by one Vaibhāṣika who follows the Topic Divisions. Others say that, in accordance with the Vaibhāṣikas, the entanglements are ten in number. In that case it would follow that wrath and concealment would be explained as entanglements because they are nonvirtuous and autonomous. In answer to this Master Saṅghabhadra says that [475] though ten entanglements exist, envy and avarice in addition tie one to pleasant rebirths because they are extremely sharp and occur frequently. They are taught separately, he says, because though many other entanglements exist in the desire realm, those two are, respectively, causes of minor power and minor enjoyment. A sūtra remarks: O Kauśika, gods and humans possess the fetters of envy and avarice.[1479]

slob dpon rgyal po'i sras ni 'di gnyis kyi rim pa ltar kun tu gdung ba'i sdug bsngal dang kun tu dga' ba dang ldan pa'i nyon mongs pa thams cad ston pa'i phyir dang*/ rab tu byung ba dang khyim pa'i phyogs gnyis ka longs spyod dang chos la phrag dog dang ser sna 'byung bas nyon mongs par byed pa'i phyir dang*/ lha dang lha ma yin gyi phyogs gnyis ka bdud rtsi dang bud med kyi phyir shin tu nyon mongs par byed pa'i phyir logs shig tu bshad do zhes 'chad do/ /

Master Jinaputra says that these two are explained separately because, respectively, [envy and avarice] reveal all afflictions that possess fully tormenting suffering or complete joy. They afflict, since envy and avarice occur for both the ordained and for laypeople regarding object fields and Dharma, and they fully afflict both gods and demigods who seek nectar and consorts.[1480]
tha ma'i cha dang mthun rnam lnga/ / gnyis kyis 'dod las mi 'da' la/ / gsum po yis ni phyir zlog byed/ / sgo dang rtsa bas bsdus phyir gsum/ / 43
There are five associated with inferior states. Due to two, one does not transcend the desire realm. Due to three, one returns there. Three because they constitute the entrance and root. (5:43)

yang bcom ldan 'das kyis mdo gzhan du tha ma'i cha dang mthun pa'i kun tu sbyor ba lnga spangs pa'i phyir 'phags pa phyir mi 'ong ba yin te/ 'di lta ste 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang*/ tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa dang*/ the tshom dang*/ 'dod pa la 'dun pa dang*/ gnod sems so zhes tha ma'i cha dang mthun pa'i kun tu sbyor ba rnam pa lnga gsungs te/

The Bhagavan discloses in other sūtras that one becomes an ārya nonreturner because one abandons fetters associated with inferior states. The five types of fetters associated with inferior states (pañcadhā avarabhāgīya) are (1) the afflicted view of the self, (2) clinging to rules and ritual as supreme, (3) doubt, (4) longing for desire-realm objects, and (5) malice.

de la tha ma ni khams gsum gyi tha ma 'dod pa'i khams te/ gcig tu mnyam par ma bzhag pa dang*/ mi dge ba dang ngan 'gro dang sdug bsngal dang yid mi bde ba dang nyon mongs pa bar mtshams med pa yod pa'i phyir tha ma yin no zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / des na dman pa la tha ma'i sgra sbyar ba yin no/ / de'i cha dang mthun pa ni lnga po 'di dag 'dod pa dang rjes su mthun pa'i phyir te/ 'di ltar 'dod pa la 'dun pa dang gnod sems gnyis kyis ni gang la de dag yod pa de 'dod khams pa kho nar nges shing khams gong ma gnyis na de gnyis med pas sgo bas btson srung ba ltar 'dod pa'i khams las mi 'da' bar byed la/ 'jig tshogs la lta ba la sogs pa gsum po yis ni lan cig btson ra nas thar kyang rjes su 'brang bas phyir bzlog pa ltar 'dod pa las 'das te gong mar skyes kyang yang phyir bzlog par byed pa'i phyir ro zhes bye brag tu smra ba zer te/ de ltar na khong khro ma gtogs pa rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa dang lta ba gzhan yang tha ma'i cha dang mthun par 'gyur te/ 'dod pa las 'das kyang phyir bzlog par byed pa'i phyir ro/ /

“Inferior” means the desire realm, the least of the three realms, because it’s a state of nonequipoise, nonvirtue, lower rebirth, pain, mental dissatisfaction, and endless affliction. Pūrṇavardhana’s commentary explains this.[1481] Therefore the term “inferior” is applied to what is lower, and “associated” means they are associated with the desire realm. Thus one does not transcend the desire realm due to two: (1) longing for sensory objects and (2) malice. They are like guards who protect a prison, since any being who has them is certain to be a desire-realm being alone and those two do not exist in the two higher realms. Though one is born in higher realms through transcending the desire realm, one returns to the desire realm due to three states, (3–5) afflicted view of the self and so on, like one released from prison who returns due to adhering to his earlier evil habits. This is said by Vaibhāṣikas. Thus the root afflictions excluding anger and the other views are inferior states, because though one may transcend the desire realm, they cause one to return there.

de'i phyir rnal 'byor spyod pa pa dag {'di dag dang ldan na ci yang med pa la 'dod chags dang bral yang so skye las mi 'da' bas } dang po gsum gyis ni sems can gyi tha ma so so'i skye bo dang*/ phyi ma gnyis kyis ni {'phags pa'i chos thob pa yang 'dod pa las mi 'da' bas } khams kyi tha dad pa'i khams las mi 'da' la/ de dag las mi 'da' bar byed pa'i nyon mongs pa gzhan yang yod mod kyi de dag gtso che ba'i phyir bstan to/ / zhes 'chad pa ltar yin no zhes slob dpon bzhed do/ / {de ltar yang*/ khyod kyi chos las mi phyogs pa'i/ / skye bo gti mug gis ldongs pa/ / srid rtse'i bar du son nas kyang*/ / sdug bsngal rab 'byung srid pa sgrub ces bshad do }

Therefore Yogācāras teach that due to the first three inferior fetters, one remains an inferior ordinary sentient being, {since if one possesses them, one may be free of attachment to the base of nothingness but one does not transcend the state of an ordinary being}. Through the latter two inferior fetters, one does not transcend different elements of the realms, {since one does not transcend the desire realm though one may obtain ārya dharmas}. There are of course other afflictions that stop trancendence, [476] but these are taught to be foremost. This was stated by Vasubandhu.[1482] {Further, it is said: Beings who do not side with your Dharma[1483] are blinded by delusion. Though they reach the summit of existence, suffering fully arises and existence continues}.

'o na ci'i phyir rgyun du zhugs pas mthong spang thams cad spangs pas lta ba lnga po thams cad dang the tshom dang drug car spangs pa yin na stong chen mo rab tu 'joms pa las/ lta ba 'di la sbyar ma thag tu ni/ / 'jig tshogs lta dang tshul khrims brtul zhugs dang*/ / the tshom dang ni nyon mongs gsum po dag /cig car spangs te 'phags pa'i bden mthong ba zhes bya ba dang*/ ming chen gyis zhus pa'i mdo las kyang*/ btsun pa ji tsam gyis na rgyun du zhugs pa lags zhes zhus pa'i lan du/ ming chen 'di ni kun tu sbyor ba gsum po 'di lta ste 'jig tshogs la lta ba dang*/ tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa dang*/ the tshom yang yongs su spangs shing yongs su shes pa yin no/ / des kun tu sbyor ba gsum po de dag spangs pas rgyun du zhugs pa yin zhes lta ba bar pa gsum bor te kun tu sbyor ba gsum kho na spangs par gsungs she na/

Objection: If stream enterers abandon six — all five views and doubt — through abandoning all objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing, as stated in the Complete Destruction of Great Emptiness: Immediately after applying this view, then afflicted view of the self, rules and ritual, doubt, and the three afflicted states are simultaneously abandoned through seeing the ārya truths.[1484] then why does the Sūtra Requested by Mahānāma state: The Buddha asked: “Venerable, how does one become a stream enterer?” In reply Mahānāma said: “One becomes a stream enterer through fully abandoning and fully understanding the three fetters that are (1) the afflicted view of the self, (2) clinging to rules and ritual as supreme, and (3) doubt. Through abandoning these three fetters, one becomes a stream enterer.”[1485] This mentions that only three fetters are abandoned, omitting the three intermediate views.

de lta yin mod kyi gsum po 'dis mthong spang rnams kyi sgo bsdus pa'i phyir dang*/ rtsa ba bsdus pa'i phyir gsum po de spangs pas gzhan dag kyang spangs pa shugs la go ba'i phyir gsum kho na spangs par bstan te/ de la 'jig tshogs la lta ba ni spang bya'i sgo gcig pa ste sdug bsngal mthong bas spang bar bya ba'o/ / de spangs par bstan pas mthar 'dzin par lta ba spangs pa'ang shugs la go ste sgo gcig par 'dra ba'i phyir ro/ / tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog 'dzin ni sgo gnyis pa ste sdug bsngal dang lam mthong bas spang bar bya ba'o/{ the tshom ni bden bzhi mthong spang sgo bzhi pa ste} de spangs par bstan pas log lta dang lta ba mchog 'dzin yang spangs par shugs la go ste/ rnam pa bzhi par 'dra ba'i phyir ro/ / de dag spangs par bstan pas mthong spang gis bsdus pa'i 'dod chags la sogs pa'ang spangs par bstan te/ 'dod chags la sogs pa ni de dag la dmigs pas de dag gi yul can yin pa'i phyir ro zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / 'o na lta ba dang po dang the tshom bor te mthar 'dzin par lta ba dang*/ lta ba mchog 'dzin dang log lta gang rung re re'i byas nas kyang kun sbyor gsum du ston par 'gyur te/ sgo bsdus par 'dra ba'i phyir ro zhe na/ de gcig pur ma zad rtsa ba bsdus pa'i phyir yang ste/ mthar 'dzin par lta ba ni bdag la rtag chad kyi mthar 'dzin pas 'jig tshogs la lta ba'i rtsa ba can yin zhing*/ lta ba mchog 'dzin ni gang gis 'dag par yid ches pa de la mchog tu 'dzin pas tshul khrims dang brtul zhugs mchog tu 'dzin pa'i rtsa ba can yin la/ log lta ni the tshom gyis log par mnyan pa dang bsam pas log par nges pa skye bas the tshom gyi rtsa ba can yin no zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'dod de/ rnam pa gcig pa la sogs pa ni mi 'thad par bshad zin pa'i phyir rtsa ba bsdus pa'am gtso che ba'i phyir yin no zhes bar bya'o/ /

Reply: Indeed, both are true. The abandonment of three alone is taught because these three constitute the entrance (mukha) to abandonment by the path of seeing and its root (mūla), and by abandoning those three the abandonment of the others is implicitly understood. (1) The afflicted view of the self is the first entrance to abandonment that is abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering. By teaching that it is to be abandoned, the fact that extreme view is also to be abandoned is implicitly understood. They are similar in having the same entrance. (2) Clinging to rules and ritual as supreme is the second entrance that is abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering and path. By teaching that it is to be abandoned, the fact that wrong view and clinging to those as supreme are also to be abandoned is implicitly understood because they are similar to (3) the fourth, {since doubt is the fourth entrance abandoned by seeing the four truths}. Teaching that these three are to be abandoned also teaches that attachment and so on included in those abandoned by the path of seeing should also be abandoned. Since attachment and so on focus on these three, they are minds aware of these three. This is explained in the Subcommentary.[1486] Objection: Leaving aside the first view and doubt, if one engages any of the three views — the view adhering to an extreme, clinging to those as supreme, and wrong view — they should be taught to be the three fetters because they are similar in constituting entrances. Reply: Not only are they entrances, but they also constitute roots. Since extreme view grasps the self to be permanent or annihilated, it is the root of the afflicted view of the self. Since clinging to those views as supreme holds as supreme the conviction that these false views purify, it is the root of clinging to rules and ritual as supreme. Since wrong view generates wrong discernment through distorted listening and contemplation, [477] it is the root of doubt. This is asserted by Vaibhāṣikas. Because it has already been explained that it is untenable that they have the same aspect and so on, those should be understood to “constitute the root” or to be foremost.[1487]
'gro mi 'dod dang lam nor dang / / lam la the tshom de snyed cig / thar pa bgrod la gegs byed pa/ / de yi phyir na gsum bstan to/ / 44
There are three impediments to proceeding to liberation, and therefore three are taught: not desiring to proceed there, mistaking the path, and doubting the path. (5:44)

slob dpon ni dper na yul gzhan du 'gro ba la ji srid 'gro bar mi 'dod pa dang*/ lam nor bar 'gro ba dang*/ lam la the tshom za ba'i bar chad gsum po de snyed cig yod pa de srid du yul gzhan du mi phyin pa ltar thar pa bgrod pa la'ang bgegs byed pa gsum yin la/ de dag spangs na thar par bgrod pa la bgegs med par bstan pa de'i phyir na rgyun du zhugs pas kun sbyor gsum kho na spangs par bstan to/ / de la kun sbyor dang pos ni bdag chad par dogs pas thar pa la skrag pa'i phyir 'gro bar mi 'dod pa yin zhing*/ gnyis pas {tshul khrims mchog 'dzin } ni lam gzhan la brten pas lam nor ba la zhugs pa yin la/ gsum pas ni lam la the tshom za ba yin no zhes 'chad do/ /

Vasubandhu explains that for as long as one possesses the three obstacles to proceeding to another place — (1) not desiring to proceed to another place, (2) proceeding but mistaking the path, and (3) doubting the path — then for that long one will not proceed there. Similarly, there are three impediments (antarāya) to proceeding to liberation (mokṣa), and if these are abandoned, it is said that no impediments remain to proceeding there. Therefore it is taught that a stream enterer abandons three fetters alone. Through the first fetter, one does not desire to proceed to liberation because one is terrified of liberation out of fear that the self will be annihilated. Through the second {fetter clinging to rules and ritual as supreme}, one mistakes the path through relying on other paths. Through the third fetter, one doubts the path.[1488]
gong ma'i cha dang mthun lnga nyid/ / gzugs dang gzugs med las skyes pa'i/ / 'dod chags gnyis rgod nga rgyal rmongs/ /
The five factors associated with higher states are the two attachments arising for the form and formless realms, excitation, pride, and confusion. (5:45abc)

bshes spring las kyang*/ tshul khrims brtul zhugs mchog 'dzin rang lus la/ / phyin ci log par lta dang the tshom ste/ / kun du sbyor ba 'di gsum thar pa yi/ / grong khyer sgo 'gog legs par mkhyen par mdzod ces 'byung ngo*/ /

Letter to a Friend states: Clinging to rules and ritual as supreme, the distorted view of one’s body, and doubt are the three fetters. One should comprehend that these block the entrance to the city of liberation.[1489]

yang mdo las/ gong ma'i cha dang mthun pa lnga spangs pa'i phyir 'phags pa dgra bcom pa'o zhes gong ma'i cha dang mthun pa lnga nyid du gsungs pa ni gzugs dang gzugs med pa'i khams las skyes pa'i 'dod chags gnyis dang rgod pa dang nga rgyal dang kun du rmongs pa rnams yin no/ / ci'i phyir zhe na/ 'di dag ma spangs par khams gong ma las mi 'da' ba'i phyir dang*/ sgom spang yin pa'i phyir ro/{ gong ma mi gtong ba'i rgyu yin pas gsum po re rer byas la/ gong ma nye bar len pa'i rgyu yin pas 'dod chags gnyis so sor byas so zhe'o/} khong khro ni sgom spang yin yang khams gong ma na med pa'i phyir ro/ /

Again, a sūtra observes: Āryas are destroyers because they abandon five factors associated with higher states.[1490] Those called the five factors associated with higher states (pañcadhaivordhvabhāgīya) are (1–2) the two attachments (rāga) arising for the form and formless realms, (3) excitation (auddhatya), (4) pride (māna), and (5) complete confusion (mohā). Question: Why? Reply: That is because without abandoning them one does not transcend the higher realms, and they are objects abandoned by the path of meditation. {Each of the latter three acts to prevent such transcendence since they are causes for not relinquishing the higher realms. Each of the two attachments prevents such transcendence since they are the substantial cause (upādānahetu) of higher realms.} However, although anger is abandoned by the path of meditation, it does not exist in the higher realms.
drug pa 'ching ba bshad pa ni
Ties
tshor ba'i dbang gis 'ching ba gsum/ / 45
There are three ties due to the power of feelings. (5:45d)

mdo las/ 'ching ba rnams gang zhe na/ 'ching ba ni gsum ste/ 'ching ba 'dod chags thams cad dang*/ zhe sdang thams cad dang*/ gti mug thams cad do zhes gsungs pa ni {'di dag gis sems bcings na rang dbang med pas 'ching ba'o/ / de yang } dge slong ma chos sbyin gyi mdo las/ bde ba'i tshor ba la 'dod chags rgyas par 'gyur ro/ / sdug bsngal gyi tshor ba la zhe sdang rgyas par 'gyur ro/ / bde ba yang ma yin sdug bsngal yang ma yin pa'i tshor ba la gti mug rgyas par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs pas

A sūtra states: What are the ties? Ties are three: the ties of all attachment, all aversion, and all delusion.[1491] {When they tie the mind, one is constricted beyond one’s control. Further} the Bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā Sūtra notes: From the feeling of pleasure, attachment increases. From the feeling of pain, aversion increases. From the feeling that is neither pleasure nor pain, delusion increases.[1492]

bde ba la sogs pa'i tshor ba'i dbang gis 'dod chags la sogs pa 'di dag gis 'khor bar 'ching bas na 'ching ba gsum du bshad de/ tshor ba bde ba la sogs pa gsum las rim pa ltar dug gsum dmigs pa dang mtshungs ldan gyi sgo nas rgyas pa'i phyir ro/ / kun las btus las ni dug gsum gyis rim pa ltar 'gyur ba dang sdug bsngal dang 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal gsum la 'ching bas na 'ching ba zhes bshad do/ / de yang phal che ba'i dbang du byas kyi res 'ga' ni dgra bo'i bde sdug la dmigs nas kyang zhe sdang dang 'dod chags rgyas par 'gyur ro/ / de yang rang rgyud kyi bde sdug la ni dmigs pa dang mtshungs ldan gnyis kas rgyas la gzhan rgyud kyi la ni dmigs pa'i sgo nas so/ / btang snyoms la'ang chags sdang gnyis ka'ang rgyas mod kyi gti mug dang gnyis mi gsal bar mthun pas lhag par rgyas par 'gyur ro zhes slob dpon gang spel 'chad do/ /

They are called the three ties (bandhana) since they tie one to saṃsāra through attachment and so on due to the power of feelings (vidvaśa), such as pleasure, where the three poisons increase by means of focal object and concomitance respectively due to the feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity. The Compendium of Abhidharma explains: They are ties since the three poisons tie one to the three sufferings, that of change, pain, and formations.[1493] [478] Further, in general, aversion and attachment temporarily increase due to observing the pleasure and pain of enemies. Again, aversion and attachment increase due to either focusing on and being concomitant with the pleasure and pain in one’s own mindstream, or they increase by means of focusing on those in others’ mindstreams. In fact, both attachment and aversion can increase through equanimity, and they further increase when associated with the unclarity of delusion and sleep. This is explained by Master Pūrṇavardhana.[1494]
bdun pa nye ba'i nyon mongs pa bshad pa ni
Branch afflictions
nyon mongs las gzhan nyon mongs can/ / sems byung 'du byed phung zhes pa/ / gang de'ang nye ba'i nyon mongs te/ / de dag nyon mongs zhes mi bya/ / 46
Any afflicted mental factors other than root afflictions that are said to be the aggregate of formation are branch afflictions. They are not called root afflictions. (5:46)

rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa drug po las gzhan pa'i nyon mongs pa can gyi sems las byung ba 'du byed kyi phung po zhes pa gang yin pa de yang rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa dang nye bar 'dug pas na nye ba'i nyon mongs te/ de dag la rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa zhes ni mi bya ste/ rtsa ba ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag kyang kun nas dkris pa dang*/ dri ma dang*/ gzhi phran tshegs las 'byung ba mi dga' ba dang*/ glal byed pa dang*/ sems zhum pa nyid dang*/ smyo ba dang*/ zas kyi drod mi zin pa nyid dang*/ tha dad pa'i 'du shes dang*/ yid la mi byed pa dang*/ lus kyi gnas ngan len dang*/ ru gdug dang*/ 'phya smod dang*/ gnam pa nyid dang*/ mi gnam pa nyid dang*/ rang bzhin du mi 'dug pa nyid dang*/ 'dod pa'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ 'tshe ba'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ nye du'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ yul mi'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ mi 'chi ba'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ brnyas pa dang ldan pa'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ rigs snyems pa dang ldan pa'i rnam par rtog pa dang*/ mya ngan dang*/ sdug bsngal ba dang*/ yid mi bde ba dang*/ 'khrug pa zhes bya ba nyer bzhi po dag ste/ 'di dag gi don ni rin po che'i phreng ba dang*/ gzhi bsdu ba las 'byung ba ltar shes par bya'o/ /

Any afflicted mental factors (caitasā) other than the six root afflictions that are said to be the aggregate of formation (saṃskāra) are branch afflictions (upakleśa), since they exist near to the root afflictions. They are not called “root afflictions” because they are not roots. Also these are restraints and stains, and the Kṣudraka Chapter declares that there are twenty-four: Joylessness, yawning, mental lassitude, bad omens, inability to digest food, discernment of what is distinct, lack of attention, physical dysfunction, hostility, abuse, stench, nonstench, not existing with an essence, speculation about sense objects, speculation about violence, speculation about one’s relatives, speculation about one’s land, speculation about the deathless state, speculation about property, class conceit, sorrow, pain, mental dissatisfaction, and agitation.[1495] The meaning of those should be understood in accordance with how they occur in Nāgārjuna’s Precious Garland and Asaṅga’s Compendium of Bases.
brgyad pa kun nas dkris pa bshad pa ni
Entanglements
'di dag gis srid pa'i btson rar kun nas 'khri ba'am/ 'di dag yod na spyod pa ngan pa dag ldang bas na kun dkris so/ / de dag kyang gang zhe na/
They are entanglements since they completely ensnare one in the prison of saṃsāra, and when they are present, one is filled with evil actions. Question: What are they?
ngo tsha med dang khrel med dang / / phrag dog ser sna rgod pa dang / / 'gyod dang rmugs dang gnyid dang ni/ / kun nas dkris pa rnam pa brgyad/ / 47
Shamelessness, nonembarrassment, envy, avarice, excitation, regret, lethargy, and sleep are the eight types of entanglements. (5:47)
ngo tsha med pa nas gnyid kyi bar kun nas dkris pa ni rnam pa brgyad yin par bstan bcos rab tu byed pa las bshad do/ /
Topic Divisions explains the eight types of entanglements (paryavasthāna) from shamelessness to sleep.[1496]
khro dang 'chab pa'o 'dod chags kyis/ / ngo tsha med rgod ser sna bslang / / 'chab pa rtsod do ma rig las/ / rmugs dang gnyid dang khrel med do/ / 48
Wrath and concealment. Attachment motivates shamelessness, excitation, and avarice. There is dispute about concealment. Lethargy, sleep, and nonembarrassment arise from ignorance. (5:48)

bye brag tu smra ba ni brgyad po de dag dang khro ba dang 'chab pa ste bcu'o zhes 'dod do/ / de dag gi ngo bo ni bshad zin la/ 'dir 'gyod pa kun nas dkris par 'gyur ba ni 'gyod pa mi dge ba yin no/ / de dag kyang rtsa nyon gyis skyed pa las rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa gang gis skyed ce na/

The Vaibhāṣikas assert there are ten entanglements: those eight, plus wrath (krodha) and concealment (mrakṣa) [of one’s faults]. Their nature has been explained.[1497] Here regret as an entanglement refers to nonvirtuous regret. Question: Those are generated by the root afflictions, but what root afflictions generate them?

'dod chags kyis ngo tsha med pa dang rgod pa dang ser sna bslang zhing bskyed pa yin te/ rang gi chos la chags pas gzhan la ma gus pa'i phyir dang*/ 'dod pa'i yon tan la chags pas sems rnam par 'phro ba'i phyir dang*/ yo byad la sogs pa la chags pas dam du 'dzin pa'i phyir ro/ / 'chab pa ni kha cig 'dod chags kyis skyed par 'dod la/ gzhan dag ni gti mug gis bskyed par 'dod do/ / la la ni gnyis kas bskyed pa yin te/ nyes pa byung bar shes pa rnams kyi 'dod chags dang*/ byung bar ma shes pa rnams kyi gti mug las skyes so zhes zer te mi mthun par rtsod do/ / 'on kyang rnyed bkur dang tshigs su bcad pa nyams kyis dogs nas 'chab pa'i phyir 'dod chags las skyes pa nyid rigs so/ / ma rig pa las sems rmugs pa dang gnyid dang khrel med rnams skye ste/ dmigs pa gsal bar 'jug pa la rmugs pa dang gnyid med pa'i phyir dang*/ sdig pa'i 'bras bu sdug bsngal yin par ma shes pas sdig pa la mi 'jigs pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: Attachment motivates and generates shamelessness (āhrīkya), excitation (auddhatya), and avarice (matsārya) because through attachment to one’s own qualities, one does not respect others. Through attachment to sense objects, minds [attracted to them] proliferate, and through attachment to possessions and so on, one is tight-fisted. There is dispute about concealment due to contrary assertions. Some assert: Concealment is generated by attachment. [479] Others assert: Concealment is generated by delusion. Some say: Concealment is generated by both because it is generated from attachment for those who know a fault has arisen and from ignorance for those who don’t. However, it is logical that concealment is generated from attachment because concealment arises out of fear of losing one’s property and respect. Lethargy (styāna), sleep (middha), and nonembarrassment (anapatrāpya) are generated from ignorance because lethargy and sleep do not clearly engage their focal object, and they don’t fear immorality since they don’t know suffering to be the result of immorality.
the tshom las 'gyod khro ba dang / / phrag dog khong khro'i rgyu las byung / /
Regret arises from doubt. Wrath and envy arise from their cause, anger. (5:49ab)

the tshom las 'gyod pa mi dge ba 'byung ste/ dge ba'i 'bras bu bde ba yin par the tshom za ba dag dge ba byas pa la 'gyod pa'i phyir ro/ / khro ba dang phrag dog ni khong khro'i rgyu las byung ba yin te/ zhe sdang las kun nas mnar sems skye ba'i phyir dang*/ gzhan gyi phun sum tshogs pa la sems 'khrugs nas mi bzod pa'i phyir ro/ /

Nonvirtuous regret arises from doubt because those who doubt that the result of virtue is blissful have regret for virtuous actions. Wrath (krodha) and envy (īrṣya) arise from their cause, which is anger, because a tormented mind arises from aversion and one is irritable due to a mind that is disturbed by the excellent qualities of others.
dgu pa dri ma bshad pa ni
Stains
gzhan yang nyon mongs dri ma drug / sgyu dang g.yo dang rgyags pa dang / / 49 de bzhin 'tshig dang khon 'dzin dang / /
Again, the stains of afflictions are six: deceit, guile, arrogance, (5:49cd) so too resentment, spite, violence. (5:50a)
gzhan yang mdo las nyon mongs pa'i dri ma rnam pa drug gsungs te/ de dag kyang sgyu nas par 'tshe ba'i bar ro/ /'di dag gi yang ngo bo ni bshad zin la/ rtsa ba'i nyon mongs pa gang las skyes pa ni

Again, a sūtra reveals that the stains (kleśamala) of the afflictions have six types because they are those from deceit (māyā) to violence (vihiṃsā).[1498] Their nature has already been explained. Question: From what root afflictions do they arise?
rnam 'tshe rgyu dang rgyags pa ni/ / 'dod chags las skyes khon 'dzin dang / / rnam 'tshe khong khro las skyes so/ / 50
Deceit and arrogance arise from attachment. Resentment and violence arise from anger. (5:50bcd)

sgyu dang rgyags pa ni 'dod chags las skyes te/ rnyed pa la sogs pa nyams kyis dogs nas sgyu byed pa'i phyir dang rang gi chos la chags pas yid bde ba'i phyir ro/ / khon du 'dzin pa dang rnam par 'tshe ba ni zhe sdang gis kun nas bslang nas khon 'dzin dang sems can la rnam par 'tshe ba 'byung bas na khong khro las skyes so/ /

Reply: Deceit and arrogance (mada) arise from attachment because one acts with deceit through fear that one’s property and so on will decline, and one experiences mental satisfaction through attachment to one’s own good qualities. Resentment (upanāha) and violence arise from anger, where resentment is motivated by aversion and violence arises in relation to sentient beings.
'tshig pa lta ba mchog 'dzin las/ / g.yo ni lta bas kun nas bslang / /
Spite arises from clinging to those views as supreme. Guile is motivated by wrong view. (5:51ab)

'tshig pa ni lta ba mchog tu 'dzin pa las skyes te/ rang gi lta ba la dam du bzung nas gzhan la 'tshig pa'i phyir ro/ / mdo las/ gya gyu ci yin sdig can lta zhes 'byung ba'i phyir g.yo ni log par lta bas kun nas bslang ba yin te/ {las 'bras las } log par lta ba dang ldan pa sems sdig pa mi 'chags par gya gyu ba'i phyir ro/{ mdo las kyang*/ rtag pa ci zhig mya ngan 'das/ / mi rtag ci zhig 'dus byas chos/ / drang ba ci zhig 'phags pa'i lam/ / gya gyu ci zhig sdig can lta/ / zhes so/ /}

Spite (pradāśa) arises from clinging to those views as supreme because it is spite directed at others through clinging to one’s own views as pure, and a sūtra declares: Any crookedness is immoral view.[1499] Therefore guile (śāṭhya) is motivated by wrong view. Such a mind possesses wrong view {as to karma and its effects}, and it does not [inspire the] confession of immorality because it is crooked. {A sūtra states: That which is permanent is nirvāṇa. That which is impermanent is conditioned phenomena. That which is straight is ārya Dharma. That which is crooked is immoral view.}[1500]
bcu pa de dag gi khyad par gyi chos bshad pa ni
Their specific attributes
de las ngo tsha med pa dang / / khrel med rmugs gnyid rgod rnam gnyis/ / 51
From those, shamelessness, nonembarrassment, lethargy, sleep, and excitation have two types. (5:51cd)
