Question: When one obtains {ordinary abidance in the result of} nonreturn that is not free from attachment to the form realm or the result of arhat, how can there be just one perfect knowledge {or just one for each of} the many abandonments?
khams las 'dod chags bral ba dang/ / 'bras bu thob phyir de dag bsdoms/ / la la gcig gnyis lnga dang drug / gtong ste thob pa lnga min no/ / 70
Because they are free of attachment to the realms and they obtain the result through combining them. Some relinquish one, two, five, or six. Obtainment of five does not exist. (5:70)

gzugs kyi 'dod chags dang ma bral ba'i phyir mi 'ong dang dgra bcom thob pa'i tshe ni rim pa ltar 'dod pa dang khams gsum las 'dod chags dang bral ba'i phyir dang*/ phyir mi 'ong dang dgra bcom pa'i 'bras bu thob pa'i rgyu gnyis gnyis kyi phyir spangs pa dang yongs shes de dag bsdoms nas tha ma'i cha mthun spangs pa dang zag pa kun zad kyi yongs shes re rer bzhag go /rgyun zhugs dang lan cig phyir 'ong la ni 'bras bu thob pa yod kyang khams las 'dod chags dang bral ba med pa'i phyir dang*/ gzugs kyi 'dod chags dang bral ba'i phyir mi 'ong la khams las 'dod chags dang bral ba yod kyang 'bras bu sngar med thob pa med pa'i phyir dang*/ gzhan dag la ni gnyis ka med pa'i phyir yongs shes sdom par mi byed do/ / yang gang zhig yongs shes du zhig gtong ba'am 'thob ce na/

Reply: When one obtains the state of a nonreturner who is not free from attachment to the form realm, or the state of arhat, it is because, respectively, one is either free of attachment to the desire realm or the three realms, or one possesses either the cause that obtains the result of a nonreturner or the cause that obtains the result of an arhat. Perfect knowledge of the abandonment of factors associated with inferior states or the perfect knowledge of the complete elimination of contaminants [494] is established in either case through combining (saṃkalana) those abandonments and perfect knowledges. Perfect knowledge is not combined for stream enterers and once returners, even though they obtain their result, because they do not attain freedom from attachment to the realms. And perfect knowledge is not combined for nonreturners free of attachment to the form realm, even though they are free from attachment to that realm, because they do not possess a result they did not previously have. For others perfect knowledge is not combined because neither exists. Question: How many perfect knowledges are relinquished or obtained?

la la ni yongs shes gcig gtong ste/ dgra bcom las nyams na sngar yongs shes tha ma gcig pu dang ldan pa de nyid gtong ba'i phyir dang*/ de bzhin du gzugs kyi 'dod chags dang ma bral ba'i 'phags pa phyir mi 'ong 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba las nyams na'ang bdun pa gcig pu gtong ngo*/ / la la ni gnyis gtong ste/ phyir mi 'ong gzugs kyi 'dod chags dang bral ba 'dod pa'i nyon mongs mngon du byas te nyams pa'am des dgra bcom thob pa na bdun pa dang brgyad pa gnyis gtong ba'i phyir ro/ / kha cig ni lnga gtong ste/ chags bral sngon 'gros skad cig ma bcu drug pa lam la rjes shes thob pa na 'dod pa'i mthong spang spangs pa'i yongs shes gsum dang*/ khams gong ma'i mthong spang spangs pa'i yongs shes gnyis te lnga gtong ba'i phyir ro/ / khams gong ma gnyis kyi lam mthong spang spangs pa'i yongs shes ni mi gtong mod kyi khams las {yang} 'dod chags dang bral ba{ 'i phyir} dang{ de'i tshe} 'bras bu thob pa'i phyir de gnyis kyi sgo nas tha ma'i cha mthun spangs pa'i yongs shes kyi nang du bsdoms pa'i phyir de las tha dad du bshad du med do/ / la la ni drug gtong ste/ 'phags pa mthar gyis pa 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba na bdun pa thob pas snga ma drug gtong ba'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: Some relinquish (jahāti) one perfect knowledge, because if one degenerates from the state of an arhat, that one final perfect knowledge that was possessed is relinquished. So too, if an ārya nonreturner free from attachment to the form realm degenerates from freedom from attachment to the desire realm, the seventh alone is relinquished. Some relinquish two, because a nonreturner free of attachment to the form realm who degenerates through manifesting desire afflictions, or who becomes an arhat, relinquishes both the seventh and eighth. One relinquishes five, because when someone previously freed from attachment obtains knowledge of the higher path of the sixteenth moment, he relinquishes five: (1–3) the three perfect knowledges abandoning objects to be abandoned by seeing in the desire realm, and (4–5) the two higher knowledges abandoning objects to be abandoned in the higher realms. Indeed, the perfect knowledge abandoning objects to be abandoned by seeing the truth of the path of the two higher realms is not relinquished. Some relinquish six, because if an ārya serial abandoner is free of attachment to the desire realm, he relinquishes the former six in obtaining the seventh.

de bzhin du 'thob pa ni gcig dang gnyis dang drug 'thob pa yod kyi lnga 'thob pa ni yod pa min no zhes bya'o/ / de la gcig 'thob pa ni mthong lam la gnas pas kun 'byung la chos shes pa'i gnas skabs na sngar med pa las dang po gcig pu 'thob pa dang*/ de bzhin du chags bral sngon 'gros 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral nas lam la rjes shes kyi tshe bdun pa gcig pu dang*/ mthar gyis pas kyang 'dod pa las 'dod chags dang bral ba'i rnam grol gyi lam dgu pa la bdun pa gcig pu dang*/ dgra bcom pa thob pa na'ang tha ma gcig pu 'thob bo/ / gnyis thob pa ni gzugs med las 'dod chags dang bral ba gzugs med kyi nyon mongs pas nyams na bdun pa dang brgyad pa gnyis 'thob pa lta bu'o/ / drug 'thob pa ni 'phags pa la mthar gyis pa phyir mi 'ong las nyams na yongs shes dang po dag 'thob pa yin no/{ 'o na chags bral sngon 'gro tha ma'i cha mthun spangs pa las nyams na dang po lngas ci'i phyir mi thob ce na/ de ni lam gnyis kyis 'thob pa'i phyir yongs su nyams pa mi srid de/} des na lnga 'thob pa ni 'ga' yang med do/ /

Likewise, there is obtainment of one, two, and six, but obtainment (āpnoti) of five does not exist. Obtainment of one is someone abiding on the path of seeing who obtains just the first perfect knowledge that has never been obtained before when abiding in Dharma knowledge of the truth of origin. So too, someone previously freed from attachment obtains just the seventh perfect knowledge when abiding in subsequent knowledge of the truth of the path, having attained freedom from attachment to the desire realm. A serial abandoner obtains just the seventh perfect knowledge on the ninth liberated path free from attachment to the desire realm alone, and when he obtains the state of an arhat, he obtains the last perfect knowledge alone.
Obtainment of two is someone free of attachment to the formless realm who obtains both the seventh and eighth perfect knowledges when freedom from attachment to the formless realm degenerates through formless affliction. Obtainment of six [495] is an ārya serial abandoner who obtains the first perfect knowledge when he degenerates from the state of nonreturn. {Question: Now, when someone previously freed from attachment degenerates from abandoning factors associated with inferior states, why does he not obtain that through the first five? Reply: Degeneration is impossible because he obtains that through the two paths}. Therefore obtainment of five does not exist in the least.
zag bcas las dang yang srid 'grub pa yi/ / rtsa ba phra rgyas spang bya rnam gnyis dang*/ / de dag spong tshul spangs pa'i 'bras bu sogs/ / shes par 'dod pas gnas 'di mnyan par gyis/ /

Since one desires to know the two types of negative tendency to be abandoned — contaminated karma and the root establishing rebirth — as well as the result of abandonment by means of abandoning those and so on, one should study this part.
chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi tshig le'ur byas pa las/ /phra rgyas bstan pa zhes bya ba ste gnas lnga pa'o// //
chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi 'grel pa mngon pa'i rgyan las phra rgyas bstan pa zhes bya ba ste gnas lnga pa'i bshad pa'o// ! //
This has been part V, the “Exposition of Negative Tendencies,” from Ornament of Abhidharma: A Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa. [496]
26. The Four Noble Truths
gnas drug pa lam dang gang zag bstan pa/
THE EXPOSITION OF PATH AND PERSON

da ni gnas drug pa lam dang gang zag bstan pa 'chad pa na mtshams sbyar ba'i tshul gyis mdor bstan pa dang*/ dmigs pa'i yul bden pa bshad pa dang*/ mngon par rtogs pa'i rim pa dang*/ sgom pa po'i gang zag rnam par bzhag pa dang*/ mngon par rtogs pa'i lam bshad pa lnga las/

In explaining the presentation of part VI, there are five headings: (1) overview, which transitions [from part V]; (2) the [four noble] truths, the focal object; (3) the stages of realization; (4) the principle of the person as meditator; and (5) the path of realization.
dang po [mtshams sbyar ba'i tshul gyis mdor bstan pa] ni
Overview

gal te gnas lnga par 'bras bu la rgyu nye bar btags pa'i phyir spangs pa ni yongs su shes pa'i ming 'thob bo zhes pa dang*/ spong ba'i gnyen por yang*/ de dag bcu dang bdun bdun brgyad/ / lta ba gsum gnyis ma gtogs pa/ / 'dod na sdug bsngal la sogs pa/ / mthong bas rim bzhin spong bar byed/ / bzhi ni bsgom pas spang bya yin/ / zhes

In part V, abandonment obtains the name of perfect knowledge because the cause is designated as the result. Regarding the abandoning antidote, the Abhidharmakośa states, “Ten, seven, seven, and eight, because three or two views are excluded. They are serially abandoned by seeing suffering in the desire realm and so on” (5:4).[1520]
bden pa mthong dang bsgoms pa las/ / nyon mongs spangs pa zhes bshad pa/ / bsgom pa'i lam ni rnam gnyis te/ / mthong ba zhes bya zag pa med/ / 1
It is said that from seeing the truth and meditating on it, the afflictions are abandoned. The path of meditation has two types. That which is called seeing is uncontaminated. (6:1)

bden pa mthong ba dang mthong don bsgoms pa las mthong sgom gyi spang bya nyon mongs pa rnams spangs pa'am spong ngo zhes bshad pa'i gnyen po mthong sgom gyi lam de dag nyid zag bcas zag med gang yin zhe na/

It is said that from seeing the truth and meditating on its meaning, the afflictions (kleṣa) to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and meditation are abandoned (prahāṇa) or will be abandoned. Question: Which of those paths of seeing and meditation that are antidotes are contaminated, and which are uncontaminated?

Reply: The path of meditation has two types, contaminated and uncontaminated. The mundane path of meditation inceases contaminants in the contaminated absorption and formless states. The transcendent path of meditation does not incease contaminants because it cultivates the meaning of four noble truths comprehended by the path of seeing that possesses those aspects.
That which is called “the path of seeing” is singularly uncontaminated because it is the antidote {of objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing} of all three realms, because it simultaneously abandons nine states — the great of the great objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing and so on — {and because it is pervasively uncontaminated}. Mundane paths do not have this capacity. {That which is abandoned by meditation is not abandoned all at once because it possesses [progressive] causes (sanidāna); it is revealed [progressively]. There are many differences between that which is abandoned by seeing and meditation. In terms of their nature, seeing is uncontaminated alone and meditation is both contaminated and uncontamined. In terms of their focal object, seeing focuses on four truths, and meditation may focus on the levels above and below. In terms of their aspect, for seeing it is the noble truths, and for meditation it even includes agriculture.[1521] In terms of being classified by their nature, seeing has perseverance and knowledge, and meditation has knowledge alone. In terms of objects to be abandoned and their mode of abandonment, seeing simultaneously abandons through knowledge of the focal object, and meditation serially abandons through cultivating the antidote. In terms of their basis, seeing occurs in the desire realm, and meditation occurs in all three realms. In terms of mindstream, seeing occurs in an ārya alone, and meditation occurs in both ordinary beings and āryas.[1522] In terms of mode of arising, seeing arises in one session, and meditation also arises in other lives.} [497]
gnyis pa [dmigs pa'i yul bden pa bshad pa] ni
The four noble truths, the focal object
'o na bden pa mthong dang bsgoms pa las zhes bshad pa'i bden pa de dag gang zhe na/
Question: What are those truths mentioned in the Abhidharmakośa: “From seeing the truth and meditating on it” (6:1ab)?
bden pa dag ni bzhir bshad do/ / sdug bsngal kun 'byung de bzhin du/ / 'gog dang lam ste de ltar na/ / de dag ji ltar mngon rtogs rim/ / 2
Those truths are explained as four. Thus suffering, origin, so too cessation and path. These are in the order in which they are realized. (6:2)

mthong ba dang bsgom par bya ba'i bden pa dag ni bzhir bshad do/ / gang du bshad ce na/ 'di nyid kyi gnas dang por zag med lam gyi bden pa dang zhes pas lam dang*/ / so sor brtags pas 'gog pa gang*/ / bral ba'o zhes pas 'gog pa dang*/ / sdug bsngal kun 'byung 'jig rten dang zhes bya bas de gnyis kyang bshad cing*/ mdo las kyang gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / ci 'di dag gi rim pa gnas dang por bstan pa de kho na ltar yin nam zhe na/ ma yin no/ / 'o na ji lta bu zhe na/

Reply: Those truths to be seen and meditated on are explained as four. Question: Where are they explained? Reply: In part I, the path is explained by the words “Uncontaminated phenomena are the truth of the path” (1:5a), cessation is explained by “Analytical cessation is freedom” (1:6a), and the remaining two truths are explained by “Suffering, origin, destructible” (1:8c), and they are also explained in the sūtras. Question: Is the order in which they are taught in part I the only way of presenting them?

sdug bsngal dang*/ sdug bsngal kun 'byung ba dang*/ de bzhin du 'gog pa dang*/ lam 'phags pa'i bden pa ste de ltar na bzhi po de dag gi rim pa ni 'di yin no/ / 'grel pa las/ de bzhin zhes bya ba'i sgra ni rang gi ngo bo ni gnas dang por ji skad bshad pa de kho na bzhin no zhes rab tu bstan par bya ba'i phyir ro zhes 'byung ngo*/ / go rim de kho na ltar ston pa'i rgyu ni 'grel par dran pa nyer gzhag bzhi dang*/ mthar gyis gnas pa'i snyoms 'jug lta bu skye ba dang*/ mthun pa rgyu 'bras kyi go rim dang*/ yang dag spong bzhi lta bu rtogs sla ba dang mthun pa'i go rim dang*/ yul ji ltar mngon par rtogs pa dang mthun pa'i go rim gsum bshad pa las 'dir bden pa de dag ni dang por ji ltar mngon par rtogs pa dang mthun pa'i rim pa ltar bstan te/ mthong lam du dang por sdug bsngal mngon par rtogs pa la sogs pa'i phyir ro/ / skye ba'i rim pa ltar ston na ni rgyu yin pa'i phyir kun 'byung dang lam dang por ston par thal ba'i phyir ro/ / mthong lam du de ltar mngon par rtogs pa la'ang dkyus sa bstan pa'i rta thags thogs med par rgyug pa ltar tshogs sbyor du yongs su rtogs pa'i rim pa ltar skye ba'i phyir te/ dper na nad mthong bas de'i rgyu dang*/ nad zad pa dang*/ de'i thabs sman 'tshol ba ltar dang po kho na gang la chags pa dang*/ gang gis gnod pa dang*/ gang las thar par 'dod pas sdug bsngal dang*/ de'i rgyu ni gang zhig ces de'i 'og tu kun 'byung dang*/ / sdug bsngal 'gog pa ni ci zhig ces de nas 'gog pa dang*/ de thob pa'i thabs ni ci zhig ces lam la rtog pas de ltar na yongs su rtog pa'i rim pa ni de yin te/ ji skad du rgyud bla ma las/ nad ni shes bya nad kyi rgyu ni spang bya la/ / bder gnas thob bya sman ni bsten par bya ba ltar/ / sdug bsngal rgyu dang de 'gog pa dang de bzhin lam/ / shes bya spang bya rig par bya zhing bsten par bya/ / zhes gsungs pa bzhin no/ /

Reply: The order of these four is thus the ārya truth of suffering, the origin of suffering, and so too cessation and path. The Autocommentary correctly maintains: The meaning of the term “so too” is that whatever is explained for the first two is just what is explained for [the latter two].[1523] Regarding the reason for teaching them in just this order, the Autocommentary explains three types of order: (1) the order of causation, which conforms with how they arise, such as the order of the four foundations of mindfulness or meditative attainments that arise serially, (2) the order of the ease of comprehension, such as the four correct abandonments, and (3) the order of how objects are realized. Here, these truths are first taught in accordance with the order in which they are realized (abhisamaya), because on the path of seeing, suffering is realized first and so on. If they were taught in accordance with their order of arising, it would follow that the truths of origin and path would be taught first, because they are the causes. They are realized in just that order on the path of seeing because [such realization] arises in just the order in which they are investigated on the paths of accumulaton and preparation, like a horse running unhindered in a long field. For example, through seeing that one is ill, one seeks to find its cause, one strives to eliminate it, and one seeks medicine as the means of eliminating it. Thus, first one investigates suffering by asking, “What am I attached to, what harms me, and from what do I desire freedom?” One investigates the origin [of suffering] after that by asking, “What is the cause of suffering.” One investigates cessation [of suffering] by asking, “What is the cessation of suffering?” And one investigates the path [to the cessation of suffering] by asking, “What is the means of obtaining cessation?” Thus this is the order of investigation. As the Sublime Continuum observes: Just as illness should be known, the cause of illness should be abandoned, abiding in bliss should be obtained, and medicine should be trusted, so too, suffering, its cause, its cessation, and the path should be known, abandoned, cognized, and trusted.[1524]

de la bden pa bzhi'i ngo bo ni sngar bshad zin la/ nges tshig ni ci'i phyir bden pa zhes bya zhe na/ 'phags pa rnams kyi yul du sdug bsngal la sogs par bden pa'i phyir te/ byis pa ni sdug bsngal la bde ba dang*/ kun 'byung la bde ba'i rgyu dang*/ 'gog pa la kha cig ma zhi ba dang*/ kha cig bdag chad pas 'jigs pa dang*/ lam la lam ma yin pa dang dka' thub sdug bsngal gyi rgyur 'dzin pa'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir mdo las/ 'phags pas bde bar gang gsungs pa/ / de ni gzhan gyis sdug bsngal rig gzhan gyis bde bar gang smras pa/ / de ni 'phags pas sdug bsngal rig ces gsungs so/ / des na 'dir zag bcas 'bras bu'i cha thams cad ni sdug bsngal dang*/ {de yang dgra bcom dang sred bral gyi phung po tha ma sdug bsngal kho nar 'dod do } de nyid rgyur gyur pa'i cha ni kun 'byung dang*/ 'gog pa ni 'dus ma byas so sor brtags 'gog dang*/ lam ni zag med 'dus byas mthong sgom mi slob pa'i lam gsum yin te/ {kha cig dang po gnyis 'phags pa'i bden pa yin yang 'phags pa min te zag bcas yin pas so phyi ma gnyis dge ba dang zag med gzhi mthun pa yin pas gnyis ka yin no zhes so }

Question: The nature of the four truths has already been explained, but what is the etymology of truth? Reply: They are called truths because suffering and so on are true as objects for āryas, [498] but childlike beings hold suffering to be pleasure and origin to be the cause of pleasure. Some childlike beings hold cessation to be the destruction of peace, and others hold cessation to be fearsome since it severs the self. Finally, childlike beings hold the path to be not a path and austerities to be a cause of suffering. Therefore a sūtra declares: Whatever āryas call pleasure, others cognize that to be pain. Whatever others call pleasure, āryas cognize that to be pain.[1525] In this context every part of a contaminated result is suffering, {where the end-stage aggregates[1526] of arhats free of craving are asserted to be the truth of suffering alone}; origin is all parts of the cause of suffering; cessation is uncontaminated analytical cessation; and path is the three unconditioned paths of seeing, meditation, and no more learning. {Some say: Though the first two truths are ārya truths, they are not ārya states since they are contaminated. The latter two are both, since they are the shared basis of a virtuous state and an uncontaminated state.}

'grel pa las/ nye bar len pa'i phung po 'bras bur gyur pa rnams ni sdug bsngal gyi bden pa yin no/ / rgyur gyur pa rnams ni kun 'byung gi bden pa yin te/ 'di las sdug bsngal kun 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / de nyid kyi phyir 'di gnyis ni rgyu dang 'bras bur gyur pas ming gi sgo nas bye brag yod kyi rdzas su ni ma yin no/ / 'gog pa dang lam ni rdzas su yang bye brag yod do zhes 'byung bas bye brag tu smra ba bden pa dang po gnyis khyab mnyam par 'dod do/ / gal te sdug bsngal{ dang yid mi bde} ni tshor ba'i phung po'i phyogs gcig yin na ji ltar zag bcas thams cad sdug bsngal gyi bden pa yin zhe na/

The Autocommentary states: The appropriated aggregates that are resultant states are the truth of suffering. Those aggregates that are causes are the truth of origin because suffering originates from them. They are differentiated in name but not in substance, since both are causes and results. Cessation and path are included in substance.[1527] Therefore Vaibhāṣikas assert that the first two truths are mutually pervasive. Question: If pain {and mental dissatisfaction} are just similar states of feeling, in what way are all contaminated states the truth of suffering?
yid 'ong yid du mi 'ong dang / / de las gzhan zag bcas rnams nyid/ / sdug bsngal nyid gsum ldan pa'i phyir/ / ci rigs ma lus sdug bsngal lo/ / 3
Those possessing pleasant or unpleasant feeling, or contaminated equanimity distinct from those, are without exception suffering because they possess any of the three types of suffering. (6:3)

zag bcas ma lus pa ni sdug bsngal lo zhes sbyar ro/ / ci'i phyir zhe na/ ci rigs par sdug bsngal dang*/ 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal dang*/ 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal nyid gsum dang ldan pa'i phyir ro/ { gang rnams sdug bsngal dang ldan zhe na/ yid du 'ong ba tshor ba bde ba dang yid du mi 'ong ba sdug bsngal dang gnyis po de las gzhan pa'i zag pa dang bcas pa btang snyoms tshogs dang bcas pa rnams so zhes sbyar ro/ /} 'grel pa las/ de'i dbang gis bde ba myong bar 'gyur ba la sogs pa'i 'du byed rnams kyang yid du 'ong ba la sogs pa'i ming 'thob bo zhes 'byung bas tshor ba de dag gi dbang gis de dag dang mtshungs ldan gyi sems dang sems byung gzhan rnams dang*/ mtshungs ldan ma yin pa bdag rkyen dang*/ dmigs rkyen rnams kyang yid du 'ong ba la sogs pa'i ming du brjod do/ / de la ci rigs zhes pa ni 'gyur ba dang 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal gyis sdug bsngal ba yin te/ ngo bo bde ba yin yang 'gyur ba na sdug bsngal ba dang zag bcas yin pa'i phyir ro/ / yid du mi 'ong ba rnams ni 'du byed dang sdug bsngal gyis sdug bsngal ba yin te/ zag bcas yin pa dang skyes pa nyid nas sdug bsngal du myong ba'i phyir ro/ / gnyis po de las gzhan pa'i 'du byed zag bcas rnams ni 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal kho nas sdug bsngal ba yin te/ las dang nyon mongs pa'i gzhan dbang can yin pas 'phags pa rnams dang mi mthun pa'i phyir dang*/ skad cig ma nyid kyis gnod pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: That is applied to the statement “contaminated states are without exception suffering.” Question: Why? Reply: Because they possess any of the three types of suffering: [the suffering of pain], the suffering of change, and the suffering of contaminated formations. Question: What states possess suffering? Reply: Those possessing blissful, pleasant feelings, those possessing unpleasant pain, and contaminated equanimity distinct from those two. The Autocommentary observes: Due to their power, even formative factors such as karma to be experienced as pleasure and so on are called pleasant and so forth.[1528] Therefore, due to the power of those feelings, minds concomitant with them and other mental factors, dominant conditions not concomitant with them, and even their objective conditions are also called pleasant and so on. The phrase “any of the three types” (6:3d) refers to suffering through the suffering of change or the suffering of contaminated formations. [The first] is by nature blissful but transforms into suffering, and [the second] is that which is contaminated. “Those possessing . . . unpleasant feeling” (6:3a) refers to that which is associated with suffering due to either contaminated formation or pain because, respectively, they are contaminated or they are experienced as pain in their mere arising. Contaminated formations distinct from the other two sufferings are associated with suffering [499] solely through the suffering of contaminated formations; they are incompatible with āryas since they are controlled by karma and affliction, and momentary change destroys.

yang na ci rigs zhes bya ba ni 'dod pa na sdug bsngal gsum dang*/ bsam gtan gsum pa man chad na gnyis dang*/ bzhi pa yan chad na 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal 'ba' zhig gis sdug bsngal ba'i phyir ro/ / gal te mi rtag pa nyid kyis 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal yin na lam bden yang sdug bsngal du 'gyur ro zhe na/ ma yin te/ lam ni sdug bsngal thams cad 'gags pa'i bde ba 'dren pa'i rgyu zag med yin pa'i phyir 'phags pa dang mthun pas sdug bsngal du mi brjod de/ sdug bsngal gyi don ni zag bcas gang zhig mi rtag cing 'phags pa dang mi mthun pas gnod pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ / zag bcas kyi 'du byed gzhan ni mdo las/ gang mi rtag pa de ni sdug bsngal ba yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir dang*/ srid pa thams cad ni thar pa'i mi mthun phyogs yin pas 'phags pa dang mi mthun pas gnod pa'i phyir sdug bsngal du 'dod de/ de'i phyir slob dpon gyis/ lag mthil spu nyag gcig 'dug pa/ / mi rnams kyis ni mi rtogs la/ / de nyid mig tu song na ni/ / mi dga' ba dang gnod skyed ltar/ / byis pa lag mthil 'dra ba yis/ / 'du byed sdug bsngal spu mi rtogs/ / 'phags pa mig dang 'dra ba ni/ / de yis shin tu yid kyang 'byung zhes pa dang*/ {'du byed kyi sdug bsngal ni 'phags pa rnams kho nas gzigs te } ji ltar 'phags pa rnams srid pa'i rtse mo pa dag la'ang sdug bsngal gyi blo 'jug pa ltar byis pa rnams ni mnar med pa'i phung po rnams la yang de ltar sdug bsngal gyi blo mi 'jug go zhes gsungs so/ /

Again, “any of the three types” (6:3d) means that beings suffer due to three types of suffering in the desire realm, due to two in the third absorption and below, and due to the suffering of contaminated formations alone in the fourth absorption and above. Objection: If impermanence itself is the suffering of contaminated formations, even the truth of path would be suffering. Reply: That is not so. The meaning of suffering is that which harms since it is contaminated and impermanent, and this is incompatible with āryas. But the path that is the cause inducing the bliss of the cessation of all suffering is uncontaminated, and since it is compatible with āryas, it is not called suffering. Regarding other contaminated formations, a sūtra remarks: That which is impermanent is suffering.[1529] Moreover, all existence is asserted to be suffering since it is the opponent of liberation and incompatible with āryas. Therefore Vasubandhu said: A single hair resting on the palm is not discerned by humans, but if lodged in the eye it generates dislike and discomfort. Childlike beings are like the palm: they do not comprehend the hair-like suffering of contaminated formations. But āryas are like the eye: they are extremely displeased with it.[1530] Just as āryas discern suffering in those existing at the summit of existence, {for the suffering of contaminated formations is seen by āryas alone,} so childlike beings do not discern suffering even in the aggregates of those in Avīci.[1531]

{zag bcas thams cad sdug bsngal du mi 'thad de bde ba yang yod pa'i phyir ro zhe na } 'dir btsun pa gzhon nu len gyis bde ba nyung ba'i sgrub byed du/ sdug bsngal bdun cu pa las/ sdug bsngal gyi ni rgyu phyir dang*/ / sdug bsngal mang pos bskyed phyir dang*/ / sdug bsngal yod na de 'dod phyir/ / bde ba sdug bsngal zhes rtogs so/ / zhes bshad pa ni yang dag pa ma yin te/ sdug bsngal gyi rgyu de ni kun 'byung gi rnam pa yin pa'i phyir des ji ltar duHkhar grub pa dang*/{phyi ma gnyis ltar na'ang }khams gong ma gnyis kyi phung po ni sdug bsngal gyi tshor ba'i rgyu ma yin pas khams de dag tu skyes pa'i 'phags pa rnams phung po la sdug bsngal gyi blo mi 'jug par thal pa'i phyir ro/ /

{Objection: It is unacceptable that all contaminated states are suffering because some are also blissful.} In this context Bhadanta Kumāralāta quotes the Seventy Sufferings, which gives a logical proof for the rarity of pleasure: Because it is the cause of suffering, because it is generated by many sufferings, and because it is asserted to exist if suffering exists, understand pleasure to be suffering.[1532] Kumāralāta then asserts that this explanation is incorrect because the cause of suffering is the truth of origin, {for how could [pleasure] establish duḥkha?} Further, {with respect to the two upper realms,} it would then follow that āryas who are born in higher realms would not discern the aggregates to be suffering since the aggregates of the two higher realms are not the cause of the feeling of pain.

gang yang btsun pa dpal len gyis bde tshor ni med de/ tshor ba thams cad kyang sdug bsngal gyi sdug bsngal kho na yin te/ bcom ldan 'das kyis gang ci tshor yang rung de ni 'dir sdug bsngal lo zhes pa dang*/ bde ba'i tshor ba ni sdug bsngal du blta bar bya'o zhes pa dang*/ mu bzhi'i tshoms kyi phyin ci log bzhi bstan pa'i mdo las/ sdug bsngal la bde ba'o snyam du 'du shes phyin ci log go zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs pa'i lung dang*/ rigs pas kyang bde ba'i rgyur mngon par 'dod pa'i zas gos la sogs pa dag kyang ha cang spyad pas sdug bsngal bskyed pas bde ba'i rgyu rnam par mi gnas pa'i phyir dang*/ mi mkhas pa rnams {bkres skom gyis ma bcos pa tsam gyi } sdug bsngal gyi gnyen po la bde ba'i blo skye ba'i phyir dang*/ phrag khur spong ba ltar sdug bsngal chung ba la bde bar 'dzin pa'i phyir 'jig rten pas bde bar gang smras pa de yang don la ni sdug bsngal yin no zhes bya bar rtogs so zhes smras pa

Moreover, Bhadanta Śrīlāta says that the feeling of pleasure does not exist because the scriptures say that all feelings are the suffering of pain alone. The Bhagavan has said, “Whatever is experienced in this context is suffering,”[1533] “The feeling of pleasure should be viewed as suffering,”[1534] the Sūtra Teaching the Four Distortions Conforming with the Four Possibilities states, “The distorted discernment that maintains suffering is pleasure,”[1535] and so on. And in terms of logic it should be understood that [500] whatever worldly beings call pleasure is really suffering: food, clothing, and so on that are desired as causes of pleasure do not endure as causes of pleasure since they generate pain through continued use; the ignorant hold that the mind of pleasure arises as the antidote of pain {produced by hunger and thirst}; and they hold that the lessening of pain is pleasure, such as when one stops carrying rocks.[1536]

de yang rigs pa ma yin te/ re zhig lung dang po ni bcom ldan 'das nyid kyis dgongs pa can du bshad do/ / 'phags pa kun dga' bos bcom ldan 'das la bcom ldan 'das kyis bde ba dang sdug bsngal ba dang bde ba yang ma lags sdug bsngal ba yang ma lags pa dang tshor ba 'di gsum yang gsungs la/ bcom ldan 'das kyis gang ci tshor yang rung de ni 'dir sdug bsngal lo zhes kyang gsungs na bcom ldan 'das kyis ci las dgongs nas gang ci tshor yang rung de ni 'dir sdug bsngal lo zhes zhus pa na/ bcom ldan 'das kyis kun dga' bo gang ci tshor yang rung de ni 'dir sdug bsngal lo zhes bya ba ni ngas 'du byed mi rtag pa nyid dang*/ 'du byed rnam par 'gyur ba nyid la dgongs nas bshad do zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / bde ba'i tshor ba ni sdug bsngal du blta bar bya'o zhes pa ni 'gyur ba'i sdug bsngal dang 'du byed kyi sdug bsngal gyi dbang du byas nas gsungs pa yin te/ lung bar ma'i dge slong ma chos sbyin gyi mdo las/ bde ba'i tshor ba ni skye ba na yang bde/ gnas pa na yang bde la 'gyur ba na sdug bsngal lo/ / sdug bsngal gyi tshor ba ni skye ba na yang sdug bsngal la gnas pa na yang sdug bsngal lo zhes pa dang*/ skye mched drug gi tshogs kyi mdo las/ gang mi rtag pa de ni sdug bsngal ba yin no zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir mdo las kyang*/ rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas rab mkhyen gyis/ / 'du byed mi rtag nyid dang ni/ / rnam par 'gyur ba nyid mkhyen nas/ / tshor ba sdug bsngal bar gsungs so zhes gsungs so/ / sdug bsngal la bde ba'o snyam du 'du shes phyin ci log go zhes pa ni 'jig rten pa rnams tshor ba dang 'dod yon dang skye ba la sdug bsngal yang yod pa la gcig tu bde bar shes pa ni 'du shes phyin ci log yin te/ de dag phal cher sdug bsngal ba'i phyir ro zhes dgongs pa ni de yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

Reply: This is illogical. Many explain the first scripture quoted to be an interpretive teaching of the Bhagavan: Ārya Ānanda said to the Bhagavan: “The Bhagavan has explained three feelings: pleasure, that which is associated with suffering, and that which is neither pleasure nor associated with pain. Yet the Bhagavan has stated that whatever is feeling in this context is suffering. With what intention has the Bhagavan stated that whatever is feeling is suffering? The Bhagavan said to Ānanda: “I stated that whatever is feeling in this context is suffering with the thought that formations are impermanent and formations transform.[1537] The Bhagavan’s statement that “feelings of pleasure should be viewed as pain”[1538] is stated from the perspective of the suffering of change and the suffering of contaminated formations. As the Bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā Sūtra states: When the feeling of pleasure arises it is pleasurable, when it endures it is pleasurable, but when it changes it is suffering. When the feeling of pain arises it is painful, and when it endures it is painful.[1539] And the Assembly of the Six Bases Sūtra declares: Whatever is impermanent is associated with suffering.[1540] Because of that, another sūtra states: Since the perfect Buddha fully discerns that formations are impermanent and changing, he states that feelings are associated with suffering.[1541] The Bhagavan’s intention in making the statement “Distorted discernment maintains that suffering is pleasure” is that the opinion of worldy beings that feelings, sense objects, and birth that are associated with suffering are entirely pleasurable is distorted discernment because such states are mainly associated with suffering.

gzhan yang bcom ldan 'das kyis tshor ba gsum dang*/ tshor ba'i dbang po lnga la sogs pa gsungs pa dang 'gal ba'i phyir dang*/{ gzhan yang sdug bsngal gyi don gang yin/} gnod pa dang mi 'dod pa sdug bsngal yin {no zhe} na {'o na } phan pa dang 'dod pa ci'i phyir bde bar mi 'dod/ sdug bsngal chung ngu la sogs pa la bde ba la sogs pa'i blo skye'o zhes bya ba'ang rigs pa ma yin te/ bde ba chung ngu la sogs pa la'ang sdug bsngal gyi blo la sogs pa skye bar thal bar mtshungs pa'i phyir dang*/ sdug bsngal gyi gnyen po la bde ba'i blo skye'o zhes bya ba'ang ma yin te/ gnyen po ni res 'ga' bde ba dang re 'ga' btang snyoms kyis byed pa'i phyir ro/ / gang yang bde ba'i rgyu rnam par mi gnas pa'i phyir ro zhes bya ba de yang rigs pa ma yin te/ zas la sogs pa yul 'ba' zhig ni bde ba'i rgyu ma yin gyi lus dang goms pa la sogs pa'ang yin te/ gzugs la sogs pa khyad par med pa nyid 'gro ba tha dad la bde ba dang sdug bsngal dang btang snyoms su 'gyur ba dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ gal te zas la sogs pa ha cang spyad drags pas sdug bsngal skye ba tsam gyis bde ba'i rgyu med par smra na sdug bsngal gyi rgyu yang rnam par mi gnas par 'gyur te/ sdug bsngal gyi rgyu dag kyang la lar bde ba'i rgyur 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / rab tu smra ba 'di bde ba'i tshor ba myong ba'i mngon sum gyis bkag pa'i phyir 'bad par mi bya ba zhig na sngon gyi slob dpon gyis mdzad pa'i phyir kho bos kyang byas so/ /

Again, this contradicts the Bhagavan’s statements that there are three feelings, five faculties of feeling, and so on. {Question: Again, what is the meaning of pain?} If it is {said that} pain is “that which harms and is not desired,” {then} why isn’t pleasure “that which benefits and is desired”? Doesn’t the awareness of pleasure arise when pain lessens? Reply: That is illogical because it would also follow that the awareness of pain [501] would arise when pleasure lessens. But it is not that “the awareness of pleasure arises as the antidote to pain” because sometimes the antidote is pleasure and sometimes equanimity [or neutral feeling]. Moreover, the statement [by Śrīlāta] that they “do not endure as causes of pleasure” is illogical because objects such as food are not the only cause of pleasure. Instead, one’s body, habits, and so on are also causes because it is observed that the same physical object can variously give rise to pleasure, pain, or equanimity in different reincarnated beings. And if it is asserted that food and so on are not the cause of pleasure since excessive consumption merely generates pain, then they also do not endure as causes of pain because such causes of pain would sometimes be a cause of pleasure. Because such assertions are refuted through actual perception that experiences the feeling of pleasure, past masters reject them effortlessly, and I also reject them.

mdo sde pa la sogs pa na re bye brag tu smra bas kun 'byung gi bden pa gang yin pa de nyid sdug bsngal gyi bden pa'ang yin no zhes smras pa ni mdo dang 'gal te/ mdo las ni kun 'byung gi bden pa gang zhe na/ gang 'di dga' ba'i 'dod chags dang lhan cig pa'i sred pa ste de dang de la mngon par dga' ba can yin no zhes sred pa kho na kun 'byung du gsungs pa dang 'gal ba'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ / bye brag tu smra ba ni lung de ni gtso che ba'i phyir dang*/ rten 'brel gyi 'grel pa las/ sred dang bral la yang srid med ces pa ltar skye ba mngon par 'grub pa'i rgyu'i dbang du byas nas gsungs pa'i phyir te/ mdo las/ las ni skye ba'i rgyu yin la/ sred pa ni mngon par 'grub pa'i rgyu yin no zhes bya ba dang*/ skye mched drug gi tshogs kyi mdo las/ las dang sred pa dang ni ma rig pa/ / phyi ma'i tshe la 'du byed rnams kyi rgyu zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / de lta na'ang de gsum ga kun 'byung du ston par 'gyur ba zhig na sred pa kho na ci'i phyir bstan zhe na/ sred pa dang bcas pa kho na 'khor bar skye ba'i phyir dang*/ rgyud gzhol ba'i phyir dang*/ lus dam du 'dzin pa'i phyir gtso che bas yin gyi gzhan dag kyang kun 'byung yin te/ des na sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung ni khyab mnyam mo zhes 'dod do/ /

Sautrāntikas and so on say: Vaibhāṣikas who advocate that whatever is the truth of origin is also the truth of suffering contradict the sūtras because they contradict the sūtra that declares that craving alone is the truth of origin: What is the truth of origin? It is craving that coexists with joyful attachment taking joy in various objects.[1542] Vaibhāṣikas say: This scripture [merely] gives the main presentation. The Detailed Explanation of the Essence of Dependent Origination also explains [craving] to be the establishing cause of birth when it mentions: One free of craving has no rebirth.[1543] That is because a sūtra states: Karma is the cause of birth; craving is the establishing cause.[1544] And the Assembly of Six Bases Sūtra observes: Karma, craving, and ignorance are the causes of formation in future lives.[1545] If those three are all taught to be the truth of origin, why should craving alone be origin? It is the main presentation that craving and its associates alone generate saṃsāra because they maintain its continuity and they tightly hold the body. But other states are also the truth of origin. Therefore we assert that “suffering and origin are mutually pervasive.”

mdo sde pa ni dgra bcom pa'i phung po tha ma sdug bsngal yin yang kun 'byung ma yin no zhes bya bar 'dod de/ kun las btus las kyang*/ dgra bcom pa tha ma pa'i mig nas yid kyi bar ni mig nas yid kyi bar du yin gyi de dag gi khams ni ma yin no zhes bshad do/ / kha cig ni sred pa dang bral ba'i phung po dang snod kyi 'jig rten yang sdug bsngal yin yang kun 'byung ma yin no zhes zer ro/ / de dag la'ang sdug bsngal gyi rgyu la kun 'byung zhes zer na ni de dag kyang kun 'byung du za/'gyur te/ de dag kyang phyi ma de sdug bsngal yin la de skyed pa'i rgyu yin pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar yin yang kun 'byung ma yin na sred pa dang bcas pa'i phung po'ang kun 'byung ma yin par thal pa'i phyir ro/ / spros pas chog go /'o na bcom ldan 'das kyis bden pa bzhi zhes kyang gsungs/ kun rdzob dang don dam pa'i bden pa gnyis zhes kyang gsungs na gnyis po'i don ci yin zhe na/

Sautrāntikas assert: The end-stage aggregates of an arhat are the truth of suffering[1546] but not the truth of origin. This is because the Compendium of Abhidharma explains: The end-stage eyes up to the mind of an arhat are the eyes up to the mind, but their elements are not.[1547] Some say: Though the aggregates free of craving and the physical cosmos are the truth of suffering, they are not the truth of origin. Others say: If you say with regard to them that the cause of the truth of suffering is “origin,” then they would constitute [502] the truth of origin, for states that occur after them are suffering and they are a cause that generates them. And if they are not the truth of origin, it would follow that the aggregates associated with craving would not be the truth of origin. But such conjecture is enough. Question: If in addition to the four truths, the Bhagavan stated both conventional and ultimate truth, what is the meaning of these two?
gang la bcom dang blo yis gzhan/ / bsal na de blo mi 'jug pa/ / bum chu bzhin du kun rdzob tu/ / yod de don dam yod gzhan no/ / 4
Any object is a conventional existent if not apprehended by the mind when the mind analyzes its parts or when it is destroyed, like a vase and water. An ultimate existent is different. (6:4)

chos gang la thob la sogs pas bcom pa dang blos gzhan bsal na chos de'i blo mi 'jug pa dang*/ yang gang la bcom pas de'i blo mi 'dor yang blo yis chos gzhan bsal na chos de'i blo mi 'jug pa de dag ni rim pa ltar dper na bum pa la gyo mor bcom na de'i blo mi 'jug pa dang chu las la sogs pa'i rdzas brgyad kyi cha shas kyi chos rnams blos so sor bsal na chu'i blo mi 'jug pas kun rdzob yin pa bzhin du kun rdzob tu yod par 'dod de/ cha shas dang bcas pa'i phyir ro/ / 'dir dpe gnyis bkod pa ni 'joms pas 'jig pa dang*/ blos 'jig pa gnyis sam/ dbyibs kyi kun rdzob dang*/ tshogs pa'i kun rdzob gnyis sam/ kun rdzob gzhan la brten pa dang*/ rdzas gzhan la brten pa'i kun rdzob gnyis yod pa'i phyir ro zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / des na 'di skad du rgyun dang rags pa ni kun rdzob yin te/ {bum pa dang chu yod do byas na kun rdzob bden pa'i phyir dang } bcom mam blos bsal na de'i blo mi 'jug pa'i phyir ro zhes bstan pa yin no/ / don dam par yod pa ni gang la bcom pa dang blos gzhan bsal na de'i blo mi 'jug pa las gzhan gang la bcom pa dang blos chos gzhan bsal ba na'ang de'i blo 'jug pa ste gzugs kyi rdul dang skad cig ma la sogs pa lta bu yin no/ / {tshor sogs kyi'ang tshogs pa dang*/ rgyun ni kun rdzob skad cig ni don dam mo } 'di dag theg pa gong ma pa dag ni shar la sogs pa dang skye ba la sogs pa'i blos bsal na de dag gi blo mi 'jug pa'i phyir kun rdzob kho na yin gyi don dam pa ni ma yin no zhes zer ro/ / sngon gyi slob dpon kha cig ni 'jig rten las 'das pa'i ye shes kyi spyod yul dang de'i rjes thob de bzhin nyid du snang ba'i yul ni don dam par yod pa yin la/ 'jig rten pa'i blo'i yul na yod pa ni kun rdzob yin no zhes 'chad do/ /

Reply: Any object is asserted to be a conventional existent (saṃvṛtisat) — if it is not apprehended by the mind (dhiyā) when the mind analyzes its parts or when that object is destroyed by a hammer and so on; or if it is not apprehended by the mind when the mind analyzes its parts even though the mind aware of that object is not destroyed when that object is destroyed — because that object possesses parts. That is, a conventional truth is like, respectively, a vase not being apprehended by the mind when it is reduced to clay particles, and water not being apprehended by the mind when the mind analyzes its eight substantial constituents. In this context the Subcommentary explains that two examples are formulated. There is destruction through annihilation and destruction through the mind, there is both conventional truth that is shape and conventional truth that is a collection, or there is both the conventional truth that depends on others and conventional truth that depends on substance.[1548] Therefore it is said that continua and coarse entities are conventional truths, {because if a vase and water exist, they are conventional truths, and} because when an object is destroyed or the mind analyzes its parts, the mind does not apprehend that object itself. An ultimate existent (paramārthasat) is different from any object that is not apprehended by mind when it is destroyed or when the mind analyzes its parts. It is any object such as a particle of form or a moment of time and so on that is apprehended by the mind even when it is destroyed or its parts are analyzed. {The collection or continuum of feelings and so on are conventional truths, and each moment is an ultimate truth.} Mahāyānists say: Because east and so on and arising and so forth are not apprehended by mind when the mind analyzes their parts, they are conventional truths alone and not ultimate. A past scholar says: Object fields of transcendent wisdom and objects appearing as suchness (tathatā) in post-equipoise are ultimate existents. If they exist as objects of the mundane mind, they are conventional truths.
gsum pa mngon par rtogs pa'i rim pa
27. The Stages of Realization
['di] la gnyis las
{THIS HAS TWO HEADINGS: overview and elaboration.}
mdor bstan pa ni
Overview
tshul gnas thos dang bsam ldan pas/ / bsgom pa la ni rab tu sbyor/ / thos stsogs las byung blo rnams ni/ / ming dang gnyis ka don yul can/ / 5

They maintain ethics, strive to listen, and having contemplated its meaning, engage in meditation. Intelligence derived from hearing and so on possesses objects such as names, both, and meaning alone. (6:5)

dang po kho nar bden pa mngon par rtogs par 'dod pas rnam par mi g.yeng ba'i rgyu so sor thar pa ris bdun gyi tshul khrims gang yang rung ba la gnas te/ mi rmongs pa'i rgyu bden mthong ba dang mthun pa'i thos pa la brtson par byed pa dang*/ de nas gtan la phebs pa'i rgyu de'i don phyin ci ma log par sems par byed do/ / don bsam pa dang ldan pas ni 'bral ba'i rgyu don de sgom pa'i ting nge 'dzin la rab tu sbyor bar byas pa yin te/ mdo las/ dge slong rtun cing rtag 'grus pa/ / tshul khrims yang dag blangs byas nas/ / sems dang shes rab sgom byed pas/ / sdug bsngal zad pa thob par 'gyur zhes pa dang*/ tshul khrims la rten cing tshul khrims la gnas te chos bsgom par bya'o zhes pa dang*/ btsun pa dge slong mang du thos pa zhes bgyi na ji ltar na mang du thos pa lags/ ji tsam gyis na de bzhin gshegs pas dge slong mang du thos par 'dogs par mdzad/ dge slong dge slong gis phung po lnga skyob dang*/ 'dod chags dang bral ba dang*/ 'gog par bya ba'i phyir chos thos par gyur na dge slong mang du thos pa zhes brjod par nus so zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na thos byung gi shes rab la sogs pa nyid gang zhe na/

Those who desire to realize the truth alone maintain the ethics (vṛttistha) of the seven types of pratimokṣa, which is the cause of not being distracted; [503] they strive to listen (śruta) to what is compatible with seeing the truth and the cause of not being confused; and they correctly contemplate the meaning of the truth that is the cause of discerning its meaning. Then, having contemplated (cinta) its meaning, they engage in the concentration that is meditation (bhāvana) on the meaning of the cause of that result. A sūtra declares: Monks who exert themselves and continuously strive, who have properly taken ethical vows, obtain the elimination of suffering by applying the mind, wisdom, and meditation.[1549] And: Through depending on ethics and maintaining ethics, one should meditate on Dharma. And: When venerable monks are said to be greatly learned, in what way are they greatly learned? By what measure does the Tathāgata designate them as greatly learned? The Buddha replied: “Monks, a monk who protects his five aggregates, who is free of attachment, and stops attachment is called one who is greatly learned.”[1550] Question: What is wisdom derived from hearing and so on?

bye brag tu smra ba ni thos pa las byung ba'i blo ste shes rab dang*/ sogs pas bsdus pa bsam byung dang*/ / sgom byung gi shes rab rnams ni rim pa ltar ming dang*/ res 'ga' yi ges don 'dren la res 'ga' don gyis yi ge 'dren pas ming don gnyis ka dang*/ yi ge la mi ltos par don la 'jug pas don kho na'i yul can yin te/ dper na rkyal legs par ma lobs pa dang*/ cung zad lobs pa dang*/ legs par lobs pa dag shing leb la sogs pa'i 'ju bya la ltos pa dang*/ res 'ga' ltos res 'ga' mi ltos pa dang*/ ye mi ltos pa bzhin no zhes 'dod do/ / slob dpon ni de lta na ming la dmigs pa thos byung dang don la dmigs pa sgom byung yin pa'i phyir{ gnyis po las} bsam byung mi 'grub par 'gyur bas bdag rkyen yid ches pa'i lung dang*/ rigs pas dpyad pa dang*/ ting nge 'dzin la mnyam par bzhag pa las don rtogs pa ni rim pa ltar shes rab gsum yin no zhes 'chad do/ /

Vaibhāṣikas say that intelligence (dhi) or wisdom derived from hearing and so on, such as wisdom derived from contemplation and meditation, possesses objects (viṣaya) since, respectively, they engage (1) names, (2) both names and meanings, since at times letters invoke the meaning and at times the meaning invokes letters, and (3) meaning alone, since [the wisdom of meditation] engages meaning not reliant on letters. For example, it is like those with no proper training in swimming, who first rely on holding a plank; those who have some training, who sometimes hold a plank and sometimes not; and finally those who are well trained, who never have to rely on a plank. Vasubandhu explains that according to this assertion, because wisdom derived from hearing focuses on names and wisdom derived from meditation focuses on the meaning, wisdom derived from contemplation would not be established as separate {from those two}. Therefore the three wisdoms comprehend the meaning, respectively, through scripture that one has conviction in, through analysis by logical reasoning, and through equipoise in concentration.[1551]
rgyas par bshad pa
ELABORATION
['di] la tshogs lam dang*/ sbyor lam dang*/ mthong lam gsum las
This has three headings: the path of accumulation, the path of preparation, and the path of seeing.
dang po
The path of accumulation
['di] la
This has two aspects: the practitioner of the path and the path to be meditated on.
lam sgom pa po ni
THE PRACTITIONER OF THE PATH
gcig pur gnas pas lus 'du 'dzin dang*/ sems mi dge ba la sogs pa nyon mongs pa can gyi rnam rtog las bsrings pa gnyis dang ldan pa zhig gis bsgom par bya'o/ /

One who meditates on the path should isolate oneself in two ways: (1) physically isolate oneself from companions through abiding alone and (2) isolate oneself from afflictive conceptions such as nonvirtuous minds.
bsring gnyis ldan chog mi shes dang / / 'dod chen can la ma yin no/ / rnyed la yang sred chog mi shes/ / ma rnyed la 'dod 'dod chen can/ / 6
Those who possess both isolations are not discontented and lack strong desire. Discontent is craving more than one has found; Strong desire is desiring what one has not found. (6:6)

bsrings pa gnyis dang ldan pa de yang 'dod pa chung ba dang chog shes pa la yin gyi chog mi shes pa dang 'dod chen can la ni ma yin no/ / gnyis po de yang gang zhe na/ chos mngon pa ba rnams na re chos gos la sogs pa gya nom pa rnyed pa la yang dang yang du sred cing 'dod pa ni chog mi shes pa yin la/ de dag ma rnyed pa la 'dod pa ni 'dod chen can yin no zhes zer te/ chos gos la sogs pa la yang dang yang du sred pa de yang ma rnyed pa kho na la yin pa'i phyir de yang 'dod chen can du thal bar 'gyur bas des na ngan nyung rnyed pas yid mi bde ba ni chog mi shes pa dang*/ bzang mang ma rnyed pa la 'dod pa ni 'dod chen can yin no zhes slob dpon 'chad do/ /

Those who possess both isolations (vyapakarṣa) have contentment and minimal desire. They are not discontented (asaṃtuṣṭa) and lack strong desire (maheccha). Question: What are those two? Ābhidharmikas say: Though one has found fine robes and so on, craving (spṛhā) and desiring more [504] is discontent (atuṣṭi). Desiring what one has not found is strong desire (maheccha). Vasubandhu explains that it would follow from this assertion that craving for more robes and so on would also be strong attachment because craving also arises when articles are not found. Therefore mental dissatisfaction due to finding inferior and few articles is discontent, and desiring superior and numerous articles is strong desire.[1552]
yang na sngon ma rnyed pa la 'dod pa ni 'dod chen pa yin la/ rnyed pa na de bas bzang mang 'dod pa ni chog mi shes pa yin no/ /
Again, desiring that which has not been found previously is strong desire. Finding that but desiring articles of finer quality is discontent.
bzlog pa de yi gnyen po dag / de gnyis khams gsum gtogs dri med/ / ma chags 'phags rigs de dag las/ / gsum ni chog shes bdag nyid do/ / 7
These are antidotes that oppose. Both belong to the three realms and are stainless. Those with nonattachment belong to the ārya lineage. From those, three are states of contentment. (6:7)

chog mi shes pa dang 'dod chen las bzlog pa ni de gnyis po'i gnyen po chog shes pa dang 'dod chung dag yin no/ / gnyen po 'dod chung chog shes de gnyis ni 'dod pa la sogs pa'i khams gsum du gtogs pa dang dri ma med pa dag yin la/ chog mi shes pa dang 'dod pa che ba ni chags pa mi dge ba yin pas 'dod khams pa yin no/ / 'dod chung chog shes de dag gi ngo bo ni ma chags pa'i dge ba dag yin no/ /

These two — contentment and minimal desire — are the antidotes (vipakṣa) that oppose (viparyaya) discontent and strong desire. Both antidotes — contentment and minimal desire — belong to the three realms, such as the desire realm and so on, and are stainless (amala). Those who possess discontent and strong desire are desire-realm beings, since attachment is nonvirtuous. The nature of those with few desires and contentment is virtuous nonattachment,

ma chags pa de dag ni 'phags pa rnams kyi rigs yin te/ de dag las 'phags pa rnams skye ba'i phyir ro/ / 'phags pa'i rigs de yang dbye na mdo las/ 'phags pa'i rigs ni bzhi ste/ chos gos la ma chags pa dang*/ bsod snyoms la ma chags pa dang*/ mal cha dang stan la ma chags pa dang*/ spong ba dang bsgom pa la dga' ba'o zhes gang gsungs pa de dag las dang po gsum ni chog shes pa'i bdag nyid do/ / gal te 'phags pa'i rigs bzhi pa ji ltar na ma chags pa'i rang bzhin yin te/ chog shes pa'i ngo bo ma yin pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ bzhi pa'ang 'dod pa dang srid pa la rgyab kyis phyogs pa'i phyir ma chags pa yin te/ spong ba ni 'gog pa dang bsgom pa ni lam yin la de dag la dga' ba ni ma chags pa dang*/ mtshungs ldan gyi dad pa nyid yin no/ / 'o na 'phags pa'i rigs bzhis ci zhig bstan zhe na/

and those with nonattachment (alobha) belong to the ārya lineage (āryavaṃśā) because āryas are born among them. Moreover, if the ārya lineage is classified, a sūtra states: There are four ārya lineages: those not attached to robes, those not attached to alms, those not attached to bedding and seats, and those who like abandonment and meditation.[1553] From among those lineages, the first three are states of contentment (tuṣṭya). Question: Since they are not the nature of contentment, how could the four ārya lineages be the nature of nonattachment? Reply: Because these four reject desire and existence, they are unattached. Abandonment is the truth of cessation, meditation is the truth of path, and that which takes joy in them is nonattachment as well as the faith concomitant with it. Question: Why are four ārya lineages taught?
gsum gyis tshul bstan tha mas las/ / sred pa skye ba'i gnyen po'i phyir/ / bdag gir bdag 'dzin dngos 'dod pa/ / de yi dus dang gtan zhi'i phyir/ / 8
Three teach method, the last action. To counter the arising of craving, to temporarily pacify phenomena held as mine, and to stably pacify phenomena held as “I.” (6:8)

de la dang po gsum gyis ni thar pa sgrub par byed pa'i kun tu spyod pa'i tshul bstan la/ tha mas ni bya ba'i las bstan te/ de ltar na mdo las/ rang gi tshul dang las kyi mtha' yongs su spangs shing thar pa don du gnyer bar khas 'ches pa'i slob ma rnams la tshul dang las gnyis bcas te/ 'phags pa'i rigs dang po gsum gyis tshul bcas so/ / bzhi pas ni las bcas te/ khyed tshul 'dis las 'di byed na ring por mi thogs par thar pa thob par 'gyur ro zhes gsungs pa'i phyir tshul dang las gnyis 'phags pa'i rigs bzhis bstan te/ gos zas la sogs pa la 'dod pa che zhing chog mi shes pa'i rang gi tshul dang*/ zhing las dang nyo tshong la sogs pa'i las kyi mtha' ngan pa de dag spangs nas yang dag pa'i tshul dang las 'dod pa chung zhing chog shes pa dang*/ spong bsgom la dga' zhing brtson pas thar pa 'thob par 'gyur ba'o/ / dgos pa ci'i phyir tshul dang las 'di lta bu bcas she na/

Reply: The first three teach the method (vṛtti) of practice that establishes liberation, while the last teaches action (karma). Thus a sūtra declares: Trainees who agree to abandon their former methods and actions and seek liberation possess method and action. They possess method through having the first three types of ārya lineage, and they possess action through having the fourth. If you practice this method and action, you will soon obtain liberation.[1554] Therefore the four types of ārya lineage teach method and action, for by abandoning their former methods such as having strong desire for robes, food, and so on, as well as discontent [when not receiving them,] and by adopting the correct method that abandons inferior activities such as field work, trade, and so on, they obtain liberation through having little desire for worldly activities, through having contentment, and through liking and making exertion in both abandonment and meditation. Question: What is the purpose of such method and action? [505]

mdo las/ sred pa skye ba bzhi gsungs pa'i gnyen po'i phyir 'phags pa'i rigs bzhi bstan te/ mdo las/ dge slong sred pa skye na chos gos kyi phyir dang*/ bsod snyoms kyi phyir dang*/ mal cha dang stan gyi phyir skye'o/ / gnas pa na gnas so/ / mngon par zhen pa na mngon par zhen to/ / dge slong sred pa skye ba na 'byung ba dang 'jig pa ste de lta bu'i phyir skye'o zhes gsungs te/ de la sred pa skye ba ni dang por ro/ / gnas pa ni rgyun gnas pa'o/ / mngon par zhen pa ni spang dka' bas dam du 'dzin pa'o/ / 'byung ba dang 'jig pa de lta bu'i phyir sred pa skye ba dang gnas pa dang mngon par zhen pa ni kye ma bdag dbang po dang 'khor los bsgyur bar gyur kyang ci ma rung snyam pa la sogs pa 'byung ba la sred pa skye ba la chags pa dang*/ ngan pas 'jigs nas kye ma bdag shi yang ci ma rung*/ med pa dang ma byung yang ci ma rung snyam pa la sogs pa 'jig pa la sred pa ste chad pa la chags pa'o/ / de la 'byung 'jig la sred pa'i gnyen po ni tha ma bstan la/ snga ma dag ni rang rang gi gnyen por ro/ /

Reply: The Buddha taught the four ārya lineages to counter (vipakṣa) the arising of the four types of craving (tṛṣṇa) that are mentioned in the sūtras: Monks, if craving arises, it arises for Dharma robes, for alms, for bedding and mats. If it is maintained, it is maintained; if it is complete longing, it is complete longing. Monks, if craving arises, then one is born compelled by [craving for] existence and destruction.[1555] “Craving arises” is the first step. “Maintained” is continuously sustaining craving. “Complete longing” is tightly holding, since craving is difficult to abandon. “Existence and destruction arise because of it” means that craving arising, being maintained, and being complete longing is craving for existence that reflects, “Listen, why shouldn’t I be born as Lord Indra or a cakravartin king?” and so on, and this is attachment to birth. Craving for destruction, in contrast, reflects, “Why shouldn’t I die, become nothing, and so on?” out of fear of evil, and this is attachment to annihilation. The last line is taught as the antidote of craving for existence and destruction, the earlier lines as antidotes of specific types of craving.

yang na bdag gir 'dzin pa'i dngos po chos gos la sogs pa gsum 'dod pa'i sred pa de'i dus su zhi bar bya ba'i phyir dang po gsum bstan la/ bdag tu 'dzin pa'i dngos po lus la 'dod cing sred pa dang bdag gir 'dzin pa'i dngos po chos gos la sogs pa 'dod pa gnyis ka gtan du zhi bar bya ba'i phyir rigs bzhi pa bstan pa yin te/ de la de'i dus su zhi ba ni re zhig spong ba yin la/ gtan du zhi ba ni ye mi skye bar byed pa'o/ /

Again, the first three are taught to temporarily pacify (śānta) desire and craving for the three things (vastu) held as mine (mama), such as robes. The four [ārya] lineages are taught in order to stably pacify both desire and craving for things held as “I” (ahaṃkāra), such as the body and desire for things held as “mine,” such as the three concerning robes and so on. “Temporarily” pacify means intermittent abandonment, and “stably pacify” means abandoning objects so that [craving for them] never again arises.
gnyis pa bsgom bya'i lam
THE PATH TO BE MEDITATED ON
['di] la
This has two types: calm abiding and generating insight.
zhi gnas ni
CALM ABIDING
de la 'jug pa mi sdug pa/ / dbugs rngub 'byung ba dran pa yis/ / 'dod chags rnam rtog lhag rnams so/ / keng rus chags bcas thams cad la/ / 9
To enter this meditation, repulsiveness and mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation are antidotes to excessive attachment and discursiveness. The skeleton for all possessing attachment. (6:9)

snod du rung ba'i sgom pa pos bsgom pa de la 'jug pa ni gang nas 'jug pa'i mtha' tshogs lam yin la/ de la'ang zhi gnas bsgrub pa'i phyir 'dod chags lhag par spyod pa'i gnyen por mi sdug ba dang*/ rnam par rtog pa lhag par spyod pa rnams kyi gnyen por dbugs te lus kyi rlung nang du rngub pa dang dbugs phyir 'byung ba dran pa yis 'jug cing sgom par byed do/ /

The entry point for a meditator who is a proper vessel to enter this meditation is the path of accumulation. In order to establish calm abiding, he engages and meditates on repulsiveness (aśubha) as the antidote to excessive attachment (adhirāga), and on mindfulness of inhalation (ānāpānasmṛti) of breath into the body and exhalation of breath (ānāpānasmṛti) back out as the antidote to excessive discursiveness (vitarka).

de dag so sor 'jug pa ci ste zhe na/ dbugs rngub pa dang 'byung ba rjes su dran pa ni rlung la kha dog dang dbyibs sna tshogs med cing kha nang du bltas pas dmigs pa gcig la 'jug pa'i phyir rnam rtog gi gnyen po byed la/ mi sdug pa ni dmigs pa kha dog dang dbyibs kyi bye brag sna tshogs la 'jug cing kha phyir bltas pa'i phyir rnam rtog 'dren pas rnam rtog gi gnyen po mi byed kyi 'on kyang 'dod chags kyi gnyen po byed de/ mdo las/ dge slong slob pa gzhon pa'i rabs/ / sems ma byung ba gang zhig ni/ / gal te 'dod chags 'joms 'dod na/ / des ni dur khrod 'gro bar gyis/ / de nas rnam par bsngos pa ltos/ / de nas rnam par rnag pa ltos/ / de nas rnam bam rus pa yis/ / rus gong la sogs blta bar gyis zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro/ / kha cig na re/ mi sdug pa ni mig gi yul la nye bar rtog pas kha phyir bltas pa'i phyir rnam rtog gi gnyen po ma yin la/ dbugs 'byung rngub rjes su dran pa ni kha nang du bltas pa'i phyir rnam rtog gi gnyen po yin no zhes zer ro/ /

Question: Why does one engage in each of these meditations? Reply: Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation acts as an antidote to discursiveness because it engages a single focal object through focusing internally on wind that lacks various colors and shapes. Meditation on repulsiveness does not act as an antidote to discursiveness since it engages focal objects of various specific shapes and colors; it induces discursiveness through focusing on external objects. However, it acts as an antidote to attachment. As a sūtra explains: Monks, if a student in the prime of youth who lacks disillusionment with the world desires to destroy attachment, he should go to the cremation ground and look at bluish corpses, then look at festering corpses, then at putrid skeletons, then look at bare skeletons.[1556] Some say: The conception of repulsiveness for an object of the eye [506] is not an antidote to discursiveness because it views external objects. Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is an antidote to discursiveness because it views internal states.

'o na mi sdug pas ji ltar 'dod chags kyi gnyen po byed ce na/ 'dod chags ni bzhi ste/ kha dog dang*/ dbyibs dang*/ reg pa dang*/ bsnyen bkur gyi 'dod chags so/ / de la dang po'i gnyen por ni rnam par bsngos pa dang*/ rnam par rnag pa dang*/ rnam par dmar ba gsum la dmigs nas mi sdug pa'i 'du shes sgom par byed do/ gnyis pa'i gnyen por ni rnam par zos pa dang rnam par 'thor ba gnyis la dmigs nas mi sdug pa'i 'du shes sgom par byed do/ / gsum pa'i gnyen por ni rnam par 'bus gzhigs pa dang*/ rgyus pas brang breng du sbrel ba'i keng rus gnyis la dmigs nas mi sdug pa'i 'du shes sgom par byed do/ / bzhi pa'i gnyen por ni shi ba'i ro g.yo ba med pa la dmigs nas mi sdug pa'i 'du shes sgom par byed do/ /

Question: How does repulsiveness act as an antidote to attachment? There are four types of attachment: attachment to (1) color, (2) shape, (3) contact, and (4) property and respect. (1) The antidote to the first is cultivating the discernment of repulsiveness that focuses on three aspects: a blue corpse, a festering corpse, and a red corpse. (2) The antidote to the second is cultivating the discernment of repulsiveness that focuses on two aspects: a corpse that is being eaten and a corpse whose limbs are scattered. (3) The antidote to the third is cultivating the discernment of repulsiveness that focuses on two aspects: a corpse disintegrating due to insects and a skeleton held together by a few tendons. (4) The antidote of the fourth is cultivating the discernment of repulsiveness that focuses on the lack of movement of a dead corpse.

bye brag med par keng rus kyi 'du shes ni chags bcas thams cad la shis shing bsngags pas thams cad kyi gnyen por sgom par byed do/ / keng rus la kha dog la sogs pa chags pa'i gzhi rnam pa bzhi med pa'i phyir ro/ / de ltar na mi sdug pa'i 'du shes ni rnam pa dgu'o/ / de la mi sdug pa sgom pa 'di ni sgro btags nas mos pa yod la byed pa'i phyir dang*/ {gzugs phung gi phyogs gcig } kha dog dang dbyibs nyi tshe la dmigs pa'i phyir nyon mongs pa rnam par gnon pa tsam yin gyi gtan nas spong ba ni ma yin no/ / mi sdug pa bsgom pa'i rnal 'byor de ni rnam pa gsum du rig par bya ste/ las dang po pa dang*/ yongs su sbyang ba byas pa dang*/ yid la byed pa yongs su rdzogs pa'i rnal 'byor ro/ /

Discernment of an undifferentiated skeleton (śaṅkala) should be cultivated as the antidote to all attachment, since it benefits and is recommended for all who possess attachment. Thus discernment of repulsiveness has nine types.[1557] Meditation on repulsiveness merely suppresses afflicted states but does not abandon them in any way, because it is resolute attention that superimposes repulsiveness on its object, and it focuses on both the color and shape {of just one part of the form aggregate}. The yoga of meditating on repulsiveness should be cognized as three types: (1) the yoga of a beginner, (2) the yoga of complete training, and (3) the yoga of complete attention.
rus pa rgya mtsho'i bar du ni/ / spro zhing sdud pas las dang po/ / rkang rus nas ni thod phyed bar/ / btang bas sbyang ba byas par bshad/ / 10
The beginner expands the bones to fill an ocean, and then he contracts them. He disperses the bones of the feet up to half the skull. This is explained as complete training. (6:10)

de la rang gi lus kyi rkang pa'i mthe bong ngam dpral ba'i dbyes la sogs pa gang mos pa nas sha 'theb gang myags te bog nas rus pa nyid du sems shing goms par byed la/ de nas rim gyis{ rang gi} lus ril po dang*/ gnas khang dang*/ mthar gyis phyi'i rgya mtsho'i bar du{ gang rus su} spro zhing*/{ yun ring du sgom} yang{ dmigs pa mtha' nas} rim gyis rang gi lus 'ba' zhig rus pa yin pa la{ sems} sdud{ nas sgom} pas ni las dang po pa'i rnal 'byor ro/ / de nas{ spros sngar bzhin la} sems bsdu ba khyad par du bya ba'i phyir rkang pa'i rus pa rnams bor zhing lus lhag ma rus pa nyid du dmigs pa nas bzung nas ni rim gyis lus phyed dang de nas thod pa'i phyed kyi bar du rus par btang zhing bor nas thod pa'i phyed rus pa nyid yin pa la sems 'dzin pas ni yongs su sbyang ba byas pa'i rnal 'byor yin par bshad do/ /

(1) The yoga of a beginner (ādikarmika) is taking any part of the practitioner’s body, from the toes to the forehead and so on, and contemplating and meditating on the bones (asthi) there, through mentally separating the potentially putrid flesh from the bones. He then gradually expands the image of {these bones until they fill his} entire body, abode, and the external ocean. {He meditates on this for a long time}. Then, in stages, he {mentally} contracts them {from the limit of the full expansion of the focal object}, until {he meditates on} the bones of his body alone. (2) Then, in order to perfect mental contraction, {he expands the bones as before} and scatters the bones of the feet. Then he focuses on the bones constituting the rest of the body and disperses and scatters them in stages, first in terms of the body, then up to half the skull. Then he visualizes the bones constituting the remaining half of the skull. This is explained as the yoga of complete training.
smin ma'i bar du sems 'dzin pas/ / yid la byed pa rdzogs pa yin/ / mi sdug ma chags sa bcu dang / / dmigs pa 'dod snang mis skyed do/ / 11

Visualizing the remaining bone between the eyebrows is the yoga of attention. Repulsiveness is nonattachment. It has ten levels. Its focal object appears in the desire realm, generated by humans. (6:11)

de thod pa phyed kyang rus pa yin pa'i dmigs pa bor nas{ sngar bzhin spros nas spyad pa na} smin ma gnyis po'i bar du rus par 'theb gang tsam la sems 'dzin pas ni yid la byed pa yongs su rdzogs pa'i rnal 'byor yin no zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'chad do/ /

(3) {Then, having expanded the visualization as before,} he scatters even the focal object of the bones constituting half the skull. Visualizing just the remaining bones between the two eyebrows is the yoga of complete attention. This is explained by the Vaibhāṣikas.

{de'i chos kyi khyad par la } mi sdug pa'i rnam par yid la byed pa 'di'i ngo bo ni ma chags pa'i dge ba dang 'khor dang bcas na phung po lnga'am bzhi yin no/ / sa ni bsam gtan gyi dngos gzhi bzhi khyad par can nyer bsdogs bzhi dang bcas pas dgu 'dod pa ste bcu dang*/ dmigs pa ni 'dod pa'i snang ba'i chos kha dog dang dbyibs la dmigs pa'o/ / gang zag ni gling gsum gyi mi kho nas skyed do/ / gzhan na ni med do/ / byang gi sgra mi snyan pa ni blun pa'i phyir dang*/ gnyen po yid la byed pa med pa'i phyir ro/ / 'gro ba gzhan dang khams gzhan na'ang med do/ { de yang ni lha dbang rtul gyis bden pa mi rtogs la dbang rnon 'di mi sgom pas so/ /} rnam pa ni mi sdug pa'i rnam pa yin no/ / dus ni 'das pa'i mi sdug pa 'das pa la dmigs pa la sogs pa'o/ / mi skye ba'i chos can ni dus gsum la dmigs pa'o/ / mos pa yid la byed pa kho na'i phyir zag bcas yin no/ / {thog med nas } sngar 'dris pa {'i byis pa }rnams kyis ni{ 'dod pa las} 'dod chags dang bral ba tsam gyis {'di 'dod chags dang bral lam yin pa'i phyir } 'thob la/ sngar ma 'dris pa {'i 'phags pa }rnams kyis ni sbyor ba'i stobs kyis 'thob bo/ / {bsam gtan thob kyang 'di sbyor bas bskyed dgos so/ /}

The nature of this attention on repulsiveness [507] {as an attribute of its object} is the virtue of nonattachment (aśubha), and if associated with sāṃsara it has five or four aggregates. It has ten levels: nine associated with (1–4) the four actual bases of absorption, (5) special absorption, (6–9) the four access concentrations, and (10) the desire realm. As for its focal object (ālambā), it is the color and shape of objects that appear in the desire realm. In terms of the person, it is generated by humans of the three continents alone. No other beings generate it because those of Northern Kuru are dull, and they do not apply such antidotes. It does not exist in other reincarnating beings or in other realms. {Further, gods of dull faculty do not comprehend the four truths, and those of sharp faculty do not meditate on it.} Its aspect is the aspect of repulsiveness. Its time is that it focuses on repulsiveness in the past and so on. It focuses on unarisen repulsiveness in the three times. It is contaminated because it is merely resolute attention focusing on repulsiveness. {Childlike beings} who have prior familiarity with it {from the beginning} obtain mere freedom from attachment {to sense objects}, {because it itself is not free from attachment}. {Āryas} without prior familiarity obtain it through the power of preparatory application. {Though they obtain the absorptions, this is necessarily generated through preparation.}
dbugs rngub dbugs 'byung dran pa ni/ / shes rab sa lnga spyod yul rlung / / 'dod rten phyi ba'i ma yin no/ / bgrang la sogs pa rnam pa drug / 12
Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is wisdom. It has five levels. Its object field is wind. Its basis is a desire being, not outsiders. It has six aspects: counting and so on. (6:12)

dbugs rngub pa dang dbugs 'byung ba rjes su dran pa'i rang bzhin ni 'byung rngub ji lta bar shes pa'i shes rab yin no/ / de la dran pa zhes brjod pa ni rgyu dran pa'i stobs kyis 'bras bu shes rab de skyed cing 'jug pas na rgyu'i ming gis 'bras bu la {bsaM gtan thob kyang 'di sbyor bas bskyed dgos so }btags pa ste dran pa nyer gzhag bzhin no/ / {de'i khyad par gyi chos la } sa ni lnga pa yin te/ bsam gtan dang po gsum gyi nyer bsdogs gsum dang bsam gtan khyad par can dang*/ 'dod pa'i sa pa yin pa'i phyir te/ 'di ni rnam rtog gi gnyen po dang mthun pas tshor ba btang snyoms dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir dang*/ {nyer bsdogs gsum yang btang snyoms kyi sa pa yin pa'i phyir dang } dngos gzhi dang po gsum na yid bde dang bde ba yod pa'i phyir dang*/ rnam rtog gi gnyen po dbugs 'byung rngub dran pa ni tshor ba bde sdug dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa'i phyir dang*/ bzhi pa yan chad na rlung rgyu ba dang bral ba'i phyir ro/ / kha cig ni dngos gzhi dang po gsum la mnyam par bzhag pa na btang snyoms dang mtshungs par ldan pa'ang srid pas sa brgyad pa yin no zhes 'dod do/ / de'i spyod yul te dmigs pa ni rlung yin no/ / sngar 'dris pa dang ma 'dris pa'i phyir{ rim pa ltar} 'dod chags dang bral ba dang sbyor bas 'thob la 'di ni de kho na yid la byed pa'ang yin no/ / 'dod khams pa'i rten can yin te/ rnam par rtog pa mang ba'i phyir ro/ / de yang blo gsal bas lha dang gling gsum gyi mi yin te/ {'gro ba } gzhan{ dang sgra mi snyan pa} dag ni blo mi gsal ba dang mthong lam gyi rten ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / dbugs rngub pa dang 'byung ba dran pa 'di ni chos 'di pa kho na'i yin gyi{ 'phags lam gyi rgyu} yang dag par ston pa'i lung med pa'i phyir dang*/ {lung med par } rang nyid kyis chos zab mo mi rtogs pa'i phyir phyi pa mu stegs pa'i ni ma yin no/ / zab mo nyid{ drug} gang zhe na/

The essential nature of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (ānāpānasmṛti) is wisdom (prajñā) that knows how to inhale and exhale. It is called “mindfulness” since resultant wisdom is generated and engaged by the power of its cause, mindfulness, where the name of the cause is imputed to the result. Thus it is the close placement of mindfulness. It has five levels {as its attributes}. There are (1–3) the three access concentrations of the first three absorptions, (4) special absorption, and (5) the desire-realm level. That is because (1) it is concomitant with the feeling of equanimity, since it is compatible with the antidote of discursiveness; (2) {it exists on the level of the three access concentrations and equanimity}; (3) mental satisfaction and pleasure exist in the first three absorptions; (4) mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation that is the antidote of discursiveness is not concomitant with feelings of pleasure and pain; and (5) there is no movement of winds on the fourth absorption and above. Some say it has eight levels, since it is possible that equipoise in the first three actual bases of absorption is concomitant with equanimity. Its object field (gocarā) or focal object is wind (vāyu). Because one is previously familiar with it or not, {respectively,} one either is free of attachment or obtains it through preparation. And it is attention focused on wind alone. Its basis (āśraya) is a desire-realm being because such beings have much discursive thought. Further, gods and humans of the three continents are bases since they have clarity of mind. Other {reincarnating beings and humans of Kuru} are not, since they do not have clear intelligence and they are not bases [supporting] the path of seeing. Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is a mundane phenomenon alone, [508] and there is no scripture authentically demonstrating it to be {a cause of the ārya path}. Outsider tīrthikas are not beings who engage in this practice. They don’t comprehend the profound Dharma {since they do not have such scripture}. Question: What are the {six} profound states?
