shes pa thams cad rnam pa gnyis su 'dus te zag pa dang bcas pa dang zag pa med pa'o/ / de la dang po zag bcas ni kun rdzob shes pa zhes bya ba yin te/ res 'ga' rang dang spyi'i mtshan nyid kyang 'dzin la phal cher bum pa snam bu dang skyes pa bud med la sogs pa kun rdzob tu yod pa'i dngos po la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / zag med ni chos shes pa dang rjes su shes pa rnam pa gnyis kho na yin te/ sdug bsngal shes pa la sogs pa ni 'di gnyis su 'dus pa'i phyir ro/ /

All knowledge is summarized in two types: contaminated and uncontaminated knowledge. The first, contaminated knowledge, is called conventional (sāmvṛta) knowledge because, though at times it apprehends real as well as abstract entities, it mainly focuses on things that are conventionally existent, such as vases, cloth, male, female, and so on. The second, uncontaminated knowledge, has just two types — Dharma knowledge and subsequent knowledge — because knowledge of suffering and so on are subsumed in these two.
kun rdzob yul ni thams cad do/ / chos zhes bya ba'i spyod yul ni/ / 'dod sdug bsngal sogs rjes shes pa'i/ / spyod yul gong ma'i sdug bsngal sogs/ / 3

All phenomena are objects of conventional knowledge. The object field of Dharma knowledge is suffering of the desire realm and so on. The object field of subsequent knowledge is suffering of higher realms and so on. (7:3)

de la kun rdzob shes pa'i yul ni 'dus byas dang 'dus ma byas kyi chos thams cad yin te/ {bsam gtan dge yul yid dgu yin zhes pa dang } mig shes kyis gzugs shes pa la sogs pa ci rigs par thams cad la 'jug pa'i phyir ro/ / chos shes pa zhes bya ba'i spyod yul ni 'dod pa'i sdug bsngal dang sogs pas bsdus pa kun 'byung dang 'gog pa dang lam rnams yin no/ / rjes su shes pa'i spyod yul ni khams gong ma gnyis po'i sdug bsngal dang sogs pas bsdus pa kun 'byung dang 'gog pa dang lam rnams yin pas{ nam mkha' dang so sor brtags min ni bden bzhir ma 'dus pas de dag gi dmigs pa min no/ /} de lta na shes pa gsum yin no/ /

All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are objects of conventional (saṃvṛta) knowledge. As {the Abhidharmakośa observes, “The object of virtuous absorption is all objects” (8:20d), and} conventional knowledge engages all types of objects, such as eye consciousness that knows form and so on. The object field (gocara) of Dharma knowledge is the truth of suffering of the desire realm. The term “and so on” includes the truths of origin, cessation, and path. The object field of subsequent knowledge is suffering of the higher realms. The term “and so on” again indicates the truths of origin, cessation, and path. {Space and nonanalytical cessation are not the focal objects of these knowledges since they are not included in the four truths}. Thus there are three knowledges.

de dag nyid bden bye brag gis/ / bzhi ste rnam bzhi de dag ni/ / mi skye ba dang zad pa shes/ / de gnyis dang po skyes pa ni/ / 4 sdug bsngal rgyu rjes shes pa yin/ / bzhi las pha rol sems rig pa/ / des ni sa dbang gang zag 'das/ / zhig dang ma skyes mi rig go/ / 5

Those are four, distinguished in terms of the truths. These four types are knowledge of nonarising and elimination. Those two that arise are subsequent knowledge (7:4) of suffering and its cause. Cognition of the minds of others is established from four. That is not knowledge of superior level, faculties, persons. It does not cognize that which is destroyed or unarisen. (7:5)

chos shes pa dang rjes su shes pa de dag nyid sdug bsngal shes pa la sogs pa bzhi yin te/ yul bden bzhi la dmigs pa'i bye brag gis so {dgur dbye ba ni }chos shes rjes shes las lta ba'i rang bzhin ma yin pa bden bzhi la dmigs pa'i bye brag gis sdug bsngal shes pa la sogs pa{ lta ba'i rang bzhin ma yin pa'i} rnam pa bzhi po de dag nyid ni mi skye ba shes pa dang zad pa shes pa gnyis su 'gyur te/ rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gyi rjes su skyes pa'i bden bzhir shes pa gang yin pa'o/ /

Those Dharma knowledges and subsequent knowledges are four [in number] — such as the knowledge of suffering and so on. Since they are distinguished in terms of the four truths they focus on {they are classified as thirty-nine}[1760] in terms of Dharma knowledge and subsequent knowledge that are not by nature view.[1761] These four types such as the knowledge of suffering and so on {that are not by nature view}, that are distinguished in terms of the four truths they focus on, are either knowledge of nonarising or knowledge of elimination. They constitute any knowledge of the four truths generated after vajra-like concentration.

zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa de gnyis dang por skyes pa ni sdug bsngal dang rgyu kun 'byung la rjes su shes pa yin te/ srid rtse'i phung pos bsdus pa'i sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la mi rtag pa la sogs pa dang rgyu la sogs par dmigs pa'i phyir ro/ / dang por skyes pa las gzhan de phyin chad kyi zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa ni bden pa gzhan dag la'ang dmigs so/ / rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin ni srid rtse'i bden bzhi la dmigs la zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa dang por skyes pa sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la dmigs so zhes bya ba ni bye brag tu smra ba'i grub pa'i mtha' ste khyad par med pa la khyad par rtag pa yin no/ /

Those two knowledges of nonarising and elimination that arise first are subsequent knowledge of suffering and its cause, the truth of origin, because they focus on the aspect of impermanence and so on of the truth of suffering and the aspect of cause and so on of the truth of origin that are subsumed by the aggregates of the summit of existence. Knowledge of elimination and nonarising that arise later, as distinct from those that arise first, focus on the other truths. Vajra-like concentration focuses on the four truths at the summit of existence, while the knowledges of elimination and nonarising focus on the truths of suffering and origin that arise first. This is the tenet system of the Vaibhāṣikas, who impute distinctions where there are no distinctions.

'o na rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin dang zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa dmigs pa gcig gam tha dad ce na/ rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gal te srid rtse'i sgom spang chung ngu'i chung ngu'i ngo bor gyur pa bden pa dang po gnyis la dmigs na ni gcig la 'on te/ bsgom pa'i lam la 'gog pa'am/ / lam la chos shes gang yin de/ / khams gsum gyi ni gnyen po yin zhes pas 'gog lam la dmigs na ni mi gcig ste/ shes pa gnyis po ni dang por srid rtse'i phung po kho na la nges par dmigs pa'i phyir te dper na dug mdas phog ste 'chi ba na thog mar dug yan lag thams cad la khyab nas mthar shi ma thag rma'i phyogs kho nar 'du ba bzhin no/ / {bcur dbye ba ni }

chos shes rjes shes dang lam shes pa dang kun rdzob shes pa bzhi las ni pha rol gyi sems rig pa bzhag ste/ {gzhan sems } zag bcas{ la dmigs pa ni} kun rdzob shes pa dang*/ zag med{ la dmigs pa ni} lam shes pa dang gnyen po'i bye brag gis chos shes rjes shes kyang yin pa'i phyir ro/ { ji ltar zhe na/ 'di ltar zag bcas kyi gzhan gyi sems shes ni so so'i skye bo rnams kyis bsam gtan la brten nas sems 'dod chags dang bcas bral la sogs pa 'jig rten pa'i rnam pa can gyi shes pa dang*/ 'phags pa rnams kyi rjes las thob pa'i tshe bsam gtan la brten nas shes pa ste kun rdzob shes pa yin no/ / 'phags pa'i zag med kyi sems shes pas gzhan gyi zag med kyi sems shes na de ni lam shes pa yin pas lam gyi rnam pa can kho na yin te/ des zag bcas mi shes pa'i phyir dang*/ sems shes pas 'gog pa shes par 'gyur ba'ang ming de 'gog pa sems ma yin pa'i phyir/ shes pa gzhan yang min te/ de dag gi rnam pa can ma yin pa'i phyir/ lam shes pa'ang chos dang rjes su shes pa gzhag pa'i phyir sems shes pa zag med ni shes pa gsum po yin no}

sems shes des ni sa 'das pa mi shes te/ bsam gtan dang po la sogs pa 'og ma'i sa pas bsam gtan gnyis pa la sogs pa gong ma'i sa pa mi shes pa'i phyir ro/{ de yang dman pa'i yul mchog ma yin pa'i phyir/ des na bzhi pa'i sems pa zag bcas kyi yul ni sa lnga yin pa nas zag med kyi yul sa bzhi yin pa'i bar du'o/ /} dbang po 'das pa'ang mi shes te/ dad mos pa'i lam gyis mthong thob pa'i lam mi shes pa dang*/ dus dang sbyor ba'i lam gyis dus dang mi sbyor ba'i lam mi shes{ te dbang po 'das} pa'i phyir ro/ gang zag 'das pa mi shes pa ni phyir mi 'ong gi lam gyis dgra bcom gyi lam mi shes la/ nyan thos kyi lam gyis rang sangs rgyas kyi lam mi shes pa la sogs pa'i phyir ro/ / {de yang rang stobs kyis mi shes pa la bsams gyi/ sangs rgyas la sogs pas byin gyis brlabs na gang zag dang dbang po 'das kyang shes so/ / 'dir 'phags pa chags bcas ma smros pa ni de dag la sems shes bkag pas so/ } 'das pa'i sgra ni 'dir gong ma la brjod par 'dod pa yin no/ / de'i phyir mnyam pa dang 'og ma ni shes par bstan to/ / gzhan yang pha rol sems shes ni gzhan gyi sems da ltar ba kho na'i yul can yin pa'i phyir dus zhig pa 'das pa dang ma skyes pa ma 'ongs pa'ang mi rig go /ci'i phyir zhe na/ 'das pa dang ma 'ongs pa shes pa ni rim pa ltar sngon gnas rjes dran dang 'chi 'pho skye shes yin la de dag kyang kun rdzob shes pa yin pa'i phyir ro/ /

That knowledge of mind is not knowledge of minds of superior levels (bhūmi) because knowledge of lower levels such as the first absorption does not know minds of higher levels such as the second absorption. {Moreover, because an inferior object is not a superior object, intention of the fourth [level knows] contaminated objects from the five levels up to [591] uncontaminated objects of the fourth level}. It is not knowledge of superior faculties (akṣa), because the path of resolute faith does not know the path that obtains results by insight, and the path arising according to circumstances does not know the path arising regardless of circumstances, {since they are of superior faculty}. It is not knowledge of superior persons (pudgala), because the path of a nonreturner does not know the path of an arhat, the śrāvaka path does not know the pratyekabuddha path, and so on. {Further, I think it is not knowledge arisen by its own power, since knowledge of superior persons and faculties arises due to the blessings of buddhas and so on. In this context, āryas who possess attachment are not mentioned, since for them the knowledge of others’ minds is obstructed}. The term “superior” refers to “higher states”; therefore it teaches knowledge of levels that are lower or even equal. Again, knowledge of others’ minds does not cognize (na vetti) past time that is destroyed (naṣṭa) or future time that is unarisen (ajāta) because it takes as its object the minds of others in the present alone. Question: Why? Reply: Knowledge of the past and knowledge of the future respectively recall previous abodes, and they know death and rebirth. They are also conventional knowledge.
chos rjes blo phyogs phan tshun min/ / nyan thos mthong ba'i skad cig gnyis/ / rig ste bse ru lta bus gsum/ / sangs rgyas sbyor ba med par kun/ / 6

Awarenesses compatible with Dharma or subsequent knowledge do not mutually cognize each other. Śrāvakas cognize two moments of seeing. Rhinoceros-like, three. The Buddha knows all without preparation. (7:6)

chos shes dang rjes shes kyi phyogs dang mthun pa'i sems shes pa'i blo yang{ rang gi rigs mthun ma yin pa} phyogs phan tshun{ gcig gis gcig} rig pa min te/ sems shes pa de gnyis 'dod pa dang khams gong ma'i gnyen po tha dad la dmigs pa'i phyir ro/{ gang la rgyab kyis phyogs pa de la mi dmigs par 'dod pas so/ /} de yang mthong lam la ni pha rol gyi sems shes pa med de/ mthong lam yun thung bas sems shes kyi sbyor ba bya ba'i skabs med pa'i phyir dang*/ de ni bden pa la mnyam par bzhag pa zag med bar ma chad yin pa'i phyir ro/ / 'on kyang sangs rgyas dang dge 'dun la shes nas dad pa ni bden pa mngon sum du shes nas yid ches pa yin gyi pha rol gyi sems mngon sum du shes pa ni med do zhes bya ba ni grub pa'i mtha' yin no/ / theg pa gong ma pa ni 'jig rten gyi khams brgya shes pa la sogs pa skad cig ma la skye ba'i yon tan du ma bzhed pa yin no/ / mthong lam ni pha rol sems shes kyi yul du 'gyur bas de'i khyad par bshad par bya ste/

Also awarenesses (dhī) of others’ minds compatible with Dharma knowledge or subsequent knowledge {are different types of awareness that} do not mutually cognize {each other}. These two types of knowledge [or awareness] of others’ minds focus on distinct antidotes to the desire realm and higher realms {since it is asserted that what one turns one’s back on is not focused upon}. Further, knowledge of other’s minds doesn’t exist on the path of seeing. Since the path of seeing is of short duration and it is uninterrupted uncontaminated equipoise on the four truths, there is no opportunity to activate knowledge of others’ minds. Still, some hold the philosophical position that faith through knowledge of the Buddha and Saṅgha exists, since it is conviction directly knowing the four truths, but directly knowing the minds of others does not exist. Those of the higher vehicle assert that many qualities can be generated in one moment, such as knowing one hundred world systems and so on. This attribute is explained since the path of seeing is an object comprehended by knowledge of others’ minds.

de la 'phags pa nyan thos kyi sems shes pas ni dbang po rtul bas mthong ba'i lam skad cig ma bco lnga las skad cig ma dang po gnyis rig ste/ rjes su shes pa'i phyogs ni de shes par 'dod pa na sbyor ba gzhan gyis sgrub dgos pa'i phyir dang*/ grub pa na'ang{ de'i bar la yun ring 'gor bas} sems bcu drug pa{ thob par 'gyur la de} thob nas { skad cig ma gsum pa sogs} 'das pa'i phyir dang*/ 'das pa'ang mi rig pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na ni skad cig ma dang po gnyis kyang mi rig par 'gyur te/ de shes par 'dod nas sbyor ba brtsams te grub pa na skad cig ma gnyis po'ang 'gag pa'i phyir ro zhe na/ skad cig ma gnyis po 'di shes par bya'o zhes sbyor ba rtsom pa ni ma yin gyi gang zag 'di'i sems shes par bya'o zhes sbyor ba rtsom pa na mngon shes grub pa dang mnyam par skad cig dang po gnyis skyes pa dag shes par 'gyur ro zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'dod mod kyi/ de lta na ni rjes su shes pa'i bzod pa la sogs pa rnams kyang shes par 'gyur ro/ / de'i phyir sbyor ba ni spyi la dmigs pa yin gyi bye brag ni ma yin gyi/ mi shes pa'i phyir ro/ / de'i phyir 'di dag kyang khyad par med pa la rnam par rtog pas khyad par du rtog pa kho nar zad do/ / rang sangs rgyas bse ru lta bu'i sems shes pas ni skad cig ma dang po gnyis dang brgyad pa gsum rig ste/ nyan thos kyi ni sbyor ba chen pos bsgrub dgos la 'di ni sbyor ba la rtsol ba chung bas dang po gnyis shes nas yang skad cig ma lnga'i bar la mngon shes 'grub pa'i phyir ro/ / des kyang skad cig ma dgu pa la sogs pa ni mi rig ste/ yang sbyor ba gzhan gyis sgrub dgos pa'i phyir dang*/ de nas dub pas skad cig ma bdun la'ang sbyor ba mi rdzogs pa'i phyir ro/ / kha cig skad cig ma dang po gnyis shes nas yang sbyor ba gzhan byas nas skad cig ma bco lnga pa dang gsum shes so zhes bya bar 'dod do/ /
nyan rang gnyis ka la yang skad cig ma dang po gnyis shes par bshad pa ni mtshon pa ste/ nyan thos kyis ni rigs mthun pa'i skad cig ma gnyis ci rigs par shes par 'gyur la rang rgyal gyis ni rigs mthun pa gnyis dang mi mthun pa gcig ste gsum ci rigs par shes par 'gyur ro/ /

Therefore ārya śrāvakas with knowledge of others’ minds cognize the first two moments of the fifteen moments (kṣaṇa) of the path of seeing. But if they desire to know aspects of subsequent knowledge, they must engage in other types of preparation. But even if they engage in them, {they are delayed in obtaining knowledge of} the sixteenth moment. And though they may obtain it, {by then the third moment and so on} has passed, and they do not cognize that it has passed. Objection: Neither do they cognize the first two moments, because these two moments cease while they prepare to generate knowledge of them. Indeed, Vaibhāṣikas assert that this is [592] not preparing to know the two moments but instead preparing to know the mind of this person {of the third moment and so on}. If one engages in this, one establishes higher perception, and one comes to know the first two moments that arise with it. Thus one comes to know perseverance in subsequent knowledge and so on. Because of that, preparation focuses on general objects and not specific objects, since it does not know them. Therefore they are not different, and conception that conceives them as being different subsides. Rhinoceros-like (khaḍga) pratyekabuddhas cognize three moments — the first two and the eighth — because though they must establish knowledge of the śrāvaka [mind] through intense preparation, here they establish higher perception through knowing the first two moments up to the fifth moment through less exertion in preparation. But they do not cognize the ninth moment and so on, because these must be established by other types of preparation, and preparation for even the seventh moment is not completed due to fatigue. Some assert: Through having knowledge of the first two moments, they develop knowledge of the fifteenth and third moments through other types of preparation.
The explanation that both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know the first two moments of the path of seeing is exemplified by śrāvakas who come to know any two moments of similar type, while pratyekabuddhas come to know any three moments — namely, two of similar type and one of dissimilar type.

sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das ni mdzad pa thams cad lhun gyis grub pas sbyor ba las byung ba'i 'bad rtsol med par mthong lam gyi ye shes kyi skad cig ma kun shes par 'gyur ba yin te/ ji skad du/ dge mthar phyin pa khyod la ni/ / sbyor byung dge ba 'ga' ma mchis/ / khyod ni gang zhig bzhed na yang*/ / bzhed pa tsam la rag las so zhes bshad pa bzhin no/ / 'o na zad pa shes pa dang mi skye ba shes pa dag la khyad par ci yod ce na/ bstan bcos las/ zad pa shes pa gang zhe na/

But the Bhagavan Buddha knows all moments of transcendent wisdom of the path of seeing without exertion arising from any type of preparation, since he spontaneously establishes all actions. As it is said: You with consummate virtue do not prepare for any virtue. Whatever you desire arises merely in reliance on your wish.[1762] Question: What is the difference between knowledge of elimination and knowledge of nonarising?
zad par shes pa bden rnams la/ / yongs shes la sogs pa nges pa'o/ / yongs shes byar med ces la sogs/ / mi skye ba yi blo 'dod do/ / 7
Some assert that knowledge of elimination ascertains the truths and fully knows suffering and so on. Awareness of nonarising ascertains that there is no more to fully know and so on. (7:7)

bdag gis sdug bsngal shes so zhes bya bar shes pa dang*/ kun 'byung spangs so/ / 'gog pa mngon du byas so/ / lam bsgoms so zhes bya bar shes pa de'i rgyu las byung ba'i shes pa dang mthong ba dang rig pa dang blo dang rtog pa dang shes rab dang snang ba dang mngon par rtogs pa gang yin pa 'di ni zad pa shes pa zhes bya'o/ / mi skye ba shes pa gang zhe na/ bdag gis sdug bsngal yongs su shes te yang yongs su shes par byar med do zhes bya bar shes pa nas bdag gis lam bsgoms te yang sgom du med do zhes bya ba'i bar du shes pa de'i rgyu las byung ba'i shes pa dang zhes pa nas 'di ni mi skye ba shes pa zhes bya'o zhes bya ba'i bar du 'byung ba'i phyir

Reply: The treatise [Topic Divisions][1763] explains: What is knowledge of elimination? It is knowledge that I know suffering, I have abandoned origin, I have manifested cessation, and I have meditated on the path.[1764] Any knowledge, seeing, cognition, insight, investigation, wisdom, appearance, and realization derived from the cause of that knowledge is called knowledge of elimination. What is knowledge of nonarising? Because that occurs from knowledge derived from the cause of that knowledge, from “I fully know suffering and there is no more to fully know” up to “I have meditated on the path and there is nothing else to meditate on,” it is called knowledge of nonarising.

zad pa shes pa ni sdug bsngal la sogs pa'i bden pa rnams la bdag gis sdug bsngal yongs su shes so zhes pa dang*/ sogs pas gzung ba kun 'byung spangs so/ / 'gog pa mngon du byas so/ / lam bsgoms so zhes mnyam gzhag gi dus su shes pa las byung ba'i rjes kyi shes pas nges pa'o/ / de bzhin du mnyam gzhag tu bdag gis sdug bsngal yongs su shes par byas te yang yongs su shes par byar med do zhes bya ba la sogs par rtogs pa las langs pa'i rjes las thob pa'i shes pas nges pa ni mi skye ba shes pa'i blor kha che bas 'dod do/ / nyi 'og pa ni mnyam gzhag na zag med kyi rnam pa bcu drug las gzhan yang yod pas des de ltar nges so zhes 'dod do/ / 'o na bstan bcos las mthong ba zhes bshad pa'i phyir shes pa de gnyis lta bar 'gyur te/ lta ba dang mthong ba gnyis don gcig pa'i phyir ro/ / 'dod na zad dang mi skye'i blo lta min zhes pa dang 'gal lo zhe na/ mi 'gal te/ mthong ba ni shes pas 'phangs pa'i rnam grangs sam/ tha snyad tsam mam/ yang na lung dang rtags las ma ltos par mig shes kyis gzugs ltar mngon sum du rtogs pas na sdug bsngal shes pa la sogs pa dang shes te yang shes par byar med pa la sogs par shes pa nyid la mthong ba zhes brjod kyi rtog pa'i bdag nyid ma yin zhing mthong ba la lta bas ma khyab pas {snga ma ni dgra bcom dbang po rno rtul gnyis ka la yod la phyi ma ni mi g.yo ba'i chos can kho na'o } lta ba ni ma yin no/ /

Kāśmīri Vaibhāṣikas assert that knowledge of elimination is subsequent knowledge that ascertains the four truths such as suffering [593] derived from the knowledge during equipoise that has established “I fully know suffering” and so on: “I have abandoned origin,” “I have manifested cessation,” and “I have meditated on the path.” So too, awareness (mati) that is knowledge of nonarising is knowledge during post-equipoise that has arisen from the realization during equipoise that ascertains “I fully know suffering and there is no more to fully know” and so on. Aparāntakas assert that they ascertain other states, since states other than the sixteen uncontaminated aspects exist in equipoise. Objection: Because the treatise [Topic Divisions][1765] says “seeing,” those two knowledges would be view, because “view” and “seeing” have the same meaning. But this contradicts the Abhidharmakośa, which mentions, “Awareness of elimination and nonarising is not view” (7:1b).[1766] Reply: There is no contradiction because “seeing” is a synonym or mere designation suggested by “knowledge.” Again, knowledge that is knowledge of suffering and so on or knowledge that there is no more to know and so forth, is called “seeing” since it is like eye consciousness that directly comprehends form without relying on scripture or signs. It is not “view” since it is not conceptual thought and seeing is not necessarily view. {The former exists for arhats of both dull and sharp faculty, the latter exists for immutable arhats alone.}

de'i phyir bstan bcos las kyang*/ re zhig shes pa gang yin pa de ni mthong ba yang yin no zhes shes pa dang mthong ba rnam grangs su bshad kyi mthong ba yin la shes pa ma yin pa yang yod de mngon par rtogs pa'i khongs su gtogs pa'i bzod pa brgyad lta bu'o zhes 'byung ngo*/ / mthong ba dang lta ba ni rnam grangs su ma bshad do/ / shes pa dag gi sdom kyi tshigs su bcad pa ni/ kun rdzob chos dang rjes su shes/ / gsum yin de dag bcur bshad de/ / kun rdzob shes pa rang dang ni/ / sems shes cha'o chos shes ni/ / rang dang bden pa bzhi shes dang*/ / zad dang mi skye sems shes brgyad/ / rjes shes kyang yin bden gsum shes/ / rang dang zad dang mi skye shes/ / chos shes rjes su shes pa dang*/ / lnga yin zad dang mi skye zhes/ / rang rang bden pa bzhi shes dang*/ / chos shes rjes su shes dang bdun/ / sems shes chos shes rjes shes dang*/ / lam shes kun rdzob shes pa dang*/ / rang dang lnga yin lam shes ni/ / rang dang chos shes rjes shes dang*/ / sems shes zad dang mi skye zhes/ / rnam pa drug tu yang dag brjod ces bya'o/ /

Therefore the treatise [Attainment of Knowledge][1767] declares: Knowledge and seeing are explained as synonyms since at times knowledge is also seeing.[1768] But seeing that is not knowledge also exists, such as the eight types of perseverance that are included as realizations. This passage explains that seeing and view are not synonyms. The Compendium of Knowledge states: Conventional knowledge, Dharma knowledge, and subsequent knowledge; are three. These are explained as ten;[1769] Conventional knowledge is (1) itself [conventional knowledge]; and (2) knowledge of others’ minds. Dharma knowledge is; eight: (1) itself, and knowledge of (2–5) the four truths; (6) elimination, (7) nonarising, and (8) [others’] minds; Subsequent knowledge is also that. Knowledge of three truths;[1770] is fivefold: (1) themselves, knowledge of (2) elimination, and (3) nonarising; (4) Dharma knowledge, and (5) subsequent knowledge; Those called knowledge of elimination and nonarising; are seven: (1) themselves, (2–5) knowledge of each of the four truths; (6) Dharma knowledge, and (7) subsequent knowledge; Knowledge of minds is fivefold: (1) Dharma knowledge, (2) subsequent knowledge; (3) knowledge of the path, (4) conventional knowledge; and (5) itself. Knowledge of the path is; (1) itself, (2) Dharma knowledge, (3) subsequent knowledge; (4) knowledge of mind, (5) elimination, and (6) nonarising; correctly described in six parts.[1771]
gnyis pa [shes pa'i grangs nges] ni
Set number
ci'i phyir shes pa gsum po de dag bcur phye zhe na/
Question: Why are these three knowledges classified as ten?
rang bzhin dang ni gnyen po dang / / rnam pa rnam pa spyod yul dang / / sbyor dang bya ba byas nyid dang / / rgyu rgyas pa las bcu yin no/ / 8
Ten knowledges arise from essence, antidotes, aspects, aspects and object fields, preparation, completed action, and enhanced cause. (7:8)

zag bcas kyi rang bzhin las ni kun rdzob shes pa ste/ / des kun rdzob shes kyi don dam mi shes pa'i phyir ro/ / gnyen po las ni chos shes dang rjes shes gnyis te/ rim pa ltar 'dod pa dang gong ma'i gnyen po byed pa'i phyir ro/ / rnam pa las ni sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung shes pa phye ste gnyis ka'ang nyer len gyi phung po la dmigs pas dmigs pa tha dad med pa'i phyir dang*/ rnam pa mi rtag pa la sogs pa dang rgyu la sogs pa mi 'dra bas bzhag pa'i phyir ro/ / rnam pa dang spyod yul te dmigs pa gnyis ka{ tha dad pa} las ni 'gog pa dang las shes pa dag phye ste/ 'gog pa la sogs pa dang lam la sogs pa'i rnam pa'ang tha dad cing dmigs pa 'dus ma byas dang 'dus byas kyang tha dad pa'i phyir ro/ {gzhan sems shes par bya'o zhes } sbyor ba las ni pha rol gyi sems shes pa phye ste/ des sems byung yang shes mod kyi gzhan gyi sems shes par bya'o zhes sbyor gyi sems byung shes par bya'o zhes mi sbyor ba'i phyir ro/ / bya ba byas pa nyid las ni zad pa shes pa ste/ bya ba byas pa'i rgyud la dang po nyid du skye ba'i phyir ro/ / skal mnyam gyi rgyu rgyas pa las ni mi skye ba shes pa ste/ zag med kyi shes pa sngar bskyed pa thams cad kyi 'bras bu yin pa'i phyir ro/ / des na rgyu bdun po de dag gis shes pa bcur rnam par bzhag pa yin no zhes bye brag tu smra ba 'chad do/ /
'on kyang 'di dag /rang bzhin dang ni gnyen po dang*/ / yul dang shes pa'i rnam pa las kun rdzob shes sogs rnam pa bcur/ / 'dren pas rab tu gsungs pa yin zhes shes par bya'o/ / chos shes 'dod pa'i gnyen po yin no zhes bya ba'ang 'dod pa'i spang bya ris lnga po thams cad kyi gnyen po yin pa'i phyir dang*/ gnyen po chos shes mthong sgom gyi lam gyis bsdus pa bden bzhi la dmigs pa thams cad yin pa'i phyir bshad pa yin gyi/ der ma zad gzhan yang chos shes kyis khams gong ma gnyis kyi gnyen po byed pa'ang yod de/ gang zhe na/

Vaibhāṣikas explain [594] that ten knowledges are posited due to seven causes. (1) Conventional knowledge arises from the essence (svābhava) of contaminated states because it knows conventional truth and does not know ultimate truth. Both (2) Dharma knowledge and (3) subsequent knowledge separately arise from antidotes (pratipakṣa) because they respectively act as antidotes to desire-realm and higher-realm affliction. Both (4–5) knowledge of the truth of suffering and [knowledge of the truth of] origin separately arise from the aspects (ākāra) of those truths because they don’t have distinct focal objects; both focus on the appropriated aggregates, and they are posited through different aspects, such as impermanence, cause, and so forth. Both (6–7) knowledge of the truth of cessation and [knowledge of the truth of] path separately arise from both {distinct} aspects and focal objects, or object fields (gocara), because the aspects such as cessation, path, and so forth are distinct and conditioned, and unconditioned focal objects are also distinct. (8) Knowledge of others’ minds, {which is called knowledge of the minds of others,} arises from preparation (prayoga); through preparing to know the minds of others it indeed knows mental factors, but it does not prepare to know mental factors. (9) Knowledge of elimination arises from completed action (kṛtakṛtya) because it is first generated in the mindstream of those who have completed action. (10) Knowledge of nonarising arises from an enhanced homogeneous cause because it is the result of all prior generation of uncontaminated knowledge. However, it is said: They are properly explained in ten aspects through enumerating conventional knowledge and so on. These arise from essence and antidotes, from objects and aspects of knowledge.[1772] Also it is said: Dharma knowledge is the antidote of desire-realm affliction.[1773] That is said because it is the antidote of all five types of desire-realm objects to be abandoned, and all are antidotes that are Dharma knowledge subsumed by the paths of seeing and meditation that focus on the four truths. Moreover, Dharma knowledge acts as an antidote to afflictions of the two higher realms. Question: Why is that?
bsgom pa'i lam la 'gog pa'am/ / lam la chos shes gang yin de/ / khams gsum gyi ni gnyen po yin/ / 'dod pa'i khams kyi rjes ma yin/ / 9
On the path of meditation, Dharma knowledge regarding cessation or path is an antidote to the three realms. Subsequent knowledge is not an antidote to desire-realm affliction. (7:9)

sgom pa'i lam la 'gog pa la chos shes pa'am/ lam la chos shes pa gang yin pa de dag ni 'dod pa la sogs pa khams gsum char gyi gnyen po yin te/ 'dod pa'i rten can gyi 'phags pas 'dod pa'i sgom spang dgu chos shes pas rim gyis spangs nas khams gong ma'i sgom spang yang sngar 'dris pa'i lam de nyid bskyed nas spong ba dag srid pa'i phyir ram yang na 'gog lam la chos shes kyi dmigs pa 'gog lam gnyis ni zag med yin pas khams su ma gtogs pas dmigs pa dman pa ma yin pas de dag la dmigs pa'i chos shes ni khams gsum ga'i gnyen po yin pa srid pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la chos shes pa yang khams gong ma'i gnyen por 'gyur ro zhe na/ ma yin te/ sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la chos shes pa'i dmigs pa ni 'dod pa'i bden pa dang po gnyis zag bcas yin pas dmigs pa dman pas de dag la dmigs pa'i chos shes ni khams gong ma gnyis kyi gnyen po ma yin te/ rnam par sun 'byin pa yid la byed pa yin pa'i{ phyir dman pas mchog sun 'byin mi nus pa'i} phyir ro zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ /

Reply: On the path of meditation, Dharma knowledge regarding the truth of cessation or Dharma knowledge regarding the truth of path acts as an antidote to the three realms. It is possible for āryas based in the desire realm to serially abandon the nine objects to be abandoned in the desire realm by the path of meditation through Dharma knowledge and then, through generating a path one is already familiar with, to abandon objects to be abandoned in the higher realms by the path of meditation. Or it is possible that Dharma knowledge focusing on both the truths of cessation and path — which are the focal objects of Dharma knowledge of the truths of cessation and path — are antidotes to afflictions of the three realms. Cessation and path are uncontaminated, they don’t belong to any level, and they are not inferior focal objects. Question: Does Dharma knowledge of the truths of suffering and origin also act as an antidote to afflictions of higher realms? Reply: The focal objects of Dharma knowledge of the truths of suffering and origin are the first two truths that are contaminated and inferior. The Dharma knowledge focusing on them is not the antidote of afflictions of both higher realms because such Dharma knowledge observes [595] states to be counteracted, {and inferior states cannot counteract superior states.} This is explained in Pūrṇavardhana’s commentary.[1774]

kha cig spang bya spong ba la de la dngos su gnod pa'am yang na spang bya de dang 'gal ba la yon tan du lta ba'i shugs la spong ba yin pa na sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la chos shes pa ni de lta ma yin te/ {sgom pa'i zhes smros kyi mthong lam ma smros pa ni } khams gong ma'i spang bya la dngos su mi dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ 'gal zla yon tan du lta ba'ang ma yin te/ 'og ma'i bden pa la dmigs nas yid skyo bar byed pa'i phyir ro/ / 'gog lam la dmigs pa'i chos shes ni khams gong ma'i spang bya dang 'gal ba la yon tan du lta ba'i phyir shugs la spong ba yin no zhes 'chad do/ / mthong lam gyi la 'gog lam la chos shes pa dag gong ma'i gnyen po ma yin pa ni bden pa la dmigs pa'i log zhugs tha dad pa'i phyir te/ mtho la mir 'dzin pa'i log rtog thag pa la der shes pas mi spong ba bzhin no/ / de'i phyir TIka byed dag gis sgom pa'i lam la zhes smros pa ni khams gong ma gnyis kyi mthong spang rnams ni rjes su shes pa'i bzod pas gzhom par bya ba yin no zhes bshad do/ / 'o na 'gog lam la rjes shes sgom lam gyis bsdus pas kyang 'dod pa'i gnyen po byed par 'gyur ro zhe na/

Some assert: Dharma knowledge of the truths of suffering and origin does not abandon objects to be abandoned by directly harming them. Neither does it indirectly abandon them through viewing the qualities of states that exclude them. {Stating “path of meditation” (7:9a) but not “seeing” indicates that} it does not directly focus on objects to be abandoned in higher realms. Also it does not view the qualities of states excluding it, because focusing on truths of lower level depresses the mind. It is said that Dharma knowledge focusing on the truths of cessation and path indirectly abandons objects of abandonment because it views states that exclude it as something that possesses qualities. Dharma knowledge of the truths of cessation and path on the path of seeing are not antidotes of higher-realm affliction because misconceptions that focus on those truths are different, just as knowing a rope is not a man does not eliminate the wrong conception apprehending a pile of stones to be one. Therefore Pūrṇavardhana writes in his commentary: The statement “on the path of meditation” (7:9a) indicates that objects of the two higher realms to be abandoned by the path of seeing are to be annihilated by perseverance for subsequent knowledge.[1775] Objection: Dharma knowledge of the truths of cessation and path would act as an antidote to desire-realm affliction since it would be subsumed by the path of meditation.

'dod pa'i khams kyi spang bya'i gnyen po ni rjes su shes pa sgom lam gyi bsdus pa'ang rnam pa thams cad du ma yin te/ {'dod pa'i spang bya } chos shes pas spangs zin pa'i phyir dang*/ 'og ma'i spang bya ma spangs bar gong ma'i gnyen po skye ba'ang mi srid pa'i phyir ro/ / gang yang slob dpon gang spel na re chos shes pas ni gong ma'i sgom spang spong ste/ de'i yul can 'dod pa'i kun 'gro spangs pa'i phyir dgra bcom nas yul 'jig par byed pa bzhin no/ / rjes su shes pa la ni de lta bu'i bya ba med pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ba de yang mi rigs te/ de lta na sdug bsngal dang kun 'byung la chos shes pa'ang gong ma'i sgom spang gi gnyen por 'gyur te/ yul can 'dod pa'i kun 'gro'i nyon mongs pa'i gnyen po byed pa'i phyir ro zhes bya ba 'di spang dgos so/ /

Reply: Subsequent knowledge subsumed by the path of meditation is not in any way an antidote to objects to be abandoned in the desire realm. Dharma knowledge has already abandoned {objects to be abandoned in the desire realm}, and it is impossible to generate antidotes to higher-realm affliction without first abandoning objects to be abandoned in lower realms. Master Pūrṇavardhana also says: Dharma knowledge abandons objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation in higher realms because it abandons minds possessing them that are pervasive minds of the desire realm, like destroying the land after having annihilated the enemy. Subsequent knowledge does not possess such action. Reply: That is illogical, since even Dharma knowledge of the truths of suffering and origin would be an antidote to objects to be abandoned by the path of meditation in higher realms because it would act as an antidote to pervasive minds that are desire-realm afflictions. Therefore this assertion must be abandoned.
shes pa'i rnam pa/
Aspects of knowledge
chos shes pa dang rjes su shes/ / rnam pa bcu drug kun rdzob ni/ / de bzhin gzhan du'ang rang rang gi / bden pa'i rnam pas bzhi yin no/ / 10

Dharma knowledge and subsequent knowledge possess sixteen aspects. Conventional knowledge similarly possesses those and also other aspects. Knowledge of truth possesses four aspects of each truth. (7:10)

gsum pa ni shes pa bcu po de dag las chos shes pa dang rjes su shes pa ni mi rtag pa la sogs pa rnam pa bcu drug can yin no/ / kun rdzob shes pa ni sbyor lam na yod pa dag gnyis po de bzhin du rnam pa bcu drug can yang yin la/ gnas skabs gzhan na yod pa ni rnam pa gzhan du'ang yin te/ mi sdug pa dang dbugs 'byung rngub dang byams sogs sgom pa na rang dang spyi'i mtshan nyid 'dzin pa'i phyir ro/ / de dag tu ma zad bum pa dang snam bu dang zo zhig 'thung zhig song zhig 'dug cig ces pa la sogs pa rang spyi'i mtshan nyid las gzhan pa'i rnam pa can yang yod do zhes TIka byed dag 'chad do/ / bden pa bzhi shes pa ni rang rang gi bden pa'i rnam pa can du 'jug pas rnam pa bzhi bzhi pa yin no/ /

From those ten knowledges, Dharma knowledge and subsequent knowledge possess sixteen aspects such as impermanence. Conventional knowledge — namely, the two existing on the path of preparation — similarly possesses sixteen aspects, and those existing elsewhere also have other aspects, because meditation on repulsiveness, inhalation and exhalation, love, and so on apprehend real and abstract aspects. [596] They possess not just those but other real and abstract aspects, such as vases, cloth, and so on, and expressions such as “eat,” “drink,” “go,” “stay,” and so forth.[1776] This is explained in Pūrṇavardhana’s commentary.[1777] Knowledge of the four truths possesses four aspects each, since they engage the aspects of each truth.
pha rol yid shes dri med kyang / / de bzhin dri ma dang bcas ni/ / shes bya rang gi mtshan nyid rnam/ / rdzas re re zhig spyod yul lo/ / 11

Knowledge of the stainless mental consciousness of another is similar to path knowledge. Knowledge of the stained possesses real aspects that are objects of knowledge. It takes each substance as its object field. (7:11)

gzhan sems shes pa'i yul gyi pha rol yid shes dri med kyang lam shes pa yin pas lam shes pa de bzhin du lam bden gyi rnam pa bzhi can yin zhing*/ dri ma dang bcas pa'i pha rol yid shes ni shes bya sems dang sems las byung ba'i rang gi mtshan nyid kyi rnam pa can yin {te 'dod chags dang bcas pa la sogs pa shes pa yin } la/ de yang sems 'dzin pa'i tshe sems byung dang sems byung 'dzin pa'i tshe sems mi 'dzin la/ tshor ba 'dzin pa'i 'du shes la sogs pa phan tshun mi 'dzin pas pha rol sems shes zag bcas zag med gnyis ka'ang sems dang sems byung rdzas re re zhig spyod yul du byed pa yin no/ / 'o na bcom ldan 'das kyis gnas mang po las 'dod chags dang bcas pa'i sems la yang 'dod chags dang bcas pa'i sems so zhes bya bar yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin du rab tu shes so/ / 'dod chags dang bral ba'i sems la yang 'dod chags dang bral ba'i sems so zhes bya bar yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin du rab tu shes so zhes bya ba nas de bzhin du zhe sdang dang gti mug dang bcas bral dang*/ kun tu bsdus pa dang rnam par g.yengs pa dang*/ zhum pa dang rab tu bzung ba dang*/ chung ngu dang*/ chen por gyur pa dang*/ rgod pa dang*/ de ma yin pa dang*/ nye bar ma zhi ba dang nye bar zhi ba dang*/ mnyam par ma bzhag pa dang bzhag pa dang*/ ma bsgoms pa dang bsgoms pa dang*/ rnam par ma grol ba dang rnam par grol ba'i sems la rnam par grol ba'i sems so zhes bya bar yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin du rab tu shes so zhes pa'i bar du gsungs pa dang 'gal bar 'gyur ro zhe na

Knowledge of others’ minds, where the object is the stainless (nirmala) mental consciousness of another (paramanojñā), possesses the four aspects of path knowledge similar to path knowledge, since its object is path knowledge. Knowledge of the stained (samala) minds of others possesses the real aspects (svalakṣaṇākāra) of the mind and mental factors that are its objects of knowledge (jñeya), {since it is knowledge possessing attachment and so on}. Further, the knowledge of others’ minds takes each substance of the mind and the mental factors, whether uncontaminated or contaminated, as its object field (gocara), since mental factors are not held when the mind is held, the mind is not held when mental factors are held, discernment is not held when feeling is held, and so on. Objection: But that would contradict the Bhagavan, who said: Minds associated with attachment to many states should be known correctly as they are, as minds associated with attachment. Minds free of attachment should be known correctly as they are, as minds free of attachment. Similarly, one should know whether the mind possesses aversion or delusion or is free of them, is fully contracted or distracted, listless or fully engaged, weaker or stronger, excited or nonexcited, nonpacified or pacified, nonequipoise or equipoise, nonmeditative or meditative, unliberated or liberated.[1778]

bye brag tu smra ba ni de dag rdzas re re ba'i spyod yul can yin pa'i phyir mtshungs ldan gnyis cig car 'dzin pa ni ma yin te/ dper na shes pas gos so snyam du 'dzin pa'i tshe dri ma mi 'dzin la dri ma'o snyam du 'dzin pa'i tshe gos mi 'dzin pa bzhin no/ / mdo las 'dod chags dang bcas pa'i sems zhes gsungs pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa ni 'dod chags dang mtshungs par ldan pa 'dres pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa dang*/ de dang mtshungs par mi ldan yang 'dod chags kyi thob pa dang bcas pa'am 'dod chags rgyas 'gyur gyi dmigs pa yin pas ldan pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa gnyis las dang po ni 'dres pa dang ldan pa gnyis kas 'dod chags dang bcas pa yin la/ gnyis pa ni de las gzhan pa'i zag bcas thams cad de/ de ni bden pa kho nas 'dod chags dang bcas pa yin no/ / de ltar gnyis las 'dir ni ldan pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa nyid la der dgongs pa yin no/ / bral ba ni gnyis ka dang bral ba ste zag pa med pa'i sems so zhes 'dod do/ / kha cig na re mdo 'dir ni 'dod chags dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i sems ni 'dod chags dang bcas pa yin la 'dod chags kyi gnyen po ni 'dod chags dang bral bar bshad pa yin te/ gal te 'dod chags dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa 'dod chags dang bral ba yin pa na ni zhe sdang la sogs pa nyon mongs pa gzhan dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i sems kyang 'dod chags dang bral ba yin par 'gyur ba zhig na 'dod chags dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa de 'dod chags dang bral ba ni ma bshad de/ zhe sdang dang bcas pa dang gti mug dang bcas pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa 'byung ba'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

Vaibhāṣikas assert that two concomitant states are not apprehended simultaneously because they are substantially distinct minds. For example, when consciousness holds the thought “cloth,” the stain is not held, and when it holds the stain, the cloth is not held. “That associated with attachment” in the sūtric statement “minds associated with attachment” refers to both (1) that associated with attachment that is mixed with that which is concomitant with attachment, and (2) that associated with attachment that is not concomitant with but obtains attachment, or that which is associated with attachment through possessing a focal object that increases attachment. (1) The first is that associated with attachment through both being mixed and concomitant. (2) The second is all other contaminated states that are associated with attachment through the four truths alone. From these two, here that associated with attachment through possession is intended. [597] “Free” means freedom from both and refers to the uncontaminated mind.[1779] Some say: In this sūtra, the mind concomitant with attachment is associated with attachment, and the antidote to attachment is explained as freedom from attachment. For if that which is not concomitant with attachment is free from attachment, then the mind concomitant with other afflictions, such as aversion, would be free from attachment. Therefore, that which is not concomitant with attachment is not explained as freedom from attachment because that which is associated with aversion, that which is associated with delusion, and so on occur.

chos mngon pa ba dag na re de lta na sems nyon mongs pa can ma yin pa ma bsgribs lung ma bstan ni 'dod chags dang bcas bral gnyis ka ma yin par 'gyur te/ rim pa ltar 'dod chags dang mtshungs par mi ldan zhing*/ gnyen po'ang ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / 'dod chags dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa tsam chags bral du mi 'dod pas nyon mongs pa gzhan dang mtshungs par ldan pa chags bral du'ang mi 'gyur ro/ / des na mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ mi ldan pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa gnyis las mdo 'dir ni ldan pa'i 'dod chags dang bcas pa nyid la bshad par rig par bya'o zhes zer ro/ / de bzhin du zhe sdang dang gti mug dang bcas pa dang bral ba'ang shes par bya'o/ / kun du bsdus pa dang rnam par g.yengs pa ni bye brag tu sra ba rnams na re rim pa ltar rnam g.yeng dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa dang ldan pa'i bye brag gis dmigs pa la sems mngon par sdud pa'i phyir dge ba dang nyon mongs can yin no zhes zer ro/ / nub phyogs pa rnams na re de gnyis ni rim pa ltar gnyid nyon mongs can dang gnyid las gzhan pa'i nyon mongs dang mtshungs par ldan pa yin pas gnyis ka'ang nyon mongs can yin no zhes zer ro/ /

Ābhidharmikas say: Thus unobscured-neutral unafflicted mind is neither associated with attachment nor free from attachment because it is not concomitant with, respectively, attachment nor the antidote to attachment. Since that which is merely not concomitant with attachment is not asserted to be free from attachment, those concomitant with other afflictions are not free from attachment. Therefore, from the two types — that associated with attachment through concomitance and that through nonconcomitance — one should understand that this sūtra explains that it is that associated with attachment through possession. Vaibhāṣikas say: “Fully contracted” and “distracted” refer respectively to virtuous or afflicted states because the first is the mind contracted to its focal object due to not being concomitant with distraction, and the second is concomitant with distraction. Western Vaibhāṣikas say: Both are afflicted, since these two are, respectively, either concomitant with afflicted sleep or concomitant with afflicted states other than sleep.

kha che ba na re de ni mi rigs te/ de lta na sems de nyid nyon mongs can gyi gnyid dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir bsdus pa'ang yin la/ nyon mongs can yin pa'i phyir rnam par g.yengs pa'ang yin par 'gyur bas de gnyis mtshan nyid 'chol ba'i skyon du 'gyur ba'i phyir dang*/ bstan bcos las/ sems kun du bsdus pa yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin du rab tu shes so/ / de shes pa'i shes pa ni bzhi ste/ chos shes pa dang*/ rjes su shes pa dang*/ kun rdzob shes pa dang*/ lam shes pa'o zhes 'byung ba dang 'gal ba'i phyir te/ gal te kun du bsdus pa gnyid dang mtshungs ldan la 'dod na rjes shes dang lam shes pas kun du bsdus pa'i sems la mi dmigs par 'gyur te/ khams gong ma na gnyid med cing*/ 'dod khams na gnyid yod kyang rjes shes 'dod khams la mi dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ lam shes pa ni lam bden kho na la dmigs la lam bden ni gnyid dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / des na khyod ltar na bstan bcos las 'di skad du de shes pa'i shes pa ni gnyis te/ chos shes pa dang*/ kun rdzob shes pa'o zhes brjod dgos par 'gyur te/ rjes shes dang lam shes pas de mi shes pa'i phyir ro/ / kho bo cag ltar na ni kun du bsdus pa'i sems ni dge ba kho na yin pas mtshan nyid 'chol ba'i nyes par yang mi 'gyur la/ bstan bcos dang 'gal ba'ang med de/ kun du bsdus pa'i sems dge ba ni khams gsum gyis bsdus pa zag bcas dang ma bsdus pa zag med gnyis ka yin pas khams gong ma gnyis kyi sems dge ba zag bcas la dmigs pa zag med kyi shes pa ni rjes shes yin la/ lam bden gyis bsdus pa'i sems dge ba zag med la dmigs pa ni lam shes pa'ang yin pas rjes shes dang lam shes kyi dmigs par yang grub pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

Kāśmīri Vaibhāṣikas say: That is illogical. The mind would contract because it is concomitant with afflicted sleep, but since it would also be distracted because it is afflicted, there would be the error that the characteristics of these two would become confused. Also, it would contradict the treatise [Attainment of Knowledge],[1780] which states: Know the fully contracted mind correctly as it is. Knowledge that knows it is fourfold: Dharma knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path knowledge.[1781] If one asserts that fully contracted states are concomitant with sleep, then subsequent knowledge and path knowledge would not focus on fully contracted minds because sleep does not exist in higher realms. And even though sleep exists in the desire realm, subsequent knowledge does not focus on the desire realm; path knowledge focuses on the truth of path alone, [598] but the truth of path is not concomitant with sleep. Therefore, according to you, the treatise must mean that knowledge that knows sleep has two types — Dharma knowledge and conventional knowledge — because subsequent knowledge and path knowledge do not know it. According to us, the fully contracted mind that possesses the error of confused characteristics [such as being distracted and afflicted] does not arise since the fully contracted mind is solely virtuous. And that does not contradict the treatise, since the virtuous contracted mind is either contaminated when subsumed by the three realms or uncontaminated when not subsumed. Therefore the uncontaminated knowledge focusing on contaminated virtuous minds of the two higher realms is subsequent knowledge, and since that focusing on the uncontaminated virtuous mind subsumed by path knowledge is also path knowledge, it is established as the focal object of subsequent knowledge and path knowledge.

de bzhin du zhum pa ni le lo dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir nyon mongs can no/ / rab tu bzung ba ni brtson 'grus dang mtshungs par ldan pa'i phyir dge ba'o/ / chung ngu ni chags sdang gnyis mtshungs par mi ldan pas gti mug dang chags sdang gnyis po gang rung re'i rtsa ba gnyis dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ 'bad pas bsgrub par bya ba ma yin pa dang*/ de dang 'dra ba ma 'ongs pa thob pa med pa dang*/ rjes su 'brang ba'i gzugs med pas rnam shes la tshor ba la sogs pa phung po gsum gyi rjes su 'brang ba dang bcas pa dang*/ log ltas kyang dge ba gtan du gcod mi nus pas rim pa ltar rtsa ba dang rin dang 'khor dang rjes su 'brang ba dang stobs chung bas dge ba chung ngu dag gis bsten pa'i phyir nyon mongs can no/ /

Similarly, “listless” is afflicted because it is concomitant with laziness. “Fully engaged” [states of mind] are virtuous because they are concomitant with effort. “Weaker” states include: (1) those not concomitant with either attachment or aversion but concomitant with both the root of delusion and either attachment or aversion, (2) those not established through striving, (3) those that do not obtain a similar state in future, (4) consciousness possessing complements of three aggregates such as feeling — since it lacks form among its complements, and (5) virtue that can never be severed by wrong view. They are afflicted because they rely on weaker virtue. They possess, respectively, weaker (1) roots, (2) value, (3) retinue, (4) complements, and (5) strength.

chen po ni ma chags pa la sogs pa gsum phan tshun med na mi 'byung bas rtsa ba gsum dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ tshogs chen pos bsgrub par bya ba yin pa{s rin che ba } dang*/ rnyed dang bsten ces bya ba ni/ / dge ba 'dus byas thob pa'o zhes pas dge ba 'dus byas la de dang 'dra ba ma 'ongs pa thob pa yod pa dang*/ rnam shes la 'khor tshor ba la sogs pa gsum dang gzugs kyi phung po bsam gtan zag med kyi sdom pas bsdus pa dang bcas pas phung po bzhi'i rjes su 'brang ba dang bcas pa dang*/ sdug bsngal la chos shes pa'i bzod pa gcig gi kyang mthong spang gi phra rgyas bcu gtan du 'joms pas rim pa ltar tsa ba dang rin dang 'khor dang rjes su 'brang pa dang stobs che bas dge ba chen po dag gis bsten pa'i phyir dge ba yin no/ / rgod pa dang rgod pa ma yin pa ni rim pa ltar rgod pa dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang de'i gnyen po yin pa'i phyir nyon mongs can dang dge ba'o/ / rnam par ma zhi ba dang zhi ba'ang de dang 'dra'o/ / mnyam par ma bzhag pa dang bzhag pa ni rim pa ltar rnam g.yeng dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang de'i gnyen po yin pa'i phyir nyon mongs can dang dge ba'o/ / ma bsgoms pa ni sngon ma thob pa las 'thob pa dang*/ thob zin mngon du byed pa'i bsten pa'i sgom pa dag gi ma bsgom pa'i phyir nyon mongs can no/ / bsgom pa ni de gnyis kyis bsgom pa'i phyir dge ba'o/ / rnam par ma grol ba ni nyon mongs pa dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang*/ nyon mongs pa zad pa'i rgyud la mi skye bas go rim bzhin du rang bzhin dang rgyud rnam par grol ba dag gis rnam par ma grol bas nyon mongs can dang*/ rnam par grol ba ni nyon mongs pa dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa dang nyon mongs pa zad pa'i rgyud la skye bas rim pa ltar rang bzhin dang rgyud rnam par grol ba dag gis rnam par grol bas dge ba yin no zhes 'dod do/ /

“Stronger” states include: (1) those concomitant with the three roots — since if the three roots of nonattachment and so on do not exist, then these do not arise, (2) those {of great value — since} they are established through a great collection of merit, (3) those called “attaining and relying” that obtain a similar conditioned virtuous state in future — since they are called “obtaining virtuous conditioned states,” (4) consciousness possessing complements of four aggregates — since they possess three such as feeling and the form aggregate subsumed by uncontaminated absorption vows, and (5) perseverance for Dharma knowledge of the truth of suffering that fully annihilates ten negative tendencies that are objects to be abandoned by the path of seeing. They are virtuous because they rely on stronger virtue. They possess, respectively, stronger (1) roots, (2) value, (3) retinue, (4) complements, and (5) strength. “Excited” and “nonexcited” are, respectively, afflicted and virtuous because they are concomitant with excitation and its antidote. “Nonpacified” and “pacified” are similar to that. “Nonequipoise” and “equipoise” are, respectively, afflicted and virtuous because they are concomitant with distraction and its antidote. “Nonmeditative” [states of mind] [599] are afflicted because they do not meditate on obtaining virtue not previously obtained or manifesting virtue already obtained. “Meditative” states are virtuous because they meditate on both. “Unliberated” are afflicted since they are not natural liberation and they do not liberate the mindstream; respectively, they are concomitant with affliction and do not eliminate affliction in one’s mindstream. “Liberated” states are virtuous since they are natural liberation and they liberate the mindstream; respectively, they are not concomitant with affliction and they generate the elimination of afflictions in one’s mindstream.

slob dpon ni de ltar byas na mdo dang mi mthun pa dang*/ so so'i khyad par ma bshad pa yin te/ de la dang po ni mdo las/ ji ltar na sems nang du kun du bsdus pa yin zhe na/ sems gang rmugs pa dang gnyid dang lhan cig par gyur cing nang du kun du 'gog pa dang lhan cig par gyur la lhag mthong dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa yin no/ / ji ltar na phyi rol tu rnam par g.yengs pa yin zhe na/ sems gang 'dod pa'i yon tan lnga rnams la rjes su g.yengs pa yin zhing rnam par 'phros pa yin no zhes kun du bsdus pa ni rmugs gnyid dang mtshungs ldan la bshad pas gnyis ka'ang nyon mongs can du bshad pa'i phyir ro/ / 'o na bstan bcos las sems kun du bsdus pa yang dag pa bzhin rab tu shes so zhes pa nas lam shes so zhes pa'i bar du bshad pa dang 'gal lo zhe na/ sangs rgyas kyis ma gsungs pas bstan bcos dang 'gal ba ni sla'i mdo'i don spong ba ni rigs pa ma yin no/ / so so'i khyad par ma bshad pa ni rnam par g.yengs pa dang zhum pa dang chung ngu dang rgod pa dang rnam par ma zhi ba dang mnyam par ma bzhag pa dang ma bsgoms pa dang rnam par ma grol ba zhes bya ba brgyad po thams cad nyon mongs can dang*/ kun du bsdus pa dang rab tu bzung ba dang chen po dang rgod pa ma yin pa dang rnam par zhi ba dang mnyam par bzhag pa dang bsgoms pa dang rnam par grol ba zhes bya ba brgyad dge ba kho nar bshad pas so so'i mtshan nyid tha dad ma bshad pa'i phyir ro/ /

Vasubandhu explains that this explanation is (1) incompatible with the sūtras and (2) does not explain the individual attributes. The first is established because a sūtra explains: What mind is fully contracted within? Any mind coemergent with lethargy and sleep and coemergent with complete internal cessation that is not concomitant with insight. What mind is distracted to external objects? Any mind that is distracted and expands to the five sense objects.[1782] Since “fully contracted” refers to that which is concomitant with lethargy and sleep, both are explained as afflicted. Question: Doesn’t this contradict the statement in the treatise:[1783] Know the fully contracted mind correctly as it is.[1784] Reply: It would be illogical to reject the obvious meaning of the sūtras just because it contradicts the treatise, a work that was not stated by the Buddha. Not explaining individual attributes is not explaining the distinct individual characteristics of all eight afflicted states: (1) distracted, (2) listless, (3) weaker, (4) excited, (5) nonpacified, (6) nonequipoise, (7) nonmeditative, (8) unliberated; and not explaining the eight virtuous states: (1) fully contracted, (2) fully engaged, (3) stronger, (4) nonexcited, (5) pacified, (6) equipoise, (7) meditative, and (8) liberated.

bye brag tu smra ba na re de dag nyon mongs can dang dge bar mtshungs kyang so so'i nyes pa dang yon tan gyi khyad par bshad zin pa'i phyir so so'i mtshan nyid ma bshad par ma grub bo zhes zer mod kyi 'on kyang mdo dang 'gal ba'i nyes pa ni yod do/ / de'i phyir mdo'i don ni 'dod chags dang mtshungs par ldan pa dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa'i sems ni rim pa ltar 'dod chags dang bcas pa dang bral ba yin no zhes bya ba la sogs par shes par bya ste/ ting nge 'dzin mi rtsom pa dang*/ rtsom la ma thob pa dang*/ thob pa'i dbang du byas nas drug dang bcu gnyis dang bzhi rim pa bzhin du gsungs so zhes 'chad do/ /

Vaibhāṣikas say: It is not established that their individual characteristics have not been explained, because each of the faults and qualities of these afflicted and virtuous states has been explained. Reply: Indeed, that is so, but the fault of contradicting the sūtras remains. Therefore you should understand the meaning of a sūtra that declares that the minds concomitant or not concomitant with attachment are, respectively, associated with attachment and free from attachment. It explains, respectively, six, twelve, and four such states from the perspective of concentration not being cultivated, concentration being cultivated but not obtained, and concentration being obtained. [600]

gzhan yang pha rol sems shes kyis sems 'di chags pa dang bcas pa'o zhes bya bar shes kyi gzugs 'di la chags pa dang bcas pa'o zhes sems de'i dmigs yul ni mi shes te/ gal te shes na gzugs la dmigs pas pha rol sems shes ma yin par 'gyur ba'i phyir dang*/ gzhan gyi sems des rang gi sems la dmigs pa na rang gi sems kyi ngobo'ang 'dzin par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / des na pha rol sems shes thams cad ni yul zag bcas zag med kyi mtshungs ldan dang*/ rang gi mtshan nyid 'dzin pa dang*/ de yang dus da ltar byung ba dang*/ pha rol gyi rgyud kyis bsdus pa dang*/ sa bsam gtan gyi dngos gzhis bsdus pa dang*/ gzugs la brten nas bsgrub par bya ba yin pas rten khams 'og ma gnyis kyis bsdus pa dang*/ lam sgom lam gyi sbyor ba dang rnam grol dang khyad par can gyi lam gyis bsdus pa yin gyi gzugs la sogs pa dang*/ spyi'i mtshan nyid dang*/ 'das ma 'ongs dang*/ rang gi rgyud dang*/ gzugs med la dmigs pa ma yin no/ /

Again, knowledge of others’ minds knows that this mind is associated with attachment, but it does not know that the mind is associated with attachment regarding a specific form as its focal object; if it knows form, it would not be knowledge of the mind of another, and if the mind of another were to focus on one’s mind, it would also focus on the nature of one’s mind. Therefore, all knowledge of others’ minds is concomitant with contaminated and uncontaminated objects, holds their characteristics, occurs at the present time, is conjoined with others’ mindstreams, is subsumed by the levels of the four actual bases of absorption, is subsumed by the desire and form realms as its basis, since it is established in dependence on the form realm, and by preparation for the path of meditation, the liberated path, and the special path. It does not focus on form and so on, abstract states, the past and future, one’s own mindstream, and the formless realm.

de bzhin du bsam gtan gyi dngos gzhi ma thob pas chags bcas la'ang pha rol sems shes med de/ gzhan yid shes pa bsam gtan bzhi zhes 'chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir ro/ / yul can yang mthong lam dang bsam gtan gyi nyer bsdogs dang*/ bar chad med pa'i lam dang*/ zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa rnams la gzhan gyi sems shes bkag ste/ de dag ni spyi'i mtshan nyid la dmigs pa dang*/ bar chad med lam la bkag pa dang*/ zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa ni rtog cing 'tshol ba'i bsam pa can ma yin pa'i phyir dang*/ de ni de lta ma yin pa'i phyir ro/ / rnam pa'ang zag med ni lam bden gyi rnam pa can yin pas smon pa med pa'i rnam pa can yin gyi stong pa dang mtshan med kyi rnam pa can ni ma yin te/ de gnyis ni rim pa ltar sdug bsngal dang 'gog pa shes pa'i rnam pa can yin pa'i phyir ro zhes byar 'dod do/ / 'di dag gi rgyu mtshan yang bye brag tu smra bas rnam par brtags pa kho na yin te/ yi ge mangs pas 'jigs pas rnam par dpyad pa ni ma bris so/ /

Similarly, those with attachment do not have knowledge of others’ minds since they have not obtained the actual base of the absorptions. As the Abhidharmakośa mentions, “Knowledge of the minds of others exists in the four absorptions” (7:15a). Also, minds such as the path of seeing, access concentration to the absorptions, uninterrrupted paths, and knowledge of elimination and nonarising block knowledge of the minds of others because they focus on abstract states; they block the uninterrupted path; and knowledge of elimination and nonarising does not possess investigative and probing contemplation. Knowledge of others’ minds is not like that. Since aspects of knowledge that are uncontaminated are also aspects of the truth of path, they are aspects that are wishless. They are not empty or signless, however, because these are, respectively, aspects of the truths of suffering and cessation. These issues are investigated by Vaibhāṣikas alone, but I have not written down this analysis here out of fear this would become too digressive.
lhag ma rnam pa bcu bzhi can/ / stong dang bdag med ma gtogs so/ / dri med bcu drug gzhan rnam med/ / gzhan yod ces pa bstan bcos las/ / 12

The remaining knowledges have fourteen aspects since empty and selfless are excluded. Stainless states have no aspects other than the sixteen. According to a treatise, others assert that they exist. (7:12)
de ltar zhar la 'ongs pa bshad nas skabs su babs pa bshad pa ni
In addition,

sngar shes pa brgyad yan chad bshad pa'i lhag ma zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa ni mi rtag pa la sogs pa rnam pa bcu bzhi can yin te/ shes pa de dag don dam pa'i yul can yin yang bdag gi skye ba zad do/ / tshangs par spyod pa bsten to/ / 'di las srid pa gzhan mi shes so zhes bya ba la sogs pa rjes thob kyi shes pas bdag gi tha snyad 'dogs shing bdag stong pa ma yin la rjes thob kyang kun rdzob kyi yul can yin pa'i phyir dang*/ mnyam gzhag kyang de dang mthun par bya ba'i phyir stong pa dang bdag med gnyis mi bsgom pas stong pa dang bdag med pa'i rnam pa gnyis ma gtogs so/ / ci zag med la rang gi mtshan nyid kyi rnam pa gzhan yod dam med ce na/

the remaining knowledges to be explained after the previous eight are: the knowledge of elimination and the knowledge of nonarising, which have fourteen aspects, such as impermanence. That is because, though they possess ultimate objects, they also possess conventional objects. Knowledge during post-equipoise knows that “Arising of a self has been eliminated,” “I rely on pure practice,” “I know of no further rebirth” and so on, but post-equipoise knowledge imputes a self and the self not being empty, and they are also compatible with equipoise. Since these knowledges do not meditate on that which is empty and selfless, the two aspects of being empty (śūnyā) and selfless (anātma) are excluded. Question: Don’t uncontaminated states have other real aspects? [601]

re zhig kha che ba rnams na re dri ma med pa la ni bcu drug las gzhan pa'i rnam pa med do{ bden pa'i rnam pa can 'dir 'dus la/ 'dus ma byas gzhan gnyis ni kun rdzob shes pa'i yul lo/} zhes zer ro/ gzhan nyi 'og pa dag ni bcu drug las gzhan yang yod ces pa 'dod de/ bstan bcos rnam shes kyi tshogs las mi ldan pa'i sems kyis 'dod pa dang ldan pa'i chos rnams shes par 'gyur ba yod dam zhe na/ shes par 'gyur te/ rigs pas bskyed pa'i sgo nas mi rtag pa dang*/ sdug bsngal ba dang*/ stong pa dang*/ bdag med pa dang*/ rgyu dang*/ kun 'byung ba dang*/ rab tu skye ba dang*/ rkyen dang*/ 'di ni gnas yod do/ / 'di ni gzhi yod do zhes bya bar shes par 'gyur ro zhes 'byung ba'i phyir ro/ / de la mi ldan pa'i sems ni zag pa med pa'o/ / rigs pas bskyed pa ni phyi ci ma log pa'o/ / gnas ni mtshan nyid do/ / gzhi ni rgyu'o/ /

Some Kāśmīri Vaibhāṣikas say: The stainless (amala) have no aspects other than the sixteen aspects. {Those possessing the aspects of the four truths are included here. But the other two unconditioned states are objects of conventional knowledge.} Others, such as the Aparāntakas, assert that aspects other than those sixteen exist. The Compendium of Consciousness states: Does the mind not associated with attachment know phenomena possessing attachment or not? It knows them since it is generated by reasoning. It knows the aspects of impermanence, that associated with suffering, empty, selfless, cause, origin, strong generation, condition, and this abides, and this is the basis.[1785] “The mind not associated with attachment” refers to the uncontaminated mind, “generated by reasoning” refers to the nondistorted mind, “abides” refers to characteristics, and “basis” refers to their cause.

gal te de ni mi rtag pa la sogs par shes par 'gyur ba gang yin pa 'di ni gnas dang gzhi yod do zhes ston pa yin gyi bden pa'i rnam pa ni ma yin no zhe na/ ma yin te/ tshig de gnyis bstan bcos kyi gzhung gi cha gzhan nas mi 'byung ba'i phyir te/ 'di ltar bstan bcos de nyid las/ mthong bas spang bar bya ba'i sems kyis 'dod pa dang ldan pa'i chos rnams shes par 'gyur ba yod dam zhe na/ shes par 'gyur te/ rigs pa ma yin pas bskyed pa'i sgo nas bdag dang*/ bdag gi dang*/ chad pa dang*/ rtag pa dang*/ rgyu med pa dang*/ byed pa med pa dang*/ skur ba 'debs pa dang*/ mchog dang*/ gtso bo dang*/ khyad par du 'phags pa dang*/ dam pa dang*/ dag pa dang*/ grol ba dang*/ nges par 'byin par byed pa dang*/ nem nur dang*/ yid gnyis dang*/ the tshom du shes par 'gyur zhing*/ chags pa dang*/ sdang ba dang*/ rlom pa dang*/ rmongs par 'gyur ro zhes gang gsungs pa der yang 'di skad du 'di ni gnas yod do/ / 'di ni gzhi yod do/ / zhes 'byung bar 'gyur ba zhig na der ma gsungs pa'i phyir ro zhes zer ro/ /

Objection: Impermanence and so on that should be known are taught to abide and act as a basis, but abidance and basis are not aspects of the four truths. Reply: That is not so. Those two words do not occur in any other part of the text of the treatise, because the treatise [Compendium of Consciousness][1786] states: Does the mind that abandons objects to be abandoned through the path of seeing know phenomena possessing attachment or not? It knows them beyond reasoning because it knows the self, mine, annihilation, permanence, causelessness, nonaction, underestimation, superior, chief, excelling, holy, pure, liberated, and acting to definitely deliver, and it knows suspicion, hesitation, doubt, and attachment, aversion, conceit, and confusion.[1787] In this statement the words “this abides” and “this is the basis” are not stated.

'di yang mdo sde pa la sogs pa kha cig ni rnam pa bcu drug tu bshad pa ni ming gi sgo nas yin gyi rjes su ni sdug bsngal gyi bden pa'i rnam pa bzhi dang bden pa gzhan gsum ni rgyu dang 'gog pa dang lam gyi rnam pa re re ba yin pas bdun yin te/ rnam pa phyi ma dag ni dang po dag gi rnam grangs tsam yin pa'i phyir dper na dbang po dang brgya byin dang grong khyer 'jig ces bya ba bzhin no zhes 'dod do/ /

Sautrāntikas and so on assert: The explanation that there are sixteen aspects is a nominal explanation. In terms of substance there are seven aspects: (1–4) four aspects of the truth of suffering and the first aspect of each of the remaining three truths of (5) cause, (6) cessation, and (7) path, because the latter aspects of each of those truths are merely synonyms for the first. It is like Indra, Śakra, and Nagaraghātaka being equivalent.
rdzas su rnam pa bcu drug go/ / rnam pa shes rab dang bcas pa'i/ / dmigs dang bcas pas 'dzin par byed/ / yod pa thams cad gzung bya yin/ / 13
There are sixteen aspects by substance. The aspects are wisdom. All possessing focal objects associated with it apprehend. All existence is apprehended. (7:13)

bye brag tu smra ba ni don dam par ni rdzas su rnam pa bcu drug go zhes 'dod de/ de la rkyen la rag lus pa'i phyir mi rtag pa'o/ gnod pa'i bdag nyid yin pa'i phyir sdug bsngal ba'o/ / bdag gir lta ba'i mi mthun phyogs yin pas stong pa'o/ / bdag tu lta ba'i mi mthun phyogs yin pas bdag med pa'o/ / sdug bsngal gyi sa bon gyi chos kyi tshul gyi rgyu'o/ / de ma thag tu 'byung bas na kun 'byung ba'o/ rgyun gyi 'brel bas na rab tu skye ba'o/ rgyu rkyen mang pos mngon par bsgrubs pas rkyen no/ / sdug bsngal gyi phung po zhig pas 'gog pa'o/ / 'dod chags la sogs pa dug gsum gyi me gsum zhi ba'i phyir zhi ba'o/ / sdug bsngal gyi 'tshe ba med pas gya nom pa'o/ / las dang nyon mongs pa'i skyon thams cad dang bral bas nges par 'byung ba'o/ / thar par bgrod par byed pas lam mo/ / thabs kyi rigs pa dang ldan pas rigs pa'o/ / myang 'das yang dag par sgrub par sgrub pa'o/ gtan du yang dag par 'da' bar byed pas nges par 'byin pa'o/ / rnam pa gcig tu na rtag pa dang*/ bde ba dang*/ bdag gir dang*/ bdag tu lta ba dang*/ rgyu med pa dang*/ rgyu gcig pu dang*/ rang bzhin rtag la gnas skabs rnam par 'gyur ba dang*/ blo sngar btang bar lta ba dang*/ thar pa med pa dang*/ sdug bsngal la thar par lta ba dang*/ bsam gtan gyi bden ba gya nom pa dang*/ yang dang yang nyams par 'gyur bas thar pa gtan du ma yin par lta ba dang*/ lam med do/ / lam 'di ngan no/ / 'di las gzhan yang lam yin no/ / lam 'di yang ldog go snyam pa'i lta ba dpyad pa bcu drug gi gnyen por go rim bzhin du mi rtag pa la sogs bcu drug yin no/ / yang rnam pa nyid gang zhe na/

Vaibhāṣikas assert: Ultimately there are sixteen aspects by substance: Suffering is (1) impermanent because it relies on conditions, it is (2) associated with suffering because it is the state of harm itself, it is (3) empty since it opposes the view of [the aggregates as] “mine,” and it is (4) selfless since it opposes the view of [the aggregates as] “I.” Origin is (5) the [602] cause that is the means of activating the seed of suffering, it is (6) origin since [suffering] arises immediately after it, it is (7) intense production since it continuously connects [to suffering], and it is (8) a condition since many causes and conditions establish [suffering]. Cessation is (9) cessation since it destroys the aggregate of suffering, it is (10) peace because it pacifies the three fires of the three poisons of attachment and so on, it is (11) sublime since it is free of the violence [or harm] of suffering, and it is (12) definite emergence since it is free from all error of karma and affliction. Path is (13) the path since it is the way to proceed to liberation, it is (14) appropriate since it possesses the appropriate method, it is (15) establishment since it correctly establishes nirvāṇa, and it is (16) definite release since it gives rise to complete and perfect transcendence. These sixteen aspects such as impermanent act as antidotes to the sixteen speculative views that regard the aggregates as (1) permanent, (2) blissful, (3) mine, or (4) the self; or that view suffering as (5) causeless, (6) possessing one single cause, (7) permanent in essence but at times changing, or (8) instigated by the prior thought of a creator; or that (9) views liberation as nonexistent, (10) views suffering as liberation, (11) views the bliss of the absorptions as sublime, or (12) views liberation as unstable since it frequently degenerates; or that holds (13) the path to be nonexistent, (14) this path to be inferior, (15) the path to be other than this, or (16) this path to be susceptible to regression. Question: What are the aspects themselves?

rnam pa ni shes rab yin la de yang yul 'dzin pa na shes rab kho nas 'dzin pa ma yin gyi shes rab de dang bcas pa'i dmigs pa dang bcas pa thams cad kyis 'dzin par byed de/ shes rab ni sa mang po ba yin pa'i phyir ro/ / gzugs la sogs pa{ rdzas dang btags par} yod pa thams cad kyang gzung bya yin{ te de dag gi mi 'dzin pa gang yang med pa yin} no/ / de ltar na shes rab ni rnam pa dang 'dzin pa dang gzung bar bya ba gsum ga dang*/ shes rab las gzhan pa'i dmigs bcas thams cad ni 'dzin pa dang gzung bar bya ba gnyis dang*/ dmigs pa med pa rnams ni gzung bar bya ba kho na yin no zhes bye brag tu smra ba rnams 'dod do/ / mdo sde pa la sogs pa rnams na re gal te shes rab rnam par 'dod na de nyid grogs su ldan pa'am ngo bo yin pas rnam pa dang bcas pa yin/ dang po ltar na shes rab nyid rnam pa dang bcas par mi 'gyur te/ shes rab shes rab dang mtshungs par mi ldan pa'i phyir ro/ / gnyis pa ltar na shes rab las gzhan pa'i mtshungs ldan rnams rnam pa dang bcas pa ma yin par 'gyur ro/ / de dag gang yang rung bas rnam pa dang bcas pa ma yin par 'dod na yang*/ sems dang sems byung dang*/ / rten dang dmigs dang rnam bcas dang*/ / mtshungs par ldan pa'ang rnam pa lnga/ / zhes 'dod pa dang 'gal bar 'gyur ro/ / de'i phyir dmigs pa ni yul dang*/ rnam pa ni blo'i 'dzin stangs te yul gyi rnam pa can{ gyi sems sems byung thams cad} la 'dod do zhes zer ro/ / yang shes pa bcu po 'di dag gi ngo bo dge mi dge lung ma bstan gang yin zhe na/

Reply: The aspects (ākāra) are wisdom (prajñā). And if [aspects] apprehend objects, it is not that wisdom alone apprehends them, for all those possessing focal objects (sālambana) associated with that wisdom apprehend objects because wisdom is a universal mental state.[1788] Also, all {substantial and nominal} existence (sat), such as form and so on, is apprehended {since there are none that are not apprehended}. Thus wisdom is threefold: (1) aspect, (2) apprehender, and (3) object apprehended. All those [states] that possess focal objects that are other than wisdom are either apprehenders or objects apprehended, while those lacking focal objects are objects apprehended alone. This is asserted by Vaibhāṣikas. Sautrāntikas and so on say: If wisdom is asserted to be an aspect, then wisdom would be associated with aspects either as a [concomitant] companion state or by its own nature. (1) According to the first, wisdom itself could not be associated with aspects because wisdom is not concomitant with itself. (2) According to the second, those concomitant with states [of awareness] other than wisdom would not be associated with aspects. If it is asserted that they are not associated with aspects by any tenable means, then it would contradict the assertion that minds and mental factors are concomitant. As the Abhidharmakośa says, “Minds and mental factors are concomitant in five ways through possessing support, focal object, and aspect” (2:34bcd). Therefore the focal object is asserted to be the object, and the aspect reflects the mode of apprehension of those [minds and mental factors] that possess an aspect of that object. [603] Question: What is the nature of these ten knowledges? Is it virtuous, nonvirtuous, or neutral?
dang po rnam gsum gzhan rnams dge /
The first has three types; the others are virtuous. (7:14a)

dang po kun rdzob shes pa ni ci rigs dge mi dge lung ma bstan rnam pa gsum char yin la/ shes pa gzhan dgu po rnams ni dge ba 'ba' zhig pa yin no/ / {'dir sems shes zag bcas kyang sgom byung gzung la lhag ma ni lam bden gyis bsdus so zhes gsung ngo }

Reply: The first, conventional knowledge, has three types: virtuous, nonvirtuous, and neutral. The other nine knowledges are virtuous alone. {Here contaminated knowledge of others’ minds is derived from meditation, and the remainder are subsumed by the truth of path}.
bzhi pa [sa dang brten pa] ni
Levels and the basis of knowledge
dang po sa rnams thams cad na/ / drug na chos shes bya bar dgu/ / rjes shes bya ba de bzhin drug / 14
The first exists on all levels. That called Dharma knowledge exists on six. That called subsequent knowledge on nine. So too, six. (7:14bcd)

shes pa dang po kun rdzob shes pa ni 'dod pa nas srid rtse'i bar gyi sa rnams thams cad na yod de/ {khams gsum la dmigs pa thams cad der 'dod pas so } bsam gtan dang po'i nyer bsdogs la sogs pa bsam gtan sa drug na chos shes pa zhes bya ba yod de/ sa de dag 'dod pa'i sdug bsngal la sogs pa{'i bden pa }la dmigs pa'i phyir dang*/ gzugs med 'dod pa la mi dmigs pa'i phyir med do/ / bsam gtan drug dang gzugs med dang po gsum ste zag med sa dgu na rjes su shes pa zhes bya ba yod la/ de yang gzugs med dang po gsum na ni rjes shes sgom lam gyis bsdus pa kho na yod do/ / ji ltar rjes shes sa dgu na yod pa de bzhin du bden pa bzhi shes pa dang zad pa dang mi skye ba shes pa gnyis te drug kyang sa dgu po de dag na yod do/ / 'dir yang chos shes kyis bsdus pa sa drug dang rjes shes kyis bsdus pa sa dgu char na yod la de yang gzugs med dang po gsum na yod pa'i bden pa bzhi shes pa ni rjes shes kyi phyogs sgom lam gyis bsdus pa kho na yod do/ /

Conventional knowledge, which is the first knowledge, {is asserted to focus on all three realms}. Thus it exists on all levels from the desire realm to the summit of existence. That called Dharma knowledge exists on six levels of absorption, such as access concentration to the first absorption, because those levels focus on {the truth of} suffering in the desire realm and so on. It doesn’t exist on the formless-realm levels because formless states do not focus on sense objects. That called subsequent knowledge exists on nine levels: the six levels of absorption, and the first three formless-realm levels. Further, subsequent knowledge subsumed by the path of meditation alone exists in the first three formless states. Just as subsequent knowledge exists on nine levels, so too six, including the four knowledges [of the noble truths] plus both the knowledge of elimination and the knowledge of nonarising, exist on nine levels. Moreover, regarding those existing on the six levels subsumed by Dharma knowledge and the nine levels subsumed by subsequent knowledge, knowledge of the four truths existing in the first three formless states are subsequent knowledge that are subsumed by the path of meditation alone.
gzhan yid shes pa bsam gtan bzhi/ / de ni 'dod dang gzugs rten can/ / chos shes bya ba 'dod rten can/ / khams gsum pa yi rten can gzhan/ / 15
